title: AI-assisted versus point-based registration for digital planning in CBCT images with metallic artifacts
abstract: BACKGROUND: Accurate registration between cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) images and intraoral scans is fundamental to digital implant planning because registration errors may propagate throughout the digital workflow and affect the accuracy of computer-guided implant surgery. Conventional point-based registration relies on manually selected anatomical landmarks and may be compromised by metallic artifacts that obscure dental structures. Artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted registration has recently emerged as a promising alternative; however, evidence comparing its performance with conventional point-based registration under clinically challenging conditions remains limited. This study aimed to compare the registration accuracy (primary outcome) and registration duration (secondary outcome) of AI-assisted and conventional point-based registration in patients presenting with metallic artifacts on CBCT images. METHODS: This study included 45 eligible patients with corresponding full-arch CBCT datasets and intraoral scans. Registration accuracy was evaluated at the arch level by measuring the mean discrepancy at three predefined anatomical landmarks using Geomagic Control X software. Registration duration was recorded for each workflow. Arches were classified according to artifact burden into mild (> 0-33%), moderate (> 33-66%), and severe (> 66%) categories. Because the data were non-normally distributed, paired comparisons were performed using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Generalized estimating equations (GEE) were used as a sensitivity analysis to account for clustering of maxillary and mandibular arches within the same patient. Intra-observer reliability was assessed using the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC). RESULTS: A total of 78 paired arch observations were available for registration accuracy analysis. AI-assisted registration demonstrated significantly lower registration discrepancies than conventional point-based registration (median 0.190 mm [IQR 0.121-0.275] vs. 0.268 mm [IQR 0.200-0.418]; p < 0.001). Registration discrepancy increased with increasing artifact burden for both techniques, although AI-assisted registration consistently demonstrated lower discrepancies across all artifact severity groups. Registration duration was comparable between the two workflows. The GEE sensitivity analysis confirmed the primary findings after accounting for within-patient clustering. Intra-observer reliability was excellent (ICC = 0.985; 95% CI: 0.968-0.993). CONCLUSIONS: AI-assisted registration achieved significantly lower registration discrepancies than conventional point-based registration while maintaining comparable registration duration in CBCTs with metallic artifacts on CBCT images. These findings suggest that AI-assisted registration may improve the accuracy and consistency of multimodal image registration within the digital implant planning workflow, particularly in clinically challenging cases. Further prospective multicenter studies involving multiple implant-planning software platforms and broader clinical scenarios are required to confirm these findings.
authors: Nehal Ibrahim Shobair; Zainab H. Abdel Rahman; Mohamed Tolba; Yassin S. Alian

title: ARCGym: Benchmarking Deep Reinforcement Learning in Autonomous Robotic Colonoscopy
abstract: Simulations for learning-based autonomous colonoscopic navigation focus mainly on fully actuated capsule robots, failing to capture the contact-rich navigation of long and flexible clinical colonoscopes. We present the Autonomous Robotic Colonoscopy Gym (ARCGym), an open-source reinforcement learning environment and benchmark for image-based navigation in clinically derived deformable colon anatomies. ARCGym supports multiple types of colonoscope robots, spanning capsule robots and flexible endoscopes, with this work focusing on flexible endoscopes including magnetic-driven tip actuation and clinically used proximally translational actuation. This work includes five CT-reconstructed colons representing typical clinical scenarios, a set of clinically meaningful navigation subtasks, and unified success metrics. We introduce a reward combining depth-based lumen alignment with a lumen-visibility score to improve learning under occlusions. Experiments across tasks, robots, and anatomies show that autonomous navigation remains challenging for both magnetic-driven and proximal-insertion flexible robots, with proximal-insertion actuation remaining an open problem.
authors: Guanglin Ji; Martina Finocchiaro; Kenny Erleben; Hang Yin

title: ARISE: Adaptive Agentic Reasoning with Image-grounded Self-Evaluation for Interpretable IBD Assessment
abstract: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) requires frequent imaging-based assessment, yet interpretation of modalities such as wireless capsule endoscopy (WCE) and intestinal ultrasound remains heavily dependent on specialist expertise. Vision-Language Models (VLMs) demonstrate significant potential in multimodal medical image analysis, but their clinical adoption is hindered by their insufficient domain-specific reasoning, susceptibility to hallucination, scarcity of high quality training data in fine-grained diagnostics and limited interpretability. We introduce ARISE (Adaptive Agentic Reasoning with Image-grounded Self-Evaluation), an autonomous planning framework that models few-shot medical image understanding as a sequential agentic workflow. ARISE structures agent execution into a transparent 5-stage workflow: hypothesis generation, image-grounded evidence summarization, evidence-conditioned refinement, symbolic verification, and final diagnosis. We apply ARISE to IBD assessment across two independent patient cohorts: wireless capsule endoscopy (WCE) images for Crohn's disease and B-mode ultrasound data for ulcerative colitis. ARISE consistently improves diagnostic performance over baseline VLMs while exposing where reasoning succeeds or fails, providing a more interpretable basis for clinical decision support and realistic deployment.
authors: Pronoma Banerjee; Anuva Shah; Jason Wu; Md. Masudur Rahman; Sanjay Mohanty; Satya V. Kurada; Juan Pablo Wachs

title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AS A DECISION-SUPPORT TOOL FOR MATERIAL SELECTION IN PROSTHODONTICS: AN ANALYTICAL REVIEW OF THE LITERATURE
abstract: Background. The rapid development of digital dentistry and artificial intelligence (AI) is expanding the range of technologies available for diagnosis, treatment planning, prosthetic design, and outcome prediction. Material selection remains a clinically important component of prosthodontic treatment because the choice of restorative material must account for mechanical, functional, biological, and esthetic requirements. Aim. To analyze recent literature on the application of AI in prosthodontics, with particular attention to its potential role in supporting restorative material selection, integrating clinical and digital parameters, predicting prosthetic outcomes, and personalizing treatment planning. Materials and methods. A narrative analytical review was developed from literature published during seven completed calendar years (January 2019–December 2025). Relevant publications were identified in PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and NCBI resources using combinations of terms related to artificial intelligence, machine learning, prosthodontics, dental materials, CAD/CAM, crowns, dental prostheses, occlusion, and treatment outcomes. Publications were thematically analyzed according to AI application, type of prosthodontic task, data source, clinical purpose, reported outcomes, and limitations. Results. The reviewed literature demonstrates that AI is increasingly applied in prosthodontic diagnostics, treatment planning, automated crown design, finish-line detection, occlusal assessment, prediction of prosthetic outcomes, and digital workflows. AI-assisted CAD systems have shown potential to improve design efficiency and, in selected studies, achieve clinically acceptable crown fit. However, the evidence remains heterogeneous with substantial differences in datasets, algorithms, validation procedures, and outcome measures. Direct evidence supporting independently validated AI systems for individualized restorative material selection remains limited. Current evidence therefore supports the use of AI primarily as a clinical decision-support tool rather than as an autonomous system for material selection. Conclusions. AI has considerable potential to support individualized material selection and prosthodontic treatment planning by integrating multiple clinical and digital parameters. At the same time, current evidence does not support treating AI as an autonomous replacement for professional clinical judgment. Direct validation of AI systems specifically designed to select restorative materials remains limited, and many predictive models require stronger external validation and prospective clinical evaluation. The most appropriate current framework is therefore a human-in-the-loop decision-support model in which AI augments, rather than replaces, clinical expertise
authors: Tetiana I. Dzetsiukh

title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN DENTISTRY: CURRENT APPLICATIONS, ADVANCEMENTS, CHALLENGES, AND FUTURE PERSPECTIVES
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as one of the most transformative technologies in modern healthcare and is increasingly influencing contemporary dental practice.Recent advancements in machine learning, deep learning, computer vision, and generative AI have enabled the development of intelligent systems capable of analyzing complex clinical, radiographic, and histopathological datasets with remarkable precision.AI applications have demonstrated substantial benefits across multiple dental specialties, including oral radiology, oral pathology, orthodontics, periodontology, prosthodontics, conservative dentistry and endodontics, oral and maxillofacial surgery, pediatric dentistry, and public health dentistry.These technologies facilitate early disease detection, automated image interpretation, treatment planning, outcome prediction, and workflow optimization.The integration of AI with digital dentistry technologies such as cone-beam computed tomography, intraoral scanners, computer-aided design/computer-aided manufacturing systems, and electronic health records has accelerated its adoption in clinical settings.Despite these advantages, challenges such as data privacy concerns, algorithmic bias, transparency issues, implementation costs, and regulatory uncertainties continue to limit widespread clinical implementation.Furthermore, ethical considerations regarding patient confidentiality and professional accountability remain important concerns.This review provides a comprehensive overview of current AI applications in dentistry, recent technological advancements, existing limitations, and future opportunities for integrating AI into routine dental practice.
venue: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology

title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN DIABETES MANAGEMENT: EMERGING APPLICATIONS, CLINICAL OPPORTUNITIES AND CHALLENGES
abstract: Diabetes mellitus is a serious chronic metabolic disease marked by continuous problems in the regulation of glucose and is linked to a wide range of cardiovascular, renal, neurological, ophthalmic and other complications. Because of the growing number of people with diabetes, the difficulty of providing individualized treatment and the large amount of health data that is produced as part of routine care, there is a growing need for more intelligent methods of managing the disease. Artificial intelligence (AI), which encompasses machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing and predictive analytics, is becoming increasingly the subject of investigation as a means of improving diabetes prevention, screening, diagnosis, monitoring, treatment selection and the management of complications. These AI systems are able to combine data fromcontinuous glucose monitors, electronic health records, laboratory tests, medication records, dietary information, physical activity, wearable sensors and medical images in order to detect patterns that are hard to spot using traditional methods. The applications involve the prediction of diabetes risk, forecasting glucose levels, the detection of both hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia, automated insulin delivery, the giving of individualized treatment recommendations, screening for diabetic retinopathy, the identification of the risk of diabetic kidney disease and digital assistance in making lifestyle changes. AI can also help healthcare professionals by decreasing the amount of information they have to deal with and allowing for more personalized decisions. Yet problems relating to data quality, algorithmic bias, explainability, privacy, cybersecurity, interoperability, regulatory supervision, cost and unequal access still constitute significant obstacles. AI should thus be seen as a decision-support tool and not as a substitute that can operate autonomously for healthcare professionals. This review looks at the principles, major applications, benefits, limitations, ethical issues and future possibilities of the use of AI in the management of diabetes, with a special focus on its potential role in achieving precision and patient-centred diabetes care.

title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE-ASSISTED EARLY DETECTION OF OCCLUSAL AND PERIODONTAL CHANGES FOR PERSONALIZED PREVENTIVE DENTAL CARE
abstract: Disorders of occlusion and periodontal diseases are among the most prevalent oral health disorders and remain one of the primary reasons for functional impairments, tooth loss, and low quality of life. In order to prevent further development of such disorders and to ensure good oral health status in the future, it is vital to identify pathological changes at an early stage. With the advancements in artificial intelligence (AI), there are new opportunities for enhancing diagnostic precision, monitoring, and individual preventive treatment in dentistry. This review paper is aimed at discussing the biological association between modification of occlusion and periodontal diseases, as well as current state of applying AI technologies in the early diagnosis and management of periodontal diseases. Machine learning, deep learning, computer vision, and predictive analytics in the analysis of radiographic images, intraoral scans, clinical histories, biomarker profiles, and other functional data are emphasized in the current review paper. It is possible to highlight the ability of AI assisted systems to diagnose teeth wear, monitor orthodontic movement, assess periodontal bone loss, evaluate TMD, and predict the course of the disease. Moreover, multimodal AI approaches, incorporating clinical, imaging, behavioral, and biological information, contribute to the transition to precision dentistry and tailored preventive approaches. Although considerable achievements have been made, there are still some issues affecting the application of the models clinically, namely, low interpretability, validation of the model and quality of the data, privacy concerns, and ethics of governance. Innovations like digital twins, federated learning, and intelligent decision support systems are likely to improve predictive power and personalized approach of providers. In summary, AI can bring about a revolution in preventive dental care, allowing for intervention at an early stage and management of risks.

title: Acoustically driven micro/nanobubbles: from fundamental mechanisms to biomedical applications
abstract: Acoustically driven micro/nanobubbles, as a bridge between macroscopic acoustic fields and microscopic biological machinery, have shown considerable promise due to their non-contact actuation, tunable mechanical responses, and favorable biocompatibility. Recent advances in bubble formulation and acoustic control have further expanded their capabilities, enabling targeted membrane permeabilization, enhanced molecular transport, and precise manipulation at the microscale. In this review, we summarize the fundamental mechanisms linking bubble dynamics to biologically relevant effects under ultrasound and establish quantitative design criteria that govern the coupling between acoustic parameters, bubble behavior, and therapeutic performance. We then organize biomedical applications across scales, spanning single-cell manipulation, tissue-level barrier modulation, and organ-scale imaging and therapeutic interventions. Particular attention is given to how acoustic modes and bubble configurations translate into measurable performance metrics, as well as the limitations that constrain reproducibility and safety in complex biological environments. Finally, we discuss key challenges for practical translation from an engineering perspective and propose strategies for improving controllability, standardization, and system integration. By providing a framework to overcome the inherent randomness of bubble-acoustic interactions in clinical translation, this review outlines a roadmap toward reliable and programmable mechano-bio platforms for closed-loop, patient-adaptive interventions.
authors: Jiaxin Wu; Tatsuo Arai; Chenhao Bai; Changsheng Li; Xingguang Duan; Toshio Fukuda; Xiaoming Liu

title: Action-conditioned latent Kalman filtering for robust spatio-temporal state estimation of deformable object
abstract: Abstract Robust spatio-temporal state estimation from noisy observations is a critical challenge in robotic manipulation. Current latent space representations derived from dynamic point clouds often suffer from severe perceptual noise and occlusions, leading to discontinuous trajectories and pronounced temporal jitter. To mitigate these artifacts, we propose an Action-Conditioned Latent Kalman Filter (AC-LKF) framework. Leveraging a hybrid architecture of PointNet++ and Gated Recurrent Units (GRU), our method models non-linear temporal dynamics within a low-dimensional latent manifold. Instead of claiming to fully model the physical causality of deformable-object dynamics, AC-LKF incorporates the robot end-effector displacement as a low-dimensional, observable, and task-relevant kinematic prior to condition the latent state transition. Furthermore, a heteroscedastic latent filtering module adaptively estimates process and measurement uncertainties, balancing the action-conditioned prior with degraded visual inputs under noise and occlusion. Evaluations using quantitative temporal metrics and reconstruction errors, supplemented by principal component analysis (PCA) and t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE) visualizations, show that AC-LKF improves latent trajectory smoothness, information retention, and dynamic robustness by reducing abrupt observation-induced state transitions. These results indicate that kinematic action conditioning can improve the temporal consistency and robustness of learned geometric state representations for interactive deformable-object manipulation.
authors: Duan Gao; Majed Melibary; Junlei Hu

title: Active sensing explains cortical variability and improves visual information
abstract: Abstract Active vision is often considered at the scale of saccades, with each fixation treated as a static visual sample. Yet the eyes continue to move during fixation, continually transforming the retinal input. Here we measured these movements at high precision while recording neuronal populations in the foveal primary visual cortex of awake marmosets viewing repeated flashed natural images. Fixational eye movements accounted for most conditional firing-rate variability and nearly all shared variability not explained by the trial-averaged response. An image-computable model captured this modulation largely from gaze-dependent retinal input; explicit eye-position and eye-velocity signals added little predictive power. Under natural viewing, retinal motion redistributed image power across temporal frequencies, and motion effects grew when this power engaged spatiotemporal tuning. In model-derived populations, fixational motion increased the spatial information carried per spike relative to stabilized input, with sharpening growing across successive nonlinear stages. Thus, activity commonly assigned to cortical noise is not just structured visual reafference generated by the movement of the observer, but is beneficial signal which sharpens spatial representations.

title: Adult Meckel’s Diverticulum Presenting with Massive Lower Gastrointestinal Bleeding and Hemorrhagic Shock: A Case Report
abstract: Meckel’s diverticulum (MD) is a congenital ileal outpouching that may contain ectopic gastric mucosa. Although typically asymptomatic, it may cause significant lower gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding in adults and, rarely, hemorrhagic shock.We report a case of a 31-year-old man who presented with sudden-onset painless hematochezia, syncope, and eventual hemorrhagic shock. Despite negative CT angiography and upper endoscopy, colonoscopy revealed active bleeding originating in the terminal ileum and entering the cecum, suggesting a small-bowel source and providing partial localization. The patient required substantial blood transfusion support, including 3 units of packed red blood cells, 2 units of platelets, and 2 units of cryoprecipitate. Ongoing hemorrhage and hemodynamic instability prompted emergent laparotomy, which identified and allowed for resection of an MD. Histopathologic examination confirmed MD containing ectopic gastric mucosa with an ulcerated bleeding focus.This case highlights the clinical challenges of MD in adults. It demonstrates that it may present with life-threatening lower gastrointestinal bleeding despite initially non-diagnostic imaging and the absence of definitive endoscopic identification of the lesion. Although uncommon, this case supports maintaining clinical suspicion for MD in adults with unexplained severe gastrointestinal hemorrhage and further characterizes its potential presentation in the adult population.

title: Advanced Diagnosis and Surgical Management of Temporomandibular Joint Disorders: Imaging, Digital Innovation and Procedure Selection
abstract: Temporomandibular disorders (TMDs) comprise heterogeneous pain and dysfunction conditions involving the masticatory muscles, temporomandibular joints (TMJs), and associated structures. Reliable care begins with standardized clinical diagnosis, assessment of psychosocial and functional contributors, and imaging selected to answer a defined clinical question. This chapter reviews functional anatomy, contemporary classification, the Diagnostic Criteria for Temporomandibular Disorders (DC/TMDs), and the complementary roles of magnetic resonance imaging and cone-beam computed tomography. It then develops a diagnosis-driven pathway from education, self-management, rehabilitation, and behavioral care to arthrocentesis, arthroscopy, open-joint surgery, ankylosis release, and alloplastic total joint replacement. Evidence is strongest for conservative multimodal care in chronic pain-related TMD; procedural evidence is more heterogeneous and often comes from observational series. Accordingly, escalation should be based on concordant symptoms, examination, imaging, functional impairment, prior treatment, and shared decision-making. Digital planning and patient-specific reconstruction are increasingly useful in complex structural diseases. In contrast, biomarkers, wearable phenotyping, and artificial intelligence remain investigational until standardized methods, external validation, and evidence of clinical benefit are established.
authors: Vikranth Ravipati; Anjan Kumar Thyagaraajen; Maha Rizvi; Qasim Khalid; Junad Khan

title: Advanced Medical Optics & Surgical Robotics: Applications of Jana's Invariant Lens Equations in Orthopedics, Neurosurgery, Ophthalmology, and Dentistry
abstract: This paper establishes a high-precision computational paradigm for biomedical optics, robotic surgery, and advanced diagnostic imaging by extending Jana’s Invariant Lens Governing Equations—specifically the dif- ferential velocity profile (dv/du + (v/u) 2 = 0), the cubic spatial matrix (Equation C), and the radical symmetry boundary (Equation K). Traditional surgical microscopes, intra-oral scanners, and autonomous robotic cutting arrays experience processing latencies when adapting to micro-scale tissue variations and localized movement-driven focal shifts. By hardcoding Jana’s non-linear spatial transformations directly into optical tracking firmware, this model eliminates computational tracking lag by roughly 65%. We de- tail direct engineering frameworks to achieve absolute focus stabilization in orthopedic bone cutting, deep micro-vascular neurosurgery, LASIK ophthalmic tracking, and intra-oral 3D dental mapping.

title: Advances in Dental Imaging and the Integration of Artificial Intelligence
abstract: Diagnostic imaging of the oral and maxillofacial region is of paramount importance in clinical diagnosis, treatment planning, and follow-up procedures in dentistry. Periapical radiographic examinations and various panoramic imaging systems are routinely employed in clinical dental practice. Cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) has become a widely used and currently preferred imaging modality in dental implantology, endodontics, maxillofacial surgery, periodontology, temporomandibular joint disorders, orthodontics, airway assessment, sleep disorders, and forensic dentistry. However, relatively high radiation doses, prolonged scanning times, and high costs limit its routine clinical use. Ultrasound imaging is also among the recommended techniques in dental practice, as it provides real-time imaging using an ionizing radiation-free, cost-effective, rapid, and user-friendly technique. Ultrasonography can be utilized in the dentomaxillofacial region for various diagnostic purposes, including the examination of the salivary glands and superficial tissues. More recently, dedicated dental magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) has been introduced, incorporating specialized software, hardware, imaging sequences, and fields of view tailored to the anatomical characteristics of the dentomaxillofacial region. Another important topic in dental and maxillofacial radiology is artificial intelligence (AI). Artificial intelligence is a field of computer science dedicated to developing systems or machines capable of performing tasks that have traditionally been associated with human intelligence. Further research and investigation in the field of dental and maxillofacial radiology are expected to make substantial contributions to diagnostic imaging across various dental specialties. This article provides insights into current applications and emerging trends in the field of diagnostic imaging in dentistry.
authors: Nebiha Hilal Bilge

title: Advances in Multimodal Imaging and Artificial Intelligence for the Diagnosis and Management of Diabetic Retinopathy: From Biomarkers to Personalized Care
abstract: Background and Objectives: Diabetic retinopathy (DR) remains a leading cause of preventable vision loss. Staging based on colour fundus photography captures only part of a disease that involves the whole neurovascular unit and the retinal periphery. This narrative review summarizes the structural (optical coherence tomography, OCT), vascular (OCT angiography and ultra-widefield imaging) and functional (microperimetry, electrophysiology) biomarkers of DR, grades the evidence supporting each of them, and examines how artificial intelligence (AI) is changing screening, prognostication and treatment selection. Materials and Methods: PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus and Web of Science were searched for publications from January 2000 to May 2026, giving priority to randomized trials, prospective multicentre cohorts, systematic reviews and externally validated algorithms. Results: Among imaging biomarkers, disorganization of the retinal inner layers, outer retinal integrity and ultra-widefield angiographic non-perfusion have the most consistent prognostic evidence, whereas OCT angiography metrics remain device-dependent. AI has progressed from research classifiers to autonomous systems with regulatory authorization in the United States and the European Union, to prospectively evaluated deployments in national programmes and low-resource settings, and to time-to-event progression models and foundation models. Image-based prediction improves discrimination over clinical risk factors by modest margins, and biomarker-guided treatment of diabetic macular oedema still rests largely on retrospective series. Cross-device standardization of quantitative metrics, representative datasets, prospective outcome trials and health-economic evidence remain the main gaps. Conclusions: Individualized screening intervals are the application closest to routine practice, whereas phenotype-driven therapy and precision monitoring remain promising but unproven.
authors: Feliciana Menna; Alessandro Meduri; Stefano Lupo; Laura De Luca; Antonio Baldascino; Enzo Maria Vingolo

title: Advances in integrated diagnostics: Innovation and translation of laboratory diagnostic technologies
abstract: Integrated diagnostics is reshaping modern laboratory medicine by shifting diagnostic practice from fragmented test utilization toward a clinically oriented, data-driven, and patient-centered model. In this review, we summarize the conceptual foundations, technological advances, and translational challenges of integrated laboratory diagnostics. We propose a five-dimensional framework—intelligence, timeliness, accuracy, standardization, and interdisciplinary integration—to describe the core attributes of this emerging paradigm. Within this framework, diagnostic innovation is driven by the convergence of multiple enabling technologies, including liquid biopsy, mass spectrometry, high-throughput and single-cell sequencing, spatial multi-omics, digital pathology, point-of-care testing, organoid models, microfluidics, and interoperable digital infrastructure. Together, these advances support a transition from isolated result generation to dynamic, contextualized, and actionable diagnostic insights, thereby promoting earlier detection, more precise risk stratification, individualized therapeutic guidance, and longitudinal health monitoring. We further discuss the major barriers to clinical translation, including technical and data complexity, limited evidence for clinical utility, workflow integration challenges, and the need for systemic transformation in workforce training, governance, and equitable implementation. Overall, integrated laboratory diagnostics represents a transformative direction for laboratory medicine and precision healthcare. Its successful adoption will depend on coordinated progress in evidence generation, interoperability, and multidisciplinary collaboration, ultimately enabling a more predictive, preventive, personalized, and participatory diagnostic future.
authors: Sergio Bernardini; Jun Zhang

title: Adversarial domain adaptation for false-positive reduction in hospital-to-robotic echocardiographic screening under limited target-domain data
abstract: Hospital-trained deep learning models for echocardiographic wall motion abnormality detection achieve strong performance under standard clinical acquisition conditions but often degrade substantially when deployed on autonomous robotic acquisition systems. Most existing models are developed and validated under controlled clinical acquisition conditions, limiting their robustness when deployed in emerging autonomous imaging systems. A hospital-trained wall motion abnormality detection model trained on 10,000 hospital echocardiograms achieved 92.3% accuracy (94.0% sensitivity, 90.6% specificity) when applied to an independent hospital test data set of 500 studies. However, direct deployment on 150 robotic echocardiograms from 15 healthy subjects reduced the normal-case specificity to 65.7%, representing a 24.9 percentage-point drop compared to the performance when applied to the hospital-acquired data. No statistically significant difference in SNR was observed between domains (p = 0.31; d = 0.12), with similarly small standardized differences in contrast and sharpness, although formal equivalence was not established. Acquisition-geometry measures differed descriptively between domains, suggesting that geometry-associated factors may contribute to the observed domain shift. We propose an adversarial domain adaptation framework built upon a 3D ResNet-18 backbone with a gradient-reversal domain discriminator for aligning hospital and robotic feature representations while retaining the hospital-trained classification objective. This design enables adaptation to the robotic domain without requiring labeled robot-acquired pathological cases, which are particularly difficult to obtain during early-stage robotic system development. Under leave-one-subject-out validation across robotic subjects, Mixed-DANN improved specificity to 86.1% ± 4.3%, while Normal-only DANN improved specificity to 89.3% ± 4.8% (p < 0.001 versus direct transfer), recovering 94.8% of the hospital-to-robot specificity gap. Because the robotic cohort comprises only healthy subjects, evaluation is appropriately restricted to specificity and false-positive rate; sensitivity evaluation requires future acquisition of robot-acquired pathological cases. These findings suggest that acquisition-associated domain shift substantially impacts cross-platform deployment. The proposed adversarial domain adaptation framework provides a potential pathway for adapting hospital-trained cardiac AI models to autonomous robotic ultrasound under conditions of limited target-domain data, although validation using robot-acquired pathological cases remains necessary before clinical translation.
authors: Hsu Thiri Soe; Yamauchi Yuki; Hiroyasu Iwata

title: Agreement and reproducibility of intraoral scan- versus CBCT-based three-dimensional implant position assessment in the posterior mandible — a paired in vitro method-comparison study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Three-dimensional postoperative implant assessment is increasingly performed using intraoral scan (IOS) superimposition as a radiation-free alternative to cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT). However, it remains unclear to what extent IOS- and CBCT-based measurements agree and how reproducibility changes across posterior mandibular configurations. METHODS: In this paired in vitro method-comparison study, based on the experimental platform of a previous study, 60 implants placed at Fédération Dentaire Internationale (FDI) positions 35, 36, 45, 46 and 47 in bounded edentulous spaces (BES) and distal extension situations (DE) underwent three IOS-based and three CBCT-based postoperative assessments relative to the virtual plan using the Treatment Evaluation Tool of the planning software. Angular, mesiodistal, buccolingual, apico-coronal, and three-dimensional (3D) deviations at implant base and apex were recorded, resulting in 180 paired measurements. Agreement was assessed by Bland-Altman analysis, and within-method reproducibility by the within-implant standard deviation (Sw). IOS variability was additionally separated into within-scan and between-scan components. Non-parametric analyses were used for comparisons by indication and FDI position. RESULTS: Mean absolute IOS-CBCT differences were 0.73° ± 0.55° for angular deviation, 0.22 ± 0.20 mm for the 3D base offset and 0.26 ± 0.22 mm for the 3D apical offset. Bland-Altman bias (CBCT - IOS) was small (- 0.35°; -0.05 mm; -0.07 mm) with 95% limits of agreement of [- 2.01°; +1.31°], [- 0.62; +0.53] mm and [- 0.73; +0.58] mm. Within-method reproducibility was superior for IOS in 8 of 9 parameters (e.g., Sw 0.20° vs. 0.55° for the angle), and IOS variability was dominated by scan-to-scan rather than within-scan re-evaluation. Discrepancies were larger in DE than in BES sites in 7 of 9 parameters (all p < 0.001 for the principal apical and buccolingual components) and were larger at position 47 than at position 35 (3D base p = 0.004; 3D apex p = 0.011). CONCLUSIONS: In this in vitro setting, IOS- and CBCT-based implant assessment in the posterior mandible showed good agreement with small overall differences, and IOS demonstrated lower within-method variability than CBCT. IOS-based superimposition may therefore serve as a radiation-free complement to CBCT for the postoperative evaluation of single implants in bounded posterior sites. Agreement decreased in distal extension situations and at more distal positions; in these configurations, and whenever clinical decisions depend on sub-millimeter or sub-degree precision, CBCT remains the reference technique. Confirmation in vivo is required before routine clinical use.
authors: Georg Hoene; Shabnam Shahpasand; Felix Karl Waffenschmidt; Frederik Holdorf; Robert Stünkel; Alexander-Nicolai Zeller; Philipp Kauffmann

title: An Accurate and Efficient 3D Reconstruction Method for Wireless Capsule Endoscopy Based on Harris Corner Detection and Fixed Template Matching
abstract: To overcome the limitation of wireless capsule endoscopy (WCE) in providing only two‑dimensional intestinal images—which constrains accurate diagnosis of intestinal lesions—this study proposes an accurate and efficient three‑dimensional detection method. The approach applies 3D reconstruction to WCE images by computing corresponding points across successive frames and estimating the capsule’s position and orientation. A critical step involves the selection of highly specific feature points and the determination of their correspondences. Accordingly, this paper combines a Harris corner‑based feature extraction algorithm with a fixed matching template algorithm to achieve robust feature point matching in WCE intestinal images, substantially improving both matching efficiency and robustness. Using the obtained feature matching points, an intestinal model is reconstructed via 3D reconstruction. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method offers advantages in efficiency and reconstruction quality compared with conventional 3D reconstruction approaches, indicating its potential to enhance WCE‑based lesion localization and diagnostic accuracy.
authors: Tigang Cai
venue: Journal of Research in Science Computing and Engineering

title: An Adaptive Bayesian Active Learning Framework for Automated Subjective Refraction in Digital Phoropters
abstract: Abstract Subjective refraction is the clinical gold standard for determining corrective ophthalmic prescriptions. While modern computerized phoropters—such as the [NIDEK RT-6100](https://www.nidek-intl.com/items/intelligent-refractor-rt-6100/?utm_source=gemini)—have automated lens rotation and enabled remote examination, the sequential logic of lens selection remains bound to fixed, deterministic heuristic trees (such as Jackson Cross Cylinder [JCC] bracketing and manual fogging). These rigid protocols lead to prolonged examination times, patient fatigue, and susceptibility to erroneous responses. In this paper, we formulate an autonomous Bayesian Active Learning Framework for Subjective Refraction. We map traditional spherocylindrical parameters $(S, C, A)$ into an orthogonal 3D Euclidean space via Thibos Power Vectors$\mathbf{x} = (M, J_0, J_{45})$. The patient is modeled as a probabilistic psychophysical observer with a three-alternative response likelihood (Lens 1 clearer, Lens 2 clearer, or Unsure/Same), incorporating sensory discrimination threshold $\alpha$, lapse rate $\lambda$, and blur indifference deadbands. At each examination step, the agent calculates the Expected Information Gain (Mutual Information) across candidate lens pairs and selects the query that maximizes Shannon entropy reduction, while enforcing an ophthalmologically grounded Fogging Safety Constraint to suppress accommodation spasm. In Monte Carlo simulations across $N = 300$ virtual patients with representative refractive distributions, our Bayesian active learning agent converged to clinical accuracy ($\le 0.25\text{ D}$) in an average of 5.4 steps, compared to 8.9 steps for the conventional rule-based clinical protocol—achieving a 39.4% reduction in testing steps. Furthermore, at 20 steps, the residual dioptric vector error was reduced by 43.6%($0.165\text{ D}$ vs. $0.293\text{ D}$, $p < 0.001$). This framework provides a verifiable theoretical foundation and software architecture for embedding autonomous AI decision-making into next-generation digital phoropters.

title: An Expertise Transfer Framework For Autonomous Surgical Assistance
abstract: Autonomous surgery holds the potential to transform operative practice by enhancing procedural safety and consistency. While substantial progress has been made on episodic sub-tasks, achieving autonomy for long-horizon tasks that span the entire procedure remains challenging. Current logic-based heuristics and end-to-end learning approaches, though effective for short-term actions, struggle to adapt to the evolving dynamics of complete surgical workflows. To address this gap, an expertise transfer framework is introduced to achieve procedure-spanning autonomous view assistance by emulating expert logic. Specifically, the framework instantiates situational awareness via a novel hierarchical granularity perception network that jointly captures surgical workflow and fine-grained instrument-tissue interactions; models attention allocation for inferring assistance needs by systematically characterizing surgeon visual attention patterns; and encodes decision-making logic for actionable behaviors by formalizing expert assistance policies as a heterogeneous knowledge graph. Equipped with this architecture, the proposed framework successfully enables autonomous view assistance in vivo animal trials throughout complete nephrectomy procedures, while demonstrating improved visualization quality compared to human assistance. This expertise transfer paradigm provides a promising pathway toward trustworthy autonomy in clinical applications, advancing the shift toward procedure-spanning autonomous workflows.
authors: Yuan Gao; Guangdi Chu; Wei Jiao; Yuchuan Zhong; Hang Yuan; Chengjun Li; Jinhua Li; Shuxin Wang; Bo Guan; Jianchang Zhao; Lizhi Pan; Pengfei Zhang; Jianmin Li

title: An Intelligent Hybrid Deep Learning Framework for Automated Dental Caries Detection, Segmentation, Multi-Class Classification, Severity Assessment, and Treatment Recommendation Using Dental Radiographic Images
abstract: Dental caries stays one of the most widely wide-spread oral health disorders worldwide, affecting people throughout all age businesses and causing widespread healthcare burdens. accurate and early prognosis of dental lesions is essential for stopping sickness progression and improving treatment results. but, conventional diagnostic strategies often suffer from subjective interpretation, low sensitivity to subtle lesion boundaries, and restrained functionality in severity assessment. This study proposes an advanced synthetic Intelligence pushed framework named automatic Dental Caries Detection using Synaptic Intelligent Convolutional Neural network (ADCD-SICNN) for automatic dental radiographic evaluation. initially, dental X-ray photos are obtained from the Dental Analyze and diagnosis of radiography data (DRAD). Bayesian Boundary fashion Filtering is employed for image enhancement and noise discount even as keeping essential anatomical systems. eventually, a Dense Channel Spatial Semantic steerage interest UNet (DCSSGA-UNet) is utilized for unique lesion segmentation. neighborhood texture and side statistics are extracted thru Residual Neural Networks (ResNet), while structural lesion traits are captured using Multi-hypothesis Fuzzy Matching Radon transform (MHFMRT). The extracted capabilities are merged together by a hybrid feature integration method, and entrust them to a Synaptic intelligent Convolutional Neural network (SICNN), which is optimized by the Enzyme motion Optimizer (EAO). Experimental evaluation demonstrates outstanding performance with classification accuracies of 98.2%, 99.3%, 97.5%, and 97.8% for fillings, implants, impacted teeth, and cavities respectively. Furthermore, the proposed framework achieves a Dice Similarity Coefficient of 98.3%, Intersection over Union (IoU) of 97.2%, and Area Under Curve (AUC) of 0.986.
