title: Analysis of the relationship between double-balloon enteroscopy docking success rates and lesion detection rates: a single-center retrospective study
abstract: Abstract Background: The small intestine poses diagnostic challenges in digestive system diseases. The advent of double-balloon enteroscopy (DBE) has significantly improved endoscopic visualization and diagnostic capabilities for small intestine diseases. Objective: To investigate the correlation between DBE docking rates and small intestine disease detection rates among patients with small intestine disorders. Design: Retrospective study. Methods: A total of 125 patients with small intestine diseases who underwent DBE at the Department of Gastroenterology of the Affiliated Hospital of Inner Mongolia Medical University between March 2024 and July 2025 were enrolled and divided into the docking group (n=48) and non-docking group (n=77). Endoscopic findings and clinical data were retrospectively analyzed and lesion detection rates of both groups were systematically documented. Patients were also categorized according to disease types to analyze the relationship between lesion detection and the docking status. Results: However, DBE docking was successful in only 48 patients (38.4%; 48/125). Lesions were detected in 78 patients (78/125 [62.4%]; docking group: 38/48 [79.2%]; non-docking group: 40/77; 51.9%). The difference in lesion detection rates between groups was statistically significant (χ 2 =9.336; P=0.002). Among 43 patients with small intestine disease, unexplained gastrointestinal bleeding was confirmed in 37 (docking group: 22/23 [95.6%]; non-docking group: 14/20 [70%]). The intergroup difference was not statistically significant (χ 2 =5.165; P=0.023). For 29 patients with small intestine ulcers, lesion detection rates were 76.5% (13/17) and 58.3% (7/12) in the docking and non-docking groups, respectively, with no statistically significant intergroup difference: χ 2 =1.081; P=0.298. Among 17 patients with tumors, lesion detection rates were 100% (3/3) and 64.3% (9/14) in the docking and non-docking groups, respectively, with no statistically significant intergroup difference: χ 2 =1.581; P=0.218. Differences in hospitalization duration, adverse events, and average hospitalization costs were not statistically significant. Conclusion: Significantly higher lesion detection rates were associated with successful DBE docking.
authors: Xinyue Hu; Chen Ping; Jie Cui; Haiying DONG; Jia Li; A Runa

title: Antioxidant Strategies for Inherited Retinal Degenerations in the Era of Gene Therapy
abstract: Inherited retinal degenerations (IRDs) are a genetically heterogeneous group of disorders characterized by progressive loss of photoreceptors and retinal pigment epithelium, leading to irreversible vision impairment. Although gene therapy has transformed the therapeutic outlook for IRDs, its efficacy remains limited by gene and variant specificity, a narrow treatment window dependent on viable target cells, and the persistence of retinal degeneration even after restoration of gene function. In this review, we summarize current gene-based therapeutic strategies, critically examine oxidative stress as a shared but heterogeneous downstream mechanism across IRDs, and review antioxidant and redox-modulating interventions with particular emphasis on the distinction between preclinical and clinical evidence. This review highlights that oxidative stress contributes to inflammation, metabolic dysfunction, and cellular damage during disease progression and may be exacerbated by interventions associated with gene therapy-including vector-induced immune activation, transgene-related cellular stress, and delivery-associated tissue injury. However, direct evidence supporting antioxidant-gene therapy combinations remains predominantly preclinical, and their clinical efficacy has not yet been established. Disease- and stage-specific integration of antioxidants and redox modulation may help preserve viable retinal cells, support retinal homeostasis during genetic rescue, and potentially improve treatment durability.
authors: Yiliu Yang; Qin Chen; Junjie Zeng; Licong Liang; Zhiyan Tao; Kaiqin She; Chengda Ren; Fang Lu

title: Application of Artificial Intelligence in Diagnostic Medical Imaging and Radiotherapy
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming healthcare, particularly in diagnostic imaging and radiotherapy. The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in the field of diagnostic medical imaging and radiotherapy has witnessed significant advancements, revolutionizing the healthcare landscape. This review delves into its diverse applications, exploring its potential to boost accuracy, streamline workflows, and improve patient outcomes. A systematic literature search identified relevant studies on AI's role in these domains. Articles covered topics like image analysis, pattern recognition, decision support, and treatment planning. AI algorithms, performance, and integration into clinical practice were critically evaluated. In diagnostic imaging, AI shines in modalities like MRI, CT, and PET. AI algorithms excel in image interpretation, aiding early detection, characterization, and staging of various diseases. Additionally, these tools show promise in predicting treatment response and personalizing treatment plans. Within radiotherapy, AI automates and improves treatment steps. Machine learning algorithms efficiently contour target volumes and organs at risk, facilitating optimal treatment planning. Real-time image guidance and AI-driven adaptive radiotherapy techniques enhance precision and safety during treatment delivery. Moreover, AI-based predictive models assist in assessing outcomes and optimizing therapeutic strategies, ultimately improving patient care. Despite the advancements, challenges like data privacy, standardization, and ethical considerations persist. This review paints a comprehensive picture of AI's current applications in diagnostic imaging and radiotherapy, highlighting its transformative impact on disease diagnosis and treatment planning. As AI evolves, its integration into clinical practice holds immense potential to revolutionize patient care, ushering in a new era of precision medicine.
authors: Buhari Samaila
venue: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF APPLIED SCIENCE AND MATHEMATICAL THEORY

title: Artificial Intelligence Approaches for Gastrointestinal Bleeding Detection in Capsule Endoscopy: A Systematic Review and Critical Analysis
abstract: Background/Objectives: Gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding is a common, potentially life-threatening condition, and capsule endoscopy (CE) is the principal investigation for suspected small-bowel bleeding after non-diagnostic upper endoscopy and colonoscopy. Because manual review of thousands of CE frames is labor-intensive, artificial intelligence (AI) has been proposed to automate bleeding detection. Methods: Following PRISMA 2020, this systematic review synthesizes 15 peer-reviewed journal studies (2020–2025) applying traditional machine learning, convolutional neural networks, transfer learning, attention-based or hybrid architectures, segmentation, or object detection to GI bleeding detection in CE. Methodological quality was appraised with an AI-adapted risk-of-bias framework informed by QUADAS-2 and PROBAST. Results: Frame-level classification accuracy ranged from 90.6% to 99.9% (median 98.5%; 13 studies), with the lowest values from evaluations closest to clinical practice; the segmentation and detection studies reported a mean intersection-over-union of 86.9% and an mAP@0.5 of 79.0%. Only two studies (13%) were at low risk of bias for validation strategy, none reported patient-level separation of training and test data, only four (27%) used clinical patient data, and none compared AI with conventional endoscopy or clinical outcomes. Conclusions: Current evidence demonstrates high performance on curated datasets but not yet generalizability or clinical readiness; patient-level, external, and prospective multicentre validation is required.
authors: Nasima Mohammad Helal; Jon Zaccary Regala; K. K. Mujeeb Rahman

title: Artificial Intelligence and Imaging Technologies in Orthodontic Assessment, Referral and Care Pathways: A Scoping Review
abstract: Abstract* Background Artificial intelligence (AI), integrated with imaging technologies, is increasingly applied across orthodontic assessment and care pathways. However, the evidence remains scattered across imaging modalities, clinical applications, AI methodologies, and stages of clinical translation. Methods A scoping review was conducted in accordance with the Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and reported in line with the PRISMA-ScR guidelines. PubMed, Scopus, and IEEE Xplore were searched for studies published between January 2016 and June 2026, with searches supplemented by Google Scholar, OpenAlex, grey literature sources, and citation searching. Eligible studies were mapped descriptively and synthesised thematically using Braun and Clarke’s framework. Results Fifty-four studies were included. AI applications used intraoral and facial photographs, cephalometric radiographs, CBCT, intraoral scans, three-dimensional dental models, and multimodal imaging. Applications ranged from landmark localisation, segmentation, and malocclusion classification to treatment-need assessment, screening, referral support, treatment planning, and remote monitoring. Evidence was strongest for bounded, anatomically verifiable image-analysis tasks, whereas applications involving referral, triage, treatment-need decisions, longitudinal prediction, and workflow integration were less mature. Common limitations included retrospective, single-centre designs; heterogeneous reference standards; limited external validation; inconsistent reporting of calibration and uncertainty; and insufficient evaluation of patient-centred, equity, and service-level outcomes. Conclusions Imaging-based AI in orthodontics has evolved from automated image interpretation to clinician-assisted decision support across the care pathway. Current evidence most strongly supports AI for structured image-analysis tasks, but does not yet support autonomous referral, triage, or treatment-planning decisions. Future research should prioritise prospective multicentre validation, transparent reporting, explainability, fairness, uncertainty handling, and workflow-integrated evaluation to enable safe and clinically useful implementation.
authors: Kayali S, Bernabe E, Golkari A.

title: Artificial Intelligence as a Catalyst for Cell-Based Therapies in Retinal Disease
abstract: Retinal degenerative diseases, including age-related macular degeneration (AMD), retinitis pigmentosa (RP), and Stargardt disease, represent leading causes of irreversible vision loss worldwide, collectively affecting hundreds of millions of people. Cell-based therapies, particularly those leveraging induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs), retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) transplantation, and CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing, have emerged as promising treatment modalities that may preserve, replace, or partially restore retinal function. However, these approaches face significant challenges in patient stratification, manufacturing consistency, surgical precision, and long-term outcome monitoring. Artificial intelligence (AI), encompassing machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), and computer vision, is increasingly being integrated across the cell therapy pipeline to address these limitations. This review comprehensively explores the role of AI in enhancing cell-based retinal therapies, spanning disease diagnosis and patient selection, stem cell quality control and differentiation optimization, CRISPR off-target detection, retinal organoid characterization, scalable manufacturing, and post-transplantation monitoring through multimodal retinal imaging. Throughout, we distinguish direct retinal cell-therapy evidence from retinal-adjacent, cross-domain, and conceptual evidence. We also propose an AI-powered end-to-end pipeline that connects patient profiling through gene editing, cell production, and transplantation to longitudinal outcomes tracking (a forward-looking framework that needs to be clinically validated in future). While AI offers powerful tools to enhance efficacy, reproducibility, and personalization, it does not replace the clinical and biological foundations of cell therapy. Critical challenges remain, including data scarcity, algorithmic interpretability, regulatory compliance, and clinical validation. This review concludes that the strategic integration of AI has plausible potential to become supportive infrastructure for scalable and reproducible cell-based treatments for retinal diseases, although its necessity has not been demonstrated and prospective clinical validation is still required, and biological insight and rigorous empirical verification remain fundamental.
authors: Girish Kumar Srivastava; Priyank Shukla; Sara Crespo Millas; Yogeswaran Lokanathan

title: Artificial Intelligence for Benign Esophageal Stricture Dilation: An Evidence‐Transferability Framework and Safety‐First Roadmap
abstract: ABSTRACT Background Endoscopic dilation is first‐line therapy for symptomatic benign esophageal strictures but remains operator‐dependent. Artificial intelligence (AI) could support assessment, risk stratification, and documentation; however, evidence from adjacent tasks is often mistaken for procedure‐specific validation. Aim To map the evidence for AI in benign esophageal stricture dilation, assess transferability and methodological quality, and propose a translational pathway. Methods We searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Europe PMC from inception through June 28, 2026, using prespecified searches in adults and children. Studies were classified by evidence provenance and appraised using design‐adapted domain considerations. Results Within the search date and eligibility criteria, no AI system was identified that guided, monitored, or assessed dilation itself; two retrospective single‐center studies applied machine learning in the target population for other tasks. Adjacent neoplasia and engineering studies support component feasibility, while clinical cohorts identify candidate predictors. Functional lumen imaging probe technology provides non‐AI measurement and potential reference labels. Recurrent concerns included selected or retrospective samples, limited external validation, and high concern about applicability to dilation. Performance cannot be transferred across mismatched target tasks, acquisition physics, reference standards, populations or operating contexts, or consequences of error. Conclusion Adjacent evidence can justify candidate components. Procedure‐specific calibration and validation remain necessary. Priorities are calibrated morphometric variables with prespecified reference standards and reproducible documentation using synchronized multimodal and outcome data. External validation should be followed by human‐controlled advisory testing before intraprocedural automation.
authors: Ahmed Salman; Mohamed Abdalla Salman

title: Artificial Intelligence in Bioengineering: Innovations, Challenges, and Future Directions: A Narrative Review
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming bioengineering, with applications ranging from diagnosis and biomedical imaging to wearable technologies, rehabilitation, biomaterials, biofabrication, and digital twins. This narrative review aims to examine the major innovations, challenges, and future directions of AI-enabled bioengineering, with particular attention to its clinical and translational development. The literature was searched in Scopus and PubMed, with emphasis on systematic reviews and meta-analyses and consideration of other relevant secondary literature across the main bioengineering domains. A total of 57 secondary publications were included in the principal evidence base. The review process was additionally informed by the ANDJ Narrative Review Checklist and an established qualification and scoring methodology applied to the selected secondary literature. The reviewed evidence shows a broad expansion of AI applications and increasing integration of intelligent technologies into bioengineering systems. However, important challenges remain, particularly regarding data quality and representativeness, validation and generalizability, reproducibility, safety, human oversight, ethical responsibility, equity, and regulatory requirements. Future developments are expected to increasingly involve multimodal, adaptive, connected, and human-centered systems integrating AI with sensing technologies, robotics, digital twins, and longitudinal data. Overall, AI-enabled bioengineering is progressing from promising technological applications toward increasingly integrated and translational systems. Its successful evolution will depend on combining technological innovation with robust clinical evidence, responsible development, and appropriate ethical and regulatory frameworks.
authors: Daniele Giansanti

title: Artificial Intelligence in CBCT for Dental Implantology: Current Applications, Limitations, and Future Perspectives - A Literature Review
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being integrated into cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT)-based workflows in dental implantology.This structured narrative literature review evaluated current AI applications in implant dentistry, critically assessed their technical and clinical limitations, and discussed future perspectives for integration into implant planning and treatment workflows.A literature search was conducted using PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and Embase.Evidence was synthesized according to clinically relevant domains, including anatomical segmentation, identification of edentulous regions and implant sites, bone assessment, virtual implant planning, comparison with expert planning, workflow optimization, and outcome prediction.AI demonstrated encouraging performance in CBCT segmentation, anatomical and bone assessment, and selected components of virtual implant planning.Automated systems showed substantial agreement with expert-generated plans in selected clinical settings and consistently reduced planning time while providing high repeatability.However, performance varied according to anatomical complexity, imaging conditions, software environment, and the specific task evaluated.Limited external validation, heterogeneous datasets and evaluation methods, and the gap between technical performance and demonstrated clinical benefit remain important barriers to generalizability.Current evidence supports AI primarily as a decision-support tool that complements professional judgment.Future research should prioritize multicenter prospective validation, standardized evaluation frameworks, multimodal data integration, explainable and uncertainty-aware models, and clinically meaningful outcomes.
authors: Nabil EL SAHILI
venue: Online Journal of Dentistry & Oral Health

title: Artificial Intelligence in Contemporary Dentistry: Applications Across Dental Specialties and Future Challenges.
abstract: Modern artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly shaping contemporary dental practice through efficient diagnosis, improved treatment planning, and patient personalization across various settings. By leveraging innovations in computer vision, deep learning, and multimodal pattern recognition, computational models are being applied across the major fields of dentistry today. These AI-based approaches are used for automated lesion detection in diagnostic imaging, precision alignment in orthodontics, root canal mapping in endodontics, and robotic assistance in surgical procedures. Despite the substantial improvements in diagnostic accuracy, objectivity, and efficiency, there are several major challenges with implementing these technologies into clinical practice. These challenges include algorithm bias, data privacy concerns, the absence of regulatory guidelines for the development of such tools, and cost. This review aims to provide an overview of the applications of artificial intelligence in the different fields of dentistry, to highlight the current challenges and directions for future research and development, and to discuss the potential of generative language models, real-time augmented reality (AR), and the prediction of dental healthcare outcomes.
authors: Sumit Bhatt; Prantika Mandal; Shweta V Sagare; Sanjay J Gawali; Kunal Nischal; Sai C Das; Pratik Surana

title: Artificial Intelligence in Dental Implant Treatment Planning: A Systematic Review
abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being integrated into digital dentistry and dental implantology, particularly for three-dimensional image analysis, anatomical segmentation, implant-site identification, bone assessment, and computer-assisted treatment planning. Because implant placement is prosthetically and anatomically driven, reliable interpretation of cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) data is central to reducing surgical and prosthetic complications. Objective: To systematically synthesize current evidence regarding AI applications in dental implant treatment planning, with emphasis on CBCT-based anatomical identification and segmentation, edentulous-site detection, bone-dimension assessment, technical assistance in planning, and emerging outcome prediction. Methods: Evidence was synthesized from recent systematic reviews, meta-analyses, scoping reviews, and representative primary studies addressing AI-assisted implant planning. The review framework follows PRISMA 2020 principles and organizes evidence according to population, intervention, comparison, outcomes, AI architecture, imaging modality, and clinical application. Because substantial heterogeneity exists in algorithms, datasets, reference standards, and reported endpoints, quantitative pooling was restricted to outcomes already meta-analyzed in the literature. Results: Published reviews consistently show high technical performance for several CBCT-based tasks. A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis reported pooled accuracy of 96% for mandibular and 83% for maxillary edentulous-site identification. A 2026 systematic review of 28 implant-planning studies reported anatomical-segmentation accuracy ranging from 66.4% to 99.1%, with 18 studies addressing segmentation and eight examining technical assistance. A 2026 meta-analysis of U-Net-based mandibular-canal segmentation reported pooled Dice similarity coefficient of 0.84 and substantial heterogeneity. AI-assisted systems can markedly reduce segmentation and planning time, but evidence remains dominated by retrospective, single-centre, and technically focused studies. Conclusion: AI has substantial potential to improve the speed, consistency, and anatomical precision of dental implant treatment planning, particularly when applied to CBCT segmentation and risk-structure identification. Current evidence does not justify autonomous implant planning. External validation, multicentre prospective studies, standardized reporting, explainability, regulatory oversight, and clinician-in-the-loop workflows are required before routine autonomous use.
authors: Dr. Sowmiya. T; Mihir Joshi; Mohammad Jalaluddin; Pawan Dawane; Jyotsna Seth; Neha Liya

title: Artificial Intelligence in Eye Disease: A Systematic Review of Screening, Diagnosis, Prognosis, Treatment-Response Prediction, and Clinical Decision Support
abstract: Background/Objectives: Artificial intelligence (AI) is expanding eye care beyond image-based detection toward prognosis, treatment-response prediction, monitoring, triage, and clinician-facing decision support. We evaluated AI across eye-disease screening, diagnosis, prognosis, treatment response, and decision support, emphasizing validation, explainability, and clinical readiness. Methods: This PROSPERO-registered review followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 statement. Six databases plus supplementary routes identified English-language literature published from 1 January 2015 through 10 August 2026. Included studies underwent design-mapped Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI)/adapted-JBI item-level appraisal; heterogeneity precluded meta-analysis. Results: The evidence base comprised 270 studies. Diabetic retinopathy/diabetic macular oedema was the largest clinical area (82), followed by retinal/multi-disease AI (52), glaucoma (46), and age-related macular degeneration (AMD)/macular disease (29); convolutional neural network (CNN)/convolutional deep learning was the largest primary method group (136). External validation was confirmed in 130 studies, including 95 with a clinical/geographic/prospective/real-world external-validation component (86 clinical-only and nine mixed clinical + technical); 49 had a strict direct clinical comparator and 90 used explainability. Pediatric/pediatric-relevant evidence accounted for 30 studies, while explicit optometry/optometrist involvement appeared in only three. Conclusions: Ophthalmic AI spans diagnosis through clinical management, but translation remains limited by heterogeneous outcomes, incomplete independent validation, few direct comparators, and sparse evaluation of safety, workflow effects, and patient outcomes.
authors: Manal M Alharbi; Emtenan M. Alharbi; Alanoud S Alsalamah; Hanan Asiri; Najla Beati; Renad AlAtawi; Amr A. Arafat

title: Artificial Intelligence in Gastroenterology: Towards Explainable, Generalisable and Clinically Actionable Decision Support
abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly used in gastroenterology for endoscopic detection and characterisation, disease-activity assessment, risk prediction, treatment-response estimation and workflow support. However, high retrospective accuracy does not necessarily translate into reliable or beneficial clinical decision support. This structured narrative review examines the clinical development of artificial intelligence across gastrointestinal endoscopy, inflammatory bowel disease, hepatology and pancreaticobiliary diseases through three translational dimensions: explainability, generalisability and clinical actionability. Communication, human oversight and lifecycle governance are considered cross-cutting determinants of implementation. The evidence is most mature in gastrointestinal endoscopy, particularly for computer-aided polyp detection, although benefits vary across operators, indications and practice settings. Applications in inflammatory bowel disease, hepatology and pancreaticobiliary care remain predominantly retrospective, with limited prospective evidence that model outputs alter management or improve patient outcomes. Explainability is commonly represented by heatmaps or feature-attribution methods, but rarely evaluated in terms of clinician understanding, calibrated trust or patient communication. External validation is becoming more frequent, yet geographic and technological transportability, calibration and performance under dataset shift remain insufficiently assessed. Prospective implementation and health-economic studies are uncommon, and available economic evidence is largely model-based. Clinical artificial intelligence should therefore be evaluated as a sociotechnical intervention comprising the model, interface, users, workflow, communication process and associated care pathway. Translation requires clinically defined use cases, representative multicentre validation, human-centred evaluation, prospective assessment of benefits and harms, and continuous post-deployment surveillance. Clinical AI in gastroenterology should complement clinical expertise through transparent, contestable and continuously monitored decision support that preserves clinician accountability and supports informed, patient-centred decisions.
authors: Ismail BAYDİLİ; Burak Taşçı; Şengül Doğan; Türker Tuncer

title: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare: From Predictive Models to Generative, Multimodal, and Agentic AI
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used across the diagnostic pathway, from screening and disease detection to differential diagnosis, prognostic stratification, and treatment-response assessment. This narrative review examines predictive, generative, multi-modal, and agentic AI through a diagnostic-science lens and evaluates the evidence required for translation into clinical practice. Predictive models can identify complex patterns in images, physiological signals, laboratory data, and electronic health records, but high retrospective accuracy does not establish diagnostic utility. Clinical validity and utility depend on the intended use, target population, disease spectrum and prevalence, reference standard, operating threshold, calibration, and the consequences of false-positive and false-negative results. Generative AI may support problem representation, differential diagnosis, information synthesis, and documentation, yet fluent outputs can omit critical alternatives, amplify false premises, or convey unjustified certainty. Multimodal systems may better reflect clinical reasoning by integrating imaging, text, signals, pathology, and molecular data, but they must demonstrate incremental value over the best single-modality test and remain robust to missing data. Agentic systems can coordinate evidence retrieval, test selection, and sequential workflows, thereby increasing the need for bounded permissions, auditability, error recovery, and human escalation. Across all paradigms, a credible pathway to diagnostic implementation requires independent external and prospective validation, representative consecutive patients, subgroup analysis, workflow and human-AI evaluation, clinical impact studies, and post-deployment surveillance. The field should therefore be judged not by model capability alone, but by whether AI measurably improves diagnostic yield, timeliness, safety, equity, and patient-relevant outcomes in real care settings.
authors: Ismail BAYDİLİ; Burak Taşçı; Gülay Taşçı; Şengül Doğan; Türker Tuncer

title: Artificial Intelligence in Invisible Orthodontics: From Digital Impressions to Adaptive Treatment Management
abstract: ABSTRACT Digital transformation in orthodontics has significantly revolutionized clinical practices over recent decades. Advancements such as intraoral scanners, 3D imaging (including cone‐beam computed tomography, CBCT), and advanced treatment planning software have increased diagnostic accuracy and the ability to design personalized treatments. These technologies have primarily focused on static aspects and still require continuous human oversight. Machine learning algorithms, particularly convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and artificial neural networks (ANNs), offer superior performance in tasks such as identifying anatomical landmarks on radiographic images, assessing skeletal maturity, and predicting treatment outcomes. Research has shown that AI in static diagnosis and planning has achieved an accuracy greater than 90%, outperforming traditional methods. Moreover, AI reduces processing time, minimizes operator performance variability, and serves as a supportive tool in digital orthodontic workflows. Despite these advancements, there remains a significant gap in research regarding adaptive AI for treatments involving clear aligners. Most studies focus on static planning, while dynamic aspects, such as real‐time treatment adjustments based on the patient's biological responses or deviations in tooth movement, are less explored. This research gap may arise from factors such as patient biological diversity, a lack of real clinical data, and the need for multi‐center validation. Adaptive AI, based on reinforcement learning and digital twin modeling, has the potential to reduce the average treatment duration by approximately 3 to 4 months and increase patient satisfaction. The aim of this review is to provide a comprehensive examination of AI's role in real‐time management of invisible orthodontic treatments, focusing on clear aligner‐based treatments. This study analyzes AI applications going from digital data processing to integration with supervisory platforms, discussing challenges, limitations, and future perspectives. This review not only summarizes current achievements but also proposes practical solutions to overcome existing barriers and presents adaptive AI as a pivotal tool for the future of orthodontics.
authors: Soodeh Hosseini; Hossein Seilani; At‐har Nasari

title: Artificial Intelligence in Ocular Surface Oncology: A Narrative Review of Multimodal Imaging, Smartphone-Based Screening, and Clinical Decision Support
abstract: Ocular surface malignancies include ocular surface squamous neoplasia (OSSN), con-junctival melanoma, and conjunctival lymphoma. These rare disorders may threaten vi-sion and, in some cases, life. Early identification may be difficult because malignant le-sions can resemble benign ocular surface conditions. Artificial intelligence (AI), including machine learning and deep learning, has emerged as a potential aid to detection, classi-fication, and referral. This structured narrative review, organized with reference to SANRA principles, synthesizes PubMed/MEDLINE literature on AI applications in ocular surface oncology available through 29 August 2026. We examine slit-lamp photography, anterior segment optical coherence tomography, in vivo confocal microscopy, ultrasound biomicroscopy, and smartphone imaging. Deep-learning models have shown promising performance in selected binary OSSN tasks, whereas multiclass studies report lower sen-sitivity for rare malignancies such as conjunctival melanoma and lymphoma. Smartphone-based screening has also been evaluated in a prospective referral pathway, although the reference standard and verification process limit interpretation of popula-tion-level sensitivity. Dataset imbalance, image-acquisition variability, limited external and prospective validation, explainability, and workflow integration remain barriers to implementation. Future work should prioritize multicenter datasets, standardized acquisition, calibrated thresholds, and prospective human-AI evaluations. Current evidence supports further evaluation of AI as an adjunct for detection and referral, not as a re-placement for specialist assessment or histopathology.
authors: F. Cappellani; Marco Zeppieri; Longo Antonio; Cosimo Giuseppe Mazzotta; Irene Gattazzo; Fabiana D’Esposito; Caterina Gagliano; Matteo Capobianco

title: Artificial Intelligence in Optical Coherence Tomography‐Based Ophthalmic Imaging: From Automated Diagnosis to Personalized Disease Monitoring
abstract: ABSTRACT Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly applied to optical coherence tomography (OCT) in ophthalmology, but evidence for automated diagnosis is stronger than evidence for longitudinal monitoring. This narrative review evaluates OCT‐based AI with emphasis on disease monitoring and progression, particularly in retinal disease and glaucoma. Literature from 2016 to 2026 was screened across major biomedical databases, and 45 verifiable sources were included. Retinal OCT models support referral triage, fluid segmentation, and treatment‐response prediction, whereas glaucoma applications face specific challenges: retinal nerve fiber layer floor effects, inconsistent progression definitions, reference‐standard circularity, spectrum bias, high myopia, anomalous discs, and device‐related domain shift. Recent meta‐analyses show high diagnostic performance for glaucoma detection, but progression prediction remains less externally validated. Clinically useful OCT‐based AI should therefore be implemented as clinician‐led decision support, with explicit intended use, external validation, calibration, post‐deployment monitoring, and lifecycle governance.
authors: Stjepan Škudar

title: Artificial intelligence for ophthalmic vessel segmentation: from multimodal imaging to clinical translation
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-based vessel segmentation converts color fundus photographs, scanning laser ophthalmoscopy (SLO), optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA), structural OCT, and anterior-segment images into quantitative vascular biomarkers. Strong performance within individual datasets has not consistently yielded reliable clinical measurements because errors can arise during acquisition, anatomical preprocessing, vessel extraction, biomarker calculation, and deployment. This structured narrative review compares segmentation tasks involving retinal vascular trees, OCTA capillary plexuses, the structural choroid and choriocapillaris, macular neovascularization, corneal neovascularization, and conjunctival microvasculature. We assess modern architectures in relation to vessel geometry, severe foreground-background imbalance, scale variation, crossings, and susceptibility to artifacts. The methods considered include multiscale feature pyramids, deformable and directional operators, Transformers, state-space models, diffusion approaches, and foundation models. We organize the synthesis around five evaluation levels: pixel overlap, centerline recovery, vascular topology, biomarker agreement, and clinical actionability. Public fundus and OCTA datasets are catalogued with their acquisition and annotation characteristics, and gaps in public anterior-segment vessel benchmarks are discussed. Because devices, data splits, labels, and post-processing differ substantially, reported metrics are summarized without ranking studies against one another. The review distinguishes structural OCT choroidal vascularity index from OCTA choriocapillaris flow-deficit mapping, as well as true vessel segmentation from global hyperemia grading. Clinical translation will require ocular-magnification correction, quality control of retinal layers and projection artifacts, external testing across devices and populations, out-of-distribution rejection, DICOM/PACS interoperability, prospective impact studies, and regulation as software as a medical device. We conclude that clinical utility depends on an auditable pipeline that measures structural error, biomarker uncertainty, and failure states throughout the workflow.
authors: Lingyan Wu; Jiahao Tang; Shanping Zhao

title: Artificial intelligence for vascular minimally invasive surgery: techniques, clinical integration, and challenges
abstract: Introduction Minimally invasive surgery (MIS), including endovascular and robot-assisted procedures, is widely used for vascular pathologies but remains limited by technical complexity, cognitive workload, and postoperative complications. Artificial Intelligence (AI) may help address these challenges through predictive analysis, decision support, image analysis, and automation. Methods A structured Google Scholar search was conducted from February 21, 2025, to January 1, 2026, and updated through September 2026. Peer-reviewed studies applying AI to vascular MIS were included, with additional targeted searches addressing clinical translation, deployment, regulation, and ethical considerations. Results Thirty primary studies were analyzed, including eight on machine learning, nine on deep learning, four on natural language processing, and nine on robotics or reinforcement learning. Machine learning supported risk stratification and outcome prediction, deep learning enabled imaging and segmentation applications, natural language processing facilitated clinical information extraction, and robotic systems supported navigation and procedural assistance. Discussion AI demonstrates substantial potential across the vascular MIS pathway, but broader clinical adoption requires stronger validation, prospective multicenter studies, standardized reporting, health-economic evaluation, and careful consideration of regulatory, liability, and accessibility challenges.
authors: Cenk Jiang; Bogdan Bortnovskii; Ijaz Gul; Mehmed Özkan; Lian Zhang; Dongmei Yu; Vijay Pandey; Runming Wang; Jian Wu; Peiwu Qin

title: Artificial intelligence in chronic atrophic gastritis: A comprehensive review
abstract: Chronic atrophic gastritis (CAG) is a significant precancerous condition associated with gastric cancer, and its accurate diagnosis and comprehensive management are of great importance for reducing the risk of gastric cancer.In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) has advanced rapidly in the field of digestive diseases, offering new approaches for the intelligent diagnosis and treatment of CAG.Early studies suggest that AI may improve diagnostic performance and assist in risk stratification.However, whether these systems reduce clinician workload or improve patient outcomes remains to be established.Most evidence comes from retrospective diagnostic accuracy studies, and no AI system has yet been incorporated into clinical guidelines.This review summarizes the research progress of AI in CAG, focusing on five key aspects: Assisted diagnosis, pathological interpretation, Helicobacter pylori infection diagnosis, risk prediction, and patient management.It aims to provide a reference for research on CAG and to highlight priorities for future research and clinical translation.
authors: Nuoya Zhou; Qi Luo; Wei Liu; Xiang-Lei Yuan; Huan Jiang; Bing Hu

title: Artificial intelligence in diabetes: Clinical applications across the disease continuum.
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly shaping the landscape of diabetes mellitus (DM) care by enabling data-driven approaches to prediction, diagnosis, classification, and management. The growing availability of continuous biometric data from wearable technologies, combined with advances in machine learning, has created new opportunities to overcome limitations of traditional diabetes metrics and population-based care models. This review summarises current clinical applications of AI in DM, with a focus on translational relevance and, critically, on the level of validation and clinical readiness of each application. AI-based models have demonstrated improved performance in predicting DM onset and diabetes-related complications by integrating electronic health records, imaging data, and longitudinal clinical variables. In diagnosis and screening, AI offers non-invasive and scalable tools, including automated retinal screening systems and emerging digital biomarkers. Data-driven clustering approaches have further refined diabetes classification. In diabetes management, AI supports personalised glucose monitoring, insulin titration, pharmacological decision-making, and lifestyle interventions. Crucially, these applications differ markedly in maturity: autonomous retinal screening and closed-loop insulin delivery are approaching or have reached routine clinical use, whereas voice-based biomarkers and simulation-evaluated lifestyle systems remain proof-of-concept. Addressing challenges of generalisability, data quality, interpretability, and ethical governance through robust validation and explainable AI will be essential to realise the full potential of AI in precision, patient-centred diabetes care.
authors: Serena Shih Yin; Viola Viola; Paolo Pozzilli
venue: Journal of diabetes and its complications

title: Artificial intelligence in diabetic retinopathy: From deep learning to foundation models, clinical translation, and real-world deployment.
abstract: Diabetic retinopathy (DR) remains a leading cause of preventable vision impairment worldwide, with its burden increasing in parallel with the global diabetes pandemic. As a progressive microvascular disorder with neurovascular unit involvement, DR is driven by retinal ischemia, inflammation, and pathological neovascularization, while diabetic macular edema (DME) continues to represent a principal cause of vision loss. This structured narrative review provides a critical synthesis of advances in diabetic retinopathy diagnosis, retinal imaging, treatment strategies, and artificial intelligence(AI)-enabled screening published from January, 2020, through March, 2026, while selectively incorporating earlier landmark studies to provide clinical and methodological context. We summarize contemporary screening pathways and emerging retinal imaging modalities, including ultra-widefield photography (up to ∼200° field of view), optical coherence tomography (OCT), and OCT angiography, examining how complementary structural and vascular biomarkers are reshaping disease severity assessment and DME characterization. We then review the evolution of AI methodologies, highlighting a transition from task-specific convolutional neural network pipelines toward transformer-based and self-supervised representation learning, including retina-specific foundation models designed to reduce annotation burden and improve robustness and generalizability under domain shift. Beyond algorithmic performance on curated benchmarks, we emphasize key translational requirements for clinical adoption, including model calibration, uncertainty-aware triage, image quality control, and external validation across imaging devices and diverse populations. Recent prospective and implementation studies across diverse healthcare systems demonstrate that the real-world effectiveness of AI-enabled DR screening depends not only on diagnostic accuracy but also on image gradability, clinically appropriate operating thresholds, uncertainty management, external validation, referral capacity, and integration with established care pathways. Evidence from the Asia-Pacific region provides important examples of these implementation challenges in heterogeneous and resource-constrained screening environments. Specific attention is given to the identification and mitigation strategies for fundus pigmentation-related performance disparities and the governance of autonomous versus hybrid human-AI screening models within evolving regulatory frameworks. Finally, we examine emerging work in oculomics for systemic risk stratification and propose a pragmatic clinical readiness framework centered on validation hierarchy, safety monitoring, and workflow integration. Particular emphasis is placed on the translational readiness of foundation models, multimodal retinal intelligence, and emerging technologies for large-scale screening, therapeutic decision-making, and longitudinal disease monitoring.
authors: Basanta Haobijam; Tourangbam Harishore Singh; Puyam Tondonba Singh; Wei-Chi Wu; Eugene Yu-Chuan Kang; Sinam Ajitkumar Singh; Anzila Laikhuram; Cheng-Ming Huang; Wei-Che Huang; Peng-Po Chun; Zhou-Yu Qin

title: Artificial intelligence in early oral cancer detection: a comprehensive review of diagnostic applications, clinical implementation, and future directions
abstract: Oral cancer causes more than 377,000 new cases annually, and delayed diagnosis remains a major contributor to poor outcomes. Conventional visual examination is subjective, while specialist access is limited in many rural and resource-constrained settings.To review the diagnostic performance, clinical implementation, and future directions of artificial intelligence (AI) for early detection and risk stratification of oral potentially malignant disorders (OPMDs) and oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC).PubMed, Scopus, IEEE Xplore, and Web of Science were searched for English-language, peer-reviewed studies published from 2015 to 2026 using terms related to AI, machine learning, deep learning, OPMDs, OSCC, screening, and early detection. Eligible diagnostic and implementation studies were synthesized narratively because of methodological heterogeneity.Meta-analyses reported pooled sensitivities of 87%-92% and specificities of 81%-92% across mixed imaging and histopathology applications. PRAYAAS achieved 94% accuracy on its held-out test set, while OralCancerPredict showed good discrimination and calibration for malignant progression risk in oral leukoplakia. Nevertheless, most evidence remains retrospective, single-center, and vulnerable to dataset bias, limited external validation, and inconsistent reference standards.AI is a promising adjunct, not a replacement, for clinician-led screening and histopathologic diagnosis. Priorities include prospective multicenter validation, representative datasets, transparent reporting, explainability, workflow integration, cost-effectiveness, and equity-focused evaluation in low- and middle-income countries.
authors: Smit Kabrawala; Akshay Ashok Katara; Ikjyot Singh Gujral; Siddharth Jena

title: Artificial intelligence in gastroenterology practice: Current perspectives and emerging prospects
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly changing the landscape of gastroenterology by improving disease detection, diagnosis, risk stratification, prognostication, and clinical decision-making.Machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, large language models, and multimodal data integration have facilitated the development of accurate diagnostic and predictive algorithms for a wide spectrum of gastrointestinal and hepatopancreatobiliary diseases.In upper gastrointestinal diseases, AI has enhanced the detection and characterization of gastroesophageal reflux disease, Barrett's esophagus, esophageal cancer, gastric neoplasia, and gastroesophageal varices.The use of AI in capsule endoscopy has facilitated small intestinal mucosal lesion detection and reduced reading time.Computer-aided detection and diagnosis systems have improved adenoma detection and polyp characterization in colorectal diseases, while AI is increasingly being applied to molecular profiling and prognostic modeling in colorectal cancer.In inflammatory bowel disease, AI facilitates more objective endoscopic and histologic assessment, as well as prediction of disease outcome and treatment response.Promising AI-based radiomics, digital pathology, biomarker discovery, and risk prediction models have been emerging in pancreatic, biliary, and liver diseases.Large language models and multimodal AI may further enable integration of heterogeneous information and support personalized decision-making.Computer-aided quality assessment represents an emerging application for standardizing procedural quality in endoscopy.Several AIassisted platforms have received regulatory approval with ongoing integration into clinical practice.However, limited external validation, population and device-related heterogeneity, dataset bias, interpretability, workflow integration, and uncertain costeffectiveness remain important barriers to generalizability and clinical adoption.Robust multicenter prospective validation and responsible implementation will be essential to optimize its clinical impact. / 85

title: Artificial intelligence in gastrointestinal endoscopy: From technical performance to clinical translation
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is being increasingly used in gastrointestinal endoscopy for lesion detection, optical characterization, procedural quality monitoring, multimodal assessment, clinical decision support, and documentation. The strongest clinical evidence supports computer-aided detection during colonoscopy and selected applications for upper gastrointestinal neoplasia. Randomized trials have shown that AI can increase adenoma detection and assist in real-time lesion recognition. However, the benefits observed in controlled studies are not always reproduced in routine practice. Evidence for optical diagnosis, invasion depth assessment, inflammatory bowel disease, capsule endoscopy, pancreatobiliary endoscopy, and endoscopic ultrasonography remains heterogeneous, and many systems have been evaluated, mainly using retrospective or selected datasets. However, technical performance alone does not establish clinical value. Higher sensitivity, specificity, and diagnostic accuracy may not lead to safer decisions, more efficient workflows, or better patient outcomes. False-positive alerts, automation bias, correction burden, geographic and platform dependence, limited external validation, and poor workflow integration can affect real-world performance. Vision-foundation models, multimodal systems, and large-language models extend AI beyond single-task image analysis to reusable representations, automated reporting, and well-defined clinical support. Their clinical transferability remains uncertain because of domain shifts, data leakage, unsupported generation, and variable performance across settings. This review examined the evidence from gastrointestinal endoscopy using two complementary dimensions: clinical function and stage of evaluation. The clinical function describes the role of AI in the endoscopic pathway. Stage of evaluation distinguishes among retrospective internal testing, independent external validation, prospective clinical evaluation, interventional evaluation, and real-world or post-deployment assessment. We also use reasoning-aligned AI to describe systems whose tasks, intermediate representations, evidence integration, and outputs are organized around clinically meaningful observations and decisions, without implying human-like cognition or causal reasoning. Wider adoption should depend on independent validation, prospective evaluation of complete human–AI workflows, appropriate clinical oversight, operational reliability, governance, economic value, and reproducible benefits in routine care.
authors: Wenxin Xue; Xueying Wang; Tongrui Yang; Honggang Yu

title: Artificial intelligence in odontology education
abstract: Introduction Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being explored in dental education as a tool to support teaching, learning, assessment, and clinical decision-making. This systematic review synthesized current evidence on the implementation and educational impact of AI technologies in undergraduate, postgraduate, and continuing dental education. Methodology A PRISMA-guided systematic review was conducted using Scopus, PubMed, and IEEE Xplore. Studies published between 2020 and 2025 evaluating AI applications in dental education were identified using predefined PICO criteria. Educational outcomes included knowledge acquisition, diagnostic accuracy, clinical reasoning, procedural skills, learner engagement, and perceptions of AI-assisted learning. Results The included literature reflects an expansion from machine learning, deep learning, and computer vision systems primarily evaluated for diagnostic support toward generative AI platforms, including large language models and retrieval-augmented generation systems. Across the included studies, AI applications were frequently associated with favorable diagnostic and examination performance and, in selected educational contexts, with supportive findings related to clinical reasoning, technical competency, feedback, and self-directed learning. However, the evidence was predominantly based on technical performance assessments and observational or cross-sectional designs. Discussion AI is increasingly being explored as a potential complementary educational resource, with applications including interactive tutoring, adaptive learning, and support for clinical reasoning. Nevertheless, heterogeneous methodologies and limited longitudinal evidence indicate the need for standardized educational evaluation and responsible curricular integration. Conclusion AI shows potential as a complementary resource in dental education. Its integration should remain pedagogically guided and ethically supervised while future research establishes its educational effectiveness through standardized and longitudinal evaluation.

title: Artificial intelligence in pediatric endoscopy for hereditary polyposis syndromes: promises and challenges.
abstract: Children with hereditary polyposis syndromes require long-term endoscopic surveillance to reduce risks of gastrointestinal complications: malignancy, bleeding, and obstruction, among others. However, surveillance remains challenging because of variable lesion distribution, subtle morphology, interobserver variability, and the burden of repeated procedures throughout the patient's lifetime. Artificial intelligence has transformed adult endoscopy, but its application in pediatric polyposis is less defined. This review summarizes current evidence and explores potential applications for children with hereditary polyposis syndromes. In adult colonoscopy, meta-analyses and randomized trials demonstrate that artificial intelligence improves adenoma detection rates (ADR) and reduces missed lesions, though evidence linking these benefits to meaningful reductions in colorectal cancer incidence remains insufficient. In capsule endoscopy, artificial intelligence demonstrates high sensitivity for lesion detection while substantially reducing review time. Pediatric data remain limited, with no studies specific to hereditary polyposis syndromes, but early studies support feasibility. Potential applications include automated polyp detection, localization, burden quantification, and longitudinal comparisons across surveillance examinations. Artificial intelligence has significant potential to improve polyp detection, diagnostic consistency, accuracy, efficiency, and longitudinal disease monitoring in pediatric hereditary polyposis syndromes. Development of pediatric-specific datasets and prospective, multicenter, and outcome-driven validation studies will be essential before widespread clinical implementation.
authors: Kennedy Tham; Nicholas Norris; Srisindu Vellanki; Isabel Rojas; Claudia Phen

title: Artificial intelligence-driven imaging in sickle cell retinopathy: Advancing early detection, risk stratification, and precision ophthalmology
abstract: Sickle cell disease (SCD) is a disorder of genetically inherited red blood cells (RBCs), wherein it is manifested clinically as sickling of RBCs, due to polymerization of hemoglobin S. SCD patients frequently face RBCs clumping, blocking of blood vessels and capillaries along with persistent hemolysis.Sickle cell retinopathy (SCR), is a SCD associated disorder in the peripheral retina, responsible for several features like vasoocclusion, ischemia, vitreous hemorrhage and neovascularization within the retina and adjoining regions.While these are manageable features, some severe cases report retinal detachment and ultimately vision impairment in patients.As early signs of SCR are not usually manifested visually, its early diagnosis becomes the limiting factor for devising effective management strategies in patients.Artificial intelligence (AI) assisted deep learning models have very recently being utilized and provides a promising alternative in assisting early diagnosis, staging, and monitoring disease progression.Traditional retinal imaging methods like fundus photography, fluorescein angiography, optical coherence tomography and optical coherence tomography angiography scans have always assisted ophthalmologists to make clinical decisions for patients.Recently, these methods were being used to train AI models for easy and efficient analysis of such scans.As a growing field, works in this area have transitioned our understanding of image analyses and promises a fast, objective and efficient interpretation.This review discusses; how traditional methods captures structural damages to peripheral retina and summarizes recent research work done in this field to integrate AI driven models based on deep learning and machine learning.We summarize here AI based strategies for SCR screening and diagnosis, while underlining their clinical applicability, utilities and future translational promises towards ascertaining personalized ophthalmology.
authors: Tarun Sahu; Deepankar Mondal; Yashwant Kumar Ratre; Henu Kumar Verma

title: Artificial intelligence-driven precision management of Helicobacter pylori: an integrated framework from endoscopy and multi-omics to vaccine design and digital care
abstract: Helicobacter pylori ( H. pylori ) infection, affecting half of the world’s population, is the principal cause of peptic ulcer disease and gastric cancer, yet its clinical management is increasingly undermined by the rapidly escalating global burden of antibiotic resistance, the suboptimal accuracy of conventional diagnostic methods, and the declining efficacy of empirical therapeutic regimens. Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly reshaping this landscape, but existing research remains fragmented across single modalities. We propose a conceptual five-module framework that integrates AI approaches across the H. pylori care continuum: (1) global disease burden and the evolutionary dynamics of H. pylori drug resistance; (2) the application of multimodal AI, from convolutional neural networks to vision-language foundation models, for endoscopic early screening, pathological identification, and functional assessment; (3) the harnessing of machine learning (ML) on genomic and electronic health record data to decipher resistance mechanisms and generate personalized eradication regimens; (4) AI-driven vaccine target discovery and generative design, spanning reverse vaccinology to de novo immunogen creation; and (5) a digital closed-loop patient management platform that leverages new media and reinforcement learning to enhance adherence and eradication rates. We further delineate the core challenges of data bias, cross-scenario generalization, and the critical absence of prospective randomized evidence, and propose a future direction anchored in multimodal foundation models, federated learning, and continuous AI quality improvement. Rather than an established clinical pathway, this framework is proposed as a conceptual blueprint that, once prospectively validated, could upgrade AI-enabled H. pylori care from isolated image recognition toward an end-to-end “perception–reasoning–intervention” system, offering a blueprint for precision prevention and control.
authors: Minglin Zhang; Nuonan Lv; Yanghui Cao; Lingqiao Lou; Ting Cai; Jiaxing Zhu; Yingting Xu; Xuelin Zhao; Zhiyuan Ma; Xuemei Liu

title: Assessment architecture, scoring, and evidence of quality in objective structured clinical examinations in dental education: a scoping review
abstract: This scoping review mapped the design, scoring, implementation, and quality assurance of objective structured clinical examinations (OSCEs) in dental education. The review followed Joanna Briggs Institute guidance and the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews. Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, PubMed/MEDLINE, ERIC, Embase, and LILACS/BVS were searched through July 25, 2026. Of the 940 records identified, 129 full-text reports were assessed and 63 studies were included. The most frequently reported evidence concerned station design, blueprinting, scoring, examiner calibration, reliability, and psychometric performance. Fewer studies examined standard setting, fairness and potential construct-irrelevant variance, classification accuracy, economic feasibility, or the consequences of high-stakes decisions. Virtual and electronic OSCEs supported assessment continuity and structured evaluation of diagnostic reasoning, interpretation, communication, and decision-making; however, they should not be assumed to replace direct observation when technical or psychomotor performance is the main target. The dental OSCE literature now encompasses both isolated station-based examinations and broader assessment systems. Future research should establish which combinations of assessment design, scoring, examiner preparation, psychometric evaluation, fairness analysis, and decision rules provide defensible evidence for specific educational purposes.

title: Assessment of uncertainty estimation and distillation for reliable 3D dental mesh segmentation in orthodontics
abstract: Abstract The integration of deep learning into computer-aided orthodontic treatment planning has enabled automated tasks such as tooth segmentation from 3D dental models. However, the reliability of these systems remains a concern due to their black-box nature and tendency toward overconfident predictions. In this work, we present a comprehensive evaluation of uncertainty estimation methods for tooth segmentation on 3D intraoral scans. We investigate several state-of-the-art neural network architectures combined with uncertainty estimation techniques including predictive entropy, Monte Carlo dropout, test-time augmentation, deep ensembles, and evidential deep learning. Evaluation on the Teeth3DS benchmark, supplemented with synthetically incomplete scans and a custom out-of-distribution dataset, shows that sampling-based approaches, particularly deep ensembles, provide the most reliable uncertainty estimates. In contrast, entropy-based methods and evidential deep learning often produce overconfident predictions and fail to identify major segmentation errors. We further demonstrate that uncertainty estimation can detect out-of-distribution samples such as scans with artifacts or missing regions. Although deep ensembles provide the most reliable uncertainty estimates, their computational cost limits practical deployment. We therefore investigate uncertainty distillation and show that a single student model can achieve ensemble-like uncertainty quality with only one forward pass.
authors: Lucas Krenmayr; Reinhold von Schwerin; Daniel Schaudt

title: Association between salivary alkaline phosphatase and inflammatory periodontal diseases among adolescents in the European North of Russia
abstract: The high prevalence of periodontal inflammatory diseases (PID) among adolescents underscores the need to develop simple, non-invasive methods for their timely detection. Oral fluid is considered a promising diagnostic substrate, enabling the assessment of various biomarkers, particularly alkaline phosphatase (ALP), which is involved in inflammatory and reparative processes in periodontal tissues. However, there is a paucity of studies analyzing the diagnostic significance of this enzyme. Objective. To investigate the association between salivary ALP levels and clinical signs of PID in individuals aged 15–17 years permanently residing in the European North of Russia. In a cross-sectional study, participants (n = 439) residing in the Nenets Autonomous Okrug (n = 171), the Komi Republic (n = 146), and Murmansk Oblast (n = 121) underwent a dental examination with recording of periodontal parameters (bleeding, dental deposits, presence of periodontitis) and provided mixed saliva samples for subsequent determination of ALP activity. Data analysis was performed using Poisson regression models; unadjusted and adjusted (for sex, age, and place of residence) relative risks were calculated, and linear trends were assessed across quartiles of ALP distribution. Results: а direct statistically significant association was observed between enzyme concentration and the number of sextants exhibiting bleeding in the multivariable regression model, p for trend = 0.037. No statistically significant association was found between ALP levels and the likelihood of detecting periodontitis (p for trend = 0.404) or dental calculus (p = 0.521). Our results suggest that elevated ALP levels in the oral fluid of adolescents are associated with a greater prevalence of gingival bleeding. This suggests that this parameter may serve as a potential indicator of the severity and extent of generalized inflammation in periodontal tissues, although it is not specific for a diagnosis of periodontitis. Further prospective studies are required to definitively establish the clinical and diagnostic utility of ALP and to justify its application in routine clinical practice.

title: Augmenting colonoscopy with artificial intelligence and robotic assistance: a human-factors scoping review toward a task-based shared autonomy paradigm
abstract: Colonoscopy is central to colorectal cancer prevention but remains a high-demand psychomotor and cognitive procedure, characterized by operator dependency, variable performance, and substantial physical and mental workload. Increasing evidence links procedural quality and safety to clinician-related factors, including musculoskeletal strain, fatigue, and non-technical skills. Concurrently, artificial intelligence (AI) and robotic technologies are emerging as potential tools to address these limitations. We conducted a scoping review with narrative synthesis of literature on human factors, ergonomics, AI, robotic technologies, and shared autonomy in colonoscopy and surgical robotics. Evidence synthesis: Colonoscopy performance remains limited by non-negligible miss rates and variability driven by both technical and human factors. Ergonomic constraints and cognitive workload contribute significantly to operator strain and may affect vigilance and decision-making. AI systems-including computer-aided detection (CADe), diagnosis (CADx), and quality monitoring-have demonstrated improvements in detection metrics and procedural standardisation, although concerns regarding cognitive offloading and potential deskilling persist. In parallel, emerging robotic and soft-robotic platforms aim to enhance navigation, improve procedural ergonomics, and reduce operator musculoskeletal strain, although clinical evidence remains limited. These technologies converge within a task-based shared-autonomy paradigm integrating physical, perceptual, and cognitive augmentation, with different procedural tasks operating at different levels of human-system control. A task-based shared-autonomy framework may provide a coherent model for integrating AI and robotics into colonoscopy while preserving human supervision and clinical judgement. Future developments should prioritise human-centred design, workflow integration, and multidimensional evaluation strategies to ensure safe and effective clinical implementation.

title: Automated Dental Calculus Mapping and Burden Estimation Using Deep Learning
abstract: Abstract Background Dental calculus is a primary etiological factor in periodontal disease, disproportionately affecting underserved populations with limited access to professional dental care. Automated photographic oral disease screening tools may help bridge this access gap by enabling early identification of calculus burden in community, school-based, and remote settings. Methods A ResNet-50 encoder integrated within a U-Net segmentation architecture was trained on intraoral photographic images sourced from a public dataset. The dataset was partitioned into training (1,361 images; 66.5%), validation (584 images; 28.5%), and an independent held-out test set (103 images; 5.0%), with the test set withheld from all model development decisions. Manual polygon segmentation masks were created using CVAT. A pixel-area calculation technique was developed to estimate the percentage of tooth surface covered by calculus. Architecture comparisons were conducted against a standard U-Net (no pretraining), VGG16/U-Net, and EfficientNet-B4/U-Net under identical training conditions. Results On the held-out test set, the model achieved a Dice coefficient of 0.731 (95% CI: 0.706–0.756), IoU of 0.698 (95% CI: 0.671–0.724), recall of 0.714, and specificity of 0.971. The pixel-level ROC-AUC was 0.931 (95% CI: 0.918–0.944) however, this value is inflated by background pixel dominance and should be interpreted alongside Dice and IoU as primary segmentation metrics. The proposed architecture outperformed all three comparators. Validation-set metrics (Dice 0.743, IoU 0.712) were modestly higher than test-set values, as expected given reduced optimization bias on unseen data. Conclusions This proof-of-concept study demonstrates that deep learning can support automated dental calculus screening from photographic images. Findings are preliminary and subject to important limitations including non-clinician annotation and a single public dataset source. With further clinical validation, such tools may contribute to scalable oral health monitoring in tele-dentistry workflows, school dental programs, and community health initiatives.
authors: Elikem Des-Amekudi; Akoto Kwame; Michael McLennon; Cierra Mayo; Clayton Clark Clayton Clark; AKM Islam

title: Automatic Trajectory Planning from Preoperative MRI images Using the AI-Optimized RRT* Algorithm for Robotic Breast Ultrasound
abstract: Ultrasound imaging is the most widely used technique for detecting and diagnosing breast cancer, as it provides real-time images in a non-invasive and inexpensive manner. However, performing ultrasound examinations requires experienced and well-trained operators either for probe manipulation during acquisition or during image interpretation, which makes this technique dependent. This dependency requires the employment of sonographers with extensive training and experience, which may limit access to this technique in remote areas and also expose experts to serious health issues due to repetitive movements. To overcome these difficulties, robotic ultrasound systems have emerged in recent years to enable conventional ultrasound examinations to be performed in an automated and standardized way. Our study contributes to this field through an integrated approach to automated planning of robotic breast ultrasound trajectories. This approach is based on the application of a developed version of the rapidly-exploring random tree (RRT) trajectory planning algorithm to pre-operational threedimensional (3D) magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) images. We performed simulations with the three versions of the algorithm RRT, RRT* and RRT* with 30% reinforcement learning (RL) on two different patients. The results obtained demonstrate the potential of the RRT algorithm with 30% RL to obtain optimized trajectories with high fluidity and a short path while ensuring total and homogeneous coverage adapted to different complex breast morphologies.

title: Automation dependence in AI-assisted colonoscopy: impact of system reliability and surgeon experience on navigation performance.
abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly introduced into endoscopic navigation, understanding how operators use and respond to AI suggestions is essential for designing safe and effective human-AI collaboration. This study investigated the effects of AI reliability and operator experience on task performance and cognitive responses in a simulated colonoscopy navigation task. A virtual simulation paradigm was used, in which 27 interns and experienced doctors completed a navigation direction judgment task under three AI reliability conditions (high, medium, and low) and a no AI condition. Navigation accuracy, task completion time, subjective trust, cognitive load, and compliance with incorrect AI prompts were recorded. The results showed that AI reliability significantly affected navigation performance and subjective trust. High reliability AI improved task accuracy and efficiency, particularly among less experienced operators. However, when AI reliability decreased, participants' performance declined, and interns showed higher compliance with incorrect AI prompts than experienced doctors. Notably, this behavior occurred even when subjective trust decreased, suggesting a potential mismatch between trust evaluation and AI following behavior. This could be interpreted cautiously, as higher compliance among interns may reflect both rational reliance under high task difficulty and the risk of inappropriate reliance when AI reliability is insufficient. These findings indicate that AI-assisted endoscopic systems should not only improve navigation performance but also support appropriate reliance calibration. Differentiated support strategies may be needed for operators with different levels of experience, especially in scenarios involving training or novice operators.

title: Autonomous Reconfigurable Modular Conductive Hydrogels for Adaptive and Degradable Bioelectronic Interfaces
abstract: ABSTRACT Bioelectronic interfaces are increasingly used in medical devices for tissue stimulation and sensing. Transient bioelectronics seek the same functionality in temporary systems, yet most available materials are nondegradable, stiff, and require surgery or external removal. Achieving tissue‐like softness, smooth injectability, stable mixed conductivity, and reliable short‐term bioresorption within a single biocompatible matrix remains challenging. Here, we decouple injectability from bulk conductive performance using a modular reconfiguration strategy. High‐filler‐content hydrogels are converted into lyophilized modules that can be resuspended, injected through a standard syringe, and then autonomously reassemble in situ into a cohesive conductive network, recovering 90% of conductivity after freeze–drying, fragmentation, and reconfiguration. The platform uses a fully degradable tannic‐acid‐crosslinked poly(vinyl alcohol) matrix with molybdenum and molybdenum trioxide nanoparticles as co‐functional fillers. Mixed ionic/electronic conduction arises from redox‐active tannic acid–Mo(VI) complexes (ionic transport) and semi‐percolated Mo nanoparticles (electron hopping). The optimized formulation matches extracellular‐matrix mechanics (Young's modulus 0.03 MPa; failure strain 998%) and fully degrades within 120 h under simulated physiological conditions. In a human skin explant wound model, conformal integration enables charge transfer, reaching 0.02 A at across a 1 cm defect.
authors: Matthew K. Burgess; Zofia B. Wolny; Zekun Liu; Karolina Cysewska; Malavika Nair

title: Autonomy, Operating Domains, and Validation in Robotic Ultrasound: Transferable Lessons and Structural Limits from Autonomous Vehicle Development
abstract: Diagnostic ultrasound is among the most portable and least expensive of the major imaging modalities, yet its reach is constrained by the availability and physical capacity of skilled operators: between 85 and 90 percent of sonographers report work-related musculoskeletal pain, and approximately one in five sustains a career-ending injury [1, 2, 3]. Robotic ultrasound systems have advanced substantially in response and learned acquisition policies now approach expert-level performance on individual anatomical targets [4, 5]. Progress in the field is, however, characterized using autonomy taxonomies inherited from surgical robotics [6, 7, 8]. These are frameworks that describe how much of a task a machine performs while remaining largely silent on the population in which that performance was demonstrated. Across the studies examined in this review, performance metrics are routinely reported, whereas explicit specification of operating conditions is considerably less common.
