title: Avoiding the Automation Trap: Designing Human-Centred AI Workflows for Dental Manufacturing
abstract: This industrial case study explores integrating machine learning into high-volume dental manufacturing. Such technologies profoundly influence existing technician workflows and laboratory operations. To address this, a legacy software audit using a localised Cognitive Dimensions of Notation (CDN) framework identified high Repetitive Viscosity, Hidden Task Status, and Workflow Rigidity. This diagnostic phase was driven by structured workshops with the digital technicians. These failings hindered quality control and forced technicians into redundant tasks. To resolve these issues, the project co-designed a human-in-the-loop application that replaced modal menus with a unified 3D editor layout, eliminated hidden states with a visual column-based progress queue, and introduced state serialisation to support flexible task management. Qualitative evaluation confirmed that these design choices effectively resolved the identified cognitive frictions by reducing interaction costs and preventing repetitive editing tasks. While improvements to backend algorithms halved baseline processing time, successful digital transformation relies equally on workflow redesign and end-user engagement. Ultimately, this method of adapting, localising, and running workshops provides a technique that can be deployed across a wide range of industrial settings when faced with the challenge of the AI-assisted automation trap. This is of particular importance in industrial sectors where machine learning-based solutions risk threatening existing work practices and disrupting established processes.
authors: Salman Ahmed; Chris Roast; Ajmal Gharib

title: BOPPPS Instructional Framework Embedding Case‐ and Problem‐ Based Strategies in Oral Pathology Education: A Teaching Reform Study
abstract: OBJECTIVE: Oral pathology education requires students to master both foundational theoretical knowledge and clinical diagnostic reasoning, yet conventional lecture-based instruction provides limited opportunities for structured participatory learning that actively engages both dimensions. This study evaluated the pedagogical effectiveness of the BOPPPS instructional framework-a six phase teaching model comprising bridge-in, objective, pre-assessment, participatory learning, post-assessment, and summary-within an oral pathology curriculum. Within this framework, case-based learning (CBL) and problem-based learning (PBL) were integrated as complementary and overlapping pedagogical strategies and incorporated into phases of the BOPPPS framework, forming a unified, discipline-adapted teaching approach. METHODS: A total of 206 undergraduate oral medicine students were randomly assigned to the reform group (the BOPPPS instructional framework integrating case- and problem-based strategies) or a traditional lecture-based control group. Outcomes and learning experience were assessed through theoretical examination scores, experimental diagnostic image-recognition performance, and student satisfaction questionnaire respectively. RESULTS: Compared with the control group, students in the reform group achieved significantly higher average scores on the oral pathology theoretical examination (adjusted p < 0.001). In the pathology experimental course, the reform group also demonstrated improved overall performance, particularly on items assessing clinical reasoning skills (adjusted p < 0.05). Students also reported high satisfaction with the instructional experience, with the mean overall learning outcome self-assessment score reaching 4.5 out of 5. CONCLUSIONS: The BOPPPS instructional framework with embedded case- and problem-based strategies was associated with improved theoretical examination performance and diagnostic image interpretation in oral pathology. Students also reported high satisfaction with the learning experience.
authors: Jiaxin Yang; Yanan Sun; Li Wang; Shaodong Yang; Jiali Zhang

title: Beyond Discrete Tokens: Preserving Numerical Continuity in Medical Vision-Language Models
abstract: Objective: To develop a unified vision-language model for prompt-conditioned quantitative ultrasound measurement that addresses the mismatch between continuous measurement targets and discrete token-based numerical prediction. Methods: This article presents HAD-VLM, a hybrid autoregressive-diffusion framework that combines autoregressive text generation with continuous measurement prediction within a shared backbone. Visual prompt tuning adapts the vision encoder to ultrasound images. A diffusion process predicts a five-component representation comprising caliper endpoint coordinates and measurement length. A post-processing strategy combining the proposed coordinate-length consistency mechanism with ensemble prediction is introduced to refine measurement estimates. We evaluate four echocardiographic measurement tasks on EchoNet-LVH, with additional assessments of medical question answering and X-ray vertebral measurement. Results: HAD-VLM achieves mean absolute errors of 1.36, 2.77, 3.05, and 1.16 mm for IVSd, LVIDd, LVIDs, and LVPWd, respectively, reducing errors by 21.4-37.6\% relative to the Vicuna-based autoregressive baseline. It also outperforms fine-tuned Qwen3-VL and direct MLP regression across all four tasks. Medical question answering performance is preserved on the evaluated dataset. For X-ray vertebral measurement, HAD-VLM reduces mean absolute error from 11.4 to 6.7 pixels. Conclusion: Integrating autoregressive language generation with diffusion-based continuous prediction improves quantitative medical image measurement while retaining prompt-conditioned task flexibility. Significance: HAD-VLM provides a unified approach to combining language interaction with anatomically grounded numerical prediction for quantitative medical image analysis.
authors: Dianye Huang; Jiamei Guo; Yue Zhou; Mingde Li; Yi Xiong; Wei Wang; Nassir Navab; Zhongliang Jiang

title: Bibliometric Data and Validation-Evidence Mapping of Robotic Ultrasound-Guided Biopsy, Ablation, and Access (2000–2025)
abstract: This repository provides supporting data and reproducibility materials for a bibliometric analysis and publication-level validation-evidence map of robotic ultrasound-guided biopsy, ablation, and access. The analysis integrates PubMed and Web of Science Core Collection records, comprising 857 unique bibliographic records after deduplication. The focused Master corpus includes 197 publications, of which 184 were classified as direct-validation reports. The deposited materials include publication-level classification matrices, application categories, V0–V3 validation settings, ablation technology pathways, supplementary data tables, and available plotting scripts and TXT data matrices. Validation settings describe the highest reported experimental or human evaluation within each publication. They should not be interpreted as clinical maturity, independent clinical trials, or unique patient cohorts. The deposited data and scripts are provided to support transparency and reproducibility. Redistribution of proprietary Web of Science records and copyrighted full-text articles is excluded.

title: Bibliometric Mapping of Transforaminal Research in Clinical Neurology: Publication Trends, Intellectual Structure, and Global Collaboration Networks
abstract: Objective: This study aimed to reveal the bibliometric profile, conceptual structure, and scientific collaboration patterns of articles containing the term “transforaminal” in their titles in the Web of Science (WoS) Clinical Neurology category. Methods: The title field was searched for “transforaminal” in WoS (data retrieved on 23 September 2026); 1,430 records restricted to the Clinical Neurology category and Article document type were analyzed. Publication distributions by year and journal and the most cited studies were assessed through performance analysis; keyword co-occurrence and institutional and country-level co-authorship analyses were performed using VOSviewer. Results: Publication output increased particularly after 2013 and peaked at 129 publications in 2025. World Neurosurgery was the most productive journal, with 222 publications (15.524%). Most of the highly cited publications concerned transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion (TLIF). In the keyword network, “transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion” was the most central concept, with 476 occurrences and a total link strength of 1,226. The United States stood out at the country level with 594 publications, 18,910 citations, and a total link strength of 122; China and South Korea were also major centers of output. Conclusion: Although transforaminal research has historically centered on TLIF, minimally invasive/endoscopic surgery, decompression, radiculopathy, and interventional pain management are prominent themes, with selected endoscopic keywords more frequently represented in recent publications. The findings show that publication productivity, citation impact, and international collaboration represent distinct bibliometric dimensions.

title: Biodigital Transformation in Dentistry: From Diagnosis and Biological Preservation to Multidisciplinary Rehabilitation
abstract: Advances in digital technologies have expanded diagnostic and treatment possibilities in dentistry while making the preservation of biological tissues and collaboration among specialties increasingly important. This book, *Biodigital Transformation in Dentistry: From Diagnosis and Biological Preservation to Multidisciplinary Rehabilitation*, was prepared to address these developments from an integrated perspective. It follows a scientific progression from biodigital diagnosis and clinical decision-making to preventive care in pediatric dentistry; from the preservation of the pulp and natural dentition to periodontal and orthodontic treatment; and from digital prosthetic planning to implant-supported rehabilitation. Written by contributors from different dental specialties, the chapters examine both the clinical applications and the limitations of current technologies. We hope this book will serve as a valuable resource for dental students, residents, academics, and clinicians, and we thank all the authors for their knowledge, time, and contributions.

title: Bioinspired soft enteroscopic robot for intestinal locomotion, steering, and intervention
abstract: Diagnosing and treating small intestinal disorders such as bleeding, inflammatory bowel disease, and tumors present challenges because of limited access to this anatomical compartment. We present BIOSENTER, a bioinspired soft enteroscopic robot for deep procedures in the small intestine that addresses locomotion, steering, and intervention constraints of existing soft robotic systems. BIOSENTER features a hollow cylinder architecture comprising a linearly deformable soft pneumatic actuator as the body, two radially expandable soft pneumatic actuators wrapped with kirigami sleeves as the head and tail, a central hollow channel for accessory endoscopic tools, and a control box for navigation. Inspired by snake locomotion, the robotic body incorporates a fiber-reinforced actuator with four embedded inflatable chambers, enabling steering and axial expansion. The dynamic kirigami sleeves generate an anchoring force of ∼1.5 newtons on intestinal mucosa while requiring substantially less radial expansion than the corresponding nonkirigami configuration. A reinforced central channel supports tool passage for diagnostic and therapeutic interventions. The control box enables locomotion and steering at autonomous speeds of ∼100 millimeters per minute in vitro and ∼43 millimeters per minute in tissue-covered tubing. BIOSENTER successfully navigated the collapsed, tortuous small intestine for 2 meters in 11 minutes, with gentle forward pushing forces of 2.2 to 6.4 newtons in pig studies. In vivo pig studies demonstrated technical feasibility of tissue biopsy, localized fluid delivery as a model for future drug administration, and real-time visualization of the deep intestine, without macroscopic overdistention or visible tissue damage under the tested conditions.
authors: Binbin Ying; Ahmad Mujtaba Jebran; Sahab Babaee; Karen Jiang; Brenda D. Fernandez Martinez; Haniyah Shareef; Mohammed Talha Faiz; Andrew Pettinari; Kailyn Schmidt; Niora J. Fabian; Alison M. Hayward; Giovanni Traverso

title: Bioresorbable batteries for transient ingestible bioelectronics
abstract: Abstract Ingestible and implantable electronic devices are transforming personalized healthcare by enabling real-time sensing, targeted therapy and diagnostic capabilities. However, powering these systems remains a major challenge owing to biocompatibility concerns and the environmental impact of conventional batteries. Here we present a bioresorbable magnesium–molybdenum trioxide (Mg–MoO 3 ) paper battery that delivers high electrochemical performance under physiological conditions and safely degrades over time. The battery provides a peak open-circuit voltage of 1.84 V and supports capsule-scale ingestible electronic systems incorporating bioresorbable power sources for two key gastrointestinal applications: battery-assisted radio-frequency identification tags for wireless medication tracking and capsule systems for electroceutical therapy. In vivo studies in swine models have demonstrated robust operation within the gastrointestinal tract and compatibility with clinically relevant use cases. This study establishes a foundation for safe, high-performance and bioresorbable power sources in biomedical electronics, enabling retrieval-free, eco-friendly devices that eliminate electronic waste in the gastrointestinal environment.

title: Boundary-complexity-guided adaptive weighting for single-image unsupervised superpixel segmentation
abstract: Abstract Superpixel segmentation provides an important mid-level representation for computer vision, but accurate boundary adherence remains difficult in images with weak contours, cluttered backgrounds, and complex textures. We propose a boundary-complexity-guided adaptive weighting framework for single-image unsupervised superpixel segmentation, termed AW-Super. The proposed Enhanced Boundary Feature Extraction Module (EBFEM) fuses semantic edge cues with gradient-based local structural information to produce a continuous complexity map, which is then used to reweight the optimization objective spatially. As a result, the method imposes stronger boundary-sensitive constraints in structurally complex regions while encouraging shape regularity in relatively homogeneous areas. We further introduce an adaptive stopping criterion into the Deep Image Prior optimization process, replacing a fixed iteration schedule with an image-dependent termination rule. Experiments on BSDS500 and SBD under matched superpixel budgets ( $$N=50$$ –500) demonstrate high boundary recall together with competitive overall segmentation performance, without requiring dataset-level training or ground-truth superpixel annotations. An additional cross-domain evaluation on DRIVE retinal images against SLIC and SEEDS further supports the applicability of AW-Super beyond natural-image benchmarks.
authors: Nannan Wang; Qianyi Zhang; Yongxia Zhang; Wei Wei

title: Bronchoscope Tip Localization With Learned Airway Constraints and an Open Source Simulator
abstract: Accurate bronchoscope localization is challenging because airway images contain limited texture and similar views across branches. We present BronchoLoc, a learning‐based framework that combines monocular video with a preoperative CT centerline graph to estimate the 3D bronchoscope tip position. Local visual tracking and global sequence context constrain predictions to the airway anatomy. The accompanying open‐source BronchoSim simulator generates synchronized images, depth, and trajectories (Traj) for training and evaluation. Averaged across Traj, localization RMSE was 5.65 mm in simulation with 82.8% branch selection accuracy and 8.72 mm in the physical phantom. Together, BronchoLoc and BronchoSim provide a framework for developing and evaluating image‐based airway localization.
authors: Emanuele Nicotra; James Davies; Bibhu Sharma; Adrienne Ji; Kefan Zhu; Phuoc Thien Phan; Nigel Hamilton Lovell; Thanh Nho Do

title: Budget-Constrained Fault-Tolerant Mutual Visibility for Autonomous Robots under the Mobility Fault Model
abstract: We investigate the mutual visibility problem for a swarm of $n\ge3$ autonomous mobile robots under the budget-constrained mobility fault model. The robots are opaque, so if three robots are collinear, the middle robot obstructs the visibility between the other two. Each robot is assigned a finite movement budget, reflecting its limited energy, that bounds the total distance it may traverse during the execution. Moreover, an arbitrary number of robots may become permanently immobile due to mobility faults. The objective is to design a distributed algorithm that enables the non-faulty robots to coordinate their movements so that, within a finite time, every non-faulty robot attains unobstructed visibility of all robots in the system, including the faulty ones, while respecting the prescribed movement budget. We consider luminous robots operating under the $\mathsf{SSYNC}$ model with non-rigid movements, without any agreement on their local coordinate systems, and equipped only with a {\it common fixed reference point}. We present a deterministic distributed algorithm that solves the problem despite an arbitrary number of mobility faults. The algorithm guarantees mutual visibility for the non-faulty robots, respects the movement budget of every robot, provides collision-free movements for the robots, and uses only 12 light colors.
authors: Prakhar Shukla; Animesh Maiti; Shivam Kumar; Subhash Bhagat

title: CAD/CAM Technologies, Three-Dimensional Printing, and Contemporary Dental Materials
abstract: CAD/CAM technologies have transformed the production of fixed prosthodontic restorations from a craft based on manual skill into a standardized and measurable digital process. This chapter addresses, for dental students in their clinical years and for early-career clinicians, the fundamental principles of CAD/CAM systems, digital and artificial intelligence-assisted restoration design, milling and three-dimensional printing technologies, contemporary restorative materials, the factors influencing material selection, accuracy and quality control in digital manufacturing, and the biocompatible and smart materials of the future, in the light of the current and verified literature. The digital workflow comprises three interdependent links—data acquisition, design, and manufacturing—and the quality of the final restoration is limited by the weakest link in the chain. Although milling remains the gold standard for definitive restorations, additive manufacturing has become established for interim restorations, models, and surgical guides, and it is a rapidly maturing alternative for definitive restorations. On the material side, the rise of monolithic zirconia, the diversification of lithium silicate glass-ceramics, and the establishment of resin-matrix ceramics in minimally invasive applications offer the clinician a broad range of options with varying levels of evidence. Current systematic-review and meta-analytic evidence shows that AI-assisted design shortens design time and improves reproducibility, but that human oversight remains indispensable. Clinical success depends on manufacturing the right material with validated parameters for the right indication and applying it with an appropriate adhesive or conventional cementation protocol. Accuracy should be defined by its trueness and precision components, marginal fit should be evaluated against clinical acceptability thresholds, and quality control should be maintained at every link of the digital chain. The graded, bioactive, self-healing, and stimuli-responsive materials of the future, together with additively manufactured ceramics, signal a transition from passive to smart materials in restorative dentistry.
authors: Muhammed Mustafa Akar; Alptuğ Kendirci

title: CROPS: Cosserat-Rod-Based Co-Design of Soft Slender Programmable Material Systems for Biomedical Applications
abstract: Programmable slender structures that deform in response to external stimuli represent a class of emerging material systems, with applications in soft robotics, minimally invasive surgery, wearable electronics, and deployable structures. In biomedical applications, the on-demand design of slender structures, encompassing both their material layout and actuation, is instrumental in leveraging their large deformation and multiphysics actuation for meeting patient-specific design requirements. However, owing to geometric and material nonlinearities, their structure-actuation-response relationship is highly non-intuitive and entails resource-intensive computation. This renders trial-and-error and conventional design approaches largely intractable for addressing patient-specific needs. To this end, we present a Cosserat-rod-based design optimization framework for the autonomous design of programmable slender structures. Capitalizing on the Cosserat rod representation, the end-to-end differentiable framework is demonstrated on two case studies: (i) design of swellable stents that morph to the shape of carotid vessels; (ii) co-design of the remnant magnetization and the applied field of magnetically-active catheters to reduce the force exerted on the patient-specific vessel wall during insertion. As the actuation types, the swelling of gel-elastomer composites and the magnetic actuation of hard-magnetic composites are considered. Additionally, the contact of the rod with itself and its surroundings is accounted for. The proposed framework presents an autonomous design platform for material-structure-actuation co-design of soft slender material systems that support large deformation and multiphysics actuation, with contact addressed.
authors: Aaditya Chandrasekhar; Lee, Dex Doksoo; Kwon, Hyunwoo; Li, Shicheng; Chen, Wei

title: Can Annotation‐Free Deep Learning Detect Periapical Bone Rarefactions on Panoramic Radiographs? A Paired Diagnostic Validation Study
abstract: ABSTRACT This study aimed to compare an annotation‐free deep learning (DL) model with human evaluators for detecting periapical bone rarefactions (PBRs) on panoramic radiographs (PRs) and to assess the clinical acceptability of AI‐supported dental imaging. A mixed‐methods diagnostic validation was conducted using 238 PRs, equally distributed between images with ( n = 119) and without ( n = 119) PBRs. Model performance was compared with that of four calibrated dentists: two oral and maxillofacial radiologists and two endodontists. The reference standard was based on internationally accepted radiographic criteria applied by calibrated researchers under expert supervision, with final classifications verified by the principal investigator. Diagnostic performance was assessed using standard diagnostic metrics, chance‐corrected agreement statistics and receiver operating characteristic analysis, while clinical acceptability was explored through questionnaires and thematically analysed semi‐structured interviews. At the sensitivity‐oriented decision threshold of 0.27, the DL model achieved a sensitivity of 0.924, a specificity of 0.109, an accuracy of 0.517, a precision of 0.509 and an F 1‐score of 0.657. Threshold‐independent binary discrimination was moderate (ROC‐AUC = 0.726). Human evaluators showed more balanced profiles, with accuracy ranging from 0.655 to 0.752 and F 1‐scores from 0.654 to 0.779. Professional perception was generally favourable, although responses varied among evaluators. The annotation‐free DL model showed high sensitivity and moderate discrimination for PBR detection. Although low specificity limits autonomous use, the findings support annotation‐free learning as a potentially scalable strategy, warranting further training with larger and more heterogeneous datasets.

title: Can We Really See the World in Three Dimensions? An Exploratory Study with Finger Alignment Task and Ponzo Illusion
abstract: Abstract Stereopsis is the perception of depth when two 2-dimensional (2D) images of an object from slightly different angles align with corresponding retinal positions in both eyes. However, when we consider the blind spot (BS), a new set of challenges arises. In binocular vision, one eye’s higher visual areas compensate for the other’s non-receptive region. However, our brain only receives information from one image patch in the BS region, and another visual patch does not contribute to constructing a comprehensive 3-dimensional (3D) representation of the scene. This suggests that the brain adeptly manages this dimensional transition. We aimed to determine the extent to which we perceive 3D across our entire field of view (FoV). We employed the Ponzo illusion, a stimulus relying on visual depth cues (pictorial depth cues), and an eye-tracking technique to assess participants’ accurate fixation and eye movement patterns. The participants attempted to align their index fingers before a chart paper to create a Horopter-like setup, supporting the hypothesis about our capacity for stereoscopic perception. The results of our exploratory pilot study with two specific tasks revealed that our ability to perceive depth diminishes beyond approximately 8° of retinal eccentricity (in the horizontal meridian) in both halves of the visual field centered around the fovea. This limitation is not apparent in our day-to-day experience.
authors: Amrita Mukherjee; Avijit Paul; Kuntal Ghosh

title: Capsule endoscopy: Emerging technologies and future clinical applications
abstract: Capsule endoscopy has evolved from a diagnostic tool for small bowel evaluation into a complex platform with expanding diagnostic and prognostic potential.This mini review aims to summarize recent advances in capsule endoscopy and explore potential clinical applications and future directions of this technology.The introduction of pan-enteric capsule endoscopy has enabled comprehensive evaluation of the entire gastrointestinal tract in a single, minimally invasive examination, supporting treat-to-target approaches and improving disease phenotyping in inflammatory bowel disease.Artificial intelligence (AI) represents one of the most important recent developments in capsule endoscopy.Deep learning algorithms have demonstrated high accuracy in lesion detection while reducing reading times.More recently, AI has been applied to automated inflammatory activity scoring, bowel cleansing assessment, and computer-assisted reporting, facilitating standardized interpretation and improving report quality.Magnetically controlled capsule endoscopy has further expanded the role of capsule technology by enabling active navigation within the upper gastrointestinal tract.Recent innovations include detachable-string systems for esophageal examination, remote 5Gassisted capsule navigation, and integration with AI-assisted image analysis, opening new perspectives for noninvasive evaluation from mouth to anus.Experimental robotic capsule prototypes have explored the feasibility of interventional functions, including tissue sampling and targeted drug delivery.These technologies remain at the preclinical stage, and their potential clinical applicability requires further investigation.
authors: Clelia Marmo; Maria Elena Riccioni

title: Carbon dots derived from traditional Chinese medicines: a novel therapeutic strategy for ocular diseases
abstract: and in acute animal studies. They also exhibit distinctive optical properties and diverse pharmacological activities. Synthesized via eco-friendly green routes using traditional Chinese medicines (TCMs) and their extracts, TCM-derived carbon dots (TCM-CDs) display distinct properties compared to conventional nanocarriers. Benefiting from their inherent nanostructures, abundant surface functional groups, and nanozyme-like activity, TCM-CDs can deliver intrinsic therapeutic effects without loading exogenous drugs or relying on residual herbal ingredients. They possess multiple bioactivities, including antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, antibacterial and neuroprotective effects, which make them potential non-invasive therapeutic candidates for refractory ocular disorders. A growing body of studies has validated the promising therapeutic efficacy of TCM-CDs in animal models against autoimmune uveitis, retinal lesions, and optic nerve injuries, highlighting their encouraging preclinical findings that warrant further investigation toward clinical translation. Focusing on the intrinsic therapeutic capacity of TCM-CDs, this review systematically summarizes their core functional mechanisms and research progress in ocular disease intervention, discusses prevailing academic controversies and unresolved research bottlenecks in this field, and proposes prospective developmental directions. This work intends to offer comprehensive theoretical evidence and guidance directions for subsequent mechanistic investigations and clinical translation of TCM-CDs in ophthalmic research.
authors: Tingyu Yang; Zongqi Feng; Xiao Zhang; Lihui Zhang; Yu Su; Ruihua Liu; Rina Sa; A Lamusi

title: Case Report: Giant adult rhabdomyoma of the parapharyngeal space: diagnostic and surgical pitfalls
abstract: Background: Adult-type extracardiac rhabdomyoma is a rare benign skeletal-muscle neoplasm that most often arises in the head and neck but is exceptional in the parapharyngeal space, where it may mimic salivary or neurogenic tumours. Case presentation: A 67-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of progressive dysphagia, globus sensation, and mild hoarseness. Computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated an approximately 9-cm, well-circumscribed right parapharyngeal mass with relatively homogeneous internal characteristics and mild-to-moderate enhancement. Because direct glottic exposure was inadequate, tracheotomy-assisted airway management preceded complete excision through a right lateral transcervical approach. Histopathology showed large polygonal cells with abundant eosinophilic granular cytoplasm. The tumour was positive for desmin and smooth-muscle actin, with focal MyoD1 and myogenin expression, a low Ki-67 labelling index, and negative S-100 staining, supporting adult-type rhabdomyoma. Recovery was uneventful, and magnetic resonance imaging at 6 and 12 months showed no recurrence. Conclusion: Adult rhabdomyoma should be considered in the differential diagnosis of a well-circumscribed parapharyngeal mass in an older adult. Integrated radiological and pathological assessment, careful airway planning, complete conservative excision, and long-term surveillance are central to management.
authors: Bingyi Dai; Hongyang Qu; Rong Liu; Changling Sun; Xiao Yin

title: Cell-autonomous restoration of splicing homeostasis and RP11 phenotype in patient-derived RPE and retinal organoids by PRPF31.AAV gene therapy
abstract: Mutations in the PRPF31 gene cause retinitis pigmentosa type 11 (RP11), a progressive blinding disease triggered by defects in the spliceosome, the cellular machinery responsible for RNA processing. Although gene replacement holds therapeutic promise, it remains unclear whether it can effectively rescue both primary target cell types across different disease stages. Here we show that viral-mediated delivery of PRPF31 to patient-derived retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells and 3D retinal organoids restores RNA splicing activity and reverses core cellular pathology. Gene delivery cleared toxic protein aggregates, restored essential RPE functions, including structural polarity, cilia integrity, and cellular waste clearance, and boosted light-evoked activity in photoreceptors. Notably, robust rescue was achievable even in mature cells, whereas combining gene therapy with autophagy-activating drugs offered no added benefit. These findings demonstrate that restoring splicing homeostasis alone drives functional recovery, supporting a broad clinical window for PRPF31 gene therapy in RP11.
authors: Maria Elia; Valda Pauzuolyte; Μαρία Γεωργίου; Mark Basche; Carina Hansohn; Elton J. R. Vasconcelos; Robert Atkinson; Sushma Grellscheid; Colin A. Johnson; Gerrit Hilgen; Henning Urlaub; Alexander J. Smith; Sina Mozaffari‐Jovin; Robin R. Ali; Majlinda Lako

title: Changing Colorectal Cancer Epidemiology Demands a Risk-Adapted European Screening Strategy
abstract: European colorectal cancer screening remains largely age-defined despite changing epidemiology, heterogeneous risk, non-participation and finite colonoscopy capacity. European guidance already anticipates risk-based thresholds, intervals and test allocation; how to test these across heterogeneous health systems remains unresolved. We propose a four-decision policy and research framework, not a validated clinical protocol, addressing when screening should begin or recur, which first-line test should be offered, what result or risk trajectory should trigger escalation, and how diagnosis and treatment should be completed. Quantitative faecal immunochemical testing (FIT) should remain a principal population-based strategy and high-quality colonoscopy the confirmatory and therapeutic standard, while national programmes may differ. Previous quantitative FIT results, age, sex, family history, comorbidity and screening behaviour can be prospectively evaluated as modifiers of interval and threshold. Multitarget stool tests, blood-based cell-free DNA, microbiome or volatile-organic-compound classifiers, colon capsule endoscopy and CT colonography should address defined pathway failures rather than act as interchangeable competitors. Because evidence for risk adaptation remains modelled or observational, implementation should proceed only through prospectively governed pilots. Evaluation should prioritise sustained participation, advanced neoplasia removed, interval cancer, colonoscopy use, equity and societal cost. Risk adaptation should optimise existing workflows through prospectively validated programmatic rules, not unvetted diagnostic layers.

title: Classification of cystoid macular edema status from retinal vasculitis fluorescein angiography images using a convolutional neural network
abstract: Introduction: Cystoid macular edema (CME) is a vision-threatening complication of retinal vasculitis, a rare inflammatory disease for which large imaging datasets are difficult to obtain. Detection of CME on fluorescein angiography (FA) requires expert interpretation, motivating automated image-based approaches to support clinical decision-making. Deep learning methods, particularly convolutional neural networks (CNNs), have shown strong performance in medical image analysis but are constrained by limited labeled data in rare diseases. Transfer learning may mitigate this limitation by adapting pretrained models to small, task-specific datasets. Methods: We analyzed 207 de-identified late-phase 55° FA images from 117 patients with retinal vasculitis. The primary target was concurrent patient-level CME status, established through specialist review of clinical records and optical coherence tomography obtained at the same clinical visit as FA. A patient was classified as CME-positive when CME was present in at least one eye. An ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-18 was evaluated using five-fold nested, patient-level cross-validation. Within each outer-development cohort, 144 candidate configurations were compared by four-fold inner cross-validation and selected according to mean inner-validation AUROC. Each selected configuration was evaluated only on its corresponding untouched outer-test fold. Results: Across 117 pooled patient-level outer-test predictions, the model-selection pipeline achieved an AUROC of 0.708 (95% CI, 0.610-0.802), an AUPRC of 0.626 (95% CI, 0.493-0.755), and an accuracy of 0.726 (95% CI, 0.641-0.803). Sensitivity was 0.694 (95% CI, 0.558-0.822), specificity was 0.750 (95% CI, 0.643-0.853), and the F1 score was 0.680 (95% CI, 0.563-0.780). Exploratory Grad-CAM analysis visualized regions associated with model predictions. Discussion: The nested model-selection pipeline showed moderate discrimination with a relatively balanced operating profile and slightly higher specificity than sensitivity. Clinically relevant false-positive and false-negative errors, together with the absence of external validation, preclude clinical deployment.
authors: Celina Wang; Koushani Chakrabarty; Stephen D. Anesi; Peter Y. Chang

title: Clinical and CBCT Based Evaluation of Residual Ridge Length in Posterior Partially Edentulous Mandibular Arches for Dental Implant Planning
abstract: Dental implants have proved to be one of the most reliable methods for treating partially edentulous patients.Successful placement of dental implants in posterior regions of the mandible requires careful evaluation of ridge length, width, and height of residual bone relative to the inferior alveolar nerve and mental foramen.Clinical examination alone does not give an exact idea of the residual ridge anatomy due to morphological variations and ridge resorption following tooth extraction.Cone Beam Computed Tomography (CBCT) is an important diagnostic tool providing high-resolution, three-dimensional images of the alveolar bone with minimal distortion and radiation.This research discusses the significance of residual ridge length analysis for implant therapy in posterior partially edentulous mandibular arches, the anatomy of ridges, methods for evaluating ridge length, importance of CBCT in implantology, patterns of ridge resorption, measurements, clinical application, disadvantages, and prospects of digital planning in implant therapy.The article concludes by comparing clinical examinations with radiographic techniques in ridge length determination and concludes that radiographic examinations prove better than clinical methods.Importance of digital workflow integration, guided implant surgery, and artificial intelligence-based imaging to enhance implant treatment results is also pointed out in the article.Evaluation of the residual ridge length becomes vital in defining the size of the implant, its inclination angle, number of implants, and necessity of performing bone augmentation.
venue: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology

title: Clinical characteristics and prognosis of emergency enteroscopy for small bowel bleeding in hospitals of different levels: A real-world study based on 297 cases from provincial, municipal, and district hospitals
abstract: Abstract Background and aims: This study aimed to compare the clinical characteristics, diagnostic efficiency, lesion detection spectrum, and follow-up outcomes of emergency enteroscopy for obscure small bowel bleeding among provincial, municipal, and district hospitals. Methods: This was a multicenter retrospective analysis of 297 consecutive patients who underwent emergency enteroscopy for obscure small bowel bleeding at a provincial hospital (n = 240), a municipal hospital (n = 25), and a district hospital (n = 32). Baseline data, ward type on admission, pre-procedural examinations, enteroscopy completion rate (total enteroscopy), endoscopic diagnoses, treatment modalities, complications, and follow-up data were collected and compared. Results: The provincial hospital admitted the highest proportion of patients to the intensive care unit (ICU) (21.3%) and performed more comprehensive pre-procedural examinations. The total enteroscopy completion rate was significantly higher at the provincial hospital (87.92%) than at the municipal (68.0%) and district (46.88%) hospitals. In terms of disease spectrum, the provincial hospital predominantly managed Crohn’s disease (33.3%), Meckel’s diverticulum (16.7%), and small bowel vascular malformations (12.5%), whereas municipal and district hospitals showed a narrower disease spectrum. Endoscopic therapy was the most common treatment across all levels. Follow-up data indicated that the provincial hospital had a lower rebleeding rate and better long-term prognosis. Among cases of incomplete enteroscopy, “bowel loop tortuosity” was a significantly more frequent cause of failure at the municipal and district hospitals. Conclusions: Significant differences exist in the diagnostic and therapeutic capacity of emergency enteroscopy and patient composition across hospital levels. Provincial hospitals demonstrate clear advantages in procedural efficiency, lesion detection, and treatment outcomes. Establishing standardized care pathways for small bowel bleeding and strengthening technical support for primary hospitals are crucial for improving overall clinical care.

title: Cognitive digital twins: A state-of-the-art review
abstract: Digital twin (DT), as a key enabling technology of Industry 4.0, have transformed real-time monitoring and simulation by offering digital representations of physical systems. However, the growing complexity of modern systems needs increasingly advanced capabilities that extend beyond replication. Cognitive Digital Twin (CDT) extend the capabilities of traditional DT by integrating cognitive functions such as perception, attention, memory, reasoning, problem solving and learning through artificial intelligence (AI) techniques such as machine learning (ML). Despite the lack of literature due to the field's infancy, CDT is becoming key tools for Industry 4.0/5.0, making systems more autonomous and adaptable. This research explores CDT developments, their differences from traditional DT, and how they operationalize cognitive functions. We investigate CDT technologies through quantitative and qualitative assessments, emphasizing particular algorithms, software, tools, and frameworks across various sectors. The review identifies current advancements, maps cognitive functions to CDT applications, and highlights critical gaps, establishing a foundation for future research.
authors: Naveed Shahzad; William Dias Ferreira; Bassant Selim

title: ColoACT: Multi-Cue Action Chunking for Smooth Autonomous Colon Navigation on a Self-Propelled Endoscopic Robot
abstract: Autonomous colonoscopic navigation can reduce operator burden and the risk of loop formation or tissue trauma, but remains challenging due to deformable anatomy, weak-texture and specular endoscopic visuals, and contact-rich viscoelastic interactions. Existing methods either rely on geometry-driven pipelines, which are efficient and interpretable yet brittle due to manually engineered features and switching logic, or adopt learning-based policies, whose inferred depth/geometry can become temporally inconsistent or overly smooth under weak texture and specular highlights while simulation-trained variants (e.g., deep reinforcement learning) may further suffer from a sim-to-real gap. We propose ColoACT, an autonomous navigation system that integrates an RGB-D-E based Action Chunking Transformer policy (ColoACT policy) for a compact self-propelled Bevel-Gear-Based Endoscopic Robot (BGER). The ColoACT policy augments RGB with estimated relative depth and a gradient-based pseudo-elevation map to enhance fold-ridge saliency and other high-frequency geometric cues, and enables smooth continuous control of the BGER by predicting overlapping action chunks and fusing them via temporal ensembling. In different \textit{ex-vivo} porcine colons (approximately 60 cm), our system achieves success rates of 85.4\% and 72.5\% in straight and curved segments, respectively, and achieves 70\% success in 90-degree turns and 60\% in double-bend sequences, with feasibility further demonstrated in challenging triple-bend segments. The project page is available at: https://Adamhu1.github.io/ColoACT/.
authors: Jian Hu; Shujing He; Leixin Chang; Zongze Li; Ding Huang; Chaoyang Shi; Chengzhi Hu

title: Colon capsule endoscopy and cost-effectiveness across colorectal care: a valuable filter, but a poor universal substitute
abstract: Colon capsule endoscopy (CCE) is a patient-friendly, minimally invasive alternative to conventional colonoscopy, but its value depends on pathway performance rather than diagnostic accuracy alone. This narrative review examines the cost-effectiveness of CCE across colorectal cancer screening, symptomatic investigation, incomplete colonoscopy, post-polypectomy surveillance, inflammatory bowel disease monitoring, and AI-supported implementation. Targeted literature searches were performed in PubMed and official guidance sources through 6 July 2026. Across broad screening populations, CCE is not yet cost-effective compared with biennial faecal immunochemical testing (FIT) or 10-yearly colonoscopy; contemporary Dutch MISCAN modelling found all CCE screening strategies dominated at full adherence, largely because unit cost and follow-up colonoscopy burden remained high. The dominant economic problem is pathway duplication: a 2025 meta-analysis found a pooled follow-up endoscopy rate of 42%, and contemporary UK/Scottish service data showed that about half of patients required further optical endoscopy or sigmoidoscopy. CCE may offer conditional value after incomplete colonoscopy, in lower-risk symptomatic triage, and in carefully selected surveillance pathways where a negative or low-risk capsule result may avoid, defer, or focus colonoscopy. Evidence from Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis monitoring is encouraging but should not be extrapolated uncritically to colorectal cancer screening or dysplasia surveillance, where biopsy and therapy remain decisive. AI-assisted CCE may reduce reading time and improve polyp detection, but robust lifetime cost-effectiveness models are still needed. The current evidence supports CCE as a pathway-dependent filter, not a universal substitute for colonoscopy.

title: Colonic diseases: epidemiology, risk factors, diagnosis, and prevention (Global trends and data from Kazakhstan). A literature review
abstract: Relevance. Colorectal cancer, Crohn’s disease, ulcerative colitis, and colonic polyposis are major public health problems. These diseases reduce quality of life, increase disability and healthcare costs, and affect screening policy. Population aging, urbanization, and lifestyle changes have altered their incidence and age distribution in many countries. This burden makes their epidemiological assessment particularly important for public health planning, prevention, early detection, and organization of appropriate healthcare services. Objective. To summarize recent evidence on the epidemiology, risk factors, diagnosis, and prevention of major colon diseases worldwide and in Kazakhstan, with attention to regional differences and gaps in knowledge. Evidence was considered globally and nationally to provide comparative perspective. Methodology. A structured narrative literature review was conducted using PubMed, Scopus, eLibrary, and Google Scholar. The initial literature search was performed from June to August 2025, and the evidence base was subsequently updated to include relevant publications available through October 2026. The review primarily covered literature published between 2015 and 2026, with earlier landmark studies included where appropriate. Eligible sources comprised original research articles, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, clinical guidelines, authoritative reference materials, and official epidemiological and statistical reports. A total of 89 sources were included in the final narrative synthesis. Results. Colorectal cancer remains a major contributor to cancer incidence and mortality worldwide and in Kazakhstan. According to GLOBOCAN 2024 estimates, colorectal cancer accounted for 3,598 new cases (12.1% of all estimated cancer cases) in Kazakhstan. National statistical data demonstrated regional differences in colorectal cancer incidence and the continued occurrence of advanced-stage disease. Colorectal carcinogenesis involves chromosomal instability, microsatellite instability, and serrated neoplasia pathways, while hereditary syndromes contribute to increased individual risk. Advances in image-enhanced endoscopy, artificial intelligence-assisted colonoscopy, capsule endoscopy, and molecular testing offer additional diagnostic opportunities. However, gaps remain in population-based epidemiological data on inflammatory bowel diseases and colonic polyposis in Kazakhstan. Conclusions. The reviewed evidence highlights the importance of risk-factor modification, organized colorectal cancer screening, early detection and removal of precancerous lesions, and risk-adapted surveillance of individuals with hereditary predisposition. For Kazakhstan, priorities include improving screening quality, strengthening national cancer registration and epidemiological monitoring, expanding access to diagnostic services, and developing population-based research on inflammatory bowel diseases and colonic polyposis. Modern diagnostic technologies should complement established clinical pathways rather than replace colonoscopy and histological examination. Keywords: colorectal neoplasms, Crohn disease, ulcerative colitis, intestinal polyposis, epidemiology, Kazakhstan.

title: Comparative Evaluation of EfficientNet-B3, Vision Transformers, and RETFound for Seven-Category Retinopathy Fundus Image Classification
abstract: Background/Objectives: Retinal fundus photography is the most widely available means of screening for sight-threatening disease, but it is difficult to read: several conditions leave overlapping signs on the same photograph, the features that separate them are often subtle and confined to small regions of the retina, and a single image carries no systemic context, so an automated reader must resolve categories on which experienced clinicians themselves agree only moderately. Methods: We compared five deep learning architectures—EfficientNet-B3, DenseNet-121, ViT-Base/16, Inception-V3, and RETFound ViT-Large—for simultaneous seven-class retinal disease classification on a multi-source fundus image benchmark, in a retrospective computational study using stratified five-fold cross-validation. We pooled 11,223 patient-eye fundus images from three publicly available, de-identified datasets (ODIR-5K, RFMiD, and APTOS 2019) spanning age-related macular degeneration (AMD), cataract, diabetic retinopathy (DR), glaucoma, hypertensive retinopathy, pathological myopia, and normal fundus; the cohort was markedly class-imbalanced (DR, 62.5%; normal, 25.6%; each remaining class < 3%), and no new patient data were collected. Images were deduplicated by MD5 hash and split at the patient level to eliminate data leakage, with a fixed 15% held-out test set and five stratified cross-validation folds; training images received Ben Graham illumination normalization and class-balancing augmentation, while validation and test images were unaugmented. Three ImageNet-pretrained CNNs (EfficientNet-B3, DenseNet-121, Inception-V3), ViT-Base/16, and RETFound ViT-Large (pretrained on 1.6 million retinal photographs via masked autoencoding) were trained; the primary outcome was the five-fold mean weighted-averaged F1 score, pairwise comparisons used paired t-tests on fold-level F1 (df= 4), and Grad-CAM was applied for explainability. Results: EfficientNet-B3 achieved the highest five-fold mean accuracy (95.53%; weighted-F1, 0.9507) and significantly outperformed RETFound ViT-Large (ΔF1=+0.0255; t=9.70; p<0.001), ViT-Base/16 (ΔF1=+0.0075; t=9.20; p<0.001), and Inception-V3 (ΔF1=+0.0103; t=8.38; p<0.001), while performing comparably to DenseNet-121 (t=2.24; p=0.089); Grad-CAM showed clinically plausible activation localization for the CNN architectures. Conclusions: A compact, resource-efficient CNN thus matched or exceeded a substantially larger retinal foundation model and Vision Transformers, indicating that larger domain-specific foundation models are not inherently superior for heterogeneous retinal screening; because such compact models run on commodity hardware, they may offer more practical screening solutions for community, rural, and resource-limited settings where ophthalmologist coverage is scarcest. External validity across imaging sources and populations remains unproven, underscoring that prospective, multicenter validation must precede clinical deployment. A provenance audit of this pooled cohort subsequently found it confounded. The audit identified five failure modes, three of them decisive: image width alone reproduced the diabetic retinopathy label at 99.98% accuracy using no retinal pixels, source and label were almost perfectly dependent with a Cramér’s V of 0.9996, and diabetic retinopathy recall was exactly 1.0000 for all five architectures. The cohort was rebuilt from a single source with per-eye labels, and nine architectures were retrained under one protocol with external validation. The corrected headline is a macro-AUC of 0.930 internally and 0.978 externally, with a macro-F1 of 0.686. No architecture is declared superior, and the pooled-cohort conclusion does not stand.

title: Comparative Evaluation of Multiple Deep Learning Models for Six-Class Keratitis Classification
abstract: Purpose: Keratitis can be classified as infectious or noninfectious, with infectious keratitis being a major cause of blindness. In this study, multiple deep learning (DL) models were applied to perform six-class classification of corneal lesions, and their diagnostic performance was systematically compared. Methods: We analyzed 3797 slit-lamp images from six categories: normal cornea, bacterial keratitis, fungal keratitis, viral keratitis, Acanthamoeba keratitis, and non-infectious keratitis. Convolutional neural network (CNN), transformer, self-supervised, and vision-language models were evaluated at image and patient levels using patient-level splits, with clinician comparison on a 240-image test subset. Results: RegNet had the best image-level performance (accuracy, 76.8%; macro-F1 score, 75.7%; macro-AUC, 0.946), and EfficientNet_B0 had the highest patient-level accuracy (77.5%; macro-F1 score, 76.6%; macro-AUC, 0.954). On the same 240-image subset, RegNet accuracy was 75.4% versus 72.7%, 56.3%, and 44.4% for senior corneal specialists, junior corneal specialists, and junior general ophthalmologists. Conclusions: CNN-based models showed stable performance under the present image-based evaluation pipeline. RegNet achieved the most balanced image-level results, whereas EfficientNet_B0 showed the strongest patient-level performance. On the same 240-image subset, RegNet showed numerically higher accuracy than clinician-group means. However, performance remains insufficient for autonomous diagnosis and requires external and prospective validation. Translational Relevance: This comparative DL framework could serve as an adjunctive image-based decision-support tool for six-class keratitis classification after further external and prospective validation, which may assist clinicians in early diagnosis and improve decision making in clinical management.
authors: Qian Tan; Yingnan Xu; Yang Zhang; Yuning Wang; Yanwu Xu; Weihua Yang

title: Compartment-specific roles of gasdermin D and E in photoreceptor degeneration: evidence and pharmacological implications
abstract: Photoreceptor degeneration arises from diverse genetic and acquired insults, yet oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and sterile inflammation repeatedly converge on membrane injury and irreversible cell loss. Inflammasome activation is frequently described as retinal pyroptosis, although upstream markers alone neither establish gasdermin-dependent lysis nor identify the executing cell. Rather than treating retinal pyroptosis as a single cell-autonomous pathway, we distinguish a myeloid gasdermin D (GSDMD) inflammatory relay from a photoreceptor-intrinsic gasdermin E (GSDME) lytic amplification program and evaluate potential interventions according to direct retinal evidence, cellular specificity, and translational readiness. GSDMD is best supported in microglia and subretinal macrophages, where inflammasome-caspase-1 signaling promotes cytokine and extracellular-vesicle release and can worsen secondary photoreceptor injury. Recent evidence in TREM2-deficient rd10 retina further supports GSDMD as a functional disease modifier, while remaining context specific. By contrast, GSDME has direct loss-of-function support in all-trans-retinal overload, in which caspase-3-dependent cleavage increases membrane rupture and is associated with mitochondrial oxidative burden and ferroptotic susceptibility. We compare NLRP3/caspase-1, interleukin-1, GSDMD pore, GSDME, and redox-directed strategies against five translational gates: target engagement, ocular exposure, cell specificity, delivery feasibility, and safety. This evidence-graded framework identifies promising pharmacological entry points while preserving the distinction between mechanistic plausibility and retinal target readiness.
authors: Ying Deng; Yasha Zhou; 派 周; Li Xiao; Jing Lu; Qinghua Peng; Yijing Yang

title: Complementary Roles of Intestinal Ultrasound and Capsule Endoscopy in Crohn’s Disease: A Prospective Blinded Comparative Study
abstract: Background and Aims: Precise and longitudinal assessment of small-bowel inflammatory activity is essential in Crohn’s disease (CD). Capsule endoscopy (CE) provides comprehensive mucosal evaluation but is limited for routine use by cost and availability. Intestinal ultrasound (IUS) has emerged as a non-invasive, accessible, and complementary imaging modality. This study compared the diagnostic performance of IUS with CE for detecting terminal ileum inflammation. Methods: In this prospective blinded study, adult patients with suspected or established CD referred for CE underwent same-day IUS. Inflammatory activity was quantified by the International Bowel Ultrasound Segmental Activity Score (IBUS-SAS) for IUS and the Lewis score for CE. Results: Ninety-eight patients were included with a mean age of 42±14 years, 42% male. IBUS-SAS showed a significant association with the 3rd tertile Lewis score (ρ=0.515, p<0.001). This association differed according to inflammatory burden, as among patients with a Lewis score <350, the correlation was weak and non-significant (ρ=0.149, p=0.198), whereas a stronger correlation was observed in those with a Lewis score ≥350. IBUS-SAS demonstrated excellent discrimination for a Lewis Score ≥350 (AUROC 0.889; 95% CI 0.807–0.972), and an IBUS-SAS cut-off of ≥13.7 yielded 90.5% sensitivity, 76.3% specificity, and 96.7% negative predictive value. Discriminative performance remained high across suspected and established CD. IBUS-SAS was the only predictor of capsule-derived inflammation, when adjusted for clinical and laboratorial biomarkers (OR 1.149 per point increase; 95% CI, 1.070–1.234; p<0.001). Conclusions: IUS accurately detects clinically significant ileal inflammation (Lewis score ≥350) and performs best in patients with higher inflammatory burden. In contrast, its performance was lower in patients with absent or low-grade inflammation, in whom the correlation between IBUS-SAS and Lewis score was weak. These findings support a complementary approach, with CE remaining the reference standard for detailed mucosal assessment and IUS serving as a practical, non-invasive tool for the assessment of clinically significant ileal inflammation.
authors: Joao Goncalves; Francisca Dias de Castro; Leite Sílvia; Joana Magalhães; Bruno Joel Ferreira Rosa; José Cotter

title: Concept-Based Explainable AI in Retinal Imaging: Core Concepts, Techniques, and Challenges
abstract: In high-stakes domains like healthcare, establishing trust in AI-assisted decisions is critical for fostering confidence among experts and researchers. However, standard explanation methods may not fully meet clinical needs, offering raw data, such as saliency maps, rather than human-readable text and auditable, transparent reasoning. To bridge this gap, researchers are increasingly adopting concept-based approaches that express model reasoning through human-readable concepts grounded in expert-backed clinical knowledge. Although this field has advanced rapidly in recent years, retinal C-XAI remains methodologically heterogeneous, with limited agreement on taxonomy, evaluation, and clinical validation. This review identifies recurring reliability gaps in retinal C-XAI and synthesises potential directions for addressing them, including independent concept-level auditing, robustness testing, and clinician-informed validation. As an illustrative example, we discuss how the established SMILE methodology could be adapted for concept-level auditing in retinal C-XAI; this is presented as a candidate research direction rather than a new or clinically validated framework.

title: Concordancia diagnóstica entre la cápsula endoscópica y la enteroscopía de doble balón en la hemorragia digestiva de intestino medio en un hospital de referencia en Perú
abstract: Introduction: The diagnostic approach to mid-gut gastrointestinal bleeding requires several examinations, primarily video capsule endoscopy followed by double-balloon enteroscopy) at tertiary care centers. Objective: To evaluate the level of diagnostic agreement between video capsule endoscopy and double-balloon enteroscopy in patients treated with mid-gut gastrointestinal bleeding at a referral hospital in Lima, Peru, during the 2020-2025 period. Methods: This was an observational, retrospective, and comparative study. Diagnostic agreement between the two procedures was calculated using the Kappa coefficient. Statistical analysis was performed using IBM SPSS Statistics v.20.0 and R software version 4.1.2, with a significant p-value < 0.05. Results: In fifty-one patients with mid-gut gastrointestinal bleeding (28 women; median age: 65 years [IQR: 55-71]), video capsule endoscopy and subsequent double-balloon enteroscopy (39 antegrade and 12 retrograde) were performed. Most patients (34/51; 66.7%) presented with overt mid-gut gastrointestinal bleeding, while the rest had occult bleeding, with a mean hemoglobin level of 7.3 ± 2.24 g/dL. The median time interval between the two procedures was 13 days (IQR 5-29). In 10 (19.6%) patients where video capsule endoscopy showed positive findings, no lesions were identified during double-balloon enteroscopy , whereas in one case (2%) with a negative video capsule endoscopy , double-balloon enteroscopy was positive. Overall diagnostic agreement was low (κ = 0.37; [95% CI: 0.10-0.64]; p = 0.002). Moderate agreement was observed regarding lesion type (κ = 0.58; [95% CI: 0.42-0.74]; p < 0.001) and lesion location (κ = 0.50; [95% CI: 0.31-0.69]; p < 0.001), with moderate agreement for vascular (κ = 0.60) and tumoral (κ = 0.60) lesions. Conclusion: Video capsule endoscopy and double-balloon enteroscopy showed low overall diagnostic agreement in patients with mid-gut gastrointestinal bleeding, and moderate agreement regarding the type and location of the lesion.

title: Constipation Not So Vibrant: A Case Report of Colonic Obstruction From Capsule Retention
abstract: Vibrating capsules represent a novel, nonpharmacologic approach for chronic idiopathic constipation, with favorable safety profiles in clinical trials, showing no reported retention events. Although generally well tolerated, patients with severe motility disorders and use of narcotics pose risk of retention of capsules. We report a case of a 73-year-old woman with a history of gastroparesis and slow-transit constipation, who developed colonic retention of multiple vibrating capsules, requiring colonoscopic retrieval. Careful patient selection, monitoring, and timely imaging may prevent complications when treating patients with vibrating capsules.

title: Contact-Adaptive Robotic Ultrasound Probe Control for Tissue Exploration and Continuous Task-Relevant Visualization Using Robot-Free Image-Motion Demonstration
abstract: Robotic ultrasound commonly targets standardized views, predefined scanning protocols, or expert-scan reproduction. We target a different role: while a clinician performs the primary procedure, a robotic assistant maintains a clinician-selected view so that changing tissue remains observable. We present contact-adaptive robotic ultrasound monitoring derived from robot-free demonstrations. Sonologger clamps a six-axis inertial sensor to the clinician-operated probe and records synchronized ultrasound and probe-frame relative rotations without a robot, camera, or tracker. Rather than imitating trajectories, the recordings measure which probe axis and sign the clinician uses to correct an image offset. A measured image latency is removed before still-move-still segmentation yields relative-rotation labels; translation is excluded from control because of inertial drift. These measurements parameterize the Demonstration-Informed Image-Motion Controller (DIMC), an interpretable, non-learned controller combined with beam-axis force regulation and an independent safety supervisor with 5 N forced retreat. On a dynamic bladder phantom, DIMC acquired and held a task-relevant view in 7 of 7 blind, pose-paired trials versus 1 of 7 for a static hold (McNemar p = 0.031), and retained the view during syringe-driven hydro-distension while the supervisor bounded the force excursion. The framework offers an operational representation of ultrasound context for contact-adaptive intraoperative monitoring; clinical validation remains future work.

title: Contact-Aware Impedance Controller for Robot-Assisted Ultrasound Imaging
abstract: Safe robot-assisted ultrasound imaging requires a reliable controller able to detect and localize probe--tissue interaction. In this paper, we present a B-mode ultrasound image-based contact perception method and a contact-aware impedance controller for robotic ultrasound imaging. The proposed method detects acoustic contact independently of force measurements, enabling contact-conditioned force/torque taring to reduce residual wrench bias. During contact, the method continuously estimates the effective contact location along the curved probe surface and uses it to update the controller interaction frame, enabling visual servoing of the physical probe--tissue contact point during imaging. Experiments on an agar phantom demonstrated a contact-localization RMSE of $\mathbf{1.46 \pm 0.14}$~mm over probe roll angles from $\mathbf{-15^\circ}$ to $\mathbf{15^\circ}$. During static rolling, the proposed controller maintained task-space tracking accuracy comparable to a conventional fixed-frame impedance controller while reducing the maximum compressive interaction force from $\mathbf{31.56}$~N to $\mathbf{20.09}$~N, corresponding to a $\mathbf{36.3\%}$ reduction. These results demonstrate the potential of ultrasound images as direct contact feedback for safe and accurate robot-assisted ultrasound imaging.
authors: Md Miraj Arefin; M Efe Tiryaki

title: Continuum Robots in Surgery: From Engineering Design to Clinical Practice
abstract: Over the past decades, continuum robots have made significant advancements, yet are still minimally used in industry. The medical field has demonstrated growing interest in these robots, particularly in research but clinical translation has been limited. Their hyper‐redundant structures enable infinite degrees of freedom, offering a wide range of benefits. Specifically, continuum robots are able to navigate torturous pathways reaching deep areas of the body with improved dexterity and minimal risk. This review provides a historical overview of continuum robots and highlights key innovations that have shaped their development. The history also traces the emergence of robotic‐assisted surgery, contextualizing the clinical motivation for the rise of continuum robots. It examines the fundamentals of continuum robot design including structural configurations, sensing technology, modeling techniques, and control strategies. Together, these provide an in‐depth understanding of continuum robots and the common underlying principles as a guide for their future design. The review also discusses medical considerations, current clinical applications, and major challenges that continue to limit the widespread adoption of continuum robots. With decades of development in continuum robots, synthesizing this information is crucial to improving accessibility in the field and fostering continued research and innovation in these highly promising medical systems.
authors: Griffin Smith; Kaitlyn Clancy; Siwen Xie; Xiaochen Li; Sarah Khalifé; Benjamin D. van der Woerd; Onaizah Onaizah

title: Current Diagnostic Approaches to Pulpal and Periapical Diseases
abstract: The success of endodontic treatment largely depends on establishing an accurate diagnosis and selecting an appropriate treatment strategy based on the available diagnostic findings. Pulpal and periapical diseases may present with overlapping clinical and radiographic features, while certain non-endodontic conditions can also mimic endodontic disease. These similarities may complicate diagnosis, particularly when symptoms are nonspecific, pulpal tests provide inconclusive results, or radiographic findings are limited. Therefore, endodontic diagnosis should be based on the integration of the patient’s history, clinical examination, pulpal and periapical tests, and radiographic findings. When necessary, advanced diagnostic methods, including cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) and histopathological examination, can provide additional information. An accurate differential diagnosis is essential not only for identifying the underlying condition but also for avoiding unnecessary endodontic or surgical procedures and establishing an appropriate treatment plan. When the expected healing does not occur after treatment or the clinical course is inconsistent with the initial diagnosis, the diagnosis should be reconsidered. In recent years, the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in endodontics has introduced new opportunities to support diagnostic assessment. AI-based applications have increasingly been investigated for tasks such as radiographic image analysis, detection of periapical lesions, assessment of root canal morphology, determination of working length, and identification of vertical root fractures. However, AI should not be regarded as an independent diagnostic method that replaces clinical assessment. Rather, it should be considered a supportive tool that may facilitate a more systematic and objective interpretation of clinical and radiographic data . Integrating clinical expertise with contemporary technological advances may improve diagnostic accuracy and contribute to more appropriate treatment planning in endodontics.
authors: Yücel Aydemir

title: Current Trends in AI and Eye Disease Diagnostics
abstract: PURPOSE: Artificial intelligence (AI) has rapidly advanced as an approach for ophthalmic disease detection, driven by the widespread use of high-dimensional imaging modalities (e.g., optical coherence tomography). This review summarises the machine learning and AI approaches for disease detection in ophthalmology and discusses emerging paradigms and highlights key challenges impacting clinical translation. RECENT FINDINGS: AI-based systems have demonstrated suitably high diagnostic performance across major ophthalmic diseases, including diabetic retinopathy (DR), diabetic macular oedema, glaucoma, age-related macular degeneration and retinopathy of prematurity. Several tools have even received regulatory approval for commercial DR screening. More recently, foundation models trained using self-supervised learning have enabled more generalisable and data-efficient disease detection across datasets and imaging modalities. In parallel, multimodal large language model systems are emerging that integrate imaging and clinical data to support more comprehensive diagnostic workflows. Early agentic AI systems extend this paradigm further by coordinating multiple models to perform disease detection, provide clinical decision support and generate reports. AI-based disease detection in ophthalmology has achieved substantial technical progress but only limited translation into routine clinical practice. Key barriers include technical, clinical, ethical, economic and regulatory concerns. Future efforts should prioritise prospective evaluation in real-world settings, addressing model transparency and bias and alignment with clinical and regulatory requirements. With continued advances, AI has the potential to expand access to care, improve diagnostic accuracy and reduce the global burden of vision loss.
authors: Maria Jessica Cruz; Siddharth Limaye; Mark Christopher

title: DIABETIC RETINOPATHY: CURRENT APPROACHES TO SCREENING, DIAGNOSIS, AND PERSONALIZED MANAGEMENT
abstract: Diabetic retinopathy remains a major cause of preventable visual impairment, despite the availability of effective screening and sight -preserving therapies. Contemporary care is moving from episodic eye examinations towards integrated pathways that combine retinal imaging, risk -based follow -up, systemic risk -factor optimisation, and timely treatment. This narrative review summarises recent guidance and evidence published predominantly during 2022- 2026 on screening, diagnostic assessment, artificial intellig ence, and individualised management. Retinal photography remains a scalable screening method, while dilated examination and optical coherence tomography support clinical confirmation and assessment of diabetic macular oedema. Validated autonomous AI systems can improve access, but require reliable image acquisition, quality assurance, referral pathways, and evaluation across diverse populations. Management is determined by disease severity, macular involvement, visual function, treatment burden, pregnancy s tatus, comorbidities, and the likelihood of adherence. Anti -vascular endothelial growth factor (anti -VEGF) therapy is a central treatment for vision-impairing centre-involving DME and an option for selected proliferative DR; panretinal photocoagulation rem ains important when durable treatment or reduced dependence on repeated injections is prioritised. Optimal glycaemic, blood- pressure, and lipid management remains foundational. A personalised model should link screening results to an actionable care plan rather than treating image classification as an endpoint.
authors: Saparbay Abuov; Nurmukhambet Mussay; Ulykbek Daurenov; Baknur Bazarbay

title: Deep Convolutional Neural Networks For Diabetic Retinopathy And Glaucoma Screening From Retinal Fundus Images: A Literature Review With Emphasis On Rural India
abstract: Diabetic retinopathy (DR) and glaucoma are major causes of preventable blindness, and both can be picked up on a colour fundus photograph before the patient notices any symptom. In rural India, though, ophthalmologists are few compared with the number of people at risk, so many patients are seen late or not at all. Convolutional neural networks (CNN) have been reported to grade fundus images about as well as trained graders, and a number of studies have tested them in Indian hospitals and community camps. This paper reviews that literature from a computer engineering perspective. It covers the clinical background, public datasets and preprocessing, the development of CNN architectures, published DR and glaucoma detection studies, and the practical problems of deploying such systems with smartphone-based cameras and poor connectivity. The review finds that DR detection is considerably more mature than glaucoma detection, that most of the evidence comes from well-resourced centres, and that image quality, dataset shift, explainability, joint multi-disease screening and regulatory readiness are still open problems. A framework for a rural screening pipeline and an evaluation plan are outlined to guide future work.
