title: Long-Term Outcomes According to a Device-Assisted Enteroscopy Strategy after Capsule Endoscopy in Patients with Small Bowel Bleeding: A Nationwide Population-Based Cohort Study.
abstract:
Background/aims

Although the use of device-assisted enteroscopy (DAE) has increased, few large-scale studies have examined long-term outcomes focused on small bowel (SB) bleeding. We analyzed National Health Insurance Service data to evaluate the clinical utility of DAE in patients with SB bleeding who underwent capsule endoscopy.

Methods

We included a cohort of 11,690 patients who underwent capsule endoscopy for SB bleeding (identified using ICD-10 codes) between 2014 and 2022. Patients were categorized into three groups: no DAE, diagnostic DAE, and therapeutic DAE. We assessed four major outcomes, including the probability and factors associated with SB rebleeding, severe SB rebleeding, rebleeding-related mortality, and all-cause mortality.

Results

Of 11,690 patients, 5,211 were included in the analysis (no DAE, n=4,960; diagnostic DAE, n=173; therapeutic DAE, n=78). The probability of SB rebleeding and severe SB rebleeding was highest in the therapeutic DAE group, followed by the diagnostic DAE and no DAE groups (p<0.001), with 7-year rebleeding probabilities of 19.8%, 15.8%, and 5.0%, respectively. Rebleeding-related and all-cause mortality were also highest in the therapeutic DAE group, followed by the diagnostic DAE and no DAE groups (p<0.001 for both), with 7-year rebleeding-related mortality probabilities of 9.3%, 5.9%, and 2.7%, respectively. Risk factors for both rebleeding-related and all-cause mortality included age, male sex, liver cirrhosis, and malignancy.

Conclusions

Patients who require therapeutic DAE for SB bleeding remain at increased long-term risk of rebleeding and mortality. These findings likely reflect their greater underlying disease burden and highlight the need for individualized long-term surveillance and careful management of comorbidities, even after therapeutic intervention.
authors: Song JH, Moon JR, Kim HG, Kim JO, Park JB, Jeon SR, Lee JS, Small Intestine Research Group of the Korean Association for the Study of Intestinal Diseases (KASID).

title: Long-term outcomes of patients with negative small bowel video capsule endoscopy for Crohn's disease: A cohort study.
abstract:
Background

In the diagnostic algorithm of Crohn's disease (CD), video capsule endoscopy (VCE) is used as a subsequent investigation when initial assessments are inconclusive (ileocolonoscopy and computed tomography/magnetic resonance enterography). The long-term clinical significance of a negative VCE remains uncertain. Therefore, we evaluated long-term clinical outcomes in patients with suspected CD and inconclusive standard investigation.

Methods

We conducted a retrospective cohort study of adults with inconclusive standard investigation for suspected CD who were referred for VCE at a tertiary inflammatory bowel diseases center between 2008 and 2017. VCE studies were scored using the Lewis score. Patients with a Lewis score <135 were defined as "negative VCE." Patients with negative VCE were followed for subsequent CD or alternative diagnoses. Final CD diagnosis was verified by review of electronic clinical charts.

Results

Among 615 consecutive patients (median age 36 years; 57.5% female), 192 (31.2%) were identified with a positive VCE suggestive of small bowel CD. Overall, 18 (4.3%) of 423 patients with a negative VCE had a subsequent diagnosis of CD over a median follow-up of 11 years (interquartile range: 10-13 years; 4665 patient-years); median time to diagnosis was 1.5 years (interquartile range: 1-3 years). An alternative diagnosis was established in ∼70% of patients with negative VCE (mostly functional disorders and noninflammatory conditions). The negative predictive value for a negative VCE to exclude CD was 95.7%.

Conclusions

A negative VCE confers a very low likelihood of subsequent CD diagnosis in patients with suspected CD after nondiagnostic standard evaluation. Diagnostic efforts should instead focus on functional evaluation and dietary intervention.
authors: Edelman-Klapper H, Avni-Biron I, Ollech JE, Hegger S, Levi Z, Dotan I, Yanai H.

title: ML‐driven Early Detection of Retinal Diseases in Primary Care Settings
abstract: The common causes of preventable blindness mainly concern retinal diseases, including diabetic retinopathy (DR), age-related macular degeneration (AMD) and glaucoma. Machine-learning (ML) models are trained on large datasets of retinal images, demographics of patients and clinical information. This chapter looks at the potential of ML in facilitating the detection of retinal disease at an earlier stage in primary care. It explains the importance of early intervention, the ML methods applied in screening, clinical performance and implementation challenges, and also future trends that may change the way diagnostic processes work in the future. ML tools can help decrease preventable blindness, maximize resources and develop effective proactive eyecare by facilitating the connection between primary healthcare and specialist diagnostics. ML has been rapidly increasing in the detection of retinal diseases, particularly with the incorporation of deep learning. ML algorithms need to be rigorously validated before being deployed to real-world clinical applications to detect retinal diseases.
authors: Vijay Hari Karambelkar; N. Patil Ashish

title: MRI-compatible skull-base pin fixation for advanced image-guided pediatric neurosurgery using augmented reality in infants younger than one year: A feasibility study.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Rigid cranial fixation in infants younger than 1 year is controversial because thin, incompletely ossified calvaria predispose to skull fractures, epidural hematomas, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leaks, and scalp injury. However, neuronavigation, augmented reality (AR), and intraoperative MRI (iMRI) require stable head immobilization. METHODS: Four infants aged 5, 4, 7, and 10 months underwent surgery for choroid plexus papilloma, pineal atypical teratoid rhabdoid tumor, hemimegalencephaly, and occipital focal cortical dysplasia, respectively. An MRI-compatible head holder served as both fixation device and iMRI coil (prone position n = 3, supine n = 1). Low-pressure skull-base pinning (below 45 N; both lateral sphenoid wings and upper mastoid) avoided thin calvarial regions. Neuronavigation, microscope-based AR, and iMRI were integrated in all cases. RESULTS: Stable immobilization sufficient for neuronavigation (registration accuracy below 2 mm), AR-guided microsurgery, and repeated iMRI was achieved in all patients without loss of fixation. iMRI confirmed gross total resection in three cases and complete disconnection on diffusion tensor imaging after hemispherotomy. No fixation-related complications, new or unexpected neurological deficits, or wound-healing disorders occurred during a follow-up of 5-12 months (median 5.5 months). CONCLUSION: In this small technical series, low-pressure skull-base pin fixation with an MRI-compatible head holder provided stable immobilization without fixation-related complications in infants undergoing advanced image-guided neurosurgery. These results demonstrate technical feasibility but do not establish safety, which requires larger studies. Careful skull-base pin placement may reduce classical pinning complications while enabling multimodal neurosurgical techniques in infants.

title: MagServo: Uncertainty-Resilient Hierarchical Magnetic Servoing via Learned Latent Representations
abstract: Magnetic navigation provides contact-free and line-of-sight-independent feedback for robotic systems, yet existing approaches typically rely on explicit pose estimation or direct use of raw magnetic measurements, making accurate control susceptible to modeling errors, measurement noise, and disturbances. This work presents MagServo, a hierarchical learning-based framework for robust 6-DoF magnetic servoing directly using the learned latent magnetic feature. MagServo learns uncertainty-resilient magnetic representations through masked reconstruction and captures state-dependent interaction dynamics between robot motion and latent magnetic transitions without analytical magnetic models or explicit Jacobian supervision. Based on the learned dynamics, a hierarchical controller combines nonlinear model predictive control for coarse approach with local Jacobian inversion for precise fine regulation. Extensive physical experiments demonstrate submillimeter and subdegree accuracy, achieving mean terminal errors of 0.386 mm and 0.479 degree for 6-DoF pose reaching. MagServo further outperforms a localization-based control baseline in complex trajectory tracking and maintains robust performance under unseen magnetic-source configurations without retraining. A supplementary video of the real-robot experiments is available at https://youtu.be/rZt1NUP1Mr0.
authors: Yuhan Tan; Yameng Zhang; Pei Liu; Yao Zhong; Zhongliang Jiang

title: Magnetic Micro/Nano Carriers for Targeted and Sustained Drug Delivery Systems
abstract: ABSTRACT This review provides a comprehensive overview of magnetic micro‐ and nano‐carrier systems for targeted and sustained drug delivery, highlighting recent advancements in formulation design, synthesis parameters, and multi‐stimuli‐responsive mechanisms to overcome conventional chemotherapy limitations. Unlike existing literature, this work uniquely synthesizes the structural and functional trade‐offs across magnetic nanoparticles, liposomes, and microspheres while critically evaluating translation‐defining synthesis parameters. Conventional chemotherapy often lacks selectivity, leading to adverse systemic effects; targeted and sustained magnetic drug delivery (MDD) uses external magnetic field gradients to guide biocompatible carriers to pathological sites. These platforms enhance therapeutic efficacy, reduce systemic toxicity, cross complex biological barriers like the blood–brain barrier, and provide controlled release. The review explores carrier design, surface functionalization, and synthesis optimization. However, key translational challenges persist, including severe batch‐to‐batch variability during scale‐up, rapid reticuloendothelial clearance due to in vivo protein corona formation, limited magnetic field penetration in deep‐tissue human anatomy, and an ambiguous regulatory landscape. Finally, we outline critical future directions, focusing on image‐guided theranostics, non‐invasive robotic endoscopic navigation, standardized characterization protocols, and biocompatible/biodegradable platforms to accelerate clinical adoption in oncology and neurology.
authors: Noble George; Harjeet Singh; Shivani Pandya

title: Magnetic based In-situ Self 3D Pose Estimation for a Modular Soft Tendon-Driven Continuum Robot via IMU-Fusion
abstract: Continuum robots are well suited for gentle manipulation because of their inherent compliance and ability to adapt to complex environments. However, their continuously deformable structure makes accurate configuration estimation challenging, particularly when external vision systems are unavailable or obstructed. In this work, we present an embedded pose sensing framework that combines inertial measurement units (IMUs) and active magnetic fields to estimate the robot configuration without relying on external cameras. The angular measurements from the IMU and magnetic-field references are fused to improve local orientation estimation and reduce accumulated orientation error during operation. This pose sensing scheme achieves an update rate of 16.7~Hz, allowing real-time feedback. The proposed system is experimentally validated through closed-loop control, where the estimated robot configuration is used to maintain the end-effector at a desired position while interacting with an object. These results demonstrate the potential of distributed magnetic--inertial sensing for real-time pose estimation and closed-loop control of continuum robots.
authors: Sue; Guo Ning Sue; Xiangyun Bu; David Quinn; Junzhe Hu; Carmel Majidi

title: Magnetically gated millimeter-scale capsule power system for leadless electrotherapy
abstract: Temporary cardiac pacing is indispensable for bridging transient bradyarrhythmic indications over days to weeks, yet existing systems remain constrained by device dimensions, surgical complexity, patient burden, and intrinsic operational principles. Here, these challenges are addressed through a millimeter-scale capsule power system with magnetically gated activation via a reed switch, which eliminates the stringent orientation and implantation-depth requirements of optically controlled approaches. In contrast to conventional reed switch-based pacemakers, this capsule system extends the functionality of the reed switch by integrating electrode materials directly onto its surface, thereby enabling a monolithic miniaturized architecture. Pulsed magnetic fields wirelessly actuate intermittent switching, enabling controlled discharge, with robust cardiac pacing demonstrated in large animals. A proof-of-concept closed-loop system is further realized, establishing the feasibility of future integration with a wearable electronic module to enable autonomous electrotherapy upon arrhythmia detection. Collectively, this strategy addresses a key limitation in temporary pacing and may provide a versatile framework for the development of temporary electrotherapeutic systems across cardiac, neural, and regenerative applications.
authors: Feiyao Yang; Yu Tian; Enyi Zhang; Lixue Yang; Ziyue You; Puguang Peng; Qian Han; Yan Du; Haiwei Li; Yongquan Wu; Houfang Liu; Anfu Zhou; Tian‐Ling Ren; Weiping Sun; Zhong Lin Wang; Di Wei

title: Mapping the new frontier: Current perspectives on evolving gastrointestinal pathophysiology
abstract: With rapid advancement in cutting edge basic research in genetics, multi-omics, bioengineering and artificial intelligence focusing on improvement in precision medicine, the study of gastrointestinal (GI) pathophysiology has transitioned from describing GI conditions as isolated structural disorders to a systems-biology approach which recognize them as a complex network of interconnected systemic and functional diseases.It emphasizes the "interactome" -the complex crosstalk between the gut microbiome, the enteric nervous system, the mucosal immune system, and the enteroendocrine system -with associative effects on distant organs, metabolic, and immune function of the body.The gut is thus a central regulatory hub for metabolic health, immune education, and possibly neurocognitive function.Current perspectives emphasize three primary pillars in disease pathogenesis, namely the role of low-grade chronic inflammation and the integrity of the epithelial barrier (leaky gut), the metabolic influence of the microbiome, and its effect on functioning of distant organs.This narrative review will broaden the above perspectives highlighting the effect of smouldering inflammation affecting the epithelial barrier (its causative metabolomic signatures, the resulting epithelial plasticity, and its involvement in local and systemic diseases), the gut-microbiomedistant organ axis, the gut-metabolic axis (contributing to systemic inflammation and atherosclerosis), immuno-gastroenterology (related to GI cancers and other diseases), and advances in bioengineering (three dimensional in vitro modelling like organ-on-a-chip and personalized organoids) for better delineation of disease pathogenesis, biomarkers and precision therapeutics.Further, the utility of artificial intelligence in precision diagnostics (radiology, histology, multi-omics) and in shaping future therapies will be discussed as also the present limitations.
authors: Gautam Ray

title: Mask2Restore: Self-Supervised Ultrasound Despeckling via Inpainting
abstract: Medical ultrasound (US) is inherently degraded by speckle, a granular interference pattern that is often treated as a complex form of noise in image restoration. However, unlike random noise, US speckle originates from coherent scattering within tissue and is therefore highly spatially dependent and deterministic under fixed acquisition conditions, making US speckle suppression fundamentally different from natural image denoising. Because speckle-free US targets are unavailable in practice, self-supervised denoising is necessary. Blind-spot networks (BSN) are the dominant self-supervised paradigm for natural images, but their pixel-wise masking strategy assumes spatially independent noise, an assumption poorly matched to US speckle, which is spatially correlated over multiple pixels rather than pixel-wise independent. To address this mismatch, we propose Mask2Restore, a self-supervised US despeckling framework that reformulates despeckling as contextual inpainting with block-wise masking on single noisy images. Unlike pixel-wise BSN masking, block-wise masking addresses this multi-pixel speckle correlation by removing locally correlated speckle neighborhoods and shifting the reconstruction cues used by the network from adjacent speckle correlations to broader anatomical context. We further introduce cross-resolution context regularization (CRCR), which suppresses residual speckle bias by enforcing consistency across multi-resolution predictions. Experiments on simulated and in vivo carotid US, unseen fine-structure cases, and downstream cardiac segmentation demonstrate improved speckle-detail trade-offs, better preservation of fine anatomical structures, and practical value for subsequent image analysis.
authors: Xuesong Li; Yingtai Xu; Zhongliang Jiang; Nassir Navab; Yuan Bi

title: Medical Magnetic Robots: From Multi-scale Actuation and Intelligent Control to Biomedical Applications
abstract: Medical magnetic robots utilize external fields for tetherless navigation, revolutionizing minimally invasive medicine. This review systematically summarizes advancements in physical principles, hardware architectures, intelligent control, and clinical translation. The article systematically reviews three principal hardware categories: permanent magnet systems, coil-based systems, and multimodal hybrid actuation platforms. It charts their evolutionary trajectories and posits that the collaborative integration of electromagnets and permanent magnets, together with multiphysics coupling, constitutes a critical strategy for resolving inherent performance trade-offs. Addressing unstructured environments, this paper discusses the shift toward intelligent autonomy, providing an in-depth analysis of deep learning-based perception, model predictive control (MPC), and reinforcement learning (RL) technologies. Furthermore, this review places significant focus on decoupled multi-robot control achieved via frequency and spatial domains, alongside environment-adaptive nano/microswarm reconfiguration mechanisms. The evaluation further extends to the clinical efficacy of this technology in gastrointestinal capsule endoscopy, and cardiovascular catheter guidance. Magnetic actuation technology is currently undergoing a critical transition from passive tools to intelligent autonomous medical systems, thereby continually bridging the gap between laboratory research and widespread clinical application.
authors: Xianjun Cheng; Zheming Zhao; Fujiang Yuan; Zebing Mao; Shaojie Gu; Zhen Tian; Yanhong Peng

title: Micro- and Nanorobots in Ophthalmology: Active Navigation Across Ocular Barriers for Precision Therapeutics—A Scoping Review of Technology Readiness, Clinical Applications and Therapeutic Gaps
abstract: This review concerns actively actuated miniaturised robotic systems investigated for ocular, adnexal and ophthalmic vascular applications. Its rationale is to distinguish such systems from passive drug carriers and conventional full-scale surgical robots, and to map how engineering capabilities relate to experimentally demonstrated ophthalmic tasks. Particular interests include movement across ocular barriers, precision delivery, surgical manipulation, tracking, retrieval, biocompatibility and translational readiness. A scoping review is appropriate to the stated objective of mapping a heterogeneous evidence base across engineering and biomedical disciplines, rather than estimating a pooled therapeutic effect. The methodological framework is the JBI approach to scoping reviews; reporting of the completed review follows PRISMA-ScR. JBI provides guidance specifically addressing protocol development, searching, data extraction and presentation. Primary objective To map the nature, extent, engineering characteristics, experimentally demonstrated applications and translational maturity of micro-, nano- and millirobotic systems investigated in ophthalmology. Review questions 1. What types of tethered and untethered miniaturised robots have been investigated for ophthalmic applications? 2. What device dimensions, materials, fabrication methods, propulsion mechanisms and actuation systems have been reported? 3. What imaging, localisation, tracking and control approaches have been demonstrated? 4. Which ophthalmic tasks and disease applications have been experimentally investigated? 5. What experimental models, comparators, efficacy outcomes and safety assessments have been used? 6. What evidence exists concerning retrieval, biodegradation, clearance and sustained ocular residence? 7. What provisional technology readiness has been demonstrated, and what gaps remain in the pathway toward clinical translation? These questions reflect the objectives and extraction domains reported in the manuscript.
authors: Islam Omar; Paria Malekahmadi; Mohamed Abosheisha; Ahmed Hafez; Tilemacos Zaimis; Meysam Keshavarz; Farid Froghi

title: MicroDLP: Microscope-Enabled Resolution-Switchable 3D Microprinting
abstract: Abstract Complex three-dimensional (3D) microarchitectures are increasingly important for microfluidics, microrobotics, organ-on-chip systems, biomedical devices, and architected materials. However, fabricating complex 3D microstructures with micrometre-scale precision remains a major manufacturing challenge. Integrating these fine features with larger supporting structures presents an additional challenge, requiring fabrication across multiple length scales within a single architecture. Although microscale 3D printing enables intricate geometries, the trade-off between resolution and build volume limits multiscale fabrication, while existing approaches often require complex optics and precise registration. Here, we introduce MicroDLP, a microscope-enabled digital light processing platform for versatile, resolution -switchable 3D microprinting. By integrating a projection module into a conventional inverted microscope, MicroDLP exploits its revolving objective turret to switch between 4×, 10×, and 20× objectives, provi ding projected pixel sizes from 1.89 to 0.378 µm. We characterize photopolymerization, voxel geometry, and lateral feature resolution across magnifications to establish suitable microscale printing conditions. MicroDLP enables the fabrication of diverse and complex 3D microarchitectures, including freestanding trusses with 170 µm struts, microvascular structures with 10 µm features, interlocking gears, suspended microbridges, and microneedles with 3–5 µm tips. Importantly, switching from 10× to 20× during fabrication produces monolithic 3D structures combining larger supporting foundations with fine micropillar arrays, without manual optical realignment. The shared optical pathway also enables coaxial in situ monitoring of photopolymerization. Together, these results establish MicroDLP as a versatile platform for microscale additive manufacturing, combining complex 3D microfabrication with resolution switching within a single monolithic structure.
authors: Dimitar Boev; Prajwal Sanjay Agrawal; Mahmoud Medany; 邓永; Gabriele Morlupi; Daniel Ahmed

title: Microvasculopathy in spinal muscular atrophy: The endothelium as a target of SMN deficiency and an amplifier of disease
abstract: Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) is caused by deficiency of the ubiquitous survival motor neuron (SMN) protein. Degeneration of anterior horn motor neurons defines the disease, but many organs are affected, including heart, liver, kidney, and bone. The vascular compartment is among them: digital necrosis in infants with the fewest SMN2 copies, capillary rarefaction in SMA mice, and decreased von Willebrand factor with fibrinogen extravasation in human post-mortem spinal cord. Whether these reflect endothelial injury by SMN deficiency itself or capillary adaptation to atrophic, denervated tissue has not been examined systematically. SMN-depleted endothelial cells form defective networks and migrate poorly in neuron-free systems, but this is based on a single unreplicated study in macrovascular and progenitor cells, which do not recapitulate human spinal cord microvascular endothelium. Ventral horn hypoxia precedes or accompanies weakness, retinal vessels fail before ganglion cells are lost, but retinal networks and patient-derived endothelial progenitors recover when SMN is restored. Demand-matched regression, reduced cardiac output, post-mortem artefact, critical illness, autonomic dysfunction and measurement confounding account for part of the phenotype, not all. Throughout, we keep vascular abnormality distinct from impaired perfusion, demonstrated only in mice. SMN has never been deleted from, or restored in, the endothelium alone in vivo. We therefore hypothesise, as a falsifiable model, not a proven mechanism, that the endothelium is injured cell-autonomously alongside other SMN-dependent lineages and amplifies rather than initiates disease, and we outline the genetic experiments required to falsify it. Retinal angiography and capillaroscopy are accessible readouts, neither visualising the cord.
authors: Stefania Paola Corti; Linda Ottoboni; Francesca Beatrice; Andrea D’Angelo; Filippo Marcotti; Martina D'Agostino; Federica Rizzo; Giulia Magni; Giacomo Pietro Comi

title: Minding the gates: dual cell-autonomous and non-cell-autonomous mechanisms of TBK1 in ALS/FTD
abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD) comprise a neurodegenerative disease spectrum characterized by TDP-43 pathology and overlapping genetic risk factors. Loss-of-function variants in TBK1 (TANK-binding kinase 1) represent one of the most common genetic causes of ALS/FTD, highlighting haploinsufficiency for TBK1 as a major contributor to disease pathogenesis. Emerging evidence from iPSC and mouse models suggests that reduced TBK1 activity disrupts interconnected autophagy, endo-lysosomal, and innate immune pathways through both cell-autonomous and non-cell-autonomous mechanisms. In this review, we discuss the multifaceted role of TBK1 as a master regulator of proteostasis and inflammatory pathways, highlight its critical role in maintaining microglial homeostasis, and explore how these convergent functions inform therapeutic strategies for ALS/FTD.

title: Mobile AI-Assisted Oral Lesion Triage for Community Oral Cancer Screening: Prospective Field Evaluation Study.
abstract:
Background

AI-based tools for oral cancer screening have shown promising performance in curated image datasets, but their performance in real-world mobile community screening workflows remains less clear.

Objective

This study evaluated the prospective field performance of a parameter-locked, mobile AI-assisted oral lesion triage system embedded in a human-supervised community oral cancer screening workflow.

Methods

We conducted a prospective community-based field evaluation in eastern Taiwan from June 17 to December 31, 2025. Trained nonspecialist personnel acquired standard white-light intraoral images using handheld mobile devices during routine screening. The AI system incorporated on-site image quality assessment and lesion-level risk stratification into green, yellow, and red triage categories. Technically inadequate images after repeated acquisition attempts were classified as ungradable and excluded from performance analysis. Three board-certified oral and maxillofacial specialists established an operational clinical reference standard through structured image review and consensus adjudication. The primary outcome was lesion-level identification of high-risk lesions requiring specialist referral, defined as red versus nonred triage. Diagnostic performance was estimated with Wilson 95% CIs; precision-recall performance and preconsensus specialist agreement were also assessed.

Results

Among 602 screened participants, 4283 interpretable intraoral images were included in expert adjudication and lesion-level analysis. The AI system flagged 68 red lesions; 12 (17.6%) were confirmed as high risk, and 4 additional high-risk lesions were identified during expert review, yielding 16 high-risk events for the primary red-triage analysis. For high-risk lesion identification, sensitivity was 75% (12/16; 95% CI 50.5%-89.8%) and positive predictive value was 17.6% (12/68; 95% CI 10.4%-28.4%); specificity, negative predictive value, and accuracy were 98.6% (3928/3984), 99.9% (3928/3932), and 98.5% (3940/4000), respectively. Area under the receiver operating characteristic curve values were 0.957 for red, 0.931 for yellow, and 0.964 for green triage; precision-recall analysis showed area under the precision-recall curve values of 0.8235, 0.9052, and 0.9476, respectively. Preconsensus specialist agreement was high, with a Fleiss κ of 0.921 and a Gwet AC1 of 0.981.

Conclusions

This mobile AI-assisted oral lesion triage system was feasibly integrated into a real-world community screening workflow operated by trained nonspecialist personnel. In this low-prevalence field setting, red triage showed moderate sensitivity and modest positive predictive value, supporting its use as human-supervised referral-prioritization support rather than autonomous diagnosis. Further multicenter studies with blinded assessment, participant-level outcomes, workflow-efficiency measures, and longitudinal follow-up are needed before clinical impact and scalability can be determined.
authors: Liu HY, Huang YC, Chen SW, Wei LY, Chou CY, Lee JJ, Chen SJ, Lee CC.

title: Modulation of Presynaptic Inhibitory Retinal Circuits for Retinal Ganglion Cell Neuroprotection in Glaucoma
abstract: Glaucoma is a leading cause of irreversible blindness, yet the circuit-level mechanisms contributing to retinal ganglion cell (RGC) degeneration remain incompletely defined. Although multiple neuroprotective strategies have been explored, clinical translation remains limited. Here, we identify early dysfunction of inner retinal inhibitory circuitry as a modifiable contributor to RGC vulnerability during ocular hypertensive stress. In mouse ocular hypertension models, inner nuclear layer neurons exhibited increased c-fos expression and enhanced oscillatory potential-associated differential electroretinography signals before substantial RGC loss was detected, suggesting early retinal circuit hyperactivity. Broad pharmacological attenuation of GABAergic and glycinergic inhibitory signaling improved RGC survival without reducing intraocular pressure, supporting a functional contribution of inhibitory neurotransmission to RGC vulnerability. Moreover, Cre-dependent AAV delivery of Lin28, an RNA-binding regulator of post-transcriptional gene expression, to Vgat-positive inhibitory interneurons increased RGC survival compared with Vgat-EGFP controls and Vglut2-lineage Lin28 expression. Vgat-targeted Lin28 also reduced c-fos expression and oscillatory potential-associated differential electroretinogram abnormalities, indicating suppression of ocular hypertension-associated inner retinal hyperactivity. In addition, ocular hypertension was associated with altered sleep architecture, and Vgat-targeted Lin28 expression was associated with mitigation of these alterations. These findings position presynaptic inhibitory retinal circuitry as an early and modifiable contributor to glaucomatous RGC vulnerability.
authors: Eun Ji Hong; Chen Lin; Wenjie Long; Ian Kim; Mengwen Xiong; Zuer Wu; Siyuan Rao; Qianbin Wang

title: Monocular depth estimation for endoscopic surgery using swin transformer and conditional random fields
abstract: Abstract Monocular depth estimation in endoscopic surgery is challenging due to weak tissue textures, uneven illumination, specular reflections, and frequent smoke or instrument interference. This paper proposes CRFDepth, a pseudo‑supervised framework for endoscopic monocular depth estimation. A Swin Transformer encoder extracts hierarchical global features under weak‑texture conditions. The proposed CRFDepth framework effectively addresses key challenges in endoscopic monocular depth estimation, achieving superior accuracy and robustness. A Pyramid Scene Parsing module aggregates multi‑scale contextual information to improve structural perception in distorted regions. A NeWCRF decoder performs cross‑scale structured inference for boundary refinement and detail recovery. A RangeAwareLoss is introduced to stabilize optimization within the narrow endoscopic depth range. The network is trained with stereo-derived pseudo-ground-truth supervision using binocular image pairs, while only monocular input is required during inference. Experiments were conducted on the da Vinci laparoscopic dataset. CRFDepth achieves 44.27 dB PSNR and 0.9942 SSIM, outperforming baseline methods, and demonstrates strong robustness to occlusion and smoke interference.

title: Multidisciplinary Perspectives in Colorectal Polyps and Polyposis Syndromes : Integrating Pharmacotherapy, Laboratory Biomarkers, Diagnostic Imaging, Rehabilitation, and Genetic Profiling
abstract: Background: Colorectal polyps are common gastrointestinal lesions with heterogeneous histological, molecular, and malignant potential. Although many polyps are benign, adenomatous and serrated lesions may represent important precursors of colorectal cancer. Hereditary polyposis syndromes further increase cancer risk and require early recognition, genetic assessment, and structured surveillance. Aim: This review aimed to provide an integrated overview of colorectal polyps, focusing on their classification, etiology, epidemiology, pathophysiology, histopathology, clinical presentation, diagnostic evaluation, differential diagnosis, and contemporary management strategies. Methods: Relevant clinical and scientific literature addressing colorectal polyps and hereditary polyposis syndromes was reviewed. Evidence concerning genetic mechanisms, environmental risk factors, endoscopic and radiological diagnosis, histopathological classification, colonoscopic polypectomy, advanced endoscopic techniques, surgical interventions, and multidisciplinary management was synthesized. Results: Colorectal polyps comprise hyperplastic, inflammatory, hamartomatous, adenomatous, and serrated lesions with substantially different biological behaviors. Molecular abnormalities involving APC, KRAS, TP53, mismatch-repair genes, BRAF, STK11, SMAD4, MUTYH, and PTEN contribute to distinct hereditary and sporadic pathways. Colonoscopy remains central to diagnosis and treatment, allowing simultaneous detection, characterization, biopsy, and removal. Cold and hot snare polypectomy, endoscopic mucosal resection, and endoscopic submucosal dissection provide increasingly tailored approaches for different lesions. Surgical and transanal procedures are reserved for selected advanced, unresectable, malignant, or hereditary disease. Conclusion: Accurate characterization and complete management of colorectal polyps are essential for colorectal cancer prevention. Integration of endoscopy, pathology, laboratory and molecular testing, radiology, genetics, pharmacy, surgery, and rehabilitation supports individualized treatment and long-term surveillance.

title: Multimodal Progress-Residual Fusion for Anticipating Navigation Retreat in Robotic Flexible Endoscopy
abstract: Flexible robotic endoscopes provide access through tortuous anatomy, where friction, deformation, and wall interaction separate commanded insertion from useful distal progress. Operators interpret this mismatch and retreat to recover a navigable configuration. Recognizing the approach to that decision requires relating motor intent to distal response and the local visual scene. We introduce Multimodal Progress-Residual Fusion (MPRF), a causal model that anticipates operator retreat from commands, electromagnetic (EM) tracking, and endoscopic video. A nominal-progress model predicts the response expected in normal or successful navigation; a temporal predictor combines its EM residual with all three observed modalities. In a 150-episode colon-phantom collection, MPRF achieves 0.580 +/- 0.007 AUPRC across three seeds, compared with 0.511 for the strongest reduced-modality control. Complete multimodal histories provide the principal ranking advantage, while the residual adds an explicit intent-response representation with a small, uncertain increment over raw fusion. Analysis of frozen alarms relates warning timing to the behavioral label and explains the increase in event recall under a longer matching window. These results establish a basis for behavioral assistance during operator-controlled navigation.
authors: Chi Kit Ng; Tianchun Wu; Jiatan Sun; Yuming Sun; Jianru Zhang; Hongliang Ren

title: Multimodal artificial intelligence and large language models in gastrointestinal endoscopy: From lesion detection to workflow-integrated report generation
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has rapidly transformed gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy, with most early applications focusing on computer-aided detection and diagnosis of lesions from endoscopic images.However, real-world endoscopic practice extends beyond image interpretation.Endoscopists must integrate real-time video, anatomical location, lesion morphology, procedural context, histopathological findings, clinical history, and standardized terminology to make diagnostic decisions and generate clinically meaningful reports.Recent advances in multimodal AI and large language models (LLMs) provide an opportunity to move beyond isolated endoscopic image analysis toward more comprehensive endoscopic workflow support.By integrating visual, textual, temporal, and clinical information, these models can support lesion characterization, anatomical navigation, procedure quality assessment, structured documentation, report generation, and patient-centered communication.Nevertheless, clinical translation remains limited by scarce high-quality multimodal datasets, heterogeneous reporting standards, insufficient external validation, hallucination risk, limited interpretability, real-time integration challenges, privacy concerns, and evolving regulation.This review summarizes current applications of AI in GI endoscopy, with particular emphasis on the emerging role of multimodal learning and LLMs in bridging lesion detection, context-aware interpretation, and automated report generation.Furthermore, the article analyzes future challenges and the methodological, clinical, ethical, and regulatory requirements for the reliable integration of these systems into clinical endoscopic practice.
authors: Hua-Wei He; In Neng Chan; Ye-Ying Qin; Tao Yan; Pak Kin Wong

title: Multimodal retinal imaging–based assessment of large language models for the differential diagnosis of retinal vascular occlusion
abstract: Aims: To compare the diagnostic and treatment recommendation performance of three large language models (LLMs)-ChatGPT-4o, Gemini, and Microsoft Copilot-in the differential diagnosis of retinal vascular occlusions using multimodal retinal imaging. Methods: This observational study included 75 patients, comprising 50 retinal vein occlusion (RVO; 25 branch and 25 central) and 25 retinal artery occlusion (RAO; 6 branch and 19 central) cases. Each LLM independently evaluated three imaging datasets: (1) color fundus photographs, (2) fundus photographs combined with optical coherence tomography (OCT), and (3) fundus photographs combined with OCT and fundus fluorescein angiography (FFA). A standardized prompt was used for all analyses. Diagnostic accuracy and treatment recommendation accuracy were compared among the models using Cochran’s Q and post-hoc McNemar tests. Results: Significant differences in diagnostic accuracy were observed among the three models under all imaging conditions (all p<0.001). Using fundus photographs alone, diagnostic accuracy was 21.3% for ChatGPT-4o, 12.0% for Gemini, and 1.3% for Copilot. After adding OCT images, ChatGPT-4o and Gemini each achieved an accuracy of 21.3%, whereas Copilot remained at 1.3%. With multimodal imaging (fundus photographs+OCT+FFA), diagnostic accuracy increased to 28.0% for ChatGPT-4o and 37.3% for Gemini, while Copilot again remained unchanged at 1.3%. Pairwise comparisons demonstrated no significant difference between ChatGPT-4o and Gemini across imaging conditions, whereas both significantly outperformed Copilot. For treatment recommendations, Gemini achieved the highest accuracy (57.3%), followed by ChatGPT-4o (26.7%) and Copilot (10.7%) (p<0.001). Gemini performed significantly better than both ChatGPT-4o and Copilot, and ChatGPT-4o also outperformed Copilot. Conclusion: Although multimodal retinal imaging improved the diagnostic performance of current LLMs, their overall diagnostic accuracy remained inadequate for independent clinical use in retinal vascular occlusions. Gemini demonstrated the greatest benefit from multimodal image integration and provided the most accurate treatment recommendations. These findings suggest that current LLMs should be regarded as supportive clinical tools rather than autonomous diagnostic systems, while future multimodal Artificial Intelligence models trained on ophthalmology-specific datasets may achieve substantially improved performance.
authors: Memduh Kurt; Ayna Sariyeva İsmayılov; Mahmut Oğuz Ulusoy

title: Nanomotors: Preparation Strategies, Propulsion Mechanisms, and Applications in Cancer Therapeutics
abstract: Cancer remains one of the leading causes of human death globally. The capabilities of tumor cells for rapid proliferation, resistance to death, and metastasis have become major hurdles in the successful treatment of cancer. Nanomotors, with distinct advantages such as tumor targeting and excellent biocompatibility, have emerged as a crucial research area in cancer therapy. This type of nanoscale dynamic system can convert external energy sources like magnetic fields, light fields, and sound fields, as well as endogenous chemical energy such as hydrogen peroxide, into autonomously driven mechanical energy. These distinctive motion characteristics remarkably enhance the penetration efficiency of nanocarriers into tumor tissue. This offers a promising approach to overcome the physiological barriers of the tumor microenvironment and improve therapeutic efficacy. In this review, the latest advancements in tumor treatment using nanomotors are systematically summarized. The content encompasses the preparation strategies, driving mechanisms, and therapeutic applications, providing crucial references for the further development of nanomotors in the field of cancer treatment.
authors: Heyi Zhang; Ben Shi; Lianzhen Li; Qinrui Fu; Zeyu Jiang

title: Neuromorphic Decoding and Dynamical Image Reconstruction from Populations of Spiking Retinal Ganglion Cells
abstract: Decoding visual stimuli from the spiking activity of retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) informs both our understanding of the retinal code and the design of visual prostheses. Natural vision is dynamic, yet state-of-the-art decoders mostly reconstruct single frames with artificial neural networks that process dense, continuous-valued signals rather than the retina's sparse, asynchronous spikes. We asked whether dynamic scenes can be reconstructed and tracked entirely within the spike domain, and at what computational cost. We built an end-to-end spiking neural network (SNN) whose neurons integrate the recorded RGC spikes over time. Populations of up to 1836 RGCs were recorded ex vivo from mouse retina on high-density microelectrode arrays while flashed images, moving bars, drifting gratings and randomly moving handwritten digits were presented. For moving digits, one shared spiking encoder fed two readouts, one reconstructing the image and one decoding the digit's position. Compute energy was estimated from counted synaptic operations. The SNN decoded what and where at once. It reconstructed the stimuli with a structural similarity (SSIM) of up to 0.93, refining the reconstruction as spikes accumulated, and tracked a randomly moving target with a mean error of 1.33 pixels on a $32\times32$ grid. Its fidelity nearly matched that of the best of 17 larger spiking and artificial decoders (5.9 million to 1.7 billion parameters, versus 5.4 million), and at a mean firing rate of 14.2% it needed an estimated $\sim$70-fold less compute energy than a dense artificial network of the same architecture. Dynamic visual scenes can thus be decoded from retinal population activity in the spike domain, with a compact network and at a compute cost compatible with implantable and wearable neural interfaces, supporting spike-native decoders for visual prostheses.
authors: Ning Zhang; Arto V Nurmikko

title: Neurovascular Dysfunction in Retinal Diseases: Biological Mechanisms and Emerging AI-based diagnostic approaches
abstract: In the world, retinal diseases are one of the most important causes of permanent vision loss, and they are now known to be more than just vascular diseases; these are diseases of complex interaction between the neuronal, vascular, glial, and immune elements.The retinal neurovascular unit, which consists of retinal neurons, endothelial cells, pericytes, Müller glia, astrocytes and microglia, is a unit that is pivotal to maintaining the homeostasis of the retina via coordinated neurovascular coupling and blood-retinal barrier integrity.This highly integrated system is disrupted in the pathogenesis of major retinal diseases such as diabetic retinopathy , age-related macular degeneration, glaucoma and retinal vein occlusion.Recent data indicates that neurovascular dysfunction usually occurs before clinically apparent vascular lesions, leading to a paradigm change from a vascular to a model of early neuronal damage, inflammation, oxidative stress, and impaired cellular communication.Research for decades pointed to the retinal neurovascular unit as a target for early therapeutic interventions in diabetic retinopathy.The development of new imaging techniques for the retina, such as optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA), adaptive optics and hyperspectral imaging, have made it possible to visualize micro-vascular and micro-neural changes in the retina like never before.At the same time, artificial intelligence (AI), especially deep learning, multimodal learning, and explainable AI (XAI), has revolutionized retinal diagnostics with automated detection of retinal diseases, their severity, and prediction of the disease prognosis and management.The recent advances in foundation models and multimodal AI systems that combine fundus photography, OCT, OCTA, and clinical metadata, signify a significant leap in precision ophthalmology.This review explores the biological mechanisms involved in retinal neurovascular dysfunction, reviews its contribution to the major retinal diseases, and critically analyzes recent advances, current limitations, and future prospects for the computational intelligence in clinical retinal care.
authors: Aditya Choudhary

title: Next‐Generation Robotic Perception Artificial Intelligence Design, Development, and Real‐World Impacts
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)–driven robotic vision is transforming the domains of autonomous mobility, healthcare, geological research, and space exploration. This work examines the integration of deep learning, sensor fusion, edge AI, and multimodal geospatial intelligence into robotic perception systems. Convolutional neural networks, transformers, LiDAR (light detection and ranging), edge computing, and AI-augmented geospatial analysis exemplify essential technologies. Advancements such as neuromorphic computing, biomimetic vision, autonomous learning, and adaptive reinforcement learning enable real-time environmental assessment, predictive geological mapping, and resource identification through hyperspectral imaging and seismic sensors. AI-enhanced vision drives autonomous navigation, surgical robots, space exploration, and disaster response. The research examines subjects such as real-time decision-making, computational efficiency, energy limitations, and ethical AI. Energy-efficient computing, self-adaptive neural networks, and interpretable AI are crucial for future advancements. The integration of AI, robotics, and geospatial intelligence heralds a new epoch of intelligent automation that will profoundly influence numerous businesses and academic disciplines.
authors: Martins Olatoye AROWOLO; Rafiu Mope Isiaka; Kingsley Theophilus Igulu; Ayodeji Nurudeen Mohammed; Adejare Adeyemo; Marvis Ayoola Arowolo; Adeola Margaret Olarewaju; Micheal Olaolu Arowolo

title: ORBIT: A Modular Multi-finger Robotic Hand Platform with Rotational Finger Reconfiguration
abstract: Despite the popularity of multi-fingered robotic hands for dexterous manipulation, there is no systematic platform to compare different hand morphologies against one another. We present ORBIT (Orbital Reconfigurable Base-actuated Integrated Theta-motion Hand), a modular platform designed to enable principled exploration of multi-fingered hand morphology. The core contribution of ORBIT is a rotating knuckle mechanism, where independent fingers travel around a cylindrical palm via a belt drive. This enables ORBIT to perform quick recon- figuration (< 1 s) of finger layout without hand disassembly. ORBITs a robust system, with finger average angular velocity of 1.57 rad / s1 and a root finger force resistance of 50 N. Using a three fingers instantiation of ORBIT, we demonstrate an initial pilot grasping study, comparing anthropomorphic, isometric, and Barrett-style finger layouts across eleven objects of varied size, shape, and texture. We further demonstrate how ORBITs nonanthropomorphic orbital DOF enables the achievement of tasks that would be difficult to perform with fixed-knuckle designs, such as cube face reorientation, lid threading, and precision pinching of sub-centimeter objects. These results establish ORBIT as a viable platform for direct apples to apples comparison of multi-fingered hand morphologies for specific manipulation tasks
authors: Benito Ribadeneira; Siqi Shang; Lillian Chin

title: Object-Centered Reconstruction for Vision-Based 3D Force Estimation
abstract: Excessive force may damage tissue and increase the risk of anastomotic leakage in robotic colorectal surgery. Although the da Vinci 5 provides force sensing, this capability is unavailable on earlier da Vinci systems and many other surgical robotic platforms. In this work, we present a vision-based pipeline for estimating 3D interaction forces from soft-tissue deformation in stereo endoscopic video. We dynamically reconstruct the tissue point cloud in an object-centered coordinate frame, track tissue points with geometric constraints, and predict the 3D force vector with a neural network. We progressively evaluate the pipeline on rubber-glove phantoms, ex vivo porcine colons, and in vivo colorectal surgical video sequences. Under varying tissue orientations and positions within the endoscopic view, as well as different camera viewpoints, the proposed method achieves average root mean square error (RMSEs) of 0.77 N and 1.30 N on the phantom and porcine colon, respectively. Compared with the camera-frame representation, the object-centered representation reduces average RMSE by 51.3% and 56.7%, while geometry-constrained tracking reduces RMSE by 19.8% and 25.3% compared with CoTracker. We further qualitatively demonstrate the feasibility of vision-based force estimation on an in vivo colorectal surgical sequence, as a step toward clinical translation of vision-based, sensorless force estimation.
authors: Zhonghao Zhang; Mingyeung Wu; Hao Yang; Ayberk Acar; Alan Kuntz; Jie Ying Wu

title: Ocular Factors Affecting AI Diagnosis in Diabetic Retinopathy Screening for Resource-Limited Regions: Cross-Sectional Study
abstract: Background: Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is the leading cause of vision loss among working-age adults worldwide. AI-assisted automated image reading has effectively alleviated the human resource challenges in large-scale remote screenings, yet there is limited analysis on the impact of complex ocular factors on the diagnostic efficacy of AI. Objective: This study aimed to systematically analyze the impact of multiple ocular factors on the diagnostic efficacy of the EVisionAI system in detecting DR and vision-threatening diabetic retinopathy (VTDR) during large-scale screening of residents with diabetes in resource-limited regions. Methods: testing, and comprehensive ophthalmic examinations (visual acuity, intraocular pressure, slit-lamp examination, axial length measurement, and fundus photography). Following data collection, 2 ophthalmologists independently graded fundus photographs according to the American Academy of Ophthalmology standards. The influence of various ocular factors on the diagnostic performance of EVisionAI was subsequently evaluated. Results: Between October 21 and November 12, 2024, 1847 participants with type 2 diabetes (aged 32-91 years) were enrolled, of whom 1748 (94.6%) completed the screening process and 3392 eyes were eligible for DR analysis. Participants had a mean age of 67.17 (SD 8.52) years and mean diabetes duration of 9.13 (SD 6.97) years, with 19.2% (335/1748) having DR and 7.4% (129/1748) having VTDR. Although EVisionAI's diagnostic efficacy was comparable to that of ophthalmologists (sensitivity: 90.61%, 95% CI 87.89%-92.79%; specificity: 98.99%, 95% CI 98.52%-99.31%), some ocular factors-including pupil size, refractive media opacity, and tessellated fundus (TF)-significantly impaired its efficiency. Severe refractive media opacity and TF reduced its sensitivity to 80.95% and 82.86%, respectively, and these factors interfered more with early-stage DR detection than VTDR (97.45% detected), particularly in eyes with severe TF changes (sensitivity decreased to 60.71%). Most notably, severe vitreous degeneration-induced opacity almost invariably led to VTDR misdiagnosis. Additionally, pupil dilation improved the sensitivity of EVisionAI for diagnosing DR (excluding early-stage DR) but had minimal impact on specificity. Conclusions: EVisionAI achieved high diagnostic accuracy for large-scale DR screening in resource-limited regions, yet its performance for early-stage disease was diminished by severe ocular factors. Optimizing for these factors is therefore essential to maximize its clinical utility in primary care settings with limited specialist access.
authors: Ying Xue; Xin Hu; Shuaijie Yuan; Junfang Zhang; Hongxia Hu; Shangbo Yang; Rongrong Zhu

title: Ocular Motor Dysfunction Versus Visual Impairment: A Two-Patient Case Series of Pituitary Macroadenoma Presentations
abstract: Patients with pituitary macroadenoma typically present to ophthalmic clinics with visual field defects or optic disc pallor. Ocular motor symptoms such as diplopia, strabismus, and cranial nerve palsies due to parasellar or cavernous sinus invasion are often missed and may be the initial presentation. We present two patients who were examined in an ophthalmology outpatient clinic and diagnosed with pituitary macroadenoma with neuro-ophthalmologic findings. The first case was a 26-year-old female presenting with persistent headache, right esotropia, and decreased abduction of the right eye more than the left eye, with a history of infertility evaluated gynecologically. Laboratory tests and magnetic resonance imaging confirmed the diagnosis. The second patient was a 58-year-old man who had one month of reduced vision and headaches. Visual acuity was 0.1 in both eyes with slightly pale optic disks and limited abduction of the right eye with diplopia on right gaze. Automated perimetry, endocrine studies, and brain MRI confirmed the diagnosis of a pituitary macroadenoma. Both patients were referred for neurosurgical evaluation and continued to be followed up on cabergoline 0.5 mg as per the plan of their medical team. These cases illustrate the importance of considering pituitary macroadenoma in patients with unexplained esotropia, abduction deficits, diplopia, headaches, visual loss, optic disc pallor, or reproductive problems and highlight the need for a comprehensive neuro-ophthalmic evaluation, formal visual field testing, endocrine investigation, and contrast-enhanced sellar MRI in a multidisciplinary setting. They also emphasize that cabergoline should only be prescribed for proven hyperprolactinemia or prolactinoma and not based on tumor size alone.
authors: Abdulbari Alshareef
venue: AlQalam Journal of Medical and Applied Sciences

title: Optimizing Ophthalmic Surgery Outcomes Using Predictive ML Algorithms
abstract: Ophthalmic surgery has experienced tremendous progresses in the past two decades. It has all been due to new surgery techniques, improved imaging and the integration of digital health. Predictive machine-learning (ML) algorithms have the potential to be helpful in enhancing decisions and outcomes. In this chapter, the authors present a review of the recent predictive ML solutions in enhancing the outcome of ophthalmic surgery. They study algorithmic frameworks, analyze how to use them in particular areas of surgery, and explain what their advantages, disadvantages and prospects are. The authors leave evidence gathered in the recent past showing how predictive ML can complement precision ophthalmology and surgeons' custom-takes on procedures specific to the patient, and increase the overall success rates of the surgery. Combining ML and cloud technology with the electronic health records scale will ensure the availability of the tools in various environments.
authors: D.B. SHIRKE; V. Patil Zunjar

title: Oral Radiology and Diagnostic Imaging: The Most Mature Frontier of Dental Artificial Intelligence
abstract: Oral radiology is the most extensively studied domain of dental artificial intelligence (AI), accounting for more than a quarter of all dental AI publications between 2011 and 2021. Convolutional neural networks have been trained to detect caries, periapical lesions, alveolar bone loss, root fractures, cysts and anatomical structures on periapical, bitewing, panoramic and cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) images, often reaching sensitivity and specificity comparable to, or higher than, those of general dental practitioners. This chapter reviews the main applications of AI in dental imaging, the quantitative evidence behind them, the first randomized and economic evaluations, and the practical issues that determine whether a radiographic AI tool helps or harms patients: dataset heterogeneity, generalisability across equipment and populations, the risk of overtreatment and the need for prospective, real-world validation. Because many orthodontic, periodontal, endodontic, surgical and pediatric tools are built on the same image-analysis architectures, the maturity of oral radiology underpins much of what is discussed in later chapters. The chapter concludes that radiographic AI is ready to act as a second reader under clinical supervision, but not as an autonomous diagnostician.

title: Orofacial pain disorder or trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia? Insights into pathophysiology and implications in medicine and dentistry
abstract: OBJECTIVE: This narrative review highlights the importance of orofacial pain considerations in the differential diagnosis of trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias (TACs)/trigeminal autonomic orofacial pains (TAOPs). In addition, we provide novel insights into the pathophysiology of the presentation of TACs in the maxillary (V2) and mandibular (V3) trigeminal distributions (TAOPs). BACKGROUND: TACs are lifelong disorders characterized by severe unilateral head pain accompanied by cranial autonomic phenomena. However, the head pain experienced may refer to the face, be present solely in the orofacial region as TAOPs, or even be experienced as a toothache. These presentations, involving V2/V3, may resemble disorders of diverse etiology and pathophysiology that may share some similarities with TACs, confusing the patient while relating symptoms, and creating a diagnostic dilemma for the clinician potentially leading to misdiagnosis. Moreover, TACs pathophysiology has not been discussed in relation to V2/V3 presentations (TAOPs). METHODS: A literature search was performed on PubMed/Scopus to find relevant literature about TACs and TAOPs, and case reports of orofacial presentations. Deep reanalysis of several of our published articles on preclinical models of TACs was conducted to assess potential of V2-V3 components. RESULTS: TACs orofacial presentations are not as common but if present can lead to misdiagnosis with significant consequences. Patients presenting TACs involving the midface as TAOPs experience an important delay for a correct diagnosis including multiple and diverse health provider visits, with a risk of having well-intended but misguided procedures. Differential diagnosis considerations need to include dental/odontogenic causes, sinusitis, temporomandibular disorders, Eagle syndrome, trigeminal neuralgia, and migraine (orofacial migraine, neurovascular orofacial pain). A reanalysis of preclinical data provides novel insights into this orofacial involvement. In two TAC-specific preclinical neuronal populations, recording either trigeminal or superior salivatory nucleus neurons, it was observed that ~20% and 37.5% of neurons, respectively, had cutaneous receptive fields that included or were exclusively within the V2-V3 trigeminal division. Whereas the numbers are not large, these demonstrate that even in rodent models in neuronal populations that could be considered TAC-like, they can extend to, or exclusively involve, the facial region, similar to TAOPs. CONCLUSION: The potential presence of TACs in the orofacial region can be observed from preclinical models to the clinical setting. The International Classification of Headache Disorders (ICHD) needs to recognize this additional localization, as well as the intraoral one, including dental structures. Education about TACs/TAOPs in the medical and dental setting is vital. Evidence has shown that dentists are one of the first providers that are seen by this patient population due to similarities with dental pain. The dentist specialized in orofacial pain is a key ally in the identification of TACs/TAOPs. The medical/neurology and dental/orofacial pain settings have a great opportunity and responsibility to work together to stop years of pain in this patient population.
authors: Marcela Romero‐Reyes; Simon Akerman

title: Outcomes and Reclassification Patterns in Inflammatory Bowel Disease Unclassified: A Multicenter Study Matched With Ulcerative Colitis From Spanish ENEIDA Registry
abstract: BACKGROUND AND AIM: Around 10% of patients with inflammatory bowel disease do not fulfill the diagnostic criteria for Crohn's disease (CD) or ulcerative colitis (UC). These cases are labelled as inflammatory bowel disease unclassified (IBDU). The aim of the study was to compare therapeutic requirements in patients with IBDU and UC and to identify predictive factors of reclassification. METHODS: This was a multicenter retrospective cohort study based on the ENEIDA registry. Patients diagnosed with IBDU or indeterminate colitis between January 2010 and December 2016 were included. All cases were matched by sex, age at diagnosis, and disease extent with at least two UC patients from the same hospital. The Kaplan-Meier method was performed to assess diagnostic changes during follow-up. Fine-Gray competing-risks regression analysis identified predictive factors of reclassification. RESULTS: Two hundred and nine IBDU patients and 465 UC patients were included. After a median follow-up of 90 months, no significant differences were observed in the use of immunomodulator (37.3% vs. 37%, p = 0.934) and advanced therapies (29.2% vs. 23.9%, p = 0.143) between IBDU and UC. No statistical differences were found in the surgical rates (5.7% vs. 4.7%, p = 0.579). Overall, 59 IBDU patients (28.2%) were reclassified (30 UC and 29 CD). Baseline extensive colitis was associated with a lower probability of subsequent reclassification to UC (SHR: 0.33; 95% CI: 0.12-0.91). No independent predictive factors for reclassification to CD were identified. CONCLUSIONS: Therapeutic management of IBDU and UC patients tended to be similar. Two-thirds of patients remained classified as IBDU.

title: Overview of Persistent Inter-Professional Rivalry Within the Laboratory Medicine Practice Domain of Tertiary Healthcare Institutions in Nigeria: A Narrative Review
abstract: The persistent inter-professional rivalry within the laboratory medicine practice domain of Nigerian tertiary healthcare institutions constitutes a systemic crisis that undermines diagnostic accuracy, jeopardizes patient safety, and disrupts healthcare delivery. This longstanding conflict between the Medical Laboratory Scientists (MLS) and the laboratory-based physicians (Clinical Pathologists) centers mainly on operational independence, leadership in clinical laboratories, and statutory boundaries. This review examines the historical, legal, educational, and socio-political causes of this rivalry in Nigerian tertiary healthcare settings. Historically, laboratory medicine practice functions shifted from physician-led to specialized, autonomous scientific roles, leading to overlapping claims over laboratory and clinical consultation domains. Conflicting laws—such as the Medical and Dental Council of Nigeria (MDCN) Practitioners Act and the Medical Laboratory Science Council of Nigeria (MLSCN) Act—have created parallel regulatory frameworks, resulting in ongoing legal disputes at the National Industrial Court. These dynamics foster operational silos, strikes, and diagnostic errors, often causing preventable misdiagnoses. To transform this rivalry into collaborative clinical efforts, the article recommends a comprehensive approach that includes legislative reforms, separation of administrative and clinical roles, formal interprofessional education in training, and joint governance boards in tertiary healthcare settings. Ultimately, resolving this conflict is vital to achieving international standards and protecting Nigerian patient care from interprofessional conflicts.
authors: Collins Amadi; Roy Amadi; Sasha Amadi; Elena Amadi; Comfort John

title: PREFERENDO: a preference for the full picture in pediatric capsule endoscopy
abstract: The PREFERENDO consensus provides a valuable framework for pediatric endoscopy reporting [1]. Its capsule domain already includes preparation quality, completeness, lesion description and interpretation. The opportunity for refinement lies in connecting these fields to the endorsed scores. We suggest an implementation principle: each reported score should include the information needed to understand what it measures and how examination quality constrains its interpretation.
authors: Anastasios Koulaouzidis; Ervin Tóth; Wojciech M. Marlicz

title: Paradigm shifts in prostate biopsy strategies in the era of precision medicine
abstract: The escalating global burden of prostate cancer necessitates continuous refinement of diagnostic strategies. Although prostate biopsy remains the gold standard for diagnosis, key procedural aspects, including biopsy template, guidance methods, and biopsy route, remain subjects of ongoing debate. Current approaches have yet to achieve the dual goals of high sensitivity and high specificity in diagnostic performance. In recent years, ongoing advancements in related fields have generated substantial clinical evidence, offering further insights into optimizing biopsy strategies. This review provides a synthesized framework for navigating the paradigm shift from traditional, standardized biopsy toward personalized, precision-based approaches. We not only trace the evolution of biopsy techniques but also offer a comprehensive, in-depth exploration of how patient-specific factors, such as prostate volume, prostate-specific antigen density, and Prostate Imaging Reporting and Data System scores, can inform individualized biopsy decisions, thereby providing practical clinical guidance. In addition to critically evaluating conventional biopsy paradigms, we systematically examine emerging biopsy strategies and synthesize high-quality studies at the forefront of this field. Finally, against the backdrop of the artificial intelligence era, we highlight the transformative potential of artificial intelligence and robotic platforms across the diagnosis. By integrating current development and future directions, this review offers a structured framework for personalized biopsy decision-making, ultimately aiming to achieve both high sensitivity and high specificity in individualized prostate cancer diagnosis.
authors: Chenhui Tang; Zhen Liang; Weigang Yan

title: Patient-Specific Implant Design: Current Evidence for Artificial Intelligence, Imaging and Computational Planning—A Systematic Review of the Biomedical-Indexed Literature
abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Patient-specific skeletal implants are designed through a pipeline of imaging, computational planning and, increasingly, artificial intelligence. Each pillar has its own validation literature, but no review has asked what evidence supports each one in implant design itself. We mapped that evidence from the biomedical-indexed literature in this paper. METHODS: A systematic review was conducted under a protocol committed before retrieval (PRISMA 2020, PRISMA-S, SWiM). MEDLINE, Europe PMC, Crossref and OpenAlex were searched on 2 and 3 September 2026 for primary studies from 2015 onwards applying artificial intelligence, an evaluated imaging pipeline or computational planning to an implant whose geometry derives from the individual patient's anatomy. Engineering indexes were unavailable, so this review maps biomedical-indexed literature, and a bounded probe was used to estimate what that omits. Two artificial intelligence screeners from different vendors screened every record; every clinical study was appraised twice, independently, by assessors from different vendors. Claims about validation quality are reported on the studies read in full. All screening, charting and appraisals were machine-performed and no human-verified subsample exists. RESULTS: Of 5059 records, 639 studies were included: 373 technical studies, 179 clinical series, 75 comparative studies and 12 randomised trials. Computational planning was applied in 601, an evaluated imaging step in 219 and artificial intelligence in 36. Randomised evidence came from 12 small trials, 10 of them craniomaxillofacial, which evaluated the delivered implant rather than the planning method; virtual surgical planning was used in 11 of them. When restricting to the four studies that measure deviation from the virtual plan, with smaller meaning better, patient-specific implants deviated less from the plan (standardised mean difference -1.21, 95% CI -1.69 to -0.74). Revision or removal was less frequent (3 of 135 against 25 of 149; risk ratio 0.28, 95% CI 0.11 to 0.72); operative time, complications and infection gave intervals compatible with a difference either way. No randomised trial was at low risk of bias, and 69 of 75 comparative studies were at serious risk, mostly of unadjusted confounding, so all estimates are of very low certainty. Among technical studies read in full, independent validation material was used in fewer than half, and files were shared in about one in fourteen. Of 36 artificial intelligence studies, 4 were evaluated on independent data, 2 were used for a real patient, none were clinically comparative, and 8 of 17 cranial studies relied on AutoImplant family benchmarks. CONCLUSIONS: The design pipeline is unequally validated: planning has clinical evidence concentrated in one region, computational methods are widely applied but rarely validated independently or shared, and artificial intelligence has benchmark evidence for cranial defect completion and little else. Outcome studies of patient-specific implants should be read as evidence about whole pipelines, and future studies should evaluate the components.
