title: Systematic Review of Artificial Intelligence in Pre-Implant Radiographic Imaging: A Structured Qualitative Synthesis of Performance Across Imaging Modalities and AI Architectures.
abstract:
Purpose

To evaluate contemporary evidence on artificial intelligence (AI) applied to radiographic imaging for pre-implant dental assessment and treatment planning, with emphasis on the distinction between technical algorithmic performance and clinically oriented planning outcomes.

Materials and methods

Peer-reviewed original studies published from January 2021 through December 2025 were identified through PubMed/MEDLINE, the Cochrane Library, ScienceDirect, JSTOR, and supplementary searches. Eligible studies used radiographic imaging as an integral input to AI for pre-implant assessment, planning, decision support, virtual positioning, or outcome prediction. Reporting completeness was assessed with CLAIM 2024. Risk of bias was assessed with QUADAS-3 for eligible diagnostic/test-accuracy studies, PROBAST+AI for the prognostic prediction-model study, and RoB 2 for the randomized clinical study. Owing to heterogeneity, findings were synthesized qualitatively.

Results

Thirty-six studies were included. CBCT was the predominant modality. Applications included anatomical detection and segmentation, bone assessment, decision support, implant-position prediction, automated virtual placement, workflow integration, and preoperative outcome prediction. Segmentation and anatomical-analysis studies generally reported high task-specific performance, while clinically oriented positional accuracy and planning outcomes were more variable. AI frequently reduced workflow time. QUADAS-3 was applicable to five studies; four had high overall risk of bias and one unclear risk. The prognostic prediction-model and randomized clinical studies also had high risk of bias under their respective tools.

Conclusions

AI shows greatest current support for anatomical analysis and selected workflow tasks. Evidence for autonomous implant positioning and outcome prediction remains limited and heterogeneous. Current findings support clinician-supervised integration, with further multicenter external testing, standardized clinically meaningful outcomes, reproducibility, and prospective evaluation required before broader routine implementation.
authors: Jeevitha M, Balaji P, Kavya BT, Rajesh KS, Keerthana GS.

title: Systemic Diseases and the Eye: A Translational Perspective on Diabetes
abstract: Diabetes mellitus is a global chronic disease that affects the whole body and not just glucose metabolism. In diabetes, non-invasive ocular changes can help understand microvascular, neurodegenerative, and inflammatory processes. This analysis looks at the eye as a biomarker platform for diabetes-related disease, with retinal imaging informing systemic pathophysiology and the emergence of AI-assisted approaches. With improvements in optical coherence tomography (OCT) and OCT angiography, it is possible to observe neurovascular changes that can occur before the clinical onset of diabetic retinopathy. Issues in the retina have also been connected to problems with the heart, brain, kidneys, and cognition. However, much of the evidence for problems involving the heart and cognition comes from studies on people without diabetes. Also, most of the available data are observational, rather than coming from controlled studies. As a result, retinal measurements should be considered candidate biomarkers rather than clinically validated predictors or surrogate endpoints for systemic outcomes. Artificial Intelligence (AI) has reached a phase of clinical maturity such that it can be used in the automated screening of diabetic retinopathy. However, it remains investigational for systemic risk prediction, such as for chronic kidney disease, cardiovascular outcomes, and cognitive decline. Equally, the therapeutic implications of retinal neurodegeneration and other imaging biomarkers are under-validated for systemic decisions. Before retinal biomarkers can be used in precision diabetes care, we need more diabetes-specific prospective studies to establish standardized measurements, the clinical meaning of thresholds, incremental predictive value above and beyond established risk factors, reproducibility, cost-effectiveness, and evidence of improved outcomes.
authors: Matteo Capobianco; Marco Zeppieri; Simonetta Gaia Nicolosi; N Castellino; F. Cappellani; Irene Gattazzo; Caterina Gagliano

title: TASTY AND HEALTHY DIET REDUCES FECAL CALPROTECTIN IN HIGH-RISK FIRST-DEGREE RELATIVES OF PATIENTS WITH CROHN'S DISEASE: PIONIR RANDOMIZED CROSSOVER TRIAL.
abstract:
Background

With the rising prevalence of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), preventing new-onset disease becomes a priority. The PIONIR (Preventing IBD ONset in Individuals at Risk) randomized controlled trial explored whether the Tasty&Healthy (T&H) diet reduces inflammatory markers in high-risk first-degree relatives (FDRs) of patients with Crohn's disease (CD).

Methods

FDRs with persistently elevated fecal calprotectin (FC, >70μg/g) and, at most, nonspecific mucosal abnormalities (edema or ≤10 aphthous ulcers) on video-capsule endoscopy or ileocolonoscopy were randomized to T&H or habitual diet (HD) for 8 weeks, followed by crossover for additional 8 weeks. Treatment effect on the primary outcome, FC response, was analyzed using generalized estimating equations for the two-period, two-sequence crossover design, following the intention-to-treat principle.

Results

Twenty-nine FDRs were randomized (n=14 T&H-first, n=15 HD-first). At week 8, median FC was lower with T&H (64μg/g [IQR 44-127]) vs. HD (112μg/g [74-227]; P=.022). FC decreased by ≥50% in 71% on T&H versus 27% on HD (RR=2.68 [95%CI 1.09-6.60]; P=.016). Across both crossover periods, estimated marginal mean FC declined from 185μg/g [95%CI 144-237] by 61% to 72μg/g [95%CI 57-91] with T&H, versus 38% to 114μg/g [95%CI 93-140] with HD (ratio 0.63 [95%CI 0.51-0.80], translating to 37% overall decrease with T&H; P<0.001). Six microbial species differed between diets after FDR correction. By week 8, 79% rated T&H acceptable and 83% had good or complete adherence.

Conclusion

These findings demonstrate the modifiability of low-grade intestinal inflammation in healthy high-risk FDRs with persistent FC elevation but without diagnostic endoscopic evidence of CD, supporting long-term dietary prevention trials (ClinicalTrials.gov #NCT05211518).
authors: Turner D, Kenigsberg S, Plotkin L, Aharoni-Frutkoff Y, Sokolik M, Focht G, Gasasa S, Turpin W, Waslyk AM, Ledder O, Griffiths AM, Martincevic I, Huynh HQ, Godny L, Avni-Biron I, Torres J, Panaccione R, Jacobson K, Otley A, Sharar-Fischler T, Li Q, Azulay A, Sigall-Boneh R, Lee SH, Croitoru K.

title: Teledentistry: Bringing Dental Care Closer to Every Home
abstract: Abstract Teledentistry represents a transformative integration of telecommunication technologies into dental practice, enabling the remote exchange of clinical data, high-resolution images, patient histories, and expert consultations for diagnosis, treatment planning, and longitudinal care management. This modality significantly enhances accessibility to oral health services, particularly in geographically isolated or underserved populations, while optimizing operational efficiency, reducing healthcare expenditures, and minimizing patient travel burdens. It effectively mitigates urban-rural disparities, facilitates interdisciplinary collaboration, and supports continuous professional education. This expanded review delves deeply into teledentistry's historical evolution, multifaceted operational frameworks, underlying technical infrastructures, diverse clinical applications across dental specialties, robust evidentiary base from global studies, and critical ethical, legal, regulatory, and economic dimensions. Furthermore, it incorporates contemporary advancements—such as artificial intelligence (AI)-augmented diagnostics, 5G-enabled real-time interactions, and blockchain-secured data transmission—and prognosticates future trajectories, including integration with robotic systems and wearable sensors, to underscore its pivotal role in reshaping equitable, sustainable oral healthcare delivery in the digital era.
authors: Avantika Tuli
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Telemedicine in Retinopathy of Prematurity: A Review of Current Evidence and Clinical Outcomes
abstract: Background/Objectives: Retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) is a leading cause of preventable childhood visual impairment, particularly in settings where access to specialized ophthalmologic care is limited. Telemedicine offers an alternative approach to ROP screening and monitoring through remote retinal imaging and expert interpretation. This narrative review aimed to evaluate the diagnostic performance, clinical benefits, implementation challenges, and future perspectives of telemedicine in ROP screening and management. Methods: A narrative literature review was conducted with consideration of the Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles (SANRA) criteria. PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar were searched in August and August 2026 for relevant publications from January 2000 to the search date. Two authors independently screened titles and abstracts, followed by full-text assessment according to predefined eligibility criteria. A total of 143 scientific articles and other high-quality sources were included in the final narrative synthesis. Evidence was evaluated qualitatively, without a formal risk-of-bias assessment. Findings: The reviewed literature indicates that telemedicine can expand access to ROP screening, facilitate remote specialist consultation, support longitudinal disease monitoring, and improve the triage of infants requiring urgent assessment. In selected settings, remote retinal image interpretation has demonstrated diagnostic performance comparable to conventional examinations for clinically significant and vision-threatening ROP. Artificial intelligence-based assessment and smartphone-based retinal imaging represent promising approaches to improving screening accessibility and workflow efficiency, particularly in resource-limited settings. However, implementation remains constrained by equipment costs, infrastructure limitations, image quality, workforce training requirements, and ethical and legal considerations. Conclusions: Telemedicine represents a promising complementary strategy for ROP screening and management, with the potential to improve access to timely specialist assessment and help prevent ROP-related visual impairment. Its successful integration into clinical practice requires sustainable infrastructure, standardized protocols, trained personnel, and reliable referral pathways that ensure timely in-person examination and treatment when indicated. Further research is needed to establish the effectiveness, cost-efficiency, and long-term sustainability of different telemedicine-based approaches across diverse healthcare settings.
authors: Ilinca-Medeea Iftime; Andreea Ramona Treteanu; Andreea Pușcașu; Mihai Craiu; Octaviana Cristea; Alina Angelica Ciolpan

title: Tensions in Dental AI Systems Adoption: A Narrative Review of Challenges and Opportunities
abstract: Artificial intelligence-based systems (AIS) are becoming part of dentistry. Their integration raises unresolved tensions for users such as trust, explainability, responsibility, professional autonomy and real-world usefulness. This concise review examines these tensions and discusses how they may shape the adoption of AIS in dentistry. This concise review was designed as a narrative review. An initial screening suggested that challenges associated with the implementation of AIS in dentistry appear to remain insufficiently explored in the dental literature. An author with expertise in marketing then formulated a list of AIS implementation issues considered well established in marketing research, drawing particularly on reference publications from leading journals. Based on these issues, the authors identified a set of tensions, and the dental authors translated them into concrete examples and implications for dental implementation. In dentistry, these tensions arise at three interconnected levels. At the human level, AIS may support diagnosis, risk communication and shared decision-making, but may also foster over-reliance or unjustified rejection. At the human–AIS interface, tools can flag lesions, prioritise cases or automate workflows that redistribute agency and require clear boundaries between assistance, delegation and responsibility. At the AIS level, dental applications face persistent issues of generalisability, privacy, adaptability and validation across populations, devices and care settings. The value of AIS in dentistry will depend less on technical performance alone than on the capacity to design, evaluate and implement user-centered tools with a co-designed approach involving all stakeholders, from patients and clinicians to institutions and decision-makers. Anticipating these tensions may help support trustworthy, context-sensitive and sustainable AIS adoption in oral health care.
authors: Maxime Ducret; Falk Schwendicke; Julien Cloarec

title: Terahertz Antenna Design for Biomedical Sensing and Imaging
abstract: Background/objectives: Research in terahertz (THz) frequency range has accelerated, bridging the gap between microwave and infrared technologies, in response to the increasing demand for quicker data transmission, improved image resolution, and effective biomedical diagnostics. The non-ionizing nature of the THz band makes it highly suitable for high-resolution imaging and noninvasive biomedical sensing. The choice of substrate, however, significantly impacts on THz antenna performance, affecting radiation efficiency, bandwidth, and biocompatibility. This study aims to construct and optimize microstrip patch antennas operating at 1 THz to determine which substrate is best suited for biological sensing and imaging applications. This study also aims to develop a comparative understanding of the impact of substrate dielectric characteristics on antenna performance and their suitability for integration into sixth-generation (6G)-enabled healthcare systems. Methods: CST Microwave Studio was used to model and simulate several THz microstrip patch antennas. A 50-Ω waveguide port was used to excite each antenna, and open boundary conditions were used to simulate free-space propagation. Several substrate materials, such as polyimide, FR4, Rogers RT/Duroid 5880, gallium arsenide (GaAs), and silicon arsenide (SiAs), were selected for comparative analysis of THz antenna performance. To assess return loss, gain, directivity, bandwidth, and radiation efficiency, frequency sweeps were conducted over 0.5–1.5 THz. Finding the substrate material with the best trade-offs between electrical and biological compatibility was the primary goal of the comparative investigation. Results: According to simulation data, polyimide and Rogers RT/Duroid 5880 substrates outperformed FR4, GaAs, and SiAs in terms of antenna performance. With gain values of approximately 5 dBi at 1 THz, these materials demonstrated improved radiation efficiency, a wider impedance bandwidth, and minimum return loss (<−30 dB). In on-body designs, polyimide offers additional benefits, such as flexibility, low dielectric loss, and consistent responsiveness, making it particularly suitable for wearable biomedical devices. The investigation confirmed that impedance matching and the overall radiation behavior are significantly influenced by the substrate’s dielectric constant and loss tangent. The findings indicate the promise of THz antennas for high-speed wireless communication, noninvasive diagnosis, and real-time biological sensing in healthcare settings. Conclusions: This study offers a methodical comparison of THz patch antennas made of various substrate materials for biomedical imaging and sensing. According to the results, polyimide and Rogers RT/Duroid 5880 are the most effective substrates because they provide the best possible balance of biocompatibility, wide bandwidth, and high gain. The integration of these materials into future implantable and wearable medical systems based on THz shows excellent promise. For 6G communication-enabled healthcare networks and next-generation biomedical equipment, the study advances the creation of high-performance antennas. Future work includes exploring flexible and miniature antenna topologies, experimental validation of the proposed designs, and evaluating real-time performance in biological environments.
authors: Mandeep Singh; Simranjit Singh; Simarpreet Kaur

title: The Clinical Efficacy and Diagnostic Accuracy of Artificial Intelligence Across Dental Specialties
abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into modern dentistry has already transformed diagnostic and treatment planning approaches; yet the impact of AI in day-to-day clinical practice remains disjointed across different disciplines. Although the laboratory findings of numerous controlled algorithmic validation trials are quite impressive, we must ask ourselves if the clinical applications of AI will indeed bring improvements to our patients' clinical outcomes as they are applied within the dynamic and unpredictable real-world conditions of dentistry. This comprehensive systematic review consolidates research assessing the diagnostic accuracy and clinical efficacy of AI throughout all specialties of dentistry - from oral and maxillofacial surgery to pedodontics to ascertain whether AI is currently an innovative new technology or an incremental advancement. The PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and IEEE Xplore literature databases were systematically searched for all prospective and retrospective studies on diagnostic accuracy and/or clinical application involving an AI tool versus a established clinical standard of care (from January 2020 to January 2026). Any peer-reviewed publication reporting new data from the use of clinical AI in direct patient care was considered eligible. Measures of diagnostic accuracy (including sensitivity, specificity, and area under the curve - AUC) along with data on AI-guided treatment planning accuracy and any patient-centered outcomes were extracted. Heterogeneity among the studies was assessed by calculating the value, defined as: low heterogeneity (I≤40%), moderate(40%<I<60%), and high(I>60%). Bias in each study was critically assessed using the QUADAS-2 tool, while clinical translation potential was assessed with the ROB-2 tool. The findings indicated considerable disparity in how the validation of AI applications in dentistry was reported. While many deep learning applications achieved impressive results for image-based diagnostics, specifically in radiology (pooled sensitivity=0.94; 95% CI, 0.89-0.97) and oral pathology (pooled AUC >0.90), the real-world clinical applications and surgical uses of AI have not been sufficiently investigated. Very few prospective clinical trials were found, and only 23% of included studies had prospective designs; nearly all studied enterprises exhibited external validity biases and did not detail the process by which AI was integrated into clinical workflows or its actual effects on patient health, leading to the limited analysis of patient-centered variables. Significant challenges exist in transitioning AI developed in laboratory settings into routine chair side clinical application, prompting the necessity for uniform methods to validate AI tools for responsible innovation. An accurate accounting of AI's real-world role in all facets of dentistry would aid clinicians, researchers, and policymakers in understanding AI's true value, informing sensible and evidence-based adoption rather than overzealous enthusiasm.
authors: Ali Ahmed Khubrani; Khalid Alamri; Ahmed Abdurabu; Ahmed Abozor; Hussan Assiri; Mutea Aljamali; Abdulwahab Saad Alamri; Gamal Hafedh; Rawan Labani; Ibrahim Al Monjem; Samar Ahmad Omier; Saba Almassri; Areej Maher Alshalian

title: The Dental Operating Microscope in Endodontics: A Narrative Review of Clinical Applications, Supporting Evidence, and Limitations
abstract: The dental operating microscope (DOM) is now widely used in endodontics, but the strength of the evidence supporting its use differs between procedures. This narrative review summarizes the historical development and technical principles of the DOM, evaluates the evidence for its use in the main endodontic procedures, and outlines its limitations. A structured PubMed search covering 1981 to 2026 was supplemented by hand-searching of reference lists. The DOM combines magnification, coaxial illumination, and an upright working posture. In non-surgical root canal treatment, magnification consistently improves the detection of canal orifices, particularly the second mesiobuccal (MB2) canal of maxillary molars, and supports the management of calcified canals, complex anatomy, separated instruments, and perforations. Direct outcome data in non-surgical treatment are limited to observational studies. In vital pulp therapy and regenerative endodontic procedures, the DOM is used mainly to assess the pulp tissue and bleeding and to place materials precisely, but its independent effect on outcomes has not been tested. The strongest outcome evidence comes from endodontic microsurgery, in which a meta-analysis reported a pooled success rate of 94% with high-power magnification, compared with 88% without it, with the benefit concentrated in molars. However, two Cochrane reviews found no eligible randomized controlled trials, and a retrospective comparison of loupes and the microscope in endodontic surgery found no significant difference between them. Longer treatment time, cost, the learning curve, and restricted access in some patients are the main practical limitations. The DOM proves most advantageous when managing microscopic features that require high magnification and significantly impact the clinical outcome. Well-designed clinical trials are needed to determine whether its diagnostic advantages lead to better long-term outcomes.
authors: Serkan Ucmak

title: The Future of Clinical Assessment in US Dental Education: Competency‐Based or Entrustable Professional Activities?
abstract: In the late 1990s, US dental education embraced competency-based education (CBE), replacing time- and procedure-based requirements with an outcomes-oriented approach centered on demonstrated abilities and readiness for independent practice. Nearly three decades later, entrustable professional activities (EPAs) is emerging as an assessment framework. Do EPAs represent a new paradigm for dentistry, or are they an extension of assessment principles already embedded in competency-based dental education (CBDE)? This paper examines the similarities and differences between CBDE and entrustable professional activities-based education (EPABE), with particular attention to terminology, assessment methods, decision-making, and the evidence required to demonstrate compliance with US predoctoral dental education standards. CBDE commonly assesses competencies, defined as knowledge, skills, and professional behaviors, through discrete examinations, simulations, structured clinical assessments, or patient-based competency examinations. These methods can establish whether a learner performs a defined task at an acceptable level, but assessments conducted at a single point in time may provide limited evidence of consistency, adaptability, judgment, or sustained performance across clinical contexts. EPABE assesses authentic, integrated professional activities through repeated observation in the clinical workplace. Entrustment decisions address the level of supervision a learner requires and are informed by longitudinal evidence of reliable performance, including technical skill, clinical judgment, efficiency, communication, and professionalism. Unlike many competency assessments, entrustment is dynamic: It may be maintained, withdrawn, or re-established as performance changes. EPABE therefore requires assessment systems capable of aggregating and displaying sequential performance data to support defensible decisions about readiness for independent practice. We argue that EPAs offer a clinically grounded evolution of competency assessment but should not be viewed as a universally sufficient method. Infrequent, unpredictable, or high-risk activities may be better assessed through simulation, case-based methods, or other summative approaches. Hybrid assessment models that combine longitudinal workplace-based observations with targeted high-stakes assessments may provide the most valid, feasible, and CODA-aligned evidence of predoctoral dental graduates' readiness for practice.
authors: Cecile A. Feldman; Emily H. Sabato; Janine Fredericks-Younger; Kenneth J. Markowitz; Kim E. Fenesy

title: The Role of Micro-Ultrasound in Prostate Cancer Detection
abstract: PURPOSE OF REVIEW: To synthesize current evidence on the role of 29-MHz micro-ultrasound (microUS) in prostate cancer (PCa) detection and to define its position relative to multiparametric MRI (mpMRI) across the diagnostic pathway. We conducted a narrative review of prospective, comparative, and randomized studies, with clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa) detection as the primary endpoint. RECENT FINDINGS: MicroUS provides ~ 70-µm axial resolution and enables real-time PRI-MUS-based risk stratification. Across head-to-head studies, microUS achieves diagnostic performance comparable to mpMRI. Evidence supports utility in biopsy-naïve patients, selected MRI-negative men with persistent clinical suspicion, repeat-biopsy settings, active surveillance, and local tumor staging, while combined mpMRI-microUS approaches have been shown to maximize yield of csPCa detection. Key limitations include operator dependence, interobserver variability, lack of validated biopsy-avoidance thresholds, and reduced sensitivity in anterior lesions. MicroUS is a practical, high-resolution platform that complements mpMRI and may enhance accessibility, efficiency, and precision in prostate cancer care.
authors: Navid Jabalameli; Feres Camargo Maluf; Fatema Bhinderwala; Thomas James Polascik; Soroush Rais‐Bahrami

title: The Smart Root Canal Era: A Review of Artificial Intelligence in Endodontics
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) technologies, especially machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) algorithms, are being used more and more to interpret radiographs, identify root canal morphology, detect periapical lesions, and accurately forecast treatment outcomes.By improving clinical efficiency, treatment planning, and diagnostic accuracy, AI is quickly revolutionizing the area of endodontics.By lowering human error, these tools help clinicians make quicker, more evidence-based judgements.Cone beam computed tomography (CBCT) analysis, automated working length (WL) determination, and retreatment requirements evaluation are all supported by AI in endodontic practice.Additionally, smart tools and robotic systems powered by AI have the potential to increase procedural accuracy during root canal therapy.Notwithstanding its benefits, issues including algorithm bias, data privacy, expense, and the requirement for physician training continue to be major obstacles.However, the use of AI in endodontics is a potential step toward more individualized, effective, and minimally intrusive patient care.To maximize its potential possibilities, dental professionals and technology developers must continue to collaborate and conduct research.This abstract gives an overview of AI in endodontics.
authors: Ragavi P Pillai; Jayanthi Govindarajan; Susila V Anand; Ottilingam Kamalakannan Preethi; Aravind Kumar Duraivel

title: The future of robotic artificial intelligence in acute care surgery: an early proving ground and a final frontier for autonomous surgical robotics
abstract: Acute care surgery (ACS), spanning emergency general surgery, trauma surgery, and surgical critical care, demands high-stakes decisions in settings characterized by hemodynamic instability, distorted anatomy, contamination, and time pressure. Artificial intelligence (AI) is proposed as a means to reduce cognitive burden, standardize technically sensitive tasks, and extend surgical capability in resource-constrained environments. This review examines the autonomy continuum in surgical AI, with ACS as the primary lens. We argue that ACS occupies a paradoxical position: it has produced the earliest preclinical demonstrations of autonomous surgical robotics, yet the very conditions that motivate autonomy in this specialty make it among the most challenging environments in which to deploy these systems safely in human patients. For ACS, the central question is less whether AI can perform surgical tasks than how autonomy should be sequenced and bounded for emergency surgery. We synthesize the literature across four domains: (1) how autonomy is defined and operationalized in surgical AI and robotics; (2) the current and emerging spectrum of automation in operative environments; (3) the technical feasibility of automation for ACS-relevant tasks; and (4) the ethical boundaries of autonomy in high-risk, time-critical cases. We argue that the safest course is incremental: deploying supervised task autonomy where safety properties are demonstrable and reserving higher autonomy for rigorously evaluated, tightly bounded domains. Realizing this course will require evaluation strategies that align autonomy level to clinical risk, preserve meaningful human oversight, support post-market monitoring, and address liability, patient trust, and equitable access.
authors: Joel Grunhut; Ruhika Iyer; Jesse Haworth; Gabriel A. Brat; Axel Krieger; Jeffrey K. Jopling

title: The future of surgery
abstract: Abstract Surgery is entering a period of accelerated transformation driven by artificial intelligence, robotics, and emerging postmodern medical technologies. Unlike prior technological shifts, innovation cycles are compressing into years, challenging established models of evidence generation, regulation, training, and professional identity. This Perspective examines plausible trajectories for digital surgery, emphasizing ethical, educational, and institutional adaptation under conditions of continuous technological acceleration rather than offering definitive predictions.
authors: Donald W. Weaver; J. Edson Pontes; David S. Edelman; S. Kiran Koya; David Ellis

title: The perceived facilitators and barriers to the potential adoption of teledentistry among dental care providers in Saudi Arabia: A systematic review
abstract: Teledentistry has emerged as a tool that holds great potential to enhance access, efficiency, and continuity of oral healthcare delivery. In Saudi Arabia, its adoption is important in the context of the health transformation programme and Vision 2030, particularly given the high prevalence of dental caries among schoolchildren. Despite this potential, actual implementation is still limited. In this context, there is a need to systematically assess the factors influencing its potential adoption from the care providers' perspectives. This review aimed to systematically identify how dental care providers perceive the facilitators and barriers to the adoption of teledentistry in Saudi Arabia, with a focus on the perception of dental care providers, including dental students. Following PRISMA 2020 and SWiM guidelines, PubMed, Scopus, Medline, Embase, and CINAHL databases were searched, covering publications up to 4 July 2025. The PICO framework was used to define the inclusion and exclusion criteria, and the CASP checklist was used to assess study quality. Data were synthesised using vote counting by direction of effect, categorising findings into facilitators and barriers. Out of 156 records, 11 studies met the inclusion criteria. Study quality ranged from 7 to11 out of 11 based on the CASP checklist for cross-sectional studies. Key findings included potential facilitators such as improved access, efficiency and cost-effectiveness, communication and referral enhancements, educational benefits, and positive perception of technology. The key reported barriers were limited awareness and training, infrastructure and equipment reliability, privacy and data security, cost and financial issues, diagnostic accuracy, and the preference for in-person meetings. While teledentistry holds great potential, its integration in Saudi Arabia could be hindered by educational and technical challenges. Addressing them through improved infrastructure, enhanced training and integration into dental curricula, and strengthened regulatory frameworks may facilitate and support equitable adoption.
authors: Amjad Hakami; Sarika Mohan

title: The rise of agentic AI in drug discovery from static tools to autonomous virtual scientists
abstract: Driven by large language models, AI agents are transforming drug discovery, enabling AI to break free from task-specific tools and advance toward the vision of autonomous virtual scientists. This perspective reviews applications across the R&D lifecycle. To evaluate system maturity, we introduce a 6-level "Spectrum of Agentic Autonomy." We advocate for novel evaluation paradigms centered on full-chain traceability and outline adoption barriers, positioning AI agents as pragmatic scientist-in-the-loop co-pilots.
authors: Donghai Zhao; Meijing Fang; Lexiao Mao; Yuchen Zhu; Qun Su; Hui Shi; Hongxia Xu; Lanqing Li; Tingjun Hou; Chang-Yu Hsieh

title: The role of 11C-Choline PET/CT scanning of the bladder in the diagnosis of late radiation cystitis (pilot study)
abstract: The aim of the study was to consider the possibilities of using 11 C-choline PET/CT for visual and ultrastructural assessment of bladder wall barrier functions in women with late radiation cystitis. Materials and methods. A comprehensive examination of four women with varying visual manifestations of late radiation cystitis was conducted. The affinity of the bladder wall for 11 С-choline was studied using PET/CT as the standardized uptake level of labeled molecules (SUV max ) coming from urine in combination with the results of scanning electron microscopy of all bladder wall elements in a single block. Results. It was found that the affinity of the bladder wall for labeled 11 С-choline molecules in late radiation cystitis correlates with the severity of ultrastructural changes in its wall, which can be used as an additional marker of bladder barrier function integrity. Conclusion. The clinical application of our developed computer program allows urologists to obtain a probable visual and ultrastructural 3D reconstruction of all elements of the bladder wall using the digital value (SUV max ) of 11 С choline PET/CT.
authors: Бердичевский Борис Аркадьевич; Grigory Zubik; Irina V. Pavlova; Artem R. Gonyaev; Д.А. Учаев; M.A. Korabelnikov Korabelnikov

title: The role of digital twin technology in transforming medical education: a scoping review
abstract: This scoping review mapped the current landscape of digital twin applications in health professions education and identified gaps in the evidence. The review followed Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and PRISMA-ScR reporting guidelines. Six bibliographic databases (MEDLINE via PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, CINAHL, and IEEE Xplore) were searched from inception to March 10, 2026, supplemented by a register search (ClinicalTrials.gov) and a search of Google Scholar as an additional source. Studies describing the development, implementation, or evaluation of digital twins in health professions education were included. Data were extracted using a standardized charting form, and methodological quality was assessed with appropriate JBI critical appraisal tools. Findings were subsequently reviewed in a one-round modified Delphi consultation with stakeholders. Seventeen studies published between 2022 and 2025 met the inclusion criteria. Because three publications report the same critical care platform, these 17 reports describe 15 distinct systems. Digital twins were applied at patient-, organ-, device-, and environment- or institutional-levels across surgery, critical care, anatomy, radiology, and dentistry. Each included system was verified against three defining characteristics of digital twins: personalization, a counterpart-derived data pathway, and generative or predictive capability. Four studies satisfied all three, eight satisfied two, four satisfied one, and one proposed all three without implementing any; only a single study reported continuous closed-loop bidirectional synchronization between a physical and a virtual counterpart. Most studies were technical reports or proof-of-concept demonstrations, and no controlled educational trials were identified. Evaluations focused primarily on learner perceptions and satisfaction, whereas only one study reported quantitative learning outcomes. No study assessed behavioral transfer to clinical practice or patient-level outcomes. Digital twin technology in health professions education is, therefore, best characterized as an active area of technical development that remains educationally unvalidated. The principal contribution of this review is a structured map of what has been built, how it has been verified against the digital twin construct, and precisely where educational evidence is absent. Future research should emphasize theory-informed development, rigorous experimental designs, and validated educational outcomes to determine the educational value of these approaches.
authors: Sogand Sarmadi; Akbar Zare‐Kaseb; Neda Sanaie; Shabnam Shariatpanahi; Mahsa Boozari Pour

title: Thirty years of paediatric colonic motility assessment modalities: a systematic review
abstract: Introduction: Disorders of paediatric colonic motility may arise following operative repair of congenital colorectal conditions, as well as spontaneously. This may lead to symptoms of faecal incontinence, in addition to constipation. Management of such typically requires several investigations, clinic appointments and treatment strategies. Different investigation modalities are available to objectively and accurately describe gastrointestinal transit time. In the paediatric setting, most of these investigations are invasive, involve radiation, or require patient hospital admission. This systematic review summarises paediatric colonic motility investigations by compiling an assessment of modalities available over the last 31 years, their uses, advantages, and limitations. Methods: The following databases (Cochrane, EMBASE, MEDLINE) were interrogated. The keywords used were "paediatric", "pediatric", "colonic motility", and "investigation", searched as keywords and Medical Subject Heading/Emtree subject heading. Studies that were included were case reports, prospective and retrospective cohort studies, case series, and reviews discussing and comparing modalities to investigate paediatric (< 18 years old) colonic motility. Inclusion criteria included papers published in the last 31 years, including data about paediatric colonic motility investigations indications, rationale for investigation of choice, advantages and limitations. The protocol was registered with PROSPERO (ID 1034832). Study selection was conducted according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) protocol. Results: The initial search yielded 1061 papers. After removing duplicates and screening abstracts and full texts, 122 papers were included for analysis. The most widely-used motility investigation types were radiopaque marker studies, scintigraphy and colonic manometry. However, these had limitations, including radiation exposure, the need for an experienced-centre, and invasiveness. Hydrocolonic ultrasonography was radiation-free, not expensive, and safely repeatable for serial monitoring or assessment, but results were operator-dependent. Newer non-invasive tests that aim to limit radiation exposure have been emerging, such as cine-MRI, wireless capsule and the electromagnetic capsule tracking system. Assessment of anorectal function was often combined with colonic motility assessment to provide a full assessment, depending upon the clinical picture and diagnostic objectives. Discussion: Over the last 31 years numerous investigations have been utilised to study bowel anatomy, function, and neuromuscular ability. Each of these modalities have advantages, but also limitations. It is crucial to know the intrinsic characteristics of each modality to help decide which is most appropriate for the clinical indication in question. Radiopaque marker studies, scintigraphy and colonic manometry were the three most widely reported colonic motility studies methods. Evidence regarding colonic motility modalities in paediatrics was limited compared with the adult population. This lack of evidence is likely due to the invasive nature of some of these investigations, costs, radiation exposure, and limited availability at specific centres. It is crucial for clinicians involved in paediatric patient care to be familiar with available tests, their properties, availabilities, and to use the most appropriate investigation to answer each specific clinical question. Conclusions: This systematic review has shown that, to date, there are several colonic motility assessment modalities that all have their advantages, limitations and different indications. It is imperative for clinicians to base their investigative plan on the specific patient, clinical/centre expertise and clinical question. In the future, there is a need to develop a non-invasive, objective, world-wide reproducible and ambulatory method that may provide information on actual day-to-day physiological colonic motility. Systematic Review Registration: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420251034832, PROSPERO CRD420251034832.
authors: Assia Comella; Hannah M. E. Evans‐Barns; Phil G. Dinning; Mark Safe; Misel Trajanovska; Sebastian K. King

title: Toward Precision Colorectal Cancer Screening: Integrating Clinical Risk Stratification, Molecular Biomarkers, and Artificial Intelligence
abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) screening reduces disease incidence and mortality through the detection and removal of precursor lesions and the earlier diagnosis of invasive cancer. However, most current programs remain predominantly age-based, applying broadly uniform tests and intervals to individuals whose underlying risk, lesion biology, screening adherence, and capacity to benefit may differ substantially. Advances in clinical prediction, molecular diagnostics, and artificial intelligence (AI) create opportunities to refine screening according to individual risk and clinical context. This narrative review examines the evolution of CRC screening from conventional population-based strategies toward a precision-screening framework comprising three complementary functions. Clinical risk stratification estimates background susceptibility using demographic, familial, behavioral, metabolic, medical, and previous-screening information. Molecular biomarkers provide biologically distinct information, ranging from inherited susceptibility to signals associated with prevalent colorectal neoplasia. AI may support multimodal risk integration, procedural lesion detection and characterization, and longitudinal reassessment as new clinical and screening information accumulates. These components should not be regarded as a mandatory sequential pathway or as interchangeable sources of evidence; rather, their value depends on the specific clinical question, predicted outcome, time horizon, and decision being supported. Current evidence shows that risk-adapted and multimodal approaches are feasible, but improved prediction or diagnostic performance does not necessarily translate into superior population outcomes. Most precision-screening strategies still lack prospective evidence demonstrating improvements in participation, diagnostic completion, advanced colorectal neoplasia yield, interval CRC, harms, resource use, equity, or cost-effectiveness compared with optimized established screening. The priority for translation is therefore not maximal technological integration, but selective use of additional information when it provides actionable incremental benefit while preserving the accessibility, effectiveness, and public-health strengths of organized screening.
authors: Sorinel Luncă; Ștefan Morărașu; Gabriel Mihail Dimofte

title: Towards Robust Prehensile Manipulation in Open-Ended Environments
abstract: We propose to use Quality-Diversity (QD) algorithms to solve robotic prehensile manipulation tasks in open-ended environments. Our approach enables the efficient discovery of a wide range robust grasp configurations, which serve as reliable starting points for generating diverse prehensile manipulation trajectories on articulated objects. The resulting diversity in manipulation behaviors enhances generalization and adaptability, enabling effective deployment continuously evolving open-world settings.
authors: Mathilde Kappel; Mahdi Khoramshahi; Louis Annabi; Faïz Ben Amar; Stéphane Doncieux

title: Tracker-Free Robotic Ultrasound Calibration with a Spherical-Marker Phantom and Threshold-Free Center Localization
abstract: Robotic ultrasound (US) calibration is essential for accurately relating US images to the robot coordinate system, but accurate and automated calibration remains challenging because existing methods often require complex phantoms or external 3D trackers. In this work, we develop a tracker-free robotic US calibration framework using a spherical-marker phantom and a highly automated perception pipeline for sphere-center localization. The proposed threshold-free image-processing method localizes the spherical feature based on each US image's intensity distribution, eliminating hand-tuned intensity thresholds and improving robustness across imaging settings without per-system retuning. Multi-pose observations of the spherical fiducial are then used to estimate the US-to-EE transformation without external tracking or prior localization of the sphere center in the robot base frame. We validate the proposed framework on a robotic US platform through repeated sphere scans and further assess the calibrated system using geometrically distinct phantoms with known CAD models. Across 12 cross-validation folds, single-marker calibration achieved sphere-center accuracy and precision of $1.75\pm0.51$ mm and $0.85\pm0.11$ mm, respectively, compared with $1.72\pm0.51$ mm and $0.84\pm0.12$ mm for three-marker calibration. Across the three reconstruction sets, the single-marker calibration yielded pooled post-registration point-to-surface MAE$\pm$SD values of $0.41\pm0.35$ mm for the cone and $0.50\pm0.41$ mm for the triangular prism, closely matching the three-marker results of $0.40\pm0.35$ mm and $0.48\pm0.40$ mm, respectively.
authors: Kyoungmo Koo; Guangshen Ma; X. P. Wang; Mark Draelos

title: Tracking in-silico Lagrangian sensors in a lab-scale stirred tank reactor
abstract: Lagrangian sensors have shown promise to improve operator awareness of conditions inside a chemical reactor but three-dimensional tracking remains a mostly unsolved challenge. We explore a setup where in-silico sensors, based on a recently proposed real-world design, are tracked using data from an accelerometer and magnetometer available from a built-in inertial measurement unit. Filtering algorithms, using a bespoke dynamical model, are used to process these readings into position estimates. We compare tracking performance of an extended Kalman filter, a particle filter and the unscented Kalman filter implemented in the pykalman library. Our numerical experiments track in-silico particles moving in an analytically given three-dimensional vortex as well as in the experimentally measured flow-field of a lab-scale stirred tank reactor. Using the Maxey-Riley-Gatignol equations for the movement of inertial particles as ground-truth, we demonstrate that the extended Kalman filter and the particle filter reconstruct trajectories from noisy synthetic data with mean relative errors below 3%.
authors: Vamika Rathi; Fatima Sehar; Finn Sommer; Sebastian Götschel; Eike Steuwe; Alexandra von Kameke; Daniel Ruprecht

title: Translational Applications of Retinal Biomarkers in Chronic Cardiovascular, Neurological, Metabolic, and Renal Diseases
abstract: Imaging the retina is a powerful non-invasive probe of systemic vascular, neurological, metabolic, and renal disease, making it a cornerstone of the new field of systemic oculomics. Advanced retinal imaging techniques like optical coherence tomography (OCT) and optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA) provide detailed imaging of structural and microvascular changes potentially associated with systemic disease. Derived from fundus photography, structural imaging, vascular imaging, and artificial intelligence-based image analysis, retinal biomarkers have been associated with cardiovascular and cerebrovascular disease, neurodegenerative disorders, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, and related clinical outcomes. However, the translational maturity of these biomarkers is variable depending on imaging modality, target disease, intended clinical use, and level of validation. Longitudinally, retinal vascular characteristics have been associated with cardiovascular as well as cerebrovascular outcomes. In addition, optical coherence tomography has provided reproducible measures of neuroaxonal injury in selected neurological conditions. This is especially true for multiple sclerosis. The majority of retinal biomarkers in Alzheimer disease, Parkinson disease, chronic kidney disease, and systemic risk prediction remain experimental because of heterogeneous methodologies, insufficient external validation, and insufficient evidence for incremental clinical utility. Diabetes is the most developed translational model with established retinal screening pathways and validated ocular applications of imaging and artificial intelligence, although these cannot be directly extrapolated to systemic diagnosis or treatment guidance. This narrative review assesses retinal biomarkers for cardiovascular, neurological, metabolic, and renal disease with a focus on analytical validity, clinical validity, incremental value, clinical utility, and implementation. The retina is increasingly accepted as a site for discovery of systemic biomarkers and adjunctive risk assessment, although most applications to systemic disease remain to be standardized, validated independently, and studied prospectively before being suitable for routine clinical use.

title: Transoral robotic reconstruction of a posterior palatal defect using an upper arm flap following polymorphous adenocarcinoma resection: a novel minimally invasive approach
abstract: Abstract Background Surgical management of malignant tumors in the orofacial region frequently necessitates extensive resection, resulting in significant functional and aesthetic morbidity. In younger patients, these sequelae carry a substantial psychosocial burden, emphasizing the need for minimally invasive reconstructive strategies that preserve quality of life while maintaining oncological safety. Case presentation A 36-year-old female patient presented with a small 1 × 1 cm swelling at the junction of the hard and soft palate on the left side. Incisional biopsy confirmed a malignant minor salivary gland tumor but did not permit definitive subtyping. The final diagnosis of a polymorphous adenocarcinoma (PAC), conventional subtype, was established only on the complete resection specimen. Following oncologically adequate resection, including partial hard palate and tuberosity removal, a 3 × 4 cm defect was reconstructed with a free upper arm flap. Supermicrovascular anastomoses to the superior labial and facial arteries (vessel diameter ~ 0.2 mm) were performed via a transoral approach using the Symani ® robotic surgical system with 20× motion scaling. Venous anastomoses to the facial vein were completed end-to-end and end-to-side via the same intraoral access. Selective lymph node sampling of the four radiologically prominent ipsilateral level II lymph nodes through a minimal cervical incision showed no metastases, both on frozen section and on final histopathology (0/4). Final histopathology demonstrated a 15 mm low-grade PAC resected in sano, without lymphovascular invasion, without unequivocal perineural infiltration and without bone invasion, classified as pT1 pN0 (0/4) cM0, R0. Postoperative course was uneventful; functional rehabilitation including speech and swallowing therapy is ongoing. Conclusions Robotic-assisted supermicrosurgery using the Symani ® system enabled safe transoral free flap reconstruction of a posterior palatal defect with anastomoses at the sub 0.2 mm scale. This approach minimizes donor-site morbidity and demonstrates the feasibility of intraoral robotic supermicrosurgery as a novel reconstructive modality in head and neck oncology.
authors: Henning Wieker; Juliane Wagner; Jörg Wiltfang; Aydın Gülses; Johannes Heinrich Spille

title: Transoral robotic surgery in otorhinolaryngology: patient perspectives and determinants of outcomes
abstract: A retrospective study in the North of the Netherlands Simple SummaryTransoral Robotic Surgery (TORS) is increasingly used for various conditions, yet its success and failure remain underexplored.In this multicenter study, we assessed 220 TORS interventions across 211 patients.Success criteria differed by condition, including tumor identification for CUP, resection margins for malignancies, and symptom improvement for benign cases like OSA and chronic lingual tonsillitis.Predictors of success varied, with factors such as patient comorbidity, tumor characteristics, and demographics playing roles.Conversely, failure predictors encompassed postoperative complications and pain, linked to patient health and demographics.These insights into TORS outcomes may aid in patient selection and counseling across different conditions, informing clinical practice and enhancing patient care.
authors: Alexandra G. L. Toppenberg

title: Trends and safety of small bowel endoscopy in Crohn’s disease in Japan: a large-scale claims database analysis
abstract: Background/Aims: Evidence on the population-level utilization and safety of balloon-assisted endoscopy (BAE) and small bowel capsule endoscopy (SBCE) for Crohn's disease in Japan is limited. We aimed to characterize trends in BAE, SBCE, and patency capsule examination, as well as adverse events (AEs). Methods: We analyzed the Medical Data Vision claims database. Annual utilization was assessed per patient-year for the complete calendar years 2009-2021. AEs were defined by claimsbased therapeutic interventions after procedures. The association between patency capsule examination and SBCE-related AEs was assessed using generalized estimating equations (GEE) adjusted for age, sex, and calendar year. Results: Among 19,881 eligible patients with Crohn's disease, 4,657 BAE and 2,679 SBCE procedures were identified. Modality switching was uncommon, with 83.9% of patients with ≥2 examinations (n =1,683) undergoing the same modality at the second examination. Utilization of both modalities increased over time, and patency capsule examination before SBCE increased from 2013 to 2021. SBCE-related AEs were rare in patients with patency capsule examination compared to those without patency capsule examination (0.88% vs. 1.47%). In the main GEE analysis, patency capsule examination was not independently associated with lower odds of SBCE-related AEs (adjusted odds ratio, 0.62; 95% confidence interval, 0.28-1.37; P= 0.235), with a similar result in sensitivity analyses. Conclusions: The use of BAE and SBCE has increased in Japan alongside the spread of patency capsule examination. SBCE-related AEs were uncommon overall and numerically less frequent when preceded by patency assessment.
authors: Shuhei Hosomi; Yu Nishida; Tsuyoshi Yanagida; Koji Fujimoto; Rieko Nakata; Akinari Sawada; Hirotsugu Maruyama; Masaki Ominami; Yuji Nadatani; Shusei Fukunaga; Koji Otani; Yasuhiro Fujiwara

title: Tribology of dental materials: from laboratory metrics to clinical durability: review and translational roadmap
abstract: The functional integrity of dental restorations is known by their resilience within the dynamic and hostile tribological ecosystem of the oral cavity. Despite significant advancements in material science, the premature failure of restorations due to wear remains a critical clinical challenge, rooted in a persistent disconnect between controlled laboratory metrics and unpredictable clinical realities. This review provides a comprehensive critical appraisal of dental tribology, delineating the complex interplay of wear mechanisms, attrition, abrasion, erosion, and abfraction, and evaluating the spectrum of current assessment methodologies, from fundamental in vitro simulations to advanced clinical quantification. We identified the primary limitations hindering accurate material prediction, specifically the lack of protocol standardization, the inability to replicate synergistic degradation processes such as tribo-corrosion, and the exclusion of patient-specific variables. To bridge this translational gap, we proposed a strategic roadmap integrating multi-tiered testing standardization, finite element analysis, and machine learning to enhance predictive capabilities. Furthermore, we advocated for the development of clinically relevant in vitro models that incorporate patient-specific parameters, such as occlusal loading profiles and salivary properties. By shifting the paradigm from descriptive testing to predictive, patient-centric material science, this review outlined a transformative pathway for the development of next-generation restorative materials, ultimately optimizing clinical longevity and treatment outcomes.
authors: Naif H. Al-Qahtani; Shahad Alqahtani; Shorooq K. Almajhad; Amjaad M. Almarzoogi; Noha Taymour

title: Trust me, I’m a robot: relational determinants of social robot acceptance among university students
abstract: Purpose Although social robots are increasingly being used in higher education‚ the relational antecedents of students’ acceptance of these robots remain unexplored. This study re-conceptualises the technology acceptance model (TAM) for social robots by shifting the theoretical focus from utilitarian beliefs toward the relational quality of the human–robot interaction (HRI), positioning trust‚ satisfaction and rapport as main relational antecedents of students’ attitudes and behavioural intentions toward social robots. The study also examines the moderating effects of user motivation‚ empathy‚ risk aversion and technology readiness on the attitude–behavioural intention relationship. Design/methodology/approach Cluster sampling was used to define the sample‚ which comprised 900 university students from six public universities in Greece. Structural equation modelling (SEM) was conducted with AMOS 29 to test the proposed model. Findings Trust‚ satisfaction and rapport are strong positive predictors of student attitude toward social robots‚ which in turn positively influences students’ behavioural intention to use social robots. User motivation‚ empathy and technology readiness motivators (optimism and innovativeness) strengthen the relationship between attitude and behavioural intention towards social robots‚ while risk aversion and technology readiness inhibitors (discomfort and insecurity) attenuate this relationship. Research limitations/implications Despite the contributions achieved here‚ there are some limitations that deserve to be mentioned and suggest promising paths for future research. Because this research used a cross-sectional design‚ it does not allow for causality and the possibility to observe how attitudes and intentions towards social robots develop over time. Future studies with longitudinal designs are needed to test whether the identified antecedents for establishing a relationship with social robots (i.e. trust‚ satisfaction‚ rapport) can increase or decrease with repeated social robot interactions (Donnermann et al.‚ 2022). Practical implications Given the tight connection of trust‚ satisfaction and rapport with students’ perceptions‚ it is important that institutions also consider the quality of the HRI when deciding whether or not to use social robots as teaching assistants. This includes the robots’ ability to build trust through reliable behaviour‚ provide satisfaction through responsive interaction and achieve rapport through attentive‚ empathic and positive communication (Buhmann et al., 2026; Lemon and Dhanesh, 2026). Originality/value This study adds to the literature by being one of the first to conceptualise social robot acceptance as a relational phenomenon‚ positioning trust‚ satisfaction and rapport as core antecedents of attitude and behavioural intention‚ a theoretical move entirely absent from existing social robot acceptance and educational HRI research. Beyond the direct effects‚ this study introduces two theoretically grounded categories of individual-level moderators: psychological-relational moderators (motivation‚ empathy and risk aversion) and technology-related moderators (technology readiness)‚ which collectively provide a coherent and empirically novel account of the boundary conditions governing social robot acceptance among university students.

title: Ultra-thin, forward-viewing OCT endoscope using a rotating angle-cleaved fiber
abstract: While ultra-thin optical coherence tomography (OCT) probes using rotating fibers have been demonstrated in side-viewing configurations, achieving fully miniaturized forward-viewing OCT endoscopy remains challenging because of the need to incorporate a lateral scanning mechanism. Here, we report a forward-viewing OCT fiber endoscope that can fit inside a protective tube with an inner diameter of 0.16 mm, enabling an endoscope with an outer diameter of 0.31 mm. The rotating fiber assembly incorporates a gradient-index fiber lens and an angle-cleaved length of no-core fiber at the distal tip. This causes the beam to exit at an angle to the endoscope axis, such that rotating the fiber using an external rotary coupler generates circular scanning of the beam over the tissue. Lateral and axial resolutions of 25 µm and 11 µm, respectively, are achieved at focus, with a usable imaging depth range of over 2 mm and an image circle circumference of 950 µm at 1 mm from the fiber tip. An exemplar application in vitreoretinal surgery is demonstrated by ex vivo porcine retinal imaging and real-time monitoring of a surgical tool interacting with the tissue.
authors: Radu-Florin Stancu; Michael R. Hughes; Manuel Jorge M. Marques; Carlo Seneci; Ross Henry; Sebastien Ourselin; Lyndon da Cruz; Christos Bergeles; Adrian Gh. Podoleanu

title: UltraDiff: Differentiable Ray Tracing in Ultrasound for Shape Optimization
abstract: Physically-based differentiable rendering enables gradient-based optimization of scene parameters by matching rendered images to measurements, but has so far mainly focused on light transport. We extend this paradigm to medical ultrasound, where image formation resembles transient rendering: echoes are binned by time-of-flight rather than projected onto an image plane. We present UltraDiff, a modular framework for differentiable ultrasound ray tracing. UltraDiff formulates ultrasound image formation as a path-space integral, gated by travel time between the transducer and tissue interfaces, and derives a Monte Carlo estimator of both the forward model and its gradients with respect to scene parameters. We demonstrate this on an inverse geometry estimation: starting from a sphere, an SDF is optimized until simulated echoes match measured ones, recovering vertebral surfaces from simulated B-mode sweeps and from a real robotic acquisition of a spine phantom. Unlike state-of-the-art ultrasound shape reconstruction methods, which rely on pre-segmented images, our approach operates unsupervised on B-mode images through analysis-by-synthesis, while achieving competitive geometric accuracy. Implemented on top of Mitsuba 3, UltraDiff brings differentiable path tracing to a new sensing modality and provides a foundation for inverse problems in acoustic imaging.

title: UltraWorld: Learning Interactive Ultrasound World Models from Untracked Clinical Videos with Acoustic Sampling Map
abstract: World models can enable autonomous ultrasound scanning by predicting the outcomes of probe motions from local observations. Learning this action--observation relationship typically relies on synchronized video--pose pairs, which are costly to collect at scale and largely unavailable in routine clinical recordings. Reliable action following further requires modeling ultrasound's cross-sectional sampling geometry. We present UltraWorld, a self-distillation recipe that transfers priors from clinical ultrasound videos into interactive world models without real action annotations. Starting from clinical videos, we adapt a video foundation model into an ultrasound generator conditioned on reference images and anatomical masks. Anatomical masks sampled along programmable trajectories through 3D anatomy provide spatial guidance for synthesizing action--video pairs. We then use these synthetic pairs to self-distill the generator into a world model that predicts future observations from local observations and actions, without requiring anatomical masks or other 3D assets at inference time. To further improve action following, we introduce the Acoustic Sampling Map (AsMap), which represents probe poses and imaging settings as pixel-wise 3D sampling positions, beam directions, and depths. Experiments demonstrate improved prediction fidelity and action following. Across nine simulated closed-loop local planning episodes, UltraWorld reduces the mean final distance to the goal and orientation error by 29\% and 38\%, respectively, compared with visual servoing. authors: Keke Yang; Erqi Wang; Sainan Guan; Hongliang Ren

title: Ultralow‐Bias‐Switchable Dual‐Mode Retinomorphic Device for Adaptive Extreme‐Exposure Image Restoration and Event‐Driven Light Source Positioning
abstract: ABSTRACT Safe operation of autonomous driving vision systems requires integrated photodetection and processing capabilities. However, existing vision systems remain constrained by separated architectures and limited adaptability to complex lighting environments. Here, we report a TiO 2 /ZnIn 2 S 4 heterostructure dual‐mode optoelectronic device, enabling on‐demand switching between photodetection and optoelectronic synaptic functions under an ultralow bias of 1 mV. The type‐I heterojunction integrates highly ordered TiO 2 nanotube arrays for directional carrier transport, oxygen vacancies for carrier trapping, and layered ZnIn 2 S 4 nanosheets for enhanced light harvesting and interfacial carrier transfer, enabling bias‐dependent carrier separation and release. As a result, the device exhibits efficient photodetection and tunable synaptic dynamics, enabling adaptive exposure compensation and dynamic image restoration for both overexposed and underexposed visual scenes. When configured into bioinspired spheroidal vision arrays, it further supports wide‐field detection, targeted localization, and early warning of potential hazards. This device highlights a promising approach for adaptive machine vision toward intelligent perception in autonomous driving scenarios.
authors: Linglong Wu; Ruotao Yu; Jiaxin Chen; Wentao Xu

title: Ultrasonography in disaster medicine: a narrative review
abstract: This narrative review aimed to critically appraise the diagnostic accuracy, clinical impact, and operational feasibility of ultraportable point-of-care ultrasonography (POCUS) across the four domains of disaster medicine. A literature search was conducted following the SANRA and PRISMA-trAIce guidelines. Records were identified through an AI-assisted literature-discovery tool (the Undermind Deep-Search platform, interrogating the Semantic Scholar corpus) run on 15 June 2025, rather than through an independent structured multi-database search. Candidate references were screened manually against pre-specified eligibility criteria by a single reviewer, with the search parameters independently verified by the senior author. Of 71 records identified, 63 met the inclusion criteria. The included studies comprised 32 original studies, 10 systematic or scoping reviews, 20 narrative or operational papers, and one guideline. In CBRN scenarios, lung ultrasound demonstrated sensitivities of 90-97% for COVID-19 pneumonia versus 60-69% for chest radiography while minimizing healthcare worker exposure. For blast and ballistic injuries, FAST showed a pooled sensitivity of 92.1% (95% CI: 87.8-95.6) and specificity of 98.7% (95% CI: 96.0-99.9) for intra-abdominal hemorrhage. In natural disasters, ultrasound altered management in up to 44% of patients. Post-disaster applications included vascular access, tube confirmation, and complication monitoring. Ultraportable POCUS demonstrates diagnostic utility and operational feasibility across multiple disaster domains. However, evidence quality varies significantly, and standardized protocols remain lacking. Prospective studies linking ultrasound deployment to improved patient outcomes are needed. KEY POINTS: Question When disasters disable conventional imaging, how does ultraportable point-of-care ultrasonography perform for diagnosis, triage, and procedural guidance across the four domains of disaster medicine? Findings Across 63 studies, FAST reached 92.1% pooled sensitivity for hemoperitoneum, lung ultrasound 90-97% versus 60-69% for radiography; management changed in up to 44%. Critical relevance statement This review critically appraises ultraportable ultrasound across all four disaster domains, showing that radiation-free bedside imaging accelerates triage, conserves scarce CT capacity, and extends radiological expertise through tele-guidance, while exposing an evidence base still lacking prospective outcome data.
authors: F. Amiot; Karim Tazarourte; G. Gorincour; Axel Benhamed

title: Ultrasound Operator Guidance Using World Modeling and Retrieval Based Action Planning
abstract: Ultrasound is widely used, but acquisition quality is heavily dependent on the operator's knowledge and expertise. With demand for examinations outpacing the supply of trained sonographers, operator-guidance systems aim to close this gap by instructing a less trained user how to move the probe toward a target view. In this paper, we propose a retrieval-induced latent transition model for ultrasound acquisition dynamics, formulating ultrasound operator guidance as multi-step planning and retrieval in a world model. Using a V-JEPA 2.1 backbone, observations are first encoded into a latent space where anatomically related views lie close together. We then retrieve similar views from a reference database containing encoded latent states and corresponding probe positions and orientations. Rather than learning a parametric transition function, we directly use physically executed transitions from the database to establish our nonparametric, retrieval-induced transition model that supports receding-horizon planning. At deployment, guidance is generated from the live ultrasound image feed alone, without any probe tracking hardware. Applied to carotid ultrasound, the proposed planner reaches the target view in 86% of retrospective closed-loop episodes, versus 52% and 43% for representative baselines, outperforming both on every target view, including the challenging longitudinal internal and external carotid artery views. A prospective feasibility study on unseen volunteers, run in real time on a CPU using distillation, reaches 83% target-view reachability. Because planning is driven by proximity to any encodable goal latent, the same world model can navigate back to any previously acquired, patient-specific frame, supporting reproducible longitudinal imaging for e.g. perioperative or follow-up monitoring.
authors: Noortje I.P. Schueler; Hans van Gorp; Ruud J. G. van Sloun

title: Ultrasound Robot Motion Perception and Control Based on Multimodal Sensing
abstract: This project develops multimodal perception and control methods for robotic ultrasound imaging. By integrating ultrasound images with robot motion, probe pose, and force information, the study aims to improve anatomical perception, probe navigation, and autonomous ultrasound acquisition. The project will generate synchronized imaging and sensor data for model development and evaluation, supporting more accurate and reproducible robotic ultrasound scanning.

title: Unsuspected intestinal taeniasis discovered on capsule endoscopy: A case report
abstract: Intestinal taeniasis is a tapeworm infection commonly encountered in endemic regions, including Asia, Africa, and Latin America. Diagnosis is often delayed due to nonspecific gastrointestinal symptoms and limited sensitivity of stool ova and parasite testing. We present a 57-year-old Nepali man undergoing capsule endoscopy for persistent microcytic anemia and abdominal pain, in whom capsule endoscopy revealed unsuspected diffuse small bowel tapeworms. He was treated with praziquantel, but his anemia was unchanged on follow-up, suggesting an alternate etiology. This case highlights capsule endoscopy's ability to visualize helminths in situ and cautions against attributing anemia to incidental findings.

title: Unveiling Glial Heterogeneity in the Inner Retina: Non-Visual Photic Spectrum Responses and Calcium Dynamics in Müller Glial Cells vs. Neurons
abstract: Traditional calcium (Ca2+) imaging analysis often overlooks the non-stationary temporal complexity inherent in retinal circuits, reducing dynamic signaling traces to static summary descriptors. To resolve these dynamic signatures, we implemented a reproducible analytical framework combining Continuous Wavelet Transform (CWT) time-frequency decomposition with Sinc baseline filtering and Ward’s agglomerative hierarchical clustering, applied directly to standardized high-dimensional feature spaces, reserving Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) strictly for low-dimensional visualization. This pipeline was deployed across three independent experimental models under blue light stimulation: mixed primary embryonic chicken retinal neurons, primary chicken Müller glial cells (MGCs), and the human MIO-M1 Müller cell line. Functional clustering resolved retinal neurons into three distinct kinetic subpopulations (k = 3), characterized by a kinetically stable core maintaining mid-frequency oscillations (Cluster 0), a cohort undergoing sharp post-stimulus period contraction with late amplitude surges (Cluster 1), and a low-frequency cohort with persistent period elongation (Cluster 2). Chicken MGCs partitioned into two operational clusters (k = 2), contrasting a period-stable, amplitude-decaying subpopulation (Cluster 0) with a dynamic subpopulation exhibiting light-evoked kinetic acceleration (Cluster 1). Similarly, human MIO-M1 glia separated into two major kinetic clusters (k = 2), distinguishing a low-amplitude, longer-period cohort from a high-amplitude, sustained subpopulation operating within an 8–80 s dynamic period band. Restricting phase-coupling and circular statistical analyses strictly to simultaneous Field-of-View (FOV) recordings revealed distinct stimulus-entrained network behaviors: primary avian MGCs maintain a decentralized, weakly coupled regime (“mosaic of autonomy”) that processes light across independent temporal windows, whereas human MIO-M1 glia and embryonic neuronal assemblies exhibit significant stimulus-evoked phase realignment and relative response latency sequencing. These findings demonstrate that inner retinal functional identity is fundamentally rhythmic and cluster-dependent, establishing a quantitative benchmark for decoding multi-scale Ca2+ signaling in healthy retinal preparations.

title: User-centered design of graphical user interfaces for telemedical robotic systems: development and usability study.
abstract: We explore an approach to develop telemedical Graphical User Interfaces (GUIs) using User-centered Design (UCD) methods. In contrast with prior work that emphasizes system integration, we center on the GUI as the clinician's primary interface. In a user-centered, two-stage process, we developed a modular and generalized GUI architecture and adapted it to a Robotic Ultrasound System (RUSS) and a robotic Tension Pneumothorax (tPTX) system. The GUIs were iteratively co-designed and evaluated with physicians using mixed methods (System Usability Scale (SUS), end-user-adapted heuristics, eye-tracking). The results of the study confirm the benefits of UCD methods for the development of GUIs for telemedical robotic systems. Repeated exposure increased efficiency across tasks and scenarios, indicating the usability (training effect) and consistency (cross-scenario learning transfer) of a modular GUI architecture. The mixed-methods design provided complementary insights via triangulation, helped to analyze outliers, and revealed additional design issues not captured by one method alone. A user-centered GUI development process with multiple evaluation rounds can improve the usability of telemedical robotic systems for medical professionals. Our findings show that a modular architecture can facilitate the transfer of training effects across implementations and clinical use cases by preserving high-level structures and interaction concepts.

title: VLM-Based Mesh Segmentation Framework for DDH Robotic Ultrasound.
abstract: For robotic ultrasound targeting developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH), reconstructed infant body-surface meshes should preserve the target surface while excluding bed, support, and background geometry. This study proposes a structured vision-language model (VLM)-based multi-view segmentation method for infant phantom mesh cleanup. Text-guided 2D masks provide foreground and background evidence; mask-quality statistics and structured VLM assessments generate view-specific foreground-support weights that undergo deterministic risk suppression before target/non-target classification of 3D vertices. Hard voting and Rule-weighted voting were baselines under identical projection and post-processing settings. We evaluated one physical infant phantom across 150 separate acquisition-reconstruction trials under controlled conditions, each comprising 40 voting views and 10 held-out evaluation views, yielding 1500 manually annotated reference masks. Structured VLM voting achieved a Balanced score (intersection over union minus the 2-pixel tolerant leakage rate) of 0.804 ± 0.085, versus 0.801 ± 0.084 and 0.793 ± 0.086 for Rule-weighted and Hard voting. This leakage rate was 0.087 ± 0.043, versus 0.089 ± 0.042 and 0.092 ± 0.043; mean Coverage remained similar (0.992-0.993). The Balanced-score gain and leakage-rate reduction relative to Rule-weighted voting remained significant after Holm correction (adjusted p = 0.029 and p = 0.033, respectively). Validation using real-infant data, 3D reference standards, and closed-loop robotic scanning is still required.
