The available measurement evidence is most compatible with human-supervised formative, supplementary, second-rater, or quality-assurance applications; autonomous high-stakes use requires stronger external validation, reproducibility, and decision-level safety evidence.
authors: Abdulmohsen M Alomair

title: Artificial Intelligence in Intensive Care: From Clinical Applications to Ethical and Medico-Legal Challenges
abstract: From a medico-legal perspective, AI functions as a clinical decision support tool without legal autonomy. Responsibility for AI-assisted clinical decisions remains subject to the applicable legal and regulatory framework and depends on the degree of human oversight. The use of artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming intensive care medicine, offering advanced tools for data processing, prediction, and clinical decision support. This narrative review explores current applications of AI in the intensive care unit (ICU), along with associated ethical, medico-legal, and regulatory challenges. AI systems, particularly those based on machine learning and deep learning, have demonstrated promising predictive performance across several intensive care applications. Systematic reviews of machine learning models for ICU prediction tasks have reported AUROC values generally ranging from approximately 0.80 to over 0.90 for early sepsis prediction and ARDS risk stratification, although performance decreases in external validation cohorts. AI has also shown encouraging performance in predicting weaning success and supporting mechanical ventilation management, while evidence of improved patient-centered clinical outcomes remains limited A narrative literature search was conducted in PubMed and Scopus for studies published between January 2015 and December 2025. Additionally, AI contributes to continuous patient monitoring, reduction in false alarms, and improved workflow efficiency. Despite these advances, most models are derived from retrospective and single-center datasets, limiting generalizability and real-world applicability. Moreover, only a limited number of AI systems have undergone prospective clinical evaluation or demonstrated improvements in patient-centered outcomes following real-world implementation. A key limitation of current AI systems is the "black box" nature of many algorithms, which reduces interpretability and may undermine clinician trust. Furthermore, algorithmic bias, data quality issues, and limited external validation raise concerns regarding safety, equity, and reliability. Importantly, improved predictive accuracy does not necessarily translate into better clinical outcomes, highlighting the need for prospective validation studies. From a medico-legal perspective, AI functions as a clinical decision support tool without legal autonomy. Responsibility for AI-assisted clinical decisions remains subject to the applicable legal and regulatory framework and depends on the degree of human oversight, the intended use of the AI system, and the relevant jurisdiction. The emergence of regulatory frameworks, such as the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act and the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), reflects the increasing regulation of healthcare AI according to the intended purpose, level of autonomy, and potential impact of each system, emphasizing requirements for transparency, human oversight, and data protection.
authors: Francesco De Lazzaro; Giovanna Barletta; Eugenia Magnanimi; Bruno Cirillo; Paola Frati; Enrico Marinelli; Francesco Rocco Pugliese; Lina De Paola; Giovanni G. Giordano

title: Artificial intelligence in male infertility from diagnosis to treatment
abstract: Male factors account for almost half of all infertility cases and afflict approximately 186 million men globally, presenting a substantial and increasing public health burden. Semen analysis is the standard of care for assessing male fertility, but subjective visual interpretation results in > 25–30% inter-observer variability and precludes non-destructive assessment of sperm DNA fragmentation (SDF). Machine learning, a branch of artificial intelligence, has the potential to streamline semen assessment and clinical decision-making throughout male infertility care by providing automated, data-driven approaches that are objective, efficient, and precise. Guided by the PRISMA 2020 statement, the manuscript included research from PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar. Two independent reviewers screened all retrieved records according to pre-specified inclusion criteria to identify peer-reviewed publications describing applications of machine learning, deep learning, artificial neural networks, natural language processing, computer vision, and explainable artificial intelligence to semen analysis, fertility status prediction, or assisted reproductive technologies. Artificial Intelligence techniques consistently outperformed conventional semen assessment methods for sperm count, motility, morphology, and predictive analyses. Feedforward Spectral Neural Networks classified sperm concentration with 93% accuracy, while a Fast Region-based Convolutional Neural Network classified sperm motility with 97.37% accuracy; both surpassed inter-observer agreement achievable through WHO-based manual visual analysis. VGG16-pretrained CNNs identified sperm morphology with a true positive rate of 94.1%, however, performance declined substantially to 62% when validated on an independent external dataset. Deep learning models demonstrated the capacity to predict SDF non-destructively, high concordance to TUNEL assay and sperm chromatin structure assay reference standards (r = 0.97, p < 0.001). Machine Learning classifiers specifically, Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), Random Forest, and CatBoost, showcased AUCs of 0.998 for the prediction of male fertility status. Furthermore, explainable artificial intelligence techniques such as SHAP and LIME improve the clinical interpretability of machine learning model outputs, an important step toward regulatory acceptance. These techniques can also be integration with computer-assisted sperm analysis systems, smartphone-based semen analysis, sperm sorting for intrauterine insemination, microTESE, ultrasonography, and multi-omics data platforms. Limitations of the current literature include retrospective study designs, single-centre data sources, small sample sizes, lack of external validation, and heterogeneity in image acquisition, outcome measures, and performance metrics. Included studies face challenges relating to algorithmic bias, insufficient model explainability, data security and governance, and the absence of standardized regulation or AI-specific reporting frameworks. Future work should prioritise prospective multicentre studies employing multimodal artificial intelligence that integrates imaging data with genomic, transcriptomic, hormonal, and electronic health record inputs, as well as federated learning and international collaboration to establish standardised and internationally recognised regulatory guidelines. In conclusion, artificial intelligence has the potential to transform clinical decision-making for patients presenting with infertility by enabling objective, high-throughput, and personalised assessment of semen samples. However, these tools should be used to augment rather than replace clinical expertise until models have been prospectively validated across diverse populations and have received appropriate regulatory clearance. Not applicable.
authors: Anuradha Dhull; Monika Lamba; Aryan Dahiya; Sushama Tanwar

title: Association of alkaline phosphatase and segmented neutrophils count with low appendicular lean mass in middle-aged women: Evidence from an American cross-sectional survey
abstract: OBJECTIVES: Sarcopenia is associated with an increased risk of frailty, falls, and mortality. Women exhibit distinct characteristics in appendicular lean mass and metabolism compared with men, and hormonal changes may further accelerate appendicular lean mass. This study aimed to identify key blood biomarkers associated with appendicular lean muscle mass index adjusted by body mass index (ALMBMI) in women and to explore their potential relationship with chronic inflammation. METHODS: Based on NHANES 2015-2018 data from middle-aged women, the ALMBMI was calculated. A multimodal machine learning framework was constructed using elastic net logistic regression and generalized linear models (GLMs) to screen core variables affecting ALMBMI. Weighted quantile sum (WQS) regression and Bayesian kernel machine regression (BKMR) jointly determined variable weights and effect directions, and restricted cubic spline (RCS) models characterized dose-response curves to identify key blood indicators and their magnitudes of change associated with low appendicular lean mass risk. RESULTS: A total of 1,082 participants were included in this study. Following variable screening, 12 variables were identified as significantly associated with ALMBMI. WQS regression indicated that segmented neutrophil count (weight: 0.25) and alkaline phosphatase (ALP) (weight: 0.22) were the predominant factors associated with low ALMBMI. BKMR analysis, which assesses all variables jointly, identified segmented neutrophil count (36.0%), and ALP (27.6%) as the core variables. RCS analysis revealed that segmented neutrophil count and alkaline phosphatase showed an L-shaped trend with ALMBMI, with inflection points at 4.00 (1000 cells/μL) and 76.00 IU/L, respectively. In each case, the curves plateaued to the right of the inflection point. Relative to participants classified as having low ALMBMI according to FNIH criteria, those with normal ALMBMI exhibited reductions of 16.01% in ALP and 11.17% in segmented neutrophil count, respectively. CONCLUSION: Among middle-aged women, higher segmented neutrophil count and ALP levels were identified as positive correlates of low ALMBMI, with both biomarkers demonstrating threshold phenomena. Such hematological alterations are consistent with chronic low-grade inflammation, underscoring their potential utility in early sarcopenia screening and prevention.
authors: Shanlan Yang; Jiaofeng Wang; Dayoung Kim; Han Xu; Sheng Zhou; Fan Yang; Zhijun Bao

title: BAARC: Uncertainty-Driven Adaptive Partial Spectral Measurement to Full Reconstruction for Material Classification
abstract: Spectroscopic instruments with limited wavenumber coverage require accurate scan positioning or multiple measurements to complete the material analysis. This often requires prerequisite knowledge about the material under diagnosis to measure the spectral regions with distinguishing peaks. In our study, we simulate a Bayesian Adaptive Acquisition with Reconstruction-driven Classification (BAARC) framework for Raman spectral measurements, using masked training to learn spectral features that dynamically drive laser channel selection until the material is identified. We present a jointly trained two-level framework that takes progressive partial measurements of small wavenumber patches across the complete spectral range and, at each step, first attempts to reconstruct the full spectra until the model uncertainty is low. Secondly, material classification is performed at each reconstruction step until stoppage. Uncertainty quantification during reconstruction steps helps determine the measurement position of our next patch, while combining it with classification uncertainty determines measurement termination. By closing the loop between hardware acquisition and deep probabilistic modeling, the proposed system minimizes physical measurement steps while maintaining both spectral fidelity and diagnostic accuracy. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that our framework achieves high-accuracy sample identification using only a fraction of full-spectrum channels, offering a scalable solution for real-time, high-throughput spectroscopic instruments.
authors: Adithya Ashok Chalain Valapil; Aishwarya Venkataramanan; Joachim Denzler

title: Beyond Anatomy in Uncomplicated Type B Aortic Dissection: Hypoxia, Physiological Reserve, and the Next Generation of Intelligent Endovascular Devices
abstract: Abstract: Type B aortic dissection (TBAD) represents a heterogeneous disease process that cannot be fully understood through anatomy alone. Although the majority of patients initially meet current criteria for uncomplicated TBAD (uTBAD), a substantial proportion later progresses despite appearing stable during early assessment and surveillance. The mechanisms underlying this deterioration remain incompletely understood and extends beyond our current understanding of traditional anatomic high-risk criteria. This article examines impaired oxygenation and physiological reserve as potential dimensions of clinical vulnerability in uTBAD, while distinguishing their possible relevance to acute deterioration from their unproven value in predicting aortic progression or selecting patients for intervention. As such, TBAD is not simply a focal vascular event, but a disease with broader systemic and physiological implications. It also discusses how future intelligent endovascular technologies could support a more personalised approach to management by integrating embedded sensors, wireless physiological monitoring, and artificial intelligence-assisted haemodynamic analysis. Moreover, a conceptual framework is discussed in which the stent graft evolves from a purely mechanical device into an active therapeutic platform capable of physiological sensing and real-time feedback. Keywords: type B aortic dissection, uncomplicated, TEVAR, intelligent stent graft, physiological reserve, hypoxia, computational fluid dynamics, aortic remodelling
authors: Mohamad Bashir; Matti Jubouri; Christopher J. Gaffney; Nimrat Grewal; Mohammed Idhrees A.; Amr Abdelhaliem; Gabriele Piffaretti; Martin Teraa; Damian Miles Bailey; Ian Michael Williams

title: Beyond Sensitivity: A Perspective on Transitioning Photonic Sensors into Real-Life Applications
abstract: Photonic sensing encompasses technologies at markedly different levels of maturity. Fiber-optic sensing systems are already widely deployed in infrastructure, energy, transportation, and industrial monitoring, whereas many integrated biosensors and plasmonic, metasurface, and wearable platforms remain at laboratory or early translational stages. This review critically examines the factors that have enabled some photonic sensing technologies to achieve sustained deployment while continuing to constrain others. Practical performance is considered not only in terms of the optical transducer but also through molecular recognition, sample composition, environmental cross-sensitivity, fabrication variability, optical interrogation, microfluidics, packaging, calibration, electronics, and data processing. Established, transitional, and emerging platforms are comparatively assessed across healthcare, environmental monitoring, industrial process control, structural monitoring, and security applications. Real-life readiness is evaluated through analytical validity, selectivity, reproducibility, stability, dynamic range, response time, manufacturability, usability, and total system value. An application-driven framework is proposed in which sensing architecture, recognition chemistry, sample handling, interrogation, packaging, and validation are co-designed according to the intended operating environment. The analysis shows that successful deployment depends on robust system integration, reproducible manufacturing, application-specific validation, and a clear practical advantage rather than record sensitivity or nominal detection limits alone. Future evaluations should therefore use representative samples, independently manufactured devices, realistic operating conditions, standardized reporting protocols, and comparisons with established analytical methods.
authors: Muhammad Ali Butt

title: Beyond morphology: A review of heterogeneous mechanisms and precision risk management in left ventricular non-compaction/left ventricular hypertrabeculation
abstract: Left ventricular non-compaction/left ventricular hypertrabeculation (LVNC/LVHT) has traditionally been regarded as a congenital cardiomyopathy caused by arrested myocardial compaction during embryogenesis. However, this classical concept is increasingly challenged by mounting clinical and basic evidence, in view of its marked heterogeneity in clinical presentation, imaging features, and genetic background. This review systematically synthesizes relevant research from recent years to propose that LVNC/LVHT is better understood not as a single discrete disease entity, but as a morphological endpoint resulting from diverse etiologies and mechanisms. This review critically appraises the phenotypic pitfalls of current imaging diagnostic criteria, highlighting the clinical dilemma of concurrent over-diagnosis and under-diagnosis that leads to inappropriate management. It then delineates two distinct pathogenic pathways: A developmental pathway associated with mutations in genes such as TAZ and MYH7 and dysregulation of signaling pathways including transforming growth factor-β and neuregulin 1–erythroblastic leukemia viral oncogene homolog; and an acquired/adaptive pathway linked to hemodynamic load-induced myocardial remodeling. Based on these insights, we propose an integrated classification framework subdividing LVNC/LVHT into development-driven, load-adaptive, and idiopathic benign trabeculation subtypes to resolve long-standing diagnostic confusion. We further introduce a multimodal risk stratification system incorporating cardiac structure and function, electrophysiology, genetics, circulating biomarkers, and systemic factors. This strategy aims to shift LVNC/LVHT management from a morphology-based, one-size-fits-all paradigm toward mechanism-guided, individualized precision care. Finally, we outline future directions, including validation of risk models, mechanistic studies, updated guidelines, and integration of artificial intelligence and multi-omics, to establish a novel precision diagnostic and therapeutic framework for LVNC/LVHT.
authors: Changying Zhao; Ran Ran; Shiquan Sun; Tao Shi; Yang Yan; Guoliang Li

title: Beyond physical access: disability-inclusive primary health care as a test of health equity in Sub-Saharan Africa
abstract: Disability inclusion in primary health care is not a peripheral issue but a fundamental test of whether health systems in sub-Saharan Africa are advancing health equity and universal health coverage. Persons with disabilities experience persistent and overlapping barriers across the care pathway, including physical inaccessibility, unaffordable services, inaccessible information, poor provider communication, stigma, weak referral systems, and limited access to rehabilitation and assistive technology. These barriers are intensified by poverty, gender inequality, rural residence, and under-resourced health systems, producing avoidable inequities in access, quality, continuity, and financial protection. This commentary argues that disability-inclusive primary health care should be reframed from a narrow focus on physical access to a broader agenda of health-system accountability. Drawing on recent evidence from sub-Saharan Africa, it highlights how exclusion is embedded in routine system design, financing, workforce capacity, data systems, and governance. The paper further argues that meaningful inclusion requires disability-disaggregated monitoring, accessible communication, reasonable accommodation, provider training, strengthened referral pathways, financing for rehabilitation and assistive products, and formal participation of persons with disabilities and their representative organizations in planning and oversight. Disability-inclusive primary health care is therefore not a specialist add-on, but a core measure of whether universal health coverage reforms are genuinely equitable, people-centered, and resilient. Embedding disability inclusion into routine primary health care performance systems offers a practical pathway to stronger accountability and more inclusive health systems across sub-Saharan Africa.
authors: Mohamed Daud Mohamed; Yakub Burhan Abdullahi; Abdikadir Ahmed Hassan; Iqro Omar Ibrahim; Liibaan Abdulahi Sudi; Nuradin Abdullahi Sheikh Rashid
venue: International Journal for Equity in Health

title: Beyond static perception: Animals, neurons and synapses move to compute efficiently
abstract: Neurons are often modelled as immobile systems that transmit information through chemical and electrical signals constrained by noise and bandwidth. However, this static view contrasts with biological reality, in which dynamical processes operate across scales, from whole-animal movements to motion at the subcellular level. Here, we combine recent experimental observations with biophysically realistic modelling to show that neural information processing, beyond electrochemical signalling, is dynamically shaped by motion, from morphodynamic ultrastructural changes to whole-body movements. In this framework, ultrafast mechanical adjustments in cellular and synaptic structures interact with retinal, eye, head, and body movements to accelerate encoding and enhance precision. Movement across scales dynamically alters the waveforms, latencies, refractoriness and ultrastructural organisation of quantal sampling events. These changes improve signal fidelity and extend spatiotemporal resolution, enabling neurons to generate reliable, high-speed representations with minimal delay. Through active sensing and morphodynamic sampling, animals can therefore enhance the speed and reliability of sensory representations. This perspective, in which self-generated movements across multiple scales enhance encoding and perception, offers new insight into how the brain achieves efficient, predictive and noise-resistant computation while providing a foundation for future experimental tests and biologically inspired AI designs. We first explain how motion-coupled encoding improves neural performance, focusing on edge computing in early sensory systems. We then extend these ideas more speculatively, proposing how motion-coupled sampling may have influenced the evolution of neural architectures at multiple levels, potentially contributing to efficient predictive cognition.
authors: Mikko Juusola; Jouni Takalo; Joni Kemppainen; HaDi MaBouDi; Bruce Yi Bu; Shashwat Shukla; Yiyin Zhou; Aurel A. Lazar; Gonzalo G. de Polavieja

title: Beyond the Oropharynx: TTMV ‐ HPV DNA Detection in a p16‐Positive Hypopharyngeal Squamous Cell Carcinoma
abstract: Plasma TTMV-HPV16 DNA provided complementary molecular evidence in a p16-positive hypopharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma, while PET/CT localized the occult left pyriform sinus primary. Serial postoperative TTMV-HPV DNA assays remained undetectable through approximately 19 months of clinical and radiographic surveillance.
authors: Jacob Beiriger; Brayden J. Seliger; Silvia M. Soule; Hilary C. McCrary; Richard B. Cannon

title: Biofilm-associated genes in Staphylococcus aureus: role in chronic infections and therapeutic challenges
abstract: One of the major contributors to persistent healthcare and community-associated infections is S. aureus , which has a remarkable ability to form biofilms that protect it against the host immune system and antimicrobial therapy. In recent years, it has become clear that biofilm development is a highly orchestrated and dynamic process, controlled by complex genetic networks, transcriptional regulators, two-component systems (TCSs), and environmental signals. The present review covers the molecular mechanisms involved in the initiation, maturation, maintenance, and dispersal of biofilms in general, and in particular, the coordinated functions of adhesins, the icaADBC operon, components of the extracellular matrix (ECM), global regulators ( agr , sarA , and sigB ), and two-component regulatory systems, as well as emerging insights from transcriptomic studies on biofilm adaptation. We then review the roles of these regulatory pathways in metabolic heterogeneity, antibiotic tolerance, immune evasion, and persistence in clinically relevant biofilm-associated infections, including infective endocarditis, osteomyelitis, prosthetic joint infection, catheter-associated infection, and diabetic foot infection. The review further outlines the latest developments in antibiofilm therapeutics, including matrix-degrading enzymes, quorum-sensing inhibitors, antimicrobial peptides, bacteriophage-based therapeutics, lysins, nitric oxide donors, nanoparticle-assisted therapeutics, and CRISPR-Cas-based antimicrobials. Incorporating molecular regulation into infection-specific pathogenesis and emerging therapeutic strategies, this review offers a new perspective on the biology of S. aureus biofilms and highlights opportunities to develop mechanism-based interventions to combat chronic biofilm-associated infections.
authors: Mohammad Asim Azhar; Tanveer Ahmad Mir; Sana Ahmed; Abdullah M. Assiri; Dieter Clemens Broering

title: Biometric verification using oral acoustic reflections
abstract: Biometric verification methods, such as voice, face, iris and fingerprint verification, are commonly used in smartphones, security systems, and medical devices. However, each involves tradeoffs in cost, accuracy, latency and susceptibility to spoofing. We present and report laboratory testing of Oral Cavity Acoustic Verification (OCAV), a biometric verification system that transmits sound waves into the user's oral cavity, characterizes the acoustic response, and returns a verification decision by comparing the acoustic response to the individual's prerecorded acoustic signature. A total of 108 healthy volunteers aged 18-60 years were recruited, and a unique acoustic profile was created for each participant. Across three recording sessions conducted one week apart, 20,860 genuine trials and 18,880 impostor trials were collected to evaluate verification accuracy. Verification accuracy was 90.1% for a single trial and 95.2% when pooling 5 consecutive trials. Unlike voice biometrics that depend on speech production and are sensitive to acoustic noise and audio playback attacks, OCAV exploits an active acoustic response from the oral cavity that may be less vulnerable to spoofing attacks. In contrast to other audio-based systems such as ear-canal acoustic biometrics, OCAV is intended for devices that already involve oral cavity contact. The potential applications include inhaler-based health monitoring, breath-alcohol tests, and the enforcement of nicotine-use restrictions. These capabilities can help support public health and safety efforts; for example, by monitoring youth access to e-vaping or detecting drivers' alcohol consumption prior to ignition.
authors: Amit Kam; Nir Iakoby; Daniel Tubiana; Eran Hochstadter; Roi Ram; Yaniv Zigel

title: Biosensors for viral and bacterial pathogen detection: From biological recognition elements to small-molecule engineering of electrochemical interfaces
abstract: Infectious diseases pose a serious threat to global public health, and the COVID-19 pandemic has clearly demonstrated the critical need for rapid, accurate, and accessible diagnostic tools. Portable point-of-care analytical systems provide an alternative to conventional laboratory methods such as ELISA and PCR, enabling rapid pathogen identification outside centralized facilities, which is essential for timely diagnosis and treatment decisions. Beyond initial detection, such systems also hold potential for quantitative monitoring of viral or bacterial load, relevant for assessing disease stage and therapy effectiveness. Electrochemical biosensing platforms most favorably combine the required analytical performance with broad possibilities for miniaturization, automation, and scaling. However, despite the exponential growth in publications, clinical translation and commercialization of such devices remain limited by insufficient stability and reproducibility of the bioreceptor layer, uncontrolled interfacial orientation, and matrix effects in complex biological samples. This review provides a critical analysis of current approaches to the directed structuring of the bioreceptor layer in electrochemical sensors, comparing biological recognition elements (antibodies, DNA/RNA probes) with synthetic and biomimetic alternatives (aptamers, engineered peptides, and molecularly imprinted polymers). Particular attention is given to the multifaceted roles of small organic molecules as structural elements — cross-linkers for oriented immobilization, redox mediators and electrocatalysts for signal transduction, and independent low-molecular-weight recognition ligands — for the design of next-generation electrochemical test platforms with operational characteristics tunable at the molecular level.
authors: Tatiana S. Svalova; Andrei V. Okhokhonin; Anna A. Saigushkina; Margarita V. Medvedeva; Elizaveta V. Galiautdunova; Elizaveta V. Tiupa; Р. Ф. Муктасибова; Козицина Алиса Николаевна

title: COMPLICATIONS OF SUBURETHRAL AND VAGINAL MESH – OUTCOMES OF REVISION SURGERY
abstract: Objective: To present a combined laparoscopic-endoscopic surgical approach for the treatment of a TVT bladder extrusion.Description: A 79-year-old woman with a history of TVT mesh placement for stress urinary incontinence.Five years later, she returned to the clinic with urgency urinary incontinence and pain.Ultrasound and cystoscopy revealed a mesh extrusion at the bladder dome of approximately 1 cm.Given the location of the extrusion, a combined laparoscopic-endoscopic approach was used.Clinically, after one year of follow-up, the pain has subsided, with mild residual urge and stress incontinence.This is an effective and reproducible approach for the management of TVT mesh bladder extrusions with difficult transvaginal access.
authors: Rui Pedrosa; Clara Velasco; Manuel Saavedra; Lira Pelari; Carlos Marquez; Marta Pérez; Luis San-José; Javier Casado; Luis López‐Fando

title: Calibrated Uncertainty for Informative Path Planning in Aquatic Environmental Monitoring
abstract: Informative Path Planning for scalar field reconstruction uses predictive uncertainty to direct sensing vehicles toward maximally informative locations. Gaussian Processes provide this signal but their stationary isotropic kernels are misspecified for non-homogeneous phenomena such as oil spills, producing miscalibrated estimates that degrade planning. We investigate whether replacing the Gaussian Process with a well-calibrated Deep Ensemble improves path planning outcomes, and whether uncertainty quality interacts with the choice of planning algorithm. Five strategies ($ε$-Greedy, Value Greedy, Uncertainty Greedy, Monte Carlo Tree Search, and Receding Horizon Orienteering) share a common Deep Ensemble backbone trained on physics-based oil spill simulations. On held-out stochastic spill scenarios, the Deep Ensemble reduces normalised reconstruction error by $83\%$ relative to the Gaussian Process baseline. Crucially, well-calibrated uncertainty amplifies the importance of the planning strategy: the performance gap between algorithms is negligible under miscalibrated models but becomes substantial under the ensemble, where multi-step lookahead planners outperform greedy selection by up to $32\%$ in reconstruction error and achieve IoU above $0.85$. Monte Carlo Tree Search is the recommended planner, matching Orienteering in reconstruction quality at an order-of-magnitude lower computational cost.
authors: Samuel Yanes Luis; Alejandro Casado Pérez; Alejandro Mendoza Barrionuevo; Dame Seck Diop; Sergio Luis Toral; Saniel Gutiérrez Reina

title: Can LLMs Value the Right Evidence? Evidence-Value Misalignment in Dynamic Medical Diagnosis
abstract: A correct diagnosis reached from insufficient or misleading evidence can pose a clinical hazard, yet outcome-based accuracy may reward such lucky guesses. We call this mismatch between diagnostic decisions and the value of available evidence Evidence-Value Misalignment (EVM). To disentangle evidential grounding independently from diagnostic accuracy, we introduce MedEVM, a dynamic benchmarking environment comprising 1,050 cases across 24 disease systems. Observations arrive turn by turn, requiring models to continuously calibrate its decision by deciding whether to wait for more evidence or submit a diagnosis. Across 9 LLMs, four interesting patterns are observed. (1) Miscalibrated evidence tracking. Making a diagnosis often fails to calibrate evidence sufficiency, even in more capable models, and even worsens in reasoning mode. (2) Misaligned diagnosis submission. Confidence in the correct diagnosis often fails to ensure timely submission despite sufficient evidence. (3) Evidence order matters. Reordering the same evidence changes diagnoses even when model confidence remains similar. (4) Misleading evidence remains influential. Added misleading evidence redirects diagnoses even after prior evidence becomes sufficient. We further verify that EVM predicts errors and that preventing premature submission improves accuracy. These findings motivate Evidence-Verified Diagnosis Harness (EVD-Harness). It decouples diagnosis generation from submission through an offline Contrastive Diagnostic Wiki and three online control stages, namely observation management, proposal and witness verification, and diagnosis submission control. Across five LLMs, EVD-Harness improves accuracy by 12.0--51.1 percentage points while mitigating EVM-related failures. Our results demonstrate that verifying evidential support before submission can make diagnostic decisions more reliable.
authors: Kehua Feng; Yunsheng Lu; Yitong Qiao; Tiantian He; Lei Liu; Yue Shen; Jian Wang; Jinjie Gu

title: Cardiolipin-Based Electrochemical Biosensor for Non-treponemal Antibody Detection Using Screen-Printed Electrodes: A Proof-of-Concept Study
abstract: Abstract Syphilis remains a major public health concern. Although non-treponemal tests are widely used for screening and treatment monitoring, their interpretation relies on visual assessment of flocculation. Here, an amperometric biosensor using isolated cardiolipin (0.03–0.12%) as the sole biorecognition element was developed on carbon/graphene screen-printed electrodes. The 0.06% concentration was selected for subsequent experiments, and the biosensor discriminated positive and negative control materials across two electrode batches. Progressive positive-control dilution produced a systematic electrochemical response (R2 = 0.921). Electrode functionalization significantly affected the response (p < 0.001), supporting the contribution of immobilized cardiolipin. Discrimination was maintained under physiological and pathological glucose conditions (adjusted p < 0.001). These findings provide a preliminary proof-of-concept for cardiolipin-based electrochemical assessment of non-treponemal antibody reactivity. Further studies using clinical samples are required to establish analytical and clinical performance and investigate semiquantitative evaluation by correlating electrochemical responses with defined serological titers.
authors: Duane da Silva Moraes; Bruna Ferri Serafini; Felipe Longaray Kadel; Gabriela Victória de Mello Jantzch; Milleny Germann Souza; Willyan Hasenkamp; Antônio Shigueaki Takimi; Júlia Konzen Moreira

title: Cirugía General y del Aparato Digestivo
abstract: La cirugía del aparato digestivo constituye uno de los pilares más antiguos y dinámicos de la práctica quirúrgica. Desde las primeras laparotomías exploradoras hasta los actuales abordajes robóticos y la cirugía bariátrica metabólica, el conocimiento de la anatomía, la fisiopatología y las técnicas de imagen ha evolucionado de manera vertiginosa. Sin embargo, el vértigo tecnológico no debe hacernos olvidar los fundamentos: el diagnóstico clínico sigue siendo el primer escalón de una toma de decisiones segura y eficaz. El presente libro nace con el propósito de ofrecer una visión integrada y actualizada de la cirugía general y del aparato digestivo, centrada en los fundamentos fisiopatológicos y su aplicación directa al diagnóstico clínico‑quirúrgico. No se trata de un compendio exhaustivo de técnicas, sino de una obra que prioriza el razonamiento clínico, la indicación precisa y la prevención de complicaciones. La obra se estructura en tres grandes bloques: Fundamentos generales: principios de fisiología digestiva, semiología, métodos de imagen (ecografía, TC, RM, endoscopia) y bases de la terapéutica quirúrgica (laparotomía, laparoscopia, robótica). Se incluye un capítulo específico sobre bioseguridad y control de daños, esencial en la cirugía de urgencias. Patología por segmentos: desde el esófago hasta el recto, cada capítulo aborda la epidemiología, la clínica, los criterios diagnósticos y las opciones terapéuticas (médicas, endoscópicas y quirúrgicas) de las enfermedades más prevalentes: enfermedad por reflujo gastroesofágico, hernia hiatal, úlcera péptica, colelitiasis, pancreatitis aguda y crónica, cáncer colorrectal, enfermedad inflamatoria intestinal, apendicitis, hernia de la pared abdominal y patología hemorroidal, entre otras. Escenarios especiales: cirugía de urgencias (peritonitis, obstrucción intestinal, isquemia mesentérica), cirugía oncológica (resecciones ampliadas, metástasis hepáticas), cirugía metabólica y bariátrica, y el paciente politraumatizado con afectación abdominal. Cada capítulo está redactado por especialistas con amplia experiencia asistencial y docente, y ha sido sometido a una rigurosa revisión por pares. Se han incorporado algoritmos de decisión, tablas de estadificación y recomendaciones basadas en la evidencia (guías de la Asociación Española de Cirujanos, la American College of Surgeons y la Sociedad Europea de Cirugía Endoscópica). Un aspecto distintivo de esta obra es el énfasis en el diagnóstico clínico‑quirúrgico como competencia nuclear del cirujano general. Frente a la tentación de apoyarse exclusivamente en pruebas complementarias, recordamos que una anamnesis minuciosa y una exploración física sistemática siguen siendo la mejor herramienta para orientar la indicación quirúrgica y anticipar las complicaciones. Los capítulos incluyen recuadros de "señales de alarma" y "errores diagnósticos frecuentes" que el lector podrá aplicar directamente en la práctica diaria. El libro está dirigido a residentes de Cirugía General, a cirujanos ya especializados que deseen actualizar sus conocimientos y a médicos de atención primaria o de urgencias que necesitan reconocer cuándo derivar a un paciente quirúrgico. Cada capítulo contiene objetivos de aprendizaje, preguntas de autoevaluación y una lista de lecturas recomendadas actualizadas a 2025-2026. Agradecemos profundamente a los autores, a los revisores externos y a las instituciones que han apoyado esta iniciativa (Hospital General de Latacunga, Universidad Técnica de Ambato, y las sociedades científicas afines). Esperamos que este libro se convierta en un compañero de consulta habitual y que contribuya a mejorar la calidad del diagnóstico y el tratamiento quirúrgico de los pacientes con patología digestiva.
authors: Juan Diego Lanchi Campoverde; David Patricio Alulema Cutiopala; Adriana Cristina Cabascango Soria; Karol Dayana Rengifo Santistevan; Juan Daniel Fonseca Vaca

title: Clinical Tasks Explain AI Readiness Across Medical Specialties
abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming clinical work, yet its potential impact is often considered at the level of medical specialties rather than their constituent clinical tasks. We developed a clinical task-based framework, medical specialty AI readiness (MSAIR), for evaluating AI readiness across 22 medical specialties, scoring 330 representative clinical tasks across six dimensions. We found AI-readiness scores varied more widely across clinical task categories than across specialties. Clinical documentation and diagnostic interpretation had the highest task-category scores, whereas emergency decision-making and medical procedures had the lowest. Clinical task explained 71.6% of the variation in AI readiness, compared with only 6.4% explained by medical specialty. These findings suggest that AI readiness is more strongly associated with the nature of clinical work than with medical specialty. The MSAIR framework is useful for planning and anticipating how AI may reshape medical practice.
authors: Bertalan Meskó; Gellért Katonai; Shangchu Chen; Bin Sheng; Tien Yin Wong; Eric Topol

title: Clinicopathological profile and surgical outcome of choledochal cysts: a prospective observational study from Bangladesh
abstract: Background: Choledochal cysts are uncommon congenital abnormalities of the biliary tract characterized by cystic dilatation of the extrahepatic and/or intrahepatic bile ducts. This study evaluated the clinicopathological characteristics, diagnostic profile, cyst morphology and surgical outcomes of patients with choledochal cysts treated at a tertiary surgical center in Bangladesh. Methods: This prospective observational study was conducted in the Department of Surgery, Bangladesh Medical University, Dhaka, from January 2013 to December 2014. Forty-two patients with choledochal cysts were included. Demographic characteristics, clinical presentation, associated hepatobiliary conditions, laboratory findings, imaging investigations, Todani classification, operative procedures, histopathological findings and postoperative complications were evaluated. Descriptive statistical analysis was performed. Results: Among 42 patients, 27 (64.3%) were female and 15 (35.7%) were male. Thirty-two patients (76.2%) were older than 20 years. Abdominal pain was the most frequent presenting symptom, occurring in 34 (81.0%) patients, followed by jaundice in 19 (45.2%). Todani type I was the predominant cyst type, identified in 20 (47.6%) patients, followed by type IV in 13 (31.0%). Type II, III and V cysts were present in 3 (7.1%), 1 (2.4%) and 5 (11.9%) patients, respectively. Ultrasonography was performed in all patients, while MRCP was performed in 38 (90.5%). Complete cyst excision was achieved in 34 (81.0%) patients, with Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy being the predominant reconstructive procedure. Seven patients (16.7%) developed postoperative complications. One postoperative death occurred. Conclusions: Choledochal cysts in this series predominantly affected females and were frequently diagnosed during adulthood. Todani type I was the commonest anatomical subtype. Ultrasonography followed by MRCP provided the principal diagnostic pathway. Complete cyst excision with biliary reconstruction was the predominant definitive treatment. Early diagnosis and appropriate anatomical delineation may facilitate definitive surgery and reduce complications associated with delayed presentation.
authors: Mahmud Hasan; M. Ashraful Islam; Z. M. Raihan Kabir; Shaffat Sabbir Khan; Sharmin Akhter; M. Tafazzul Hossain Bhuiyan

title: Comparative study of robot-assisted versus laparoscopic surgery for rectovestibular fistula
abstract: OBJECTIVE: To compare perioperative outcomes and 30-day complications between robot-assisted anorectoplasty (RAARP) and laparoscopic-assisted anorectoplasty (LAARP) for rectovestibular fistula (RVF), and exploratorily assess bowel function and operative time trends after RAARP. Comparative evidence specific to RVF remains limited. METHODS: This single-center retrospective cohort included 63 patients treated during 2019-2024. Given nonrandom treatment and differing enrollment periods, the primary analysis used the contemporaneous 2021-2024 cohort (RAARP, n = 25; LAARP, n = 23). Propensity scores were estimated by Firth bias-reduced logistic regression including calendar year, and overlap weighting estimated the average treatment effect in the overlap population. The primary outcome was total operative time. Core operative time excluded robotic docking time; for LAARP, it equaled total operative time. Thirty-day complications and Krickenbeck bowel function were analyzed exploratorily. RESULTS: RAARP was associated with longer total operative time (overlap-weighted difference, 18.00 min; 95% CI 9.90 - 26.10; P < 0.001) but shorter core operative time (- 6.81 min; 95% CI - 10.36 to - 3.26; P < 0.001). Docking time averaged 26.24±11.29 min. Postoperative length of stay did not differ significantly (- 0.53 days; 95% CI - 1.52 to 0.46; P = 0.290). Thirty-day complications did not clearly differ, and no fistula recurred. Within the RAARP group, case sequence correlated negatively with total, docking, and core operative times (Spearman ρ = - 0.987, - 0.975, and - 0.896; all P < 0.001). Among 33 patients with complete Krickenbeck assessments, soiling was less frequent after RAARP [1/12 (8.3%) vs 10/21 (47.6%); exploratory P = 0.027], but missing and non-contemporaneous data limited interpretation. CONCLUSIONS: RAARP had shorter core but longer total operative time because of robotic docking. Operative times decreased across consecutive RAARP cases, although no proficiency threshold was estimated. Functional findings remain exploratory.

title: Comparison of three malnutrition assessment criteria for predicting postoperative complications and overall survival in colorectal cancer
abstract: Background Malnutrition is highly prevalent in patients with colorectal cancer and is associated with adverse postoperative outcomes and shortened survival. However, the comparative predictive performance of commonly used nutritional assessment tools—PG-SGA, ESPEN, and GLIM criteria—remains unclear. Methods A total of 1,258 patients who underwent radical resection for colorectal cancer were retrospectively enrolled. Malnutrition was diagnosed simultaneously using the PG-SGA, ESPEN, and GLIM criteria. Agreement among the three tools was evaluated using Cohen’s kappa coefficient. Multivariable logistic regression, an exploratory random forest analysis, and Cox proportional hazards models were applied. For the logistic regression models, ROC curve analysis and pairwise AUC comparisons using DeLong’s test were performed; for the Cox models, bootstrap-based C-index comparisons were conducted. Propensity score matching (PSM) was performed for the GLIM criterion as a post hoc sensitivity analysis to explore the association between GLIM-defined malnutrition and clinical outcomes. Results The prevalence of malnutrition defined by PG-SGA, ESPEN, and GLIM was 24.7%, 15.7%, and 29.9%, respectively, with pairwise agreements ranging from moderate to substantial. All three criteria were independent risk factors for postoperative complications, with GLIM having the highest odds ratio (OR = 1.869, p < 0.001). AUC comparison further showed that the GLIM-incorporated model achieved the numerically highest AUC (0.781), with a significantly higher AUC than the ESPEN-based model ( p = 0.023), whereas no significant difference was observed between GLIM and PG-SGA ( p = 0.172). For OS, PG-SGA (HR = 1.364, p = 0.014) and GLIM (HR = 1.415, p = 0.004) were independent prognostic factors, whereas ESPEN was not ( p = 0.129). Bootstrap C-index comparisons showed that the GLIM-based model provided modestly better prognostic discrimination than both the PG-SGA- and ESPEN-based models (both p < 0.05), although the absolute C-index improvement was small (approximately 0.015). After PSM balancing baseline characteristics, GLIM-defined malnutrition remained significantly associated with prolonged postoperative hospital stay, higher complication rates, and reduced 5-year overall survival. Conclusion The three malnutrition diagnostic criteria are not interchangeable. For postoperative complications, GLIM demonstrated better discriminative ability than ESPEN but was comparable to PG-SGA. For long-term OS, GLIM provided modestly better prognostic discrimination than both PG-SGA and ESPEN, although the absolute improvement was small. These findings support the potential clinical utility of GLIM for perioperative nutritional risk assessment; however, the clinical relevance of these relatively small performance differences warrants further validation.

title: Complexity-informed osteopathic care for chronic low back pain in a 60-year-old woman: a case report
abstract: Background Chronic low back pain is a pervasive condition that challenges healthcare systems and can compromise healthy ageing. This case report describes a person-centred osteopathic approach in a 60-year-old woman. Case presentation A 60-year-old woman presented with a 10-year history of chronic low back pain (working diagnosis) radiating to the coccyx, accompanied by shoulder pain and recurrent cervicogenic headaches. Her clinical picture was complicated by diabetes, depression, and a history of trauma, illustrating a complex case of multimorbidity. Prior physical therapy had been only partly undertaken and prescribed glucocorticoid injections were declined, with limited relief and progressive functional decline. A structured conventional examination preceded a personalized osteopathic assessment informed by reasoning based on the Cynefin Framework—a complexity-science approach to making sense of her presentation—with the complete framework mapping assembled retrospectively for this report. The multimodal osteopathic care plan, delivered by a single practitioner, comprised osteopathic manipulative treatment (including myofascial release and balanced ligamentous tension), patient active-participatory graded movement (such as functional neuromyofascial activity), prescribed home activity, shared decision-making, and reassurance addressing kinesiophobia. Progress was monitored with the RAND-36 Health Survey (scored at baseline and the third session, with unchanged scores confirmed at the two subsequent encounters, through ∼10.6 months) and the Visual Analogue Scale (VAS, current pain, recorded at every encounter). The VAS decreased from 7 to 2, and substantial numerical improvements were recorded across multiple RAND-36 domains, temporally associated with the course of osteopathic care. Discussion In this single, uncontrolled case, clinical improvement occurred but cannot be attributed to the intervention alone, as regression to the mean, natural symptom fluctuation, expectancy effects, and the therapeutic alliance cannot be excluded. The case suggests a potential role for a holistic, biopsychosocial approach grounded in complexity-informed, person-centred reasoning and shared decision-making, and may inform wider discussions of non-pharmacological care within universal health coverage and healthy-ageing strategies, including tertiary-prevention objectives that minimize morbidity and maximize functional and psychosocial recovery in long-term conditions. These broader implications are, however, hypothesis-generating and not established by a single case. Controlled prospective research is required to evaluate efficacy and clarify the underlying mechanisms.

title: Concordance of p16 status between US-guided core needle biopsy and surgical specimens in oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma
abstract: With the increasing prevalence of human papillomavirus (HPV)-driven oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (OPSCC), there is a need for efficient, minimally invasive methods to evaluate p16 status. This study aimed to assess the concordance of p16 status between ultrasound (US)-guided core needle biopsy (CNB) of cervical lymph nodes and surgical specimens, and to describe the numbers of CNB and surgical sessions required to establish the histopathologic diagnosis. This retrospective study included 39 patients diagnosed with OPSCC or head and neck squamous cell carcinoma of unknown primary (SCCUP) at a single tertiary hospital between March 2019 and March 2024. All included patients underwent US-guided CNB of cervical lymph nodes and a surgical procedure (biopsy or resection), and had evaluable p16 immunohistochemistry (IHC) results on both specimen types. The concordance rate for p16 status between US-guided CNB and surgical specimens was 100.0% (39/39; 95% CI, 91.0-100.0%; 35 p16-positive and 4 p16-negative cases). Sensitivity was 100.0% (35/35; 95% CI, 90.0-100.0%) and specificity was 100.0% (4/4; 95% CI, 39.8-100.0%). In all 39 included patients, a diagnosis of metastatic squamous cell carcinoma and an evaluable p16 result were obtained at the first CNB session. Among the 35 patients with OPSCC, 10 (28.6%) required more than 1 surgical session at the primary tumor site. No immediate complications were observed following US-guided CNB. In this cohort, US-guided CNB of cervical lymph nodes showed complete observed concordance with surgical specimens for p16 status, and a diagnosis with an evaluable p16 result was obtained at the first CNB session in all patients. Prospective, multicenter validation including more p16-negative cases is required before wider adoption.

title: Content, implementation, and evaluation of artificial intelligence literacy education for nursing students : A scoping review
abstract: Abstract Background Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in nursing education, but evidence on AI literacy as a nursing-specific educational competency remains fragmented. Methods The review was informed by Arksey and O'Malley's framework. Nine databases and Google Scholar were searched for publications from 1 January 2018 to 5 June 2026. Two reviewers independently screened the records and charted the data. Study characteristics and evaluation approaches were summarised descriptively, while educational content, pedagogical strategies, and AI-related learning tasks were synthesised using inductive thematic analysis. Results A total of 14 sources were included. AI literacy education primarily focuses on the responsible use of AI, the critical evaluation of AI-generated content, applications in nursing contexts, and professional judgement. In terms of teaching strategies, guided AI practice and prompt scaffolding are the most common. Assessment primarily employs standardised scales, task rubrics, and qualitative feedback; short-term assessments based on scales are more common, while performance-based assessments grounded in nursing tasks are less frequent. Conclusions AI literacy education for nursing students is still in its early stages, and its focus has expanded from mere technical application to responsible, critical, and context-sensitive nursing judgement. In the future, we should promote the gradual integration of AI literacy into the nursing curriculum and strengthen performance-based assessments of AI-assisted nursing judgement in real-world learning contexts.

title: Cryptococcal Meningitis in an Apparently Immunocompetent Patient With a Ventriculoatrial Shunt: Diagnostic Challenges of Negative Serum Cryptococcal Antigen
abstract: Objective:Rare disease Background:Cryptococcal meningitis usually occurs in people with impaired cellular immunity, but it can also affect patients without a recognized immunodeficiency.Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) shunts complicate recognition because symptoms may be subtle and serum studies may be unrevealing.We describe a case of a patient with a longstanding ventriculoatrial (VA) shunt whose CSF findings established the diagnosis despite a negative serum cryptococcal antigen result. Case Report:A 60-year-old man with a remote ventriculoperitoneal shunt subsequently converted to a VA shunt developed persistent headache and an episode of seizure-like activity 3 days after robotic cholecystectomy.He had no focal neurological deficit, and electroencephalography showed no epileptiform activity.Brain magnetic resonance imaging showed no mass lesion or hydrocephalus.Lumbar puncture revealed lymphocytic pleocytosis (101 cells/μL), CSF protein of 61 mg/dL, and glucose of 44 mg/dL.Serum cryptococcal antigen was negative, whereas CSF cryptococcal antigen was positive at a titer of 1: 40 and CSF culture grew Cryptococcus neoformans.The discordant serum result has an uncertain mechanism because assay-platform details and repeat or dilution testing were unavailable.He received liposomal amphotericin B and flucytosine, underwent VA shunt removal and external ventricular drainage, and later had shunt revision.Following clinical and microbiologic improvement, he received fluconazole consolidation and maintenance therapy and remained clinically well at 4-week follow-up. Conclusions:A negative serum cryptococcal antigen result did not exclude meningitis in this patient with a CSF shunt.Persistent unexplained neurological symptoms warrant CSF evaluation when cryptococcosis remains clinically plausible.This case also illustrates the importance of antifungal therapy and coordinated neurosurgical management for suspected shunt-associated infection.

title: DLST-driven metabolic alterations link skin to blood glucose: A translational study from mouse to human
abstract: To investigate the link between skin features and diabetes, we performed a multi-modal study combining a diabetic mouse model, a human pilot cohort, and keratinocyte response assays. Our goal was to identify molecular signatures in skin, cells, and sweat that correlate with glycemic control and could serve as early biomarkers of hyperglycemia. This integrative approach advances understanding of diabetes-associated dermatological changes and supports the development of targeted, non-invasive diagnostic tools for early detection. Following glucose tolerance tests, proteomic and metabolomic profiling was performed. We identified dihydrolipoyl-succinyltransferase (DLST) as a promising biomarker whose protein and transcript levels consistently correlated with glycemic status across models. In HaCaT keratinocytes, DLST was found to drive metabolic reprogramming toward glutamine utilization as part of an antioxidant protective response. Chromatin immunoprecipitation assay revealed that Sp1 binds to the DLST promoter region, while functional studies, including Sp1 overexpression and knowdown, further confirmed that Sp1 regulates DLST at transcriptional level. Furthermore, DLST knockdown reproduced metabolic shifts in glutamine pathways, findings supported by proteomic analyses and stable isotopic flux analysis. Reduced DLST expression in healthy skin corresponded with glutamine metabolism changes observed in keratinocytes upon oral glucose ingestion. While healthy skin and sweat displayed opposing metabolic trends, pre-type 2 diabetes samples showed aligned trends, suggesting sweat metabolomics could serve as an early systemic metabolic indicator. These findings identify DLST as a glucose-responsive biomarker reflecting skin and sweat responses to systemic glucose, providing a foundation for the development of targeted, non-invasive diagnostic tools for early detection of diabetes.

title: Deep Learning for Sequential Decision Making Under Uncertainty: Foundations, Frameworks, and Frontiers
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is moving increasingly beyond prediction to support decisions in complex, uncertain, and dynamic environments. This shift creates a natural intersection with operations research and management sciences (OR/MS), which have long offered conceptual and methodological foundations for sequential decision-making under uncertainty. At the same time, recent advances in deep learning, including feedforward neural networks, LSTMs, transformers, and deep reinforcement learning, have expanded the scope of data-driven modeling and opened new possibilities for large-scale decision systems. This tutorial presents an OR/MS-centered perspective on deep learning for sequential decision-making under uncertainty. Its central premise is that deep learning is valuable not as a replacement for optimization, but as a complement to it. Deep learning brings adaptability and scalable approximation, whereas OR/MS provides the structural rigor needed to represent constraints, recourse, and uncertainty. The tutorial reviews key decision-making foundations, connects them to the major neural architectures in modern AI, and discusses leading approaches to integrating learning and optimization. It also highlights emerging impact in domains such as supply chains, healthcare and epidemic response, agriculture, energy, and autonomous operations. More broadly, it frames these developments as part of a wider transition from predictive AI toward decision-capable AI and highlights the role of OR/MS in shaping the next generation of integrated learning–optimization systems.

title: Deep learning–based estimation of entrapment status of survivors under debris from 3D measurements for disaster medical response
abstract: Severe earthquakes, landslides, and tsunamis can cause structural collapse, trapping survivors beneath debris and limiting direct observation of the entire body. In confined spaces, voice calls, still images, and videos may be inadequate for conveying a survivor’s posture, contact with debris, and surrounding spatial conditions. We therefore developed a deep learning–based pipeline that takes a textured 3D scene mesh as input and integrates multiview, disaster-adapted human pose and shape estimation, dual-label RGB-D segmentation, scene-constrained SMPL fitting, and voxel-based geometric reasoning. The pipeline reconstructs a full-body survivor mesh, identifies candidate debris–body contact regions, and estimates the mass of load-contributing debris using a simplified geometric criterion. We evaluated the pipeline in 23 controlled entrapment cases involving clothed mannequins and representative wood and concrete blocks. Across these cases, the complete pipeline achieved a contact-region intersection-over-union of 0.391, an F1-score of 0.538, and a relative debris-mass error of 26.1%. Although these results do not establish the method’s suitability for clinical diagnosis, crush-syndrome severity assessment, or autonomous medical or rescue decision-making, they demonstrate its technical feasibility for generating preliminary situational information from 3D scene measurements.

title: Delayed sequential lung, acral cutaneous and brain metastases after radical nephrectomy for clear cell renal cell carcinoma: a case report
abstract: Renal cell carcinoma may recur after nephrextomy. Approximately 25-30% of all RCC patients develop metastases, most commonly involving the lungs, bones and brain. Cutaneous metastases are exceptionally rare (about 3% of all RCC patiens) and are associated with a favorable prognosis. While the surgical interventions remain the cornerstone of the management of RCCs, chemotherapy and biological therapies are also available, therefore a complex approach is a must in order to reach the best possible outcome. This is a case report of a 62-year-old male patient with obesity, type 2 diabetes mellitus and smoking history, who underwent a laparoscopic transperitoneal radical right nephrectomy in 2019. Later the histological examination confirmed clear cell renal cell carcinoma. During the course of the disease, he developed multiple metastases involving the lungs, the skin and the brain. He received oncological therapies as well as surgeries – involving robot-assisted thoracoscopic surgery and CyberKnife surgery - and tolerated the therapeutic methods well. This case emphasizes that even small acral lesions in patients with prior renal cell carcinoma may represent metastatic disease and demonstrates the value of prolonged surveillance and multidisciplinary treatment in rare delayed metastatic presentations.

title: Design Guidelines for Block Copolymer‐Templated In 2 O 3 Nanowires: Linking Morphology, Sintering, and Volatile Organic Compounds Sensing Performance
abstract: We provide design guidelines for obtaining functional indium (III) oxide nanowire (NW) (In 2 O 3 NW) meshes for chemiresistive sensing via a practical, single‐step templating route that utilizes a precursor‐infused block copolymer (BCP) ink. This approach realizes a long‐sought promise of BCP‐templated functional nanostructures: reproducible patterning of active sensing materials with tunable morphology and high scalability potential. By varying BCP molecular weight, we systematically tune NW geometry and network connectivity, correlate morphology with baseline resistivity and chemiresistive metrics toward volatile organic compounds (VOCs), and identify an optimal BCP molecular weight that maximizes sensitivity. An optimized thermal annealing protocol sinters the sensory NW mesh, increasing its electrical conductivity by two orders of magnitude and stabilizing chemical and microstructural state, which yields durable, repeatable responses. Using the optimized morphology and annealing protocol, we evaluate sensing against six types of model VOC air pollutants, demonstrating robust high sensitivity. By correlating the performance with structural parameters, we establish quantitative guidelines linking BCP molecular weight, NW geometry, percolation, electrical resistivity, and VOC detection sensitivity. This method combines the nanoscale precision and tunability of BCP templating with the practicality of spin‐coating processes, establishing a reproducible process blueprint compatible with large‐area deposition techniques, pending future optimization of strict process control parameters.

title: Design and Simulation of Multilayer SPR Biosensor Based on BK7/Ag/BN/BlueP/WSe 2 /BP for Label‐Free Detection of A549 Lung Cancer Cells
abstract: ABSTRACT A label‐free surface plasmon resonance (SPR) biosensor was explored for the detection of A549 lung cancer cells. The proposed sensing platform uses a multi‐layer platform consisting of a BK7 prism, Ag, BN, BlueP/WSe 2 heterostructure, and BP layers. To excite the surface plasmons, a silver coating was applied to the BK7 prism using the Kretschmann arrangement. These BN, BlueP/WSe 2 , and BP layers increase the confinement of the electromagnetic field and light–matter interaction and reduce the dissipation of plasmonic energy. The transfer matrix method (TMM), which uses angular interrogation at an operating wavelength of 633 nm, was used for the numerical analysis. The optimized multilayer architecture exhibited excellent sensing capability, with a sensitivity of 366.589°/RIU, quality factor of 100.054 RIU − 1 , detection accuracy of 1.8010 deg − 1 , and full width at half maximum (FWHM) of 3.6639°. The results show the efficiency of the proposed design for A549 lung cancer detection.

title: Design and Simulation of an Event Driven Sensorless IoT System for Automotive Battery Monitoring and Fault Detection
abstract: In the automobile industry, lead acid battery failure continues to be a major factor in vehicle immobility. In traditional monitoring systems, high inactive current draw, which adds to parasitic drain, or a lack of remote accessibility for real time user notification are common problems. A unique, event driven Internet of Things (IoT) framework for real time vehicle power diagnostics is proposed in this research. The sensorless architecture that uses straightforward resistor divider network to transmit voltage data straight into Analog to Digital Converter (ADC) of the microcontroller, is a significant innovation since it prevents the need for external sensors. Also, this suggested framework makes use of a state machine that alternates between an active sensing mode and a deep sleep period that is only activated by abnormal voltage occurrences. The proposed design validated through an electrical system and supervisory state logic modelled using MATLAB/Simulink, where Python serving as a secondary simulation and communication layer. Five main operating conditions are distinguished by the monitoring algorithm: parked, engine cranking, regular operation, alternator failure, and critical shutdown. The automotive voltage is scaled to an ADC compatible range using a 10 kΩ/2.7 kΩ resistor divider network, and signal filtering is provided by a 0.1 µF capacitor. With voltage settings of 12.60 V during parked operation, 9.80 V during engine cranking, 14.20 V during normal charging, 11.74 V during simulated alternator failure, and 10.30 V at critical shutdown, the simulation replicated the desired vehicle operating sequence. 1000 separate Monte Carlo runs with additive Gaussian measurement noise made up the stochastic validation. Relative mean voltage errors for the statistically assessed parked, alternator failure, and shutdown states were 0.0016%, 0.0009%, and 0.0029%, respectively, whereas the empirical detection success rate under the simulated conditions was 100%. The findings show that the suggested state machine architecture can reduce the need for ongoing high-power monitoring while differentiating between sustained abnormal voltage circumstances and normal beginning transients. As a result, the system offers a useful basis for controlled automotive validation and future ESP32 based physical implementation.

title: Design and optimization of an Ag/Cu–black phosphorus/Franckeite heterostructure for high-sensitivity surface plasmon resonance biosensing
abstract: Introduction Surface plasmon resonance (SPR) biosensors enable label-free, real-time detection, but simultaneously achieving strong field confinement, near-critical coupling, and a high figure of merit (FoM) remains challenging, particularly when low-loss silver must be protected from aqueous media. Methods A CaF 2 /Ag/Cu/black phosphorus (BP)/Franckeite Kretschmann heterostructure was modeled at λ = 633 nm using the frequency-domain Maxwell wave equation and the transfer matrix method under TM-polarized angular and phase interrogation. The Ag and Cu thicknesses were optimized individually and jointly, size-dependent Drude damping corrections were applied, and performance was benchmarked against a Cu-only reference with identical BP/Franckeite overlayers. Fabrication tolerance to BP layer number and Franckeite thickness was also evaluated. Results Joint optimization identified a near-critical-coupling configuration at approximately 31 nm Ag and 7 nm Cu, with a minimum reflectance of 1.1 × 10 −3 within the sensing window. Over 1.328–1.336 RIU, the sensor reached a peak angular sensitivity of 372°/RIU and a FoM of 47.0 RIU −1 at n s = 1.332, approximately 62% and 78% higher than the Cu-only reference. Phase interrogation reached 29,200°/RIU, corresponding to a minimum detectable refractive-index change of approximately 3.4 × 10 −7 RIU. The 1/e evanescent-field penetration depth was 178–201 nm. Size-dependent damping reduced the FoM by approximately 5%, and realistic 2D-layer thickness variations reduced it by no more than approximately 10%. Discussion The Ag/Cu/BP/Franckeite architecture is a promising platform for label-free biosensing, including carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) detection, subject to experimental validation of long-term stability, surface functionalization, and thermally compensated phase readout.
authors: Jacob Wekalao; Tobias Otieno

title: Designing Noble Metal Nanoparticle Interfaces for Biosensing: A Fabrication-to-Validation Roadmap
abstract: Abstract Noble metal nanoparticles have become central components of biosensor design, yet their contribution is often described mainly in terms of signal enhancement or diagnostic performance. This review takes a complementary perspective by focusing on how gold, silver, and platinum nanoparticles become functional biosensing interfaces through controlled synthesis, interfacial incorporation, surface functionalization, characterization, and analytical validation. We first examine how colloidal synthesis, direct substrate growth, electrodeposition, thin-film-derived nanostructuring, organized film assembly, and nanocomposite formation produce interfaces with distinct optical, electrical, catalytic, and surface-chemical properties. We then discuss how linker chemistry, receptor immobilization, blocking, and antifouling strategies determine whether a nanoparticle-modified surface becomes a selective biosensor. Characterization is treated as a question-driven framework for verifying nanomaterial formation, interfacial assembly, biorecognition-layer immobilization, charge-transfer or optical response, and analytical reliability. Representative electrochemical, conductometric, colorimetric, and plasmonic platforms are analyzed to show that noble metal nanoparticles do not act as universal enhancers, but rather as catalytic domains, conductive modifiers, immobilization supports, signal tags, or plasmonic transducers depending on the sensing architecture. Finally, we highlight reproducibility, matrix effects, fouling, scalability, and validation in real samples as key barriers to translation. By reframing noble metal nanoparticle biosensors as engineered interfaces, this review emphasizes that analytical performance depends on aligning material properties, interface architecture, and sensing mechanism.

title: Diagnosis, Treatment, and Current Controversies in Multiligament Knee Injuries: A Narrative Review
abstract: Multiligament knee injuries are infrequent but potentially severe, defined by the simultaneous rupture of two or more major knee ligaments, with a considerable risk of neurovascular injury. This narrative review, based on a search of PubMed, the Cochrane Library, and Google Scholar covering 2010 to 2026, examines their diagnosis, treatment, and outcomes, with emphasis on current controversies in surgical management. The Schenck classification remains the reference system, but its initial category is imprecise, and it does not reliably predict neurovascular injury; it should be interpreted alongside the full injury profile. Diagnosis requires a high index of suspicion and systematic physical examination; magnetic resonance imaging is the diagnostic standard, with a low threshold for computed tomography angiography when vascular injury is suspected. Surgery is the treatment of choice in active patients. Single-stage anatomic reconstruction of all injured structures within the first two to three weeks is associated with less secondary meniscal and chondral injury. Autograft is preferred for the anterior cruciate ligament in young patients, whereas autograft and allograft perform comparably for the posterior cruciate ligament and collateral complexes. Early mobilization is associated with less arthrofibrosis without compromising the grafts. Functional outcomes are acceptable in the short and medium term but deteriorate from seven years onward, with post-traumatic osteoarthritis in up to 71.7% of patients in some series. This should be discussed in preoperative counseling. Arthrofibrosis and residual instability are the most frequent complications, and neurovascular injury is the most severe. Surgical timing, graft selection, and the sequence of reconstruction remain the main open questions and will require comparative studies.

title: Diagnostic limitations and procedure-related implantation in follicular-patterned thyroid tumors: a focused review with two illustrative cases
abstract: The rapid adoption of thyroid radiofrequency ablation (RFA) and remote-access thyroid surgery has changed the therapeutic landscape for thyroid nodules. These approaches can reduce visible scarring, shorten recovery, and offer alternatives to conventional surgery in appropriately selected patients. However, their expansion has also exposed a persistent diagnostic vulnerability: follicular-patterned thyroid tumors cannot be definitively classified as benign or malignant by cytology alone, because the diagnosis of follicular thyroid carcinoma requires histologic assessment of capsular and/or vascular invasion. This review first summarizes the current clinical context of minimally invasive thyroid intervention, the diagnostic boundaries of fine-needle aspiration and Bethesda reporting in follicular-lineage lesions, the definitions and published evidence for needle-tract or surgical-tunnel implantation, and the molecular context of DICER1-altered follicular-patterned tumors. Two implantation-related cases are used as illustrative clinical scenarios rather than as the primary evidentiary basis. The Discussion then addresses the major controversies, including procedural expansion, the role of benign cytology as a preprocedural gatekeeper, the uncertain role of molecular testing before ablation, terminology, patient selection, surveillance, research gaps, and potential developments. The available literature remains dominated by case reports and small series, and causal inference is limited. Nevertheless, repeated reports of tract- or tunnel-aligned deposits in follicular-lineage tumors suggest that implantation risk should be considered when selecting patients for ablative or remote-access interventions. Molecular alterations such as DICER1 RNase IIIb hotspot mutations may provide biological context, but they should not replace histologic classification. Future progress will require standardized reporting, prospective registries, molecularly annotated cohorts, and preprocedural algorithms that integrate imaging, cytology, molecular testing, procedural anatomy, and patient preference.
