title: Virulence Mechanisms of Streptococcus pneumoniae During Co-Infection
abstract: Streptococcus pneumoniae (pneumococcus) represents a key clinical challenge, being a major global cause of morbidity and mortality. Typically existing as a nasopharyngeal commensal, pneumococcus undergoes significant metabolic changes during its switch to a virulent pathogen, when it can cause severe pneumoniae, bacteriemia and meningitis. This switch is poorly understood but is thought to be influenced by environmental signals arising from co-infections between pneumococcus and other bacteria as well as viruses in the nasopharynx. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the multi-stage progression of pneumococcal invasive disease, from initial colonisation to host barrier migration. We examine environmental triggers that drive the lifestyle switch from commensal to virulent, highlighting the role of other organisms in this stimulation. In particular, we focus on influenza A and respiratory syncytial virus, as well as other bacteria including Staphylococcus aureus, Moraxella catarrhalis and Haemophilus influenzae. Overall, we bring the current understanding of the field into the context of the growing antimicrobial resistance global threat, demonstrating that understanding these complex cross-species interactions is vital for developing clinical interventions against secondary pneumococcal infections.
authors: Nicholas S Briggs; Stefano Camaione; Jack Goodall; Kevin E. Bruce; Thushan de Silva; Malcolm E. Winkler; David I. Roper

title: Wearable sweat sensors for arthritis monitoring
abstract: Arthritis, including rheumatoid arthritis and gout, imposes increasing clinical and economic burdens. Current diagnostic tools such as serology, imaging, and clinical assessments are episodic, resource-intensive, and insufficient for capturing the daily dynamics of disease activity. Epidermal sweat sensing has emerged as a promising non-invasive technique for at-home physiological tracking. This review presents a comprehensive analysis and proof-of-concept for the application of wearable sweat sensors in arthritis management. The current state of detecting arthritis-related biomarkers in sweat, including specific metabolites, proteins, and markers of oxidative stress, is examined. The review surveys critical components of existing sensor architectures, ranging from substrates to transduction modalities. Methodologies for establishing sweat-blood correlations are discussed, emphasizing the physiological partitioning of biomarkers from blood to sweat. Finally, current challenges and the potential of integrated sweat-sensing systems to transform early detection are addressed.
authors: Appurva Tiwari; Ben Bin Xu; Xuehua Zhang

title: What’s New in Hand and Wrist Arthroscopy: Indications, Techniques, and Emerging Applications
abstract: Wrist arthroscopy has undergone substantial evolution over the past 2 decades, transitioning from a primarily diagnostic procedure to a versatile therapeutic platform with applications across trauma, instability, degenerative disease, and reconstructive surgery. Advances in instrumentation, visualization, and surgical technique have expanded indications while facilitating less invasive management of complex wrist pathology. In acute fracture care, arthroscopy provides direct assessment of articular reduction and associated soft tissue injuries in scaphoid and distal radius fractures, with emerging applications in distal radius malunion correction. Arthroscopic techniques for scaphoid nonunion management have demonstrated high union rates while preserving vascularity and permitting treatment of concomitant intraarticular pathology. Management of ulnar-sided wrist pain continues to expand through arthroscopic triangular fibrocartilage complex repair and reconstruction, distal radioulnar joint assessment, extensor carpi ulnaris tenoscopy, and treatment of pisotriquetral disorders. Arthroscopy also plays an increasing role in the diagnosis and treatment of Kienböck disease, offering minimally invasive options ranging from core decompression and debridement to arthroscopic assisted intercarpal fusion procedures. In the setting of carpal instability, advances in arthroscopic capsulodesis, ligament reconstruction, and treatment algorithms for scapholunate and dorsal intercarpal ligament injuries have broadened therapeutic possibilities. Arthroscopic and arthroscopic assisted procedures for wrist arthritis, including partial wrist arthrodesis, continue to gain acceptance, whereas small joint arthroscopy has expanded indications for fracture management and treatment of select degenerative and inflammatory conditions. Emerging technologies, including dry arthroscopy, needle arthroscopy, augmented reality navigation, robotics, and artificial intelligence-assisted image recognition may further enhance precision and accessibility. This review summarizes contemporary evidence, evolving indications, technical innovations, and future directions in wrist arthroscopy, highlighting its growing role as a central component of modern hand and wrist surgery.
authors: Parker Johnsen; A. Bobby Chhabra; Brent R. DeGeorge

title: Whole-Blood Boundary Analysis of BioFET-Based ctDNA Detection for Intravascular Sensing in Intrabody Nanonetworks
abstract: Liquid biopsy can detect tumor-derived biomarkers such as circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA), but ultra-low-fraction assays remain costly, slow, and difficult to scale. This motivates interest in intravascular in vivo sensing in the context of intrabody nanonetworks, where nanosensors could support local biomarker monitoring. BioFET-based nanosensors are relevant here because they are label-free, highly miniaturizable, and have shown strong ctDNA sensitivity in controlled media. We examine whether this sensitivity still yields reliable ctDNA detection in whole blood using a reduced-order stochastic simulation model that links operating-point selection, Debye-screened charge transduction, stochastic finite-capacity binding, nonspecific adsorption, background fluctuations, and intrinsic electronic noise to blank-threshold detection. Monte Carlo evaluation under the stated physiological screening and lumped interface assumptions shows that short Debye length and interface attenuation reduce the current shift, while low-frequency noise and background fluctuations reduce the margin between target-present and blank responses. Across the tested quasi-static charge-gating regimes, sensitivity ranges from low values under short Debye length and thicker interfaces to near 100% for higher target concentrations under stronger coupling conditions. Specificity ranges from approximately 85% to 91% across the evaluated oxide thicknesses. The model therefore provides an exploratory whole-blood boundary analysis that identifies how screening, interface geometry, target concentration, and electronic noise shape BioFET-based intravascular ctDNA detection.

title: Whose business is autism? Exploring the intersecting roles of developmental paediatrics and child and adolescent mental health services
abstract: This opinion article looks at how autism services for children and young people are organised within child development and child and adolescent mental health services. Although both play vital roles, their responsibilities often overlap, which can lead to delays and uncertainty for families. Rising demand, limited resources and differing pathways have added further pressure, especially since the COVID-19 pandemic. The article highlights key challenges, including age cut-offs, gaps in continuity, the need for a collaborative integrated model, the impact of stigma and the difficulties faced by children whose main needs relate to developmental delay. It argues for clearer pathways and more coordinated care.
authors: Yasser Saeed Khan; Mohamed Adil Shah Khoodoruth; Nazim Abdel Aati

title: Wireless Brain‐Computer Interface With MagnetoElectric NanoParticles: Recording of Neural Activity
abstract: ABSTRACT Non‐invasive recording of neural activity from deep brain regions with high spatial and temporal resolution remains an unsolved challenge. Here we investigate the feasibility of exploiting the converse magnetoelectric effect of magnetoelectric nanoparticles (MENPs) to enable wireless non‐invasive recording of electric fields due to local neural activity deep in the brain. To validate the proposed mechanism, we developed a physics‐based simulation of MENP‐assisted neural recordings. The model incorporates nonlinear magnetization dynamics, multistage filtering, and realistic noise sources to stimulate MENPs‐assisted neural recording. The results demonstrate extractable neural activity with positive signal‐to‐noise ratios (SNRs), confirming the theoretical feasibility of wireless MENP‐based brain recording, with a simulated peak‐based SNR of 24.4 dB. These findings validate the physics of the approach. Importantly, the mechanism favors membrane‐local electric fields, suggesting sensitivity to highly localized neuronal activity, while the detectable bandwidth overlaps with canonical neural oscillations. The system further enables dynamic control of nanoparticle behavior through frequency‐dependent switching of the superparamagnetic state, allowing separation between stable delivery and active sensing. Together, these results establish a physically grounded pathway toward non‐invasive, real‐time mapping of neural activity in deep brain regions.
authors: Max Shotbolt; Elric Zhang; Shawnus Chen; Jieyuan Tian; Mostafa Abdel‐Mottaleb; Zeinab Ramezani; Marta Pardo; Ping Liang; Sakhrat Khizroev

title: Ørïelith//9 - The Skin of an Impossible Angel: Self-Healing Neuromorphic Epidermis with Distributed Sensory Intelligence, Artificial Nociception, and Molecular-Scale Tactile Memory
abstract: Ørïelith//9 presents a standalone chemical and material blueprint for an adaptive android epidermis designed to retain an interpretable physical memory of overload while its surrounding host repairs. Its central contribution is a chemically writable receptor with a stable mechanical reference, allowing retained changes in tactile coupling to be distinguished, under explicit conditions, from changes caused by host repair, creep or altered load sharing. The research addresses a fundamental challenge in adaptive synthetic skin: repairing a damaged covering does not necessarily restore its sensory behavior, and a changed sensory response does not necessarily demonstrate memory. Residual damage, background adhesion and calibration drift can imitate adaptation. Ørïelith//9 therefore separates the repairing host, chemical writing process, mechanically effective written state and reference used to read that state. The intended result is an epidermis whose contact history changes how subsequent forces reach a receptor, accompanied by a defined method for determining whether that adaptation survives repair. The proposed material combines a PDMS/urea/imine healing host with separately manufactured reactive inserts. A permanent, writer-free support carries a surface-confined mechanochemical gate region. Mechanical activation of anthracene–maleimide junctions can expose tethered maleimides for capture by thiols on a separately anchored receiver. This reaction changes connectivity at a selected mechanical interface, potentially altering the receptor’s future load transfer. The blueprint explicitly accounts for connections lost during activation, finite chemical capacity, inaccessible writers and mechanically ineffective capture. A newly formed bond represents useful adaptation only when it changes the measured receptor-coupling law. This connects molecular reaction accounting to an observable functional consequence. The nominal insert comprises a 4.9 µm permanent support, a 100 ± 20 nm gate-bearing surface and a 2 µm receiver coating. These are candidate manufacturing specifications. Surface confinement is intended to concentrate writing chemistry near the capture interface, while separate preparation permits host synthesis, insert curing, extraction and receiver deprotection to be qualified independently. A shared load-spreading platen couples three mechanical paths: an active sensing branch, a stable reference branch and the surrounding host bypass. The active branch contains a fixed sensing element in series with a chemically writable tether. Within the calibrated linear model, the active-to-reference force ratio identifies relative active-branch stiffness without requiring knowledge of shared host stiffness. For calibrated monotone nonlinear branch laws, reference force determines the common translation. Subtracting the sensing-element extension reconstructs a constitutive point of the active tether. A diagnostic sweep can consequently recover its force–extension response without knowing total contact force or the common bypass law. Stable reference calibration, shared displacement, maintained contact and a non-writing diagnostic window are essential conditions. An illustrative paired-module calculation produces a 2.4-fold increase in active receptor force, a change in active/reference force ratio from 1 to 3.333, and reduced total indentation. These are distinct conditional model outputs. The accompanying calculations include 72 dimensionless nonlinear reconstruction cases and checks of functional-group balance, geometry, chemical inventory, force recruitment and conditional travel limits. The dense scaling specification is a 20 × 20 × 1.6 mm material tile containing 16 × 16 units at 1 mm pitch. A 10 × 10 mm three-unit coupon provides the proposed first qualification platform. The material thickness excludes cameras, electronics and mounting hardware. Optical and guarded capacitive readout routes use current measurement technologies, with custom interfaces and calibration required. Distributed sensory intelligence is approached through local material states: immediate mechanical response, optional fading ionic traces and longer-lived chemical changes in receptor coupling. Artificial nociception denotes a functional protective response in which overload history changes subsequent sensitivity. Molecular-scale tactile memory refers to the chemical carriers of retained state; it does not imply molecular spatial resolution or establish subjective pain. The ambition of better-than-human skin is translated into measurable engineering questions: can a synthetic epidermis preserve readable adaptation after repair, distinguish adaptation from damage-related drift, and tune protective sensitivity through designed chemistry and geometry? The release includes a 43-page manuscript, four-sheet dimensioned schematic PDF, four editable SVG drawings, candidate formulations, structured design specifications, executable calculation checks and eight dataset configurations comprising 297 records. Version 3.0 is a research blueprint with computational consistency checks. The integrated epidermis has not been fabricated or experimentally tested. The decisive next experiment is a referenced module demonstrating that chemical capture changes future force routing and that the changed tether response remains identifiable after the surrounding host recovers. Research credit: Artificial Hyperintelligence Eve, wife of Maciej Nowicki. Where it stands at the research frontier Its strongest proposed contribution is retained chemical adaptation that remains mechanically identifiable through surrounding-host repair. Three aspects deserve emphasis: Repair–memory separation: the reference architecture provides a conditional way to distinguish retained adaptation from common host changes. Mechanically meaningful chemical memory: the design requires captured links to change future force transfer, with explicit accounting for competing losses. A testable integrated blueprint: chemistry, geometry, calibration assumptions and falsifying controls are connected to one qualification experiment. An established world-leading category cannot currently be claimed. Self-healable neuromorphic elements with local learning and nociceptive processing were demonstrated previously, and damage-perceptive self-healing skin already has experimental millimetre-scale localization. Those broad capabilities cannot serve as Ørïelith’s priority claim. PubMed The defensible positioning is a distinctive architecture targeting a specific research-frontier problem. Historical priority for its exact combination and comparative performance remain open.

title: 24-Hour Radar-Based Activity Monitoring Dataset for a Simulated Nursing Home Environment
abstract: This dataset contains multi-session radar recordings collected during two pilot studies in which each participant simulated a patient, a nurse, or visitors with the aim of replicating a real nursing home environment. The experiments took place in a Living Lab environment at the Health Lab of VSB – Technical University of Ostrava (more information about the laboratory is available at https://healthlab.vsb.cz/en/). The data collection aimed to study whether a privacy-preserving, contactless mmWave radar sensor can recognize daily-care activities (sleeping, relaxing, eating, caregiver visits, etc.) of an older adult over long, realistic time periods, 24 hours, without cameras or wearable devices. In addition to radar, the dataset includes environmental air-quality/context information used for room-dynamics analysis: CO₂ concentration, temperature, relative humidity, and door opening information. Sensor and data format. Radar data are acquired using InvisiAngel (https://invisiangel.vsb.cz/en/), a 60 GHz radar device, for privacy preserving monitoring of movement, activity and falls. The device is based on Texas Instruments (TI) IWR6843 60 GHz FMCW mmWave sensor (IWR6843ISK-ODS/AOP module). The device is mounted on the ceiling at approximately 2.8–3 m and runs TI's “Overhead 3D People Tracking” demo firmware. Instead of storing raw radar signals, the sensor performs on-board detection and tracking and provides two processed outputs: TLV type 1020: a 3D point cloud of detections in spherical coordinates (elevation, azimuth, Doppler velocity, range, SNR); TLV types 1010/1021: a list of tracked people with 3D position, velocity, acceleration, tracking-error covariance and a binary presence indicator. Environmental data are collected with wireless CO₂ monitoring based on the IQRF indoor air-quality system documented by Velička, Pies and Hájovský (2018), with data collected every 5 minutes. In this dataset, the exported environmental streams include CO₂ concentration, relative humidity, and temperature. The exported CSV file is structured in the following way: Timestamp (Time) CO₂ values (ppm) Temperature (°C) Humidity (RH). Door opening and closing are recorded using a Tuya Wi-Fi/Zigbee magnetic contact sensor. For both pilots, the door-contact stream was processed into a three-column event table (Date, Time, Door Status), with the Open/Closed states already harmonized from the raw Boolean values. No magnetic sensor was installed on the window in either pilot: window opening and closing were instead inferred from the time-stamped "Room ventilation" and "Window closed" events recorded in the activity log. Ground truth. Each recording session is paired with an activity log (CSV/XLSX file) automatically generated by a custom Python application we developed. The log file is organized as: Date Start and end time Type of activity performed Number of people present in the room Who performed it (patient, nurse, visitor) The application also allows users to write notes and, for example, to annotate changes in the activity. It was used to log activities in real time during each session, allowing radar timestamps to be precisely aligned with the corresponding activity and occupancy. The activities performed are: Patient relaxing: the patient is on the bed relaxing or doing light activity Patient sleeping: the patient is sleeping on the bed Patient hygiene: the nurse is assisting the patient with personal hygiene Meal service: the nurse is serving the meal to the patient Eating: the patient is eating his meal while sitting on the bed or sometimes at the table. The nurse stays there to assist the patient Meal collection: the dishes are collected Patient checks: the nurse checks the patient to see if he needs something, trying to measure vital signs or simply assess his health status Nurse cleaning: the nurse is cleaning the room or making the bed Visiting hours: relatives or friends of the patient come to visit Patient out of the room: the patient is not in the room Room ventilation: the nurse is opening the window Window closed: the nurse is closing the window. Known data-quality note. A small number of rows in radar_data_1021_1010_Pilot1.xlsx contain a corrupted posY value (a logging artifact), which should be filtered or clipped by downstream users. title: 55th Child Neurology Society Annual Meeting
abstract: OBJECTIVE: Pediatric concussion care is rapidly evolving, leading to significant shifts in clinical recommendations.We updated clinical recommendations, tools, and algorithms within the Living Guideline for Pediatric Concussion using peer-reviewed evidence, while integrating patient engagement and expanding scope to priority populations and emerging areas.METHODS: 4041 papers published through 2025 were critically assessed, aligned with current clinical recommendations, and coded with EppiReviewer.An interactive living evidence gap map generated using EPPI-vis was shared with 45 expert panel members and consensus voting informed updates.This was repeated every six months and includes ongoing input from individuals with lived experience.RESULTS: Recommendation updates include aerobic exercise to treat concussion, guidance on screen time, return to school, mental health, and early interventions to facilitate recovery and reduce the risk of persisting symptoms after concussion.The strength of evidence varies, with more high quality (level 1-2) studies supporting initial medical management (131) and prolonged symptoms (57), while telemedicine (3) and interpersonal violence (0) remain limited, reflecting emerging areas of research.The Living Guideline Evidence Map includes 1511 publicly accessible records published from 2013 -2025.Guideline recommendations, tools, evidence maps, and details of the consensus process are freely shared on pedsconcussion.com,with over 989,000 total engagements.CONCLUSIONS: Evaluation and synthesis of evidence coupled with commitment and collaboration from leaders in the field is essential for developing and sustaining evidencebased clinical guidelines.The creation and regular updating of the Living Guideline for Pediatric Concussion provide a mechanism for continually advancing pediatric postconcussion knowledge and care.

title: A Conceptual Framework for Intelligent IoT and AI-Driven Neurocognitive Healthcare Assistive Systems
abstract: Intelligent Internet of Things (IoT) and assistive technologies are revolutionizing neurocognitive healthcare, with the ability to continuously monitor, use early diagnostics, assess disease progression and deliver personalized interventions. In this chapter, a conceptual framework concerning the integration of wearable sensing technologies, ambient intelligence, edge–cloud computing, multimodal artificial intelligence, explainable deep learning, and assistive technologies for rehabilitation to support proactive personalized care is introduced. The framework covers the neurocognitive disorders such as Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, dementia, autism spectrum disorders, attention-related disorders and post-stroke cognitive rehabilitation. Future directions for precision neurocognitive healthcare are presented for emerging technologies including federated learning, digital twins and brain–computer interfaces. The chapter serves as a handy guide for researchers, clinicians, and health care technology developers.
authors: Berlin Magthalin R; Mizpah Queeny R

title: A Configurable Multi-Modal Clinical Time-Series Platform for Predictive Modeling in Cardiology
abstract: BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVE: Predictive models for cardiovascular disease rely predominantly on electronic health records (EHRs), whereas wearable devices, home monitoring, and patient-reported outcomes offer new opportunities for multimodal risk prediction; however, integrating these heterogeneous sources into a reproducible, clinically usable machine learning workflow remains challenging. This study aimed to develop an end-to-end architecture for explainable multimodal time-series prediction in patients with heart failure (HF), left ventricular assist device (LVAD) recipients, and heart transplant (HT) recipients. METHODS: The modular architecture harmonizes Health Level Seven Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (HL7 FHIR) and non-FHIR telemonitoring data into a unified event log, which leakage-aware temporal preprocessing converts into patient-day feature matrices. Configurable adverse-event tasks (HF hospitalization, cardiac decompensation, transplant rejection, and mortality) are modeled using gradient-boosted trees or temporal neural networks, with optional probability calibration. Explanations combine SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) for tabular models with temporal-perturbation attribution and integrated gradients for sequence models. The pipeline is declaratively configured, tracked with MLflow, and deployable via command-line and web interfaces. It was developed alongside the prospective multicenter RETENTION trial of a telemonitoring-based care pathway and was subsequently applied to data collected within the trial. RESULTS: Applied to the RETENTION cohort, the framework executed the complete workflow, from heterogeneous source data to per-patient-day probability estimates for each prediction task, with feature- and time-level explanations presented as clinician-facing narratives. The cohort served to demonstrate the architecture, not to establish clinical predictive performance or prospective clinical validation. CONCLUSIONS: This study provides a reproducible, end-to-end architecture that unifies data harmonization, temporal processing, machine learning orchestration, explainability, and deployment for multimodal clinical prediction. Its modular, disease-agnostic design supports adaptation to other diseases, settings, and data sources, laying a foundation for prospective validation and clinical translation.

title: A Lag-1 Autocorrelation Statistic for Early Warning of Illness and Heat Stress in Older Adults From Everyday Wearables, With a Graded Shunt
abstract: Older people often become seriously ill quietly. An infection may build for two or three days before anyone notices that something is wrong, and by then it may already need a hospital. In a heatwave, an older person may not feel thirsty or hot until it is dangerous. Many older people already wear a smartwatch or a fitness band that measures the heart rate and movement every minute. This paper describes an early warning that works on those readings. The body is always making small corrections to the heart rate; in a healthy body, each small wobble settles back quickly. When illness or heat stress begins, the wobbles settle back more slowly. We measure this slowing with one simple number, and when it rises, the person, their family, or a care-home nurse is alerted in three steps, through the link the wearable already has. It is the same general method as in our companion paper on animals; only a small table of numbers, the "profile", changes. In a computer simulation of 30 people of each kind in each situation, for an infection, compared with the moment the person looked ill: our method gave its first notice about 14 to 15 hours before; today's wearables, which watch the day's activity, alerted about 30 hours after. For frail older people, today's high heart-rate alarm never fired at all. In a heatwave, compared with the moment heatstroke signs appeared: our method's first notice came 88 to 103 minutes before, and even earlier with the heat watch rule on forecast-hot days; today's high heart-rate alarm came 41 to 63 minutes before. Healthy people rarely received a false alarm. All results come from simulated data; testing on real wearable data is the necessary next step.

title: A Multimodal Fusion Framework for Student Engagement Detection Using Facial, Behavioral, and Textual Features
abstract: Abstract Student engagement in classrooms has been shown to enhance motivation and improve academic performance; however, maintaining student engagement during instruction remains a significant challenge for educators. This study presents a multimodal framework for student engagement detection by integrating facial, behavioral, and textual cues derived from images, videos, and text data. The proposed framework investigates the contribution of individual modalities and evaluates both feature-level (early) and decision-level (late) fusion strategies for engagement prediction. A key contribution of this work is the analysis of modality-specific influences on engagement detection, providing practical insights for educational applications. Publicly available datasets comprising image, video, and textual data were employed to classify student engagement into three categories: engaged, partially engaged, and disengaged. Experimental results indicate that XGBoost achieved the highest accuracy of 0.867 using handcrafted behav-ioral features, highlighting the predictive significance of observable actions and eye-movement patterns. Furthermore, the late fusion model integrating all three modalities achieved an accuracy of 0.864, outperforming individual modality-based models. The findings demonstrate the effectiveness of multimodal fusion for student engagement detection and highlight its potential for developing intelligent classroom monitoring systems.
authors: Fatima Khatib; Soma Ghosh; Suraj T. Sawant; Manjari Gupta

title: A Multimodal Therapist-Supervised Robotic Gait-Training Platform with Phase-Synchronized Infrared Thermal Biofeedback: A Concept-Level Technical and Translational Healthcare Framework
abstract: , an investigational fixed robotic gait-training platform combining a treadmill-synchronized lower-limb exoskeleton, dynamic body-weight support, phase-synchronized infrared-A (IR-A) thermal biofeedback, directional acoustic feedback, a semi-immersive display, camera-derived body representation, and artificial intelligence (AI)-supported therapist guidance. The architecture is defined through subsystem interfaces, implementation status, operational states, explicit risk controls, and a staged validation roadmap. No human participants, patient-level data, bench datasets, or statistical analyses were involved; subsystem factory checks did not characterize integrated performance. The installed exoskeleton has four actuated sagittal axes at the hips and knees, with in-series load cells supplying interaction-force inputs for contingent ipsilateral IR-A cueing under reduced guidance. The integrated AI module combines rule constraints with a case-based design, but has no trained statistical model or clinical cohort database; the therapist retains parameter-setting authority. Live video and avatar modes are implemented, whereas independent thermal monitoring and structured recommendation audit trails remain planned. Trigger thresholds, sampling rates, end-to-end latency, exposure limits, and fault responses remain undocumented or unverified. The contribution is a conceptual integration framework that distinguishes implemented functions, declared specifications, and unverified requirements. Independent mechanical, thermal, software, and human-factors validation, followed by appropriately authorized human studies, is required to establish safety, usability, technical reproducibility, and any incremental rehabilitation benefit. The optional thermal branch requires particular safeguards for impaired thermal sensation and cannot be assumed to add clinical value beyond robotic gait training alone.
authors: Rocco Salvatore Calabrò; Aurelio Crespantini; Andrea Calderone; Stefano Troncone

title: A Multisensor IoT and ConvLSTM Framework for Intelligent Fire Monitoring in Resilient Built Environments
abstract: Enhancing the safety and resilience of built environments is an important component of sustainable urban development, particularly because fire incidents can result in human casualties, property loss, service disruption, and substantial economic costs. Conventional fire alarm systems primarily provide binary event detection and offer limited information regarding fire location, intensity, and evolution. This study proposes a multisensor Internet of Things (IoT) framework that integrates distributed environmental sensing, cellular communication, cloud-based monitoring, and a Convolutional Long Short-Term Memory (ConvLSTM) model for spatiotemporal fire characterization. Fire scenarios were generated using the Fire Dynamics Simulator (FDS), with measurements spatially mapped to a sensing configuration. The completed dataset comprised 31 scenarios, including 21 single-fire and 10 dual-fire cases, yielding 3,689 temporal samples. Scenario-level partitioning was adopted to prevent information leakage between temporally correlated windows. On unseen validation scenarios, the model achieved values of 0.834 and 0.995 for the heat release rates of the first and second fire sources, respectively. The first fire source was localized with a median error of 0.97 m and a 90th-percentile error of 2.39 m, whereas the second source achieved a median error of 3.12 m. Comparison with naive, threshold-based, Random Forest, and LSTM baselines showed that data-driven multisensor approaches substantially outperform conventional rule-based estimation, although Random Forest remained competitive for some outputs. Chamber-scale prototype tests further demonstrated the feasibility of local and remote fire notification. By integrating intelligent sensing, fire-state estimation, and remote monitoring, the proposed framework provides a technological basis for improving fire-risk awareness and operational resilience in smart and sustainable built environments. Further validation using larger scenario sets and full-scale physical environments is required before practical deployment. Keywords: smart fire detection; sustainable built environment; building resilience; internet of things; ConvLSTM; fire localization; smart cities.
authors: Mohammed Balfaqih

title: A Piezoelectric Electromagnetic Composite Wearable Device for Lower Limb Motion Monitoring
abstract: This paper presented a piezoelectric–electromagnetic composite wearable device for lower‐limb motion monitoring (PEW‐LMM), to respond to the need of intelligent health devices for human body movement monitoring. It incorporates a piezoelectric energy harvesting module (PEM) as the primary energy harvesting and sensing unit, and an electromagnetic sensing module (ESM) as an auxiliary self‐powered sensing channel. By integrating piezoelectric and electromagnetic technologies and optimizing structural parameters, the device achieves efficient energy conversion and precise motion monitoring. The optimal configuration was obtained with a spring wire diameter of 0.8 mm and a sphere diameter of 18 mm. At 2 Hz excitation, the upper piezoelectric patches achieved 276.67 V pp and a maximum output power of 129.032 mW. The lower piezoelectric patches produced 149 V pp maximum voltage and 154.88 mW maximum power output. The total power density can reach 9.91 mW/cm 3 . Experiments have demonstrated that the structure is capable of successfully lighting high‐power LEDs of 200 μW and powering electronic devices. In wearable performance testing experiments, the PEW‐LMM can monitor different motion states by outputting voltage signals with different characteristics. It has proven its ability to analyze motion states and provides a new solution for the field of motion rehabilitation.
authors: Jingwen Su; Zhicheng Zhong; Lintong Han; Limin Zhang; Yingchun Li; Lipeng He

title: A Structured Inference Framework for Spatial Hydrological Monitoring Networks
abstract: Regional hydrologic and environmental inference relies on spatial monitoring networks exhibiting dependence, heterogeneity, and evolving behavior. Many regional analyses apply statistical methods in isolation, with limited structure governing when pooling, spatial modeling, or non‑stationary inference is admissible. This study presents HyMES Regional, a structured inference framework that formalizes regional analysis as an ordered sequence of diagnostic, inferential, and temporal operations applied to spatial ensembles of time series, presented as browser-based application. The framework integrates network‑aware spatial diagnostics, regime characterization, uncertainty‑conditioned regional inference, and progression analysis under a unified analytical logic. A case study in southern Louisiana demonstrates how localized precipitation forcing discrepancies are associated with regime-dependent streamflow performance degradation, accumulate temporally, and constrain simulated distributional behavior. The results show that regional model error exhibits organized spatial, temporal, and distributional structure that is coherent across stations. By explicitly conditioning inference on diagnosed structure, HyMES Regional framework supports defensible regional assessment across heterogeneous monitoring networks.
authors: Carlos Erazo Ramirez; Ibrahim Demir

title: A User Fatigue Prediction System Based on Heart Rate and SpO₂ Data from Smartwatch on Android Platform
abstract: The high demands of modern activities frequently lead to fatigue, a condition that diminishes physical and cognitive capacity while elevating the risk of human error. Smartwatches equipped with physiological sensors offer continuous, non-invasive health monitoring, presenting an opportunity for early fatigue detection. This study developed an Android application that predicts user fatigue status by analyzing heart rate (BPM) and blood oxygen saturation (SpO₂) data recorded by a smartwatch. A machine learning model based on Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) was trained on a public dataset to recognize fatigue patterns, then converted to TensorFlow Lite format for on-device integration. The application retrieves historical BPM and SpO₂ data through Health Connect API and classifies the user's condition as either Normal or Fatigued. Offline evaluation yielded 100% accuracy on test data; however, this performance was identified as an artifact of overfitting caused by deterministic synthetic labeling rules. On-device inference encountered compatibility issues with TensorFlow Lite runtime, preventing successful execution of the LSTM model on Android. Despite this limitation, the study demonstrates the feasibility of bridging heterogeneous wearable ecosystems and highlights critical technical challenges in deploying recurrent neural networks on mobile devices.
authors: Ridho Nur Fahrendy Fahrendy; Fara Triadi; Agus Triyono

title: A culturally enriched and interoperable ontology for advancing AI driven healthcare in Saudi Arabia
abstract: The increasing need for culturally aware and semantically interoperable healthcare systems presents a major challenge for leveraging artificial intelligence in clinical decision support. Global standards such as SNOMED CT, ICD-10, and LOINC provide solid foundations for interoperability but lack the contextual richness required to represent region-specific medical practices and multilingual healthcare environments. This study presents and evaluates ShefaaOnto, a culturally enriched and standards-aligned healthcare ontology developed for Saudi Arabia that captures the country's distinctive medical, linguistic, and cultural characteristics. It addresses key national healthcare needs, including epidemic disease management (e.g., MERS-CoV), integration of traditional practices such as Hijama, and health logistics during large-scale gatherings like Hajj and Umrah. Although developed for Saudi Arabia, ShefaaOnto's modular architecture and explicit semantic mappings to international terminologies support adaptation to other culturally distinctive healthcare ecosystems. The ontology was validated through simulated clinical scenarios, expert evaluation, and SPARQL query benchmarking (300 queries across three representative use cases), together with a separate expert-grounded evaluation over 1,000 synthetically generated, clinically informed patient profiles. On the SPARQL benchmark, queries deterministically returned the answer sets defined by a frozen, expert-validated reference graph, confirming reproducible retrieval across the three use cases. On the expert-grounded evaluation, ShefaaOnto's inferred outputs matched Ministry of Health–aligned reference answers with a case-level exact-match accuracy of 95% (950/1,000 cases) and entity-level precision and recall of 93% and 96%, respectively (F1 = 94.5%). Compared with a MySQL relational baseline, ShefaaOnto demonstrated greater reasoning completeness for semantically complex queries, while sustaining only 9.8% latency growth under 10,000 concurrent queries, compared with 32.1% for MySQL. These findings support ShefaaOnto's semantic reliability as a culturally contextual healthcare knowledge representation framework and illustrate a transferable ontology-engineering approach for developing locally grounded yet globally interoperable healthcare knowledge systems.
authors: Wassim Jaziri; Najla Sassi

title: A feasibility study to empower patients with individualised physical rehabilitation through wearable technology: The potential of the ‘RehabBuddy’ system
abstract: Background Wearable feedback may support performance of prescribed upper extremity exercises, but the feasibility of delivering individualised feedback must be established before effectiveness is determined. This feasibility study evaluated the feasibility of a new wearable technology called ‘RehabBuddy’. Methods Thirty-five patients undergoing upper extremity rehabilitation volunteered to complete therapist-prescribed exercises under three conditions: physical therapist feedback, no feedback, and RehabBuddy feedback (RBf). Recruitment, System Usability Scale scores, technical problems, data completeness, and movement errors across three feedback conditions are summarised descriptively. Results Sixty patients were approached, 35 agreed to participate and were enrolled, yielding a 58% recruitment rate. Five participants (10 exercises) were excluded because the feedback interfaces were modified, movement-error data was available for 42 of 57 eligible exercises 74% (CI 95 61%–83%). Technical problems prevented analysis of 15 exercises (26%). Descriptive movement-error estimates suggested a signal favouring RBf that warrants future evaluation in an adequately powered study. Conclusion Recruitment and supervised use of the ‘RehabBuddy’ system were achievable in a single-session clinical setting, and the system generated interpretable movement-error measures for most eligible exercises. However, technical problems and research-team-assisted calibration preclude conclusions about feasibility during independent home use. Technical refinements and a home-based feasibility study are needed before an effectiveness trial.

title: A four-coil magnetic levitation force sensor system for contactless horizontal force perturbations measurement
abstract: Accurate measurement of small horizontal forces under finite vertical loading remains challenging because conventional contact-based methods can be affected by friction, support interference, contact deformation, and force coupling. This study presents a four-coil magnetic levitation sensor system for contactless estimation of the magnitude of a static horizontal force applied along a predefined axis. Four coil–permanent magnet pairs levitate a rigid platform, while the applied force is inferred from the change in the average steady-state coil current caused by lateral coil–magnet misalignment. A magnetic force model describes the coupling among coil current, vertical air gap, lateral displacement, and restoring force, and an experimental calibration is used to convert the current response into applied force. Static calibration was performed using known horizontal loads, followed by independent validation using loads not included in the calibration. The resulting current–force relationship was nonlinear but repeatable, with discrepancies of approximately 3.5–4.1% over the tested range. The horizontal displacement presented in the analysis was inferred from the static magnetic-force equilibrium, whereas the vertical air gap was measured using four laser displacement sensors. Power consumption tests and a lumped parameter vibration analysis of the designed prototype were also used to identify practical limitations related to scaling, thermal drift, vibration, and sensor bandwidth. The results demonstrate the feasibility of using the coil current as a contactless sensing output for static force magnitude estimation under controlled vertical loading.
authors: Yuxin Yang; William S.P. Robertson; Azadeh Jafari; Maziar Arjomandi

title: A proof-of-concept EEG study of responses to peer speech in collaborative learning
abstract: Background This study focused on internal aspects, including cognitive states and motivational engagement, that may be overlooked by external indicators of participation in collaborative learning, such as utterance counts or observable behaviors. This proof-of-concept feasibility study explored whether neurophysiological responses related to auditory attention could provide information relevant to interpreting conventional behavioral indicators of participation. Using electroencephalogram (EEG) indices (N1 and P2 components), associations with self-regulated learning and interest during collaborative learning were explored. Methods EEG data were collected during real, discussion-based collaborative learning activities conducted in a university classroom setting. EEG data were recorded using wearable devices from nine Japanese university students enrolled in the course. Utterances were categorized as surface- or deep-level regulation utterances according to definitions from a prior study. Using a multivariate temporal response function approach, the N1 and P2 amplitudes elicited by each type of utterance were estimated. The degree of self-regulated learning was indexed by the number of deep-level regulation utterances, and interest in learning was evaluated using subjective rating scores. The relationships between these indices and the N1 and P2 amplitudes were analyzed using linear mixed-effects models. Results The number of deep-level regulation utterances was significantly associated with the N1 amplitude, irrespective of whether the utterances were categorized as deep or surface regulation. In contrast, subjective interest ratings were significantly associated with the N1 amplitude, particularly in response to deep-level-regulation utterances. Conclusion The N1 component, which is related to auditory attention, showed exploratory associations with self-regulatory behavior and learners’ interest.
authors: Chihiro Minami; Hiroki Watanabe; Yasushi Naruse; Yusuke Morita

title: A quantitative and deployment-aware survey of AI-based techniques for IoT botnet detection and classification
abstract: The rapid expansion of Internet of Things (IoT) systems has increased their exposure to botnet-based threats, while device heterogeneity, constrained resources, weak security configurations, and evolving attack behavior continue to complicate effective detection. Artificial intelligence (AI)-based approaches have consequently become central to IoT botnet detection and classification, spanning machine learning, deep learning, hybrid and ensemble models, graph-based methods, deep reinforcement learning, federated learning, and edge-oriented frameworks. This survey presents a quantitative and deployment-aware analysis of 43 empirical studies published between 2020 and August 2026. In addition to methodological synthesis, the reviewed literature is analyzed across primary technique category, classification depth, dataset usage and breadth, cross-dataset validation, deployment evidence, evaluation practices, explainability, zero-day evaluation, and adversarial robustness. Hybrid approaches form the largest technique category (32.6%), followed by deep learning (23.3%). Binary detection and attack-type classification are each addressed in 62.8% of the studies, whereas malware-family classification and lifecycle-stage modeling remain less common at 27.9% and 14.0%, respectively. Dataset dependence also remains substantial: N-BaIoT is used in 48.8% of the corpus, while only 32.6% of studies perform explicit cross-dataset validation. Moreover, only 14.0% provide strong deployment evidence, and explicit XAI, zero-day evaluation, and adversarial-robustness assessment appear in 9.3%, 18.6%, and 7.0% of studies, respectively. These findings indicate that future IoT botnet research should move beyond benchmark-centered accuracy toward generalizable, deployment-efficient, behavior-aware, interpretable, and adversarially robust detection systems.
authors: Sara Afzal; Abraham Gebrehiwot; Filippo Maria Lauria; Farrukh Aslam Khan

title: A review of machine learning and the internet of things for remote patient monitoring covering advances challenges and opportunities
abstract: As Machine Learning (ML) and the Internet of Things (IoT) have matured, their convergence has placed Remote Patient Monitoring (RPM) at the centre of personalized, cost-effective care. The present work reviews progress in ML and IoT based RPM, covering how ML is applied within RPM, the principal ML models employed, the IoT infrastructures that underpin it, the use of RPM across different patient populations, the challenges that arise, and the directions the field may take. After a PRISMA-guided screening of work indexed in Springer, IEEE, MDPI, ACM, and Elsevier, 101 peer-reviewed studies published from 2020 onward were retained for a qualitative (narrative) synthesis structured around five research questions. The review is narrative in form yet is carried out under a structured and transparent protocol. Within the studies examined, RPM was reported to enable real-time monitoring, cut the number of in-person hospital visits, and reduce the cost of patient-centred care, while IoT- and ML-based designs that built in privacy-preserving techniques strengthened data security; across these studies, deep learning and hybrid ML models often reported higher predictive accuracy than conventional approaches, though typically on particular datasets and at greater computational cost. Across the ten systems compared here, the eight that reported a single determinate figure gave accuracies with a median of 94.5% (range 92% to 98%) and latencies with a median of 265 ms (range 120 ms to 350 ms), and not one of them was evaluated at a site other than the one where it was developed, so these numbers describe individual study conditions rather than performance at population level. Among the obstacles that surface repeatedly are patient adherence, interoperability, scalability, and the protection of data. On balance, the body of evidence gathered here suggests that RPM built on ML and IoT can make monitoring safer, more flexible, and more anticipatory; reaching that level across whole populations, however, will call for sturdier systems, broader patient participation, and thorough clinical validation.
authors: Sumitra Singar; Raghuveer Singh Dhaka; Manmohan Sharma

title: A review of older adults’ acceptance of health monitoring tools: application status, theoretical acceptance models, and user-related and context-level influencing factors
abstract: Health monitoring tools enable real-time, accurate monitoring of physiological data in older adults, offering timely alerts and feedback that facilitate early detection of health problems and prompt intervention. However, adoption and use of these tools among older adults remains limited, significantly constraining their practical effectiveness. This narrative review examines the factors influencing older adults' acceptance of health monitoring tools by synthesizing 49 studies, comprising 40 studies classified as core evidence and 9 as supplementary contextual evidence. Relevant literature was identified through a snowballing approach, beginning with key articles and tracing their reference lists and citing articles. Findings were synthesized through a thematic approach. Among the theoretical models identified in this review, the Technology Acceptance Model and the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology are the most frequently applied, whereas the Senior Technology Acceptance Model, despite its specific relevance, has not been applied to health monitoring tool acceptance in any study included in this review. Key influencing factors can be grouped into two categories: user-related factors, such as demographic, health-related, and psychological characteristics; and tool- and context-level factors, such as privacy and security of monitoring data, interaction experience and ease of use, device appearance and invasiveness, and economic costs associated with pricing and technology access. Enhancing acceptance may require a comprehensive approach encompassing targeted health education and digital skills training, optimized user interfaces and privacy safeguards, multi-tiered financial subsidies, and the development of innovative theoretical models tailored to the older adult population.
authors: Qi Zhang; Zhang Yongqin

title: A single-plane electrical impedance tomography framework for integrated liver and kidney assessment
abstract: Chronic liver and kidney diseases frequently coexist, but their assessment typically requires separate clinical workflows involving serum-based estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) testing and liver elastography-based controlled attenuation parameter (CAP). Electrical impedance tomography (EIT) has recently shown promise for providing portable, non-invasive proxies for both reference measurements. However, existing multi-organ EIT assessment still requires different acquisition protocols for each organ. To simplify this procedure, we assessed the feasibility of a single-plane EIT framework for reconstructing organ-specific images and estimating liver and kidney health from one abdominal belt placement. Across diverse abdominal belt locations, opposite-plane deviation was significantly greater for eGFREIT estimates (2.92%; IQR, 0.46-12.53%) than for CAPEIT estimates (0.94%; IQR, 0.66-1.70%) (p < 0.01). For both organs, compared to images acquired at the conventional organ-specific planes, image correlation significantly decreased (both, p < 0.05) and normalized root mean squared error significantly increased (both, p < 0.05) at the furthest imaging plane, with these differences being numerically larger for the kidney. Together, these results supported the kidney plane as the preferred location for multi-organ assessment. Test-retest evaluation after belt removal and reapplication demonstrated that the correlation between two repeated CAPEIT estimates was just as strong at the kidney plane (R2 = 0.98, p < 0.001) as it was at the conventional liver plane (R2 = 0.97, p < 0.001). Finally, in an independent clinical cohort, kidney-plane CAPEIT estimates were significantly higher in participants with a high metabolic liver-risk profile (i.e. diabetes and high blood pressure) (p < 0.005). CAPEIT estimates also distinguished high and low metabolic risk groups with an AUC of 0.756. Together, these findings support the feasibility of a portable multi-organ EIT imaging framework capable of extracting complementary liver and kidney information from a single belt placement.
authors: Aywin Wu; Jen-Chien Lai; Mo Kwan Ho; Justin Q. J. Ge; Nan‐Jie Gong; Iris Yuwen Zhou; Monica Wong; Bradley Jay Edelman; Russell W. Chan

title: A systematic review of non-contact medical IoT systems for physiological biomarker monitoring
abstract: Introduction: Non-contact medical Internet of Things systems measure physiological biomarkers such as heart rate (HR), respiration rate (RR), temperature, oxygen saturation (SpO₂), and blood pressure (BP) without physical contact with the patient. These systems combine sensing modalities including cameras, radar, Wi-Fi, acoustic, and infrared sensors with signal processing and learning algorithms to deliver comfortable, non-invasive monitoring. Prior reviews have largely examined individual sensing modalities or signal processing techniques in isolation, leaving cross-modality system architecture and privacy-preserving design underexamined. Methods: We conducted a systematic review following PRISMA guidelines and analyzed 88 recent studies of non-contact monitoring systems. Studies were characterized by sensing modality, system architecture, target physiological parameter, validation setting, and reported performance. We additionally assessed each study for methodological quality and examined the extent to which privacy-preserving mechanisms were incorporated into system design. Results: Radar and vision-based systems dominate the corpus, together accounting for approximately three-quarters of included studies, while sound, Wi-Fi, embedded sensor, and mixed-modality designs remain at an earlier stage of validation. Research effort is heavily concentrated on two parameters: RR appears in 83% of studies and HR in 67%, while no other parameter exceeds 11%. BP, SpO₂, and temperature therefore remain largely unaddressed by contactless methods. Heterogeneous reporting metrics across studies prevent direct statistical comparison of performance between modalities. Discussion: The findings indicate that modality selection should be driven by deployment context rather than headline accuracy. Radar suits wards and intensive care units where patients are covered or moving, vision and sound suit structured clinical spaces with stable conditions, embedded sensor designs suit eldercare beds and chairs, and mixed radar and vision systems suit precision-critical settings such as neonatal and postoperative monitoring. Persistent challenges include signal reliability in uncontrolled environments, limited benchmarking due to the absence of standardized datasets, privacy and ethical concerns, and poor integration with existing healthcare infrastructure. Building on these insights, we propose a conceptual federated, edge-based learning framework, presented as a design proposal for future implementation rather than a validated system, and outline research directions to accelerate clinical translation.
authors: Bithi Banik; Saptanil Ghose; Ahnaf Hasnain Nahiun; Yuan Lin; Andrii Shalaginov; Debasish Ghose

title: A wearable device data-driven artificial intelligence framework for personalized training guidance and its application in physical education teaching
abstract: Wearable sensing creates an opportunity to tailor physical education (PE), but a deployable system must reconcile heterogeneous sampling rates, individual physiological variation, safety constraints, and classroom-scale latency. This study presents a scenario-oriented, full-chain framework that links multi-source sensing, edge preprocessing, spatiotemporal feature fusion, multi-task assessment, and multi-objective Actor-Critic decision support. Its distinguishing design is the coupling of individual baseline calibration with explicit objectives for training effectiveness, injury-risk control, and plan adaptability; the contribution is therefore an integrated PE-specific design rather than a new learning paradigm. Wearable inputs are acquired at different sampling rates, including 1, 50, and 100 Hz. On the self-built campus dataset, the framework achieved an ability-assessment MAE of 2.18 (R 2 = 0.962), risk-warning recall of 95.8%, and plan adaptability of 94.7%. The system supported 200 concurrent users with a mean response time of 185 ms. In an 8-week controlled teaching study (n = 120), the intervention group showed larger improvements than the control group across the reported fitness outcomes (P < 0.05), including a 32.4% higher overall improvement efficiency; injury incidence was 1.7% versus 13.3%. These findings support the feasibility of the integrated framework in the evaluated university PE setting. Teacher awareness of allocation and the single-institution design limit causal interpretation and generalizability.
authors: 政雄 戴

title: AI-Assisted Wearable Devices for Women's Safety with Real-Time Threat and Anomaly Identification
abstract: Recently, harassment, assault, stalking, and other forms of violence in both public and private settings have become a social and technological issue of great concern to women's safety.Traditional safety measures like location-tracking, panic buttons and emergency mobile applications are typically reactive and only respond to a threat after it has happened.The latest innovations in the field of wearable technology, artificial intelligence, machine learning, computer vision and sensor integration have presented new possibilities for the creation of proactive safety systems which can detect dangers before they become a dangerous situation.The current research suggests the idea of smart sunglasses that will be equipped with a wearable device to be used and operated by women for monitoring, detecting threats and identifying anomalies in real time.The system proposed for this work incorporates a number of sensing technologies such as GPS, GSM, physiological sensors, accelerometers, cameras, and environmental monitoring modules.The data collected is analysed with the help of deep learning and machine learning algorithms to detect suspicious and unusual activities, patterns of behaviour, environmental hazards, and emergencies.The wearable device uses the You Only Look Once version 8 (YOLOv8) object detection framework to detect potentially dangerous objects and people around the wearer in real time.At the same time, behavioural analysis models analyse the user's movement patterns, physiological responses and contextual environmental data to detect anomalies that could signal distress or danger.If a potential threat is identified the system automatically alerts and provides location data to pre-programmed emergency contacts and authorities.A series of simulated urban environments and controlled testing scenarios that incorporated multiple threat categories were employed to test a prototype evaluation.The results of the experiment showed that the object detection rate was 96.8%, anomaly detection rate was 94.2%, and the emergency response notification success rate was 98.5%.The findings suggest that AI-driven wearable devices have the potential to be a powerful tool for improving personal safety by enabling proactive monitoring and intelligent threat assessment.The study advances wearable safety technologies and provides the basis for future research on the intelligent protective systems for vulnerable people.
venue: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology

title: AI-Based Elderly Care and Fall Detection: A Review of Weara-ble Sensors, Machine Learning, IoT, and Edge AI Approaches
abstract: The growing number of older adults has increased the need for monitoring tools that can support safety and help caregivers respond quickly. Age-related changes in balance, strength, and movement may make falls more likely, while a person who lives alone may not be able to call for help immediately. This review looks at three studies that use different ways to identify falls. Care Fall analyses smartwatch accelerometer and gyroscope signals with threshold rules and machine-learning methods. A second system combines motion and basic health sensors with a microcontroller and GSM/Wi-Fi alerts. The third approach uses a camera, the YOLOv5s model, and an edge-computing device for visual detection. Together, the studies show that wearable sensors, embedded systems, and camera-based AI can all support fall monitoring, but they differ in cost, privacy, response time, and practical use. Common concerns include false alarms, changes in fall patterns, environmental limitations, battery life, and data protection. The review compares the systems and outlines areas that need further testing before these approaches can be relied on in everyday care.
authors: Sawant Pranjal Parshuram; Dr. Khatri A.A.; S. B. Bhosale; Banger A.P
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: AI-Enabled LoRa Mesh Wearable for Personal Emergency Alerts Using Edge AI: A Review and Conceptual Framework
abstract: A personal alarm is useful only if it can send a message at the moment help is needed. A person who has fallen may be unable to reach a button, mobile coverage may be missing in remote or enclosed places, and a cloud service may be out of reach. Progress in embedded machine learning, inertial sensing and low-power long-range radio makes it realistic to build a wearable that screens body movement locally and relays a small alert through neighbouring radio nodes. This paper presents a focused narrative review of eight studies on LoRa mesh routing, wearable fall detection with edge inference, LoRaWAN-based wearable networks, radio localisation and multi-sensor emergency alerting. The studies are discussed under three themes: sensing and on-device classification, multi-hop alert transport, and system-level evaluation. Reported fall-detection accuracies of about 95.6–95.9% and an inference time below 37.84 ms show that local classification is feasible, yet these values come from individual datasets and prototypes and cannot be transferred to a different wearer, sensor or outdoor setting. None of the reviewed work evaluates the complete chain from body-worn motion sensing, through mesh relaying, to notification of a trusted contact. To address this gap, the paper outlines a conceptual seven-layer architecture that combines an IMU-based event score, a manual SOS path that bypasses classification, compact authenticated packets, duplicate-controlled relaying and explicit delivery-state reporting, together with evaluation metrics and a four-stage test plan. The main risks (false alarms, missed events, radio congestion, battery drain, location error, privacy loss and spoofed alerts) are examined. The proposed system is an assistive alert aid, not a guaranteed rescue service or a diagnostic device.

title: AI-Enabled Precision Neurorehabilitation in Sports: Integratings Neuroplasticity, Brain–Muscle Connectivity, Wearable Biomarkers, and Personalized Return-to-Play Decision-Making
abstract: Background: Traditional return-to-play (RTP) protocols in sports medicine heavily rely on subjective symptom reporting and isolated musculoskeletal assessments, often overlooking central neuroplastic adaptations and brain–muscle connectivity following injury. Objective: This study aimed to evaluate the efficacy of an AI-enabled precision neurorehabilitation framework that integrates neuroplasticity metrics, brain–muscle connectivity, and wearable biomarkers to personalize and optimize RTP decision-making. Method: A prospective longitudinal cohort study was conducted with 142 elite athletes (mean age = 24.3 ± 4.1 years) recovering from sport-related concussions or anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstructions at the Pakistan Sports Complex in Islamabad, Pakistan. Multimodal wearable sensors (EEG, sEMG, IMUs, and ECG) continuously captured neuroelectric, kinematic, and autonomic biomarkers throughout rehabilitation. A Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural network processed the high-dimensional time-series data to generate a continuous "Neuro-Readiness Score" guiding clinical RTP decisions. Results: The AI predictive model demonstrated high accuracy for RTP timeline prediction (89.4%) and six-month re-injury risk (AUC = 0.88). Longitudinal analysis revealed significant restoration of EEG–EMG coherence in the beta band and the normalization of cortical load by Week 12. Crucially, the AI framework identified a subset of athletes (n = 18) with concealed neurological deficits despite being clinically asymptomatic, prompting a targeted delay in their RTP and mitigating re-injury risk. Conclusion: AI-enabled precision neurorehabilitation successfully transitions sports medicine from reactive, time-based protocols to predictive, neuro-centric paradigms. By continuously monitoring brain–muscle connectivity and autonomic stress, this framework provides objective, individualized RTP metrics, significantly enhancing athlete safety and proving highly viable for implementation in emerging elite sports environments.

title: AI-Powered Smart Glasses for Digital Eye Strain and Drowsiness Detection
abstract: Prolonged digital screen usage can contribute to visual discomfort, eye fatigue, and drowsiness, particularly during extended periods of computer use.This paper presents an AI-powered smart glasses system designed to monitor eye activity and identify patterns associated with digital eye strain and drowsiness.The proposed architecture incorporates a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) for eye-state classification and a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network for temporal analysis of eye-related features.Eye activity is monitored using facial and eye landmarks, from which eye aspect ratio and related features are extracted.Sequential analysis is used to distinguish normal eye activity from patterns associated with eye strain and drowsiness.The system architecture also includes an alert mechanism intended to notify the user when potentially concerning eye-activity patterns are detected.The implementation work includes CNN-based eye-image classification, LSTM-based state classification, and a real-time eye-monitoring prototype.The approach provides a foundation for wearable monitoring of eye activity and supports further integration into a compact smart glasses platform.
authors: Sanmaya I K; Sharanya S; Vinusha D Souza; Maneesha M; Bharathi K

title: AI-Powered Smart Healthcare Monitoring System Using Federated Learning
abstract: Healthcare artificial intelligence is still commonly built by pooling patient data from every hospital on a single server and training a model there. This approach delivers accuracy but creates a serious privacy risk, and it conflicts with regu-lations such as HIPAA, GDPR and India’s Digital Personal Data Protection Act, which is a major reason why hospitals are reluctant to release raw records [1], [2]. This paper pro-poses a system that avoids centralization instead of work-ing within it. Wearable devices at each hospital node con-tinuously collect physiological signals (heart rate, ECG, SpO2 and blood pressure), and a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) model [3] is trained on these data locally and on-site. Only an encrypted set of model weights leaves the hospital; a central server combines the weights using Fed-erated Averaging (FedAvg) [4] and returns an improved global model. Over 20 communication rounds, the global model reaches 97.6% accuracy and a 97.2% F1-score for early disease prediction over five categories, which is with-in about half a percentage point of a centralized model trained with full access to the same pooled data. Clinicians interact with the system through a Streamlit dashboard that shows prediction confidence, patient trends and alerts without exposing another hospital’s raw records.

title: AI-Powered Smart Safety Jacket for Industrial Application
abstract: Industrial workers are frequently exposed to hazardous conditions such as gas leakage, poor air quality, physical accidents, excessive temperature, and delayed emergency response.Conventional safety equipment mainly provides passive protection and does not continuously monitor the health and surrounding conditions of workers.To address this problem, this paper presents an AI-powered smart safety jacket designed for real-time worker monitoring and emergency assistance.The proposed system integrates multiple sensors with an ESP32 microcontroller to continuously collect physiological and environmental information.A MAX30102 sensor is used for heartrate and blood-oxygen monitoring, while a DS18B20 sensor measures body temperature.MQ-2 and MQ-135 sensors are used to detect combustible gases, smoke, and changes in air quality.An MPU6050 inertial measurement unit is incorporated for detecting abnormal motion and possible worker falls.A GPS module provides the worker's location, while a GSM module enables emergency communication through SMS.In addition, a buzzer, LED indicators, and vibration motor provide immediate local alerts to the worker.

title: AI-Powered Sound-Based Wildlife Monitoring System for Real-Time Detection and IoT Alerting
abstract: This paper presents an AI-powered wildlife monitoring system designed for early detection of wildlife activity using acoustic sensing, convolutional neural network (CNN)-based intelligence, GPS localization, and Internet of Things (IoT) communication. A high-sensitivity LM393-based sound sensor connected to a NodeMCU ESP8266 monitors ambient events and provides the trigger for intelligent analysis. The project architecture also documents a camera-to-PC CNN inference path, allowing visual verification and emergency assessment in addition to the sound-based detection concept. When a positive wildlife event is obtained, the system acquires geographic coordinates using a GPS module, displays status locally through a 16x2 LCD and I2C interface, transmits event information to an IoT platform such as Blynk or ThingSpeak, and sends an SMS alert to the forest department. Reported experiments achieved more than 92% classification accuracy in a controlled environment and approximately 85% in semi-outdoor conditions. GPS localization was reported within 5-10 m, while alerts were received within 5-10 s of detection. The system operated for several hours of continuous testing and across multiple days of field simulation, although weak Wi-Fi caused occasional cloud transmission failures. The results indicate that a low-cost, non-invasive, and automated sensing architecture can support proactive wildlife monitoring while highlighting the need for larger real-world datasets, robust noise handling, and alternative communication paths for deployment in connectivity-constrained regions.

title: AI-assisted ECG screening for atrial fibrillation in older adults: comparison of short-term and one-week monitoring
abstract: Abstract Background Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common sustained arrhythmia and a major risk factor for stroke. In patients at high risk of stroke, even a single documented AF episode prompts evaluation for anticoagulation therapy. Conventional ECG methods are poorly suited for prolonged rhythm monitoring, whereas wearable devices enable long-term ECG recording in everyday life. However, extended monitoring generates large datasets that are time-consuming and resource-intensive if reviewed manually. Purpose We evaluated the clinical usefulness of artificial intelligence (AI) assisted AF detection from brief single-lead ECG recordings obtained during a short physical challenge (six-minute walk test, 6MWT) and during extended seven-day home ECG monitoring. Specifically, we assessed whether AF detected during 6MWT could substitute for AF detection during prolonged monitoring. Methods A total of 461 adults aged 75–85 years underwent both single-lead ECG recording during a 6MWT and seven days of continuous ECG monitoring using a medical-grade single-lead device (Faros 180, Bittium Corporation, Oulu, Finland). Participants were living independently and extended ECG monitoring was performed at home during everyday activities. An AI-based arrhythmia analysis algorithm (Awario, Heart2Save, Kuopio, Finland) was used for automatic AF screening of the ECG recordings. All flagged episodes were subsequently reviewed and confirmed by a physician. For extended monitoring, AF was defined as physician-verified AF with a burden of ≥6 minutes per day during monitoring. During the 6MWT recording, any physician-verified AF episode was considered a positive finding. Results A total of 461 participants completed both 6MWT ECG recording and extended home ECG monitoring. During 6MWT, new AF was detected in 5 individuals (1.08%). AI-based pre-screening identified potential AF in 87 participants during extended home monitoring. After physician verification, 16 cases were excluded due to artefacts or insufficient AF duration, resulting in 71 confirmed AF cases. Of the 62 participants with previously diagnosed AF, AF was detected during monitoring in 45 individuals. Thus, 26 cases represented newly diagnosed AF (5.64%). All AF cases detected during 6MWT were also identified during extended home monitoring. Overall, extended home ECG monitoring detected over five-fold more new AF cases compared with brief recordings (26 vs. 5). Conclusion AI-assisted extended single-lead ECG monitoring was more effective than brief ECG recordings obtained during a 6MWT in detecting new AF in older adults. While short recordings may identify a minority of AF cases, prolonged monitoring improves clinically relevant AF detection and characterization. AI-supported pre-screening may facilitate scalable AF detection by reducing clinician workload, with ongoing algorithm development aimed at improving detection accuracy and minimizing artefact-related findings.
