title: DRW-CNN: A Dilated Residual Wavelet CNN for ECG-based Severe Heart Failure Screening
abstract: Electrocardiogram (ECG)-based heart-failure screening requires clinically valid labels, record-independent evaluation, and uncertainty analysis at the level of independent records. This study evaluates a Dilated Residual Wavelet Convolutional Neural Network (DRW-CNN) for discrimination of clinically confirmed severe Congestive Heart Failure (CHF) from normal sinus rhythm. The primary cohort comprises all 15 available BIDMC CHF records and 18 MIT-BIH Normal Sinus Rhythm Database records. Records are partitioned before segmentation, yielding 528 training, 96 validation, and 168 held-out test segments from mutually exclusive records. The network applies level-4 Daubechies-4 wavelet denoising, z-score normalization, residual blocks with dilation factors 1, 2, and 4, global average pooling, and sigmoid classification. Class-weighted binary cross-entropy addresses imbalance without deleting independent records. At the prespecified threshold of 0.5, held-out predictions achieve 95.238% accuracy, 95.833% sensitivity, 94.792% specificity, 93.243% precision, 94.521% F1-score, MCC 0.903, ROC-AUC 0.988, and average precision 0.989. Record-cluster bootstrap intervals, calibration, threshold sensitivity, record-level aggregation, leave-one-record-out stability, and auxiliary non-HF domain-shift stress analyses are also reported. The study provides a leakage-resistant severe-CHF screening evaluation that separates disease-specific evidence from auxiliary abnormality testing and quantifies uncertainty at record level.

title: Decentralized Epidemic Tracking using Federated Learning and Edge AI on Consumer Wearables
abstract: Early detection of infectious-disease outbreaks depends on how quickly weak, distributed signals can be turned into a public-health decision, yet conventional surveillance relies on clinic visits, laboratory confirmation, and syndromic reporting that lag infection by days. Consumer wearables such as smartwatches, fitness bands, and smart rings continuously record resting heart rate, heart-rate variability, skin temperature, blood-oxygen saturation, respiration, sleep, and activity, and prior studies show that deviations from a person's own baseline can appear before symptoms. Centralizing this data, however, creates serious privacy, security, and regulatory exposure. This paper proposes a decentralized epidemic-tracking framework that combines Federated Learning (FL) and Edge AI on consumer wearables. Personalized anomaly detectors run on the device; only privacy-protected model updates and coarse, thresholded anomaly flags leave the user's phone; and a hierarchical wearable, smartphone, regional-edge, and health-authority architecture converts local signals into population-level outbreak indicators. Building on a recent wearable-centric review of federated AI, the framework adds eight design innovations: personalized baseline-deviation modelling, hierarchical hybrid aggregation, outbreak-risk-adaptive differential privacy, energy-aware client participation, federated analytics with secure aggregation and k-anonymous geo-cells, a permissioned-ledger audit trail kept off the critical path, federated unlearning for erasure rights, and a pathogen-agnostic cold-start strategy. Six learning approaches are compared conceptually, and detection, timeliness, communication, energy, and privacy metrics are defined. As no field deployment or labelled dataset was collected for this study, the work is presented as a proposed framework and illustrative experimental design rather than a report of empirical results, and all performance figures shown are clearly marked as illustrative placeholders. The discussion covers practical significance for public-health agencies, limitations such as sensor noise, non-IID data, client dropout, dataset shift, and regulatory classification, and the future directions needed to move from prototype to field-ready deployment.

title: Decision-centered wearable biosensors for personalized rehabilitation: integrating multimodal monitoring, artificial intelligence, and closed-loop intervention
abstract: Personalized rehabilitation requires repeated assessment of movement, physiological tolerance, fatigue, and adherence, yet conventional clinic-based measurements provide only intermittent snapshots. The convergence of wearable biosensors with artificial intelligence, edge-cloud computing, and connected data infrastructures creates an opportunity to convert continuous multimodal signals into timely rehabilitation decisions. This critical narrative review synthesizes physiological, biochemical, electrophysiological, biomechanical, and behavioral sensing within a monitoring-interpretation-feedback-adaptation-outcome framework. We first evaluate analytical validity, real-world robustness, biocompatibility, wearability, calibration drift, and power continuity. We then examine signal-quality control, multimodal fusion, digital biomarkers, federated learning, digital twins, and predictive models according to latency, uncertainty, generalizability, privacy, and decision utility. The review follows biosensor-derived information across a graded spectrum of action, from clinician-reviewed monitoring and real-time biofeedback to assist-as-needed adaptation, functional electrical stimulation, and state-responsive neuromodulation. Applications include motor and physiological assessment, fatigue-aware dose adjustment, musculoskeletal and neurological rehabilitation, posture correction, sensor-rich prosthetics, and Internet of Things-enabled home rehabilitation. Across these settings, greater autonomy increases the evidence and safety requirements: models should expose confidence, systems should degrade safely when signal quality falls, and digital infrastructures should preserve interoperability, version traceability, privacy, and accountable clinician oversight. The central translational gap is not sensor sensitivity alone but whether an integrated biosensor system produces a reliable metric, supports an explicit and proportionate decision, and improves an outcome important to the patient. Decision-centered evaluation can help move wearable biosensing from fragmented technology demonstrations toward secure, personalized, continuous, and clinically accountable rehabilitation.

title: Deep learning analysis of contactless facial video and remote photoplethysmography for acute heart failure detection
abstract: Abstract Background and Purpose Early identification of acute decompensated heart failure (HF) is essential to enable timely treatment and prevent clinical deterioration. Current diagnostic tools require blood testing or imaging, limiting rapid, scalable screening. We evaluated the feasibility of contactless camera-based photoplethysmography (rPPG) derived from facial video for detection of decompensated HF. Methods In this prospective cohort study, 275 hospitalized patients from July 2024 to February 2026 were enrolled, including 87 with acute decompensated HF (irrespective of ejection fraction) and 188 controls admitted for non-HF conditions. A standardized 2-minute facial video was recorded during index admission and at 1-month outpatient clinic follow-up. Videos were segmented into 10-second clips and processed using facial region detection, motion stabilization, and remote PPG signal extraction, which have been previously validated for non-contact cardiovascular signal measurement [1–3]. To prevent information leakage, dataset partitioning was performed at the participant level, in accordance with best practices for clinical machine learning studies. After stratification, patients were randomly allocated into training (80%) and validation (20%) sets. HF classification was performed using a PhysNet-based deep neural network. Final model performance was evaluated on the validation set. Results Baseline characteristics are summarized in Table 1. The overall cohort had a median age of 64 years and was predominantly male (74.9%). There were no significant differences between HF and control groups with respect to age, sex distribution, body mass index, diabetes mellitus, dyslipidaemia, hypertension, or prior acute myocardial infarction (all P>0.05).Patients with HF were more frequently current smokers (32.2% vs 14.4%, P=0.002) and less frequently non-smokers. Among HF patients, mean left ventricular ejection fraction was 47%, reflecting inclusion across the ejection fraction spectrum. Both video-based and rPPG-based approaches demonstrated comparable discriminative performance. The video-based model achieved an accuracy of 0.82, AUPRC 0.78, F1-score 0.80, and AUROC 0.76. The rPPG-based model achieved an accuracy of 0.78, AUPRC 0.80, F1-score 0.82, and AUROC 0.74. These findings support the feasibility of extracting diagnostically relevant cardiovascular signatures from facial video for HF detection. Conclusion Contactless facial video analysis using rPPG enables non-invasive identification of decompensated HF. This approach may support scalable screening and remote monitoring applications.Table 1 baseline characteristics table

title: Defect-Engineered ZIF-8-Derived Nanoporous Carbon for Ultra-Stable Flexible Cryogenic Thermistors and Ultra-Miniature Physiological Sensors.
abstract: In cryogenic electronics and biomedicine, there is a growing need for flexible temperature sensors operating reliably down to liquid-nitrogen temperatures while conforming to complex, moving surfaces. However, state-of-the-art metal or ceramic thermistors are rigid and bulky, whereas polymer and hydrogel sensors lose conductivity or drift severely below -150°C, making robust cryogenic sensing extremely challenging. Herein, we design a ZIF-8-derived nanoporous carbon as a cryogenic thermistor material by rational defect engineering. By tuning the carbonization temperature, the heteroatom/vacancy defect landscape (N, O, Zn, and carbon vacancies) is programmed to balance percolated graphitic pathways and dense ionized impurity centers, leading to ionized-impurity-scattering-dominated transport at deep cryogenic temperatures. The printed carbon thermistors exhibit a wide operating window from 150 to -190°C, a high cryogenic temperature coefficient of resistance (TCR) up to -4.7%/°C, a temperature resolution of 0.05°C, and a response time of 0.58 s. After 100 days of immersion in liquid nitrogen, the TCR drift remains within ±0.2%, evidencing outstanding long-term cryogenic stability. Benefiting from the printable nature, 0.3 × 0.3 mm2 micro-thermistors are integrated into cryopreservation needles and oxygen tubes for real-time in vivo freeze-thaw monitoring and contactless sensing, demonstrating the promise of defect-engineered MOF-derived carbons for next-generation flexible cryogenics.

title: Demo: Surface Material and Roughness Sensing via mmWave Vibrometry
abstract: mmWave sensing has emerged as a promising contactless solution for object detection and material sensing. While existing material-sensing approaches exploit differences in mmWave signal reflectivity, their performance in understanding fine-grained surface characteristics, such as texture and roughness, is limited by sensing wavelength and spatial resolution. We propose mmTexora, a novel system that extends mmWave material sensing to surface roughness sensing for robotic grasping and manipulation. mmTexora adapts vibrometry principles to mmWave radar by leveraging ambient vibrations from sources such as air conditioning or machinery, which subtly modulate surface scattering and embed roughness-related information in the received radar signals. By extracting these vibration-induced features, mm-Texora enables texture and roughness sensing in quasi-static scenes. In this demonstration, we show that a simplified mmTexora prototype using a single TI AWR1843 mmWave radar can identify surfaces made of different materials and distinguish surfaces with different textures and roughness levels, even when they are made of the same material.

title: Detection of clinically significant atrial fibrillation in patients with ahre: diagnostic value of long-term wearable ECG monitoring
abstract: Abstract Background Atrial high-rate episodes (AHREs) represent a subclinical phenotype of atrial tachyarrhythmias and may precede atrial fibrillation (AF). Brief episodes (<30 s) detected during standard 24-hour Holter monitoring have uncertain prognostic value and may remain underestimated. Prolonged wearable ECG monitoring may improve detection of clinically significant AF and enhance risk stratification. Aim To assess the diagnostic value of long-term wearable ECG monitoring for detecting clinically significant AF in patients with AHRE identified during 24-hour Holter ECG prescreening. Materials and Methods The study was conducted in two stages. Stage I included 157 patients with AHREs (<30 s) detected on 24-hour Holter ECG monitoring. The mean number of paroxysms was 3.37 ± 6.03 per day, the total duration of atrial arrhythmia was 39.6 ± 92.8 seconds per day, and the mean AF burden was 0.22 ± 2.06%. Stage II involved long-term wearable ECG monitoring in 13 selected patients. The mean age was 57.7 ± 9.8 years; 7 (53.8%) were men. Obesity (BMI ≥30) was present in 5 (38.5%) patients, arterial hypertension in 10 (76.9%), chronic heart failure in 4 (30.8%), and ischemic heart disease in 3 (23.1%). The mean CHA2DS2-VA score was 1.77 ± 1.09, and the mean AFEQT score was 76.1 ± 9.8. The device performed photoplethysmographic rhythm monitoring at rest and triggered alerts in case of suspected arrhythmia, prompting a short single-lead ECG recording (Lead I). The protocol included four scheduled ECG recordings daily, with additional patient- or device-initiated recordings. All ECGs were physician-verified for AF. Results Monitoring lasted 12.9 ± 2.6 days with 93.8 ± 5.1% valid recording time. A total of 1200 short (30-second) ECG recordings were obtained (92.3 ± 55.5 per patient), generating 124 arrhythmia alerts (9.5 ± 5.3 per patient). An average of 10.3 ± 12.7 ECGs per patient were performed at night. Subjective symptoms were reported by 9 (69.2%) patients, whereas asymptomatic episodes were documented in 6 (46.2%). AF of any duration was newly detected in 3 of 13 patients (23.1%). Clinically significant AF (≥30 s) was identified in 2 patients (15.4%), despite prior negative 24-hour Holter monitoring. Baseline Holter-derived atrial arrhythmic burden was higher in patients with subsequent AF detection compared with those without AF (median 140 [136–142.5] vs. 8 [5–27] seconds per day). Conclusions In patients with AHRE (<30 s), long-term wearable ECG monitoring identified clinically significant AF (≥30 s) in 15.4% of cases and AF of any duration in 23.1%. Higher baseline Holter-derived arrhythmic burden was associated with subsequent AF detection. These findings suggest that short AHREs may represent an early stage of AF and warrant prolonged monitoring for timely diagnosis and improved risk stratification.Two-week summary of wearable ECG monitoring.Single-lead ECG confirming AF episode

title: Developing an AI-Powered Occupational Health Surveillance System for Real-Time Detection and Management of Workplace Health Hazards
abstract: The increasing complexity of workplace environments necessitates advanced solutions for monitoring and managing occupational health risks. Traditional occupational health surveillance systems often struggle with inefficiencies, delayed hazard detection, and limited adaptability to dynamic workplace conditions. This study proposes the development of an Artificial Intelligence (AI)-powered occupational health surveillance system designed to enable real-time detection, assessment, and management of workplace health hazards. The system leverages machine learning (ML) algorithms, predictive analytics, and Internet of Things (IoT) devices to enhance workplace safety and improve health outcomes for employees. Central to the proposed system is the integration of wearable devices and IoT sensors to collect real-time data on environmental conditions, such as air quality, noise levels, and temperature, as well as employee health metrics, including heart rate, stress levels, and fatigue. These data streams are processed using AI algorithms capable of identifying patterns, detecting anomalies, and predicting potential risks. Predictive analytics further support proactive interventions, enabling organizations to mitigate hazards before they escalate into critical incidents. The system incorporates a user-friendly dashboard for visualizing insights, generating automated reports, and delivering actionable recommendations to managers and employees. Additionally, the framework supports compliance with occupational safety regulations by providing detailed documentation and audit trails. By combining real-time monitoring with AI-driven insights, the system promotes a culture of safety, minimizes workplace injuries, and enhances employee well-being. Moreover, the scalability of the framework allows it to be adapted across industries, addressing sector-specific challenges and operational requirements. This innovative approach bridges the gap between emerging technologies and occupational health, providing a comprehensive solution for organizations aiming to foster safe and healthy work environments. title: Development of a Model for Health Monitoring Using Machine Learning and Data Mining System
abstract: Mobile Health is an emerging field that allows for real-time monitoring of individuals between routine clinical visits. It also makes it possible to remotely gather health signals, track disease progression and provide just-in-time interventions. Data Mining is the process of extracting valid, previously unknown, comprehensible and actionable information from large databases and using it to make crucial, critical business and logical decisions. The motivation is to improve on the existing by designing a medical bio-card, where the patient’s medical history can be accessed by any readily available medical personnel, other than the registered one (probably due to network issues or remote location), to proscribe drugs and commence treatment when the patient is in critical condition. The Objective of this research is to improve on the current system that focused on key risk factors such as High/ low Blood Pressure (H/LBP), Sugar level, Blood level, High Body Temperature (Fever), Tobacco use, Alcohol use, Inadequate Physical Inactivity, Unhealthy Diets, Abnormal Sleep Patterns etc which plays key roles in many chronic diseases. Hence, there is a need to continuously monitor at risk individuals for their health status and activities over extended periods of time in their natural settings with the goal of improving their health and well being using wearable sensors. Wearable devices are devices worn on, in or around the body, and it has highly reduced form factors, longer battery life and enhanced network capabilities to continuously and remotely monitor individuals in their natural settings over extended period of time. The Methodology employed for the study of the existing system and adopted for the design of the new system is Object-Oriented Analysis and Design Method (OOADM) since it is object-oriented in nature. The improved system implemented with an accelerometer, gyroscope and/or magnetometer will detect motion, orientation and direction. The mobile App developed using Python programming language, MySQLite and a Cloud Infrastructure (AWS). The result is in form of coupling these wearable devices with smart phones and cloud computing, where large volume of data can be remotely analyzed to find interesting patterns, detect abnormalities and detect target activities from continuous stream of data.

title: Diagnostic accuracy of wearable technologies for atrial fibrillation detection: a systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common sustained cardiac arrhythmia and a major cause of ischemic stroke. Because AF is frequently paroxysmal and asymptomatic, conventional short-term monitoring often fails to detect it. Wearable technologies have emerged as promising tools for AF screening, but their diagnostic performance requires comprehensive evaluation. We conducted a systematic review and diagnostic test accuracy meta-analysis following PRISMA-DTA guidelines. PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched from inception to 25 February 2026 for prospective and retrospective studies using electrocardiographic reference standards. Bivariate random-effects and Bayesian hierarchical models were used to pool diagnostic accuracy estimates. Fifty-one studies involving 33,374 participants from 15 countries were included. PPG-based smartwatches demonstrated the highest sensitivity (96.3%) with specificity of 93.6%. ECG-based smartwatches achieved sensitivity of 89.0% and specificity of 92.8% (DOR 103.9). Smartphone-based ECG devices showed the strongest overall diagnostic performance, with sensitivity of 94.5%, specificity of 95.8%, DOR of 396.4, LR+ of 22.6, and LR− of 0.057. Smartphone-based PPG applications achieved sensitivity of 92.0% and specificity of 91.9%. Apple Watch demonstrated sensitivity of 94.1% and specificity of 94.6%. Meta-regression revealed no statistically significant differences in diagnostic accuracy between device categories despite slightly higher point estimates for PPG-based smartwatches. No significant publication bias was detected (Deeks' test, p=0.18). Wearable devices demonstrate excellent diagnostic accuracy for AF detection, particularly smartphone-based ECG applications. These technologies support scalable AF screening and monitoring, although heterogeneity in study populations and diagnostic thresholds should be considered when applying these findings to routine clinical practice.
authors: Alina Abbas; Gauhar Hamid; Beesham Kumar; Sajida Moiz Hussain Qamari; Hira Riaz

title: Digital transformation of clinical trials with remote patient monitoring solutions
abstract: Remote patient monitoring (RPM) is becoming increasingly feasible to implement in clinical trials. A framework is presented for developing RPM digital solutions incorporating the needs and perspectives of patients and healthcare professionals, and regulatory requirements/guidance. This framework is illustrated with recent examples of RPM deployments in the context of skin toxicities and stomatitis. Strategies to overcome challenges in the adoption of RPM solutions in clinical trials are discussed.
authors: Elisabeth Piault; Ramya Sita Palacholla; SIMON PULMAN‐JONES; Emmett Alton Sartor; Sergio Simön; Jill Bell

title: Disease progression shapes circadian and locomotor disruption in a model of multiple sclerosis
abstract: ABSTRACT Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an autoimmune demyelinating disease of the central nervous system featuring a wide range of debilitating symptoms. Wearable activity recording devices have recently been adopted to improve symptom monitoring in MS, capturing symptoms related to sleep/wake cycles, circadian disruption, and fatigue. However, comparable measures of activity have yet been established in pre-clinical models of MS, the most widely used being experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE). We therefore sought to characterize changes in continual home-cage activity over the course of EAE, and establish whether home-cage monitoring can be used as an observer-independent measure of disease progression. Our results showed that locomotor activity in the mid-active/dark phase was most severely affected by EAE. Disrupted circadian (24-hour) activity was observed during the peak and onset stages of disease. Bout activity analysis revealed >40-minute long activity bouts as a sensitive indicator of non-motor symptoms independent of clinical score-based motor deficits. Current assessment of disease progression in EAE relies on clinical scores, which primarily assess motor deficits through visual observation prone to observer bias. Various computed activity parameters were found to be altered during key disease stages, suggesting that a combination of activity measures can serve as objective indicators of disease progression. Overall, our results show that home-cage activity effectively captures signs of non-motor symptoms in the EAE model of MS and can serve as an observer-independent measure of EAE disease progression.
authors: Vina Wenyu Li; Julia P. Segal; Nader Ghasemlou

title: Disruption of the Muscle–Brain Axis in Ageing: Role of Myokines in Sarcopenia and Neurodegeneration
abstract: This narrative review analyzes how myokines act as key links in communication between skeletal muscle and the brain, focusing on the impact of aging on this axis. Although the current literature links defects in this signaling pathway to sarcopenia, neurodegeneration, and cognitive decline, we still do not know exactly what role each molecule plays individually. Among the main gaps in our understanding are questions about how these substances are transported to the nervous system, what their specific receptors are, and what cause-and-effect relationship actually exists between losing muscle mass and developing neurological problems. In fact, in humans, it remains unclear whether myokines actually reach the brain in truly effective concentrations or whether their benefits are due more to peripheral metabolic, vascular, and inflammatory changes. Today, most of the mechanistic evidence comes from animal and cellular models, while observational studies predominate in humans. This is further complicated by uncertainties regarding the actual origin of these proteins in tissues, their passage through the blood-brain barrier, and their measurement in the blood, making it difficult to determine whether these proteins act as causes, consequences, or simply compensatory responses to aging and disease. On the other hand, although exercise remains the most robust tool for maintaining muscle health and protecting cognitive function, it is still unclear whether we could replicate those same benefits by isolating and stimulating specific myokines. The major challenge for the future is to develop human studies that combine standardized biomarkers with long-term monitoring of muscle function, cognition, and brain structure. Only then will we know whether this fascinating muscle-brain axis can move beyond being a promising hypothesis to become a real therapeutic target.
authors: Víctor Agustín Morales Molina; Cecibel Nicole Ludeña Salinas; Celina Andrade Vásquez; Andri Matos; Diego Aldeán Riofrío

title: Domestic sensor-based monitoring for supporting independent-living older adults: A scoping review
abstract: Population ageing is accelerating globally, placing increasing pressure on local health and social care systems. Older people who remain living independently generally have better health outcomes and use fewer care resources. Moreover, many older people express a preference for living independently. Therefore, supporting independent living represents a cost-effective objective for health and care systems. One potential means for supporting such ageing in place is domestic sensor-based activity monitoring technologies; however, to date evidence on their effectiveness, usability, and real-world implementation has been inconclusive. A scoping review has been undertaken following PRISMA-ScR guidance to map the latest evidence on domestic passive sensor-based monitoring for older adults. Twenty-nine studies met the inclusion criteria; the evidence they provide suggests domestic sensors can support monitoring of activities of daily living, detect early functional or cognitive decline, and are generally acceptable to users. However, robust evidence for improved clinical outcomes, cost-effectiveness, and effective integration into health systems remains limited.
authors: Afia Murshida; Stephen Potter; Mark Hawley

title: DuBCG: Unlocking In-Home, Clinically Comparable mmWave Cardiac Monitoring for Co-Sleepers via Physics-Informed Spatial Sensing
abstract: Continuous, fine-grained cardiac monitoring during sleep is vital for cardiovascular health. Emerging as a promising alternative to cumbersome wearables, mmWave radar offers a contactless, privacy-preserving modality capable of capturing minute skin vibrations. However, transitioning mmWave radar from labs to real-world bedrooms remains challenging. Our rigorous empirical evaluation of state-of-the-art systems reveals a severe reliability gap: valid Inter-Beat Intervals (IBI) are captured for only 24%-42% of the night within an error threshold of 50 ms. Since clinical HRV analysis requires millisecond-level precision (e.g., RMSSD changes), such coarse and intermittent tracking renders existing methods medically insufficient. We attribute this failure to two fundamental hurdles: (i) instability driven by overwhelming respiratory interference and postural diversity, and (ii) signal entanglement in co-sleeping scenarios where angular separation defies hardware resolution. To bridge this gap, we present DuBCG. First, to tackle instability, we introduce a Head-Facing configuration to capture the Radar Ballistocardiogram (R-BCG). By leveraging the body's longitudinal recoil, this approach achieves orthogonal respiratory suppression and posture-invariant robustness. Second, to resolve entanglement, we propose the Multi-point Scattering Spatial Selectivity Model, theoretically proving that signal separability is achievable beyond physical resolution limits. Extensive real-world benchmarks demonstrate that DuBCG achieves a median IBI error of 8.4 ms—an 8× improvement over existing methods. This precision bridges the gap from existing intermittent monitoring to long-term, clinically comparable continuous HRV assessment.
authors: Xusheng Zhang; Duo Zhang; Jingfu Dong; Ruiqi Yu; Hongliu Yang; Junzhe Wang; Zizhou Fan; Z X Yin; Daqing Zhang

title: Dyadic technology-based interventions for community-dwelling people with dementia and their informal caregivers in low- and middle-income countries: a scoping review
abstract: OBJECTIVES: Over 60% of people living with dementia reside in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), where limited awareness and scarce supportive services can intensify caregiver burden. Although dyadic technology-based interventions (DTIs) show promise in high-income countries, their scope in LMICs remains unclear. This scoping review aimed to identify the types of DTIs used for dementia dyads in LMICs and to map reported outcomes, with particular attention to caregiver burden. METHODS: This review followed JBI methodology for scoping reviews and was reported according to PRISMA-ScR. MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, CINAHL, Scopus, and Cochrane Library were searched without date restrictions. RESULTS: Twelve studies from six middle-income countries were included. Five technological platforms were identified: videoconferencing-based interventions, mobile applications, computer software, robotics, and ambient intelligence. Most DTIs were multifunctional, commonly supporting telemedicine or telerehabilitation and targeted health information or therapeutic content. Outcomes were heterogeneous and primarily focused on feasibility, acceptability, usability, and implementation rather than health-related outcomes. Most studies did not report caregiver burden directly, though two case studies suggested that ambient intelligence may reduce caregiver burden. CONCLUSION: Evidence on DTIs in LMICs is limited, fragmented, and largely excludes low-income countries. Further rigorous, context-sensitive studies on DTIs are needed to explore feasibility and effectiveness.
authors: Chi Linh Bui; Susan Rampling; Linh Kim Le Nguyen; Maayken van den Berg

title: EETANet: A Human-Centered Intelligent Framework for Exercise Posture Quality Assessment.
abstract: As physical rehabilitation and fitness monitoring increasingly shift toward autonomous and home-based healthcare, accurate and intelligent posture assessment systems have become essential for supporting personalized rehabilitation and clinical decision making. This study proposes the Edge-Enhanced Temporal Attention Network (EETANet), a human-centered ambient intelligence framework for automated exercise posture assessment and quality evaluation. The proposed framework is designed as an end-to-end computational pipeline that transforms raw multivariate motion signals into posture quality predictions using a compact set of core biomechanical posture features. The pipeline integrates data preprocessing, signal enhancement, multi-domain feature representation, and deep neural classification to capture the relevant spatial and temporal characteristics of human movement. Signal preprocessing incorporates data cleaning, z-score normalization, and Savitzky-Golay smoothing to improve signal quality while preserving temporal dynamics. Subsequently, informative posture representations are extracted through complementary temporal, spectral, and morphological descriptors, enabling the model to characterize motion variations associated with posture quality. These representations are learned using a Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) classifier within the proposed EETANet framework to model nonlinear relationships between posture features and quality levels. Experimental evaluation demonstrates that the compact five-feature configuration achieves an accuracy of 90.83%, precision of 90.99%, recall of 90.83%, and F1-score of 90.84%. Notably, this compact configuration outperforms the corresponding 24-feature MLP configuration, which achieves 88.83% accuracy, indicating that a reduced set of core posture features can provide effective discriminative information while avoiding unnecessary feature redundancy. These findings demonstrate the potential of EETANet as an efficient framework for automated posture quality assessment in rehabilitation, fitness monitoring, and ambient healthcare applications.
authors: Esraa Hassan; Amira Samy Talaat; Aliya Aleryani; Rana Albelaihi; M A Elsabagh

title: EITWatch: Smartwatch-Integrated Planar Electrical Impedance Tomography for Hand Gesture Recognition
abstract: Wrist Electrical Impedance Tomography (EIT) senses hand gestures from muscle- and tendon-driven impedance changes, but prior wrist-EIT systems require electrode coverage beyond the watch-back contact patch and separate analog front ends. We present EITWatch, the first wrist-EIT system built around smartwatch case-back geometry, asking whether this contact patch alone can support gesture recognition: eight planar electrodes in a 31 mm ring acquire 35 impedance measurements at 48 Hz. Because a planar array cannot encircle the wrist, EITWatch uses multi-depth scanning to sample multiple source-sink distances and current paths; it beat matched adjacent injection by 15.1/10.4 percentage points (macro/micro) across all 12 participants. In a prompted study, within-session leave-one-round-out accuracy reached 91.4%/92.5% (window/trial) for six macro-gestures, and 90.1%/91.5% (window/segment) for five micro-gestures plus relax; window-level cross-session and leave-one-user-out transfer reached 73.2%/70.4% and 63.1%/55.3% (macro/micro).
authors: Xuanyou Liu; Novel Alam; Karan Ahuja

title: EMERGING BLOOD-BASED BIOMARKERS IN ALZHEIMER’S DISEASE: FOCUS ON TAU, NFL, AND GFAP
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is characterised by progressive neurological disorder marked by the gradual decline of memory and cognitive abilities, affecting daily functioning and quality of life, imposing a leading socioeconomic disruption and healthcare burden.For the effective interventions, treatment and management, early diagnosis is important though conventional techniques like imaging and cerebrospinal fluid tests are invasive and costly.The inclusion of blood-based biomarkers provides a transformative approach for the early detection and disease monitoring.The purpose of this review is to critically evaluate the emerging evidence on Tau181, Tau217, NfL, and GFAP, aiming to delineate their role in reshaping future strategies for detection, monitoring, and intervention.Tau 217, among the tau isoforms biomarkers, demonstrated as a superior candidate with regards to diagnostic accuracy and stronger co-relation with Amyloid Positron Emission Tomography and disease progression, while compared to Tau 181.As the frontrunner biomarker, Tau 217 has emerged for AD with NfL and GFAP that provide precious complementary insights.Axonal degeneration is reflected by NfL while astrocytic activation is indicated by GFAP.Both serve as complementary markers.Combined multi-marker panels integrating these biomarkers enhanced sensitivity and specificity for AD detection.Therefore, these blood-based biomarkers provide a potential and revolutionary AD diagnosis and management by enabling non-invasive, early, and precise disease characterization.
authors: Sakina Turabi
venue: Indian Journal of Health Care Medical & Pharmacy Practice

title: ENERGY-Matched Heart-Rate Sensing Schedules for Pre-Symptomatic Infection Detection on Low-Cost Wearables
abstract: Most wearable infection-detection studies have assumed that more sensing is better, and focused on deviations in resting heart rate preceding self-reported symptoms; however, not much consideration has been given to when sensing is needed when there is a limited budget for the amount of energy the device can expend. This study asks: Is there a difference in pre-symptomatic warning performance when the timing of the heart-rate acquisition is considered in addition to the amount of sensing? Two publicly released data sets (Stanford Phase 1 and Stanford Phase 2) were re-analyzed using a preregistered causal pipeline. The final frozen base cohort included 38 participants; 30 contributed to the primary paired comparison after arm-specific calibration requirements. On the primary, modelled-energy budget (E3), sparse schedules were employed with 7 acquisition bursts per day of 10 minutes each. The confirmatory comparison tested nocturnally sensing (S3) against uniform block (S2) through the personalized time-of-day-normalized resting-heart-rate detector, with an identical alert burden (no more than two alert-days/person-month) and with a hierarchical paired endpoint of detection and warning time. S3 did not outperform S2: W/L/T = 8/12/10, θ = 0.433 (95% BCa CI 0.300-0.583), exact two-sided p = 0.5034. Detection rate was 63.3% for S3 and 66.7% for S2 and median warning time was 13 and 14 days respectively for the detected cases. Due to H1 failure, the fixed-sequence gate was closed and the remaining schedule comparisons were estimation-only. For all sensitivity analyses reported in H1, θ was kept at or below 0.5. These results do not demonstrate equality, but they do not offer any evidence that heart-rate acquisition focused at night is superior to an energy-matched uniform heart-rate acquisition schedule in warning about infection prior to symptoms onset in this sample. The study presents a framework for evaluation of sensing placement, alert burden, missingness and modeled device energy that is reproducible and suggests the need for larger prospective validation and measured hardware-energy experiments.
authors: Hassan Jalal; M.Usman Riaz

title: EXTENT OF AWARENESS OF WEARABLE TECHNOLOGY DEVICES AND HEALTH BENEFITS AMONG LECTURERS OF EBONYI STATE UNIVERSITY, ABAKALIKI
abstract: The study investigated the extent of awareness of wearable fashion technology devices and their health benefits among lecturers of Ebonyi State University Abakaliki. Specifically, the study determined the extent of awareness of fashion clothing technology devices among lecturers at Ebonyi State University Abakaliki and the extent of health benefits of fashion clothing technology devices in the area of the study. Using a descriptive survey research design, the population of the study comprised nine hundred and sixty lecturers (960) in Ebonyi State University. A cluster sampling technique was adopted to select a sample of 100 lecturers. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire administered by hand to the study respondents. The data collected was analyzed using mean statistics. Findings revealed that the respondents were unaware of seven out of the ten identified fashion clothing devices; these include smart clothing, smart jewellery, smart rings, smart watches, and others. In the same vein, the respondents were unaware of seven out of the ten identified health benefits; these include control of hypertension, monitoring heart health, control of sleep, and reduction of anxiety, among others. Based on the findings, the study recommends that the university management and relevant public health organizations should initiate targeted digital health literacy programmes focused on clearly demonstrating the health benefits of these devices to lecturers. This is essential for converting low awareness into an active intention to utilize and eventual adoption.
authors: OKORO Victoria Ifeyinwa; Tessy EDE-AUGUSTINE; FRED Chidinma Vivian

title: Edge AI on Constrained Devices for Binary Sleep-Wake Classification in Dynamic Environments
abstract: This paper presents an Edge AI-based system for detecting sleep and wake states in non-stationary mobile environments using resource-constrained embedded hardware. Conventional approaches relying on accelerometer-based activity metrics are highly susceptible to motion and vibration artifacts and are limited by strict compute and energy budgets of wearable and IoT devices. To address these challenges, a multimodal pipeline is designed and implemented on an ESP32-S3 microcontroller. The system combines inertial sensing for head movement analysis and visual pose classification. A dual-core architecture with FreeRTOS enables parallel execution of real-time data acquisition and on-device inference. Sleep detection follows a two-stage strategy: low-movement detection over a temporal window, followed by visual validation of poses. Experimental results show accuracies of 96.5% for motion-based detection and 89% for pose classification, yielding robust binary sleep-wake classification. Field tests confirmed feasibility in representative mobile scenarios. The results demonstrate that privacy-preserving, local sleep detection is achievable on edge hardware through careful co-design, while highlighting limitations in sensing intrusiveness, dataset scale, and system integration.
authors: Stefan Reitmann; Lena Oden

title: Editorial: Revolutionizing obstetric and pediatric pharmacology through artificial intelligence and digital health innovations
abstract: Zhang et al. (https://doi.org/10.3389/fphar.2026.1817282) combined a population pharmacokinetic model of linezolid with machine learning in critically ill children, using SHAP to trace predictions back to clearance, dose, weight, and renal function. Notably, the authors flag their own strong validation metrics as optimistic, since the pharmacokinetic parameters used as model inputs were derived from the same concentration data being predicted, a transparency that usefully clarifies what leakage-free, prospective validation will need to look like before such hybrid models reach the bedside. Westvik et al. (https://doi.org/10.3389/fped.2026.1881474) took a related approach in very preterm infants, estimating serum phosphate levels from routinely collected blood gas, anthropometric, and nutritional data, with small-for-gestational-age status emerging as the dominant risk factor for early hypophosphatemia. Both studies point to the same opportunity that has long motivated modelinformed dosing: extracting more clinical value from data already being collected, rather than adding burden to already vulnerable patients. Recent physiologically based pharmacokinetic modeling of pediatric antibiotic dosing offers a complementary, developmentally grounded route to the same goal (Tanaka et al., 2025).A second cluster of studies extends prediction into real-time obstetric care. Li et al. (https://doi.org/10.3389/fmed.2025.1686637) evaluated a consumer smartwatch for detecting spinal anesthesia-induced hypotension during cesarean delivery, finding moderate accuracy at a clinically relevant threshold (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUC] 0.87, sensitivity 79.2%, specificity 82.0%) but reduced sensitivity at a milder one, appropriately positioning the device as a screening aid rather than a diagnostic replacement. Wang and He (https://doi.org/10.3389/fmed.2026.1794753) developed logistic regression, Naive Bayes, random forest, support vector machine, and XGBoost models to predict intrapartum labor analgesia efficacy from preoperative demographic, clinical, ultrasound, and psychological indicators in 137 parturients; their XGBoost model showed strong discrimination in training (AUC 0.875) that declined in validation (AUC 0.759), an instructive reminder that external testing must precede clinical use. He et al. (https://doi.org/10.3389/fmed.2026.1908970) studied nalbuphine-ropivacaine infiltration along the epidural puncture tract in a prospective cohort of 473 women undergoing cesarean delivery, reporting lower rates of post-neuraxial puncture-site pain alongside an interpretable XGBoost risk model (AUC 0.912); as the authors themselves note, SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) values describe statistical association within the model, not causal mechanism, so the treatment comparison still needs confirmation in an appropriately controlled trial.None of the above is clinically useful without infrastructure that turns knowledge into action at the point of prescribing, the kind of routinely collected, real-world clinical data that increasingly underpins broader evaluations of drug safety and effectiveness (Corrigan-Curay et al., 2018). Wu et al. (https://doi.org/10.3389/fped.2026.1736268) describe the construction of China's first Pediatric Rational Medication Intelligent Decision System, a database of more than 400,000 entries across 1,030 medications covering dosing, interactions, infusion parameters, pharmacogenomics, and compatibility with traditional Chinese medicines. Embedded into the hospital information system with real-time access to patient biochemical and disease data, the system was associated with a significant reduction in higher-severity prescription alerts. This contribution is a reminder that predictive algorithms and curated, governed knowledge bases are not competing approaches but necessary complements; sophisticated models still depend on structured, pediatric-specific, continuously maintained medication data to reach the bedside. It also highlights the adoption, implementation, and governance of the underlying systems that support this application, with the intention of improving patient outcomes.These six contributions sit within a much broader shift already reshaping drug discovery and clinical trial design (Paul et al., 2021) and raising ethical and regulatory questions across the clinical pharmacology discipline (Petkovic et al., 2024); obstetric and pediatric applications carry that broader shift into two of medicine's least evidence-rich populations. Across the six studies specifically, common priorities emerge: external validation across institutions, developmental stages, and healthcare systems; evaluation that extends beyond discrimination to calibration, transportability, workflow burden, and effect on patient outcomes; and transparent, explainable models with human clinical oversight retained wherever predictions influence dosing, monitoring, or intervention. These considerations carry strong emphasis when the populations affected are pregnant women, neonates, and children. The next challenge is translating these advances into routine pediatric and obstetric practice beyond specialist centers (Thompson et al., 2024).The contributions to this Research Topic show that AI and digital health can strengthen obstetric and pediatric pharmacology. The next phase of this work should shift from retrospective prediction and single-center feasibility to prospective evaluation and interoperable implementation. Ultimately, the success of artificial intelligence in obstetric and pediatric pharmacology will not be measured solely by algorithmic performance, but by its ability to support safer, more effective, and more individualized pharmacotherapy for mothers and children. As confidence in these approaches increases, we can hopefully expect more routine deployment, with vigilance in place to ensure they continue to perform as expected as our knowledge and experience improve.Artificial intelligence tools were used to assist in creating the figure; Claude (Anthropic) was used for schematic layout generation. The authors reviewed, edited, and verified the accuracy of all AI-generated visual content. AI tools were not used for reference selection, data interpretation, or the generation of scientific conclusions. The authors assume full responsibility for all content in this publication. title: Effect of a wearable-based individualised multidomain lifestyle intervention on cognitive and physical function in older adults at risk of decline (INSPIOR): a single-centre, open-label, randomised controlled trial
abstract: Background Multidomain lifestyle programmes are the leading preventive approach to cognitive decline, but they rely on intensive face-to-face delivery that is hard to scale. We assessed whether an automated, wearable-based multidomain programme of activity, sleep, and optional nutrition prompts changed cognitive and physical function in at-risk older adults. Methods INSPIOR was a 6-month, single-centre, open-label, randomised controlled trial in Kashiwa, Japan. Adults aged 65–92 years with low body-mass index, pre-frailty, frailty, or sarcopenia-related decline were randomly assigned 1:1, in permuted blocks of four and without stratification, to the Fitbit-based intervention or an assessment-only control; allocation was not concealed and outcome assessors were not masked. Co-primary outcomes were the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA), Trail Making Test (TMT), and skeletal muscle mass index (SMI), with no pre-specified hierarchy or multiplicity adjustment; analyses used intention-to-treat analysis of covariance with multiple imputation. This trial was registered with UMIN-CTR, UMIN000052707, and ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT06135740. Findings Between Nov 8, 2023, and Jul 31, 2024, 355 participants were randomly assigned to the intervention group (n = 178) or control group (n = 177); all were analysed. Adjusted between-group differences were 0·58 MoCA points (95% CI 0·03–1·13; p=0·039; Holm-adjusted p=0·12), 0·16 s (−5·07 to 5·40; p=0·95) for TMT-A, 5·59 s (−3·88 to 15·05; p=0·25) for TMT-B, and −0·01 kg/m 2 (−0·09 to 0·07; p=0·88) for SMI. Mild skin irritation and dietary-recording stress occurred; no serious adverse event was intervention-related. Interpretation The intervention was associated with a small difference in a global cognitive screening score that did not survive multiplicity adjustment and is of uncertain clinical significance; the other two showed none. Larger, longer, masked trials are needed. Funding University of Tokyo–NH Foods Collaborative Research Programme, Google, Mitsui Fudosan.
