title: Metal Hypersensitivity Reactions Following Spinal Implants
abstract: BACKGROUND: Metal hypersensitivity reactions are infrequently reported but clinically significant after spinal implant surgery. Clinical presentation can mimic infection or mechanical failure, making diagnosis difficult. Evidence to guide diagnosis and management is largely limited to short case series and case reports. The purpose of this study was to systematically review the clinical presentation, diagnostic methods, and outcomes of metal hypersensitivity associated with spinal implants. METHODS: A systematic review was conducted of PubMed, Embase, and Scopus from inception through June 22, 2026, in accordance with Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines. Title and abstract screening, full-text review, and data extraction were performed independently by 2 reviewers with conflicts resolved by a third reviewer. Eligible studies included adult patients with suspected or confirmed metal hypersensitivity following spinal implant surgery that reported patient-level clinical outcomes. RESULTS: Fifteen studies with a total of 19 patients met inclusion criteria (53% female, 42% male, and 5% not reported). The median patient age was 47 years (range, 19-69). Twelve procedures (63%) were fusion-based, while 7 (37%) were motion preserving, including disk arthroplasty and artificial facet replacement systems. Common clinical presentations included persistent pain, with 8 patients (42%) exhibiting dermatologic manifestations. Metal hypersensitivity was immunologically confirmed by positive patch testing and/or lymphocyte transformation testing in 11 patients (58%), while 8 (42%) were diagnosed clinically. Onset of symptoms ranged from immediately postoperatively to 15 years after implantation. Eighteen patients underwent removal or revision with clinical improvement in 14 of 16 with a reported outcome (88%). CONCLUSION: Metal hypersensitivity reactions following spinal implants are infrequently reported but may present either immediately or in a delayed manner with symptoms that mimic more common postoperative complications, such as infection or pseudarthrosis, or may present with dermatologic manifestations. In cases where other etiologies are ruled out, hardware removal was frequently, though not invariably, associated with clinical improvement, which was reported narratively rather than by validated outcome measures. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Therapeutic Level V. See Instructions for Authors for a complete description of levels of evidence.
authors: Joseph Abbo; Jacob Thomas; Christian Stipho; Erik Nakken; Rakesh Patel; Joshua David Piche; IIyas Aleem

title: Millimetre-Wave Radar for Sports Engineering Applications: A Scoping Review of Current Evidence, Validation, and Future Directions
abstract: Millimetre-wave (mmWave) radar has emerged as a promising non-contact sensing technology capable of capturing human movement and physiological information without requiring wearable devices or continuous visual recording. Although mmWave radar has been extensively investigated in general human sensing applications, its current role and potential translation in sports engineering remain unclear. This scoping review aims to systematically map current evidence regarding mmWave radar applications relevant to sports engineering, including localisation and tracking, movement recognition, pose estimation, and physiological monitoring. The review will summarise sensing configurations, experimental designs, validation approaches, performance metrics, and engineering limitations reported in existing studies. The review will follow the methodological framework for scoping reviews and will be reported according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) guidelines. The findings will identify current capabilities, evidence gaps, and future directions for translating mmWave radar technologies into practical sports engineering applications.
authors: Rouli Ye; Xu Wen

title: Minute-Scale Sleep-Onset HRV as a Candidate Risk-Stratification Biomarker for Diabetic Retinopathy: An Exploratory Pilot Study
abstract: Background: Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is the most common microvascular complication of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), yet DR screening coverage remains inadequate worldwide. Diabetic autonomic neuropathy typically precedes DR, and heart rate variability (HRV) provides a non-invasive autonomic measure; however, whether HRV can screen for DR remains unexplored. Methods: This pilot study investigated whether sleep-onset minute-scale HRV indices—SDANN1 (standard deviation of 1-min segment means of normal-to-normal intervals) and SDANN2 (2-min segments)—serve as candidate screening biomarkers. Using a public 24-h Holter ECG dataset of T2DM inpatients (N = 39; 11 DR-positive, 28 DR-negative), sleep-onset time-points from cardiopulmonary coupling analysis were used to extract 30 min of post-onset ECG. Results: SDANN1 was significantly lower in the DR group (median 23.6 vs. 44.8 ms, p = 0.028, d = 0.74), with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.731 (95% CI: 0.530–0.901). At the optimal threshold of ≤ 25 ms, the odds ratio was 8.1 (95% CI: 1.7–38.4), with DR prevalence of 58% in the high-risk versus 12.5% in the low-risk group. Among 12 candidates, only the SDANN family reached significance. Conclusions: sleep-onset minute-scale HRV shows promise as a candidate risk-stratification biomarker for DR; prospective longitudinal validation in larger, sex-balanced cohorts is required before any screening application.
authors: Yi-Ting Cheng; Yu-Cheng Lin; Yu‐Ting Ho; Terry B. J. Kuo; Cheryl C.H. Yang

title: Mobile Health Technologies for Long COVID Management: A Scoping Review
abstract: Background: Long COVID affects an estimated 400 million worldwide. Individuals with long COVID face a range of fluctuating and often debilitating symptoms including myalgia, fatigue, and cognitive difficulties. Psychological effects such as anxiety, depression, and reduced quality of life are also commonly reported. Together, these symptoms present barriers to accessing traditional healthcare services. Furthermore, a lack of satisfaction in traditional healthcare services is often reported. Mobile health has been proposed as a solution to improve long COVID symptom management whilst overcoming some barriers and improving patient experience of healthcare services. This scoping review aimed to identify mobile health technologies to support long COVID symptom management or tracking and to synthesise their reported outcomes. Methods: Following JBI guidelines and the PRISMA-ScR checklist, five databases (CINAHL ultimate, MEDLINE, ScienceDirect, Cochrane, and Scopus) were searched. Articles were eligible for the review if they examined the use of mobile health technologies for long COVID symptom management or tracking. Articles which involved individuals under 18 years or non-human samples or focussed on conditions alongside long COVID where results could not be separated were not eligible for inclusion. Risk of bias was assessed using JBI, ROB 2, and ROBINS-1 V2, and is presented using both visual summaries and narrative descriptions. Results: Of 737 articles screened, 38 met the eligibility criteria and were included in the current review. These articles totalled 3541 participants across 14 countries. Technology modality varied, with the current review synthesising findings from mobile apps, web pages, video-calling platforms, wearables, and virtual reality headsets. Findings showed that mobile health technologies were acceptable and feasible, although a one-size-fits-all approach cannot be adopted due to individual differences in symptomatology and support needs. Conclusions: Promising improvements in symptom-based outcome measures and fitness tests were reported, although intervention and methodological heterogeneity limits our conclusions regarding comparative effectiveness.
authors: Gabrielle Humphreys; Lawrence D. Hayes; Ethan C J Berry; Eleanor Daniels; Abby Pritchard; Ramna A. Bukhari; Barbara Budai; Siyra Sabah; Nilihan E. M. Sanal‐Hayes

title: Mobility Enhancement of Patients Body Monitoring based on WBAN with Multipath Routing
abstract: One of the promising applications of wireless sensor networks (WSNs) is monitoring of the human body for health concerns. For this purpose, a large number of small sensors are implanted in the human body. These sensors altogether provide a network of wireless sensors (WBANs) and monitor the vital signs and signals of the human body; these sensors will then send this information to the doctor. The most important application of the WBAN is the implementation of the monitoring network for patient safety in the hospital environment. In this case, supporting patients’ mobility is one of the basic needs, which has been underestimated in recent studies. The problem that involves providing the required energy for the units used in this type of network is challenging; for this reason, sent/ received units with very low power consumption and with a very small radius are used in order to save energy. The resulting small sending range, leads to the lack of support for patients' mobility. In this paper, the AD HOC mode is suggested for use to establish a network and a multi-path routing algorithm, for the purpose of importing patients’ mobility in hospital setting. The results of the simulation show that in addition to supporting patients' mobility, the use of the proposed idea instead of previously presented protocols, reduces delays in data transmission and energy consumption; and it also increases the delivery rate depending on the destination and the lifetime of the network, while on the other hand, it increases routing overhead.
authors: Nastooh Javan

title: Molecular Mechanisms and Biochemical Alterations in Huntington’s Disease: Current Perspectives and Emerging Insights
abstract: Huntington disease (HD) is a progressive, inherited neurodegenerative disorder with motor, cognitive, and psychiatric manifestations.This review aims to synthesize current knowledge on the epidemiology, pathogenesis, and management of HD, and critically evaluate advances in emerging therapeutic strategies.Key findings reveal that HD is frequently underdiagnosed in non-European populations due to limited data and awareness, and that significant disparities exist in access to care and genetic testing worldwide.Although current therapies are limited to symptomatic management, recent research has clarified the molecular mechanisms of neuronal degeneration, including excitotoxicity, mitochondrial dysfunction, and oxidative stress.The review highlights promising developments in RNA-targeted therapies, gene-editing technologies such as CRISPR-Cas9, stem cell approaches, and antioxidant interventions, though none have yet to demonstrate disease-modifying effects in clinical trials.Overall, continued research and improved global surveillance are essential for advancing early diagnosis, expanding access to care, and ultimately developing effective, disease-modifying treatments for HD.
authors: Moses Adondua Abah; Micheal Oladosu Abimbola; Nathan Rimamsanati Yohanna; Abdulkabir Abdulquadri Ola; Ahmed Olajide Akinlabi; Yunusa Rahima

title: Monitoraggio contactless e stima del dispendio energetico notturno da segnali balistocardiografici sotto-materasso su una coorte clinica
abstract: La quantificazione accurata del dispendio energetico e la comprensione della dinamica metabolica costituiscono ambiti di primaria importanza per la ricerca biomedica, con riscontri diretti nella nutrizione clinica, nella diagnostica endocrinologica e nel trattamento dell'obesità.Alla base dell'aumento ponderale e dei disordini metabolici vi è infatti un'alterazione cronica del bilancio energetico, ovvero dello sbilanciamento tra le calorie introdotte con la dieta e l'energia spesa dall'organismo attraverso i processi ossidativi a carico dei substrati energetici.Le metodiche di riferimento per la misurazione di tale consumo a livello individuale presentano però evidenti barriere pratiche ed economiche.L'acqua doppiamente marcata (Doubly Labeled Water, DLW) permette la misura in vita libera ma ha costi molto elevati, richiede laboratori specializzati e fornisce solo una media su più giorni senza dettagli orari.La calorimetria indiretta a stanza intera (Whole-Room Indirect Calorimetry), pur rappresentando il gold standard per accuratezza e risoluzione temporale, richiede ambienti confinati, elevata complessità gestionale e costi considerevoli.Questi vincoli ne limitano l'uso su larga scala e impediscono il monitoraggio continuo del paziente nella sua quotidianità.Per superare queste barriere si sta dedicando crescente attenzione ai sistemi di monitoraggio contact-free, tecnologie non invasive e completamente invisibili all'utente.I comuni dispositivi indossabili (wearable), sebbene diffusi, possono risultare invasivi o fastidiosi, riducendo l'aderenza al monitoraggio a lungo termine, soprattutto durante il sonno.In questo panorama si colloca la balistocardiografia, metodica basata sulla rilevazione delle forze meccaniche di rinculo generate dall'eiezione cardiaca sistolica e dai movimenti respiratori.L'adozione di sensori piezoelettrici o ferroelettrici alloggiati sotto il materasso o sotto il lenzuolo rende possibile l'acquisizione passiva e continuativa dei segnali biologici durante il riposo notturno, azzerando il disturbo per il soggetto e garantendo una totale aderenza al monitoraggio.Nel caso del dispositivo impiegato in questo studio (Emfit QS), la letteratura scientifica ha ampiamente validato la sua affidabilità nella misura a riposo di frequenza cardiaca e frequenza respiratoria.Al contrario, la possibilità di impiegare tali informazioni per ricavare una stima quantitativa del dispendio energetico notturno costituisce un obiettivo innovativo che nessuno studio ha ancora affrontato.

title: Multi-Omics and Digital Biomarkers for Dynamic Cardiometabolic Risk Prediction
abstract: Cardiometabolic risk changes as metabolic state, vascular injury, behavior and treatment evolve. Multi-omics assays characterize the underlying molecular state, whereas wearable sensors and continuous glucose monitoring capture physiological responses during daily life. This review asks whether combining these measurements improves a defined clinical decision beyond established clinical information in type 2 diabetes, atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and heart failure. We distinguish biological association, prediction and clinical utility, and define dynamic risk prediction as repeated estimation of future event probability over a specified horizon using only information available at each prediction time. Large cohorts link proteins and metabolites with future disease, and intensive studies connect molecular variation with activity, nutrition and glycemic responses. However, evidence for joint molecular-digital integration remains predominantly observational. Trials of glucose monitoring and structured telemanagement show that monitoring can improve outcomes when it is embedded in an effective care pathway, but they do not establish the incremental value of multi-omics. We therefore organize the evidence around three requirements: temporal alignment of stable genomic information, intermittent molecular assays and dense digital trajectories; validation against a strong clinical comparator; and prospective assessment of patient outcomes, cost and burden. Emerging sensors, dynamical network biomarkers and digital twins may eventually extend this framework, but they remain experimental or conceptual for integrated cardiometabolic event prediction.
authors: Kexin Ding; Xiaoyi Li; Jun Zhang; Dafang Chen

title: Multimodal deep learning with particle swarm guided feature refinement for automated pain detection
abstract: Pain assessment remains a significant challenge in clinical practice because conventional self-reporting methods are subjective and unreliable for non-verbal, cognitively impaired, and critically ill patients. Existing automated pain detection approaches primarily rely on single-modality data or limited multimodal integration, resulting in inadequate feature representation, feature redundancy, and reduced classification performance. To address these limitations, this study proposes a multimodal deep learning framework that integrates physiological signals, facial images, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and clinical text for objective pain detection. The physiological branch employs a hybrid architecture comprising a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network, Bidirectional Gated Recurrent Unit (BiGRU), and Deep Neural Network (DNN) to learn hierarchical spatial-temporal representations. The facial branch combines EfficientNet and Residual Network (ResNet) to extract discriminative facial features, while a CNN-based architecture processes MRI images. Clinical narratives are encoded using Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) and BioBERT to capture contextual semantic information. An Adaptive Feature Refinement Layer (AFRL) enhances modality-specific feature learning, followed by Particle Swarm Optimisation (PSO) for feature selection and a novel PSO-Guided Feature Refinement Layer (PFRL) for adaptive feature weighting prior to multimodal fusion. We implement the framework in TensorFlow and PyTorch and evaluate it on the BioVid, UNBC-McMaster, and Trigeminal Neuralgia MRI datasets. Experimental results achieve 96.2% accuracy, outperforming Support Vector Machine (82.4%), K-Nearest Neighbors (79.6%), Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (88.9%), and AdaBoost (90.7%). The proposed framework provides a robust, scalable, and clinically applicable solution for automated multimodal pain detection and improved clinical decision support.
authors: Karim Gasmi; Sarah Almaghrabi; Ibrahim Rizqallah Alzahrani; Adil Mahmoud Mohamed Mahmoud; Alameen Abdalrahman Eltoum; Abdullah Sawdi Alenzi; Osama R. Shahin; Ahmed I. Taloba; Fatma Al Zahraa Hamed Abdel Hameed

title: Navigating human-robot interaction challenges in private and residential aged care homes
abstract: This chapter explores how robotic systems and ambient intelligence can enhance care for older adults in residential aged care (RAC) homes and private homes. Although these settings differ, we frame both as extreme and challenging environments for human-robot interaction (HRI), characterised by cluttered and dynamic layouts, diverse resident needs, and limited on-site technical support. We review embodied and non-embodied systems that assist with daily living, safety monitoring, and social engagement, highlighting hybrid deployments where robots complement fixed and wearable sensors. To ensure these technologies are usable and effective, design considerations consider the cognitive, physical, and social needs of older adults. Interaction design prioritises accessibility for older adults with low digital literacy, using robust but simple voice interfaces, small sets of non-verbal cues, accessible screen-based companions, and safe object handovers. Privacy, trust, and acceptability are addressed via practical strategies such as on-device inference, data minimisation, visible consent controls, and transparent data handling aligned with emerging artificial intelligence (AI) and privacy regulation. Evaluation emphasises real-world metrics including false alarms per day, time to recover from faults, staff workload, and long-term system reliability. We close by outlining open research challenges and future directions for scalable, regulation-ready deployments that support aging with dignity, safety, and independence.
authors: David Ahmedt-Aristizabal; Mohammad Ali Armin; Akila Pemasiri; Harshala Gammulle; Tharindu Fernando; David Silvera-Tawil; Simon Denman

title: NeuroCareIoT for reliable multimodal edge based Alzheimer’s home monitoring using NeuroFuseNet
abstract: Continuous, reliable assessment of falls and night-time wandering, routine deviations and physiological instability must be provided for people with Alzheimer’s disease at home. Current methods, however, typically address only a single modality of sensing, are grounded in fixed decision thresholds, and fail to appropriately consider probability calibration and predictive uncertainty, resulting in too many false alarms at night, delayed detection of subtle changes, and diminished trust by caregivers. To fill these gaps, we present NeuroCareIoT, an edge-first IoT framework that integrates motion, location, routines, and vitals while accounting for reliability and uncertainty. It consists of four task-specific backbones (IMU micro-dynamics: SafeFallNet; room-level localisation with path entropy: WanderSenseNet; temporal deviation modelling: DailyRoutineNet; motion-aware HR/HRV: VitalRhythmNet), coupled by NeuroFuseNet, a reliability-aware fusion layer that weighs modalities based on quality scores ( $$qi$$ ) and outputs a calibrated risk. On top of this, NeuroFuseNet applies Platt scaling at the internal node level for calibration and includes an entropy-based gate to suppress low-confidence windows and drive tiered escalation. NeuroCareIoT was shown to provide better performance in terms of precision (86.9%) and recall (90.3%) across five random seed data sets than both the heuristic baseline, the best-performing single-modality model and naïve average fusion. It also achieved better probability calibration (Brier score = 0.061), lower expected calibration error (2.6%), and more stable performance across decision thresholds. Ablation analysis revealed that reliability weighting and uncertainty gating had the greatest effect on precision, and SafeFallNet had the greatest effect on sensitivity, while maintaining a 95th-percentile decision latency under 200 ms on both the Raspberry Pi 4B and Jetson Nano platforms. Personalisation reduced the number of false alarms by 0.54 per night and shortened the time to detect routine deviations by 1.7 minutes. Quiet-hours alert burden was further lowered, and the precision of night-time alerts was further improved by tuning the policy for caregivers. In addition, case studies of SHAP-based care notes were given to facilitate transparent decision-making, along with risk and entropy trajectories. All results show that NeuroCareIoT is a viable prototype for implementing a multimodal monitoring framework that can be realised through an edge-first approach and tested in controlled, synchronised replay experiments built on publicly available datasets. The suggested framework serves as a basis for future validation through longitudinal real-home studies with Alzheimer’s patients, caregivers, and clinician-adjudicated incident records. Not applicable.
authors: K Venkata Naganjaneyulu; Sajja Suneel; Dheeraj Sundaragiri; Thanniru Pavan Vinayak; V R D Swathi Nellipudi; Bakkala Santha Kumar

title: New Oxygen Sensor with Polyaniline Spin Probe and Low Frequency EPR (L-Band) Detection System
abstract: Our research demonstrates the potential of certain PANI samples to serve as sensitive and reliable spin probes for oxygen detection, while also highlighting the advantages of the lowfrequency EPR technique. Compared to other methods of measuring oxygen concentration, the new sensor—based on a PANI spin probe and a low-frequency EPR detector—offers unique benefits: it ensures high sensitivity to changes in oxygen concentration and does not require direct contact between the EPR detector and the sensor itself (the polyaniline probe). This sensor can be placed in isolated environments, including biological samples (tissues), and - thanks to the use of nanodispersed polyaniline - even inside living cells.
authors: Mikolaj Baranowski; Sebastian Golczak; Jerzy J. Langer

title: Next-Generation Brain Health Monitoring Enabled by Integrated Wearable AI Infrastructure.
abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases are difficult to detect during their pre-symptomatic stages, when intervention is most effective. Advances in wearable biosensors, artificial intelligence (AI), and neuroscience now enable continuous monitoring of brain-related physiological signals in real-world settings. However, progress in sensing technologies, signal analytics, and machine learning remains fragmented, limiting the biological specificity, robustness, and clinical translation of many digital biomarkers. This review presents an integrated framework that links molecular pathology and neural circuit dysfunction to sensor-detectable digital phenotypes across sleep, autonomic regulation, gait, speech, and ocular dynamics. We evaluate emerging wearable platforms, including bioelectric, optical, and neuromotor sensors, and discuss critical design considerations such as signal quality, user-centered form factors, and ultra-low-power edge AI systems. We further examine how self-supervised learning, federated AI, mechanistic modeling, and fairness-aware validation can improve biomarker reliability, interpretability, and generalizability. To facilitate clinical deployment, we introduce the Personalized Brain-Health Operating System (pBH-OS), a privacy-preserving reference architecture for scalable digital phenotyping. The framework maps conceptual layers to existing technologies while identifying key validation gaps. We also address practical challenges, including adherence, device dropout, informative missingness, regulatory compliance, and accountability. Together, these advances provide a pathway toward biologically grounded and regulation-ready systems capable of identifying neurodegenerative risk years before clinical symptom onset.
authors: Muhammad Hasan Masrur; Bangul Khan; Rana Talha Khalid; Sumaira; Saad Abdullah

title: Non-Sustained Ventricular Tachycardia on Long Term Ambulatory ECG Monitoring in the Pediatric Population Without Prior Cardiac Diagnosis
abstract: Background Non-sustained ventricular tachycardia (NSVT) may predict adverse outcomes in adults, but its significance in pediatric patients without prior cardiac diagnosis is unclear. Objective To assess NSVT prevalence in undiagnosed pediatric patients, its association with cardiac disease, and the utility of clinical testing. Methods We reviewed 2,207 patients <18 years who underwent ambulatory ECG (AECG) monitoring. NSVT was defined as ≥4 consecutive ventricular complexes at tachycardic rates for age. Patients with cardiomyopathy or congenital heart disease were excluded. Data on medications, echocardiography, MRI, exercise testing, and resultant diagnoses were analyzed. Results NSVT occurred in 62 patients (3%). These patients had longer wear times (246 vs. 178 hours) and more ventricular ectopy (p<0.001). Stimulant and albuterol use was not correlated with NSVT burden. Testing included echocardiography (82%), MRI (32%), repeat AECG monitoring (40%), and exercise testing (39%). No sustained ventricular tachycardia occurred during exercise testing; no deaths were reported. Two patients (3%) were diagnosed with cardiomyopathy; four had nonspecific dilation or dysfunction without a diagnosis. NSVT frequency and shorter duration to first occurrence correlated with any abnormal testing (p = 0.032) and specifically ventricular dilation/dysfunction (p=0.038). After adjusting for ventricular ectopy, duration to first episode remained significant while NSVT burden lost significance. Conclusions Incidental NSVT was infrequent in this pediatric cohort. Cardiomyopathy was diagnosed in two patients. Ventricular dilation/dysfunction was seen in 3% and was associated with earlier occurrences of NSVT on AECG monitoring. These findings support further evaluation to exclude cardiomyopathy.

title: Non-contact Cardiorespiratory Monitoring in a Smart Triage Chair using Laser Speckle Pattern Dynamics
abstract: Emergency triage requires rapid, simultaneous vital-sign acquisition, yet contact-based sensors create throughput bottlenecks during surge events. We present a triage chair that measures heart rate (HR) and respiration rate (RR) simultaneously without patient contact, using time-varying laser speckle patterns projected onto the posterior thorax. We conducted our experiments in a cohort of 34 volunteers (19 males, 15 females, age 39.6 ± 11.4 years). RR estimation showed good agreement with an MAE of 1.9 br/min and an RMSE of 3.4 br/min (95% CI: [0.9, 2.9] br/min). For HR estimation, an MAE of 10.68 BPM and an RMSE of 19.0 BPM were obtained (95% CI: [5.2, 16.2] BPM).

title: Noninvasive assessment of the anaerobic threshold in endurance athletes: an evidence-based narrative review of methods, validity, and field feasibility
abstract: INTRODUCTION OR BACKGROUND: The anaerobic threshold (AnT) marks the transition between heavy and severe exercise intensity domains and guides training prescription and performance monitoring. Criterion methods (blood lactate and gas exchange) are accurate but invasive, costly, or impractical outside laboratories, prompting the search for noninvasive surrogates. This review evaluates the validity of these estimation procedures rather than the underlying physiology. SOURCES OF DATA: MEDLINE (via PubMed) was searched from inception without language restrictions, supplemented by reference-list and citation searching. Eligible studies compared noninvasive AnT indices, including heart rate variability (HRV; including detrended fluctuation analysis [DFA] α1), cardiac repolarization instability, heart rate deflection/field slope-variation methods, critical power (CP)/ critical speed (CS), near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS), the talk test, and machine-learning (ML) models, with criterion standards. Risk of bias was assessed using QUADAS-2. Eighty-eight reports were synthesized narratively; no meta-analysis was performed. AREAS OF AGREEMENT: DFA α1, NIRS breakpoints, and CP/CS show strong associations with laboratory criteria and increasing field applicability through wearables. Accuracy and feasibility trade-offs require method selection according to the threshold, sport, and required precision. AREAS OF CONTROVERSY: Correlation indicates group-level association rather than individual agreement; Bland-Altman and reliability analyses are more informative for substitution. Criterion standards are not interchangeable, and heart rate deflection is not consistently identifiable. Evidence in female athletes remains limited. GROWING POINTS: Multimodal wearables integrating HRV, muscle oxygenation, and running power with ML may improve field-based threshold estimation. AREAS FOR DEVELOPING RESEARCH: Priorities include standardized reporting, transparent bias assessment, female-athlete validation, and broader systematic and meta-analytic synthesis.
authors: Nicola Maffulli; Johnny Padulo; Francesco Oliva

title: Nurse-led mobile health interventions for heart failure self-care: A systematic review
abstract: Heart failure places a heavy and growing demand on health systems, and much of its everyday management depends on what patients do at home: taking medicines as prescribed, weighing themselves, limiting salt and fluid, and noticing the early signs of decompensation. Nurses have traditionally led the education and follow-up that sustain these behaviours, and mobile health tools now allow that support to continue well beyond the clinic. This systematic review examined whether nurse-led mobile health interventions improve self-care and related outcomes in adults living with heart failure. Guided by PRISMA 2020, we searched PubMed/MEDLINE for studies published between January 2010 and October 2026 and supplemented this with citation and targeted keyword searching. Sixteen studies from fourteen countries were included, fifteen of them randomised. Interventions ranged from structured telephone support and messaging to smartphone applications, wireless telemonitoring and wearable-guided coaching. Most trials that used validated instruments reported better self-care, especially daily weighing, self-care maintenance and medication adherence, although some gains faded once active support ended. Effects on rehospitalisation were inconsistent; reductions appeared mainly where nurses acted promptly on transmitted data. Quality of life improved in several, but not all, trials. Small samples, short follow-up and the impossibility of blinding limit certainty. Nurse-led mobile health appears to strengthen heart failure self-care when technology is paired with timely clinical response, and it warrants rigorous testing in low- and middle-income settings, including India.

title: Oculomics using artificial intelligence derived retinal biomarkers for cardiovascular health
abstract: This narrative review synthesizes evidence from retinal vascular morphology, structural and perfusion imaging, retinal aging, metabolomics, and artificial intelligence models linking retinal biomarkers with cardiovascular risk factors, subclinical disease, clinical events, and cardiorenal and metabolic outcomes. These biomarkers may complement conventional risk assessment, but clinical utility is unproven and integration into cardiovascular digital twins remains conceptual. Prospective validation, standardized acquisition, interoperability, interpretability, and equitable evaluation are required before implementation.

title: Optimasi Parameter Pemesinan CNC Turning untuk Meminimalkan Deviasi Dimensi dan Kekasaran Permukaan
abstract: Deviasi diameter pada komponen collar roda depan sepeda motor berbahan Aluminium 6061 merupakan indikator kualitas kritis karena penyimpangan yang melewati batas toleransi ±0,02 mm dapat menyebabkan sambungan longgar dan getaran saat kendaraan beroperasi. Penelitian ini bertujuan menentukan kombinasi optimal parameter CNC turning untuk meminimalkan deviasi diameter menggunakan metode Taguchi. Tiga parameter yang dikaji meliputi putaran spindel (1300, 1900, 2500 rpm), laju pemakanan (0,10; 0,20; 0,30 mm/rev), dan kedalaman potong (1,50; 2,00; 2,50 mm) yang disusun dalam matriks ortogonal L9 dengan tiga kali replikasi menggunakan mesin CNC Turning SL-25 Mori Seiki dan pahat insert carbide CNMG 120402-HA. Karakteristik kualitas Smaller-the-Better diterapkan pada analisis rasio signal-to-noise dan analisis varians (ANOVA). Hasil penelitian menunjukkan kedalaman potong sebagai faktor paling dominan dengan kontribusi 60,09%, diikuti putaran spindel 28,08% dan laju pemakanan 10,71%, dengan galat 1,12%. Kondisi optimal diperoleh pada putaran spinoh anova di abstrak gasdel 2500 rpm, laju pemakanan 0,10 mm/rev, dan kedalaman potong 2,00 mm, menghasilkan prediksi deviasi diameter 0,031 mm pada interval keyakinan 95% antara 0,020 mm hingga 0,049 mm. Uji konfirmasi menghasilkan deviasi rata-rata 0,044 mm yang masih berada dalam rentang prediksi, sehingga memvalidasi model yang dibangun. Metode Taguchi terbukti efektif mengidentifikasi parameter pemesinan optimal untuk menghasilkan dimensi collar Aluminium 6061 yang presisi dan konsisten. Kata kunci: Aluminium 6061; ANOVA; CNC turning; deviasi diameter; metode Taguchi.
authors: Tio Suhendri; Husman; Yuliyanto

title: Optimization of Wear Behavior Analysis in MWCNT-Reinforced GFRP Composites Using RSM and ETLBO
abstract: This study aims to optimize the fabrication process of Multi-walled Carbon Nanotube (MWCNT)-filled Glass Fiber-reinforced Polymer (GFRP) composites to enhance their tribological performance during the hand layup process. A structured experimental approach based on the Box–Behnken design within the Response Surface Methodology (RSM) framework was used to evaluate the influence of wt.% MWCNT loading, applied load, and sliding velocity. The fabrication was performed, ensuring a uniform MWCNT dispersion via mechanical stirring and probe sonication. The performance of the composites was assessed in terms of their Specific Wear Rate (SWR) and Wear Coefficients (WCs). Statistical analysis, including ANOVA and Pareto charts, revealed that the load and sliding velocity significantly affected both the SWR and WC, whereas interactions such as the MWCNT content and sliding velocity also played a crucial role. Mathematical models were developed for SWR and WC and optimized using Elitist Teaching-learning-based Optimization (ETLBO). The optimal fabrication settings were found to be 1 wt.% MWCNT loading, 30 N load, and 2 m/s sliding velocity, yielding improved wear characteristics. Confirmatory tests validated the model predictions and showed minimal errors. Scanning electron microscopy further confirmed that optimal nanotube dispersion led to a more uniform and durable composite structure, supporting its potential for high-performance engineering applications. The proposed integrated approach demonstrates the effectiveness of combining RSM and ETLBO to develop high-performance MWCNT–GFRP composites with superior wear resistance. The findings of this study provide practical guidelines for fabricating durable, wear-resistant composite structures for automotive brake systems, aerospace joints, and industrial machinery parts, where reliability under continuous sliding conditions is essential.
authors: Ch. Rajeswari; Namala Kiran Kumar; P. Saritha

title: PS2-15. Multimodal Video and Audio Signal Processing for Estimating Cattle Forage Intake.
abstract: Abstract Accurate quantification of forage intake and rumen digesta during grazing is important for nutrition research but remains difficult to measure at scale. This pilot study evaluated whether contactless video and audio recordings collected during grazing contain kinematic and acoustic signatures that can be related to forage disappearance and rumen digesta dry matter measured via cannulation. Two Angus cattle were recorded across three days during controlled feeding trials in which cereal rye was presented in ground-level pots (three pots per animal per day) and consumed while a fixed-position action camera captured video with onboard audio. Jaw and head keypoints were tracked from video using SLEAP, and grazing-associated audio features were extracted from the video soundtrack using standard digital signal processing implemented in librosa. Features linked to biting events were used as inputs to a linear regression model to estimate forage dry matter disappearance and rumen digesta dry matter recovered after each trial. In this pilot dataset, recovered rumen digesta dry matter was highly correlated with forage disappearance (R² = 0.99), supporting the use of disappearance as a closely aligned intake-related endpoint under these controlled conditions. The results motivate expanded validation across more animals, forage types, and grazing conditions to assess model generalizability and the potential for contactless intake-related monitoring using invasive ground truth for calibration. title: Passive Monitoring for Suicide Risk Prediction in U.S. Military Personnel: Detecting Behavioral Changes with Wearable Data
abstract: Abstract Suicide rates in U.S. military personnel exceed national averages, with crises escalating rapidly outside clinical hours. Passive wearable sensing offers a continuous and objective approach to detect proximal suicide risk that may go unnoticed by periodic clinical assessments. This secondary analysis evaluated whether behavioral changes passively captured by wearable devices could predict suicidal events in a high-risk military sample. We analyzed 28-day Fitbit data from 86 U.S. military service members and veterans, including physical activity, heart rate variability, and sleep, alongside self-reported suicidal events collected through ecological momentary assessment. Probabilistic heterogeneous mixture models were used to generate daily behavioral profiles, and Bayesian change-point detection identified instability preceding events within a 72-hour window. Source contribution analysis was then conducted to determine the most informative passive feature combinations. The model achieved AUC scores of 0.90 for suicide attempts, 0.85 for preparatory acts, and 0.82 for non-suicidal self-injury, with an average AUC of 0.79 across suicidal behaviors. Performance was lower for suicidal urge, suggesting that passive sensing may better capture observable behavioral crises than subjectively reported ideation. These findings support wearable-based change detection as a scalable strategy for real-time suicide prevention in military populations.

title: Perceived Acceptability, Design Preferences, and User Requirements for a Proposed Ear-Worn Device for Heart-Rate and Ear-Temperature Monitoring with Localized Neck Cooling: A Pre-Prototype Mixed-Methods Study in People with Multiple Sclerosis.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Heat sensitivity in multiple sclerosis (MS) can worsen neurological symptoms and impair daily functioning and quality of life. As current cooling strategies are largely reactive, wearable technology may offer a proactive approach, provided it is acceptable to users. This pre-prototype study evaluated the perceived acceptability of a proposed ear-worn device, not yet fabricated, that would measure ear-site temperature and heart rate, alert the user, and direct localized airflow at the neck, and identified the user priorities that should guide its development. No technical feasibility or device-performance testing was performed. Methods: Adults with MS completed an electronic questionnaire on design preferences, functional features, and overall acceptability; a subset took part in semi-structured interviews analyzed thematically. Results: Forty-seven participants completed the survey. Comfort during prolonged use (72.3%) and compatibility with prescription glasses (66.0%) were the design features most often rated important; health reports (93.6%), communication with healthcare providers (91.5%), symptom monitoring (89.4%), emergency contact (85.1%), and automatic cooling activation (83.0%) were each rated important by more than 80% of participants, with overlapping confidence intervals that do not permit these functions to be ranked. Anticipated acceptability of the concept was uncertain: 46.8% (95% confidence interval [CI] 33.3-60.8) expressed some degree of acceptability (34.0% when only 'acceptable' or 'very acceptable' responses were counted), 36.2% were neutral, and 17.0% found it not acceptable. Six interviews generated four themes: uncertainty, the impact of heat on daily life, independence through self-management, and practical considerations for implementation. Conclusions: These findings reflect anticipated, concept-level acceptability rather than acceptability after use of a physical device. Because the proposed device would measure ear-site temperature and heart rate rather than neurological symptoms, the priority given to symptom monitoring is addressed through physiological early warning combined with user-reported symptoms. The identified priorities are translated into measurable specifications and verification tests for the next prototype; the technical performance of the device, including its cooling capacity, remains to be demonstrated.
authors: Almuwais A, Alotaibi M, Binshaye D, Alhumaid D, Almohsen F, Alsubaie S, Alshareef R, Alkhushayban N.

title: Perceived occupational HIV risk, stigma, and discriminatory attitudes among healthcare professionals in Jeddah and Riyadh, Saudi Arabia: a comparative cross-sectional study
abstract: Background Even with the presence of institutional policies, training programs, and various interventions, stigma associated with Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) still obstructs fair access to healthcare services. In Saudi Arabia, there is a scarcity of research focusing on the regional variations among healthcare workers regarding their Fear of HIV Infection/Perceived Occupational Risk, their attitudes towards individuals living with HIV (PLHIV), and the stigma and discrimination they observe. Aim This research aimed to compare these aspects among healthcare professionals in Riyadh and Jeddah. Methods This study employed a comparative cross-sectional design involving 466 healthcare workers, including doctors, nurses, and allied health professionals, from selected healthcare facilities in Riyadh and Jeddah. Data collection was carried out using a validated, self-administered questionnaire that evaluated Fear of HIV Infection/Perceived Occupational Risk, attitudes towards PLHIV, observed stigma and discrimination, infection-control practices, the healthcare facility environment, and institutional policies. Descriptive statistics, comparisons between groups, and multiple regression analyses were utilized to explore regional differences and factors influencing attitudes towards PLHIV. Results In Riyadh, participants tended to be older and possess more experience than those in Jeddah. Specifically, 39.7% of individuals from Riyadh were between 30 and 39 years old, while 55.0% of those from Jeddah were aged 20 to 29. Additionally, those in Riyadh were more likely to have extensive professional experience and prior training related to HIV. Both groups showed moderate levels of fear regarding HIV infection and perceived occupational risk, along with similar levels of support from institutional policies. Differences between regions were noted in terms of observed stigma and discrimination, with Riyadh scoring higher, and in infection-control practices, where Jeddah had slightly better scores. Multivariable regression analysis revealed minimal evidence that factors such as region, previous HIV-related training, fear of HIV infection, perceived occupational risk, or health facility policies independently influenced attitudes toward people living with HIV (R 2 = 0.006, p = 0.596). Conclusion In both areas, healthcare workers exhibited moderate levels of fear regarding HIV infection and perceived occupational risks. However, misconceptions and discriminatory attitudes towards people living with HIV (PLHIV) were still apparent. These results highlight the necessity of ongoing, evidence-based HIV education, initiatives to reduce stigma, and enhanced institutional support systems to foster compassionate and fair treatment of individuals with HIV in Saudi Arabia.
authors: Amal Ibrahim Khalil; Seham Ahmed Mohamed El-Gamal; Sitah S Alshutwi; Waad Alsulami; Hanaa M. Abo Shereda

title: Perspectives and experiences of youth and caregivers on screening and monitoring islet autoimmunity
abstract: Aims Screening and monitoring programs for islet autoantibodies, which signal risk of clinical type 1 diabetes, are being implemented globally. No studies have qualitatively explored youths’ perspectives on islet autoimmunity screening and monitoring, nor integrated their views with those of caregivers. Methods We interviewed 35 Australian youth (aged 9–18 years; median age = 11.5 years; n = 18 girls) with one or more islet autoantibodies and 49 caregivers of affected youth. Youth had been monitored for approximately 9 years (median). All families, except one, had a relative with type 1 diabetes. Twenty-one (42.86%) caregivers lived with clinical type 1 diabetes. Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Results Seven themes reflected our findings. Youth had limited understanding of the advantages of monitoring outside of research. They were predominantly focused on testing experiences rather than clinical risk. Caregivers generally displayed strong psychological responses, as did older adolescents. Family experience of diabetes shaped psychological responses in multifaceted ways. Caregivers further emphasised flexible service delivery and specific logistical considerations for screening and monitoring. Conclusions Youths’ focus on the practicalities of testing, rather than health risk, is reassuring in the context of planning international screening and monitoring programs. However, it highlights the need to prioritise procedural experiences. Youth should also be educated on the real-world benefits of monitoring. Psychosocial support is needed, particularly for caregivers and older adolescents, with healthcare individualised to the unique influence of family history of clinical diabetes. Caregivers further need reliable, structured monitoring pathways to manage distress, with equity and accessibility prioritised for sustained engagement.
authors: Mia Majstorovic; Kelly J. McGorm; John M. Wentworth; Tony Huynh; Fergus Cameron; Maria E. Craig; Elizabeth Ann Davis; Kirstine J. Bell; Georgia Soldatos; Megan A. S. Penno; Alyssa C. P. Sawyer; Melissa Oxlad; Jennifer Couper

title: Phishing URL Detection using CNN-BiLSTM Attention with Character-Level Embeddings
abstract: Phishing is a critical cybersecurity issue since malicious URLs are often used to trick users and acquire sensitive data such as passwords, bank account information, and personal details.Current approaches for phishing URL detection typically rely on blacklist matching, hand-designed lexical features or domain-specific rules.These methods are effective for detecting known attacks, but they may not work for emerging, obfuscated, or novel (zero-day) phishing URLs.In this work, we present a deep learning approach to detect phishing URLs by encoding URL strings with embedded characters and an attention mechanism.Our approach converts each URL into dense vector embeddings by an embedding layer, considering URLs as a sequence of characters.The proposed model combines convolutional and bidirectional long shortterm memory (BiLSTM) layers to learn local suspicious features and contextual information in URL strings.We then use an attention mechanism to give more weight to the most relevant parts of the URL, including deceptive subdomains, suspicious characters, fake login pages, encoded characters, and irregular paths.The PhiUSIIL Phishing URL Dataset, comprising 235,795 URLs (134,850 legitimate and 100,945 phishing) is used to validate the model.For this analysis, only the URL string and label are employed, without using the web page content, WHOIS data, DNS records, blacklist, and reputation providers.The effectiveness of the proposed method is evaluated using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, ROC-AUC, and confusion matrix.
authors: Chandrashekhar B. Banad; L Chaitanya; Chetna Sagar; Bhavani Kadiyala; Devulapalli Shyam Prasad

title: Photoplethysmography-based smartwatches for atrial fibrillation detection in stroke survivors: The Liverpool-Huawei Stroke Study
abstract: Abstract Background Detecting atrial fibrillation (AF) in stroke survivors is critical for preventing recurrent stroke. However, the diagnostic accuracy of photoplethysmography (PPG)-based smartwatches in this high-risk population remains uncertain. The Liverpool-Huawei Stroke Study evaluated the performance of Huawei smartbands for AF detection following an ischaemic stroke. Purpose 1. To determine the clinical effectiveness of Huawei smartband by assessing the negative predictive value (NPV) and positive predictive value (PPV) for identifying incident and known AF in a post-stroke population. 2. To identify clinical predictors associated with AF detection. Methods Between June 2022 and June 2024, patients hospitalised with a recent ischaemic stroke were recruited from 8 National Health Service Trusts. Participants wore a Huawei smartband paired with an Android smartphone for one month. The device automatically screened for AF at regular intervals, transmitting data via the Huawei Health App. Following alerts generated by the device, clinical evaluation with ECG and 5-14 days Holter or ECG patch monitoring were used to confirm AF diagnosis although these were not done concurrent with the alert. Results 491 patients (median age: 62 [QR 54, 72]; 35% female) were recruited (Table). During the one-month monitoring period, 192 (39.1%) individual AF alerts were received, 15 (7.8%) were confirmed as incident AF, 114 (59.4%) were confirmed AF-negative, and 39 (7.9%) identified as known AF. (Figure). The resulting NPV and PPV were 0.89 (0.85, 0.93) and 0.32 (95% CI: [0.25, 0.40]), respectively. Multivariable logistic regression indicated that age (OR: 1.06, 95%CI [1.03, 1.11]), current smoker (0.35 [0.10, 0.96]) and systolic blood pressure (0.98 [0.96, 0.99]) were independently associated with AF detection (Figure). Conclusions The Huawei smartband revealed incident AF in 15 (7.8%) patients post-stroke with a high NPV (89%), but a low PPV (32.1%). This may reflect that ECG monitoring was not done concurrent with the alert and ectopic beats (common in this population) were flagged as an alert due to irregular PPG rhythm; however, the absence of an alert likely reflects the absence of AF post-stroke. Baseline age, smoking status, and systolic blood pressure were independent predictors for AF detection.Figure

title: Physical activity in preclinical Alzheimer disease: current evidence and implications for multimodal longitudinal research
abstract: Alzheimer disease (AD) pathology may be detectable years before cognitive symptoms, but biomarker testing of cognitively unimpaired people is not recommended for routine clinical use. Objective physical activity (PA), gait, and rest-activity measures are attractive research signals because they are repeatable and relatively inexpensive; however, none are specific to AD. This narrative review examined evidence linking PA, gait, and rest-activity measures to AD-related outcomes and considered their role in multimodal longitudinal research within biomarker-characterized cohorts. Targeted searches of PubMed, Scopus, and IEEE Xplore were conducted from inception through 25 August 2026, and reference lists of pivotal studies and guidance documents were hand-searched. Priority was given to guidelines, longitudinal cohorts, randomized trials, studies using objective behavior measures and AD biomarkers, and externally evaluated prediction models. Observational evidence links higher activity with lower dementia risk, but reverse causation remains plausible. In biomarker-characterized cohorts, greater baseline step count has been associated with slower amyloid-related tau accumulation and slower cognitive and functional decline, not with lower amyloid burden. Rest-activity fragmentation has shown cross-sectional and prospective associations with amyloid-related measures, whereas a 1-year aerobic-exercise trial did not reduce amyloid accumulation. Recent multimodal AI studies demonstrate that non-PET (positron emission tomography) data can estimate amyloid and tau status. Yet, they do not establish the incremental value of free-living PA in cognitively unimpaired community samples. We therefore outline a framework for longitudinal behavioral research in cohorts whose biomarker status has been characterized independently of PA-based selection. Its primary purpose is to examine associations between behavioral measures and subsequent cognitive, functional, and tau trajectories. Whether PA improves individual prediction beyond clinical information and baseline biomarkers remains a separate, unresolved question. PA is considered a contextual behavioral measure, and the framework does not propose using it to determine eligibility for biomarker testing or research recruitment.
authors: Liang Wang; Wei Lai; Tianqi Wei; Yunbang Zhang; Youliang Wen

title: Physics-Informed and Explainable Artificial Intelligence for Nanomaterial-Based Biosensors: From Sensor Design and Signal Processing to Clinical Translation
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in biosensing, yet its role is often limited to post-processing or high-accuracy regression on simulation-generated datasets. This critical narrative review examines physics-informed and explainable AI for nanomaterial-based biosensors, emphasizing graphene and other two-dimensional materials, surface plasmon resonance (SPR), terahertz (THz) metasurfaces, electrochemical platforms, field-effect transistors, surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy, and wearable systems. Recent peer-reviewed studies and relevant technical guidance were critically compared with respect to sensing physics, data provenance, AI task, interpretability, validation strategy, and evidence level. Across these modalities, AI supports forward surrogate modeling, inverse design, spectral interpretation, classification, calibration, and uncertainty-aware decision support, but predictive accuracy alone does not establish translational maturity. Particular attention is given to explainable AI, the distinction between physics-guided and genuinely physics-informed learning, small-data validation, fabrication tolerance, drift, and the simulation-to-experiment gap. Quantitative comparisons place reported SPR and THz sensitivities in context, while independent experimental studies provide benchmarks for real-device and biomedical validation. Clinically credible intelligent biosensors should combine mechanistic constraints, uncertainty quantification, device- and batch-aware validation, interpretable features, realistic biological matrices, and prospective evaluation.
authors: Stefano Bellucci A

title: Plasma immune signatures associate with neurodegeneration in frontotemporal lobar degeneration
abstract: Abstract Frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD) encompasses clinically and biologically heterogeneous syndromes that are unlikely to be captured by a single blood biomarker. Although plasma neurofilament light (NfL) chain reflects neuroaxonal injury, multiplex profiling may identify complementary inflammatory, vascular and proteostatic processes relevant to clinical phenotype and progression. We characterised plasma CNS-related and inflammatory proteomic signatures across FTLD-related clinical syndromes and tested their associations with neuroaxonal injury, clinical severity, regional brain atrophy and survival. Plasma samples from 177 participants with behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD), primary progressive aphasia (PPA), progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) or corticobasal syndrome (CBS) and 67 healthy controls were analysed using the high-sensitivity nucleic acid-linked immuno-sandwich assay (NULISA) platform. We quantified 130 CNS-related and 250 inflammation-related proteins. Differential expression and multivariate classification analyses were complemented by hierarchical clustering, penalised regression and survival analyses. Canonical correlation analysis tested multivariate associations between disease-associated proteins and regional MRI brain volumes. Sixty-one CNS-related and 61 inflammation-related proteins differed between participants with FTLD-related syndromes and controls after false-discovery-rate correction. NfL was the strongest individual discriminator between all patients and controls, with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.91. In exploratory full-cohort models, the multivariate CNS signature achieved an area under the curve of 0.93, compared with 0.82 for the multivariate inflammation signature. However, inflammatory proteins provided stronger discrimination for selected syndrome comparisons, including PPA versus PSP. Among inflammation-related proteins, SPP1 and CD276 showed the strongest positive associations with NfL. Higher CD276 and SPP1 were associated with increased mortality, whereas higher amyloid-β42 was associated with lower mortality. A multivariate protein signature weighted towards tumour necrosis factor and immune signalling was associated with lower regional brain volumes across predominantly frontotemporal and limbic regions (canonical correlation 0.43; permutation p=0.018). Plasma multiplex proteomics identified complementary dimensions of neuroaxonal injury and immune dysregulation across frontotemporal lobar degeneration-related syndromes. CNS-related proteins, particularly NfL, predominantly captured case-control neurodegeneration, whereas inflammatory signatures provided additional information about syndrome heterogeneity, structural brain changes and survival. SPP1, CD276 and broader immune-related signatures are candidates for independent biomarker validation and mechanistic investigation.

title: Portable Devices for Diagnosis of Sleep-Disordered Breathing
abstract: What Is the Issue? Sleep-disordered breathing (SDB) includes a range of conditions that make it difficult to breathe while sleeping and can lead to heart failure, neurodegenerative diseases, cognitive impairment, and poor quality of life. Many people in Canada have obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), a type of SDB, but they often remain undiagnosed. The gold standard for diagnosing SDB is polysomnography (PSG), which is referred to as a level 1 test. PSG is conducted in a sleep laboratory and attended by a sleep technician. Because access to this test can vary, is often limited geographically, and can have long wait times, portable devices for diagnosing SDB have emerged for use at home and may help speed up diagnosis and access to treatment. Provincial decision-makers requested this report to assess the evidence available on using portable devices for diagnosing SDB. The findings will inform whether results from these devices can be used with confidence as an alternative to PSG. What Did We Do? We conducted a rapid review to identify and summarize evidence that compared the diagnostic accuracy and clinical utility of these devices as well as evidence-based guidelines published in the past 5 years. Two clinical experts reviewed the report, and 1 expert identified devices to supplement the literature available. We conducted a horizon scan to identify any new devices emerging in the field. What Did We Find? A total of 92 portable sleep devices were identified. Ten systematic reviews were identified that examined the diagnostic accuracy or clinical utility of more than 60 portable diagnostic sleep tests compared to those of PSG. Five guidelines with recommendations for adults or people who are pregnant were identified, of which 1 guideline reported on 6 specific portable diagnostic sleep devices. An expert identified an additional 26 devices to consider. A Canadian guideline on the diagnosis of OSA in children was published in 2026 while this report was being written, and relevant information from that guideline has been included in this report. Sleep diagnostic devices have traditionally been categorized using levels. Unlike PSG studies, tests using devices categorized as level 2, 3, or 4 are unattended by a technician. Level 3 devices usually have at least 3 channels that measure airflow, respiratory effort, and oximetry. Airflow-based measurement is considered necessary to inform diagnosis. Level 4 devices usually have 1 channel measuring blood oxygen saturation and are not generally used for diagnostic purposes. Some emerging or novel devices fall outside these levels. Of the 92 devices identified in this report, 25 were identified as having active licensing from Health Canada and are currently being manufactured. Current evidence was identified for 6 of these devices. For adults suspected of having OSA, level 3 devices and some wearables (e.g., WatchPAT devices) were generally reported in systematic review evidence as having adequate sensitivity, while level 4 devices tended to have varying sensitivity and specificity. There was less evidence for other devices (e.g., noncontact systems, smartphone-based tools); generally, the evidence reported adequate sensitivity, but specificity varied by factors such as OSA severity and device type. For adults, guidelines recommend level 3 sleep tests for adults with a high pretest probability for moderate to severe OSA and who do not have complicated comorbidities such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease; heart failure; neuromuscular conditions; and physical, sensory, and cognitive impairment. The AcuPebble SA100, Sunrise, WatchPAT 300, and WatchPAT ONE are 4 specific devices recommended for assessing people aged older than 16 years; the WatchPAT 300 device is licensed for sale in Canada. There are several evidence gaps regarding the use of portable devices for the diagnosis of SDB in specific populations. Yet, for people who are pregnant, guidelines state that home sleep apnea testing, but not overnight pulse oximetry, can be considered, and for children aged between 6 and 17 years without significant comorbidities, a Canadian guideline published in 2026 recommends PSG to diagnose OSA. It also recommends that overnight oximetry (level 4 testing) should not be used. What Does This Mean? Some portable sleep devices can be considered for the diagnosis of adults suspected of having moderate to severe OSA who do not have comorbidities. Portable sleep devices are generally not recommended for those who have complicated comorbidities. It is also unclear whether these devices work for people of all genders and/or sexes or for people with darker skin tones given that pulse oximetry cannot accurately measure oxygen saturation in melanated skin. Careful consideration should be given to the following points regarding the use of portable sleep devices to diagnose SDB: the patient’s potential SDB severity and the presence of comorbidities; the number of channels the device measures; whether the device uses airflow or indirect measurements potentially generated by artificial intelligence; the accessibility and cost of the device; the security of the patient sleep data collected; whether devices and software are regularly updated or out of use; and the training or education required to support patients administering tests at home and to interpret sleep test results.

title: Precision Exercise Support for University Students: A Scoping Review of Assessment, Prescription, Monitoring, Feedback, and Adaptation
abstract: Objective: To map how exercise and physical-education research with university students has implemented assessment, subgroup targeting, individualized prescription, monitoring, feedback, and response-based adjustment, and to identify what is still required for a reproducible closed-loop precision-support system. Methods: This scoping review followed JBI guidance and the PRISMA extension for scoping reviews. PubMed, Scopus, and CINAHL Ultimate were searched on August 21, 2026, for English-language studies, supplemented by an existing 28-report full-text seed set. Eligible studies involved university students and evaluated an exercise, physical-education, fitness-testing, monitoring, or feedback component relevant to tailoring exercise support. A five-level framework was applied: standardized provision (level 0), subgroup targeting (level 1), assessment- or feedback-informed adaptation (level 2), individual prescription (level 3), and response-adaptive closed loop (level 4). Results: The searches and seed set identified 403 records; 358 unique records were screened, 48 reports were assessed in full text, and 30 studies entered the evidence map. Fifteen studies used standardized provision, three targeted a predefined subgroup, six implemented assessment, monitoring, or personalized feedback without a complete individual prescription, and six reported individual exercise prescriptions. No study fully specified a level-4 closed loop with prospective monitoring variables, decision thresholds, and reproducible rules for changing frequency, intensity, time, or type. Exercise programs improved selected fitness, body-composition, physical-activity, and mental-health outcomes, but effects were outcome-specific and heterogeneous. Wearables and mobile platforms made monitoring scalable, yet fixed goals, multicomponent designs, and limited use of monitored data for treatment decisions constrained personalization. Assessment feedback could also reduce competence and intrinsic motivation when interpreted negatively. Conclusions: The literature has progressed beyond uniform exercise delivery, but digital monitoring should not be equated with precision. A defensible university model requires an auditable chain from multidimensional assessment to stratification, FITT prescription, process monitoring, interpretable feedback, and threshold-based adjustment, alongside evaluation of safety, equity, adherence, teacher workload, and operational efficiency.
authors: Wenshan Du; Yingsoon Goh

title: Predicting creativity in everyday life: an additional HRV reduction algorithm simulation and its Bayesian replication
abstract: Creative ideas happen in everyday life; however, some may be better than others, and we know little about the dynamics of idea quality as life unfolds. Research suggests that situations of reduced heart rate variability (HRV) might indicate moments of higher (verbal) creative performance. Therefore, this study investigated appropriate settings of an additional HRV reduction (AddHRVr) algorithm to predict creative performance in everyday life. In the first sample of 76 participants, who worked on verbal creative ideation tasks during five consecutive days, we simulated potential AddHRVr algorithm settings to identify higher creative performance. The simulation showed that short-lived periods of AddHRVr predicted higher creative performance in a given moment. In a second independent sample ( n = 65), the very same algorithm setting predicted higher creative performance, indicating robustness. This study provides first evidence for the predictive value of an AddHRVr algorithm to forecast creative performance in real life. As the next step, real-time field applications of these specific AddHRVr algorithm settings via wearables are needed to establish causality in the relationship between HRV reductions and creativity.

title: Prediction of acute mountain sickness from overnight pulse oximetry during ascent to Everest Base Camp: a field-based machine learning study
abstract: Background: Acute mountain sickness (AMS) affects a large proportion of individuals ascending to high altitude every year. While AMS is not life threatening, if left untreated it can progress to serious illness (e.g., high altitude cerebral oedema). Current assessment tools rely on subjective symptom reporting and do not enable prospective prediction. Objective, field-deployable methods for early risk stratification remain limited. This study evaluated whether physiological biomarkers derived from overnight pulse oximetry can predict subsequent AMS during ascent to Everest Base Camp (EBC). Methods: ) and heart rate recordings. Supervised machine-learning models were trained to classify physician-diagnosed AMS at Lobuche (~4,940 m) using: 1) physiological biomarkers alone and 2) biomarkers combined with clinical and contextual metadata. Model performances were assessed using repeated stratified k-fold cross-validation, with area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) as the primary metric. Results: Biomarker-only models demonstrated consistent above-chance discrimination at both altitudes (mean AUC 0.74 at both Namche and Dingboche-level). At lower altitude, predictive performance was achieved using a small set of physiological features, and inclusion of metadata did not improve model performance. At higher altitude, combining biomarkers with contextual variables improved discrimination (AUC 0.84 ± 0.08; sensitivity 0.73 ± 0.23). Selected features were primarily related to nocturnal oxygenation burden, desaturation dynamics, and heart rate variability. Conclusion: Overnight pulse oximetry captures physiological signals associated with subsequent AMS development prior to symptom onset. These findings support the feasibility of objective, non-invasive risk stratification during early ascent. Integration of wearable monitoring with computational modelling may provide a complementary tool to support preventative decision-making along high-altitude trekking routes.

title: Preliminary laboratory analytical comparison of quantitative at-home urinary hormone monitoring systems using artificial urine
abstract: Background Quantitative at-home urinary hormone monitoring systems are increasingly used for reproductive health tracking, but their analytical behaviour requires systematic characterization. This preliminary laboratory comparison aimed to provide an analytical framework to compare multiple commercially available at-home urine hormone monitoring devices across key performance metrics under controlled artificial urine conditions. Methods Laboratory experiments were informed by Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute’s (CLSI) validation principles. Four urine hormone monitoring devices were evaluated using a pre-registered analytical framework for luteinizing hormone (LH), follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), estrone-3-glucuronide (E3G), and pregnanediol glucuronide (PDG). Metrics included coefficients of variation (CV, for precision), relative deviation (RD, for accuracy), linearity, limit of blank (LoB), limit of detection (LoD) for each device, using artificial urine samples with standard hormone concentrations. Cross-reactivity was tested with other hormones including human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), cortisol, thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) and progesterone subtypes. Device-specific evaluations, including the impact of ambient light and various camera systems, were also conducted for relevant devices. Results There were device- and analyte-specific differences in precision, accuracy, linearity and detection limits. Precision and accuracy ranged from CV/RD values near the 15% acceptability threshold to levels exceeding 50% at some concentrations. External lighting conditions affected camera-based strips at low hormone concentrations. False positive results for LH can occur in the presence of 100 mIU/mL hCG, which could lead to misinterpretation in the context of pregnancy. One device that measures the LH-beta subunit avoided this cross-reactivity. Conclusions A preliminary analytical framework was applied to evaluate the performance of quantitative urinary hormone devices for at-home use. This framework can be used in future research and development of menstrual health monitoring technologies. Longitudinal clinical studies using human urine samples and appropriate ovulation reference standards are required before conclusions can be drawn regarding ovulation detection, fertile-window estimation or menstrual-phase classification.
authors: Thomas Paul Bouchard; Paul J. Yong; Patricia K. Doyle–Baker

title: Prescription of oral anticoagulation after an irregular pulse notification: findings from the apple heart study
abstract: Abstract Background Patients with atrial fibrillation (AF) are at increased risk for cerebral thromboembolic complications, and oral anticoagulation (OAC) is the standard treatment to mitigate this risk. Management strategies following irregular pulse notifications (IPNs) from wearable devices remain under explored. Purpose We aimed to examine management strategies for OAC therapy following an IPN from a smartwatch in the Apple Heart Study (AHS) that was conducted in the United States. Methods Participants in the AHS that completed the end-of-study (EOS) survey were included. Those who reported pulmonary embolism (PE) were excluded. Participants were grouped according to their IPN status, diagnosis of AF and CHA2DS2-VASc-Score with low risk defined as <1 for men and <2 for women. IPN was recorded on smartwatch devices. Diagnosis of AF or atrial flutter (AFL) and OAC prescription were self-reported in the EOS survey. Results Of the 419,297 participants enrolled in the AHS, 293,678 (70%) completed an EOS survey and did not have a PE. Median age was 39 years, 124,188 (42%) were women and 923 (0.3%) received an IPN (elusive AF). Those who received an IPN were more likely to be prescribed an OAC compared to those without an IPN ([216 (23%) vs. 1,108 (0.4%), standardized mean difference=0.76]). Of the participants who received an IPN, 333 (36%) self-reported AF/AFL and 169 (51%) of these reported an OAC prescription (Table 1). Despite not reporting an AF/AFL diagnosis, OAC prescription was reported by 47 (8%) participants who received IPNs, without any strokes or TIAs. Among the 362 participants receiving IPN with a low CHA₂DS₂-VASc-Score, 41 (11%) participants reported OAC use, compared with the non-IPN cohort (386 [(0.2%), SMD=0.49]) (Table 1). Despite, OAC being frequently prescribed in participants of female sex, with at least one comorbidity, or >65 years, the effect of receiving an IPN on OAC prescription was more pronounced in participants <65 years old, with low CHA2DS2-VASc-Score or without co-morbidities compared with the ones with a high CHA2DS2-VASc-Score or the ones reporting concomitant risk factors (Figure 1). Conclusions Among AHS participants who received an IPN 23% were prescribed an OAC, with apixaban being the most frequently prescribed DOAC. Notably, 8% of individuals who received an IPN without reporting prior diagnosis of AF were prescribed an OAC, suggesting potentially enhanced medical management in this cohort. Although, OAC prescription following IPN receipt was more frequent among females, elderly participants and those of elderly age, participants with low stroke risk reported OAC prescription rates of 11%. These findings highlight the need for further investigation into stroke risk stratification and optimal medical therapeutic strategies for patients with elusive AF.

title: Probing and Sensing Layer-Dependent van der Waals Interaction via Induced Anisotropy
abstract: Van der Waals (vdW) interaction, a fundamental force, plays an important role in two-dimensional (2D) systems by enabling atomically sharp assemblies and giving rise to many emergent phenomena. However, experimentally probing and sensing the evolution of vdW interaction between 2D layers remains challenging due to its extreme weakness, very short range, and the difficulty of keeping two atomic layers perfectly parallel while finely adjusting the interaction. Here, we demonstrate an optical strategy to indirectly probe vdW interactions by exploiting induced anisotropy in MoS2/NbIrTe4 heterostructures. We construct heterostructures using isotropic MoS2 and anisotropic NbIrTe4 to ensure perfect parallelism. We modulate and probe the vdW interaction by varying the NbIrTe4 thickness and monitor the vdW-interaction-induced anisotropy in MoS2. We find such induced anisotropy to strongly depend on the NbIrTe4 thickness and clearly observe its fast-decaying nature. This work provides a simple, noncontact approach for indirectly probing interlayer vdW interactions.
