title: Prototyping an inductive conductivity sensor with wide amplitude and frequency range using low cost components
abstract: Abstract Quick and cheap water quality monitoring is an increasingly important tool to make the best use of an increasingly valuable resource. Fluid conductivity is an important parameter and can be measured contactless using inductive or capacitive coupling while maintaining low cost. Only the inductively coupled sensors are completely free of electrode polarization effects due to the absence of electrodes. In this work, a sensor based on a newly developed tubular inductor (patented) is presented. It has a high dynamic range and excellent high frequency properties as it does not have multiple (toroid) windings. An analytical derivation of the generated electromotive force based on the Maxwell equations is presented which provides insight for dimensioning the sensor parameters. The use of ferrites will also be discussed, as they play an important role in magnetics, especially for high frequency applications. The novel drive electronics combine low cost with more than three decades of dynamic (amplitude) range at frequencies from 50 kHz to 100 MHz. Key components are a NanoVNA Vector Network Analyzer and high frequency op-amps. A fluid circuit is constructed with simple silicone tubing to form a closed loop with separated drive and detect tubes to exclude crosstalk. Test results are presented measuring five different salt solutions in four decades of concentration, demonstrating a proof of principle and opening a wide field of potential applications.
authors: F. B. Segerink; Herman Leonard Offerhaus

title: Pushing Bistatic Wireless Sensing toward High Accuracy at the Sub-Wavelength Scale
abstract: Contactless sensing using wireless communication signals has garnered significant attention due to its non-intrusive nature and ubiquitous infrastructure. Despite the promise, the inherent bistatic deployment of wireless communication introduces clock asynchronism, which leads to unknown phase offsets in channel response and hinders fine-grained sensing. State-of-the-art systems widely adopt the cross-antenna channel response ratio to cancel these detrimental phase offsets. However, the channel response ratio preserves sensing feature accuracy only at integer-wavelength target displacements, losing sub-wavelength fidelity. To overcome this limitation, we derive the first quantitative mapping between the distorted ratio feature and the ideal-channel sensing feature. Building on this foundation, we develop a robust framework that leverages raw channel response amplitude to recover the ideal sensing feature from the distorted ratio. Real-world experiments across Wi-Fi and LoRa signals demonstrate that our method can effectively reconstruct sub-wavelength displacement details, achieving nearly an order-of-magnitude improvement in accuracy.

title: QUANTUM HEALTH INFRASTRUCTURE & MOLECULAR OBSERVATORY CIVILIZATION AT THE LIMIT Safety, Privacy, Equity, Nanomedicine, Wearables, Autonomous Care, Molecular Observatories, Longitudinal Health, and Life-Centered Governance
abstract: QUANTUM HEALTH INFRASTRUCTURE & MOLECULAR OBSERVATORY CIVILIZATION AT THE LIMITSafety, Privacy, Equity, Nanomedicine, Wearables, Autonomous Care, Molecular Observatories, Longitudinal Health, and Life-Centered Governance Feng Cheng-en (33) x Starli How much continuous molecular observability should a health civilization build, and when does measurement burden exceed health benefit? QUANTUM HEALTH INFRASTRUCTURE & MOLECULAR OBSERVATORY CIVILIZATION AT THE LIMIT is a large-scale research monograph exploring what happens when quantum-enabled measurement moves beyond isolated devices and becomes longitudinal health infrastructure. Its flagship Three-Coupling is: Longitudinal Insight x Human Rights x Life-Centered Utility The Quantum Health Civilization Index (QHCI) is introduced as a book-defined research heuristic linking longitudinal insight, rights integrity, health gain, and continuity/trust while explicitly accounting for privacy risk, overdiagnosis, and measurement overreach. QHCI is not a natural law, clinical score, diagnostic threshold, regulatory standard, or policy mandate. Across 82 chapters, the volume develops research architectures for exposure safety, nanomaterial fate, molecular privacy, high-dimensional consent, equitable access, nanomedicine, AI-interpreted health, wearables, portable sensing, home calibration, autonomous and remote care, cybersecurity, human override, molecular observatories, personal baselines, longitudinal molecular information, digital twins, missingness, overdiagnosis, incidental findings, intervention thresholds, watchful waiting, measurement restraint, data minimization, health infrastructure, standards, manufacturing readiness, interoperability, health economics, dual-use risk, environmental lifecycle, hype resistance, responsible communication, trust, intergenerational governance, failure science, and successor handoff. Every chapter begins with a Three-Coupling System, a named Core Relation, and an artistic geometric research model. The geometric research grammar includes the Longitudinal Molecular Observatory Helix, Health-Rights Corridor, Personal Molecular-State Manifold, Intervention Threshold Boundary Surface, Wearable-Home-Hospital Lattice, Autonomous Care Oversight Torus, Civilization Health Constellation, and Measurement-Burden Basin. The volume contains 200 Research Gates and 33 Answer Embryos. The Research Gates are designed as falsifiable entrances for safety studies, molecular-rights research, longitudinal validation, threshold experiments, wearable and autonomous-care stress tests, molecular-observatory infrastructure, standards work, governance, negative-result programs, measurement-restraint research, and successor reconstruction. The 33 Answer Embryos remain deliberately provisional. Each provides a working answer structure, evidence that could strengthen it, evidence that could weaken or falsify it, a design consequence, and a question for the next research hand. The central distinction is simple: More measurement does not automatically produce more health. A civilization capable of measuring nearly everything still needs a rigorous science of what not to measure, when not to alert, when not to intervene, how to preserve the right to refuse observation, and how to hand unresolved uncertainty to the next research generation. Better measurement becomes better life only when technical capability remains subordinate to health gain, dignity, access, trust, proportionality, and human agency.

title: Quick fabrication of 3D-printed prosthetic sockets with embedded sensors to track limb motion
abstract: Introduction A simple time-efficient method to fabricate prosthetic sockets with embedded sensors to track limb motion may facilitate the clinical application of continuously collected quantitative data in prosthetics practice. Methods A 3D-printed inner structure of the socket shape with debosses on the outside surface to hold sensors was fabricated, the sensors were affixed in place, and the socket was laminated and trimmed. Results The time to fabricate an embedded sensor socket was 12% less than that required to fabricate a traditional carbon-fiber socket with sensors. The investigational sockets increased in volume slightly, <0.2%, over the course of 4 weeks of take-home use, likely because of compression of the inner structure material during ambulation. Sockets with a vapor-smoothed finish had a significantly lower coefficient of friction (COF) with the liner fabric backing than sockets with a normal surface finish ( P < 0.01), though participant preference for the lower COF socket was mixed. Discussion The speed, quality, and durability of the investigational sockets warrant clinical studies to determine which quantitative limb motion metrics (e.g., pistoning, volume, anterior distal motion) help prosthetists meaningfully enhance their patient care.
authors: Joan E. Sanders; Amy P. Culter; Mathew J. Weissinger; Paul Fallon; Joseph C. Mertens; Katheryn J. Allyn; Benjamin N. Sanders; Joseph L. Garbini

title: REVIEW ON COMPREHENSIVE SMART EYE RELIEF SYSTEM USING HEAT & VIBRATION
abstract: The project "Comprehensive Smart Eye Relief System using Heat& Vibration" was a wearable device designed to reduce Digital Eye Strain (DES) caused by prolonged use of smartphones, laptops, and computers. The system used controlled heat and mild vibrations to relax eye muscles and improve blood flow. The device was built using an Arduino Nano or ESP32 microcontroller, a heating pad, and a vibration motor inside a soft eye mask. A 10k NTC temperature sensor maintained the temperature between, and an automatic shut-off timer turned the device off after 10 to 15 minutes for safety. The system was powered by a rechargeable 18650 Li-ion battery and charging module, making it portable and energy-efficient. Overall, it demonstrated a low-cost and effective wearable healthcare solution for eye relaxation and stress reduction.

title: RailGuard: Vision-Based Railway Track Inspection and Fault Detection Using a Pole-Mounted Camera
abstract: Railway tracks require frequent and reliable inspection because geometric irregularities, rail-surface defects, fastener failures, ballast deterioration, and objects on or near the track can affect safety, ride quality, and maintenance planning. Conventional manual patrols and specialized track-recording vehicles provide valuable measurements, but they can be labour-intensive, costly, and difficult to scale for frequent monitoring. This paper reviews contactless railway monitoring approaches based on computer vision, LiDAR, GNSS/RTK, inertial sensing, machine learning, ground-penetrating radar (GPR), and InSAR, and uses the findings to motivate an indigenous Integrated Track Monitoring System (ITMS). The proposed direction combines stereo or line-scan cameras, LiDAR, GNSS/RTK, IMU, an encoder, onboard edge computing, SSD storage, and real-time alerts. A practical system should not only detect a defect but also estimate its severity, associate it with a reliable track position, retain evidence, and communicate an actionable maintenance alert. The review highlights calibration, weather and lighting variation, vibration, limited labelled data, computing constraints, and the integration of detection with localization as key engineering challenges.

title: Real-Time Fall Detection in Indoor Environments Using FMCW Radar and Lightweight Ensemble CNN on Edge Devices
abstract: Falls are a leading cause of injury and mortality among the elderly, particularly indoors where privacy concerns limit real-time monitoring. This study developed a privacy-preserving, real-time fall detection system using a frequency-modulated continuous wave radar sensor and a lightweight convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture deployed on an edge device. To address the limitations of wearable and vision-based methods, the system leverages contactless radar sensing and an ensemble of two independent CNN models, namely, a base model designed to capture the entire fall sequence for high recall and a sub-model aimed at pinpointing the fall moment with high precision. The final decision is executed through a voting mechanism that triggers a fall alert only when both models agree, significantly reducing false positives. On 14 recording sessions withheld from the training of both models, the ensemble detected 13 of 14 falls (recall 92.9%, 95% CI 68.5-98.7%) without false alarms, and in a 24-trial on-device test comprising 4 falls and 20 non-fall activities it detected every fall with no false alarm. Running on a low-power microcontroller, the system indicates the feasibility of privacy-preserving on-device fall detection, while validation with older adults and in real living environments remains necessary.
authors: Ju-Hong Oh; Young-Joon Park; Seon-In Kim; Ji-Hyeoung Kim; Jin-Yong Lee; Yogesh Shankar; Eui-Jong Kim

title: Real-World Marijuana Use Is Associated With Altered Nocturnal Cardiac Autonomic Function, Reduced Sleep Quality, and Declining Consumption During Wearable Monitoring
abstract: ABSTRACT Background Marijuana is among the most widely used controlled substances, with use rising as risk perception declines. Despite growing acceptance, concerns remain regarding its effects on cardiovascular and autonomic physiology, sleep, and risk of cannabis use disorder. Although laboratory and epidemiological studies have characterized these associations, objective evidence from real-world settings is limited. Methods We studied cardiac autonomic function, sleep, and marijuana use patterns in 16,965 consumer-wearable device users, contributing a total of 5,226,739 person-days of data with or without self-reported use of marijuana. Linear mixed models related day-level use to nocturnal cardiac autonomic function (resting heart rate [RHR], heart rate variability [HRV]) and sleep (duration, fragmentation, architecture) at the within- and between-person levels. Binomial mixed models were used to estimate use probability across 72 weeks of marijuana tracking. Results Members reported marijuana use on a median of 25.1% of logged days (IQR, 7.1–62.6%). Within individuals, use was associated with lower RHR (−0.12bpm; 99.5% CI: [−0.14, −0.10]) and lower HRV (−0.47ms [−0.53, −0.42]). Sleep was longer (+7.60min [7.37, 7.83]) but more fragmented, with more disturbances (+0.47 [0.45, 0.48]), greater wake time (+1.79min [1.70, 1.89]), and altered wearable-estimated sleep architecture. Daily use probability declined over 72 weeks (−11.1% [−11.5, −10.8]). Conclusions Marijuana use was associated with altered nocturnal cardiac autonomic physiology and longer but more disrupted sleep. Marijuana use declined after commencing tracking, raising the possibility that longitudinal self-monitoring may influence use. These findings extend laboratory evidence on marijuana use to real-world settings and demonstrate the potential of consumer wearables for studying substance use and its physiological correlates at scale. Highlights Marijuana-use nights were associated with lower resting heart rate and heart rate variability. Sleep was prolonged but more fragmented with marijuana use. Marijuana use fell over 72 weeks of wearable tracking.
authors: Dylan J. Curran; William von Hippel; Finnbarr Fielding; Summer R. Jasinski; Josh Leota; Jenna G. Cohen; Kristen Erika Holmes; Gregory J. Grosicki; Christian P. Cheung

title: Real-time Detection of Psychological Fatigue in Middle-Aged and Elderly Individuals During Physical Exercise Using Wearable Devices
abstract: As the global aging population continues to accelerate, exercise-related health management for older adults has emerged as one of the key research priorities in the field of public health. Psychological fatigue incurred during physical exercise is a critical factor contributing to the interruption of exercise activity among older adults, an increased risk of exercise-related injuries, and the development of exercise-related burnout; however, conventional subjective assessment methods and offline monitoring approaches are often inadequate for the continuous and real-time detection of psychological fatigue states. This study develops a real-time detection system for exercise-related psychological fatigue in middle-aged and elderly individuals, leveraging multimodal wearable devices and deep learning technologies. This system collects physiological signals-such as heart rate variability, three-axis acceleration, and skin conductance response-during physical exercise in elderly individuals. Following data preprocessing and feature extraction, it constructs a multimodal deep learning model combining temporal features, namely a CNN-LSTM architecture, to enable quantitative assessment and real-time prediction of psychological fatigue status. Experimental results demonstrate that this model achieves a prediction accuracy of 82.3% for psychological fatigue in middle-aged and elderly individuals, with a root mean square error (RMSE) of 1.25 and a Pearson correlation coefficient (r) of 0.81, significantly outperforming traditional single-feature linear regression models. This system provides an objective technological solution for intelligent and personalized monitoring of exercise-related health in middle-aged and elderly populations, while also offering data support for the development of exercise intervention strategies within the field of smart healthcare.
authors: Jinyu Wang; Bing Lin
venue: Insights in computer, signals and systems.

title: Recent advances and challenges in electronic nose technology for agricultural commodities and food quality assessment
abstract: Traditional methods for analyzing agricultural produce and food quality, such as chromatography and sensory evaluation, are often expensive, time consuming, and require skilled professionals, making them hard to implement for rapid and large-scale testing. The advent of Electronic nose (E-Nose) technology presents a promising alternative by emulating the human olfactory system through sensor arrays that identify volatile compounds and produce distinctive response patterns. This review examines the principles, evolution, and applications of E-nose systems for assessing the quality of food and agricultural products across diverse categories, including fish, meat, dairy products, tea, coffee, and edible oils. These systems provide non-destructive and smart analytical solutions for modern food-processing industries. Their role in identifying contamination, freshness assessment, authenticity, and monitoring fermentation plays a crucial role in modern food processing. Recent advancements integrating artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) methodologies have significantly enhanced the efficacy of E-nose systems, enabling superior pattern recognition, data interpretation, and precise prediction capabilities. This enables objective and accurate quality assessment. Despite these advantages, the widespread adoption of this technology is hindered due to sensor drift, low sensitivity, high initial costs, and the difficulty of processing such complex data. Future research should focus on enhancing sensor stability, formulating resilient data analytics models, and decreasing system costs to facilitate scalability. Overall, E-nose technology has potential to transform food-quality assessment by providing the food industry with rapid, non-destructive, and intelligent analytical methods.
authors: R V Maneysha; Vakalapudi Sanjani; Kirthika Suresh

title: Recent progress of biomaterials-based hydrogels for wearable electronics and health monitoring
abstract: Soft bioelectronics integrated with biological tissues are reshaping the landscape of personalized medicine, health diagnostics, and human-machine interfaces, yet they are frequently bottlenecked by the mechanical and biocompatibility discrepancies of conventional rigid hardware. Biomaterials-based hydrogels, defined as hydrogel systems constructed from natural polysaccharide or protein macromolecules, featuring extracellular matrix-like compliance, well-documented biocompatibility in numerous prior biomaterial studies and abundant functional groups, have emerged as promising interfacial materials to bridge this mechanical and biological mismatch. This review comprehensively surveys the state-of-the-art developments in polysaccharide-based (alginate, chitosan, and cellulose) and protein-based (collagen, silk fibroin, and bovine serum albumin) hydrogel platforms. It also analyzes their internal structures, crosslinking network topologies, and approaches to mechanical property regulation. Additionally, the deployment of these engineered hydrogels in capturing high-purity electrophysiological signals (e.g., electroencephalograms (EEG), electrocardiograms (ECG), and electromyograms (EMG)), as well as conducting respiratory monitoring and motion monitoring, is systematically evaluated. This review highlights critical structure-property trade-offs: reconciling mechanical softness, conductivity, biocompatibility and environmental stability remains a major unsolved bottleneck. In closing, the review concludes major contemporary challenges and future research routes for robust long-term wearable and implantable bioelectronics, to motivate original material designs of advanced soft biointerfaces for both wearable epidermal and implantable bioelectronic scenarios.
authors: Danyang Ren; Jieyun Ma; Zhenpeng Han; Yawen Lei; Yiming Liu; Yan Zhu; Yanchao Mao

title: Recommendations for the development, implementation, and evaluation of technology-assisted physical activity interventions to support healthy aging: insights from PhysAgeNet
abstract: Digital health technologies offer substantial potential to support physical activity among older adults, yet their development and implementation often remain driven by technological possibilities rather than clinical evidence and user needs. This position paper, developed within the PhysAgeNet COST Action, synthesizes current evidence and expert consensus to provide recommendations for designing, evaluating, and implementing technology-assisted physical activity interventions for older adults. We first outline key technology categories and functions relevant to physical activity promotion, including wearables, exergames, mobile applications, telehealth platforms, and smart environments, and highlight critical technical requirements such as accuracy, reliability, connectivity, interoperability, and data security. We then emphasize the need to align digital interventions with established clinical guidelines for physical activity, falls prevention, frailty, and sarcopenia, including explicit specification of exercise dose according to FITT-VP principles and robust monitoring of dual adherence to both physical activity and technology use. Building on technology acceptance models and behavior change theories, we describe how user-centered and co-creative design processes can translate theoretical constructs into concrete digital features that enhance motivation, enjoyment, and long-term engagement. Finally, we propose stakeholder-specific guidance for developers, researchers, and clinicians, including recommendations on user assessment, recruitment of vulnerable groups, implementation frameworks, and clinically grounded evaluation of outcomes and usability. Together, these recommendations provide a pragmatic roadmap for moving from a technology-push paradigm toward evidence-based, acceptable, and equitable technology-assisted physical activity interventions that can be sustainably integrated into routine practice for older adults.
authors: Nadja Schott; Jana Pelclová; Eleftheria Giannouli; Antoine Langeard; Christopher L. McCrum; Rosemary Dubbeldam; Rafael A. Bernardes; Arben Boshnjaku; David Beckwée

title: Reduced-parameter damage detection in cantilever beams using magnetoelastically measured bending frequencies
abstract: This study presents an approximately material-invariant framework for vibration-based damage detection in cracked cantilever beams using normalized modal frequencies and magnetoelastic vibration sensing. A finite element formulation combined with fracture mechanics theory was developed to model stiffness degradation caused by transverse cracks and implemented in MATLAB to evaluate the first eight bending modes under varying crack locations, crack depths, and material properties. The influence of Young’s modulus, mass density, and Poisson’s ratio on both the natural frequencies (NFs) and normalized frequency ratios (NFRs) was systematically investigated. The results demonstrate that the absolute natural frequencies are strongly governed by stiffness and inertia effects, whereas the normalization procedure substantially suppresses the dominant dependence on Young’s modulus and mass density, yielding NFRs that remain nearly invariant across different engineering materials. In contrast, Poisson’s ratio retains a weaker but systematic influence on the normalized response. Experimental validation was performed using Al 6063, Al 7075, and AISI 1018 cantilever beams instrumented with magnetoelastic sensors for contactless signal detection of modal frequencies. Excellent agreement was obtained between the numerical and experimental results, with deviations below approximately 1.5% for the natural frequencies and below 0.5% for the averaged NFRs. The findings confirm that the proposed normalization framework preserves sensitivity to structural damage while significantly reducing material-dependent scaling effects. In addition, the study demonstrates the effectiveness of magnetoelastic sensing as a contactless signal detection technique for vibration-based structural health monitoring applications.
authors: Georgios Samourgkanidis

title: Renegotiating autonomy and safety: disentangling tensions emerging for older adults living with smart monitoring systems
abstract: Smart monitoring systems (SMS) are increasingly deployed in community-based care to empower older adults to live safely and independently. However, existing research largely treats monitoring as a process in which continuous data collection and real-time alerts are intended to translate into improved outcomes. What remains underexplored is how older adults experience monitoring and how it shapes their behavior over time. In this qualitative longitudinal study, 21 older adults are accompanied from SMS installation for more than one year, with individual semi-structured interviews conducted across four data collection phases. Findings reveal that older adults actively anticipate how the system interprets their behavior, producing three responses: reactance, that is, disengaging from devices to reclaim autonomy over safety; preemptive behavior, for instance, restructuring daily routines to avoid triggering alerts constraining their autonomy and safety; and performative compliance, that is, managing behavior to satisfy caregivers rather than personal needs, leading to a loss of autonomy. These constitute autonomy-safety value tensions: a technology designed to advance both values instead produces conditions under which protecting one systematically undermines the other. To this end, this study provides empirical insights into unintended consequences and a conceptual model explaining how value tensions emerge, with implications for practitioners and caregivers.
authors: Laura Madeleine Detels; Mingsong Zhai; Zhao Cai; Manuel Trenz

title: Required components of a sleep-wake online daily diary for accurate and efficient human research
abstract: Accurate documentation of sleep timing (enabling calculation of duration and variability) is imperative for research, health, and safety recommendations. Methods in real-world settings include one-time self-report, diaries, and wearables that vary by ease, expense, and accuracy. Here we highlight how programmable online daily diaries compare to gold-standard polysomnography for measuring sleep timing, should be preferred over one-time self-report, and complement wearables for longitudinal clinical and research studies and real-world applications.
authors: Andrew W. McHill; Melissa A. St. Hilaire; Akane Sano; Jason P. Sullivan; Salim Qadri; Taylor Sara; Laura K. Barger; Andrew J. K. Phillips; Erin E. Flynn‐Evans; Conor O’Brien; Steven W. Lockley; Charles Andrew Czeisler; Elizabeth B. Klerman

title: Research Progress and Development Trends in Smart Hospital Operations Management under Digital Transformation
abstract: Digital transformation is changing hospital management from fragmented information processing toward integrated, data-driven, and increasingly intelligent operations. Smart hospitals combine electronic health records (EHRs), interoperable data platforms, artificial intelligence (AI), the Internet of Medical Things (IoMT), cloud computing, automation, real-time dashboards, and emerging digital twin technologies to support clinical services and organizational management. This narrative review synthesizes recent research on the progress, management value, implementation barriers, and development trends of smart hospital operations. Current applications are concentrated in patient flow and bed management, operating-room scheduling, workforce and equipment allocation, medication and supply-chain management, quality and safety monitoring, and administrative automation. Evidence suggests that digital technologies can improve information visibility, forecasting, coordination, and process standardization; however, technology deployment alone does not guarantee better outcomes. Benefits depend heavily on interoperability, data quality, workflow redesign, organizational leadership, user acceptance, cybersecurity, governance, and continuous performance evaluation. In particular, poorly designed EHR workflows may increase documentation burden, while AI systems introduce risks related to bias, transparency, accountability, and lifecycle monitoring. Future smart hospitals are likely to evolve toward integrated command platforms, multimodal AI, ambient intelligence, predictive and prescriptive analytics, and digital twins capable of simulating operational scenarios before real-world implementation. From a medical management perspective, the central task is therefore to shift from technology-centered construction to value-oriented digital governance. Hospitals should align digital investment with measurable operational objectives, establish multidisciplinary governance mechanisms, and evaluate efficiency, quality, safety, workforce experience, equity, and return on investment simultaneously.
authors: Zhijuan Geng; Xiaotian Hu; Haiying Bao; Xiaokang Yao

title: Research on Smart Helmet for Coal Miners with Locking System
abstract: The Smart Helmet for Coal Miners with Locking System represents a practical and effective approach to improving worker safety in underground mining environments. The system combines helmet-lock detection, hazardous gas monitoring, automatic work-time recording, and real-time communication into a single wearable device, making it more than just a conventional safety helmet. The paper contributes to creating a safer and more organized working environment while encouraging better compliance with workplace safety practices. The proposed smart helmet demonstrates how affordable IoT technology can be integrated with personal protective equipment to improve workplace safety, reduce operational risks, and support better monitoring in hazardous environments. It offers a reliable foundation for smarter mining practices and highlights the importance of combining technology with safety to protect workers in challenging underground conditions.
authors: Parth Mehare; Sagar Nikode; Vedant Dange; Yogesh Yadav

title: Role of Chatbots and Virtual Assistants in the Management of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
abstract: The rising prevalence of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM) calls for new digital tools and chatbots and virtual assistants are emerging as important enablers of patient care. In this article, we review their core technologies, including rule-based designs and advanced AI models using natural language processing, machine learning, and dialogue systems, and their roles in T2DM support, such as education, medication compliance, blood glucose tracking with tailored insights, dietary and physical activity changes, and connections with wearable devices and electronic health records. Clinical data from meta-analyses, randomised trials and implementation studies show significant impacts, including HbA1c reductions of 0.5–1.2%, increased patient engagement, and economic benefits. But there are still challenges, including technological limitations (such as accuracy issues), privacy concerns, moral questions (such as bias and access inequality), and issues with broad adoption by diverse groups. Future directions include next-generation AI with multi-sensory capabilities, harmonised regulations, and embedding into pharmacy-led clinical workflows to enable inclusive and effective T2DM management.
authors: Manish Kumar; Pranav Bhati; Ritu Mishra; Rajiv Yadav; Sushma Chaturvedi

title: Role of artificial intelligence in the diagnosis of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis via biomarkers, neuroimaging, and wearable health technologies: a narrative review
abstract: Abstract Background Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterised by upper and lower motor neuron loss. Diagnosis is frequently delayed because of phenotypic heterogeneity, overlap with ALS mimics, and the absence of a single definitive biomarker. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers complementary analytical tools across neuroimaging, biomarker panels, clinical records, and wearable sensor streams. Objective To synthesise the evidence on AI applications for ALS diagnosis, prognosis, and longitudinal monitoring, and to critically appraise the methodological quality, generalisability, and translational readiness of this literature. Methods We conducted a narrative review based on a PRISMA 2020-guided search of PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, and Google Scholar for studies published between January 2012 and March 2026. Eligible studies applied any AI method (machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, multimodal fusion) to ALS diagnosis, progression prediction, or biomarker discovery, and reported at least one quantitative performance metric. No minimum accuracy threshold was imposed. After de-duplication, title/abstract screening, and full-text review, 103 studies informed the narrative synthesis. Risk of bias in studies contributing quantitative performance estimates was appraised with an adapted QUADAS-2 framework covering patient selection, index test, reference standard, and flow/timing. Findings Across modalities, AI models reported a wide performance range — from modest discrimination in small single-centre imaging studies to reproducible accuracy in a prospectively validated blood-based miRNA classifier (area under the curve [AUC] 98.3% in discovery, > 98% across external validation cohorts). Multimodal fusion consistently outperformed unimodal approaches, but most studies relied on small convenience samples, lacked prospective external validation, and did not report calibration, subgroup performance, or fairness metrics. Risk of bias was judged high or unclear in patient selection and flow/timing domains for the majority of included studies. Conclusions AI-enabled approaches show promise for earlier and more objective ALS detection, but the current literature is dominated by small, retrospective, single-site studies. Translation into clinical practice will require prospective multicentre external validation, transparent reporting under TRIPOD + AI and CONSORT-AI, regulatory-grade explainability, and equitable deployment across diverse populations.
authors: Dhinesh Selvaraju; Kishore Durairaj; Krishna Ravi

title: SAGE: Efficient Protected Vision-Language Inference on Smart Glasses
abstract: Smart glasses are a promising platform for vision-language assistants, but private split inference remains expensive: protecting visual representations before transmission does not remove the cost of on-device vision encoding, wide protected tokens, or hardware-unaware execution. We present SAGE (Smart-glasses-Aware Guarded Encoding), a hardware-aware framework for efficient protected VLM inference on smart glasses. SAGE keeps raw images and unprotected visual tokens on the trusted device, reduces visual input cost, executes shape-specialized INT8 graphs, and compresses protected representations into compact 256-dimensional INT8 packets before transmission. Unlike efficiency methods optimized only for nominal model size, SAGE selects its operating point using downstream answer quality together with measured latency, memory, and thermal behavior on real Mentra Live glasses. On a matched Qwen workload, SAGE reduces glasses inference latency by 39.18%, device-sensor temperature rise by 21.91%, and protected packet size by 96.56%, while retaining 85.62% of the protected reference's relaxed utility and comparable prompted containment. Direct glasses-to-phone tests deliver all 192 packets and reduce median packet-plus-acknowledgment time from 71.3 to 10.0 ms. The compact protected interface also transfers across four additional VLM families. These results show that private wearable VLM inference must be optimized jointly across representation protection, communication, and real-device execution rather than through model compression alone.
authors: Zhimin Li; Pan Wang; Jingxian Chen; Yuantao Tang; Qian Lou; Jingtong Hu

title: Safe Learning of Adaptive Control Policies for Remote Patient Monitoring
abstract: Remote Patient Monitoring (RPM) enables continuous observation of patients in their daily environments, improving both health outcomes and quality of life. A key challenge in RPM is determining the optimal monitoring intensity, while balancing patient safety and monitoring costs. This problem is further complicated when system parameters, such as transition probabilities and costs, are initially unknown. We develop a learning-based control framework that estimates these parameters and adapts the monitoring policy in real time. The proposed approach is an online model-based reinforcement learning algorithm tailored to RPM, with patient safety explicitly prioritized during exploration. We provide theoretical guarantees on safety and convergence to the optimal policy. Simulation results show that the algorithm converges to the optimal threshold-based policy, maintains low treatment costs, and reduces the risk of patients reaching critical health states.
authors: Ramanan Tamizholi; Siddharth Chandak; Isha Thapa; Nicholas Bambos; David Scheinker

title: Safe-Motion: An AI-Based Wearable for Enhancing Women’s Safety through Stress Detection
abstract: In densely populated cities such as Bogotá, harassment in public transportation represents a persistent threat to women, highlighting the urgent need for innovative technological solutions to improve safety. Safe-Motion is a technological initiative focused on the development of an AI-based wearable device designed to explore the detection of physiological signals associated with anxiety in potentially unsafe situations. The proposed system integrates biometric signals such as electrodermal activity (EDA), heart rate, and temperature, using machine learning techniques to classify stress-related states. The methodology is based on the use of the WESAD dataset, including signal preprocessing, feature extraction, and supervised classification. A Random Forest model is proposed as the main approach due to its robustness for this type of data, along with a comparison with other classical machine learning methods. Additionally, a preliminary hardware architecture based on low-power and cost-effective components is proposed, enabling physiological signal acquisition and the development of a wearable prototype. Expected results include the development of a functional prototype and an initial evaluation of the classification model. These results aim to assess the feasibility of this type of system for improving women’s safety in public transportation.
authors: Gerhaldine Alejandra Suárez Bernal; Paula Nicole Quiroga Romero; Indaliria Valentina Cardona Corredor; Juliana Gongora Rasmussen; Alina Idaly Ortiz Martínez; Maribel Anaya

title: Scentronic: An artificial intelligence–assisted olfactory interface for remote odor sharing and transmission
abstract: Recent years have witnessed the surge of human-machine interfaces (HMIs) for various applications. Olfaction is a fundamental chemical sense crucial to perception, memory, and emotion. Current limitations arise from the difficulty of accurately capturing, transmitting, and reproducing odor signals, and the lack of standardized, network-enabled platforms. This work presents an internet of things (IoT)-enabled olfactory interface for remote odor sensing and stimulation. The system integrates an artificial intelligence-assisted odor sensing platform with a wearable piezoelectric olfactory actuation system. We demonstrate the design, characterization, and application of this framework, which integrates devices, circuit architecture, and software algorithms. Applications in medical contexts include psychophysical testing to study olfactory pathways and evaluate sensory loss. We further showcase multisensory stimulation through integrated olfactory and gustatory interfaces for enhanced immersion. This study establishes a scalable framework for IoT-based olfactory interaction, advancing HMIs toward a future that includes the long-overlooked chemical senses.

title: Self-swab enhanced respiratory pathogen surveillance – A scoping review
abstract: Background Self-swab enhanced surveillance of respiratory pathogens is an emerging public health tool that could expand the reach of existing surveillance, providing real-time monitoring of circulating pathogens in the community. Methods We conducted a literature search using terms covering self-swabbing, respiratory infection, and surveillance. For inclusion, publications had to describe a study on the use of serial unsupervised self-swabbing for the purpose of tracking the frequency of respiratory infections in the general population. Results We found 42 publications originating from 27 unique studies on self-swab enhanced surveillance for respiratory infection. Twenty-six studies (96%) were conducted in a high-income setting. Eleven studies (41%) included children under the age of 12 years. Most studies involved a central laboratory conducting polymerase chain reaction testing on returned self-swabs which permitted testing for a wide range of pathogens. Among studies reporting the number of invitees, <20% of invited individuals typically agreed to join. In studies requiring regular symptom reporting, adherence was commonly >75%. Adherence rates for self-swab return were more variable (between 42-96%). Eight studies (30%) explored rapid antigen testing which appears to reduce the time taken between symptom onset and test result notification but limits the number of pathogens that can be evaluated compared with polymerase chain reaction testing. Based on our findings we present a list of suggestions to guide future implementation and investigation. Conclusions Further work is needed to characterise self-swab enhanced surveillance approaches that optimise community participation and protocol adherence, generate as close to real-time data as possible, and minimise costs.
authors: David Charles Boettiger; Camille Esneau; Joshua Saul Davis

title: Semiconductor Technologies for Predictive, Preventive, and Personalized Healthcare
abstract: Purpose: This narrative review investigated how semiconductor technologies contribute to predictive, preventive, and personalized healthcare and considered their clinical value, technological maturity, and implementation challenges. Methods: A structured narrative-review search of literature published from January 2015 through August 2026 was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, and ScienceDirect. Eligible publications had to describe a semiconductor-based technology with a clear or potential healthcare application related to prediction, prevention, personalization, diagnosis, monitoring, or therapeutic decision-making. Forty-seven publications met the eligibility criteria and were critically appraised and synthesized thematically. Results: The evidence set included 47 publications published from 2016 to 2026. Major technology categories included wearable and flexible physiological sensors, biosensors and lab-on-chip systems, implantable devices, complementary metal oxide semiconductors and application-specific integrated-circuit platforms, edge processing hardware, and semiconductor imaging detectors. Across the evidence, semiconductor platforms supported continuous physiological monitoring, rapid biochemical and molecular detection, early risk identification, individualized treatment management, and local processing of health data. Signal instability, calibration drift, limited external validation, power constraints, biocompatibility, interoperability, cybersecurity, affordability, algorithmic bias, and unequal access remained important barriers. Conclusion: Semiconductor technologies can strengthen predictive, preventive, and personalized healthcare, but technical performance alone is insufficient. Near-term translation is strongest for established sensing, imaging, and implantable platforms linked to defined care pathways, whereas flexible biochemical sensors and in-sensor computing platforms require stronger clinical validation. Wider adoption requires representative validation, long-term safety evidence, interoperable systems, equitable design, clear regulation, sustainable lifecycle planning, and demonstrated improvements in patient outcomes.
authors: Jasmin Akter Toma; Samia Mahmuda; Moustaq Karim Khan Rony; Ashok Ghimire; S M Mainul Islam; Lamiya Rahman Mim; Md Abu Bakkar Siddique; Al Modabbir Zaman; Jakir Hossain Ridoy; Timotei István Erdei

title: Sensitive detection of chloroplast movements through changes in leaf cross-polarized reflectance
abstract: Abstract We show that the positioning of chloroplasts in plant cells affects the ability of photosynthetic organs to depolarize linearly polarized light through diffuse reflection. We apply this phenomenon for the detection of blue-light-induced chloroplast movements using light reflected from leaves and green stems. High-light-induced chloroplast avoidance leads to an increase in reflectance, while chloroplast accumulation in low light has the opposite effect. The changes in reflectance are correlated with an increase in the leaf’s ability to depolarize linearly polarized light. Inclusion of polarization information in the detection procedure allows for the mitigation of the effects of sample orientation and for an increase in the specificity of detection. We have employed this approach to examine chloroplast movements in the model plant Arabidopsis thaliana and 4 flowering plant species collected in the field. Despite the importance of chloroplast movements for the optimization of photosynthetic efficiency and biomass production, high-throughput reflectance-based methods are not routinely employed. Our approach opens the possibility of noninvasive, noncontact detection of chloroplast movements in a manner insensitive to the orientation of the leaf.
authors: Paweł Hermanowicz; Aleksandra Giza; Katarzyna Sowa; Paweł Korecki; Justyna Łabuz

title: SensorW: Open-Source Wear Operating System Platform for Continuous Global Positioning System and Multimodal Sensor Data Collection in Real-World Settings
abstract: Digital phenotyping requires continuous, real-world collection of multimodal behavioral and physiological data. Although several smartphone-based sensing frameworks have been developed and used, open-source platforms for long-term smartwatch sensor data acquisition remain limited. To bridge this gap, SensorW was developed, an open-source Wear operating system (OS)-based framework for direct lifelog data collection from smartwatches without requiring a paired smartphone or manufacturer cloud service. SensorW includes a front-end Wear OS application for sensor data collection and a back-end server for application initiation, secure data submission, and storage. The front-end application uses battery-management strategies, such as hybrid Global Positioning System sampling and wake-lock management, to continuously collect multimodal sensor outputs, including location data, physical activity-related metrics, barometric pressure, and device wear status, and submit data to the back-end server. A preliminary technical evaluation of SensorW was conducted with seven participants who wore SensorW-enabled devices continuously for at least seven consecutive days. The technical evaluation demonstrated multimodal data collection during 17-42 days of monitoring, with operational data availability ranging from 0.73 to 1.00 across participants. These findings support the technical feasibility of SensorW as a practical and extensible platform for continuous digital phenotyping using consumer-grade smartwatches.
authors: Yichi Yang; Kazushige Ihara; Felipe Alfonso Sandoval Garrido; Koki Hirata; Tao Jiang; Hua Lan; Han Wu; Hongyue Yu; Yoshinori Tamada; Koichi Murashita; Ken Itoh; Kazutaka Yoshida

title: Seroprevalence, Risk Factors, and Farmer’s Knowledge and Practices on Contagious Bovine Pleuropneumonia in Morogoro Rural District, Tanzania
abstract: Background: Contagious Bovine Pleuropneumonia (CBPP), a highly contagious disease of cattle, is a major constraint to cattle production in Tanzania. Purpose: This study aimed to determine the seroprevalence of CBPP, identify animal and herd level risk factors of the disease, and assess the knowledge and practices (KP) of cattle farmers regarding CBPP. Method: Data were collected from August to November 2025 through a cross sectional study involving three cattle production systems; pastoral, agropastoral, and ranching. Overall, 409 cattle with no history of vaccination against CBPP were randomly selected, and blood samples were collected for the cELISA test. Results: Most respondents practiced pastoralism (61.8%), followed by agro pastoralism (35.9%) and ranching (2.3 %). Majority reared indigenous cattle (71.0%), with cattle herd sizes ranging from fewer than 100 to over 200 animals. Risk related management practices were common among the respondents, with all reporting the use of communal grazing and watering points, followed by seasonal movement of cattle beyond village boundaries for grazing (64.9%) and herd mixing (61.8%). Overall animal and herd level seroprevalence of CBPP were 3.4% and 16.1%, respectively. Seroprevalence was higher among young cattle (3.8%) than adults (3.1%), females (4.0%) than males (1.2%), and crossbred cattle (5.5%) compared with indigenous breeds (2.7%). Moreover, cattle reared under the ranching production system exhibited the highest seroprevalence (4.6%), followed by agro pastoral (1.8%) and pastoral (1.7%) systems. Conclusion: This study detected CBPP exposure across pastoral, agro pastoral, and ranching cattle systems, with the highest seroprevalence in ranching cattle at Morogoro Rural District.
authors: Mark Joseph Mark; Julius John Medardus; Isaac Pastory Kashoma
venue: Journal of Applied Veterinary Science And Technology

title: Shifting the paradigm: from reactive to proactive and precision rehabilitation across the lifespan in pediatric neuromuscular disorders
abstract: Advances in molecular diagnostics, newborn screening, and disease-modifying therapies have transformed the natural history of pediatric neuromuscular disorders, creating an urgent need to redefine rehabilitation. Traditional reactive models, focused on managing established disability and its complications, are increasingly inadequate given earlier diagnosis, improved survival, and opportunities to preserve developmental potential, optimize functioning, and enhance participation. This narrative review proposes a conceptual framework for proactive rehabilitation in pediatric neuromuscular disorders. Grounded in the biopsychosocial perspective of the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF), proactive rehabilitation is defined as a preventive, anticipatory, person-centered, and adaptive approach. Core elements include early identification, dynamic risk stratification, habilitation and rehabilitation across developmental stages, prevention of secondary complications, optimization of functioning, promotion of physical activity and participation, integration with disease-modifying therapies, digital health technologies, and family-centered life-course care. Rather than responding to established disability, this model emphasizes functional surveillance and interventions aimed at preserving developmental trajectories, maximizing participation, and improving quality of life. Proactive rehabilitation should be regarded not simply as earlier rehabilitation, but as a comprehensive model of care that adapts interventions to the individual’s developmental stage, clinical trajectory, environmental context, and personal goals. The framework organizes established and emerging rehabilitation practices around anticipated risk, longitudinal functional trajectories, timely adaptation of interventions, providing a bridge from disease-specific Standard of Care to precision rehabilitation, across the life course.
authors: Antonio Trabacca; Maria Carmela Oliva; Camilla Ferrante; Giuseppe Accogli

title: Should I “stay” or should I “go”? Influence of an anticipated stop on cortical correlates of overground walking
abstract: Real-world walking frequently requires pedestrians to maintain proactive inhibition to safely navigate unpredictable environments. While cortical modulations occurring during locomotion under environmental uncertainty are well-established, the specific proactive mechanisms underlying this state of inhibitory anticipation remain unexplored. This study aimed to investigate the behavioral and cortical shifts associated with anticipating a stop during overground walking. Fourteen healthy young adults performed fluent and cautious walking tasks with an expected stop. Cortical activity and trunk acceleration were recorded using a 32-channel mobile electroencephalography and an integrated accelerometer. Step-1 latency and step-interval variability were calculated via heel strike detection. Gait-phase-related power modulations were computed, and spectral principal component analysis was applied to attenuate artifacts. The results revealed that cautious walking significantly increased step-interval variability, whereas step-1 latency remained unaffected. At the cortical level, left frontotemporal areas exhibited an attenuated and delayed theta desynchronization during the swing phase. Furthermore, centroparietal regions demonstrated an altered temporal profile of alpha and beta synchronization, characterized by enhanced late-stance synchronization and reduced swing-phase synchronization. The present findings suggest that anticipating a potential stop may alter the rhythmic consistency of gait and reorganize phase-specific cortical dynamics. Being prepared to stop may shift the neural control of automated locomotion toward active monitoring, highlighting the relevance of proactive inhibition during everyday mobility.
authors: Daghan Piskin; Saskia Kurtzhals; Jochen Baumeister

title: Sistem Pemantauan Aktivitas Manusia Menggunakan Sensor Human Presence Radar HLK-LD2410C Dan ESP32
abstract: Pemantauan aktivitas manusia di dalam ruangan penting untuk keamanan dan otomasi Internet of Things (IoT). Namun, sensor Passive Infrared (PIR) dan kamera terbentur kendala deteksi minim pergerakan serta masalah privasi. Penelitian ini mengimplementasikan Human Presence Radar HLK-LD2410C berbasis mmWave 24 GHz dan ESP32 untuk mengklasifikasikan aktivitas secara real-time. Parameter Presence, Distance, P_Energy, dan M_Energy dari komunikasi UART diklasifikasikan menggunakan thresholding ke dalam kategori No Presence, Static, Light Movement, dan Heavy Movement. Pengujian menunjukkan deteksi Static mencapai jarak 5,2 m, Light Movement 5,3 m, dan Heavy Movement 3,8 m. Evaluasi confusion matrix menghasilkan accuracy 97,50%, precision 97,73%, recall 97,50%, dan F1-score 97,49%. Nilai M_Energy dipengaruhi jarak serta intensitas gerakan, sementara kondisi multi-object merepresentasikan aktivitas dominan. Sistem ini terbukti menjadi solusi pemantauan aktivitas manusia secara non-contact, responsif, dan menjaga privasi pengguna.
authors: Mikha Viyo Nugroho; Gogor Christmass Setyawan; Yo’el Pieter Sumihar

title: Smart Chronic Disease and Weight Management in an Ageing and Low-Fertility Society: An IoT-Enabled Endocrine–Metabolic Monitoring Model from Macao
abstract: Macao is experiencing a unique convergence of accelerated population ageing and persistently ultra-low fertility. Chronic disease care demand continues to rise, while the medical workforce and family caregiving capacity contract in parallel, forcing health systems to transition from fragmented outpatient follow-up towards continuous, life-context monitoring coupled with closed-loop intervention. This chapter proposes an Internet of Things (IoT)-enabled endocrine–metabolic monitoring model – that uses weight management as an entry point and metabolic risk clusters as the clinical core. The model integrates three data streams: high-frequency physiological and behavioural data from wearables and home devices; medium-frequency contextual patient-reported data; and low-frequency, high-value clinical laboratory and diagnostic data. Risk stratification drives nurse–physician collaborative remote follow-up, behavioural prescription, medication adjustment, and early complication alerts. The chapter also illustrating how care-economy constraints in a low-fertility society limit the feasibility and equity of chronic disease management. Drawing on Macao’s healthcare access strategy and governance tools such as the electronic Medical Subsidy Scheme, the healthcare-integration trends of the Guangdong–Hong Kong–Macao Greater Bay Area (GBA), and the needs of bariatric-metabolic surgery – including laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy (LSG) – and post-operative nutritional management, we propose a full-module mobile application (App) design and governance architecture that concurrently serves community adults, older adults with multi-morbidity, and pre- and post-bariatric-surgery patients, with the aim of simultaneously improving adherence, accessibility, and long-term outcomes.

title: Smart Shoe for Women Safety Device
abstract: This paper presents a smart safety sandal designed to enhance the personal security of women using GSM and GPS technology. When the wearer presses a panic switch, the system sends a real-time location alert to pre-defined emergency contacts. The sandal also includes a non-lethal electric shock mechanism that serves as a self-defence measure. The device is compact, wearable and designed for quick response in emergency situations.
authors: S Soni, Zaveria M Sheikh, Drakshayani V; Hanumantha Rao A Priyanka VJ

title: Smart Tourist Safety Monitoring and Incident Response System Using AI
abstract: Tourists travelling through remote, forested, hilly, wildlife, and adventure destinations may encounter disorientation, restricted areas, accidents, health emergencies, crime, or communication failure. Conventional mechanisms often separate location tracking, emergency reporting, identity verification, and authority coordination, which can delay intervention when a tourist cannot communicate or when a location signal lacks behavioural context. This paper proposes a unified Smart Tourist Safety Monitoring and Incident Response System that combines a mobile application, GPS tracking, geo-fencing, artificial-intelligence and machine-learning analytics, blockchain-based digital tourist identity, authority monitoring, and optional IoT wearable devices. After registration, a tourist receives a Digital Tourist ID associated with the mobile application or wearable. Location, movement, activity, and optional health signals are processed to identify unsafe-zone entry, route deviation, prolonged inactivity, fall-like events, and explicit SOS requests. Alerts are delivered to an authority dashboard for verification, prioritisation, escalation, and response recording. The paper presents the research foundation, system architecture, operational methodology, implementation plan, and evaluation framework. It does not claim completed experimental results; accuracy, latency, scalability, privacy, and field effectiveness remain evaluation objectives.

title: Smartwatch-Detected Sinus Tachycardia Unmasking AL Cardiac Amyloidosis in a Young Adult.
abstract: The clinical presentation of immunoglobulin light-chain (AL) can be very heterogenous resulting in delayed diagnosis and treatment. The use of wearable health technology is rapidly expanding. This case explores the important role this technology can play in the diagnosis of cardiac amyloidosis particularly in younger adults. A 36-year-old woman presented with frequent high heart rate alerts on her smartwatch with mild nonspecific symptoms. Further investigations led to cardiac magnetic resonance imaging that raised suspicion for amyloidosis with Mayo Clinic stage III immunoglobulin A lambda AL cardiac amyloidosis confirmed on laboratory and histological testing. The sinus tachycardia was attributed to atrial amyloid infiltration. Plasma cell therapy resulted in an excellent cardiac and hematological response with normalization of resting sinus heart rates. This case highlights an atypical presentation of cardiac AL amyloidosis. Smartwatch monitoring and alerts were central to early diagnosis and treatment. This case demonstrates the potential role that wearable-technology has in early detection of AL cardiac amyloidosis. To achieve a timely diagnosis of AL cardiac amyloidosis, physicians should remain inquisitive; subtle abnormalities in cardiac biomarkers or electrocardiograms should prompt further investigation.
authors: Grace O'Dea; Peter O'Gorman; Gerard T Giblin

title: Software-defined radio sensing for self-harming behaviour detection using CWT transformation and deep learning
abstract: Self-harming, prevalent among youths and adolescents, is highly linked to coping difficulties, emotional distress, trauma, and low self-esteem. Such behaviors are a serious problem as regards social well-being, mental health and emotional stability, which are detrimental to individuals, society and healthcare systems. Early detection of self-harming behavior is vital for enabling timely intervention and mitigating long-term psychological risks. In this article, we propose an intelligent human self-harming behavior detection system leveraging Software Defined Radio (SDR) signals-based non-contact platform and deep learning. The proposed system uses a multi-carrier orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) signal to extract wireless channel state information for self-harm detection. It employs the Continuous Wavelet Transform (CWT) to convert raw one-dimensional (1D) OFDM signals into two-dimensional (2D) spectrogram representations, enriching the feature set for deep learning models. A customised convolutional neural network (CNN) is designed to capture abrupt physical movements associated with self-harm while maintaining low computational complexity for real-time deployment. The customised CNN is rigorously evaluated against benchmark pre-trained deep learning models, including AlexNet, ResNet18, and GoogleNet, to demonstrate competitive sensitivity and specificity. Comprehensive comparisons are conducted based on performance metrics such as accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and computational efficiency parameters. The proposed customised model achieves competitive accuracy (96%) and F1-score (94%) while being significantly more computationally efficient, requiring only 3,305,801 trainable parameters, 12.61 MB of memory, and 45.09 ms inference time.
authors: Farman Ullah; Shumayla Yaqoob; Ali Mustafa; Ammar; Irfan Hussain; Mobeen Ur Rehman

title: Stable and Interpretable Cognitive Status Screening Using Longitudinal Wearable Data
abstract: Abstract Wearable devices repeatedly measure activity, sleep, and nocturnal physiology, but their value for three-class cognitive screening remains uncertain. We developed an interpretable hierarchical framework to distinguish cognitively normal (CN), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and dementia (DEM) without the Mini-Mental State Examination or device-generated composite scores. Data from 174 adults aged 55 years or older were represented by seven-day windows encoding level, variability, trend, transitions, bouts, and complexity. Stage 1 separated DEM from non-DEM using the top-3 mean of window probabilities; Stage 2 separated CN from MCI using participant-median slope-and-change features. Participant-level cross-validation and repeated 3- to 6-fold sensitivity analyses preceded evaluation on an internal holdout of 38 participants. Accuracy was 0.711, balanced accuracy was 0.738, and macro F1 was 0.692; recall was 0.682, 0.700, and 0.833 for CN, MCI, and DEM, respectively. TreeSHAP and correlation grouping yielded four preliminary DEM patterns---activity complexity, device-state organization, rest, and light-sleep structure---and three exploratory MCI domains spanning activity persistence, sleep-wake timing, and nocturnal physiology. These findings support risk screening and hypothesis generation rather than diagnosis or validated biomarker claims; external multicenter validation is needed.
authors: HaEun Kim; Taewan Cho; Andrew Jaeyong Choi; Seon-Heui Lee

title: Status Quo of Artificial Intelligence- and Machine Learning-Supported Medical and Administrative Processes in Ambulatory Care Practice Management Systems: Systematic Review (Preprint)
abstract: BACKGROUND Electronic health records (EHRs) and practice management systems represent the digital foundation of outpatient care worldwide. Integrating artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML)-supported medical and administrative processes (AMP) into these platforms offers a profound opportunity to streamline clinical workflows and standardize patient care. However, existing research remains highly fragmented and focused on isolated tools. This creates a critical research gap, as there is currently no comprehensive mapping of how these diverse medical and administrative workflows collectively integrate and perform within the real-world clinical environment of ambulatory care. OBJECTIVE This study aims to address this research gap by comprehensively mapping the global status quo of natively EHR-integrated AMP in ambulatory care. Specifically, we explore the types of digital processes currently available and how physicians and medical assistants interact with these technologies in clinical environments. METHODS We conducted a systematic review of PubMed and Scopus databases (searching from inception to March 24, 2026) following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. We targeted empirical studies evaluating outpatient clinical and administrative processes driven by AI, ML, or AI-enabled decision-support algorithms natively embedded within EHR or practice management systems. To ensure literature saturation, backward citation searching of included studies was conducted (yielding no additional eligible studies). Study selection, data extraction into a standardized matrix, and methodological quality assessment using Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) critical appraisal checklists (tailored to RCTs, quasi-experimental, cohort, cross-sectional, and qualitative studies) were conducted by one reviewer and independently verified by a second reviewer. RESULTS A total of 39 empirical studies were included. Methodological quality assessed via JBI tools was moderate to high, with common limitations being a lack of participant and personnel blinding (system-inherent) and selection bias due to reliance on voluntary early adopters. Our synthesis identified 5 primary categories of natively EHR-integrated AMP: point-of-care clinical decision support systems (CDSS) (16/39, 41%), active background screening and triage (9/39, 23%), ambient intelligence for clinical documentation (8/39, 21%), administrative processes and patient communication (4/39, 10%), and remote patient monitoring (RPM) (2/39, 5%). While ambient AI demonstrated success in reducing documentation effort and burnout, point-of-care CDSS was heavily hindered by alert fatigue (with override rates up to 96%), and active background screening was constrained by algorithmic opacity (“black-box” characteristics) and clinician distrust. CONCLUSIONS Rather than achieving full automation, AMP technologies currently function as assistive tools within primary care. Real-world utilization requires a strict human-in-the-loop verification process, where medical professionals actively oversee both AI- and ML-driven outputs. Successful integration depends on addressing critical workflow barriers, particularly minimizing alert fatigue and enhancing algorithmic transparency to foster clinician trust. title: Stratification of salivary sIgA variability identified by time-series feature clustering
abstract: Salivary secretory immunoglobulin A (sIgA) is a biomarker of mucosal immunity, but its day-to-day variability hampers interpretation of single-timepoint measurements. We sampled saliva daily from 46 healthy adults for 56 consecutive days, extracted 23 time-series features per trajectory and retained twelve for clustering. Clustering of component scores gave three groups: Stable-balanced ( n = 26; intermediate levels, low variability), High-variable ( n = 7; high concentrations, large fluctuations) and Low-unstable ( n = 13; lowest concentrations, greatest variance instability). Neither the gap statistic nor a parametric bootstrap null supported three natural clusters (silhouette 0.283, P = 0.246); we therefore present an exploratory stratification. Mean level and variability drifted little between the two halves in 18/25 (72.0%, 95% CI 52.4–85.7), 5/7 (71.4%, 35.9–91.8) and 4/13 participants (30.8%, 12.7–57.6) respectively, intervals that overlap widely. Individual-level prediction was poor; the residual component held 75–85% of the variance (an upper bound). Cough was most frequent in the Low-unstable group (5/13, 38.5%, 17.7–64.5, versus 3/26 and 0/7), but this exploratory association was not significant ( P = 0.072). A single measurement therefore cannot separate an individual’s level from day-to-day fluctuation: characterising salivary sIgA requires repeated sampling over weeks, for which this stratification is a starting point.
authors: Yu Akiyama; Takahiro Shiga; Hirotaka Minagawa; Tomoko Fujita; Ikuo Shiratori

title: Strengthening Real‐World Evidence: Recognizing and Overcoming Methodological Pitfalls in Observational Health Data
abstract: Introduction: Real-world health data (RWD), typically derived from electronic health records, administrative claims, patient registries, wearable devices, and other non-experimental sources, are increasingly used to generate real-world evidence (RWE) in public health and clinical medicine. While RWD offers multiple advantages over traditional randomized clinical trials (RCTs) in cost, feasibility, speed, and generalizability, methodological pitfalls can undermine the reproducibility and validity of findings based on RWD analysis. Methods: In this manuscript, we highlight key methodological challenges in RWD analysis and illustrate them with published case studies. We then review published methodological solutions, including target trial emulation, propensity score adjustment, instrumental variable approaches, and inverse probability of sampling weighting, that can improve the validity and generalizability of empirical results derived from RWD. Results: We contend that awareness of RWD limitations is not a justification for avoiding its use, but a mandate to use it more carefully. Conclusions: Pre-specifying sampling and analytic plans, applying robust inferential methods, and continuing to invest in novel bias-reduction methods are essential to ensuring that RWE fulfills its promise for public health research and policy.
authors: Daniel L. Gillen

title: Symptom-agnostic endpoints in tuberculosis vaccine efficacy trials
abstract: Tuberculosis vaccine prevention-of-disease efficacy trials traditionally rely on symptom-triggered case detection. This approach captures only a subset of bacteriologically confirmed disease and can miss cases that occur between scheduled trial visits or outside trial procedures, slowing endpoint accrual and complicating interpretation of results. At the same time, the diagnostic landscape for tuberculosis is changing rapidly. Advances, including near point-of-care (NPOC) molecular assays using sputum and non-sputum specimens, portable chest radiography with computer-aided detection, and digital tools for decentralised monitoring, now make symptom-agnostic screening strategies increasingly feasible in large clinical trials. A 2026 WHO policy recommending the use of NPOC molecular diagnostics for tuberculosis further highlights the relevance of these approaches. In this Health Policy paper, we outlined a framework for integrating symptom-agnostic screening into tuberculosis vaccine efficacy trials and reviewed emerging diagnostic technologies that could enable this transition. Using parameters informed by the placebo arm of the M72/AS01 E phase 2b trial, we present a worked example illustrating a possible effect on endpoint detection and case-verification burden. In this illustrative scenario, an NPOC-based symptom-agnostic screening strategy was estimated to increase detection of bacteriologically confirmed tuberculosis endpoints by approximately 1·4-fold, as compared with that by symptom-based screening alone, although this finding should not be interpreted as a direct estimate of overall trial efficiency. Realising these benefits will require analytical validation of diagnostic tools, clinical qualification for trial use, and early alignment with regulators and policy bodies. If evaluated through staged evidence generation and implemented with stringent confirmation algorithms, then symptom-agnostic screening could support more interpretable assessments of vaccine impact across the bacteriological spectrum of tuberculosis disease while preserving endpoint specificity.

title: TELEMEDICINE AND MONITORING DEVICES AS TOOLS FOR IMPROVING THE QUALITY OF LIFE OF OLDER ADULTS
abstract: Research objectives: The aim of the study was to gather current evidence on the impact of telemedicine and remote monitoring technologies on quality of life and clinical outcomes in older adults. It also aimed to identify the public health implications of such interventions. Methods: A structured narrative review of peer-reviewed articles published in English between 2016 and 2025 was conducted. These were identified through searches in PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, and Google Scholar using keywords related to telemedicine, telecare, remote monitoring, wearable devices, older adults, and quality of life. Quantitative, qualitative, and review studies involving patients aged 60 years and older with cardiovascular and respiratory diseases, diabetes, neurological and psychiatric disorders, frailty syndrome, rehabilitation needs, and in the postoperative period were included. Key findings: The included studies indicated that telemedicine contributed to improvements in quality of life and in physical and mental health status, and it also had a positive impact on increasing the level of self-care. These interventions favorably affected clinical parameters such as blood pressure control and glycemic control, which was particularly important in patients with multimorbidity. In many geriatric populations, a reduction in the number of hospitalizations and healthcare costs was also observed. Conclusions: Telemedicine and remote monitoring devices are promising tools supporting aging in place and reducing the burden on the public healthcare system in the context of population aging. Full and effective use of teleinterventions still requires adaptation of the technology to fit the functional and cognitive abilities of older patients.

title: The Case for Evaluating Continuous Glucose Monitoring as a Diagnostic Tool for Diabetes
abstract: Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) provides information about real-time glycemic exposure that is not captured by measurements of fasting plasma glucose (FPG), changes in glycemia during oral glucose tolerance testing (OGTT), or Hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c). We propose that (1) CGM can identify dysglycemia earlier than existing approaches, (2) CGM may serve as an adjunctive diagnostic tool, and (3) CGM may eventually support independent diagnostic criteria. The strongest case is for Stage 2 type 1 diabetes (T1D), because this stage represents a critical opportunity for intervention before progression to Stage 3 disease. CGM as a diagnostic tool could identify individuals at risk of progression to Stage 3 T1D, particularly those with islet autoantibodies, by detecting progression of dysglycemia, supporting disease staging, and identifying candidates for confirmatory testing, closer monitoring, or future prevention trials. Beyond T1D, CGM might also prove to be a reliable diagnostic test for type 2 diabetes (T2D) in selected populations. Overall, there is a need for prospective clinical studies to compare the value of using CGM-derived metrics directly with existing diagnostic standards, including OGTT and HbA1c. For both T1D and T2D, earlier diagnosis by CGM has the potential to improve patient outcomes by creating opportunities for prevention and treatment early in the natural history of the disease. This article presents an outcome-based framework for deriving and validating CGM-based diagnostic thresholds. The framework emphasizes that future diagnostic criteria should be based on clinically meaningful outcomes, rather than concordance with existing tests.

title: The Efficacy of Auditory and Haptic Cues Delivered via a Wearable Device to Guide Walking Intensity
abstract: Walking is one of the most common forms of physical activity in the UK, promoted by the National Health Service (NHS) through guidelines recommending moderate-intensity exercise. However, the subjective interpretation of "moderate" intensity can lead to inconsistent adherence. Cadence-based thresholds, such as at least 100 steps per minute, have been proposed as an objective alternative, but these absolute markers may not reflect individual fitness levels. Wearable technologies offer an opportunity to personalise physical activity intensity using physiological markers like percentage heart rate reserve (%HRR), and to guide behaviour using nudge-based approaches such as cadence cueing. This study investigated whether metronome (auditory) and haptic cadence cues delivered via an Apple Watch app could guide users to criterion moderate-intensity walking (40 - 59% HRR). Seventy-four adults (18–65 years) completed three 10-minute overground walking trials on a ~60 m figure-of-eight track: (1) self-paced walking guided by NHS moderate-intensity guidelines, (2) walking to an auditory cadence cue, and (3) walking to a haptic cadence cue. Cadence and %HRR were recorded in each condition. Bayesian posterior distributions showed the following mean %HRR (95% credible intervals): self-paced = 41% (39–44%), auditory = 45% (42–47%), and haptic = 43% (41–45%). The proportion of participants reaching 40 - 59% HRR was highest in the auditory (76%) and haptic (65%) cueing conditions, compared to self-paced (41%). These findings suggest wearable-guided cadence cueing, particularly auditory cues, more effectively supports individuals in achieving moderate-intensity walking compared to current NHS guidelines.
