title: The Temporal Investigation of Multimodal Elements (TIME) Study: protocol for an observational, longitudinal study to characterize the dynamic structure of molecular and digital data in older adults in stable health
abstract: Background Biological systems exhibit dynamic patterns over multiple temporal scales—from minutes to months—that are poorly captured by conventional cross-sectional or low-frequency longitudinal studies. These patterns, including diurnal variations and underlying continuous rhythms, may be critical determinants of health, resilience, and disease risk in aging. Existing longitudinal studies in older adults lack high-frequency, multimodal measurements that integrate molecular, physiological, and digital health data streams. Objectives The TIME Study aims to: (i) Characterize temporal patterns in molecular, physiological, and digital health measures in healthy older adults; (ii) determine how these patterns vary across biological domains and relate to each other; and (iii) assess how physiological systems respond to defined perturbations (oral glucose tolerance and maximal exercise). Methods TIME is a single-site, observational, longitudinal study enrolling up to 150 adults aged ≥55 years. Over an 11-week main phase, participants complete seven weekly low-frequency visits, two perturbation challenge visits, and two, two-day high-frequency sampling epochs. Biospecimens, clinical measures, cognitive and physical performance tests, and continuous digital health data are collected. Follow-up visits occur at 6 and 12 months. Expected impact By integrating multimodal, temporally resolved data, TIME will provide a foundational dataset for understanding the role of biological rhythms in aging and inform future precision health strategies. Clinical Trial Registration: https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT07107386 , identifier NCT07107386.

title: The Use of Mobile Applications in Health Promotion and Disease Prevention
abstract: Thesis. Mobile health applications can support the prevention of noncommunicable diseases by facilitating self-monitoring, encouraging healthier behaviours, and extending preventive support beyond conventional healthcare settings; however, their public health value depends on sustained engagement, reliable evidence, data protection, and equitable access. Concept. This narrative review synthesizes peer-reviewed studies and reports concerning mobile applications used to address major modifiable risk factors for noncommunicable diseases. It considers applications supporting physical activity, nutrition and weight management, and the monitoring of physiological parameters, while examining their functions, documented benefits, and implementation challenges. Results and conclusion. The reviewed evidence indicates that mHealth applications can improve physical activity, dietary behaviours, weight management, and selected physiological outcomes, particularly when they incorporate goal setting, personalized feedback, reminders, gamification, and integration with wearable devices. Nevertheless, effects vary across interventions and populations, and long-term adherence frequently declines. Concerns regarding measurement accuracy, limited clinical validation, privacy and security, unequal digital access, and the geographical concentration of the evidence restrict broader implementation and generalizability. Mobile applications should therefore complement rather than replace professionally delivered prevention and should be integrated into public health systems using evidence-based, interoperable, secure, and user-centred approaches. Originality. The article provides an integrated public health perspective that connects the preventive functions of mHealth applications with the behavioural, technological, ethical, and equity-related conditions required for their responsible use in noncommunicable disease prevention. Keywords: mHealth, mobile health applications, noncommunicable diseases, disease prevention, health promotion, digital health, lifestyle interventions
authors: Agnieszka Kiedik; Zuzanna Pietruk; Dzianis Dashkevich; Przemysław Siemiątkowski; Kacper Zima; Dominik Ryszard Płaza; Michał Kozicki

title: The association between wearable device use and exercise adherence: a chain mediation model of exercise self-efficacy and positive experiences
abstract: Objective To examine the association between wearable device use and exercise adherence and to investigate the chain-mediated roles of exercise self-efficacy and positive experiences in this relationship. Methods A questionnaire survey was administered to individuals who used fitness apps or smart wearable devices ( N = 367). Structural equation modeling (SEM) was conducted to examine the hypothesized associations and mediation pathways. The Bootstrap method with 5,000 resamples was applied to assess indirect effects. Results Wearable device use showed a statistically significant total association with exercise adherence ( β = 0.430, p < 0.001); after the two proposed mediators were included, the direct association was β = 0.197 ( p < 0.001). Exercise self-efficacy and positive experiences each showed significant independent indirect associations, and the sequential (chain) indirect pathway involving both variables was also statistically significant (indirect association = 0.059, 95% CI [0.035, 0.086]). The indirect associations statistically accounted for 54.0% of the total association. Conclusion Among physically active users of digital fitness technologies, wearable device use was positively associated with exercise adherence, and this association was partially accounted for by a chain mediation pathway involving exercise self-efficacy and positive experiences. The findings are consistent with, but do not confirm, the proposed directional model; they identify psychological factors associated with exercise adherence among wearable device users and may inform future research on technology-assisted approaches for supporting sustained exercise behaviour.
authors: Ziqi Qin; Ying Guo; Xinlong Liu

title: The associations between wearable device feedback perception and athletes’ training load management behavior: the chain mediating role of physiological data literacy and recovery self-regulation
abstract: Introduction: Despite the rapid proliferation of wearable devices in sport, athletes vary considerably in their ability to interpret device-generated physiological feedback, and the psychological pathways linking feedback perception to training load management remain insufficiently understood. This study introduces physiological data literacy (PDL) as a content-specific form of data literacy and examines whether PDL and recovery self-regulation (RSR) sequentially mediate the association between wearable device feedback perception (WFP) and training load management behavior (TLM). Methods: Using a cross-sectional design, 357 active athletes (189 males and 168 females; mean age = 22.76 years, SD = 3.68) completed the wearable device feedback perception scale, physiological data literacy scale, recovery self-regulation scale, and training load management behavior scale. Path analysis with bias-corrected bootstrapping (5,000 resamples) was conducted. Results: = 0.511). Significant specific indirect associations were observed through PDL (standardized indirect effect = 0.083, 95% CI [0.032, 0.136]) and RSR (standardized indirect effect = 0.085, 95% CI [0.048, 0.128]). A significant sequential indirect association was also observed for the theoretically specified WFP → PDL → RSR → TLM ordering (indirect effect = 0.065, 95% CI [0.040, 0.098]). The direct WFP-TLM association remained significant after inclusion of both mediators. However, the reverse sequential model yielded identical AIC and BIC values. Discussion: The findings are statistically compatible with a theoretically motivated sequential framework linking WFP, PDL, RSR, and TLM, but the cross-sectional design does not establish temporal precedence or causal direction. PDL represents a conceptually distinct competency that, together with RSR, warrants further examination in longitudinal and intervention research on wearable-supported training.
authors: Yufeng Han; Junli Fan

title: The dose-response association between wearables-quantified incidental physical activity and type 2 diabetes: a prospective cohort study
abstract: AIM: This prospective cohort study aimed to quantify dose-response associations between intensity-specific incidental physical activity (IPA) and the incidence of type 2 diabetes (T2D) in a large cohort of UK adults. A secondary aim was to estimate the T2D-specific equivalence of 1 minute of vigorous-intensity IPA relative to moderate- and light-intensity IPA. METHODS: Participants were adults from the UK Biobank accelerometry sub-study who self-reported as nonexercisers. Individuals were excluded if they had T2D at baseline, were using insulin therapy, or received a T2D diagnosis within 12 months of follow-up. T2D status was primarily derived from primary care records. Device-measured IPA was categorized into light (LIPA; 1.5 to <3 METs), moderate (MIPA; 3 to <6 METs), and vigorous (VIPA; ≥6 METs) intensities. Additional analyses examined the T2D-specific equivalence of 1 minute of VIPA to MIPA and LIPA. The reference group comprised participants accumulating neither MIPA nor VIPA. RESULTS: The primary analysis included 22 857 nonexercisers (mean age 62.1 ± 7.7 years, 42.8% male). Over a 7.8-year follow-up period, 721 (3.2%) participants developed T2D. MIPA and VIPA, but not LIPA, exhibited near-linear inverse associations with T2D risk. Median VIPA (4.75 minutes/day) was associated with a hazard ratio (HR) 0.62 [95% confidence interval (CI) 0.53-0.73], and median MIPA (23.70 minutes/day) showed a HR of 0.67 (95% CI: 0.52-0.86). One minute of VIPA/day was associated with an equivalent T2D risk reduction of 5.9 minutes MIPA/day and 46.6 minutes LIPA/day. CONCLUSION: MIPA and VIPA were associated with lower T2D risk in a dose-dependent manner. Although median LIPA was linked to reduced risk, it did not demonstrate a consistent dose-response relationship.
authors: Angelo Sabag; Raaj Kishore Biswas; Nicholas A. Koemel; Monique E. François; Shelley Elizabeth Keating; Martin J. Gibala; Jonathan P. Little; Nathan Anthony Johnson; Emmanuel A. Stamatakis; Matthew N. Ahmadi

title: The effect of low-temperature-induced immune activation in elderly idiopathic facial palsy: the association between Th1/Th2 imbalance and facial nerve inflammation
abstract: The pathogenesis of idiopathic facial palsy in the elderly has not been fully elucidated. Recent studies have shown that exposure to low temperatures may participate in the pathological process through immune-mediated pathways. This article reviews that cold stimulation can disrupt the Th1/Th2 immune balance, manifested as reduced secretion of Th1-type cytokines and upregulation of Th2-type cytokines, thereby inducing peripheral inflammatory responses around the facial nerve, leading to nerve edema, demyelination, and conduction dysfunction. Due to the immune aging characteristics of the elderly population, including the reduction of the initial T cell pool, the imbalance of pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory factor ratios, and the decline in regulatory T cell function, they are more sensitive to the immune dysregulation induced by low temperatures and have a significantly increased risk of facial palsy. Clinical and animal experimental evidence supports this mechanism, suggesting that the serum IL-4/IFN-γ ratio may serve as a prognostic marker. Future multi-center studies are needed to verify the effectiveness of targeted immune regulation intervention through the Th2 pathway and explore the application value of low-temperature warning and individualized warming strategies in the prevention of facial palsy in the elderly.
authors: Xing Tang; Ziqin Ji; Xueling Xiao; Tongtong Zhu; Shoujen Lan; Yeayin Yen; Xin Shao; Shune Tan; Chao Wang; Jicheng Zhang

title: The nutritional and metabolic impact of night shift work in a real-world setting
abstract: Abstract Growing evidence from epidemiological and lab-controlled studies links night shift work to adverse health outcomes, but evidence from real-world occupational environments remains limited. Using multiple wearable devices and mobile health apps, alongside other objective and subjective assessment tools, we assess nutritional intake and cardiometabolic parameters among 72 shift workers recruited from a single-center Swiss hospital (82% female; median age 31 years; body mass index 22.7 kg/m 2 ) during three consecutive night shifts and three consecutive day shifts. While intake of calories, protein, and fat is reduced during night shifts, glycemic variability and postprandial glucose spikes are increased compared to day shifts. After three consecutive night shifts, plasma cortisol is reduced, and the 24-h heart rate and heart rate variability are altered. Exploratory analysis reveals higher protein intake correlates with lower glycemic variability, whereas nighttime eating is associated with increased glycemic variability. Future interventional studies should explore whether adjusting meal composition and timing could improve glycemic variability in night shift workers.
authors: Friedrich C. Jassil; Nick E. Phillips; Alexandra Hemmer; Céline Joris; Andrew D. Biancolin; Steffen Lutz Hartmeyer; Victor Dorribo; Stephen H. title: Theorizing future phenomena: Metaverse, wearables, and humanoids
abstract: Abstract Research Summary We propose that entrepreneurship and strategy research can develop theory about phenomena of the future rather than only explain those of the past. Research has potential for practical relevance when researchers make claims towards applications to decisions practitioners have yet to make. Theory grounded in a world that may differ from the observed world can be built through a process of extrapolation from technological trends, a practice utilized by entrepreneurs and science fiction authors alike. Assuming advances in artificial intelligence, we apply this process to three emerging phenomena: governing scarcity in metaverse virtual worlds, redesigning organizations around pervasive monitoring via wearable devices, and allocating the intellectual property rights of humanoid robots. We argue that embracing theory that speaks to the future can enhance the practical and educational relevance of management research. Managerial Summary Assuming artificial intelligence continues to improve, we highlight three impending phenomena poised to transform conventional approaches to entrepreneurship and strategy. First, in metaverse virtual worlds, managers must manage resources governed by artificial scarcity. Second, with wearable devices allowing continuous monitoring, managers must consider alternative structures for vertical hierarchy and horizontal collaboration. Third, deployment of humanoid robots will complicate intellectual property rights and asset ownership. We propose that scholarship towards developing theoretical frameworks addressing these and other phenomena of the future will be relevant to both managers and students.

title: TinyML-Optimised Multimodal Lstm for Unsupervised Anomaly Detection in Smart Home IoT Systems
abstract: The rapid rise in IoT smart home devices generates extensive time-series datasets, while anomaly detection solutions remain largely dependent on cloud-based processing, resulting in latency, privacy concerns, and connectivity requirements. Existing approaches often rely on a single modality and insufficiently address concept drift and edge-device constraints. This study proposes a TinyML-optimised multimodal LSTM model for unsupervised anomaly detection in smart home applications deployed on a Raspberry Pi edge device. Temperature, humidity, and power consumption modalities were combined to capture cross-modal relationships. A simulated dataset represented normal diurnal and seasonal behaviour and incorporated three anomaly types: heat spikes, power outages, and midnight appliance usage. Model training used only normal-value sequences within a 250-timestep sliding window. TinyML optimisation reduced the stored LSTM model size to 196 KB, which represents the model storage size and should not be interpreted as total runtime memory or direct evidence of real-time or low-power operation. An online learning strategy was employed to address concept drift through periodic retraining. On the simulated test set, the model achieved 98.97% recall, 8.79% precision, 8.86% F1-score, 0.294 Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC), and an AUC-ROC of 0.9984. The confusion matrix comprised 83,416 true negatives, 3,994 false positives, 4 false negatives, and 385 true positives. Although the model detected nearly all injected anomalies, its low precision indicates a substantial false-alarm burden and limits claims regarding deployment readiness.
authors: Osaretin Edith Okoro; Nurudeen Mahmud Ibrahim; Kirubakaran Prema; Suleiman Aliyu Muhammad

title: Topological Dielectric Fiber Networks for Self‐Powered Teleperception
abstract: Noncontact sensing is indispensable for intelligent human–machine interaction (HMI), autonomous robotics, and distributed Internet of Things (IoTs). However, the sensing range of existing triboelectric sensors remains fundamentally constrained because dense dielectric architectures limit charge trapping and dielectric polarization. Here, we develop a self‐powered triboelectric teleperception sensor (TTS) based on an electrospun poly(vinylidene fluoride)/barium titanate (PVDF/BTO) topological dielectric fiber network. COMSOL simulations, together with experimental characterizations, reveal that the three‐dimensional porous topology synergistically enhances charge trapping, electrostatic confinement, and dielectric polarization, while BTO nanoparticles further amplify the interfacial electrostatic field through enhanced dielectric response. These synergistic effects establish an efficient electrostatic induction mechanism for teleperception. Consequently, the TTS achieves a maximum sensing distance of 1.1 m, enables reliable discrimination of target materials and motion frequencies, and supports remote interaction with a robotic arm. Furthermore, a one‐dimensional convolutional neural network (1D‐CNN) enables intelligent recognition of approaching, receding, waving, walking, and running behaviors with an accuracy of 91.67%. By engineering dielectric topology to regulate electrostatic field coupling, this work establishes a general design strategy for self‐powered teleperception, providing a versatile sensing platform for intelligent robotics, HMI, and next‐generation embodied systems.
authors: Yan Du; Z. Zhang; Cong Li; Zihan Wang; Jiaxin Guo; Zhong Lin Wang; Di Wei

title: Translational maturity of artificial intelligence-enabled electrocardiography varies across cardiovascular diseases
abstract: Electrocardiography is a widely available and low-cost cardiovascular test, and artificial intelligence-enabled electrocardiography (AI-ECG) can identify latent electrical phenotypes beyond conventional interpretation. However, high retrospective discrimination does not necessarily translate into clinically reliable or actionable benefit. This critical narrative review evaluates the translational maturity of AI-ECG across arrhythmias, acute myocardial infarction, heart failure, valvular heart disease, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and cardiac amyloidosis. PubMed, IEEE Xplore, and Web of Science were searched from January 1, 2022, through July 10, 2026, with earlier landmark studies added by backward citation tracking. Seventy-seven publications informed the review. Evidence was appraised using five clinically oriented criteria: intended use, reference-standard reliability, external validation and transportability, clinical actionability, and effects on workflow or patient outcomes. AI-ECG has progressed furthest in ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction triage and reduced-left-ventricular-ejection-fraction screening, where prospective or randomized studies have demonstrated workflow or diagnostic-yield benefits, whereas acute myocardial infarction rule-out has reached prospective multicenter diagnostic validation. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy screening has also advanced through international validation and prospective implementation. By contrast, occlusion myocardial infarction detection, prediction of occult or future atrial fibrillation, valvular heart disease, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, long-term heart-failure prediction, and cardiac amyloidosis remain primarily validation-stage or risk-enrichment applications. Across domains, broader adoption is constrained by label quality, calibration, transportability, operating-threshold selection, and limited patient-outcome evidence. AI-ECG is therefore best positioned as clinician-supervised decision support linked to explicit downstream testing and care pathways.
authors: Huanhuan Chen; Jingjuan Huang; Xumin Hou

title: Transport–Reaction–Signal Coupling in Lateral Flow Assays for Next‐Generation Point‐of‐Care Diagnostics
abstract: Lateral flow assays (LFAs) remain central to point-of-care diagnostics because they combine low cost, portability, and operational simplicity. Emerging diagnostic demands, including low-abundance biomarkers, complex sample matrices, quantitative readout, and multiplexed analysis, increasingly expose limitations that cannot be solved by signal-label enhancement alone. This Review examines recent LFA advances through a three-phase framework that couples porous-material mass transfer, interfacial reaction engineering, and signal transduction. The framework clarifies how membrane and flow design regulate analyte delivery and residence time, how antibody orientation, reaction amplification, and hook-effect mitigation improve capture efficiency and dynamic range, and how advanced nanolabels, integrated readers, multiplexed formats, and AI/ML-supported design and analysis expand performance across the assay workflow. By distinguishing intrinsic performance gains from strategies that transfer complexity to reagents, devices, or software, this Review provides design principles for sensitive, quantitative, and translation-oriented LFA systems.
authors: Yan Pan; Yuewei Li; Chao Mi; Zhengwen Yang; Lana McClements; Steven James Langford; Jiayan Liao

title: Triboelectric Nanogenerators for Human‐Robot Motion Energy Harvesting and Sensing: Structures, Embodied Artificial Intelligence, and Self‐Powered Applications
abstract: The rapid development of humanoid robots and embodied artificial intelligence (EAI) is accelerating the transformation of elderly care and rehabilitation toward interactive, adaptive, and personalized human-robot collaboration. In this context, motion sensing technology is of critical importance. Triboelectric nanogenerators (TENGs), which convert biomechanical motions into electrical signals, offer a promising route toward self-powered motion perception in embodied healthcare. This review summarizes recent advances in TENG-based multimodal motion sensing for human-robot interaction, covering inertial vibration sensing, tactile sensing, non-contact sensing, continuous trajectory sensing, and joint rotation sensing. The influences of structural configuration, motion mode, sensing direction, detection range, sensitivity, resolution, electrical output, and channel number on sensing performance under specific application scenarios are analyzed. Particular attention is paid to how TENG design strategies influence sensing universality, signal effectiveness, and the reliability of health monitoring and rehabilitation evaluation. Furthermore, the integration of TENGs with artificial intelligence (AI) technologies, including multimodal fusion, network architectures, edge computing, transfer learning, and large language models, is reviewed. Finally, applications in adaptive rehabilitation sensing, self-powered electrical stimulation, fully self-powered systems, and human‑robot interfaces are highlighted, offering perspectives on closed-loop "sensing-evaluation-regulation" frameworks for green, low-carbon EAI healthcare.
authors: Jian Li; Gefan Yin; Zhen Sun; Chenhao Li; Yadong Mo; Cong Gu; Xiangyan Zhang; Sikai Wang; Xiangjie Xu; Runxiao Liu; Jiahe Wang; Pengyu Chen; Ziyang Li; Shimin Wei

title: USE OF MODERN SMARTWATCHES IN EARLY DETECTION OF HEART RHYTHM DISTURBANCES AND PREVENTION OF CARDIOVASCULAR COMPLICATIONS: A NARRATIVE REVIEW
abstract: Atrial fibrillation (AF) and other cardiac rhythm disturbances represent a major and growing global health burden, contributing substantially to stroke, heart failure, and cardiovascular mortality worldwide. Because AF is frequently asymptomatic or paroxysmal, timely diagnosis remains a persistent clinical challenge. This narrative review aims to synthesize current evidence on the technological principles, diagnostic performance, clinical utility, and limitations of consumer smartwatches equipped with photoplethysmography (PPG) and single-lead electrocardiography (ECG) for the detection and prevention of heart rhythm disturbances. Large prospective cohorts, including the Apple Heart Study and the Fitbit Heart Study, together with multiple systematic reviews and meta-analyses, demonstrate that smartwatch-based PPG and ECG algorithms achieve high sensitivity and specificity for AF detection. This enables opportunistic screening and supports targeted secondary prevention of thromboembolic events, particularly ischemic stroke. However, real-world implementation raises concerns regarding false-positive alerts, overdiagnosis, patient anxiety, and the necessity of physician-confirmed diagnosis. Smartwatch-based rhythm monitoring constitutes a clinically meaningful, evidence-supported adjunct to conventional arrhythmia detection, but its integration into routine cardiological practice requires structured confirmatory pathways, clinician education, and further research addressing diverse populations and long-term outcomes.
authors: Michal Balenkowski; Mateusz Antonow; Agnieszka Górska; Anna Kozieł; Amelia Sztangierska; Konrad Kowalski; Michał Kardela; Katarzyna Gołąbek; Mariusz Siemiński

title: Understanding nosocomial influenza transmission in acute-care and chronic-care wards using an agent-based model
abstract: BACKGROUND: Nosocomial influenza remains a major challenge in hospital settings. However, the effects of activities of daily living (ADL)-based care dependency, healthcare worker (HCW) contact structure, community importation, and near-field and far-field exposure pathways on ward-level transmission remain unclear. We therefore used an agent-based model to investigate influenza transmission dynamics in acute-care and chronic-care wards and to evaluate the relative contribution of ADL-based HCW contact and airborne exposure pathways. METHODS: The agent-based model of nosocomial influenza transmission incorporated community importation, ward structure, ventilation, nurse shift schedules, symptomatic and asymptomatic/presymptomatic infection pathways, ADL-based patient-HCW contact patterns, and near-field and far-field exposures. Simulations were performed over 1 year, with 1000 stochastic iterations performed for each scenario. Intervention strategies included no isolation, prophylaxis alone, isolation, and isolation with prophylaxis. RESULTS: Chronic-care wards had a higher nosocomial infection burden and more HCW-contact-associated patient infections, whereas the acute-care ward showed more frequent patient turnover and more community-associated imported infections. Isolation-based interventions reduced nosocomial and HCW-contact-associated patient infections more clearly than did prophylaxis alone, although residual HCW-contact-associated infections under isolation-based scenarios were linked to asymptomatic/presymptomatic HCWs. Far-field-only infections were uncommon. CONCLUSIONS: Chronic-care wards may be particularly vulnerable to nosocomial influenza transmission following viral introduction, as greater care dependency may increase opportunities for HCW-patient transmission. Mathematical modelling provides a useful approach for identifying otherwise unobservable transmission mechanisms and highlights the importance of symptomatic isolation, asymptomatic/presymptomatic transmission, and exposure pathways in hospital influenza control.
authors: Yasuhiro Umekage; Takashi Watanabe; Kiichi Nitanai; Hiraku Yanada; Ryotaro Kida; Ryohei Yoshida; Yoshinori Minami; Yoshinobu Ohsaki; Takaaki Sasaki

title: Validation of a contactless radar system for continuous respiratory rate and heart rate monitoring in clinical and simulated use conditions
abstract: Abstract Continuous monitoring of respiratory rate (RR) and heart rate (HR) remains limited in post-acute and long-term care (PALTC) settings, where intermittent spot checks may delay detection of clinical deterioration. Contactless radar-based sensing offers an unobtrusive alternative suited to these environments. This study validates the performance of the C300 Monitor, a contactless frequency-modulated continuous-wave (FMCW) radar system operating at 58.0–61.5 GHz, for continuous RR and HR monitoring across clinical and simulated use conditions. In a clinical validation study conducted in such PALTC facilities, C300-derived RR and HR were compared against carbon dioxide capnography and electrocardiography, yielding Bland-Altman limits of agreement of -1.9 to 2.7 breaths per minute for RR, and -2.9 to 2.5 beats per minute for HR, with accuracy rates of 99.8% for RR and 95.1% for HR within a ±5 breaths per minute and beats per minute error margin, respectively. A complementary laboratory study evaluated system performance across representative conditions, including varying device distances, body positions, and motion scenarios. Under motion-free conditions, accuracy rates exceeded 96.3% for RR and 90.6% for HR within the same error margin, while expected system behavior was observed during patient motion or absence. Across both studies, the C300 Monitor demonstrated reliable, continuous RR and HR monitoring under conditions representative of real-world care environments, supporting its suitability for unobtrusive vital sign monitoring in these settings.
authors: Piyush Sharma; Volodymyr Bondarenko; Nikko Martin; Max Denning; Michal Maslik; Guy Doron Leschziner; Timo Lauteslager

title: Visually similar prints expose a benchmark validity gap in computational art history
abstract: Abstract Digitised cultural collections increasingly use visual retrieval to connect related images, yet visual resemblance does not by itself establish a historical relation between physical objects. This distinction is acute for prints: two sheets may preserve the same composition while deriving from different blocks, states, workshops or copying events. The study tests whether a retrieval benchmark can appear successful because it omits such historically consequential alternatives. A diagnostic repeated-design task is compared with a controlled candidate-pool intervention built from 39 Metropolitan Museum of Art woodcut records. Across 240 transformed queries, Pool A contains an intended same-design target and other-design negatives; Pool C changes nothing except adding one catalogue record explicitly marked as a same-design copy. Raw pixels, histograms of oriented gradients and ORB rank the intended target first for all Pool A queries, but only 187, 177 and 237 times in Pool C. The added copy becomes the unique top result 53, 63 and 3 times. An abstaining ORB/HOG gate also accepts a copy for two queries. These are catalogue-class ranking errors, not findings about matrix identity or authenticity. The results show that candidate composition is part of construct validity: a benchmark of design recurrence cannot support a claim about historical sameness unless relation-confusable candidates are represented. A relation-aware evidence architecture is proposed that separates visual discovery, confusability testing and source-bearing historical judgement. The approach gives digital humanities and cultural-heritage projects a reproducible way to test when useful similarity becomes an invalid historical inference.
authors: Jiongming Fang

title: Water-cut measurement using a planar microwave resonant sensor under flowing operating conditions
abstract: Accurate monitoring of water content in flowing oil/bitumen pipelines remains a critical challenge in the petroleum industry, as it directly affects production optimization, custody transfer, and reservoir management. In this study, we present a new microwave sensor approach for real-time, noncontact quantification of water content in flowing oil-water mixtures under operating conditions. The sensing approach exploits the strong dielectric contrast between water and oil/bitumen by monitoring the flowing stream over a defined microwave frequency range and tracking resonance frequency shifts associated with changes in effective permittivity. The sensing system consists of a planar battery-less sensing tag electromagnetically coupled to a reader at a specific distance, enabling contactless monitoring. The sensor shows high sensitivity within the 600–850 MHz frequency band and a total resonance frequency shift of about 18 MHz across the full water-cut range. To replicate oilfield-relevant operating conditions, we constructed a laboratory-scale flow loop to circulate two-phase oil-water emulsions. The experiments were conducted at water cuts from 0 to 100 wt% and temperatures from 24 to 110 °C at 150 psig. The sensor shows a continuous, monotonic response across the entire emulsion spectrum ( i.e ., water-in-oil, oil-in-water, and phase-inversion regimes). The proposed technique offers fast, instantaneous response, high sensitivity, and robust performance under elevated temperature and pressure, while remaining low-cost, passive, and easy to integrate with existing pipeline infrastructure.
authors: Shadi Kheirollahi; Nima Karbaschi; Mabkhot S. BinDahbag; Zahra Abbasi; Hassan Hassanzadeh

title: Wearable abdominal acoustic biofeedback for dietary self-regulation among Taiwanese university students: an exploratory randomized pilot study
abstract: Background Manual dietary self-monitoring can impose a burden on university students, limiting sustained engagement with digital nutrition tools. AbSound was developed as a wearable abdominal-acoustic biofeedback system that converts candidate gastrointestinal sound events into uncertainty-aware reflective prompts, rather than validated diagnoses of hunger, satiety, dietary intake, diet quality, or eating speed. This exploratory, randomized pilot study assessed feasibility, acceptability, user experience, preliminary self-reported behavioral signals, and agreement in acoustic event detection among Taiwanese university students. Method Sixty first- and second-year university students in Taipei were randomized 1:1 to AbSound plus a companion app or to an active app-based dietary-tracking comparator for 4 weeks. Primary feasibility outcomes included retention, daily wear time, days worn, prompt exposure, prompt acknowledgment, reported burden, and adverse events. Exploratory behavioral outcomes included self-reported late-night eating, perceived eating speed, a brief dietary-quality score, self-regulation of eating behavior, weight, and waist circumference. TAM ratings, Kano feature classifications, brief interviews, and descriptive acceptance-path analyses characterized adoption and design priorities. Acoustic performance was evaluated post hoc against selected manually reviewed event segments. Results All participants completed follow-up. AbSound users wore the device for 9.2 ± 2.2 h per day on 25.7 ± 2.0 of 28 study days, corresponding to approximately 91.8% of possible study days. Prompt acknowledgment averaged 78% ± 9%. Selected, manually reviewed segments showed approximately 88% agreement in event detection, but this estimate does not establish physiological-state validation. Compared with the active comparator, AbSound users showed larger exploratory reductions in self-reported late-night eating. They reported lower perceived eating-speed scores, higher brief dietary-quality scores, and a marginally greater increase in eating self-regulation. Weight and waist circumference showed no clinically interpretable between-group differences. Acceptance ratings were high; comfort and privacy emerged as must-be design attributes, while feedback agreement and timeliness were performance attributes. Conclusion AbSound demonstrated short-term feasibility and acceptability as a reflective abdominal-acoustic biofeedback tool for non-clinical Taiwanese university students. The findings support further user-centered development but do not establish clinical efficacy or validated detection of nutritional or physiological states. Larger preregistered trials require independent acoustic validation, objective or repeated dietary reference measures, longer follow-up, and explicit psychological-safety monitoring.
authors: Chen Han; Sheng-Ming Wang; Chuan-Chia Wang; Jwo-Shiun Sun; Tung-Jing Fang

title: Wire-Level Interrupt-to-Decision Latency of On-Sensor MLC Versus Host Inference on the NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano: A Preregistered Measurement Study
abstract: The Machine Learning Core (MLC) embedded in the STMicroelectronics LSM6DSOX IMU is widely cited as a low-latency alternative to host-side inference, yet wire-level decision-delivery latency is rarely measured. Using a Saleae Logic Pro 8 logic analyzer on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano, we measured interrupt-to-decision latency (sensor INT1 edge to host decision GPIO) for three pipelines (a host-side decision-tree classifier, the standard MLC bank-switch read protocol, and an MLC binary-fast variant) under idle, I2C bus contention, and CPU stress. The protocol was pre-registered with 13 externally-timestamped Zenodo amendments before confirmatory data collection (4,770 of 4,860 trials included, 98.15%, across nine cells). The host pipeline exhibits lower median latency than the MLC pipeline under all conditions: 321.7 vs 681.5 us at idle (2.1x faster) and 574.5 vs 1,325.4 us under I2C contention (2.3x faster). The three-transaction I2C read protocol, not the silicon's classification, is the dominant latency contributor. We additionally characterize a reproducible 706.5 ms MLC decision cadence that bounds full stimulus-to-decision latency. Code, data, and pre-registration: github.com/akulswami/sensor-mlc-latency.
authors: Akul Swami; Dnyaneshwar Sonawane

title: Yearning to Be Our Younger Self: The Relationship Between Grief and Yearning to Internalized Ageism and Ableism
abstract: Internalized ageist and ableist beliefs significantly influence health outcomes, happiness, and longevity. Idealization of youth and pervasive ageist and ableist narratives devalue aging, contributing to perceptions of later life and potentially fostering grief over lost opportunities. To develop evidence-based interventions, it is essential to examine the potential relationship between grief, yearning, and fears about aging. A cross-sectional survey was conducted using ResearchMatch, and 384 individuals responded to questions regarding ageism, ableism, and experiences with grief. Yearning was significantly associated with internalized ageism, excessive fear of aging, and loss of physical health. Grief was significantly associated with age, internalized ageism, and excessive fear of aging. Interventions to address feelings of loss as we age, both experienced and anticipated, can be developed to address and improve personal attitudes toward growing older.
authors: Tracey L. Gendron; Kris Geerken

title: Your Programming Students' Cognition with ChatGPT: Higher Performance, Lower Retention, and Reduced Ownership
abstract: Generative AI can improve students' programming performance, but successful task completion may not reflect what they retain. We examined performance, retention, cognitive load, and ownership in a controlled between-subjects experiment with 59 undergraduate computer science students, 55 were retained for analysis. Participants completed three introductory C programming tasks with access to ChatGPT-4.5 or conventional web search without generative AI. We measured task performance, self-reported mental effort and difficulty, pupillary responses, heart rate variability, and ownership, and assessed cued recall immediately and 48 hours later. ChatGPT-assisted students achieved higher coding scores (89% vs. 69%) but lower recall scores immediately (41% vs. 53%) and after 48 hours (39% vs. 52%). There was no significant difference in the loss of recall information over 48 hours between the groups. Self-reported mental effort increased less across tasks in the ChatGPT condition (Holm-adjusted p = .047), and students attributed less of the submitted code to themselves (45% vs. 81%). Confirmatory physiological tests did not detect significant differences in trajectories between conditions; substantial data loss limits their interpretation. These findings reveal a gap between assisted task performance and subsequent recall and sense of ownership in this setting. They motivate the need for assessment practices and AI learning tools that require students to explain, retrieve, and contribute to the work they submit as active participants in their education.
authors: Christian Henrik Bergh; Benjamin Tag; Alexandra Vassar; J. Renzella

title: 3D-printed reconfigurable magnetic soft millirobots for intelligent digital microfluidics
abstract: Magnetic digital microfluidics (MDM) offers an attractive approach to miniaturised in vitro diagnostics, but most conventional platforms remain limited to predefined, planar droplet handling without the ability to rectify operation failures. Here, we present an intelligent MDM platform in which magnetic soft millirobots (MSMRs) function as reconfigurable robotic end-effectors for 3D droplet manipulation under closed-loop control based on 2D visual detection and height-dependent perspective correction. A magnetic pick-and-place mechanism exchanges a 3D-printed MSMR gripper and pipettor on demand. These MSMRs transport, merge, dispense, and split droplets, as well as collect and resuspend bacterial colonies in an oil-immersed workspace. The MSMR gripper captured 10–30 μL droplets with a success rate above 95%, and the MSMR pipettor dispensed 5.19 μL droplets with a coefficient of variation of 2.1%. Both tools retained their droplet-handling function after 10 000 reversible actuation cycles. The computer vision module enables real-time recognition and tracking, spatial calibration, operation verification, failure rectification, and result interpretation. With samples, reagents, and protocols preloaded, the platform autonomously completed the Carba NP assay for detecting carbapenemase-producing Enterobacteriaceae. These results establish MSMRs as a promising strategy for adaptive, failure-aware MDM platforms for diagnostic automation.
authors: Aiwu Zhou; Yuxuan Tang; Zhengnan Sun; Liang Zhou; Hanyu Yang; Qian Wang; Kang Li; Ciprian Iliescu; Xiaosheng Zhang; Yi Zhang

title: 4D bioprinting in advanced cancer model: technologies, drug delivery, and translational challenges
abstract: Recent advances in 3D and 4D bioprinting have enabled the development of physiologically relevant cancer models that better mimic the spatial and temporal complexity of tumor biology. 4D bioprinting integrates intelligent biomaterials, stimuli-responsive bioinks, and computational design to produce constructs capable of planned, time-dependent modifications in structure or function after printing. Such dynamic features could be useful for modeling tumor microenvironment (TME) evolution, cancer progression, therapeutic responses, and spatio-temporally controlled drug delivery. Prior reviews predominantly address 4D printing technologies, stimuli-responsive materials, or general tissue-engineering applications. This review proposes an oncology-centered framework to critically discuss whether temporal actuation grants measurable biological and predictive advantages over traditional static 3D cancer models. Special focus is placed on distinguishing dynamically changing 4D cancer constructs from advanced 3D systems with restricted stimulus-responsive behavior and on relating dynamic material behavior to TME remodeling, invasion, drug response, and therapeutic delivery. The review also incorporates AI-based analytics (Artificial Intelligence), microfluidics, computational modeling, and quantitative benchmarking into a framework for predictive validation. Finally, the translational readiness is critically assessed for reproducibility, standardization, scalability, biosafety, and regulatory and clinical applicability. We identify critical gaps in the evidence and propose a biology-to-translation paradigm that integrates dynamic biofabrication, tumor biology, quantitative validation, predictive drug-response assessment, and translational concerns. Current 4D-bioprinted cancer models are at Technology Readiness Levels 3-5 (experimental proof-of-concept to active preclinical validation), and no 4D-bioprinted cancer therapy has yet entered the clinical trial stage. Realization of predictive, clinically relevant oncology platforms will require significant advances in standardization, scalable manufacturing, and regulatory clarity.
authors: Santoshini Nayak; Snehamayee Mohapatra; Rajat Kumar Kar
venue: Journal of Biomaterials Science Polymer Edition

title: A CRISPR/Cas12a-based digital microfluidic platform for parallel detection of foodborne pathogens.
abstract: Rapid and automated on-chip detection of multiple foodborne bacterial pathogens remains challenging because conventional molecular assays require multistep liquid handling and are difficult to integrate for parallel analysis. Here, we developed an EWOD-based DMF platform integrating RPA with CRISPR/Cas12a for parallel detection of S. aureus, E. coli O157:H7, L. monocytogenes, and C. sakazakii. The 16-site DMF chip was organized into four pathogen-specific detection modules, each containing a positive control, a negative control, and two replicate sample sites, enabling programmable droplet manipulation and sequential on-chip amplification and fluorescence detection without external pumps or complex valves. Assay conditions were systematically optimized for fluidic compatibility and CRISPR/Cas12a performance. Following off-chip sample preparation and genomic DNA extraction, the automated on-chip RPA amplification and CRISPR/Cas12a detection workflow was completed within approximately 50 min. Under these conditions, the platform achieved detection limits of 103, 102, 10, and 102 CFU/mL for S. aureus, E. coli O157:H7, L. monocytogenes, and C. sakazakii, respectively. No apparent cross-reactivity was observed among 35 food-associated bacterial strains. In artificially contaminated milk, milk powder, and chicken samples, comparable detection limits were obtained after off-chip sample processing, despite matrix-dependent variations in fluorescence intensity. These results demonstrate that integrating EWOD-based digital microfluidics with RPA and CRISPR/Cas12a enables rapid, parallelized, and programmable molecular detection of multiple foodborne bacterial pathogens on a compact platform. By integrating droplet manipulation, amplification, and fluorescence detection on-chip, the proposed system reduces reliance on external fluidic components and provides a promising basis for further development toward automated and integrated food-safety testing.
authors: Yinglin Wang; Yafang Wu; Xiaotian Huang; Yachen Tian; Qing Liu

title: A Calibrated Lightweight CNN Ensemble with CIELABCLAHE Preprocessing for White Blood Cell Classification and Hematological Disorder Screening
abstract: White blood cell (WBC) classification is a clinically critical task in hematology, underpinning the diagnosis of blood malignancies, including leukemia, as well as infections and immune disorders. Accurate automated WBC differential counting is essential for early detection of conditions such as chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) and acute myeloid leukemia (AML), where abnormal leukocyte counts and morphology are primary diagnostic indicators. Manual differential counting is time-consuming, subjective, and prone to inter-observer variability. This paper proposes a weighted ensemble framework combining three lightweight pretrained convolutional neural networks (CNNs): EfficientNet-B0, MobileNetV3-Small, and MobileNetV3-Large for automated four-class WBC classification on Paul Mooney’s Blood Cell Images dataset (BCCD, Kaggle). A standardized preprocessing pipeline was employed to enhance nuclear contrast and normalize photometric variability. Each backbone was finetuned under a two-phase transfer-learning protocol with AdamW optimization and cosine annealing scheduling. Model evaluation was conducted via stratified 3-fold cross-validation, and ensemble predictions were aggregated using accuracy-weighted soft voting. The proposed ensemble achieved a classification accuracy of 98.57%, a weighted F1-score of 0.9857, a Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) of 0.9810, and a mean AUC of 0.9994. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of ensemble-based transfer learning combined with targeted preprocessing for robust, well-calibrated WBC classification, with direct applicability to clinical laboratory automation.
authors: Aya Achir; Ilham Battas; Ikram Debbarh; Hicham Medromi; Fouad Moutaouakkil
venue: International Journal of Online and Biomedical Engineering (iJOE)

title: A Highly Efficient DLD Microfluidic Chip With Two‐Stage Inclined Elliptical Pillars for Particle Separation and Purification
abstract: Deterministic lateral displacement (DLD), a hydrodynamic particle manipulation technology, has been extensively studied for the development of fast and efficient microfluidic chips for particle manipulation and detection. However, particles are prone to clogging in DLD chips with closely spaced pillars, which can reduce sorting efficiency. Previous studies have shown that elliptical pillars provide better separation performance than equilateral triangular pillars. In elliptical-pillar DLD, a negative angle of inclination (Aoi) reduces the particle period and facilitates efficient isolation of large particles, whereas a positive Aoi decreases the critical diameter, thereby improving the sorting of smaller particles. On the basis of these findings, we designed a two-stage DLD microfluidic chip with inclined elliptical-pillar arrays, using an Aoi of -45° in the first stage and 45° in the second stage. The combination of negative and positive Aoi values enhanced the isolation of large particles, improved the purification of medium- and small-sized particles, and reduced the risk of clogging. This design provides a practical approach for improving the separation and purification performance of DLD devices and offers potential for efficient multi-size particle separation.
authors: Di Jiang; Yujiang Li; Jiawen Guo; Pengcheng Zhao; Bin Wu

title: A LITERATURE REVIEW OF RADIAL BASIS FUNCTION NEURAL NETWORKS FOR BLAST EXPLOSIVE PREDICTION
abstract: This review paper examines the development and application of Radial Basis Function Neural Networks (RBFNN) for predicting blast explosive effects. Addressing the complexities of nonlinear and multi-physics blast phenomena, it highlights the advantages of data-driven approaches over traditional analytical methods. The paper presents the fundamentals of RBF networks, including their architecture, training techniques, and optimization strategies, emphasizing their capacity for universal function approximation and adaptability. A broad range of application domains such as mechanical control systems, energy and environmental modelling, medical diagnostics, and materials science underscore the versatility of RBF models. Performance evaluations demonstrate their robustness and accuracy in handling nonlinearities and uncertainties, although challenges related to computational complexity and data limitations persist. The review discusses hybrid modelling approaches and emerging methodologies like quantum kernels and interpretable artificial intelligence to address existing gaps. Ultimately, this synthesis underscores the significant potential of RBF neural networks in advancing blast effect prediction and suggests pathways for future research integrating novel computational techniques to further enhance prediction accuracy and reliability.
authors: Fakroul Ridzuan Hashim; Muhamad Izzuddin Abd Rahman; Kamsani Kamal; Mohd Fauzy Mohd Nor; Mohammed Alias Yusof; Suwimol Jungjit
venue: Journal of Defence Science Engineering & Technology

title: A Modular Micro‐Chemostat System for High‐Throughput Continuous Cultivations
abstract: ABSTRACT Improving the fidelity of computational eukaryotic models will require an enormous amount of high quality and reproducible data from biological experiments. In this study we present and demonstrate a modular 12‐channel micro‐chemostat system. This micro‐chemostat is designed for use by Genesis, a Robot Scientist developed to automate scientific research in yeast systems biology. We performed bioreactor characterization experiments to evaluate the performance of the micro‐chemostat system. We also cultivated the Saccharomyces cerevisiae reference strain, BY4741, at three different dilution rates (0.1, 0.2, and 0.3 h −1 ) and under two aeration conditions (microaerobic and aerobic), resulting in six different conditions. The bioreactor performance fulfilled our requirements, and enabled substrate‐limited continuous cultivation of yeast. Furthermore, the empirical results from the biological experiments were consistent with the literature, suggesting that results obtained from our system are comparable to those reported for other platforms in the field. Based on the evidence presented in this study, we conclude that the 12‐channel micro‐chemostat system is a suitable platform for yeast systems biology research. The modular design of the micro‐chemostat system enables future scaling to hundreds or thousands of concurrent chemostats and facilitates integration with autonomous agents for automated optimization and improvement of eukaryotic model systems.
authors: Erik Y. Bjurström; Filip Kronström; Ronald S. Reiserer; David K. Schaffer; Dmitry A. Markov; John P. Wikswo; Ross D. King; Ievgeniia Tiukova

title: A Safety-Governed Architecture for Adaptive Sequential Evidence Selection from Pre-Recorded Gait Data
abstract: Sequential evidence selection can reveal which parts of an existing sensor record reduce model uncertainty, while providing a computational test bed for future adaptive sensing. This work introduces the Embodied Evidence Acquisition and Reasoning Loop (EARL), a typed architecture in which five role-specialized critics score evidence requests and a deterministic safety governor retains exclusive execution authority. Observed, derived, and simulated evidence remain provenance-distinct in a replayable, hash-linked ledger. The primary experiment sequentially disclosed precomputed feature bundles from pre-recorded gait data; it did not acquire new measurements. EARL was evaluated on 64 unique subjects from the PhysioNet Gait in Neurodegenerative Disease Database using repeated subject-level cross-validation, 11 predeclared conditions, and 3520 replay-verified runs. The primary endpoint was area under cumulative posterior-entropy reduction. EARL achieved 7.689 (95% CI 7.535-7.840), exceeding fixed-order and random selection by 0.459 and 0.763, respectively; the EARL-minus-EIG difference was -0.321. EARL had descriptively higher macro accuracy (55.8% versus 49.5%) and a lower Brier score (0.781 versus 0.813) than pure expected-information-gain selection. This measures an entropy-efficiency trade-off under additional selection criteria, not universal superiority. All 10 original software safety challenges produced their expected outcomes. Separately identified post hoc analyses examine probe use, a sensitivity analysis excluding the record-quality probe, critic influence, illustrative resource costs, early stopping, and safety-constrained simulated execution. The small retrospective cohort and illustrative simulations establish software behavior, not clinical diagnostic performance, treatment benefit, physical-robot safety, or patient efficacy.
authors: Giulio Leone; Daniela D’Auria

title: A Scalable Droplet Microfluidic Platform That Overcomes Large‐Cell Constraints for Long‐Term Plant Cell Culture and Embryogenesis Analysis
abstract: Microspore-derived embryogenesis (MDE) is essential for doubled haploid (DH) plant breeding, but conventional bulk culture systems are limited by poor scalability and difficulty for automation. Adapting droplet microfluidics for plant cell culture is promising but challenging due to the large size and fragility of plant cells involved in embryogenesis, such as maize microspores (60-85 µm) and their expanding embryo-like structures (200-500 µm). Here, we present a droplet microfluidic platform engineered for large plant cells, integrating a tubing-based loading strategy that minimizes sedimentation losses, robust generation of stable 20 and 200 nL droplets optimized for large-cell encapsulation, and scalable 3D reservoir incubation for long-term culture. Optimized flow conditions and surface treatments enabled cell encapsulation with high fidelity, sustaining viability for over two weeks. Multi-modal viability assessment using fluorescence spectroscopy and microscopy (bright-field and fluorescence) confirmed that droplet culture preserves cell health comparably to bulk methods. The platform supports both single-cell and few-cell encapsulation modes, and increasing droplet volume and cell loading density further enhances embryogenesis rates and total embryo yield, respectively. Together, these advances establish a scalable, modular droplet microfluidic platform for high-throughput embryogenesis analysis and embryo production, offering new opportunities in plant developmental biology, precision breeding, and doubled-haploid technology.
authors: Arman Mirmiran; Fangchi Shao; Gregory Datto; Tathansh Joshi; Elizabeth C. Chatt; Yashar Bashirzadeh; Dan Stessman; Lai Wei; Hsieh KuangWen; Hena Guo; Tza‐Huei Wang

title: A comprehensive review of machine learning in proton-exchange membrane fuel cells: From materials to intelligent systems
abstract: Machine learning (ML) is rapidly transforming proton-exchange membrane fuel cell (PEMFC) science by enabling advances across materials design, multiscale modeling, diagnostics, and intelligent control. Persistent barriers to widespread PEMFC deployment—including high cost, limited durability, and complex multiscale transport phenomena—arise from nonlinear interactions that conventional modeling and experimentation struggle to resolve. This review presents a comprehensive synthesis of ML approaches tailored to the PEMFC value chain, showing how numerical, experimental, imaging, and hybrid datasets support surrogate models that reduce Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) computational costs by orders of magnitude while maintaining physical consistency through physics-informed and multi-fidelity learning. ML-guided optimization accelerates the rational design of catalyst layers, membranes, gas-diffusion media, and bipolar plates, uncovering non-intuitive structure–property relationships. Deep-learning-based diagnostics and hybrid residual frameworks significantly improve fault detection, state-of-health estimation, and remaining-useful-life prediction. At the system scale, ML-enhanced model predictive control and deep reinforcement learning enable adaptive, autonomous operation under dynamic conditions, while emerging digital-twin architectures integrate physics-based solvers with real-time data assimilation to deliver predictive, self-correcting fuel-cell management. By unifying methodological advances, cross-scale opportunities, and critical challenges, this review establishes ML as a foundational enabler for the next generation of high-performance, durable, and economically viable PEMFC technologies.
