title: Aptamers as a sandbox for lab-in-the-loop agentic molecular discovery
abstract: Despite breakthroughs in AI-driven molecular generation, existing discovery pipelines operate largely in silico, with wet-lab feedback reserved for validation rather than iterative improvement. Whether large language model (LLM)-based reasoning agents can accelerate de novo discovery by iterating with lab data remains unproven. Here we use protein-binding aptamer design as a sandbox (1-2 week cycles, \$1-\$3 per candidate) to demonstrate a wet lab in a closed loop with AI systems. We tasked agentic pipelines with developing aptamer binders against $α$-thrombin and myoglobin across three design-test-improve cycles ($\sim$1,000 candidates per round; $\sim$4,400 constructs). Statistically significant, bead-corrected on-target hit rates among new candidates rose across rounds from 0.0% in Round 1 to 26.0% in Round 2 and 42.1% in Round 3 on $α$-thrombin (37.1% excluding literature motif descendants), and from 10.2% in Round 1 to 3.7% in Round 2 and 33.5% in Round 3 on myoglobin. Single-clone bead-binding titrations of eight full-length $α$-thrombin candidates confirmed concordance with pooled sequencing enrichment (Pearson $r = 0.90$). In these assays, literature-derived motifs engineered by the agents to reduce off-target reactivity in the pooled screen reached apparent affinities of $K_D = 24.6$--$133$ nM, whereas de novo scaffolds showed low-micromolar binding ($K_D > 1\ μ$M). We also report how our pipelines used myoglobin binding data to exploit the G-quadruplex binder space, diagnose cross-reactivity as on-target specificity dropped from 75.0% to 19.1%, and recover by developing strategies that restored specificity to 72.4%. We demonstrate that empirical lab data is more valuable than existing computational proxies, showing how iterative experimental feedback enables AI agents to diagnose assay artifacts and refine molecular designs across rounds.
authors: Zachary Cutts; John Coller; Rachel Chen; Hua Tang; Mathias Bellaiche; Ryder Easterlin; Dina Zverinski; Petar Sirkovic; Avinatan Hassidim; Yossi Matias; Pooja Rao; Annalisa Pawlosky

title: Artificial Intelligence Virtual Organoid Laboratories (AIVO-Labs)
abstract: Organoids reproduce important tissue features, but variability in biomaterials and culture, labor-intensive workflows, limited standardization, and predominantly endpoint readouts constrain reproducibility and longitudinal interpretation. We propose Artificial Intelligence Virtual Organoid Laboratories (AIVO-Labs), a closed-loop experimental paradigm that couples physical organoid experiments with Artificial Intelligence Virtual Organoids (AIVOs) as continuously updated digital twins. Unlike an AIVO, which represents an individual organoid-scale computational counterpart, an AIVO-Lab is a laboratory-level, cross-experimental platform that coordinates data acquisition, model calibration, experiment selection, and prospective wet-lab validation across repeated cycles. In this bidirectional workflow, each physical result updates the AIVO, while model predictions prioritize the next experiment, directly addressing slow iteration, variable protocols, and endpoint-focused analysis. The framework builds on Artificial Intelligence Virtual Cells (AIVCs), which encode multimodal cell states as universal representations that can be interrogated by virtual instruments, and extends them to organoid scale through models of cell-cell and cell-matrix interactions. We outline a three-layer architecture comprising data, model, and interaction layers and discuss applications in drug screening, mechanism and resistance mapping, developmental and disease trajectories, and toxicology. AIVO-Labs are presented as a research framework whose predictions require prospective validation, transparent uncertainty estimates, and appropriate governance.
authors: Long Bai; Jian Wang; Jiacan Su

title: Artificial Intelligence and Sensing Technologies for Vascular Access in Hemodialysis: A Narrative Review
abstract: Vascular access performance determines the adequacy, safety, and cost of hemodialysis. Stenosis, thrombosis, cannulation difficulty, infection, and access-related cardiac stress remain major sources of morbidity. This narrative review examines artificial intelligence and sensing technologies for vascular access care, based on PubMed and ClinicalTrials.gov searches through 22 August 2026 with citation chaining. Existing reviews have examined artificial intelligence in dialysis broadly or prediction models in isolation. In this review, the vascular access itself is kept as the unit of analysis, and the evidence is followed across four connected stages: systemic risk stratification; prediction of maturation, dysfunction, and complications from clinical, ultrasound, and multimodal data; longitudinal monitoring with optical, acoustic, vibration, thermal, and pressure sensors; and procedural support with robotics and visualization technologies. Reported discrimination is high in retrospective, recording-level analyses, reaching areas under the curve of 0.99 and sample-level accuracy of 100%, but falls to approximately 0.71 in longitudinal designs that predict future events in the same patients; patient-level external validation and calibration are also rarely reported. No approach has yet been demonstrated to reduce thrombosis, prolong patency, avoid interventions, or lower cost relative to standard care in prospective multicenter studies. Deployment is further constrained by power budgets, duty cycling, and transmission bandwidth in wearable devices. Technical feasibility should not be read as clinical utility.
authors: Concetto Sessa; Elettra Lomeo; Walter Morale; Tito Gianni; Bibiana Bonerba; Giuseppe Grandaliano; Francesco Pesce

title: Artificial Intelligence in Infection Prevention: From Prediction to Protection
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), first defined by John McCarthy in 1955, refers to the science of developing intelligent machines capable of performing tasks that traditionally require human reasoning, learning, and decision-making. Since its early development in the 1960s and rapid expansion in the 2000s, AI has evolved substantially, driven by the availability of large digital health datasets, advances in machine learning, and increased computational power. In infection prevention and control (IPC), AI is emerging as a powerful tool for strengthening surveillance, improving diagnostic accuracy, predicting outbreaks, and supporting timely clinical interventions. AI-powered systems can analyze electronic health records (EHRs), laboratory results, antimicrobial prescribing patterns, microbiological data, patient demographics, and real-time hospital surveillance information to identify patients at high risk of infection and detect potential healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) at an early stage. Furthermore, AI can support antimicrobial stewardship by identifying inappropriate prescribing patterns and predicting antimicrobial resistance trends. Integration of data from wearable devices, environmental sensors, imaging systems, and unstructured clinical notes can provide continuous, real-time monitoring of infectious diseases and infection risks. AI-enabled computer vision and sensor-based technologies may also facilitate automated hand hygiene monitoring, helping healthcare facilities improve compliance with infection-control practices. Predictive models can identify emerging clusters of infection and assist public health teams in forecasting potential outbreaks, enabling earlier containment measures. Thus, AI effectively bridges prediction and protection, enhancing patient safety, healthcare quality, and operational efficiency. However, successful implementation requires high-quality data, robust validation, privacy protection, ethical governance, transparency, and recognition of the limitations of correlation-based predictions.
authors: Madhumita Das

title: Artificial intelligence across the drug discovery pipeline: From data integration to precision therapeutics
abstract: Bringing a single medicine from an idea to a patient's prescription still typically takes over a decade, costs well beyond a billion dollars, and fails more often than it succeeds, and artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a data-centric response to this long-standing inefficiency by analysing complex biomedical datasets at a scale and speed that traditional, hypothesis-driven pipelines cannot match. This review offers a forward-looking synthesis of AI-enabled drug discovery, tracing how multi-omics data integration, knowledge graphs, generative modeling, and structure-based computation are converging into a single computational discipline, drawing on a narrative review of recent peer-reviewed literature to assess progress in data harmonization, multi-omics integration, protein structure prediction, molecular docking, de novo molecule design, molecular dynamics, biologics engineering, clinical trial design, and autonomous laboratories. Across these domains, AI has shown potential to improve interoperability through knowledge graphs and FAIR data ecosystems, sharpen the analysis of disease mechanisms and biomarkers, and accelerate target identification in computational and retrospective studies. Protein structure prediction, generative molecular design, and structure-based discovery have shortened selected lead-optimization cycles in preclinical settings. AI is also being explored in biologics development, precision medicine, adaptive clinical trials, and closed-loop autonomous experimentation, although prospective clinical validation and regulatory adoption remain limited. Overall, AI is becoming a foundational technology of contemporary drug discovery by combining biological data, computational modeling, and laboratory automation into a single feedback loop, and realizing its full potential will depend on continued progress in model explainability, data standardization, and rigorous translational validation.
authors: Abhishek Kumar; Pranesh Kumar; Namrata Singh; Prashant Kumar Singh; Anshi Singh
venue: The Journal of Precision Medicine Health and Disease

title: Artificial intelligence for extracellular vesicle engineering and therapeutic design
abstract: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are promising platforms for next-generation drug delivery and regenerative therapeutics, yet biological heterogeneity, limited targeting specificity, variable cargo composition, and continued reliance on empirical optimization hinder clinical translation. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers new opportunities to make EV engineering more predictive and data-driven. Building on prior work in AI-assisted EV delivery and emerging virtual-EV modeling, this review presents an evidence-aware, multiscale framework that integrates parental-cell programming, vesicle design, recipient-system modeling, and experimental feedback. At the source level, AI virtual cells (AIVCs) may help predict how perturbations to parental cells influence EV biogenesis and composition. At the vesicle level, AI-guided approaches may support cargo prioritization, surface engineering, and loading optimization. At the recipient level, digital twin models could help simulate EV uptake, intracellular trafficking, microenvironmental interactions, and downstream therapeutic responses. These components may ultimately be integrated with experimental validation into iterative design-test-refinement workflows. Importantly, this review distinguishes direct EV-specific evidence from technologies transferable from adjacent fields and concepts that remain prospective. By defining these evidence boundaries and linking them to key challenges in data quality, model interpretability, manufacturing, and validation, this framework provides a practical roadmap for advancing AI-enabled EV therapeutics from conceptual modeling to testable, translationally relevant engineering strategies.
authors: Yunwei Wang; Qingchen Meng; Hui Li; Bonan Zhang; Dan Xing
venue: Extracellular Vesicles and Circulating Nucleic Acids

title: Artificial intelligence for precision gene therapy: emerging technologies, clinical applications, and future directions
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is revolutionizing gene therapy from an empirical and iterative process to a predictive, data-driven and increasingly intelligent therapeutic development approach. This review covers the application of AI extensively throughout the gene therapy development process, from target therapeutic discovery, identification of disease genes, variant interpretation, integration of multi-omics data, optimization of CRISPR, engineering of the vector, prediction of immunogenicity, manufacturing, and clinical development and post-marketing surveillance. The role of machine learning, deep learning, foundation models, generative AI and digital twins for advancing therapeutic design, boosting vector performance, manufacturing optimization, patient stratification and enabling precision medicine is discussed. Lastly, we provide directions for future research and highlight the need for close multidisciplinary cooperation between computational scientists, biologists, clinicians, industry, and regulatory agencies to facilitate the development of safe, effective and personalized genetic medicines responsibly.
authors: Govinder Flora; Abhinay Thakur

title: Artificial intelligence in mechanical engineering: foundations, opportunities, challenges, and responsibilities
abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming mechanical engineering (ME) practice, influencing activities that range from modeling and simulation to optimization, diagnostics, design, and technical communication. This article consolidates perspectives discussed at a dedicated round-table during the 28th ABCM International Congress on Mechanical Engineering—COBEM 2025—and offers a structured reflection for the Brazilian and international ME communities. Rather than providing an exhaustive survey, the paper develops a coherent narrative around the conditions under which AI can strengthen—rather than dilute—engineering rigor. The article begins by clarifying how contemporary AI systems operate, distinguishing statistical learning from human cognition and outlining their capabilities, limitations, and emerging agentic AI systems. It then examines industrial adoption, workforce transformation, and the growing role of AI in scientific discovery and engineering workflows. Particular attention is devoted to the energy and infrastructure demands of AI-driven computation and their implications for sustainability, power systems, and thermal management. Building on these constraints, the paper discusses integrating physical knowledge, structured reasoning, and domain expertise into AI systems for safety-relevant engineering applications. Emphasis is placed on representative ME applications, physics-informed and hybrid learning frameworks, model development under physical constraints, validation, uncertainty quantification, and certification challenges. The paper also addresses the educational, epistemological, and ethical implications of AI, including curriculum modernization, human-agent collaboration, professional accountability, and the long-term sustainability of engineering knowledge. It concludes with a synthesis of principles for the responsible adoption of AI in ME, encompassing physical consistency, validation, awareness of uncertainty, energy sustainability, human oversight, and ethical responsibility. Our central message is that AI should be viewed not as a substitute for engineering judgment, but as a powerful tool whose value depends on disciplined integration with physical reasoning, scientific rigor, and professional responsibility.
authors: Américo Cunha; Chandrasekhar Nataraj; Luciano M. Lorenzo; Hervé Panetto; Américo Scotti; JOSÉ VIRIATO COELHO VARGAS
venue: Journal of the Brazilian Society of Mechanical Sciences and Engineering

title: Artificial intelligence in mental health: benefits and challenges of electronic health records
abstract: A incorporação de novas tecnologias de inteligência artificial aos electronic healthcare records (EHRs) tem proporcionado um forte aumento na capacidade de acumular e analisar dados dos pacientes. E a área de saúde mental tem sido uma das beneficiárias deste potencial de melhorias, proporcionando aos seus profissionais ganhos de tempo e eficiência na gestão de informações médicas. Entretanto, há relatos de problemas que estão surgindo na medida em que a utilização das tecnologias de IA se intensifica. Este quadro inclui questões referentes à gestão de informações sensíveis dos pacientes, à falta de padronização dos dados de saúde mental, prejudicando a interoperabilidade dos mesmos, o receio de que o relacionamento terapêutico paciente-profissional seja prejudicado, além da preocupação que os profissionais estão tendo pela possibilidade de serem substituídos pelas tecnologias de IA. Considerando este contexto, o presente artigo tem por objetivo identificar e analisar a dinâmica de incorporação das tecnologias de IA à área de saúde mental. Para realizar este objetivo, foi realizada uma revisão de literatura envolvendo publicações sobre o tema dos últimos seis anos. Ao final, são oferecidas algumas sugestões para desenvolvimento de futuras pesquisas que possam explorar mais possíveis soluções para os problemas identificados, ao longo do processo de adoção de novas tecnologias de IA na área de saúde mental que está em curso.
authors: Bento Alves Costa Filho; Daniel Sousa Jorge; Felipe Luiz de Morais

title: Artificial intelligence in microfluidic biosensors: From signal processing to closed-loop detection
authors: Rong Xu; Veronika Le; Maria Abbasi; Mariam Shakeel; Shengnan Ma; Gong Jiale; Xiaoya Wan; Ge Ni; Fang Liu; Aiqin Luo; Tianyu Huang; Lina Geng

title: Atoms to Processes: The Role of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning in Chemical Engineering
abstract: Abstract The rapid maturation of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) has catalyzed a profound shift in how chemical engineering problems are formulated, analyzed, and solved. Advances in computing, data availability, and learning algorithms have enabled AI/ML methods to impact applications spanning atomic-scale simulations, materials and catalyst discovery, transport and thermodynamics, separations, process systems engineering, and industrial operations. This Perspective provides an account of recent methodological developments and representative applications, emphasizing how AI/ML tools are being integrated with first-principles models to address challenges of predictive accuracy, data scarcity, extrapolation, interpretability, and model life cycle management. Across domains, a unifying trend is the move away from purely black-box approaches toward hybrid and physics-informed frameworks that explicitly respect conservation laws, thermodynamic consistency, and known structural constraints. These approaches not only improve robustness and reliability but also enable meaningful human–AI collaboration by providing information at an appropriate level of abstraction for the task and decision context. We conclude that AI and ML are not replacing the core principles of chemical engineering; rather, they are amplifying them. As the field advances toward increasingly autonomous, adaptive, and sustainable systems, the thoughtful integration of AI/ML with first-principles understanding and domain expertise will be essential to realizing their full potential across both research and industrial practice.
authors: Michael Bâldea; Linda J. Broadbelt; Marianthi Ierapetritou; Akhilesh Jain; Ankur Kumar; Thomas Alan Kwan; Fèlix Llovell; Andrew James Medford; Ilias Mitrai; Joel A. Paulson; Junyi Qiao; Matthew P. Rivera; Kirti Chandra Sahu; Lev Sarkisov; Zachary P. Smith; Calvin Tsay; Ching-Mei Wen; Ví­ctor M. Zavala; Huacheng Zhang; Dan Zhao

title: Auditing LLM Chemical Priors for Multi-Objective Bayesian Optimization of Chemical Reactions: A Validity, Alignment, and Diversity Benchmark
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed as priors for cold-starting Bayesian optimization (BO) of chemical reactions, yet their benefit–risk profile in multi-objective reaction optimization remains poorly characterized. We present a systematic benchmark asking when LLM knowledge helps, is neutral, or hurts multi-objective BO (MOBO). Across seven public reaction benchmarks (6,384 candidate experiments), we compare nine strategies—including LLM-initialized BO, an LLM-only initializer, and established baselines (TSEMO, EDBO+-style scalarization, LLAMBO)—with 20 seeds per configuration (1,120 main-grid plus 360 ablation campaigns), scored by hypervolume completion and its sampling-efficiency integral (AUC), with paired Wilcoxon tests and two-family Benjamini–Hochberg correction against a random-init BO control. Three regimes emerge. On Suzuki–Miyaura, LLM initialization significantly improves sampling efficiency (ΔAUC +2.0 points, q = 0.026; alternative backbone +2.7 points, q = 1.4 × 10⁻⁴). On Buchwald–Hartwig, LLM priors are statistically indistinguishable from random. On a process-development coupling, LLM initialization significantly harms efficiency (ΔAUC −11.1 points, q = 0.0016) despite a 0% out-of-pool rate, whereas the Suzuki benefit coexists with a 45% out-of-pool rate—the prior’s direction, not its syntactic validity, controls the outcome. Diversity-based initialization (farthest point sampling) matches or exceeds LLM initialization wherever LLMs help, and no LLM-derived benefit exceeds what the knowledge-free diversity control already provides. A five-category diagnostic protocol intercepts 100% out-of-pool suggestions on the flow cases at zero experimental cost. LLM priors are not yet a reliable default for multi-objective reaction optimization; we provide a cost-free pre-campaign screening heuristic for deciding when to trust them.
authors: Fan Zhang

title: AutoPruner: Agentic Depth Pruning for Vision-Language-Action Models
abstract: Layer pruning reduces the size and inference cost of vision-language-action (VLA) models, but selecting a deployable configuration requires deciding both which layers to remove and how to recover task performance. These decisions depend on the model and task, and a failed trial can reflect either the deletion set or insufficient recovery. We present AutoPruner, an agent-driven framework that jointly searches pruning structures and recovery recipes through closed-loop experimentation. Offline layer interventions measure changes in action output to provide functional evidence. An LLM agent combines this evidence with evaluation history and retained diagnoses to propose deletion sets and recovery recipes within a search budget. Each proposal is executed and evaluated on the target tasks, and the resulting feedback guides the next experiment. Across OpenVLA-OFT, StarVLA, and FastWAM on four LIBERO suites, AutoPruner removes 16.7--87.5% of backbone layers while maintaining task success above 90%, with measured inference speedups of up to 2.50$\times$. Further analysis shows that functional probes identify action-sensitive layers despite high representation similarity, and that recovery can make previously failing structures viable.
authors: Tao Lin; Yikeng Chen; Qiwei Liang; Zinan Xie; Zhengtu Liang; Renjing Xu

title: Automated DNA-Encoded Library Synthesis on Magnetic Anion Exchange Resin
abstract: Abstract DNA-encoded libraries (DELs) access vast chemical spaces for drug discovery, but split-and-pool DEL synthesis remains the sole and very manual portion of the DEL workflow. Here, we automate DEL construction using diethylaminoethyl-functionalized weak anion exchange (WAX) magnetic resin and a KingFisher Apex particle-handling instrument. DNA encoding occurs in solution, followed by selective immobilization of DNA conjugates under low-salt conditions that exclude > 95% of unused encoding oligonucleotides. On-DNA chemistry then proceeds using the WAX resin-adsorbed “WAX-ON” DNA substrate in neat organic solvent. The platform supports amide formation, reductive amination, copper-catalyzed azide–alkyne cycloaddition, and Fmoc removal. Automated bead transfer enables iterative reaction and washing cycles. We synthesized two-cycle 9,216-member DELs from 96 Fmoc-protected amino acids and 96 carboxylic acids. Control selections reproducibly enriched the carbonic anhydrase ligand sulfamoylbenzoic acid. Magnetic WAX-ON DEL synthesis is compatible with diverse chemistries and uses the same instrumentation to automate DEL construction and affinity screening.
authors: Valerie J. Cavett; Santino L DeGirolamo; Erika Černá; Robert D. Damoiseaux; Brian M. Paegel

title: Automated Materials Data and Knowledge Extraction using Machine Learning and Large Language Models
abstract: Over the past decade, substantial efforts have been devoted to developing machine learning (ML) methods for extracting materials data and, where possible, materials knowledge directly from the scientific literature. This review traces the evolution of these methods from heuristic, rule-based pipelines through natural language processing (NLP) models and transformer-based encoders to, lastly, large language models (LLMs) and agentic systems capable of extracting materials information across multiple modalities, including text, tables, and figures. Beside construction of large, queryable materials databases and knowledge graphs that support downstream materials discovery, we discuss how these advances have enabled new capabilities, such as, generic question answering across materials science, AI co-scientists and chatbots for research assistance, and closed-loop optimization and discovery when integrated with autonomous laboratories. We critically assess the datasets generated using these approaches, their extraction accuracy and computational costs, and the respective strengths and limitations of different methodologies, and even provide practical guidelines for developing more reliable and scalable materials data extraction pipelines. Finally, we identify key open challenges, including the extraction of full materials structure-property-processing-performance tetrahedron at the sample level, the scarcity of reliable benchmark datasets for systematic evaluation, and the resolution of non-standard materials terminology across different document modalities.
authors: Arjun Sundaram; B. Pabitramohan Prusty; Rohit Batra

title: Automated Perovskite Film Fabrication with High-Resolution Data Acquisition and Machine Learning Analysis
abstract: Abstract Lead halide perovskite solar cells have emerged as promising candidates for next-generation photovoltaics; nevertheless, fabrication of the perovskite photoactive layer remains highly intricate with film formation strongly modulated by various processing and environmental factors. Here, we report an environment-controlled, robot-assisted platform for automated thin-film fabrication designed to quantify and visualize perovskite crystallization in situ. Beyond precise control of each processing step, the system captures dynamic phenomena spanning subsecond color evolution and millisecond antisolvent droplet behavior while simultaneously recording slower environmental parameters (temperature, humidity/moisture, and concentrations of oxygen and volatile organic compounds). For optoelectronic assessment, we implemented time-resolved microwave conductivity (TRMC) measurements together with photoluminescence intensity quantification by using a complementary automated evaluation system. By combining machine-learning regression with SHAP (Shapley additive explanations) analysis, we identify the environmental parameters that most impact film properties and propose a feedback strategy to refine data and extract precise effects of process factors. A comparative study of a two-cation perovskite, (FAPbI3)0.87(MAPbBr3)0.13, and a three-cation perovskite, FA0.85MA0.10Cs0.05PbI3, further reveals markedly different sensitivities to environmental factors (FA, formamidinium; MA, methylammonium), in particular, temperature and resultant phase transition kinetics during thermal annealing. Based on the ML analysis and feedback, we tuned the antisolvent droplet velocity and obtained the maximized power conversion efficiency of 24.4%. Notably, this manual device fabrication was consistent with the results obtained by the automated system. This work establishes a practical route to stable, quantitative, and mechanistically informed investigation of solution-processed photovoltaic films.
authors: Ryosuke Kado; Fumiya Iwai; Ryosuke Nishikubo; Fumitaka Ishiwari; Akinori Saeki

title: Autonomous AI research agents in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma immunology: from multimodal evidence to experimental validation
abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains one of the most challenging malignancies due to profound biological heterogeneity, complex stromal organization, and limited responsiveness to current immunotherapies. Recent advances in single-cell sequencing, spatial omics, digital pathology, and multimodal profiling have revealed that PDAC immune states are shaped not only by cellular composition but also by spatial organization, treatment context, and patient-specific evolutionary trajectories. However, the increasing complexity and fragmentation of biomedical evidence create substantial challenges for conventional artificial intelligence (AI) approaches that are typically optimized for predefined analytical tasks. Autonomous AI research agents represent an emerging paradigm that extends beyond predictive modeling by integrating scientific reasoning, retrieval of heterogeneous biomedical knowledge, computational tool orchestration, workflow adaptation, and evidence traceability. In this Review, we examine how agentic AI systems may contribute to PDAC immunology research, from characterization of immune ecosystems and spatial cellular interactions to biomarker discovery, neoantigen prioritization, and experimental protocol design. We distinguish AI agents from conventional task-specific models and discuss essential capabilities required for reliable biomedical research, including planning, tool use, verification, memory, provenance tracking, and human oversight. Despite promising technical demonstrations in biomedical domains, direct evidence supporting fully autonomous AI-driven discovery and validation in PDAC remains limited. Therefore, we propose a disease-oriented evaluation framework emphasizing benchmark task design, appropriate human and computational comparators, reproducibility assessment, and experimental validation. Future PDAC-specific AI research agents should prioritize evidence-aware reasoning, multimodal integration, calibrated uncertainty, and transparent computational-experimental workflows. Such systems may ultimately accelerate mechanistic discovery and precision immunology, while maintaining rigorous standards for biological validity, reproducibility, and responsible scientific practice.
authors: Li Yang; Yu Li; Rong Huang; Zhi-qiang San; Junfeng Ye

title: Autonomous Droplet Navigation via Model-Based Reinforcement Learning: Zero-Shot Transfer and Emergent Dynamics
abstract: Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) are transforming chemical and materials discovery through closed-loop automation, yet automated infrastructure for physical manipulation of soft, deformable matter remains beyond current robotic platforms. A critical instance is autonomous droplet transport on an open surface, where contact-angle hysteresis, capillary pinning, and surface heterogeneity produce partially observable dynamics that pose significant challenges for classical model-based controllers. We introduce the first robotic platform for closed-loop autonomous liquid droplet navigation on an open, unconfined surface using model-based reinforcement learning. A two-axis tilting board coated with a thin silicone oil film drives the droplet, while an overhead camera provides real-time feedback. A learned policy was trained on just 50 to 150 physical episodes depending on geometric complexity, without simulation or analytical models. Beyond performance alone, the platform demonstrates three capabilities of interest to the SDL community: it robustly transfers zero-shot to unseen geometries; it autonomously discovers an oscillatory depinning strategy to free the droplet when it sticks; and it completes its full training pipeline in under 90 minutes. These results extend reinforcement-learning manipulation from rigid microrobots to deformable soft-matter systems for next-generation SDLs.
authors: Rajneesh Anand; Mayuresh V. Kothare

title: Autonomous Experimentation Enables Rapid Optimization of Photochemical Continuous-Flow Synthesis of Diazaxanthilidene Fluorophores
abstract: Photoconvertible diazaxanthilidene dyes enable optical labeling and tracking in live cells, but the batch photocyclization that generates them requires days of irradiation and analog-specific optimization. Here we report a closed-loop continuous-flow platform that uses Bayesian optimization to tune light intensity, temperature, flow rate, and concentration. In campaigns on the parent diazaxanthilidene and four analogs, the platform improved throughput for four of five compounds. For the parent diazaxanthilidene, photoconversion yield rose from approximately 69% in batch to 79%, while throughput increased from 0.52 to 87 nmol min-1. The platform autonomously performs >40 optimization experiments to turn a multiday, analog-specific batch synthesis into a same-day flow synthesis.
authors: Joao Luiz P. de Albuquerque; Scott Laverty; Mao Niimura; Ari Bortman; David M. Chenoweth; Andrew F. Zahrt

title: Autonomous Materials Discovery Framework and Self-Healing Interface Architecture for High-Energy Solid-State Batteries: Operation SOLID GENESIS (サブタイトル / 和題: AGI駆動型自律材料探索による次世代全固体電池の開発基盤と界面自己修復アーキテクチャ)
abstract: Abstract (English) All-solid-state lithium secondary batteries (ASSBs) represent the foremost architecture for reconciling ultra-high energy density with non-negotiable intrinsic safety. However, severe bulk ionic transport bottlenecks within solid electrolytes and dynamic chemo-mechanical interface degradation (contact loss, interphase delamination, and lithium dendrite penetration during cycling) constitute persistent physical barriers to commercial viability. This treatise reports the theoretical framework and implementation architecture of "Operation SOLID GENESIS," an autonomous materials discovery platform integrating generative AI, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs / GNoME), and high-throughput robotic Self-Driving Laboratories (A-Lab). The architecture anchors its computational synthesis loop upon the Structure of Inviolable Decision Rules (SIDR) and an algorithmic Causal Auditor, systematically vetting and vetoing thermodynamically infeasible or hazardous reaction pathways prior to robotic execution. To eliminate structural supply chain vulnerabilities and reliance on critical scarce elements (Sc, Ge), a Scarcity Cost Vector is embedded directly into the GNN objective function, redirecting computational throughput toward earth-abundant chemical spaces (Na, Mg, Fe, Al, Mn systems). Furthermore, we formulate an intelligent "Sentient Battery" architecture combining Functionally Graded Materials (FGM) for interface stress mitigation, dynamic self-healing mechanisms via mobile ionic species (iodide-assisted recrystallization), and real-time feedforward impedance diagnostics coupled with AGI-driven Battery Management Systems (BMS). title: Autonomous Quantum Measurement with Agentic AI
abstract: Quantum materials exhibit diverse electronic and functional phenomena, but their characterization requires extensive experimental expertise, iterative decision-making and accumulated laboratory knowledge that is difficult to document and transfer. Here we introduce Quantum Agent (QUANTA), an agentic artificial intelligence (AI) framework for autonomous quantum-materials characterization. Using a widely adopted Physical Property Measurement System (PPMS) as an experimental platform, QUANTA combines retrieval augmentation using scientific literature, experimental protocols and prior measurements with specialized agents for experimental planning, troubleshooting, and data interpretation. A separate deterministic control layer validates instrument actions. Guided by incoming data, QUANTA evaluates measurement quality, revises experimental plans and selects subsequent measurements. We demonstrate these capabilities through transport measurements of the topological Weyl semimetal TaP, as well as investigations of nonlinear responses in magnetic material Co2MnGa. These results establish QUANTA as a generalizable framework for evidence-driven, safeguarded and closed-loop quantum-materials characterization.
authors: Eunbi Rha; Abhijatmedhi Chotrattanapituk; Mouyang Cheng; Chung-tao Chou; Shenyong Ye; Ashley S. Dale; Long Ju; Luqiao Liu; Mingda Li

title: Autonomous Science Bench: Evaluating AI Agents for Autonomous Scientific Discovery
abstract: AI agents for autonomous scientific discovery must decide which experiments to run under a limited budget. Most benchmarks for science agents provide fixed datasets, while others that support active experimentation largely rely on simulation. We introduce Autonomous Science Bench, an initial release comprising six budgeted design-build-test-learn campaigns grounded in published experiments across biology, chemistry, and materials science. Agents select batches of designs, receive measurements from a lab service, and use the results to guide subsequent experiments before delivering a predictive model. Success requires passing two calibrated gates: a discovery gate, which evaluates the designs the agent measured, and a learning gate, which evaluates its model's ranking of held-out designs. In a pilot evaluation of eight agent-model configurations and 144 trials, the best configuration succeeds in 67% of trials, while the hardest campaign is solved in only three of 24 attempts. The two gates reveal different weaknesses: some agents build accurate rankings but find too few promising designs, while others find promising designs but fail to predict which unseen designs will perform well. These differences are obscured by overall success rates alone. We release version 0.1 of the campaigns, lab runtime, and public leaderboard at https://yibow.me/autonomous-science-bench.
authors: Yibo Wen; Han Liu

title: Autonomous adaptive spectral analysis with an LLM agent for self-driving laboratories
abstract: Self-driving laboratories accelerate materials exploration through autonomous closed-loop integration of synthesis, characterization, and next-experiment selection. However, characterization does not always directly provide the target property; measured spectra or images often require automated analysis to extract quantitative descriptors based on physically motivated assumptions and predefined criteria. Such procedures can fail for measurements outside these criteria, requiring a decision on whether a reliable value can be recovered or no numerical value should be reported. Here, we implemented an autonomous adaptive spectral-analysis agent using a large language model (LLM) to supervise a deterministic numerical-analysis routine. For each spectrum, the agent executes the predefined analysis script and assesses the result using the measured spectrum and fitting diagnostics. Valid results are accepted unchanged, recoverable failures are reanalyzed through bounded adjustments of predefined fitting parameters, and NaN (not a number) is returned when no scientifically defensible value can be obtained. We evaluated the workflow on optical transmittance spectra from 203 epitaxial beta-Ga2O3 films grown during a previously reported self-driving thin-film growth campaign. The predefined optical analysis script returned Urbach energy, an optical-quality metric, for 183 spectra and failed for 20. The agent retained those 183 values and evaluated 20 exception cases, recovering 16 through bounded parameter adjustments and returning NaN for 4 when the spectral evidence did not support a reliable Urbach tail. The audit records captured spectral features, parameter changes, and rationale for each decision. These results demonstrate autonomous scientific exception handling by an LLM agent while leaving quantitative property extraction to deterministic numerical analysis.
authors: Yuki K. Wakabayashi; Yui Ogawa

title: Autonomous hardware security evaluation from reconnaissance to physical validation
abstract: Abstract Physical hardware-security evaluation requires both target-specific reasoning and control of laboratory instruments. This study presents a large language model (LLM) agent that links reconnaissance, vulnerability hypotheses, laser fault-injection experiments and reporting through human approval gates. The agent reverse-engineers firmware and instruction behaviour, combines this evidence with documentation and chip imagery, and generates bounded experiments with predefined rules for classifying outcomes. On an ATmega328P microcontroller, agent-derived experiments produced a skipped processor load instruction, acceptance of an incorrect personal identification number (PIN), and the same two-byte Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) encrypted-output difference in 14 trials, with 29 paired fault-free controls. Photon-emission imaging narrowed the physical search region. A second campaign on an Artix-7 field-programmable gate array (FPGA) tested transfer to programmable logic using firmware-binary analysis, optical-to-layout registration and cryptographic-output classification. Recorded agent and operator decisions connect observations to experimental revisions and documented conclusions, demonstrating an autonomous workflow across two hardware architectures.
authors: Raphael Viera

title: Beyond Candidate Generation: A Validation-First Protocol for AI-Assisted Transition-State Discovery
abstract: Machine-learned models can now propose three-dimensional transition-state (TS) geometries in seconds, but a candidate geometry is not a validated TS. The gap between a plausible structure and a mechanistically meaningful barrier—one imaginary frequency, the intended atom pair, the correct connectivity, and a consistent electronic state—remains the bottleneck in AI-assisted computational chemistry. We present a validation-first protocol that separates candidate generation from physical validation. The protocol combines (i) a chemical preflight that fixes reactive pairs, spin surfaces, connectivity, and conformers; (ii) a per-point independent scan that localizes the barrier without fragile collective scans; (iii) a constrained reference calculation that produces the Hessian; (iv) an OptTS stage that reuses that Hessian; and (v) a validation stage based on imaginary-mode localization, key bond lengths, IRC endpoints, spin diagnostics, and energy-convention checks. The protocol is implemented as a portable, open-source skill package for local ORCA/xtb and Gaussian/Slurm execution. Case studies from Ni/Fe catalysis illustrate the failure modes the protocol is designed to catch: a generative model produced candidates with 3.6–4.4 Å heavy-atom RMSD for an 84-atom broken-symmetry organometallic system, a collective scan failed three times where a per-point strategy completed 16/16 points, and a single-conformer R/S comparison would have misread a conformerdominated difference. The reported gains of multi-sampling and conformer enumeration are taken from the published benchmark, not measured here. We argue that the near-term role of AI is not to replace electronic-structure judgment but to shrink the search space before it and to make the validation layer reproducible.
authors: Haofan Li

title: Bio-Inspired Self-Healing Nanostructures for Environmental Pollutant Degradation and Biomedical Diagnostics
abstract: Bio-inspired self-healing nanostructures mimic biological repair processes skin regeneration, bone remodeling, plant vascular reconnection using dynamic covalent chemistry, supramolecular assembly, hydrogen bonding, and metal-ligand coordination to recover mechanical strength, conductivity, and catalytic activity after damage. In environmental remediation, they resist the catalyst deactivation and fatigue limiting conventional photocatalysts, adsorbents, and membranes, sustaining degradation of dyes, pharmaceuticals, pesticides, and heavy metals over far more cycles. In biomedical diagnostics, the same repair logic enables biosensors, wearables, implants, and wound dressings that tolerate repeated mechanical deformation without losing sensitivity. AI and computational modeling are now accelerating design by predicting healing efficiency before synthesis, though scalable fabrication, long-term stability, nanotoxicity, and regulatory approval remain unresolved. This review covers the biological inspiration, material classes, healing mechanisms, applications, and key challenges facing this field.
authors: Sawera Malik Albina; Neelam Zeb; Hafsa Urooj; Kiran Fatima; Atiqa Parveen; Rabiya Bashir

title: BioNICs: Biomaterial-enabled neural interfaces with closed-loop control for brain disorders
abstract: Biomaterial-enabled neural interfaces with closed-loop control (BioNICs) integrate neural sensing, state estimation, and responsive intervention within one therapeutic framework. Material composition and architecture influence tissue coupling, signal transduction, therapeutic actuation, and chronic stability. Mechanically compliant polymers and hydrogels can reduce interfacial strain; conductive and mixed ionic-electronic materials can improve electrical and electrochemical coupling; and stimulus-responsive materials can enable localized energy conversion or controlled drug release. BioNICs are therefore relevant to brain disorders requiring continuous physiological monitoring and state-dependent treatment. However, substantial translational gap remains. Clinically established closed-loop therapies rely mainly on metallic electrodes, polymer insulation, and hermetic packaging, whereas conductive polymers, nanocomposites, hydrogels, microbubbles, biohybrid interfaces, and integrated drug-delivery systems have been evaluated chiefly in vitro , in rodents, or over short implantation periods. Greater complexity in materials and functionality does not necessarily enhance therapeutic performance and may, in fact, give rise to delamination, electrochemical degradation, stimulation artifacts, calibration drift, and packaging failure, as well as additional safety risks. This review examines BioNIC architecture, including sensing, intervention, control algorithms, biomaterials, and system integration, and illustrates applications in episodic network disorders, psychiatric conditions, neurodegenerative diseases, and structural brain injury. We focus on trade-offs in combining high-fidelity electrophysiological recording, neurochemical and physical sensing, localized electrical, optical, acoustic, or magnetic actuation, and microenvironment-responsive drug delivery. Ultimately, this review emphasizes that translating the intrinsic advantages of intelligent biomaterials into clinical benefit requires moving beyond isolated component innovation toward long-term system-level validation linking material performance to reliability, biological safety, algorithmic interpretability, and clinically meaningful outcomes.
authors: Yongxu Ju; Zheng Dou; Yiyuan Yang; Fang Yang

title: Biocompatible Microscale DNA Hydrogels with Programmable Swelling and Sequence-Specific Dissolution.
abstract: Stimulus-responsive DNA hydrogels with swelling capabilities are a promising class of materials for biomedical applications such as drug delivery and biosensing. However, translation of these systems to microscale applications requires fabrication methods that are both biocompatible and material-efficient, while enabling precise control over stimulus-induced swelling and its impact on molecular transport. Here, we present a biocompatible fabrication and characterization platform for microscale DNA-hydrogels (μSDs) with tunable isotropic swelling and dissolving properties. Our approach includes a biocompatible, material-efficient fabrication workflow that conserves valuable DNA reagents by minimizing dead volume and process loss. We then demonstrated modular control over isotropic swelling in μSDs, achieving up to a two-fold size increase through programmable DNA design parameters. We further established a quantitative reaction-diffusion workflow to estimate effective diffusivity and characterize swelling dependent transport of a DNA binding fluorescent probe in spherical μSDs. Finally, we demonstrate the dissolution of μSDs using a DNA strand and find that dissolution kinetics are governed by the rates of coupled strand-displacement reactions and diffusive transport. This platform enables programmable swelling and structural disassembly in μSDs. Swelling-induced network expansion further modulates transport of a DNA binding fluorescent probe within the μSD network, highlighting the potential of programmable structural remodeling for future biosensing, controlled release, and single-cell assay applications.
authors: Corinna Torabi; Takayuki Suzuki; Emily Helm; Harrison Khoo; Sophie Tanenbaum; Rebecca Schulman; Soojung Claire Hur

title: Bioelectronics beyond proof-of-concept demonstration
abstract: Biomedical electronic devices are developed to monitor physiological activity and deliver interventions at specific sites in the body. Their operation requires stable biological interfaces, suitable power delivery and reliable interpretation of electrical signals. These requirements become particularly important during movement and prolonged use, when changes in the interface can affect device performance. Developing clinically useful systems therefore requires an understanding of how materials and device architectures preserve the intended function under these conditions. Recent contributions to APL Electronic Devices address these requirements through advances in wearable sensors, biomolecular detection, soft actuators and power sources. We argue that the next stage of development requires closer integration of these capabilities around defined clinical needs. This Editorial examines the resulting design priorities for biological interfaces, feedback control, functional lifetime and reproducible fabrication.
authors: Yeon Sik Choi

title: Bioengineering strategies for next-generation female reproductive organoids: A roadmap to clinical translation
abstract: The human female reproductive system is characterized by highly dynamic tissue remodeling, cyclical endocrinology, and the precise orchestration of maternal–fetal immune tolerance. Historically, deciphering reproductive pathologies ranging from infertility to obstetric complications and malignancies has been hampered by the fundamental physiological and interspecies disparities inherent in 2D cultures and animal models. While three-dimensional (3D) organoid technology has initiated a paradigm shift, conventional static cultures relying on poorly defined, xenogeneic matrices (e.g., Matrigel) introduce profound immunogenic confounding factors and severe bioengineering bottlenecks. To bridge this gap, this review comprehensively delineates the advanced bioengineering strategies driving the next-generation of female reproductive models. We first outline foundational engineering pillars, highlighting the transition toward intelligent biomaterials, deterministic 3D bioprinting, and microfluidic microenvironments. Subsequently, we critically evaluate state-of-the-art organoid models across the ovary, fallopian tube, the maternal–fetal interface containing endometrium and placenta, cervix, and vagina. We emphasize how multi-lineage “assembloids” and multiorgan microphysiological systems successfully recapitulate transient implantation events and bidirectional endocrine crosstalk. Finally, we propose a strategic roadmap for the field, demonstrating how the integration of materials science, genetics, multi-omics, and engineering methods will overcome current limitations, ultimately accelerating the transition from benchtop in vitro models to standardized clinical diagnostics and reproductive regenerative therapeutics.
authors: Bowen Gao; Jianing Gao; 魏文博; Yixuan Hu; Chengran Hu; Wentao Su; Shuo Chen; Li Wang

title: Bioinspired Surface Enabled by Anisotropic Pyramid Structure Arrays for Directional Liquid Self‐Transport
abstract: ABSTRACT Inspired by the phenomenon of directional liquid transport in natural organisms, various bionic surfaces with customized topological structures have been designed and fabricated, contributing to advances in such fields as microfluidics, microreactors, energy harvesting, biomedicine, etc. Despite extensive progress, bionic surfaces with directional liquid self‐transport capabilities still suffer from high technical thresholds, cumbersome fabrication processes, and contamination‐induced failure, limiting their widespread applications. In this work, a bioinspired surface with anisotropic inverted pyramid groove arrays was developed to achieve directional self‐transport of diverse liquids, from water to blood. Bioinspired by the nepenthes alata peristome, a discretely anisotropic inverted pyramid model was theoretically constructed, and then the surface with inverted pyramid groove arrays was efficiently and simply prepared via three‐dimensional (3D) printing and cast molding. This bioinspired surface exhibited rapid, long‐distance, and continuous liquid self‐transport with high unidirectionality under the optimal structural parameters. Moreover, this bioinspired surface was innovatively applied to achieve efficient removal of blood cells from diluted blood without complex operations, providing a proof‐of‐concept foundation for future applications of bioinspired surfaces in microfluidics, plasma separation, and biomedical detection.
authors: Yi‐Ke Wang; Chaowei Sun; Pin Lv; Shengjun An; Zhao Meng-qian; Hu‐Chen Zhang; Si‐Yu Tian; Yan‐Yan Sun; Jun‐Yue Chen; Yu‐Yin Xu; Fan Zhang; Li‐Yun Zheng; Shegan Gao; Hong‐Xing Xu

title: Biological-Digital-Twin-Driven Microrobotic Sampling Decisions at the Limit STARLI Research Institute XXIX — Flagship Research Monograph 10 What if the next scientific sample could be selected not merely to collect more data, but to distinguish between competing explanations of biological behavior? Biological-Digital-Twin-Driven Microrobotic Sampling Decisions at the Limit explores a prospective research architecture combining versioned biological digital twins, active learning, microrobotic sampling, uncertainty quantification, and mechanistic model discrimination. The central question is whether a computational twin can identify safe, informative sampling actions that distinguish competing biological mechanisms more effectively than conventional experimental schedules, while retaining the ability to recognize model inadequacy and abstain from unsupported decisions. The proposed framework treats biological digital twins as revisable scientific models rather than exact replicas of living systems. Its reference environment is a controlled, nonclinical microfluidic platform containing two declared dynamical mechanisms and a third withheld mechanism reserved for evaluating open-world uncertainty and model failure. The research architecture is organized around five interconnected layers: versioned biological modeling, explicit prior assumptions and knowledge gaps, physically constrained predictive interrogation, comparative adaptive experimentation, and independent requalification. The manuscript develops thirty candidate mathematical research plates covering Bayesian mechanism inference, conditional information gain, experimental identifiability, observation uncertainty, transport dynamics, calibration, model discrepancy, and decision safety. These mathematical structures are connected to eighty-two research chapters, five independently paginated investigation sections per chapter, two hundred detailed Research Gates, and thirty-three Phoenix Answer Embryos. Each Research Gate is intended as a transferable research question that future investigators may test, challenge, refine, or reject. The proposed evaluation compares twin-guided sampling against optimized fixed schedules, established experimental-design approaches, and alternative active-learning policies under matched physical constraints and experimental budgets. Particular attention is given to blinded mechanism identification, probabilistic calibration, out-of-distribution rejection, specimen integrity, model-version accountability, and explicit stopping conditions. The volume includes DOI-linked methodological literature and a staged nonclinical verification pathway. Scientific status and limitations: This manuscript presents a conceptual methodological research program, not completed experimental validation. Its integrated hypotheses, mathematical proposals, and experimental architectures remain subject to independent technical review and empirical testing. The manuscript does not establish clinical efficacy, diagnostic reliability, therapeutic benefit, or proven superiority of microrobotic digital-twin systems. The work also acknowledges remaining editorial limitations, including recurring methodological language that requires further substantive review before the manuscript can be regarded as a fully refined scientific monograph. The broader purpose of this research is to develop scientific systems that can remain useful even when their initial models are incomplete. Rather than demanding certainty from a digital twin, the proposed framework asks whether future autonomous research tools can become more transparent, corrigible, experimentally accountable, and capable of recognizing the boundaries of their own knowledge. Within the STARLI research continuum, this volume is intended as an evolving research inheritance for future human and artificial-intelligence investigators. title: Bioprinting-Enabled Customization of Biohybrid Actuators: Scaling Dimensions and Functional Complexity
abstract: Biohybrid actuators integrate living contractile cells with engineered materials, combining biological force generation with the structural and functional control offered by synthetic components. However, translating engineered muscle tissue into reproducible, high-performance biohybrid robots remains limited by tissue organization, matrix degradation, force transmission, and long-term functional stability. This review analyzes how biofabrication parameters and material properties influence tissue maturation and actuator-level performance, with particular emphasis on bioprinting. We compare muscle cell sources; extrusion-based, embedded, and light-assisted fabrication strategies; and scaffold biomaterials using reported structural and functional outcomes. We also evaluate electrical and optical activation and mechanical conditioning, distinguishing their roles in controlling contraction and promoting maturation. The comparison highlights a gap between architectural control during fabrication and reproducible robotic performance: methods that produce complex muscle constructs do not necessarily yield integrated devices with validated force transmission or locomotion. Tissue maturation, tissue-material interfaces, and nutrient transport emerge as closely coupled priorities for scaling functional constructs. We conclude with a framework for standardized benchmarking and discuss multimaterial printing, data-driven design, and feedback control as complementary routes toward more reproducible and capable biohybrid actuators.
authors: Maede Pajouhande; Nehar Celikkin; Saeed Rafieyan; Maria Celeste Tirelli; Fabio Maiullari; Maryia Piletskaya; Marco Costantini

title: Blood test on a chip: Sample-to-answer immunoassay on a structurally programmed microfluidic chip
abstract: During COVID-19, rapid antigen tests (RATs) have demonstrated their enormous potential to relax and decentralize the healthcare system for timely results. However, disease diagnosis mostly requires blood tests with quantitative readouts, which are hardly achieved by conventional lateral flow strips. Here, we report a concept of “Blood Test on a Chip” (BTOC) that streamlines the entire sample-to-answer immunoassay process on a single microfluidic chip. Without any external processes, the BTOC can operate independently based on a series of structurally programmed capillary events, including automated blood plasma separation, on-chip reaction, and a length-based quantitative result displayed on the chip. This platform demonstrated a limit of detection (LOD) of 3.78 ng/mL of prostate-specific antigen (PSA) in whole blood, which is below the clinical threshold of 4 ng/mL for PSA abnormality. Clinical validation involving 77 volunteer samples showed strong agreement between the BTOC and standard hospital tests (Lin's concordance correlation coefficient ρ ̂ c = 0.932 ). This all-in-one, self-contained chip eliminates the need for peripheral laboratory settings, offering a simple, affordable, and quantitative at-home test for telemedicine, large-scale screening in primary care and disease self-management.
authors: Jiaheng Li; Zhuoting Han; Hogi Hartanto; Lin Pang; Jianpeng Wu; Zhibing Chen; Lok Ting Chu; Ting-Hsuan Chen

title: Breaking Bottlenecks in Solid Electrolyte Discovery With Large Artificial Intelligence Models
abstract: Solid electrolytes (SEs) are central to next-generation metal batteries, yet their discovery remains constrained by fragmented data, limited transferability of simulations, and slow experimental iteration. Unlike catalysis, where surface reactivity dominates, SEs require simultaneous optimization of bulk ion transport, defect chemistry, mechanical integrity, and interfacial stability. Here, we outline a framework for autonomous SE discovery enabled by large artificial intelligence (AI) models, including machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) and large language models (LLMs). We discuss the evolution from static materials databases to dynamic, self-updating knowledge systems, the role of MLIPs in bridging density functional theory (DFT) and long-timescale ion migration, and the emergence of LLMs as engines for literature mining, hypothesis generation, and scientific reasoning. We further describe a closed-loop architecture integrating AI-driven candidate design, multiscale simulation, uncertainty-aware selection, and experimental validation. Such systems shift SE research from intuition-guided exploration to data-informed, self-improving cycles. We conclude by highlighting challenges in data standardization, interfacial complexity, and reproducibility, and we propose design principles for building autonomous laboratories for solid-state battery materials.

title: Building the Rural Nursing Workforce of the Future: Education, Research, and Partnerships to Address Persistent Health Challenges
abstract: Background: Rural populations experience healthcare disparities, including workforce shortages, geographic isolation, limited access to specialty services, and adverse social determinants of health. These challenges are particularly evident in South Dakota, where nearly half of the population resides in rural or frontier communities. Because of these unique challenges associated with rural life, preparing nurses to work in rural America is critical in preparing a workforce capable of meeting the unique healthcare needs of this population. Methods: This article describes how South Dakota State University College of Nursing, located within a rural land-grant institution, has developed and adapted educational programs, workforce initiatives, community partnerships, and re-search programs to address persistent rural health challenges across the state and region. The College of Nursing (CON) includes three campus locations: Brookings, Sioux Falls, and Rapid City and includes undergraduate and graduate nursing education. Nursing education is designed to allow students to blend their nursing education with South Dakota's unique rural environment. Results: The CON offers multiple pathways into the profession, including traditional and accelerated Bachelor of Science in Nursing (BSN) pro-grams, an online BSN option utilizing a train-in-place model, master's-level nursing education and administrator programs, Doctor of Nursing Practice (DNP) programs, and PhD education. Through strategic academic-practice partnerships and federally funded work-force initiatives, the college prepares nurses for rural practice across primary care, acute care, long-term care, and underserved settings. Additional initiatives support Native American student success, rural workforce recruitment and retention, oral health outreach, care coordination for children and youth with special healthcare needs, and research focused on workforce well-being, workplace violence, and healthcare access. Conclusions: A multi-site college of nursing can serve as a model for improving rural healthcare access, strengthening the nursing workforce, and addressing the complex and persistent health needs of rural and frontier populations. South Dakota State Universi-ty CON demonstrates how innovative educational delivery models, community partnerships, and targeted workforce initiatives can contribute to sustainable rural healthcare solutions.

title: CRISPR‐Scan: Cas13a Mismatch Tolerance Enabled Ultra‐Multiplexed Detection of Same‐Site Indels in Acute Myeloid Leukemia
abstract: Detection of gene mutations related to acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is crucial for its early diagnosis, personalized treatment, and recurrence monitoring. However, accurate detection of diverse mutations occurring at the same locus remains technically challenging. The CRISPR/Cas system, with its unique programmable nucleic acid recognition capabilities, provides a promising solution. Here, we elucidated that CRISPR/LwaCas13a is tolerant to consecutive substitutions but highly sensitive to insertions or deletions (indels) at specific positions of the spacer sequence, enabling rational CRISPR RNA (crRNA) design for multiplex detection of same-site indels. Guided by these principles, we achieved effective detection of ultra-multiplex nucleophosmin 1 (NPM1) c.863_864 4-bp insertions with a single crRNA, while maintaining specificity against the wild-type transcripts. We further established a one-pot CRISPR system, CRISPR-Scan, by integrating recombinase polymerase amplification with LwaCas13a cleavage. CRISPR-Scan enabled detection of mutations in backgrounds as low as 0.01%. In clinical validation, it identified NPM1 mutations in 43 of 120 AML patients, consistent with next-generation sequencing (NGS). Continuous monitoring of four AML patients indicated early recurrence with higher sensitivity than first-generation sequencing (FGS) and full concordance with NGS. A microfluidic chip and portable device further facilitate accurate AML mutation detection. This platform offers an efficient and convenient approach for early AML diagnosis and measurable residual disease (MRD) monitoring.

title: Carrier-Limited Release Risk in Electrospun Nanofibers for Regenerative Endodontics: Constraint Discovery from 25 Formulations
abstract: Regenerative endodontics needs an intracanal carrier that keeps disinfecting across a dressing interval that clinicians schedule at one to four weeks, without harming the stem cells that rebuild the pulp. We ask what one completed 25-formulation electrospinning campaign of poly(vinylpyrrolidone) (PVP) fibers carrying metronidazole, ciprofloxacin, minocycline and Ca(OH)2 can decide, and use machine learning for constraint discovery and decision support rather than as a new predictor. After an audit against the source thesis, logistic regression predicts fine-fiber formation at 96% leave-one-out accuracy, but a one-threshold rule does as well, the gain over the 80% majority baseline is not significant (exact McNemar p = 0.125), and accuracy falls to 84% when mixture loading is encoded per component. Diameter models interpolate within formulation families (ridge MAE 193 nm, 95% CI 96 to 317 nm) and fail across them (R^2 < 0). Because the campaign never measured release, we assemble a same-drug, cross-carrier evidence table: 17 bounded metronidazole and ciprofloxacin observations from seven studies, with two-sided censoring. Water-soluble carriers (PVP, PVA) completed release within 80 h (PVP within 8 h); no water-insoluble monolithic carrier reached 90% within its observation window, releasing 1.5 to 50%; both within-study comparisons separate at matched loading; and blend, core-shell and thick-mat architectures released over 3 to 28 days. The PVP mats therefore carry a carrier-limited release risk, not a proven ceiling, and one dissolution experiment can confirm or overturn it. A censoring-aware screen keeps three necessarily and one possibly nondominated formulation, and fixed-budget replays show that uncertainty sampling finds failed formulations sooner, except the one it is confidently wrong about.

title: Cascade-Amplified Microfluidic Detection of Tumor Biomarkers via Metal-DNA Nanospheres Activating CRISPR-Cas12a Assay.
abstract: The development of ultrasensitive protein detection platforms is pivotal for early cancer diagnosis, yet existing methods are often constrained by inefficient "protein-to-signal" conversion and complex instrumentation. While CRISPR-Cas-based biosensors offer higher sensitivity for nucleic acids, their application in protein analysis is fundamentally limited by the low nucleic acid loading capacity and tedious functionalization of traditional inorganic signal carriers such as gold nanoparticles and metal-organic frameworks (MOFs). Herein, we report a highly efficient signal-transduction strategy utilizing Fe-coordinated DNA nanospheres (FDNSs)─a programmable, metal-nucleic acid assembly─as a high-capacity DNA reservoir for amplified biomarker sensing. Unlike conventional surface-modified inorganic nanoparticles, the solid-core FDNSs achieve an unprecedented DNA loading density and exhibit specific stimulus-responsive degradation. In this FACC (FDNS-activated CRISPR chip) platform, the recognition of tumor biomarkers triggers the rapid collapse of FDNSs, releasing a massive flux of barcode DNA that subsequently activates the CRISPR-Cas12a system within a microfluidic device. This dual-amplification architecture enables the ultrasensitive quantification of prostate-specific antigen (PSA) and carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) with detection limits of 0.028 fg/mL and 0.0265 fg/mL, respectively. By replacing complex inorganic carriers with this programmable DNA assembly, our platform simplifies the sensing workflow and significantly enhances sensitivity, providing a robust and portable solution for cancer screening in resource-limited settings.
authors: Wenjian Zhao; Xiaowei Luan; Wenxiu Long; Zhi Li; Ping Dong; Bangshun He; Yanfeng Gao; Hongmei Liu; Yi Yin; Yujun Song

title: CircuitATLAS: Agentic reasoning over a systems neuroscience knowledge graph for target discovery in circuitopathies
abstract: Drug discovery for neurological disease has traditionally centered on the molecules altered by disease. But the molecules that cause pathology are not necessarily the best points from which to reverse it. Here, we ask which otherwise unaltered molecular control points can be engaged to restore pathological neural circuits toward functional states. We present CircuitATLAS, a provenance-grounded systems-neuroscience knowledge graph and agentic framework for target discovery in circuitopathies. It structures literature-derived relationships across diseases, phenotypes, electrophysiology, circuits, brain regions, cell types and molecular effectors, while deliberately excluding direct disease-gene and disease-protein edges to reduce shortcut reasoning. The graph contains 3.83 million nodes and 7.66 million edges, including 5.31 million LLM-extracted relations, and incorporates structured datasets such as the Human Cell Atlas and new multimodal in vivo measurements. We then introduce an agentic workflow that reasons from measurable disease phenotypes through their circuit and cellular substrates to molecular interventions, therapeutic feasibility and clinical constraints. Finally, we introduce a human-governed in vivo lab-in-the-loop linking hypothesis generation to experimental iteration. Within this framework an agent nominated ATP1A3, the neuronal alpha3 Na+/K+-ATPase, as a control point on cortical excitability; interneuron-restricted expression of ATP1A3 abolished the beta- and gamma-band response to a focal 4-aminopyridine challenge in vivo, and the validated target was then carried into a structure-guided small-molecule campaign terminating in a defined assay to resolve the direction of modulation. CircuitATLAS thus provides a framework for discovering therapeutics based not only on what is molecularly disrupted in disease, but on what can be controlled to restore circuit function.
authors: Gabriel Ocana-Santero; Marko Tvrdic

title: Closed-Loop Reinforcement Learning in De Novo Molecular Design: Bridging Generative AI with Automated Chemical Synthesis
abstract: Closed-loop reinforcement learning offers a promising approach to integrating generative molecular design with automated chemical synthesis and experimental evaluation. However, translating autonomous chemical optimization into pharmaceutical discovery remains challenging because biological measurements are often delayed, variable, and affected by assay limitations. This critical review and perspective examines current autonomous discovery platforms and evaluates the challenges associated with incorporating physical experimental feedback into molecular optimization. It proposes an uncertainty-aware, multi-objective reward architecture and a four-gate qualification framework covering operational synthesizability, analytical identity and purity, biological assay validity, and governed policy updating. Particular attention is given to distinguishing statistically censored measurements from pharmacologically confounded or invalid observations. The article also introduces supervised autonomy as a practical governance approach in which automated systems perform routine experimental operations while scientific experts retain responsibility for critical decisions. The proposed framework provides a foundation for improving the reliability, interpretability, and practical implementation of experimentally informed molecular discovery. Prospective validation remains necessary to establish its effectiveness.
authors: Michele Covington
