The findings demand a "right to mental self-determination" and a transition toward "soft assembly" mechanisms where distributed competencies are valued over individual ability. Ultimately, the summary calls for a global framework -similar to the one recently issued by UNESCO -that balances rapid innovation with the protection of human rights and dignity, ensuring that neurotechnology remains a benefit to humanity at large rather than a tool for surveillance or control.In general, we would highlight that despite the wealth of data and arguments in this collection, several "unsolved mysteries" remain at the heart of the neuroprivacy debate: what are the long-term post-trial responsibilities of manufacturers when a device becomes an essential part of an individual's identity, but the company ceases operations? Also, as enhancement technologies become increasingly available on the consumer market, who decides (and how) what constitutes "unlocking human potential" versus "distorting behaviour"? And, finally, how can we prevent the of dual-usage of neurotechnology -where media hype and military interests oscillate between fear and enthusiasmfrom dictating global policy?In conclusion, the research presented here indicates that we are entering an era of unprecedented human-machine interaction, with the risk of existential dependency on neurotechnology, which, therefore, necessitates transdisciplinary science discussion (possibly -the editors claim -a new fertile branch for science diplomacy). The collection demonstrates that neuroprivacy cannot be addressed as a series of isolated technical hurdles, because it is a fundamental challenge to human dignity that requires a cohesive legal and ethical framework. We must delve deeper into the multidisciplinary connections between neuroscience, IT, law, and ethics to allow researchers from diverse backgrounds to understand and address these phenomena together. We invite the academic community and policymakers to move away from the intrusive paradigms emerging from for-profit neurodevices development and join the scholars presenting their results in this collection in defining a social framework that protects the sanctity of the mind while responsibly unlocking the hybrid potentials of the future.
authors: Gianluigi M. Riva; Simona Tiribelli; Giovanni Ziccardi; Surjo Raphael Soekadar; Sara Colantonio; Agustí Solanas

title: Embedded Droplet Velocity Sensor for Lab-on-PCB Systems: A Case Study on Velocity and Monodispersity in Flow-Focusing Systems
abstract: Droplet velocity measurement in miniaturized Lab-on-PCB (LoPCB) platforms is essential for monitoring flow regime stability, monodispersity, and downstream processing in applications such as nanoparticle synthesis and clinical diagnostics, yet conventional optical techniques require bulky external instrumentation unsuitable for autonomous operation. This work presents a fully embedded opto-electrical velocity sensing system that performs sensing, signal conditioning, and data processing on-board, without requiring external instrumentation. The sensor architecture was designed following a Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) workflow and validated through simulation prior to microcontroller deployment. The maximum detectable velocity, set by photoresistor response dynamics, increases linearly with droplet length. Experimental validation was performed in a 1.4 mm flow-focusing geometry using water-in-oil emulsions across flow-rate ratios (ϕ) from 0.5 to 2.0 under a fixed continuous-phase flow rate (Qc). The system achieved an average deviation of 5.32% from optical reference values across 195 droplets, with per-condition deviations ranging from 0.74% to 12.07% and below 6.4%, excluding the highest-dispersion condition. Embedded analysis of 797 droplets revealed a linear trend between velocity and droplet length (R2=0.993) and a power-law relationship between velocity and monodispersity (R2=0.912) over the 3.7-7.4 mm/s range. These results demonstrate suitability for autonomous, real-time droplet characterization in Lab-on-PCB platforms.
authors: Daniel Solano; Jair Gonzalez-Pina; Antonio M. Luque; Sérgio Camacho-León

title: Endometrial Hyperplasia as an Actionable Precursor to Endometrial Cancer: Narrative Review
abstract: Purpose. The aim of this paper is to evaluate endometrial hyperplastic disorders as an actionable precursor to EC from a public health perspective, analyzing risk determinants, early detection triage mechanisms, and population-based prevention strategies. Material and Methods. We employed general scientific methodologies, including comprehensive literature search, analytical review, synthesis, and generalization. Relevant studies were retrieved from the PubMed and Google Scholar electronic databases using terms “endometrial cancer”, “endometrial hyperplasia”, “epidemiology”, “abnormal uterine bleeding”, “risk factors”, “early detection”, “screening” and “prevention”. Results. EH constitutes a spectrum of abnormal endometrial proliferative changes ranging from benign glandular overgrowth to precancerous lesions, among which atypical EH/EIN represents an actionable pre-malignant phase along the continuum toward EC. Effective secondary prevention relies on elevating public awareness of AUB as an urgent diagnostic signal. Broadening access to outpatient diagnostic triage using transvaginal ultrasound and endometrial sampling enables prompt identification of precursor lesions while avoiding costly, invasive inpatient curettage. Mitigating the population burden of EC requires integrating metabolic health management into primary care, establishing risk-stratified clinical pathways, and integration of cascade genetic testing for families at high risk of hereditary cancer syndromes. Conclusions. Atypical EH/EIN is a critical, actionable target for secondary prevention of endometrial cancer. Effectively mitigating population disease burden requires embedding metabolic risk management into primary care, expanding outpatient diagnostic triage for AUB, and establishing national precursor registries alongside cascade genetic testing to address healthcare disparities.
authors: Іnna Krynytska; Ю. М. Орел; Olena I. Hladii; Anna Z. Mykolenko; Tetyana Golovata

title: Engineering Construction and Risk Management Practice of Intelligent Rail Logistics System in Multi Building Tertiary A Hospital
abstract: To meet the requirements for the high‑quality development of public hospitals and solve practical problems such as low efficiency of in‑hospital material transportation, high labor costs and heavy pressure of nosocomial infection control in multi‑building tertiary‑A hospitals, Chengdu Hospital of Integrated Traditional Chinese and Western Medicine has launched the reconstruction‑and‑expansion project of an intelligent rail‑logistics system. As an intelligent renovation project constructed under the premise of uninterrupted medical services, it is restricted by multiple factors including existing building conditions, nosocomial‑infection control requirements and extreme weather, with engineering risks running through the whole project lifecycle. Combined with project practice, this paper carries out whole‑lifecycle risk identification and assessment, establishes a risk matrix, formulates corresponding countermeasures, and builds a closed‑loop management system of “risk identification‑assessment‑disposal‑review”. Risk control is implemented through multi‑party collaboration, phased construction, on‑site operation and maintenance, special training and emergency disposal. A total of 48 stations are planned with a total rail length of 2567 m, among which 32 stations have been put into operation. The system completes an average of 320 delivery tasks per day, with a 30‑minute task completion rate of 93 %. The labor cost for full‑time delivery staff is reduced by 50 %. The construction objectives of cost reduction and efficiency improvement, nosocomial‑infection prevention and refined operation of intelligent logistics support have been achieved. Practice proves that whole‑lifecycle engineering risk management is critical to the successful implementation of hospital intelligent reconstruction‑and‑expansion projects, and can provide practical references for similar domestic hospital intelligent‑logistics projects.
authors: Hong Lyu

title: Engineering Strategies for Enhanced Extracellular Vesicle Production: Mechanisms and Applications
abstract: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) have emerged as key mediators of intercellular communication and hold great promise for liquid biopsy and therapeutic applications. Their molecular composition and abundance dynamically reflect the pathophysiological state of their parental cells, endowing EVs with significant value for biomarker discovery and precision medicine. However, inefficient biogenesis, limited production yield, and considerable heterogeneity remain core bottlenecks to their clinical translation. This review systematically surveys recent engineering strategies aimed at enhancing EV production, encompassing diverse physical stimuli and biochemical interventions, with a particular focus on the underlying molecular mechanisms that govern EV quantity, composition, and functionality. Despite their varied modes of action, these approaches share a convergent regulatory principle-remodeling the fate of multivesicular bodies (MVBs) by promoting MVB biogenesis, intracellular trafficking, and plasma membrane fusion, while suppressing their diversion toward lysosomal degradation. Importantly, yield-enhancing strategies not only facilitate the scalable manufacturing of therapeutic EVs, but also enable the functional activation of EV-producing cells, enriching disease-relevant molecular signatures and directing the cargo composition for improved diagnostic performance. Crucially, the synergy between yield-enhancing strategies and advanced biosensing platforms is reshaping the entire EV research workflow. Emerging integrated analytical systems-encompassing microfluidics, electrochemical sensors, and acoustic detectors-now enable real-time monitoring of EV secretion kinetics, providing dynamic feedback to optimize stimulation parameters and harvest windows. Moreover, lab-on-a-chip platforms are beginning to merge EV production, in-line purification, and multiplexed detection into a single automated workflow, facilitating simultaneous quality control and functional characterization. Highly sensitive biosensing technologies further allow precise assessment of EV cargo composition, surface marker profiles, and biological activity, ensuring product consistency and potency. Looking forward, the deep integration of EV biogenesis engineering with these smart detection platforms holds the potential to overcome current translational bottlenecks, accelerating the development of scalable EV therapeutics and next-generation liquid biopsy systems for early diagnosis, dynamic disease monitoring, and precision medicine.
authors: Xianyue Ji; Yi Luo; Haozhang Ma; Xingyu Tao; Shuangshuang Wan

title: Engineering and optimization of microfluidic platforms for phospholipid-based ocular drug delivery
abstract: Ocular drug delivery remains a major challenge due to anatomical, physiological, and pathological barriers that limit drug penetration and retention. Liposomes offer a promising strategy to address these constraints; however, their effectiveness depends on physicochemical properties such as size, surface charge, and interfacial functionality, which govern transport across ocular tissues. Microfluidic technology provides a powerful platform to achieve precise control over these properties through tunable flow conditions and controlled self-assembly, enabling the reproducible fabrication of liposomes with tailored characteristics. In this context, this review establishes a barrier-informed framework that links ocular transport limitations to liposome design requirements and microfluidic processing strategies. In this review, we systematically examine microfluidic mixer geometries, including hydrodynamic flow, Dean-flow-based designs, and chaotic advection mixers, and discuss their impact on liposome formation. Methods for evaluating mixing performance are reviewed alongside the advantages and limitations of different chip materials and fabrication approaches. In addition, strategies for tuning liposome properties, including size, polydispersity, lamellarity, and stability, are critically analyzed in relation to ocular delivery requirements. Finally, emerging directions such as integrated single-step platforms, hybrid and 3D-printed systems, machine learning-assisted process control, solvent-free fabrication, and non-spherical liposomes are discussed. Collectively, this review provides a conceptual and engineering framework for the rational design of microfluidic platforms for liposome-based ocular drug delivery, bridging transport physics with translational applications.
authors: Shakila Dikowita Kankanamlage; Thilini Rasika Thrimawithana; Francisco Javier Tovar-Lopez

title: Engineering ex vivo T-cell expansion for CAR-T therapy: bridging biological fidelity and bioprocess scalability through platforms, functional consumables, and integrated closed manufacturing
abstract: Background Chimeric antigen receptor T (CAR-T) cell therapy has changed the treatment of relapsed or refractory B-cell malignancies and multiple myeloma, but manufacturing time, cost, variability, and access remain major barriers. Scope In this critical narrative review, we position ex vivo T-cell expansion at the interface of biological signaling and engineering design and dissect how each unit operation—from selection and activation to harvest and formulation—influences the final therapeutic product. Key advances Static gas-permeable culture, rocking-motion and stirred-tank bioreactors, hollow-fiber and perfusion systems, biomaterial scaffolds, microcarriers, and defined activation nanoparticles offer distinct routes to scalable expansion. Closed automated platforms now integrate multiple unit operations, while microfluidic systems, rapid manufacturing, and process analytical technologies (PAT) create new possibilities for monitoring and control, with data-driven and AI-assisted prediction emerging as supporting tools rather than established capabilities. Challenges Expansion remains constrained by the trade-off between cell number and preservation of memory phenotype, metabolic fitness, and potency. Donor variability, raw-material quality, consumable dependence, limited interoperability, and incomplete potency assays complicate standardization. Outlook Future progress will depend on coordinated development of defined raw materials, functionally designed consumables, closed-system engineering, interoperable automation, and data-driven process control. The goal is not simply to expand more cells, but to reproducibly manufacture the right cells at an acceptable cost.
authors: Qingzhi Wu; Menghui Jiang; Yuanyuan Li; Hui Huo; Haoyuan Cheng; Tian Jia; Yushu Wang; Ziwei Wang; Mengdie Ji; Jingjing Lin; Deyue Jiang; 张娜; Fuliang Chen

title: Engineering multifunctional materials and smart recognition probes for holistic electrochemical affinity biosensing
abstract: Affinity-based electrochemical biosensing evolves from conventional molecular detection platforms toward intelligent, multifunctional, and decentralized systems capable of making decisions in near real time based on comprehensive biochemical information. This transformation has been driven by advances in multifunctional materials and smart recognition probes that improve sensitivity, selectivity, signal transduction, robustness, analytical versatility and decentralized applicability. Multifunctional materials, including sustainable and functional hybrid nanomaterials, enable interface engineering, affinity bioassays, and signal amplification, while smart probes comprise structure-changing, multiblock, multifunctional, multivalent, and fully synthetic recognition elements. This review highlights representative strategies that integrate these innovations to develop simple, cost-effective, reagent-free, fully integrated, and adaptive biosensor platforms for continuous, multiplexed, and real-time analysis, expanding their capabilities beyond conventional detection. Finally, current challenges and future perspectives are discussed, emphasizing how advances in materials and probe engineering are driving the development of intelligent, adaptive, autonomous electrochemical biosensors for personalized, sustainable, and decentralized healthcare and environmental monitoring.
authors: Susana Campuzano; María Gamella; Víctor Ruiz‐Valdepeñas Montiel; Rebeca Magnolia Torrente-Rodríguez; Verónica Serafín; Marı́a Pedrero; José Manuel Pingarrón

title: Enzymes can activate and mobilize dense biomolecular condensates across scales
abstract: ABSTRACT Biomolecular condensates have so far been studied in terms of their structural, compositional, and functional properties. However, condensate enzymatic activity —a key aspect of cellular metabolism— remains unexplored due to the complexity of the system. In this study, using a combination of experimental, computational and theoretical techniques, we have discovered that the non-equilibrium activity which originates from catalytic reactions couples with the environment through various feedback mechanisms across five orders of magnitude of length scales. We observe that condensed enzymes catalyse more rapidly in the presence of crowding proteins and show that the increased enzymatic activity within these droplets stems from the emergence of lower-energy protein conformations induced by the highly crowded environment. Despite the crowding in the environment of the droplet, which might suggest an effective increase in its overall viscosity, we find that it becomes more agile, as evidenced by the observation of enhanced diffusion and macroscopic flow, due to the enzymatic activity. These findings shed new light on the dynamic interplay between enzymatic activity, composition and crowding in condensates, and their roles on the mobility and accessibility of various functional units in these environments, offering a novel perspective on liquidliquid phase separation in metabolically active conditions.
authors: Mirco Dindo; Jakob Metson; Weitong Ren; Michalis Chatzittofi; Kiyoshi Yagi; Alessandro Bevilacqua; Erika Fukuhara; Yuji Sugita; Ramin Golestanian; Paola Laurino

title: Experimental Analysis of Droplet Transport in Miniaturised Digital Microfluidic Platforms
abstract: Mikrofluidika obravnava obnašanje in manipulacijo tekočin na submilimetrskem merilu. V digitalni mikrofluidiki se diskretne kapljice aktuira z elektroomočenjem na dielektriku (EWOD), kar omogoča programiran transport brez klasičnih črpalk ali kanalov. Miniaturizacija elektrod lahko poveča hitrost aktuacije in prostorsko ločljivost, vendar prinaša tudi večje izzive pri izdelavi in zmanjšano zanesljivost delovanja. Zato je pomembno določiti praktične meje delovanja miniaturiziranih odprtih in zaprtih sistemov EWOD. Izdelana je bila koplanarna matrika 4 × 4 zlatih elektrod dimenzij 1 × 1 mm z razmiki 40 µm, prekrita s 15 µm debelo plastjo SU-8 in hidrofobno plastjo FluoroPel. Kvazistatične meritve kontaktnega kota pri elektroomočenju so bile izvedene med 0 V in 250 V, transport kapljic pa je bil analiziran s hitro kamero na podlagi nazivne hitrosti, ročnega štetja slik in algoritma v Pythonu za sledenje dejanski poti kapljice. Kontaktni kot se je zmanjšal s približno 120° na okoli 76° pri 170 V, od idealne Young–Lippmannove krivulje pa je začel odstopati že pri 70–75 V. Transport po predpisani poti je bil dosežen med 100 V in 200 V, pri nazivnih hitrostih od 1 do 145 mm/s. Analiza dejanske poti je pokazala povprečne hitrosti glavnine kapljice med 78,8 in 112,0 mm/s. Dejanska hitrost je bila nižja od nazivne, saj se je kapljica med gibanjem raztezala in krajšala pot čez vogale. Zaprta konfiguracija je zmanjšala pripenjanje kapljice zaradi kontaminacije ter omogočila zanesljiv transport do hitrosti 80 mm/s. Rezultati kažejo, da obratovalno območje miniaturizirane platforme v veliki meri določa debelina dielektrične plasti, način določanja hitrosti pa pomembno vpliva na poročano vrednost, saj uporaba predpostavljenega koraka med elektrodami dejansko hitrost sistematično precenjuje.

title: Experimental reasoning in large language models
abstract: Abstract Scientific reasoning requires interaction with the physical world: designing experiments, interpreting outcomes, and deciding what experiment should come next. Here we show that general-purpose large language models (LLMs) already possess substantial capabilities for experimental reasoning. We connected LLMs to a liquid-handling robot and camera through PEARL, which provides perception, action, and persistent state. Given objectives rather than prescribed workflows, the system designed and successfully executed experiments, interpreted observations, and revised its approach as evidence accumulated. When information was insufficient, PEARL autonomously designed and performed intermediate experiments to acquire it. In quantitative enzyme characterization, it judged whether measurements were sufficient, new data were required, or conditions needed to change. Across eight scenarios, these behaviors were reliable with limited agent scaffolding and no supplied scenario-specific recovery recipes. More broadly, general-purpose LLMs may provide a reasoning layer between scientific objectives and physical experimentation, shifting laboratory automation from executing predefined procedures toward AI systems that participate directly in the experimental process.
authors: Jeongyheon Kim; Philip Romero

title: Expert consensus on neuro‐musculoskeletal functional reconstruction for post‐stroke spastic hemiplegia
abstract: Persistent motor dysfunction in post-stroke spastic hemiplegia may result from impaired voluntary motor control, abnormal muscle overactivity, fixed structural restriction, muscle force imbalance, or their combination. Advances in brain-computer interfaces (BCIs), peripheral nerve surgery, and tendon and soft-tissue reconstruction have expanded therapeutic options, yet optimal indications and sequencing remain unclear. A multidisciplinary expert panel reviewed current evidence, addressed key clinical questions, and developed consensus recommendations for noninvasive BCI, diagnostic motor nerve block (DNB), selective or hyperselective peripheral nerve surgery, and reconstructive procedures. The consensus emphasizes evaluation of four major components: central voluntary motor impairment, dynamic abnormal muscle overactivity, fixed structural limitations, and muscle force imbalance. Treatment should be guided by the patient's functional goals and the primary factor restricting performance. Task-oriented motor training remains fundamental when voluntary motor control is impaired, with BCI-based closed-loop training as a potential adjunct in selected patients. Focal, functionally significant muscle overactivity caused by abnormal neural drive may be considered for selective or hyperselective peripheral nerve surgery, with DNB assisting patient selection. Fixed structural restrictions may require tendon or soft-tissue procedures, while muscle force imbalance may benefit from tendon transfer or other dynamic reconstruction. When multiple impairments coexist, combined reconstruction followed by targeted motor retraining and comprehensive reassessment may be appropriate. Overall, neuro-musculoskeletal functional reconstruction should follow an individualized pathway linking functional goals, dominant pathophysiology, treatment targets, and outcomes. Given the variable evidence quality, no universal treatment sequence or combination strategy is currently supported.
authors: Peng Wen; Y.-Z. Wang; Zhongzheng He; Zhizhong Zhu; Chunbing Chen; Kaifeng Wu; Xiaohong Fu; Guoguang Zhao; Liu‐Lin Xiong

title: Explore or Confirm? LLM Agents Misallocate Measurements Under Noise
abstract: As model reasoning gets cheaper, the physical experiment becomes the slow and costly step in discovery. Each experiment returns a noisy reading: a high value can mean a good candidate or a lucky draw. With a fixed budget, an AI agent must keep choosing between exploring a new candidate and confirming a promising one by re-testing it. We measure that choice in Wellocate, a simulated assay campaign with known true values. It is built on a generated landscape and on two real protein datasets, GB1 and PhoQ, scrambled so no model can answer from memory. We test five language models as minimal agents, with no tools and no memory beyond the history in each prompt. They misallocate in both directions. Three over-confirm, spending most of the budget re-testing. On the generated landscape one under-confirms, trusting single readings, and there every model ends with a worse final pick than a basic scripted strategy. Each failure has its own cause. The over-confirmers run short of new candidates worth trying: a list of untried candidates cuts their re-testing and, on real protein data, makes two of them pick much better. A running summary of their readings or a description of the landscape changes it by at most five percentage points. For the under-confirmer, re-testing its top candidates in a final round, replayed on its own campaigns, recovers only about a quarter of what it loses by picking the wrong candidate. This suggests confirmation has to run through the whole campaign. We release Wellocate as a benchmark and reinforcement-learning environment with frozen splits and scripted baselines. With it, anyone can measure how an agent splits its budget before trusting it with real experiments, and train agents to split it better. Code, data and the environment are available at https://github.com/Xstendyl/wellocate.
authors: Abdul Karim; Matt Keon

title: Fallopian Tube Organoid-Integrated Microfluidic Platform for Real-Time Imaging and Outflow Analysis
abstract: Abstract The fallopian tube is a dynamic, hormonally regulated epithelial conduit whose luminal microenvironment governs oocyte transport, fertilisation, early embryo development, and the initiation of gynaecological diseases including ectopic pregnancy, hydrosalpinx, and serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma (STIC), yet existing models such as 2D monolayers, intact organoids, and static Transwell systems fail to recapitulate a polarised epithelium lining a perfused lumen under physiological fluid shear while preserving native organoid secretory function. We present a robust and accessible workflow integrating mechanically opened fallopian tube organoids into a custom-designed polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) microfluidic device, in which organoid fragments form epithelial sheets and re-establish luminal-like architecture under controlled perfusion. The focus of this study is organoid integration and the characterisation of the resulting organoid-derived epithelium, rather than establishing chip cultures from individual cell lines. As this epithelium is built from expandable organoid stock rather than primary tissue, which typically survives only a few days in culture, the approach removes a major bottleneck to establishing organ-on-chip models, and we maintain viable cultures for up to 10 days. Epithelial sheets reproducibly covered more than 90% of the channel area by day 6 (n = 5 devices) and formed continuous ZO-1-positive tight junctions. The platform supports longitudinal brightfield and fluorescence microscopy at subcellular resolution, continuous collection of conditioned flow-through for ELISA, and quantitative analysis of cell coverage and health using CellProfiler software. We characterise the organoid-derived epithelium by benchmarking against tissue culture (TC) formats, comparing nuclear morphology on-chip with conventional well culture, and showing that the damage-associated cytokine interleukin-1α (IL-1α) was detectable in organoid lysates but below the assay limit of detection in both chip outflow and intact-organoid secretions. These findings indicate that culturing mechanically opened organoids on-chip did not produce a detectable increase in IL-1α release relative to intact organoids. Computational flow modelling characterises perfusion through the device and predicts how factors secreted by healthy epithelium and by tumour cells are distributed along the channel. The feasibility of tumour– epithelium co-culture was explored using OVCAR3 ovarian cancer spheroids as a proof-of-concept model to investigate interactions between tumour cells and the fallopian tube epithelium. Together, these results establish the technical feasibility of the platform and support its further development as an accessible system for studying reproductive health conditions affecting the fallopian tube, including tubal damage from infection, endometriosis, STIC lesions, and occlusion.
authors: Dolan Evans; Heidi Savey-Bennett; Kimberley Perkins; Alice Thompson; Daniel Joseph Netherwood; Eleanor A. Doman; Christine K. Schmidt; Peter T Ruane; Raveen K. J. Tank

title: Feedback control via H3K9 methylation and siRNA biogenesis autonomously maintains RNAi heterochromatin through continuous low-level transcription
abstract: The logic of RNA-based silencing involves nascent RNA molecules that serve as scaffolds to recruit proteins that repress transcription. Despite transcription and silencing being antagonistic, RNA-based recruitment mechanisms have been widely adopted in organisms ranging from yeast to humans. In fission yeast ( Schizosaccharomyces pombe ), the nuclear RNAi pathway that establishes heterochromatin at pericentromeric repeats to silence transcription exemplifies this paradox. Current models propose that cells reconcile these opposing activities by confining pericentromeric transcription to S phase while maintaining silencing during the rest of the cell cycle. Here, using strand-specific single-molecule RNA FISH (smFISH), we detect forward and reverse pericentromeric transcripts with high sensitivity and single-cell resolution. We find that repeat-associated transcription is rare, heterogeneous and happens independently of cell-cycle control. Instead, transcript production is governed solely by feedback involving small RNA biogenesis and H3K9 methylation. By combining mathematical modeling with experiments, we show that low levels of H3K9me or siRNAs prevent heterochromatin establishment, whereas high levels of H3K9me cause stochastic switching. Our work reveals that the same RNA-based feedback architecture can sample distinct transcriptional regimes, with feedback strength determining how often cells produce transcripts without any external regulatory inputs.
authors: Sumanth Kumar Maheshwaram; Amith Z. Abdulla; Serena Chiu; Dionysus Morris-Evans; Jané Kondev; Kaushik Ragunathan

title: Female Reproductive System Assembloids in Health and Disease
abstract: In just over a decade, in vitro modeling of the female reproductive tract has advanced from planar monolayers of immortalized cells to self-organizing epithelial organoids and, most recently, to increasingly complex multicellular and multicompartment 3D models, including assembloids that combine organoids with additional organoid modules or specialized cell lineages and demonstrate post-assembly integration and self-organization. This review concentrates deliberately on organoid, assembloid, and related multicellular 3D models rather than on reproductive physiology per se. We first establish a criterion-based framework that distinguishes organoids, assembloids, co-cultures, organ-on-chip systems, and blastoids according to assembly strategy, cellular composition, and evidence of structural and functional integration, and trace the rapid consolidation of the assembloid concept from neuroscience into reproductive biology. We then survey, organ-by-organ and with a critical eye, what these models have demonstrated in the endometrium, the ovary and follicle, the fallopian tube, and the embryo-maternal interface, together with the enabling technologies (including microfluidics, vascularization strategies, biomaterials and bioprinting, and single-cell and spatial benchmarking) and the limitations that still constrain the field. We close with emerging translational opportunities in disease modeling, drug and toxicology screening, and personalized reproductive medicine, while highlighting the requirements for physiological validation, reproducibility, standardization, and appropriate ethical and regulatory oversight.
authors: Mete Hakan Karalök; Burcu Biltekin; Turgay Barut; Süleyman Ergün

title: Fermentative valorization of edible algae: nutritional potential, food applications, safety considerations, and industrial challenges
abstract: Edible algae, including microalgae and macroalgae, are recognized as sustainable aquatic bioresources for future food systems, with high areal productivity, low reliance on arable land and freshwater, and rich nutrients including proteins, polyunsaturated fatty acids, pigments, minerals, vitamins and functional polysaccharides. Yet their wider application in mainstream foods is limited by low digestibility, rigid cell walls, marine off-flavors, variable safety and high processing costs. This review examines the nutritional potential, food applications, fermentation strategies, safety considerations and industrial bottlenecks of edible algae, focusing on fermentation-mediated valorization as an enabling strategy beyond conventional preservation. Lactic acid, alcoholic and mixed-culture fermentation can boost shelf stability, release intracellular nutrients, modulate sensory attributes, generate bioactive metabolites, and support circular use of residual algal biomass. Meanwhile, advanced technologies like enzyme-assisted extraction, non-thermal extraction, microfluidics and nanoencapsulation help enhance ingredient functionality and bioactive delivery. The review also notes that the future value of algae-based foods relies on matrix-specific formulation, standardized safety control for heavy metals and iodine, strain improvement, biorefinery integration and consumer-oriented sensory design. Overall, fermentative and precision-processing strategies offer a promising route to transform algae from niche supplements into safe, palatable, multifunctional ingredients for sustainable food innovation.
authors: Donglin Ma; Chaokang Xia; Aiming Jia; Guilan Zhang; Yuzong Zhao; Haiwei Ren; Xiaogang Liu; Fengjun Li; Lilang Li; Rui‐Bo Jia; Kuntai Li

title: Field‐Driven Active Colloids as Distributed Micromachines: Bridging Physics, Control, and Function Across Length Scales
abstract: Field-driven active colloids offer a route to microscale machines whose behavior can be programmed by external electric and magnetic fields. At the micron scale, thermal fluctuations, hydrodynamic interactions, interparticle forces, and field-mediated actuation combine to connect active matter physics with control and function. In this Perspective, we frame field-driven active colloids as distributed micromachines, where power delivery, sensing, control, and function are distributed across particles, applied fields, imaging modalities, and feedback architectures. Electric and magnetic fields enable programmable propulsion, trajectory regulation, collective interactions, and dynamic reconfiguration, but practical deployment remains limited by energy delivery, material compatibility, and feedback constraints in complex environments. We emphasize that progress should be evaluated not only by motion, but by controlling task-relevant variables that determine successful localization, transport, capture, treatment, release, assembly, and reconfiguration. Closing the loop between sensing, AI/ML, computation, and field-based actuation will be essential for advancing field-driven colloids toward adaptive, task-oriented micromachines.
authors: Ruchi Patel; Bhuvnesh Bharti

title: FluOpti: an open-source system for programmable whole-plate optogenetics and multi-fluorescence imaging
abstract: Bacteria are able to self-organize into complex spatial communities, such as colonies, biofilms and swarms. Probing cells and gene networks with dynamic stimuli while preserving their spatial organization is therefore essential for understanding how bacterial communities organize across spatial and temporal scales. Optogenetics offers a powerful approach for such a task given the precise control of stimulus delivery without the perturbations normally associated with the addition of liquid inducers. However, most optogenetics devices have been developed to work with liquid cell cultures or to deliver a spatial pattern without the concurrent recording of gene responses and colony growth. Here, we describe FluOpti, an open source, low-cost device for controlling gene expression, through programmable light inputs, and recording multi-fluorescence responses and colony growth across whole petri dishes. White light LEDs are used for brightfield imaging while green and red LEDs are used as optogenetic inputs to activate and inactivate target genes via the CcaS/R two component system in E. coli. Low cost blue and orange acrylic are used as excitation and emission filters for fluorescence imaging, respectively. We developed custom software to analyze colony growth and optogenetic responses from 72-hour time-lapse experiments. A mathematical model was developed to predict gene expression levels in response to green-to-red light ratio stimuli. We use FluOpti to reveal a spatially structured response to optogenetic stimuli, with gene activation rates differing in cells located at the center and edge of colonies. to validate its use at a whole petri dish scale, FluOpti was used to depict how Voronoi territories can act as predictors of colony size, in congruence with previous studies. Together, these results demonstrate the utility of the device for studying gene networks at multiple spatio-temporal scales, from individual colonies to the whole petri dish. Performing optogenetics studies in whole petri dishes while preserving spatial arrangements could offer valuable insights into the spatial biology of gene networks in microbial populations.
authors: Isaac Nuñez; Tamara Matúte; Alejandro Aravena; Wladimir Araya; Daniel Nuñez; Severine Cazaux; Valentina Ferrando; Patricio Obregón; Francisco Javier Quero; Gustavo Düring; Timothy Rudge; Fernán Federici

title: Framework-Templated Single Clathrate Hydrate Cages in Metal–Organic Frameworks
abstract: Molecular simulations identify metal–organic framework (MOF) pores that retain single methane hydrate cages and, for a nonstandard 16-water cage, support its assembly from disordered water. In smooth spherical pores, a methane molecule assembled twenty waters into the pentagonal dodecahedron of structure I hydrate and sixteen waters into a 435661 cage, a polyhedron that no known hydrate crystal contains. These idealized models were built by language-model agents and then walked back toward real materials, an approach referred to here as agentic doodling, and they guided a screening of 120,419 experimental MOF structures. Most size-matched pores pulled the cage apart, but a small set of frameworks kept it intact at 216 K, better with methane than without, and ELOZIQ kept the dodecahedron up to 270 K, near the melting temperature of the water model. In XODDED and GUQMAH, the nonstandard cage was held at least as well as in an ideal spherical pore, and it self-assembled around methane from randomly placed water, with nearly all of its edges hydrogen bonded. The pores template the cages through a moderate attraction spread over the cage corners rather than through strong binding sites placed at the corners. These results open a route to designing MOFs that hold single hydrate cages, including cages that do not occur in bulk hydrates.
authors: Jihan Kim

title: From Algorithm Performance to Laboratory Deployment: A Critical Review of Artificial Intelligence in Clinical Chemistry
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being applied in clinical laboratories to support laboratory processes and interpretation of test results. Recent developments in machine learning, deep learning, and large language models have expanded the potential applications of AI across different stages of laboratory testing. However, the use of AI in clinical laboratories also raises important questions regarding validation, analytical performance, and transferability between laboratories. This narrative review examines recent applications of AI across the total testing process in clinical chemistry. Recent English-language scientific literature published from 2023 to 18 August 2026 was identified through searches of PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar. It describes AI-assisted test utilization; specimen handling and quality assessment; detection of laboratory errors; patient-based quality control; interpretation of complex analytical outputs, including signals from emerging AI-integrated biosensors and nanomaterial-based analytical platforms; result verification; and laboratory-report interpretation. The review also discusses major implementation challenges, including analytical variability, data quality, sensor and platform reproducibility, model generalizability, interoperability, and limitations of large language models. Particular attention is given to external validation, transportability, and real-world implementation. Among the studies considered in this review, many applications remain supported mainly by retrospective or internally validated studies, while prospective and operational evaluations are less common. Finally, practical considerations for validation, local verification, quality assurance, and performance monitoring are discussed. AI has considerable potential to support clinical chemistry laboratories, but safe use requires appropriate evaluation and continued involvement of laboratory professionals.
authors: Abdelraheem A. Bani Ahmad; Sulieman Bani‐Ahmad

title: From Cell Clusters to Complexity: Testicular Organoids as Emerging Platforms in Male Reproductive Research and Biotechnological Innovation
abstract: BACKGROUND: Conventional 2D cultures and animal models incompletely recapitulate the human testicular niche, limiting translation for male infertility, toxicology, and endocrine research. Limited and highly variable access to human testicular tissue restricts translational research. Testicular organoids (TOs), self-organizing assemblies of germ and somatic cells within biomimetic scaffolds, microfluidic chips, or bioprinted constructs, can reproduce seminiferous cord/tubule-like organization, elements of the blood-testis barrier and steroidogenic function, and increasingly support germ-cell progression. By integrating defined media, matrix cues, and controlled microenvironments, TO platforms enable mechanism-driven studies and human-relevant new approach methodologies for toxicology, disease modeling, and fertility-preservation research. This, in turn, supports endocrine and reprotoxicology testing, disease modeling, and prepubertal fertility-preservation strategies. Broad and responsible adoption will require clinically concordant read-outs, stable long-term cultures, reproducible and complete human spermatogenesis, and a robust ethical framework. This review aims to comprehensively evaluate TO systems, spanning cell sources, biomaterials, and microenvironmental control to functional read-outs of morphogenesis, steroidogenesis, and germ-cell progression. By synthesizing recent advances, we clarify mechanistic determinants of organoid performance and outline their translational implications for male infertility research, toxicology, and fertility-preservation strategies.
authors: Merve Görgülü; Leyla Satı

title: From Displacement Physics to Intelligent and Sustainable EOR: Multiscale Evolution of Enhanced Oil Recovery Mechanisms, Technologies, and Strategies Aligned with the Sustainable Development Goals (2000–2026):
abstract: Enhanced Oil Recovery (EOR) is a fundamental approach for increasing oil production from mature reservoirs, in which a significant fraction of the oil remains trapped due to capillary forces, unfavorable mobility ratios, heterogeneity, and preferential flow. This review analyzes the evolution of physics applied to EOR between 2000 and 2026, highlighting the transition from methods based on the optimization of isolated properties toward integrated, multiscale, and reservoir-specific strategies. The main mechanisms associated with low-salinity water and smart water, polymers, surfactants, ASP processes, miscible CO₂ and CO₂-foam, nanotechnology, microfluidics, and digital rock physics are discussed. The analysis demonstrates that mobility, capillarity, wettability, interfacial tension, miscibility, rheology, and transport act in a coupled manner, making it inadequate to evaluate any technology based on a single performance parameter. The development of microfluidics, computed tomography, and digital rock reconstructions has expanded the ability to directly observe pore-scale phenomena and relate them to macroscopic responses. More recently, physics-informed machine learning, Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs), neural networks, and neural operators have been used to integrate experimental data and physical laws for the prediction and optimization of recovery processes. Parallelly, it is demonstrated that the evolution of contemporary EOR extends beyond production maximization by directly aligning with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) of the 2030 Agenda, highlighting resource optimization in mature fields (SDG 12 - Responsible Consumption and Production), digitalization and AI innovation (SDG 9 - Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure), permanent geological carbon storage via CCUS (SDG 13 - Climate Action), and transitional energy efficiency (SDG 7 - Affordable and Clean Energy). It is concluded that the main frontier of contemporary EOR does not lie in the search for a universal technology, but rather in the combination of physical mechanisms, experimental characterization, computational modeling, artificial intelligence, and global sustainability guidelines. This integration establishes the foundations for intelligent, adaptive, multiscale, sustainable EOR guided by the characteristics and uncertainties of each reservoir. It is concluded that the main frontier of contemporary EOR does not lie in the search for a universal technology, but rather in the combination of physical mechanisms, experimental characterization, computational modeling, and artificial intelligence. This integration establishes the foundations for intelligent, adaptive, multiscale EOR guided by the characteristics and uncertainties of each reservoir.
authors: Landson Soares Marques; Geruza Iolanda Aparecida Capovilla Mendes; Michel da Costa

title: From Experiment Execution to Verifiable Capability: An Assurance Architecture for Self-Driving Laboratories
abstract: Self-driving laboratories increasingly select experiments, orchestrate resources, execute protocols and update scientific models. Yet existing architectures often under-specify a critical runtime question: what evidence shows that the current physical system can satisfy a particular task under its operating conditions? Device availability, command completion and internal feedback do not establish that delivered volume, end-effector pose or sample temperature meets task-specific limits. Periodic calibration provides essential baseline evidence, but cannot support every operation through a single static pass label. We propose a three-layer architecture comprising task planning and scheduling, task-level capability assurance, and execution and physical operations. The assurance layer translates formal tasks into machine-readable capability requirements, represents measurement evidence through versioned, uncertainty-aware records with explicit applicability and validity, and uses these records to admit, constrain, reject, reassign or trigger verification of tasks. Maintenance, collisions, environmental excursions and version changes dynamically invalidate affected records. Parameter correction is treated as an optional bounded recovery process requiring authorization, readback, independent re-verification and commit or rollback. Examples in liquid handling, robotic positioning and temperature control illustrate the framework. Trustworthy self-driving laboratories must therefore maintain machine-actionable evidence that they are currently qualified to perform each task.
authors: Chao Wang; 李彦锋; Yuchi Shen; Yuming Chen; Jianqing Li; Bin Liu

title: From Roadmap to Response: A Community Assessment of Autonomous Science
abstract: Autonomous science couples instruments, robots, data systems, and AI agents into workflows that plan and interpret experiments with progressively less human intervention, and a two-year community roadmap published in July 2026 set eighteen milestones for the field. The second Annual Autonomous Workflows Workshop was convened to write such a roadmap and, finding one already published, answered it instead. Over two days, participants from national laboratories, universities, instrument and platform vendors, applied research institutes, and federal program offices tested those milestones against what their own organizations run today. This report presents the resulting assessment, which rests primarily on the recorded plenary discussion. We find that the milestones closest to model capability have advanced while those requiring another party's cooperation have not, that decision-relevant state does not cross the laboratory boundary, and that cross-framework provenance applied to three deployed agentic workflows exposed a silent error in each. We argue that the binding constraint is ownership rather than coordination, because implementable proposals surfaced repeatedly and no organization held the mandate, the budget, and the staff to carry them. We propose ten candidate milestones for the gaps the roadmap does not cover, and we set out an investment agenda that includes the applied mathematics autonomous laboratories need.

title: From Static Classrooms to Living Systems
abstract: This chapter explores how Digital twins (DTs) are changing in their roles across the educational spectrum. DTs play both theoretical and practical roles, facilitating immersive, feedback-intensive and personal experiences beyond traditional simulations. DTs in life sciences and agricultural engineering enable safe, repeatable and data-rich learning environments where learners can practice realistic simulations of poultry farm management, disease control and performance analytics without endangering living animals in the laboratory. DTs have been applied to reinvent introductory programming education in computing education. DTs have been identified as potential solutions for schools in developing countries such as Mozambique and Rwanda that lack physical laboratory facilities. In chemical engineering education, virtual reality twins of extraction columns enable interactive manipulation of flow parameters and AI-based image analysis to optimize droplet size, introducing students to the fusion of process control and data analytics in an accessible, hardware-light format.
authors: Marwa M. EID

title: From Trial-and-Error to Learn-by-Experiment: The Future of Materials Research in Perovskite and Organic Photovoltaics
abstract: The next major change in perovskite and organic photovoltaic research may not come from a new material or device architecture, but from a new way of doing and analyzing experiments. Conventional trial-and-error optimization, often a onevariable-at-a-time (OVAT) approach, typically varies a limited number of parameters sequentially, making it difficult to resolve interactions within the increasingly complex processing spaces of complex, multilayer solar cells and demands a large number of experiments. We argue that robotic experimentation combined with machine learning can fundamentally alter this approach. The key advantage of robotics is not simply higher throughput, but highly precise and reproducible fabrication together with comprehensive recording of processing and environmental conditions. This transforms individual experiments into reliable, machine-readable data points and provides the foundation for machine learning to explore multidimensional parameter spaces, identify hidden correlations and autonomously select informative experiments. Optimization can consequently move beyond maximizing power-conversion efficiency toward understanding how parameters interact, with simultaneous consideration of efficiency, lifetime, stability, reproducibility, resource consumption and environmental impact. Such a transition could replace sequential trial-and-error optimization with reproducible, data-rich and closed-loop experimentation. Rather than replacing researchers, robotic laboratories may enable them to investigate materials and processing spaces that are too complex to explore manually. We propose that the long-term impact of autonomous experimentation in photovoltaics will therefore be measured by how much more can be learned from every experiment.
authors: Maria Azhar; Stefan Kraner; Nikky Chandrakar; Nathanael Füssinger; Lukas Schmidt‐Mende; Udo Bach

title: From communication to computation in neurons-on-a-chip: an in silico study of neurotopomorphic computing
abstract: Living neuronal networks transform inputs through recurrent cellular and population dynamics, yet it is unknown which network architecture supports which computation. Neurons-on-a-chip turn this question into a design problem because microchannels guide axonal growth and set the network architecture. We introduce IC$^3$, an Integrated Characterisation of Communication-Driven Computation, which characterizes network state through neuronal dynamics, functional communication, and structural support. We implemented nine architectures \textit{in silico} as conductance-based spiking networks and tested each on frequency decoding, temporal-order discrimination, and fading memory. Predominantly feedforward circuits decoded best. Sequential Chain and Microchannel Diode had the lowest IC$^3$ and recruited a third of reachable neurons, yet achieved the two highest scores on both classification tasks. Across architectures, higher IC$^3$ went with lower classification scores. We term this new direction \emph{neurotopomorphic computing}, in which the physical organisation of neuronal connectivity is engineered as part of the computing substrate.
authors: Michael Taynnan Barros

title: From deterministic to adaptive magnetic micro-robots
abstract: Abstract Robotics has long pursued the development of systems that can control physical objects remotely and precisely in diverse environments. With ongoing miniaturization, micro-robots have emerged as promising platforms for a wide range of applications. In particular, magnetic micro-robots are compelling because external magnetic fields provide a wireless and biocompatible means of actuation, overcoming the constraints of on-board power sources in confined and complex settings. Despite extensive studies, the classification of magnetic micro-robots has often remained indistinct. This review seeks to contribute a more systematic understanding by defining four major categories—rigid, reconfigurable, shape-changing, and swarm—while also discussing emerging hybrid systems that bridge these paradigms. We synthesize the fundamental actuation principles and representative designs of each category. By examining the capabilities and limitations of each paradigm, we identify challenges and outline future directions for the advancement of adaptive and intelligent magnetic micro-robotic systems.
authors: 조은화; Seungyeon Kim; Koohee Han

title: From living actuators to architected machines: Biomimetic 3D and 4D printing for biohybrid robots
abstract: ABSTRACT Muscle-powered biohybrid robots are emerging at the intersection of living tissue engineering and soft robotics, and as the field matures, the primary bottleneck is shifting from biological feasibility toward manufacturability. Additive manufacturing therefore plays a central role by enabling precise control over geometry, material heterogeneity, and cellular organization, thereby improving reproducibility and scalability in increasingly complex biohybrid systems. In this perspective, we examine how biomimetic 3D printing transforms contractile tissues into architected functional systems with predictable performance through programmable anisotropy, hierarchical structures, and integrated material interfaces. We further introduce biomimetic 4D printing as a complementary paradigm that enables post-fabrication morphogenesis, dynamic shape transformation, and spatiotemporal control over structure-function relationships. Building on these advances, we propose a manufacturing-oriented roadmap centered on four primary engineering axes: programmable anisotropy, soft-hard material integration, diffusion-aware architectural design, and standardized benchmarking. Together, these axes provide a framework for translating biohybrid actuators from laboratory prototypes into reproducible and scalable engineering systems. Finally, we highlight how biomimetic hybrid additive manufacturing enables the integration of neural control, metabolic support, and immune functionality within unified architectures, thereby advancing biohybrid robots toward autonomous, scalable, and functionally robust living machines.
authors: María José Veana Hernandez; Alan de Jesús Alarcón Rodríguez; Yipei Yang; Lei Zhang; Su Ryon Shin; 이지현; Kannan Govindaraj; Cheolwoo Ha; Niyou Wang

title: From medical to pedagogical care
abstract: BACKGROUND: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) agents, including chatbots and virtual tutors, into education has expanded rapidly; however, systematic quantitative analysis of research trends in this field remains limited. Notably, the intellectual foundations of AI agent research lie not in education but in medicine, where AI agents were first extensively deployed and studied in clinical, experimental, and pedagogical contexts. METHODS: In this study, a bibliometric analysis of 377 records retrieved from the Web of Science was conducted using VOSviewer to map the evolution, thematic focus, and collaborative networks within this field. RESULTS: The study showed AI agent research originated strongly in healthcare, with educational applications emerging more recently. Key research themes encompassed AI technologies, human-computer interaction, pedagogical applications, and ethical considerations. Collaborative efforts were led by the USA and China, supported by active European and Asian research hubs. The findings revealed a dual narrative of significant benefits for personalized learning and learner well-being alongside persistent challenges such as algorithmic bias and accessibility gaps. CONCLUSION: To realize the transformative potential of AI in education, future research should prioritize the development of adaptive algorithms, robust ethical frameworks, inclusive design, and interdisciplinary collaboration. By focusing on these areas, the field can work toward overcoming technical, ethical, and logistical barriers, thereby ensuring that AI acts as a sustainable force for equity and excellence in education.
authors: Xinhuang Tang; Shukun Chen; Jinyan Chen

title: From predictive AI to autonomous food bioprocessing: a critical review of real-time quality monitoring, energy optimization, digital twins, and intelligent process control
abstract: Food bioprocessing is transitioning from conventional automation towards intelligent, data-driven, and increasingly autonomous manufacturing. A substantial gap nevertheless remains between accurate process prediction and reliable autonomous control. This critical narrative review examines the convergence of real-time sensing, artificial intelligence (AI), energy and process optimisation, hybrid physics–AI modelling, digital twins, and intelligent closed-loop control in food bioprocess engineering, with explicit attention to what has been demonstrated experimentally, at pilot scale, or only in simulation versus what remains conceptual. A structured narrative review informed by SANRA principles was conducted using Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, IEEE Xplore, and Google Scholar, with literature published up to 17 August 2026 considered and supplemented by a second, targeted search cycle addressing process analytical technology, electronic sensing, convolutional-network quality evaluation, and digital-twin applications in thermal, baking, and cold-chain processes. Evidence was synthesised according to the technological progression from monitoring and prediction to optimisation, digital twins, intelligent control, and autonomy. The evidence indicates substantial advances in smart sensing, machine learning, multimodal quality assessment, and multi-objective optimisation, with demonstrated opportunities to improve product quality, energy efficiency, productivity, and resource utilisation. Nevertheless, most applications remain concentrated at monitoring, predictive-modelling, and offline-optimisation stages, while validated industrial closed-loop and self-learning systems remain comparatively limited, and quantitative sustainability and economic evidence specific to autonomous food bioprocessing remains scarce. Digital twins and hybrid physics–AI approaches provide an important bridge towards autonomy by integrating physical process knowledge, real-time data, prediction, optimisation, and feedback control. This review proposes a six-level Food Bioprocess Autonomy Framework (FBAF), progressing from manual processing to self-learning autonomous bioprocessing, and situates it explicitly against ISA-95, RAMI 4.0, and SAE J3016-derived autonomy scales, providing measurable per-level criteria and illustrative classification of published systems. Future progress requires robust external validation, uncertainty-aware decision-making, interoperable infrastructure, cybersecurity, fail-safe control, and simultaneous optimisation of quality, safety, energy, productivity, and environmental and economic performance. The framework provides a foundation for benchmarking technological maturity and guiding the development of safe, scalable, and resource-efficient autonomous food-processing systems.
authors: Chinyere Nneoma Ugwu; Fabian Chukwudi Ogenyi; Jovita Nnenna Ugwu; Okechukwu Paul-Chima Ugwu; Micheal Ben Okon
venue: Frontiers in Food Science and Technology

title: From smart sensing to adaptive remediation: artificial intelligence and Internet of Things for persistent organic pollutants
abstract: Persistent organic pollutants (POPs) remain a major environmental challenge because of their persistence, long-range transport, bioaccumulation, and resistance to degradation. Conventional monitoring and remediation systems provide reliable analytical performance but are largely fragmented, laboratory dependent, and unable to deliver the continuous, predictive, and adaptive management required for complex, dynamic contamination scenarios. Recent literature reports substantial advances in biosensors, Internet of Things (IoT)-enabled sensing, machine learning (ML), and artificial intelligence (AI) for pollutant detection, forecasting, source identification, and remediation optimization. However, these developments often operate separately, with limited coordination between environmental sensing, data analytics, treatment processes, and decision-making. The literature further highlights persistent barriers to field deployment, including limited and geographically heterogeneous datasets, inconsistent sensor performance and calibration, restricted model transferability, insufficient independent validation, uncertainty in AI predictions, and the lack of mature regulatory frameworks for AI-assisted environmental assessment. From our perspective, the next advance in POP management should move beyond isolated AI applications toward integrated, closed-loop AI-IoT architectures that continuously connect sensing, prediction, remediation, and feedback control. Such systems could transform POP management from reactive assessment to proactive and adaptive environmental governance. Future progress will depend on standardized, Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable (FAIR) environmental datasets, explainable and uncertainty-aware AI, robust field validation, and interoperable sensing infrastructures.
authors: Khaled Chawraba; Abrar Hussain; Obaid A. Alharbi; Amal Abdelhaleem

title: From stretchable materials and functional fibers to intelligent textile sensing systems
abstract: Wearable sensors that offer significant adaptability and comfort demonstrate substantial potential for discrete, seamless integration into garments, enabling diverse applications for remote monitoring. The transformation of rigid electronic devices into flexible and stretchable sensors, achieved by integrating conductive materials with compliant dielectrics, has enabled the development of robust sensors. However, several factors must be addressed to enable widespread adoption, including garment integration, wireless communication, data pipelines, signal processing, multimodal fusion, privacy and security concerns. Addressing these challenges is essential for establishing the technological and social infrastructure necessary for the widespread adoption of wearable technologies. This review highlights innovations in material and mechanical design strategies that have shaped the current landscape of wearables, and points out some remaining challenges.
authors: Maria Papaefstathiou; Mohamed Elgendi; Carlo Menon

title: Functional double-emulsion droplets enable multiplexed CRISPR quantification of cancer-related miRNAs.
abstract: Accurate, multiplexed microRNA detection is critical for early cancer diagnosis. We present a droplet-based digital CRISPR/Cas13a platform for simultaneous, amplification-free detection of multiple miRNAs. By integrating double emulsion (DE) microfluidics with programmable crRNAs, the system achieves orthogonal, interference-free readouts, enabling precise absolute quantification in complex biological samples. The assay demonstrates high sequence specificity, robust orthogonality, and consistent performance across target combinations and matrices. Fluorescence-positive droplet counts correlate linearly with input concentrations, allowing quantification of miRNA-21, miRNA-29a, and miRNA-92a with 10 copies/μL representing the lowest concentration experimentally evaluated in this study. The applicability of the platform is further evaluated in a small proof-of-concept cohort of plasma samples from healthy controls and colorectal cancer (CRC) patients. This platform provides an amplification-free approach for multiplexed miRNA quantification and supports further development for clinical biomarker analysis.
authors: Yang Zhang; Fei Deng; Rui Sang; Ling Liu; Tracie J Barber; Ewa M Goldys; Ming Li

title: Fungal hyphae through the lens of microfluidic devices: From biological properties to novel therapeutic opportunities
abstract: Fungal diseases are increasingly being recognized as a major health problem worldwide. Advancing therapeutic approaches against fungal pathogens require comprehensive knowledge of their biological properties, which enable fungi to explore host environments, interact with host cells and coinhabiting microorganisms, adopt colonization and infective strategies. Thus, fungus intrinsic as well as extrinsic mechanisms functionally cooperate for successful host infection and disease development. In this regard, fungal hyphae, i.e. long, filamentous structures with polarized tip growth, represent a unique feature of multicellular fungi and play critical roles during the infectious process, calling for in-depth characterization of their functional and structural properties. In this context, reproducing hyphal growth in physiological conditions represents a fundamental prerequisite for disease modeling and therapeutic development. For their potential to accommodate and interconnect cells and miniature tissues, microfluidic devices stand as unique opportunities in this direction by overcoming acknowledged limits of animal models and traditional cell cultures. Based on these premises, we herein provide an overview of the use of microfluidic devices in the study of fungal hyphae, from the investigation of their biological properties to the analysis of inter-organismal networking, including the interaction between fungal hyphae and host cells. By dissecting hyphal strategies of environmental navigation as well as modalities of cell-cell interactions, resorting to microfluidics devices may provide novel opportunities for therapeutic targeting of fungal pathogens, in line with the objectives of the World Health Organization.
authors: Angela Di Battista; Lassi Sukki; Consuelo Fabi; Sarah Balucchi; Marilena Pariano; Pasi J. Kallio; Claudio Costantini

title: Gap Analysis and Recent Advances in HPLC and UPLC
abstract: Objective: To systematically review the advances of High-Performance Liquid Chromatography (HPLC) and Ultra-Performance Liquid Chromatography (UPLC) since the year of 2020 in the fields of analytical performance, sustainability, automation, and emerging technologies. Data Sources: Databases were searched for all literature related to HPLC and UPLC published from 2020 to 2026 using Scopus, PubMed, Web of Science, and Google Scholar as resources. Study Selection: A total of fifty-five peer-reviewed papers were chosen based upon predefined eligibility criteria to be included as part of this literature surveythese comprised fifteen reviews, twenty-nine articles, and eleven abstracts. Summary of Contents: Advances in the following areas are reviewed: Sub-2 µm and superficially porous columns, Q-TOF MS, green analytical chemistry metrics, automated processes, AI, and miniaturized sample preparation. Challenges include limited transfers of existing methods, lack of open access databases, and inadequate validation of AI-assisted method development by regulatory bodies. Conclusion: HPLC and UPLC have the potential to evolve into faster, more eco-friendly, and innovative analytical platforms. Addressing current limitations will allow for further integration of HPLC and UPLC with nanotechnology, microfluidics, and sustainable analytical chemistry.
authors: Snehal Shete; Deotale Kiran; Gayatri Katole; Vinod Thakre
venue: Asian Journal of Pharmaceutical Research and Development

title: Going beyond labels: Semi-supervised learning for enzyme kinetic parameter prediction
abstract: Abstract Enzyme kinetic parameters, such as the turnover number ( k cat ), underpin enzyme engineering and metabolic modeling. Machine learning models can predict these parameters from sequence and substrate representations, but their accuracy is limited by the scarcity and narrow coverage of experimentally labeled data, particularly for out-of-distribution enzymes. Existing strategies to exploit unlabeled data rely on homologous sequences, pseudo-labels or synthetic perturbations of labeled samples, limiting their potential to fully leverage unlabeled data for model improvement. Here, we show that regularization-based semi-supervised learning improves model performance by leveraging biologically meaningful unlabeled samples alongside labeled data during task-specific training, without assigning pseudo-labels to the unlabeled samples. Specifically, enzyme-substrate pairs lacking k cat , but characterized for other kinetic parameters, can serve as unlabeled data that improve k cat prediction. Using the clustered CataPro dataset at 40% sequence identity as a stringent benchmark, neural consistency regularization and graph-Laplacian regularization each performed better when unlabeled records were added, beyond the gains from regularization on labeled data alone. The benefit required sufficient labeled data, saturated at a few thousand unlabeled records for the neural model, and depended on the density of the unlabeled data in the feature space rather than on their proximity to labeled data. Gains extended to wild-type and mutant enzymes and to a local low-data adenylate kinase landscape. These findings show that incomplete kinetic records specifically, and unlabeled data points generally, are a valuable resource for enzyme kinetics prediction.
authors: Ali Malli; Denys Vasyutyn; Anuj Majumder; Jin Ryoun Kim

title: Graphene-oxide-microfiber aptasensor for dynamic neutrophil monitoring: Bridging cytokine release syndrome and point-of-care sepsis diagnosis
abstract: Neutrophil granule release is critical for host defense, yet its dysregulation underpins cytokine release syndrome (CRS) in both acute (such as sepsis) and sustained inflammatory states. Distinguishing these phases requires real-time monitoring of early markers like neutrophil elastase (ELANE) and lactoferrin (LF), but conventional assays lack requisite sensitivity. Here, we developed a graphene-oxide-functionalized optical microfiber biosensor with high-affinity DNA aptamers (NE-AP and LF-AP) to quantify ELANE and LF via aptamer-protein binding-induced spectral red shifts. The sensor achieved ultralow detection limits (3.57 × 10 −20 M for ELANE and 1.28 × 10 −19 M for LF), eight orders below ELISA, with excellent selectivity. In a lipopolysaccharide-induced murine model, it resolved distinct temporal release profiles of ELANE and LF, and in clinical validation, it showed distinct spectral responses between septic patients and healthy controls in a preliminary clinical cohort. This platform provides a highly sensitive, real-time tool for decoding neutrophil dynamics, with preliminary translational potential for early sepsis diagnosis.
authors: Zhiheng Yu; Han Dong; Xiaolin Chen; Mengjiang Xu; Ren Liu; Jin Wang; Cunliang Yang; Ke Wang; Xianyuan Zhao; Hao Jia; Jijun Feng

title: Green synthesis of silicon nanoparticles for solar cell applications: methods, characterisation, performance, and commercialisation pathways. A critical review
abstract: Green synthesis of silicon nanoparticles is widely described as a lower-carbon alternative to conventional routes. This review tests that claim against primary inventory data, and it does not hold for the only route with enough published data to assess. Rice husk valorisation followed by magnesiothermic reduction requires 1.90 to 2.42 kg of magnesium per kg of silicon at the molar ratios reported in the literature. Primary magnesium carries 17.8 to 25.8 kg CO2-eq/kg. Including that reagent within the system boundary gives 34 to 62 kg CO2-eq per kg of silicon, compared with roughly 9.7 for conventional metallurgical-grade silicon. The green route is three to six times more carbon-intensive, not the substantial environmental improvement commonly claimed. The apparent advantage comes from excluding the magnesium burden, a system-boundary artefact rather than a result. Plant-mediated and microbial routes cannot be assessed at all, since the peer-reviewed literature contains no life cycle, energy, water, waste, or cost inventory for either. Size-distribution coefficients of variation also overlap between routes, so the conventional size-control advantage is narrower than usually claimed. Device performance remains the strongest evidence for the field. A rice husk-derived nano-silicon and activated carbon counter electrode reached 8.01 per cent efficiency in a dye-sensitised solar cell, compared with 7.20 per cent for platinum under identical conditions. On the technology readiness scale, no route exceeds level 5. The case for green silicon nanoparticles rests on replacing platinum and valorising waste, not on carbon.
authors: Abdulrahaman Ogunji; Taiwo Aiyelero; Sola Adedokun; Johnson Momoh; Oluremi Olaleye
