title: Group-Aware and Explainable Machine Learning Framework for Heart Disease Prediction Using Optimized CatBoost
abstract: Accurate and reliable heart disease prediction can support early risk assessment and improve clinical decision-making. However, repeated or duplicate observations in widely used heart disease datasets can introduce data leakage and lead to overly optimistic performance estimates. This study proposes a duplicate-aware and explainable machine learning (ML) framework for heart disease prediction. A combined dataset containing 1,328 records and 13 clinical features was systematically analyzed, resulting in 605 unique feature groups. To enable reliableA classification model which can identify a decision boundary that maximize the separation between the two outcome classes was added to SVM, one of the kernel-based classification models evaluation, the feature groups were partitioned into 484 development groups and 121 independent test groups. Six ML models, including Logistic Regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, and Support Vector Machine (SVM), were comparatively evaluated using five-fold group-aware stratified cross-validation. CatBoost achieved the highest mean ROC-AUC among the evaluated models and was subsequently optimized using the development data. The optimized CatBoost model achieved an accuracy of 88.64%, precision of 89.92%, recall of 87.22%, F1-score of 88.55%, and ROC-AUC of 93.32% on the independent test set containing 264 records. At the unique feature-group level, the model achieved an accuracy of 86.78%, precision of 90.91%, recall of 81.97%, F1-score of 86.21%, and ROC-AUC of 93.28%. SHAP-based explainability analysis identified chest pain type, thalassemia status, ST-segment slope, number of major vessels, and resting electrocardiographic characteristics as among the most influential clinical features. The findings demonstrate that combining duplicate-aware evaluation, optimized CatBoost modeling, independent group-level testing, and SHAP-based explainability can provide a more reliable, robust, and transparent framework for heart disease prediction.
authors: Romaan Khan; Tufail Ahmad Khan; Muhammad Tahir; Habib Un Nabi; Waqar Saeed; Muhammad Khan
venue: International Journal of Innovations in Science and Technology

title: Harnessing microfluidics for microbiology: from bacteria-host interactions to emerging cancer therapies
abstract: Microfluidics has emerged as a powerful technology for precisely controlling mechanical and chemical environments across a wide range of biological systems, from single cells to complex co-cultures. In microbiology, the microscale dimensions of bacteria pose experimental challenges that microfluidic systems have effectively addressed, offering compatibility with live imaging and enabling quantitative investigations of bacterial behaviors and host-bacteria interactions. Historical microfluidic designs are now routinely used to quantify bacterial growth and lineage with unprecedented temporal-spatial resolution and precise control of external conditions. In parallel, organ-on-chip technologies are increasingly applied in microbiology to study host-bacteria interactions within physiologically relevant and well-controlled microenvironments. Recently, cancer tissues have been recognized as unexpected hosts for bacteria, with mounting impactful evidence showing that intratumoral microbes can influence cancer progression and response to therapy. Despite growing interest, the application of microfluidics to cancer-bacteria interactions remains limited. Addressing this gap requires the development of appropriate methodological tools that replicate the relevant tumor microenvironment features and allow the quantification of both cellular responses and bacterial colonization dynamics upon the bacterial-host interaction. In this review, we first outline the foundational applications of microfluidics in microbiology from single-cell to collective behavior studies. We then describe how organ-on-chip technology enables the fine-tuned formation of organ-specific conditions, which are critical for modeling the complex tumor microenvironment. We further examine recent findings on intratumoral bacteria across cancer types and discuss how microfluidics, especially tumor-on-chip approaches, can advance this emerging field, from mechanistic insights to therapeutic development.
authors: Léa Pinon; Auriane Debache; Alexandre Thuaud; Luca Tiraboschi; Gerlanda Vella; Jessica Riou-Ramon; Céline Cordier; Clara Helal; Pascal Hersen; María Rescigno; Maria Carla Parrini; Stéphanie Descroix

title: Harnessing the Power of Artificial Intelligence in the Fight against COVID-19: A Comprehensive Review
abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic accelerated the development and application of artificial intelligence (AI) across disease surveillance, epidemiological forecasting, medical imaging, prognosis, drug discovery, vaccine research, contact tracing, and public-health decision support. This review synthesizes the literature on these applications while critically examining the evidence needed for translation into clinical and public-health practice. A structured literature-search and selection framework was used to organize evidence published from the emergence of COVID-19 through the contemporary literature, with emphasis on peer-reviewed studies and recent reviews. The evidence was synthesized according to the pandemic-response pathway: early warning and surveillance; diagnosis and differential diagnosis; severity and prognosis; clinical and resource decision support; therapeutic and vaccine discovery; genomic surveillance; and privacy-preserving and responsible AI. Across these domains, AI demonstrates potential to process heterogeneous data and support time-sensitive decisions, but reported performance does not by itself establish clinical utility. Recurring limitations include small or non-representative datasets, dataset shift, limited external validation, class imbalance, information leakage, insufficient calibration and interpretability, privacy and security risks, and uncertainty about workflow integration and regulatory accountability. Recent systematic reviews also indicate that multimodal, federated, and privacy-preserving approaches remain less developed than conventional centralized models. The principal contribution of this review is a unified critical framework that links technical performance with data quality, external validation, clinical relevance, fairness, privacy, interpretability, and implementation readiness. The review therefore identifies not only where AI has been applied to COVID-19, but also the conditions required for responsible translation to clinical practice and future pandemic preparedness.
authors: Dasaradharami Reddy Kandati; Anusha S; N Ashalatha; Mohammed Azharuddin Ahmed

title: Head-to-head comparison of MRI-based PI-RR scoring system and 68 Ga-PSMA-PET/CT: enhancing prostate cancer recurrence detection after radical prostatectomy
abstract: PURPOSE: To compare the diagnostic performance of MRI using the PI-RR scoring system and PSMA-PET/CT in detecting prostate cancer (PCa) local recurrence after radical prostatectomy (RP), and to identify clinical and imaging variables independently associated with recurrence. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This retrospective, multicenter study evaluated 119 patients with suspected PCa recurrence who underwent both MRI and PSMA-PET/CT; MRI was performed within a time window ranging from up to 3 months before to a maximum of 1 month after the PET/CT examination; the time range was defined within MDTs. Both radiologists and nuclear medicine physicians were blinded to clinical and opposite imaging data during image interpretation. Exclusion criteria included insufficient follow-up, recent pelvic radiation (within 6 months), and history of hormone therapy. Reference standard was defined using histopathologic findings, follow-up imaging, or clinical response to treatment. Sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, and accuracy were calculated. The Cohen's kappa coefficient was used to determine inter-reader agreement. Univariable and multivariable logistic regression analyses were performed. RESULTS: MRI, considering a PI-RR ≥ 3, detected recurrence in 69 patients versus 48 with PSMA-PET/CT (p = 0.006). MRI showed significantly higher sensitivity (86%, 95% CI 75-92% vs. 71%, 95% CI 59-80%; p = 0.03) and a trend toward higher specificity (78%, 95% CI 65-87% vs. 52%, 95% CI 39-65%; p = 0.06), PPV (74% vs. 51%), NPV (89% vs. 73%). Overall accuracy was also superior for MRI (81%, 95% CI 74-87% vs. 63%, 95% CI 54-71%). ROC analysis confirmed a higher AUC for MRI (0.87, 95% CI 0.80-0.93) compared with PSMA-PET/CT (0.62, 95% CI 0.52-0.72; ΔAUC = 0.25, p < 0.001). Multivariable analysis showed that only age (p = 0.002) and PI-RR score ≥ 3 (p = 0.001) were independently correlated with recurrence. Postoperative risk grouping was correlated only at univariable analysis. Among the 119 included patients, histopathologic confirmation was available in 3% (n = 4), treatment response (either biochemical or imaging based) in 31% (n = 37), follow-up with imaging in 33% (n = 39), and clinical-laboratory follow-up in 33% (n = 39).The median follow-up was 12 months (IQR, 9-18). The effective recurrence rate was 58%. CONCLUSIONS: MRI demonstrated strong diagnostic performance in detecting prostate cancer local recurrence. These findings suggest that MRI may be particularly useful for rule out local recurrence in low-risk patients, while PET/CT could be more appropriate for rule in, both local and distant in higher-risk patients. However, this proposed risk-adapted imaging strategy should be considered hypothesis-generating and warrants further validation through prespecified risk-stratified analyses. Limitations include the retrospective design, the composite reference standard, and the relatively high recurrence prevalence, which may have influenced predictive values.
authors: Ludovica Laschena; Martina Pecoraro; Emanuele Messina; Marco Bicchetti; Antonella Borrelli; Ailin Dehghanpour; Francesca Mezzapesa; Nicholas Landini; Giuseppe De Vincentis; Valeria Panebianco

title: Hemin Triggers Cytoprotective Lipid Droplet Formation in Pulmonary Microvascular Endothelial Cells
abstract: Sickle cell disease (SCD) is characterized by chronic and episodic hemolysis, inducing endothelial cell dysfunction and death. Lipid droplets (LDs) accumulate intracellularly in response to stress but the role of LDs in hemin-stressed pulmonary microvascular cells remain unexplored. We hypothesized that LD formation is an adaptive response that improves endothelial cell survival during hemin-induced stress. We utilized cultures of human lung microvascular endothelial cells (hLMVECs) to test this hypothesis. Hemin alone was able to induce LD biogenesis in culture. In response to hemin treatment, we found an increase in cellular death by lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) assay when LD biogenesis was inhibited with a small molecule inhibitor of diacylglycerol acyltransferase 1 (DGAT1), A922500. Induction of LDs by treatment with oleic acid (OA) coupled with hemin resulted in improved endothelial cell survival. Hemin treatment was able to activate p-JNK and p-P38 signaling, while treatment with OA alone could not induce either signaling pathway. Hemin treatment combined with DGAT1 inhibition resulted in an increase in endothelial cell secreted IL-6 and IL-8 levels as measured by enzyme linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), demonstrating an increase in endothelial cell dysfunction and stress. Induction of LD formation with oleic acid (OA) treatment resulted a reduction in secreted IL-6 and IL-8. Mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) production was decreased by OA treatment, as evidenced by MitoSOXRed assay. These data suggest that hLMVECs are protected from hemin-induced inflammation and death by the presence of LDs. Further studies are needed to explore the Hemin-LD-Cell Death axis for translational therapeutic use.
authors: Carneiro AdB, Wysocki RW, Zhang X, Gordeuk VR, Machado RF.

title: Hierarchically Structured Microparticles Encapsulated With Multiple Plant‐Derived Bioactives for Psoriasis Therapy
abstract: Traditional Chinese medicine bioactives have considerable therapeutic value in psoriasis management, while their clinical applications are still constrained by the insufficient therapeutic efficacy of single components, uncontrolled release, and low local bioavailability. In this study, we report a hierarchically structured microparticle system loaded with multiple plant-derived bioactives for psoriasis therapy. The microparticles of sodium alginate (SA) hydrogel with polydopamine (PDA)-modification were fabricated through microfluidics, co-loaded with paeoniflorin (PF) and ginger-derived exosome-like nanoparticles (GELNs). Benefiting from the porous structure of hydrogel and adhesive property of PDA, the microparticles enable stable co-encapsulation of multiple plant-derived bioactives and achieve sustained release at lesion sites, enhancing local bioavailability. The encapsulated PF and GELNs exert complementary anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and anti-proliferative effects, collectively regulating key pathological processes associated with psoriasis. These results prove that the microparticle-based multiple plant-derived bioactives delivery system provides a safe, cost-effective, and translatable approach for long-term topical treatment of psoriasis, highlighting their therapeutic potential in inflammatory skin diseases.
authors: Dingyuan Chen; Minhui Lu; Y ZHAO

title: High-Throughput Experimentation in Practice: Hidden Bottlenecks and Digital Gaps
abstract: Abstract High-throughput experimentation (HTE) has become an increasingly important approach for reaction discovery, optimization, and AI-ready data generation in synthetic chemistry. However, despite rapid adoption, many practical limitations associated with implementing HTE workflows remain underreported, particularly outside industrial settings. In practice, experimental reliability is frequently constrained by factors such as solvent compatibility, evaporation, sealing performance, plate geometry, liquid handling limitations, and the physical constraints introduced through miniaturization. These effects can strongly influence reproducibility and data quality, yet are often treated as secondary implementation details rather than core considerations. Alongside these operational challenges, digital HTE workflows remain fragmented, with limited interoperability between software, hardware, analytical systems, and data structures. In this perspective, we discuss a range of practical and digital bottlenecks encountered during plate-based HTE, drawing on direct experimental experience, supporting experimental data, and recent developments across the field. In particular, we present new observations relating to solvent evaporation and sealing performance in common HTE formats, highlighting how seemingly minor physical effects can substantially influence experimental reliability and downstream interpretation. By making these practical considerations more explicit, we aim to support the development of more reproducible, interoperable, and scalable HTE workflows across academic and industrial chemistry.
authors: K. Cheung; Henrique Magri Marçon; Matthew T. Pratley; Daniel S. Wigh; Alexander Pomberger; Connor J. Taylor

title: High‐Sensitivity Self‐Sensing Hydrogels With Reconfigurable Island–Bridge Networks for Human–Machine Interaction and Intelligent Bioinspired Recognition
abstract: ABSTRACT Intelligent hydrogel actuators with self‐sensing capabilities have shown broad prospects in flexible electronics, bioinspired robotics, and human–machine interaction. However, most reported self‐sensing hydrogel actuators still suffer from insufficient sensing sensitivity and low efficiency in structural‐response coupling, which restrict their application in highly integrated self‐sensing systems. Here, we develop a high‐sensitivity self‐sensing actuating hydrogel through embedding micro‐nano collaborative island‐bridge conductive network of liquid metal (LM) and carbon nanotube (CNT) within thermal‐responsive poly(N‐isopropylacrylamide) (PNIPAM) matrix, allowing external strain and photothermal actuation to be translated into amplified electrical signals through reversible fracture and reconstruction of conductive pathways. The as‐prepared hydrogel exhibits ultrahigh strain sensitivity (Gauge Factor = 38.9) and precise actuation self‐sensing capability ( ΔR/R 0 > 200%). Benefiting from the excellent sensing performance, the proposed LM/CNT‐PNIPAM (LCP) self‐sensing hydrogel not only enables high‐fidelity monitoring of human motion and physiological signals in wearable electronics, but also exhibits potential as gesture‐controlled remote navigation of intelligent vehicle by integrating with machine‐learning algorithm. Moreover, through combining with IoT communication technique, a bioinspired self‐sensing tentacle with high‐accuracy recognition capacity was developed based on the excellent self‐sensing feature of the LCP hydrogel. This study lays a material foundation for developing intelligent soft systems with accurate feedback regulation and further human–machine interaction capacity.
authors: Zhilin Zhang; Yuhang Li; Zhaoyang Chen; Lina Wang; Deliang Li; Jiaqi Miao; Hanyang Li; Baoyang Lu; Ye Tian; Tieqiang Wang

title: How the fruit fly connectome can help autonomous materials discovery
abstract: Autonomous laboratories for two-dimensional semiconductors pair a recipe planner with instruments that return in situ spectra every few seconds. Some decisions are too fast for the planner: stop a failing selenization anneal, flag a flake that is not the logged material, or end an ion irradiation at a set vacancy density, from a few examples, on a small computer at the instrument. The fruit fly takes decisions of this form with two structures whose wiring is measured at synapse level: the mushroom body, a one-shot memory for odours, and the ventral nerve cord, which turns a few descending commands into local reflexes. We asked which instrument jobs models wired from these connectomes do better than engineered tools. A mushroom-body model of 685 projection neurons and 5,177 Kenyon cells read one Raman band per glomerulus; over 20 paired seeds, on simulated selenization Raman streams and on Ar + irradiation anchored in published in situ spectra, it lost the fewest flakes when one failed run taught a stop rule (3.3 of 30, against 3.9 for a nearest neighbour), read vacancy density from its sparse code with less error than from the raw spectrum (5.5 % against 6.4 %), and ran in 0.30 ms on a Raspberry Pi 5 within 152 kB. A stop decided at the furnace, as the nerve cord decides reflexes, prevented the losses of a planner that needed 60 s per turn (0.15 against 10.7 flakes of 30). It did not choose recipes. In three animals and after training, measured wiring matched a degree-preserving shuffle, and the nerve-cord wiring matched a ridge regression: the connectome contributes an architecture and wiring statistics, not a partner map. As hardware, the fixed wiring can be binary and each plastic synapse needs about 64 levels. The connectome supplies a low-cost reflex layer under the planner, not a replacement.
authors: Ka Chun WONG; Taylor D. Sparks

title: Hydrogen-Assisted Reduction of Metal Oxides: Reaction Mechanisms, Process Optimization, and AI/ML-Enabled Pathways for Sustainable Materials Processing
abstract: Hydrogen reduction of metal oxides has been identified as a promising approach for producing some engineering (metallic) materials, both through primary production and the reprocessing of waste materials. Such an approach offers a viable promise for the production of value-added materials in a sustainable manner. Unlike in other reduction processes, where obnoxious gases get 2 released as byproducts, hydrogen reduction, on the other hand, generate water vapor as the clean principal byproduct. Such an approach renders the overall mcheaping process inexpensive because of the use of metal oxides as the cheap feedstocks. However, the manufacturing process offers several challenges, upscaling being one of the major ones. In the present review, an attempt has been made to assess the overall reduction process in an integrated manner, which relates thermodynamic principles, reduction mechanisms, reactor-scale phenomena, and specific application requirements. The principles of thermodynamic constraints related to oxide reducibility are described in relation to the role of reduction temperature, gas compositions, and the gas-solid reaction mechanisms to determine rate-controlling processes, diffusion coefficients, and the role of catalysis for the production of metallic materials by primary manufacturing processes and environmental remediation. There is also the consideration of an enabling role of automation, modeling, and digital twin technologies. The manuscript describes practiced hydrogen reduction processes to produce some of the specific metals, such as iron, nickel, cobalt, and refractory metals, but also the need to improve hydrogen access, efficiency, scalability, and ensure catalyst longevity. Enhanced research in hydrogen, renewable power coupling, AI-assisted process control and reactor design are some of the aspects that have been observed to be the major enablers. The manuscript not only describes the status and future projections but also provides a roadmap for improving the status quo.
authors: Kunal Mondal; Rigoberto C. Advíncula; Prabhat Kumar Tripathy; Nagaraj P. Shetti

title: Implementation of next-generation sequencing to guide care and public health action in settings with high burden of rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis: 32 stakeholder consensus statements generated using Delphi principles
abstract: Background: Comprehensive knowledge of resistance to the novel all-oral regimens for treatment of rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis (RR-TB) is important, but challenging variant detection by next-generation sequencing (NGS) in combination with variant interpretation software can diagnose resistance early. We aimed to generate a consensus on strategic issues for the implementation of NGS for routine RR-TB care. Methods: We employed a stakeholder consensus process informed by Delphi principles. First, stakeholders participated in an online survey to provide feedback on statements using a 3-point Likert scale and free text. Responses were then summarised and follow-up discussion fora with stakeholders were held to revise statements until a consensus was reached. Findings: Of the 116 invited stakeholders, 58 participated, representing RR-TB research (n=28), clinical care (n=11), diagnosis (n=5), RR-TB survivors and advocacy communities (n=5) from 14 countries in five of the six WHO regions. A consensus was rapidly reached for most statements with limited editorial changes needed. The debate mostly focused on statements covering performing sequencing at centralised facilities, acting on variants without statistical association with resistance in the WHO catalogue of mutations, strengthening WHO-endorsed regimens and the need for informed consent for the use of NGS for care and surveillance. Interpretation: The consensus-building process grounded in real-world experience from a diverse group of stakeholders generated 32 consensus statements covering five strategic domains. The blueprint generated is not a definite prescriptive framework but a document that can support policymakers when developing country-specific policies for NGS-guided precision medicine and RR-TB care. title: Improvement of micro-ridge parameters for enhanced microfluidic fuel cell performance
abstract: Microfluidic fuel cells (MFCs) are emerging electrochemical power sources that offer compact size and precise control over fluid flow. MFCs rely on laminar co-flow of reactants within microscale channels, eliminating the need for complex membranes and enabling efficient reactant utilization. The small dimensions of these devices enhance mass transport, reduce ohmic losses, and facilitate rapid thermal management, making them particularly suitable for portable power applications and microscale energy systems. The performance of MFCs is strongly influenced by the design of the microchannel architecture and the incorporation of flow-modifying features such as micro-ridges. These microstructures can enhance lateral flow, increase reactant contact with the electrode surface, and modify the boundary layer, ultimately improving current density and fuel utilization. Understanding the effects of individual geometric parameters—such as ridge height, spacing, and orientation—is crucial for optimizing cell performance. In the present study, a systematic parametric investigation incorporating gravity effects was performed to evaluate the influence of ridge height, spacing, and orientation on the electrochemical performance of a microfluidic fuel cell. The combined improved micro-ridge configuration resulted in an increase of 60.7% in current density and 50.8% in fuel utilization at a ridge height of 350 μ m and an angle of 40° with respect to the flow direction. This improvement demonstrates the effectiveness of carefully designed micro-ridges in enhancing fuel cell performance. Furthermore, detailed investigations of design parameters reveal new insights into the interplay between fluid dynamics and electrochemical reactions, offering practical guidelines for the design of next-generation, high-efficiency microfluidic fuel cells.
authors: T. Tagizade; S. Jafarmadar; S. Khalilarya

title: In Situ Closed‐Loop Control of Polarization via Dual‐Axis Magnetic Field Modulation
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper addresses the issue of susceptibility to longitudinal magnetic field interference in in situ closed‐loop polarization control and introduces an innovative in situ closed‐loop control method for electronic longitudinal polarization via dual‐axis magnetic field modulation. This approach effectively suppresses interference from the longitudinal magnetic field and significantly enhances system stability. By varying the pump rate and analyzing the system's response characteristics, it is observed that, under dual‐axis magnetic field modulation, changes in electron polarization and the longitudinal magnetic field notably influence the amplitude‐frequency response of the system output. Both theoretical derivations and experimental results show that using the calculated amplitude‐frequency response of the system output, as calculated, as a feedback signal enables real‐time in‐situ closed‐loop control of electron spin polarization. Compared to the traditional single‐axis magnetic field modulation approach, this method offers substantial advantages in mitigating noise interference. Compared with the conventional method, the noise amplitude spectral density of the proposed method at 0.1 Hz is improved from 0.0004098 to 0.000129. This technique holds considerable promise for a wide range of applications, including optical pumping magnetometers, nuclear magnetic resonance gyroscopes, and various co‐magnetometer systems.
authors: Lihong Duan; Lihong Duan; Wenfeng Fan; Wei Quan

title: In-molecule machine learning with microfluidic integrated DNA neural computing
abstract: DNA-based computing enables the processing of complex molecular information within a biological context, particularly suitable for diagnostic and therapeutic applications. However, the complexity of molecular dynamics of DNA-based chemical reactions poses challenges to integrating large-scale neural networks with complex topologies, which restricts their effective feature recognition. Here, we present a hybrid bioelectronic computing architecture, the DNA-encoded microfluidic integrated computing (DMIC) chip to enhance the scalability and complexity of DNA neural networks for in-molecule machine learning. The DMIC chip employs controllable droplets as micro-containers to store, transport, and process DNA elements, coupled with a 2D electrode array that precisely organizes DNA-encoded droplets array. This design enables the formation of complex DNA reaction networks and supports efficient on-chip computation through targeted droplet movement and reconfigurable fluidic pathways. Using the DMIC chip, we achieved the monolithic integration of up to twenty-six DNA neurons, which learn and model patterns of simple to moderate complexity. Programmable droplet pathways support the execution of machine learning algorithms, including support vector machines (SVM), convolutional neural networks (CNN), and fully connected neural networks (FCNN). The DMIC chip supports in-situ learning via on-chip DNA convolutional neural networks trained, achieving the classification of three 12-bit binary patterns. Furthermore, we demonstrate the implementation of the DMIC chip to simultaneously analyze thirty-six disease-related microRNAs for multi-class diagnosis of three cancer types. This integrated computing architecture offers exciting potential for large-scale molecular data processing and diagnostic applications.
authors: Fan C, Cao M, Xiong X, Wang J, Li N, Li B, Zhu Y, Zhu T, Wang F, Xu L, Ji J, Yao Q, Li L, Pei H, Chang C.

title: Information coding strategies in biological reservoir computing for multiclass time-series classification
abstract: Abstract Physical reservoir computing (RC) using biological neural networks (BNNs) offers a framework for probing how high-dimensional dynamics arising from multicellular systems support complex information processing in the brain. However, how electrical inputs and extracellular readouts should be designed to suit different task demands remains unclear. Here, using primary rat cortical neurons cultured on a high-density microelectrode array, we investigated how input encoding and spike detection methods influence neural representations and the resulting RC performance in BNNs. Comparison of pulse amplitude modulation and latency coding revealed that the latter exhibited superior performance in demanding multiclass conditions, including a 10% improvement in a 10-class spoken digit classification task. Spike sorting further improved classification performance by enhancing class separability, while largely preserving the low-dimensional structure of population activity. These findings highlight the importance of designing information coding strategies according to task difficulty.
authors: Yusei Nishi; Hideaki Yamamoto; Yuichi Katori; Shigeo Sato

title: Information-Dense Synthesis for Molecular Discovery
abstract: Machine learning can accelerate molecular discovery by designing molecules and planning experiments. However, many scientific challenges demand molecules with very rare properties, and in this sparse setting, existing algorithms offer little gain over random guessing. We propose a method to efficiently search large regions of molecular space using algorithmically controlled stochastic synthesis. Rather than design, make and test individual molecules, we design and make complex mixtures, test them as a pool, then deconvolute the molecule-activity map. We optimize synthesis to encode maximal information. Theoretically, this approach can reduce the number of experiments required to find the optimal molecule among $d$ candidates from $\mathcal{O}(d)$ to $\mathcal{O}(\log d)$ or $\mathcal{O}(1)$. In simulation, on estimated protein fitness landscapes, it finds active molecules with an order of magnitude fewer experiments than existing Bayesian optimization methods.
authors: Kasper Krunderup Jakobsen; Eli N. Weinstein

title: Integrated Antigen–DNA Co‐Detection Using Digital Microfluidics for Improving Diagnostic Accuracy in POCT Analysis
abstract: Simultaneous detection of protein and nucleic acid (NA) provides complementary information essential for accurate analysis of complex samples. Conventional approaches for the analysis of protein and NA typically rely on separate workflows and instruments, limiting the reliability of point-of-care testing. Here, we present a digital microfluidics-based dual-mode molecular assay for simultaneous detection of both protein and NA from the same microscale sample. The protein is captured by a gold nanoparticle-antibody conjugate, while NA is enriched by magnetic beads. Magnetic manipulation separates the protein-containing fraction from NA, enabling separate analysis of the two molecular classes within an automated workflow. By integrating the analysis of protein and NA, the platform enables more accurate analysis than either modality alone. In 56 clinical samples, the combined analysis of hepatitis B surface antigen and DNA reduces the false-negative rate to 1.79%, compared with 12.5% for HBsAg alone. In food safety assays, simultaneous detection of Staphylococcus aureus-associated toxins and PMA-treated bacterial NA provides information not only on protein-based toxins, but also the presence and viability of bacteria within milk. This automated DMF-based dual-mode molecular assay provides a highly integrated strategy for multimodal POCT and public health risk assessment.
authors: Fengli Chai; Fenggang Li; Jiangjiang Zhang; Zheng Li; Jianzhao Zhai; Binwu Ying; Xicheng Zhang; Xingyu Jiang

title: Integrated Droplet Microfluidic Platform for Single-Spheroid Photothermal Nanotherapy and Morphology-Driven Response Prediction.
abstract: Photothermal therapy (PTT) is a promising cancer treatment modality, but its evaluation remains limited by the lack of physiologically relevant and quantitatively controlled in vitro platforms. Here, we present a droplet-based microfluidic platform that enables single-spheroid formation, programmable nanoparticle delivery, and in situ laser irradiation with real-time thermal monitoring. The platform enables temperature multiplexing within a single experiment, allowing construction of single-spheroid dose-response relationships and the definition of a temperature-based inhibitory metric (IT50). This provides a direct and physically meaningful quantification of photothermal efficacy. In parallel, a label-free, spheroid morphology-based machine learning approach predicts treatment response across cell types, nanoparticle incubation conditions, and therapeutic regimes while preserving intrinsic single-spheroid variability. Despite a limited dataset size and biological heterogeneity, the system achieves robust and reproducible predictive performance. Overall, this work establishes a scalable and versatile microfluidic framework for quantitative photothermal nanotherapy screening, integrating controlled thermal dosing, 3D tumor models, and morphological data-driven analysis within a single-spheroid platform.
authors: Hasti Honari; Léo Dancert; Caroline Parent; Guilhem Bousquet; Jean-Louis Viovy; Claire Wilhelm

title: Integrating artificial intelligence into medical laboratories: A structured implementation framework
abstract: This article presents a structured framework for integrating artificial intelligence (AI) into medical laboratory workflows. As laboratories face increasing demands, workforce shortages, and technological complexity, AI offers promising solutions to enhance efficiency, diagnostic accuracy, and predictive capabilities. The paper outlines key benefits of AI, including automation, quality assurance, and administrative optimization, while also addressing critical challenges such as bias, legal and ethical concerns, workforce disruption, and over-reliance on automated systems. A multi-level implementation strategy is proposed, spanning international, national, and organizational domains, with emphasis on standards, guidelines, training, and oversight. Importantly, the article underscores that AI is a supportive tool, not a replacement for laboratory professionals, whose expertise remains essential for validation and interpretation. The framework aims to guide responsible AI adoption while safeguarding quality and patient safety.
authors: Avi Peretz; Hanoch Goldshmidt; Sari Peretz; Marielle Kaplan; Orna Schwartz; Ronit Marco; Maya Azrad

title: Integration of liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry into total laboratory automation: technical challenges and clinical advantages
abstract: The clinical laboratory is undergoing a paradigm shift toward the integration of liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry(MS) into Total Laboratory Automation workflows. While historically relegated to specialized satellite units due to manual pre-analytical requirements, recent technological advancements have enabled the development of fully automated, 'sample-to-result' MS modules. This review provides an authoritative analysis of the technical integration of systems such as the Roche cobas® i 601 and Shimadzu CLAM-2040 in core laboratories. We examine the role of intelligent middleware and artificial intelligence-assisted algorithms in ensuring standardized data validation and quality control tracking and real-time operational monitoring. Furthermore, we evaluate the clinical impact of this integration on diagnostic accuracy for low-concentration analytes in endocrinology and therapeutic drug monitoring. By transitioning from batch-based processing to continuous automated streams, MS establishes itself as a robust, high-throughput tool for routine clinical diagnostics.
authors: Carlos José Sánchez Ovejero; Sergio Luis Lima; Irene Chaves‐Coira; A. Rey-Catena

title: Intelligent Agriculture for Plant Disease Management: A Critical Review of Operational Value, Field Reliability, Adoption Barriers, and Research Priorities
abstract: Plant disease management increasingly integrates artificial intelligence (AI), Internet of Things (IoT) sensing, remote and proximal sensing, disease forecasting, robotics, cloud–edge computing, and decision-support systems (DSS). This critical narrative review evaluated their operational value, reliability under production conditions, barriers to adoption, and priorities for improving field performance. An initial 99-record bibliography was screened, yielding 45 eligible sources; targeted searches of DOI/indexing services and publisher databases from 2010 to July 2026, while retaining earlier foundational studies, identified 35 additional DOI-verified sources, producing an 80-reference corpus. Evidence was appraised across five deployment-oriented domains: field representativeness, diagnostic ground truth, comparator quality, uncertainty and failure reporting, and operational outcomes. Intelligent tools provide three main benefits: earlier or more scalable detection, continuous and spatially explicit risk assessment, and targeted intervention. Field evidence is strongest for established disease-warning systems and selected precision-spraying applications, whereas image classifiers, foundation models, and autonomous robots remain more commonly validated in curated or crop-specific settings. Distribution shift is a major reliability concern, with commercial-field studies showing substantial performance losses under open-set conditions. Wider adoption is constrained by interoperability, cost, maintenance, connectivity, data governance, trust, liability, and unequal access. The most credible near-term pathway is supervised, context-sensitive autonomy. Future progress requires multi-farm and multi-season validation, explicit uncertainty reporting, FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) data architectures, economic evaluation, climate-adaptive hybrid models, and end-to-end comparisons with best conventional practice. Intelligent agriculture should therefore be developed as accountable plant-health infrastructure that keeps plant pathologists, advisers, and farmers in the decision loop.
authors: Emna Bouazizi; Yâakoub Gharbi

title: Intelligent drone-based biosensor for the detection of dengue virus antigen towards smart unmanned aerial-vehicle platform-based virus diagnosis
abstract: In the current work, we established a smart system for dengue diagnosis that enables on-site detection while removing the need for human intervention and continuous monitoring in difficult-to-reach areas. The system comprises of 4-smart technologies: i) drone, ii) biosensor, iii) Yolov5 AI-module, iv) a QR-code-derived digital website linked patient E-Prescription barcode, where the biosensor acts as a smart detector, and the drone as a vehicle for transporting the biosensor to the testing zone. Deep learning analysis was done by an expert using an artificial intelligence module; additional QR-code-based websites were added to the system, allowing users to scan the code and send detection data to laboratory authorities, and the patient got a medical e-prescription from the doctor. The proposed system has lightweight materials, optimized power sources, and weather-resistant housing to ensure reliable on-site diagnostics. However, practical challenges associated with drone-based diagnostic deployment, including environmental conditions, flight stability, battery capacity, payload constraints, and reliable operation in remote settings, should be considered when evaluating the field applicability and scalability of the proposed system. The suggested detection platform used the instrument-less lateral flow colorimetric approach, enabling naked-eye detection of dengue virus antigen with an LOD of 0.91 µg/mL within 5 s. As a consequence, the Drone-based approach allows clinicians to monitor the dengue virus antigen in remote populations. Accordingly, governments and non-profit organizations can utilize this technology to monitor the red alert zone, receiving precise and reliable data for informed decision-making.
authors: Mohd. Rahil Hasan; Sameer Khan; Dakshita Naithani; Pradakshina Sharma; Yashomita Mehta; Samra Ansari; Sushil Kumar; Ubaid Mushtaq Naikoo; Anupam Baliyan; Mohamed Abbas; Muneer Parayangat; Shaeen Kalathil; Jagriti Narang

title: Intelligent material recognition from thermal signatures using hybrid deep learning frameworks
abstract: Accurate material identification using thermal infrared signatures has significant implications for industrial inspection, autonomous systems, and non-contact diagnostics. In this study, we propose a physics-informed deep learning framework for intelligent material recognition based on transient thermal behavior. A large-scale dataset, ThermalMat-85K, comprising 85,000 long-wave infrared (LWIR) images across ten material classes, was constructed under controlled multi-angle, multi-distance, and multi-environment conditions. Each sample was validated through Fourier transform infrared (FT-IR) spectroscopy and X-ray diffraction (XRD) to ensure chemical and structural integrity prior to thermal acquisition. Seven deep learning architectures were systematically evaluated, including VGG-16, ResNet-50, MobileNet-V3, DenseNet-121, EfficientNet-B4, a CNN+LSTM temporal hybrid, and a proposed Hybrid Net integrating convolutional, transformer, and recurrent modules with cross-modal attention gating. EfficientNet-B4 achieved the highest Top-1 accuracy (93.1%) and macro F1-score (92.8%), demonstrating superior class-wise stability. Residual and dense connectivity architectures also exhibited strong performance, while lightweight and temporal hybrids revealed trade-offs between efficiency and discriminative power. Class-wise confusion analysis indicates that misclassification trends correlate strongly with thermophysical proximity, particularly thermal conductivity and emissivity overlap. These findings confirm that transient thermal decay dynamics encode physically meaningful features suitable for material discrimination. The results establish a robust benchmark for physics-informed thermal material recognition and provide guidance for selecting architectures based on deployment constraints and robustness requirements.
authors: Venkateswarlu Sunkari; T Kishore BABU; V.N.S.R. Murthy; Boddu L. V. Siva Rama KRISHNA; P V V S D Nagendrudu; Sriharsha Vikruthi

title: Intestinal Villi‐Inspired Living Biobatteries via Habitat‐Engineered Conductive Hydrogel Architectures
abstract: ABSTRACT Microbial bioelectrocatalysis demands more than electron‐conducting surfaces—it demands living microenvironments that hydrate, protect, and nourish whole‐cell biocatalysts. This biological imperative remains unaddressed by conventional electrode design. Here, we fundamentally reframe microbial biobattery architecture through living habitat engineering, drawing inspiration from the human small intestine—a biological interface evolutionarily optimized to sustain dense, metabolically active microbial communities through high‐surface‐area villi, mucus‐mediated hydration, and short‐path nutrient exchange. We translate these principles into spore‐programmed conductive hydrogel pillar arrays, in which dormant Bacillus subtilis endospores are embedded within poly(3,4‐ethylenedioxythiophene):poly(styrenesulfonate)–poly(vinyl alcohol)/reduced graphene oxide hydrogel villi that simultaneously serve as microbial reservoirs, bioelectrochemical scaffolds, and electron‐harvesting conduits. Upon nutrient contact, spores germinate on demand into electroactive cells. This villi topology delivers an 8.3‐fold volumetric power density enhancement (8.04 to 66.45 µW cm − 3 ) over planar controls under volume‐matched conditions. A 24‐device geometry matrix uncovers a coupled radius–height design rule, with peak single‐villus power of 8.35 µW at optimal dimensions. Conformable villi patches demonstrate nutrient‐triggered electricity generation in a simulated pipe environment using a wastewater‐mimicking nutrient/electrolyte solution, while a separate self‐powered array achieves spatially resolved bioelectrochemical sensing. This work establishes living habitat engineering as a transformative paradigm for activatable, architecture‐programmed, and potentially shelf‐stable microbial biobatteries.
authors: Ruohan Zhang; Botian Wang; Seokheun Choi

title: Investigating nozzle-based additive manufacturing dynamics with high-speed imaging and machine learning
abstract: Abstract Additive manufacturing (AM) offers great design flexibility but remains constrained by the complexity of tuning processing parameters from a vast parameter search space either by traditional trial-and-error experimental approach or expensive computational fluid dynamics simulations. Further, AM processes involve critical transient phenomena at very small timescales ranging from microsecond to millisecond, which are difficult to observe and characterize experimentally. This work presents a novel approach that combines high-speed photography with machine learning (ML) to model and predict dynamic printing behavior. We used jet printing data obtained from Electrohydrodynamic (EHD) jet printing as a representative AM process. A Gaussian Process (GP) classifier is trained on 123 high-speed video sequences captured at 15,000 frames per second accurately predicts five printing regimes, including cone-jetting, micro-dripping, dripping, unstable, and no-print, across a wide range of parameters. Further, a deep learning model combining a 3D convolutional encoder and transformer-based temporal predictor provided highly accurate quantitative estimation of frame-by-frame droplet dynamics at a computational cost orders of magnitude less than equivalent computational fluid dynamics simulations. These results establish a data-driven framework for the simulation, predictive control, and rapid optimization of EHD printing dynamics, demonstrating the potential of high-speed imaging-informed machine learning as a computationally efficient surrogate for complex AM processes.
authors: Stanford White; Damian L. Stoddard; Prashant Ghimire; Joshua Russell; Yiwei Han; Samrat Choudhury

title: Isothermal Strand Displacement Amplification for Chemical Sensing: From Molecular Design to Integrated and Intelligent Platforms.
abstract: Strand displacement amplification (SDA) provides a versatile isothermal framework for chemical and biosensing, coupling polymerase-driven strand displacement with programmable nucleic-acid signal generation. Its analytical scope now extends beyond direct nucleic-acid detection because aptamers, DNAzymes, antibodies, and responsive probes can convert diverse recognition events into amplifiable DNA triggers. This review develops a unified view of SDA from molecular design to practical implementation, with particular emphasis on programmable amplicon generation, recognition-to-DNA transduction, interfacial confinement, cascaded amplification, and CRISPR coupling. The review follows SDA across biomedical, food, and environmental applications, including RNA biomarkers, liquid biopsy, genetic and epigenetic targets, proteins, enzymes, small molecules, and viruses. It also considers how these assays are being transferred into microfluidic, paper-based, lateral-flow, self-powered, regenerative, and intelligent systems. The important distinction is that analytical sensitivity does not necessarily predict practical performance. Extremely low detection limits often depend on cascaded processing beyond SDA itself, whereas real samples expose weaknesses in matrix tolerance, background suppression, reagent stability, fluid control, assay duration, and manufacturing reproducibility. Comparison with commercially established isothermal methods further shows that wider adoption will depend on converting flexible molecular chemistry into robust, standardized, sample-to-answer systems.
authors: Chia-Chun Lee; Wei-Ting Hsueh; Chin-Chung Tseng; Lung-Ming Fu

title: Judgment by agents, numbers by code: auditable automated speciation analysis towards a chemistry world model
abstract: Chemical speciation governs the reactivity, solubility, and toxicity of a solution, yet assembling speciation calculations from evaluated thermodynamic data remains a manual expert task whose reasoning is discarded once the figure is drawn. To mirror real-world research, automation belongs within a chemistry world model (CWM) where language agents curate and analyze data. As a first module, our agentic framework converts plain-language questions into deterministic equilibrium calculations grounded in NIST Standard Reference Database 46 (SRD-46). Agents resolve intent, curate records, adjudicate duplicates, design calculations, and estimate values beyond database coverage through induction-deduction-validation loops, while deterministic code validates every agentic commitment before it reaches the solver and compacts diagram topology into text readable without a vision stage. Across four case studies of escalating difficulty, quoted constants, patched records, and boundary coordinates reproduced their sources essentially exactly, whereas the same model without the framework missed phases or failed to build a solver. Residual errors surfaced only as auditable narration flaws, from misread topology to a sign-flipped hydrogen-evolution argument. The framework serves as a human-in-the-loop instrument delivering consensus-grade starting points, turning evaluated databases into active discovery instruments, mapping where language-model chemical reasoning still fails, and providing a general agentic template for finetuning.
authors: Yunkai Sun; Adwaith Ravichandran; Hassan Harb; Rajeev S. Assary; Brian J. Ingram; Zhenzhen Yang

title: LLM-IDEA: Identifiability-Driven Experimental Agent for Autonomous Discovery of Mechanistic World Models
abstract: Large language model agents are being increasingly deployed as autonomous scientists, designing experiments and inferring mechanistic world models with minimal human oversight. Yet identifiability is often overlooked: when a plateau is reached, the agent needs to know whether it is not yet capable enough or the model simply is not identifiable from the data, in which case no amount of further experimentation of the same kind can help. We propose the Identifiability-Driven Experimental Agent (LLM-IDEA) for closed-loop discovery with an identifiability engine that returns a three-way plateau verdict: capability limit, resolvable within the design class, or certified exhausted. On ODEBench, 60 of the 62 systems with free constants are identifiable at round 0; the RC circuit is certified exhausted for every experiment that protocol can run, and a harvesting model is resolvable by one added initial condition. The identifiability engine reproduces known verdicts on Lotka-Volterra, Van der Pol, Lorenz, and a pharmacokinetic model, where it recommends the intravenous arm pharmacologists use, and it ranks the depth scorer of our own benchmark last among four observation designs. On the DiscoverPhysics benchmark, it finds two public worlds whose explanation rubric rewards a distinction no legal experiment can make, and every model there with accurate trajectories failed the explanation grade (15 of 15, against 5 of 9 in identifiable worlds, p = 0.012). On the Alien Universe, a two-body testbed we propose in which a force law switches between a provably non-identifiable and an identifiable protocol, LLM-IDEA on the identifiable protocol reaches discovery depth at least three on 8/8 seeds versus 1/8 without it. An autonomous discovery agent can thus compute, rather than guess, whether a plateau calls for more search, a better experiment of the same kind, or a different kind of experiment.
authors: Surya Shetty; Ulisses Braga-Neto

title: LOOP-MEDIATED ISOTHERMAL AMPLIFICATION VERSUS POLYMERASE CHAIN REACTION IN VETERINARY SCIENCE: A COMPARATIVE REVIEW
abstract: Rapid and accurate detection of pathogens is central to animal health, zoonosis control and food safety. The polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and its variants, particularly real-time PCR, remain the reference molecular tools in veterinary diagnostic laboratories because of their high sensitivity, specificity and capacity for quantification. However, PCR depends on thermal cyclers, trained staff and well-equipped laboratories, which limits its use in field and resource-limited settings. Loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP), introduced in 2000, amplifies nucleic acids at a constant temperature of 60–65 °C using a strand-displacing DNA polymerase and four to six primers that recognise six to eight regions of the target. Results are obtained within 30–60 minutes and can be read by turbidity, fluorescence or a visible colour change without electrophoresis. LAMP is also more tolerant of inhibitors present in clinical samples, allowing simplified nucleic acid extraction. This review compares the principles, performance characteristics, cost and practical requirements of LAMP and PCR, and summarises their applications in the diagnosis of bacterial, viral and parasitic diseases of livestock, poultry and companion animals, including leptospirosis, brucellosis, foot-and-mouth disease, African swine fever, avian influenza, peste des petits ruminants, lumpy skin disease and rabies. Limitations of LAMP, such as complex primer design, carryover contamination and false-positive amplification, are discussed together with emerging solutions including uracil-DNA-glycosylase-supplemented LAMP, CRISPR-coupled detection and microfluidic point-of-care devices. LAMP and PCR are complementary: LAMP suits rapid field screening, while PCR remains the confirmatory and quantitative standard.
authors: Hrishikesh Jagtap; Prafullata Bashetti; Anil B. Bhosale Deepali T. Sakunde; Chandrakant Dadaso Bhong
venue: World Journal of Biology Pharmacy and Health Sciences

title: LabCompiler: A Framework for Verifiable Human-Machine Laboratory Execution from Imperfect Protocols
abstract: Closing the loop of AI-driven science requires reliably translating natural-language protocols into executable laboratory workflows despite protocol defects and heterogeneous hardware. Existing approaches often couple scientific interpretation with device-specific code generation, making errors difficult to localize and limiting reuse across laboratory platforms. We introduce LabCompiler, a robust protocol-to-execution framework that transforms imperfect natural-language protocols into verifiable human-machine workflows. Its protocol firewall diagnoses and repairs defects before compilation while preserving unaffected content, guided by troubleshooting knowledge accumulated through perturbation-guided self-evolution. A two-level, device-agnostic graph representation separates experimental semantics from hardware-specific implementation and supports capability-based device assignment with coordinated human execution. We further introduce a protocol recovery benchmark covering four controlled perturbation types and naturally occurring errors collected from protocols written by iGEM participants. Experiments show that LabCompiler outperforms frontier LLMs in protocol error correction while enabling coordinated human-machine execution across heterogeneous, partially automated laboratory settings.
authors: Jingyuan Li; Dongzhan Zhou; Minting Pan; Yujie Liu; Yuan Gao; Yankai Jiang; Xinyu Gu; Zhe Liu; Yang Li; Bo Zhang; Lei Bai; Tong Si; Weinan Zhang

title: Labference: Benchmarking the Reasoning-Action Connection in Robotic Laboratories
abstract: Realizing Embodied AI for Science requires robots to translate experimental goals into reliable physical procedures, reducing hazardous and repetitive human work while generating evidence for scientific discovery. Although language-based planning and learned manipulation provide complementary capabilities, their integration requires robots to adapt subsequent operations to actual execution outcomes. For example, an unsuccessful placement changes what must be done next, even when the experimental goal remains unchanged. Existing benchmarks assess planning, manipulation, and laboratory workflows through task completion and reasoning or execution metrics; however, aggregate performance leaves the connection between outcome-dependent choices and physical execution unresolved. To address this evaluation gap, we introduce Labference, a benchmark for evaluating how observed physical outcomes guide subsequent choices and how those choices translate into robotic laboratory actions. Its evaluation protocol is designed to test outcome-dependent behavioral adaptation through controlled evidence variations, while independently measuring operation selection, physical execution, and task completion. Matched Oracle-assisted continuations from shared checkpoints then assess which forms of support improve subsequent choices and task completion. Initial weighing evaluations reveal target-selection errors in the tested VLA policies despite successful object transfers, whereas GPT-driven control achieves correct selection but encounters execution failures and substantial computation costs. Together, these findings highlight the need to connect task-appropriate reasoning with reliable, timely action. By making this connection measurable and diagnosable, Labference supports targeted improvements toward autonomous experimentation for Embodied AI for Science.
authors: Shitong Liu; Jingwei Zhang; Sheng Lian; Xinyu Zhuang; Kaiwen Guo; Quan Liu; Chunhai Zhao; Jiaxin He; Fan Yang; Manli Tao; Tingyu Yuan; Jinqiao Wang; Hongwei Shi; Chaomin Guo; Xiaojing Liu; Xiangyu Zhu; Zhuang Xiong; Feichan Yang; Chaoyang Zhao; Zhiyong Liu

title: Laboratory 4.0: on the path to the fourth generation of laboratory medicine
abstract: Abstract Laboratory medicine has witnessed three generational paradigm shifts over the past 75 years – from manual work to early automation, from batch processing to patient-oriented selective analysis, and from human perianalytics to Total Laboratory Automation (TLA). Drawing on a personal trajectory spanning half a century of the discipline, this essay argues that a fourth generation, called “Laboratory 4.0”, is not a distant utopia but an expected reality, just like the so-called “Industry 4.0,” which is emerging in other areas of technological development. Three converging forces are driving this transformation: miniaturization (microfluidics, lab-on-a-chip platforms, and painless capillary sampling), decentralization (pervasive diagnostics available at any point and time without a central laboratory as intermediary), and artificial intelligence (from classical decision-support systems to generative large language models). A hybrid model is proposed in which incremental modernization within existing structures (until ∼2035) gives way to genuine decentralization and democratization of diagnostic services (∼2035 to 2045), followed by a fundamental redefinition of the discipline’s role in society from 2045 onwards. Underlying these technical developments is a new epistemic responsibility: as AI transforms raw data into medical knowledge autonomously, laboratory professionals must claim their irreplaceable role as the sole legally and professionally qualified institution responsible for translating laboratory data into medical insight. The future of laboratory medicine is not a swan song, it is an invitation to actively shape the laboratory 4.0.
authors: Georg Hoffmann

title: Laser-induced local wetting on self-assembled monolayers for microscale fluid control
abstract: Precise spatial control of surface wettability is central to emerging technologies in microfluidics, biosensing, and medical applications. However, current methods for wetting control can be limited by low spatial resolution, a narrow range of achievable wettability modulation, or reliance on masks that are time-consuming to fabricate. Here, we introduce Laser-Induced Local Wetting (LILoW), a maskless technique that uses nanosecond ultraviolet laser pulses to selectively change the wettability of self-assembled monolayer (SAM) coated surfaces. By locally irradiating the SAM coating near its ablation threshold to expose selected regions of the underlying substrate, LILoW combines the broad wetting tunability of coating-based approaches with the high-resolution patterning capabilities of laser systems. We describe the principle of the technique and analyze the contrast in wettability—up to nearly 90 ° —as a function of laser parameters, including laser pulse energy and irradiation pitch, all without inducing damage to the substrate. As a proof of concept, we fabricated an open-air, pumpless Y-shaped microfluidic guide that facilitates capillary-driven laminar co-flow, with high interfacial stability in the absence of physical wall confinement. The rapid and cost-effective platform represented by LILoW can pave the way to democratizing high-resolution wettability patterning for bioanalytical sensing and surface-guided chemical applications.
authors: Lidia Lozano‐Martín; Olga Bantysh; José María Gómez; Jordi Ignés‐Mullol; Martí Duocastella

title: Laser-matter interactions in intrinsically soft materials for biointegrated systems
abstract: Abstract Biointegrated systems are emerging as a new class of technology that redefines how electronic devices interact with the human body and surrounding environments through intimate integration with biological tissues. To establish such interfaces, intrinsically soft materials, including liquid metals, conducting polymers, hydrogels, elastomers, and composites, have attracted significant attention because their low modulus minimizes mechanical mismatch with soft tissues. However, conventional fabrication strategies are often incompatible with intrinsically soft materials due to harsh processing conditions. In this regard, laser processing has emerged as a powerful manufacturing strategy for soft biointegrated systems by delivering highly localized and programmable energy with exceptional spatial and temporal precision. Depending on the laser-matter interaction mechanism, laser irradiation can induce localized heating, structural reconfiguration, chemical conversion, and interfacial reconstruction within soft materials. In this article, we explore the fundamental mechanisms of two representative laser-matter interactions, photothermal and photochemical. Then we deal with laser processing strategies for soft materials, followed by representative biointegrated systems enabled by laser-based approaches. Finally, we discuss current challenges and future opportunities for scalable, adaptive, and intelligent biointegrated systems. Collectively, these discussions highlight the emerging role of laser processing in tailoring structural properties and generating conductive functionalities in intrinsically soft biointegrated systems.
authors: Jung Jae Park; Minwoo Kim; Seung Hwan Ko

title: Liquid Metal Resistive Sensing Architectures for Measuring Diaphragm Strain Responses on Obstructed Surfaces
abstract: ABSTRACT The mechanical response of diaphragm actuators for microfluidics and soft robotics is typically characterized on flat surfaces rather than the obstructed interfaces encountered in practical devices. Upon diaphragm actuation on textured or obstructed interfaces, geometric constraints redirect the strain from uniform bending to a constrained draping mode, which is not transduced by standard strain sensing. We formulate a liquid metal‐based strain sensing architecture integrated on a circular diaphragm to measure and control diaphragm deformation on even and uneven surfaces, using a rigid bead to create an obstructed diaphragm interface. Using finite element simulations, the electrical readouts from the strain sensor on the actuated diaphragm are correlated to its progression from symmetric diaphragm deformation to constrained geometry‐induced nonlinear diaphragm deformation and eventually to saturated diaphragm deformation at the bead center, with the predicted bead‐constrained deformation showing close agreement to the cross‐sectional confocal measurements across the diaphragm. The electrical readouts from the strain sensor reflecting the deformation regimes under geometric interruptions are utilized to control diaphragm‐induced confinement on an array of beads, which is validated based on its biomolecular immobilization level. This electromechanical basis for transducing diaphragm displacement on obstructed surfaces provides a roadmap to control actuation in microfluidic and soft‐robotic systems.
authors: Abdullah‐Bin Siddique; Jui‐Hong Weng; Deng‐Kai Yang; Chia‐Fu Chou; Nathan S. Swami

title: Livestock disease monitoring using artificial intelligence, machine learning and deep learning algorithms: A review
abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML), and Deep Learning (DL) in livestock disease detection has ushered in a new era of precision farming. These technologies facilitate early detection and diagnosis of diseases, thereby minimizing the impact on livestock health and improving overall farm productivity. AI-driven systems analyse vast datasets from various sources such as images, videos, and sensor data to identify patterns and anomalies indicative of disease. Machine Learning algorithms enhance the predictive accuracy by learning from historical data, while Deep Learning models further refine disease detection by analysing complex patterns in real-time. In this article an attempt was made to review the detection of different livestock diseases using several machine and deep learning algorithms. An array of livestock disease conditions such as mastitis, cardiovascular diseases, diseases during postpartum period, and animal skin ailments were detected using different machine learning and deep learning algorithms and among them, decision tree model, ResNet101, Support Vector Machine (SVM), Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), YOLOv5, EfficientNetB7 and EFMYOLOv3 were found to be most efficient algorithms for detection of the livestock diseases.
authors: Jahnavi AP; Ramesh BK; Harish Menpadi; Srinivasa DK
venue: International Journal of Advanced Biochemistry Research

title: Long-term natural aging alters the mechanical and thermal response of PDMS for microfluidic applications
abstract: Polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) is widely used in microfluidics; however, its long-term natural aging under routine storage conditions remains insufficiently characterized. PDMS was classified by curing age and compared across two macro-groups: young PDMS ( < 30 days) and aged PDMS ( > 3000 days). Specimens were evaluated by uniaxial compression, hyperelastic fitting, Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR), and thermogravimetric analysis (TGA). The average small-strain modulus rose from 0.65 MPa in young samples to 2.01 MPa in aged samples, a threefold increase ( p = 4.5 × 1 0 − 11 ). The large-strain tangent modulus did not differ significantly (119.6 versus 125.0 MPa), whereas Poisson’s ratio ν remained close to the incompressible limit in both groups (0.499 versus 0.497). Seven phenomenological hyperelastic models were compared using R 2 and the normalized root mean square error. The Mooney–Rivlin five-parameter model gave the lowest residual error, but its coefficients are not identifiable from a single deformation mode, so the three-parameter Yeoh formulation is recommended ( R 2 = 0.9940 young, 0.9890 aged). FT-IR spectra retained the characteristic PDMS bands, and the Si–CH 3 to Si–O–Si band-area ratio, the most diagnostic of methyl loss, differed by 0.3% between groups (one specimen each). TGA showed a degradation onset shifted from approximately 300 to 350 °C, a derivative thermogravimetric (DTG) peak from 423.8 to 503.3 °C, and residual mass reduced from 63.31% to 41.66%. At 10 kPa, a compliance analysis indicates that an aged microchannel deforms 67% less than a young one of identical geometry. Curing age is therefore an experimentally relevant material-state variable: aged PDMS remains chemically the same material but becomes mechanically and thermally distinct.

title: Lookahead Bayesian Optimisation for Molecular Growth in Self-Driving Laboratories
abstract: Self-driving laboratories can autonomously execute iterative design-make-test-analyse cycles, but molecular optimisation presents a distinctive challenge: selecting which compound to elaborate determines not only the next experiment, but also the chemical space accessible in subsequent rounds. Conventional molecular Bayesian optimisation typically evaluates compounds without considering how their selection changes what can subsequently be synthesised. Here, we introduce Lookahead Bayesian Optimisation (LABO), which instead values candidate molecules according to the predicted value of the synthetically accessible chemical space they unlock, enabling optimisation to account for future experimental opportunities. We evaluate LABO in simulated five-round molecular optimisation campaigns across 30 lead-like starting compounds and five kinase targets. LABO outperformed established molecular optimisation strategies from the literature across all 30 optimisation landscapes, as well as random, greedy and Bayesian optimisation controls. LABO was shown to improve ligand-lipophilicity efficiency by 1.25 units over random selection, equivalent to approximately 18-fold greater potency at equal lipophilicity, and by 0.34 units (2.2-fold) over greedy elaboration. These results demonstrate a general principle for autonomous molecular optimisation: under synthetic constraints, the value of a molecule depends not only on its predicted properties, but on the future experiments that selecting it makes possible. By explicitly incorporating this future experimental value into molecular selection, LABO provides a framework for planning successive rounds of molecular growth in self-driving laboratories.
authors: Connor J. Taylor

title: MICROROBOTIC SAMPLING AND QUANTUM BIOSENSING CO-DESIGN AT THE LIMIT An Exploratory Engineering Monograph on Sample Handling, Reference Control, and Biological Risk Boundaries This research monograph examines whether controlled micromanipulation can improve the positioning, transport, recovery, and reproducibility of biological research samples without increasing sample alteration, cross-contamination, thermal exposure, or misleading biosensor signals. The guiding three-coupling is Sample Handling × Reference Control × Biological Risk Boundary. Its guiding question is not whether an autonomous microrobot can move a sample, but whether the resulting measurement remains traceable to an authentic, independently verifiable sample state. The work synthesizes three mother research architectures: (S) Swarm Manufacturing and Robotic Matter at the Limit, particularly chapters 9–16 and 33–40, for embodied manipulation and collective transport; (QH) Autonomous Quantum Health Infrastructure at the Limit, especially chapters 9–24 and 67–74, for raw-to-result lineage, uncertainty-aware decisions, human authority and recovery; and (QB) Self-Calibrating Quantum Biosensing Networks at the Limit, particularly chapters 57–73, for fabrication variation, reference transfer, calibration, drift and measurement integrity. These sources contribute methods rather than evidence that the cross-domain integration is already demonstrated. Across 82 chapters and 12 single-section research studies per chapter, the monograph examines non-clinical microfluidic sample environments, magnetic and acoustic micromanipulation, optical and electrokinetic methods, nanoscale surface chemistry, quantum-enabled and classical biosensing, correlated uncertainty, sample-to-signal provenance, authorized closed-loop control, physical damage and carryover detection, interlaboratory replication, lifecycle burden, and successor reconstruction. Thirty mathematical and physical derivation plates introduce assumptions and validity boundaries. Every chapter presents a distinct candidate engineering relation and a geometric three-dimensional research portrait. The validation approach prioritizes synthetic phantoms and permitted ex-vivo research standards in closed non-clinical environments. It calls for blinded comparison of skilled manual pipetting, passive microfluidics, and robotic operation under matched sample identity, measurement time, contamination constraints, and independent calibration. A perceived improvement in robotic throughput or algorithmic readout quality does not establish improved sample authenticity. Any claim of quantum advantage must be compared against an appropriate, strong classical sensing baseline end to end. The research architecture closes with 200 independently framed Research Gates and 33 provisional Phoenix Answer Embryos, each accompanied by one of 233 indexed equation eggs. Gates specify questions, comparators, pass criteria, and veto conditions; answer embryos can be challenged, decomposed, recombined or retired. An accompanying Research Gates spreadsheet maps these questions to chapters, physical relations, evidence packets and future experiments. The study is explicitly exploratory and non-clinical. It does not establish the existence of mature autonomous in-body nanorobotic medicine, grant permission for diagnosis or therapy, or imply that quantum-enabled detection is intrinsically superior. Candidate indices and equations are design hypotheses unless identified as established physical relations; many passages use a recurring structured research grammar and require independent experiments, domain expert review, and peer assessment. The aim is to leave a reproducible and falsifiable research architecture that subsequent investigators are free to revise, reject, or extend.
