title: MOF-VERIFY: A Failure-Aware Agentic Harness for MOF Hypothesis Verification
abstract: Large language models are increasingly used as reasoning components in AI-driven materials Co-Scientists, yet the reliability of the resulting verification pipeline remains unclear. Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) provide a particularly challenging setting because structures may appear under different identifiers, synthesis outcomes depend strongly on experimental conditions, evidence is distributed across heterogeneous sources, and some hypotheses require computation rather than literature alone. We introduce a diagnostic benchmark with four task families covering structural grounding, synthesis-condition verification, evidence-sufficiency verification, and MLIP-based computational verification. T-MOF-1-3 are evaluated under closed-book, retrieval-enabled, and oracle-evidence settings to localize failures in knowledge access, evidence acquisition, and reasoning, while T-MOF-4 separately evaluates computational verification. Guided by these diagnosed failure modes, we develop MOF-Verify, a failure-aware agentic harness that targets structural, literature, evidence-sufficiency, and computational bottlenecks before producing a final verdict. Across multiple backbone LLMs, MOF-Verify substantially improves hypothesis-verification performance over direct inference and retrieval-based baselines. Benchmark datasets are released at https://github.com/IMMS-Ewha/MOF-Verify-Benchmark.
authors: Donghyun Lee; Taehoon Lee; Geonhee Ahn; Jieun Kim; Jihyun Park; Suyeon Cho; Yoona Kim; Chaerim Shin; Hoi Ri Moon; Jonggeol Na; Sukho Hong; Jihwan Oh; Soo Kyung Kim

title: Machine Learning-Based Taylor Cone Analysis for Electrospinning Process-Window Identification and Cell-Laden Nanofiber Scaffold Fabrication
abstract: Electrospinning is a powerful biofabrication technique for constructing fibrous scaffolds that mimic extracellular matrix architectures. However, the process is highly nonlinear and involves strongly coupled parameters, making fiber architecture and biological performance difficult to control empirically and limits reproducibility. Most machine learning (ML) studies still focus on static correlations between processing parameters and outcomes rather than on dynamic modeling of electrospinning evolution and regulation, thereby hindering real-time, precise process control. Here, we establish a data-driven framework that links process parameters, Taylor cone geometry, and nanofiber/cell outcomes through high-speed imaging and ML. A custom image-processing pipeline is developed to automatically extract cone angle, height, and width from in situ images with improved accuracy via a rotating-ray-based geometric algorithm. Using datasets collected from three representative polymer systems (PVDF, PVB, and PEO), random forest models outperform support vector machine and minimum description length, achieving moderate-to-good prediction of Taylor cone descriptors (R²≈0.57-0.83) across varied voltages, flow rate, and needle-collector distances. We further extend this framework to PEO-based cell electrospinning. By correlating predicted cone geometries with experimentally measured viability of 293T cells and umbilical cord mesenchymal stem cells, we identify a Taylor cone "safe window" that simultaneously stabilizes jet formation and preserves cell survival (>95%). Guided by this window, a bilayer cell-laden scaffold comprising a PVB support layer and a PEO-cell layer is fabricated with improved process robustness. This enables stable delivery of high-density, highly viable cells and facilitates the fabrication of three-dimensional cell-laden nanofiber scaffolds. Overall, this Taylor cone analysis, ML-guided strategy provides a quantitative framework for process-window identification in polymer and cell electrospinning, and may support future integration with real-time monitoring, online inference, and closed-loop control in intelligent biofabrication.
authors: Huazhen Liu; Kaidi Luo; Jiayao Gu; Wenbin Sun; Xiaoyi Wang; Yongjun Zheng; Zhijian Li; Su Xiao; Yuanyuan Liu

title: Machine Learning–Assisted Fluorescent Eu@ZnMOF for the Enoxacin and Glyphosate Detection in Food by Suppressing Sensitization and Ligand–Metal Charge Transfer
abstract: ABSTRACT The antibiotics and pesticides in the ecosystem environment, owing to their extensive application in veterinary medicine and insecticides, present a significant hazard to public health. Herein, we developed a novel bimetallic metal‐organic framework (MOF) as a ratiometric fluorescent sensor for the simultaneous monitoring of enoxacin (ENX) and glyphosate (GLY). To fabricate a dual‐responsive probe, we synthesized the ZnMOF by reacting Zn 2+ ions with the ligands (2,2′‐bipyridine‐5,5′‐dicarboxylic acid, 8‐hydroxyquinoline, and 2‐aminoterephthalic acid). Subsequently, the bimetallic Eu@ZnMOF was synthesized by loading europium (Eu 3+ ) ions into the ZnMOF based on the coordination with the 2,2′‐bipyridine‐5,5′‐dicarboxylic acid sites. The Eu@ZnMOF‐based detection system exhibits a distinct green emission due to the suppression of excited‐state intramolecular proton transfer in 8‐hydroxyquinoline by Zn 2+ ions. In the detection system, ENX enhances the red emission of Eu@ZnMOF by sensitizing Eu 3+ ions. Accordingly, the ENX fluorescent sensing system was fabricated. Moreover, ENX‐modified Eu@ZnMOF was fabricated. Upon the addition of GLY, suppression of sensitization and ligand‐to‐metal charge transfer (LMCT) occurs, which quenches the red emission of Eu 3+ and boosts the blue emission, resulting in a distinct color transition from red to blue. The ratiometric fluorescent sensor allows detection limits of 0.05 and 0.10 mg/L for ENX and GLY, respectively. Moreover, we integrated this material into a microfluidic chip. By combining this platform with smartphone imaging and machine learning algorithms, we constructed a rapid detection protocol capable of simultaneous multi‐sample analysis. These results demonstrate the promising application potential of Eu@ZnMOF for advanced environmental and food‐safety testing.
authors: Ze Li; Yan Man; Qingju Liu; Jilong Han; Zhikun Zhang

title: Machine-Vision-Assisted Automated Closed-Loop Manipulation of Open-Surface Droplets.
abstract: Automated manipulation of open-surface droplets is important for microscale sample handling, reaction assembly, and biochemical analysis, yet existing systems often lack obstacle-aware planning, control-state monitoring, and disturbance recovery. Here, we present a machine-vision-assisted closed-loop system for programmable, noncontact droplet manipulation on a photogated corona microfluidic (PGCM) platform. The system integrates real-time localization, rapidly exploring random tree planning, robotic laser actuation, and hierarchical feedback control. An inner loop guides the laser spot along the planned path, while an outer loop monitors the droplet-laser binding state. Obstacle changes trigger online replanning, whereas loss of binding triggers laser return, droplet recapture, and task recovery. The system transported 1-50 μL droplets, performed sequential coalescence, static and dynamic obstacle avoidance, complex-path manipulation, multistep reactions, and droplet-mediated transport of a flexible porous solid target. Following a manually imposed voltage interruption, it automatically detected loss of binding and resumed the task after actuation was restored. This work provides a programmable and disturbance-tolerant visual closed-loop framework for automated open-surface droplet manipulation.
authors: Biao Cheng; Jialin Yang; Chengjun Wang; Yongliang Sun; Lei Zhou; Qiang Zhao; Huanyu Li; Yifan Meng; Qiang Tang

title: Magnetic Field-Based Intervention in Cardiovascular Diseases: Biological Basis, Therapeutic Strategies, and Translational Challenges
abstract: Cardiovascular diseases remain the leading cause of death worldwide, and their burden continues to rise. As a noninvasive physical intervention, magnetic fields offer deep tissue penetration, remote programmability, and favorable spatiotemporal controllability, making them uniquely valuable for modulating cardiovascular function. This review systematically summarizes the biological basis of magnetic field actions on the cardiovascular system, including multi-scale effects on cardiac electrophysiology and ion channels, vascular endothelial function and microcirculatory perfusion, and cardiac autonomic regulation. On this basis, we synthesize therapeutic advances in three areas: electrophysiological intervention in arrhythmias, cardiac autonomic neuromodulation, and cardiac repair and regeneration. Preclinical evidence indicates that magnetic fields can mediate nonpharmacological intervention in arrhythmias, myocardial infarction, and heart failure, although clinical validation to date is limited to a single small randomized trial. Finally, we analyze translational bottlenecks (standardization of stimulation parameters, long-term in vivo safety assessment, and intelligent closed-loop control) and outline future directions integrating magnetic fields with regenerative medicine and artificial intelligence, aiming to provide new strategies for precision cardiovascular care.
authors: 孔德汶; 唐杨烽

title: Making Self-Driving Laboratories Auditable:A Unified Framework for Hybrid Actions,Measurements, and Safe Execution
abstract: Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) are laboratory systems that couple experimental planning, automated execution, and measurement feedback in a closed loop. Integrating flexible robot control with the typed application programming interfaces (APIs) and continuous measurements exposed by laboratory instruments remains an execution-interface challenge. To address this challenge, we propose a traceable framework comprising four components: LAM (Lab Action Model), OpenSDL, Safe-SDL, and L3-Bench. LAM is a proposed measurement-conditioned policy architecture that extends vision-language-action paradigms to generate both continuous robot trajectories and typed instrument API calls. OpenSDL is an execution substrate with an initial control implementation, designed to map role-level operations to heterogeneous devices, coordinate execution, and record timestamped causal events. The proposed Safe-SDL runtime gate combines pre-dispatch schema and resource checks with signal temporal logic monitoring during execution, including extended waiting periods. L3-Bench (Level-3 Laboratory Benchmark) specifies an episode-level evaluation protocol covering physical outcomes, timing, reproducibility, safety violations, and fault recovery. Together, these components provide an end-to-end design for linking hybrid action generation, monitored device execution, measurement feedback, and experimental evaluation, addressing coordination and traceability challenges in SDL workflows.
authors: Zihan Zhang; Zeyu Wu; Xin Zhang; Mingyu Luo; Haohui Que; Tong Zhu

title: Management of acute necrotizing pancreatitis: Current evidence, controversies and future perspectives
abstract: Acute necrotizing pancreatitis affects 10%-20% of patients with acute pancreatitis and carries substantial morbidity and mortality, ranging from 15% in sterile necrosis to 30-40% in infected necrosis.Over the past two decades, management has shifted from early aggressive intervention to a delayed, minimally invasive "step-up" approach, though several aspects remain non-standardized.This narrative review synthesizes evidence from randomized controlled trials, systematic reviews, meta-analyses and current guidelines across diagnosis, supportive care, antibiotics, intervention indications, step-up strategies, minimally invasive and open necrosectomy.Initial management should favor moderate fluid resuscitation, early oral/enteral feeding, and appropriate intensive care unit triage.Antibiotic prophylaxis is unsupported by evidence and therapy should be reserved for confirmed or strongly suspected infected necrosis, guided by clinical/radiological reassessment.When intervention is needed, step-up remains standard of care.Endoscopic and surgical step-up show broadly comparable survival, though not uniformly across anatomical patterns and settings, with endoscopy favoring fistula rates and length of stay.Minimally invasive necrosectomy is associated with lower mortality and fewer complications than open necrosectomy.However, these findings are largely observational and prone to confounding by indication.Based on this evidence, we propose a risk-adapted algorithm separating risk stratification from treatment escalation.

title: Mapping the technology–demand interface: how brain organoid evolution is reshaping the translational landscape of stroke
abstract: Stroke research faces a dual modeling barrier: interspecies divergence and oversimplified 2D cultures have contributed to the failure of many neuroprotective trials. Brain organoids, which provide human genetic backgrounds and 3D neural networks, offer a promising but incomplete solution. Existing reviews often address isolated technological aspects without linking them to stroke-specific demands. This narrative review establishes a “technological iteration–clinical demand” mapping matrix (Figure 1). We trace organoid evolution from static oxygen–glucose deprivation models to vascularized, assembloid, and microfluidic chip-integrated systems, and toward multi-organ coupling. We highlight how these advances may uncover human-specific neuroinflammation, proposed PANoptosis-like spatiotemporal cascades, and synaptic deficits mediated by human-specific genes such as SRGAP2C. We argue that the inability of animal models to resolve certain human-specific targets is driving organoids from static endpoint models toward dynamic platforms with perfusable vasculature and immune integration, although current systems remain at an early stage. We critically evaluate the preclinical role of organoids, defining scenarios where they may partially replace animal testing and where they cannot. Major bottlenecks include fetal-like organoid maturity (transcriptome approximately equivalent to gestational weeks 12–20) versus the average stroke onset age of about 70 years, and the absence of peripheral immune infiltration, which mediates a large fraction of secondary injury. We outline potential solutions including multi-omics integration, inducible aging, gene editing, and multi-organ chip coupling, and emphasize that standardized evaluation frameworks are needed to translate organoid findings into personalized stroke therapy.
authors: Caohang Qiu; Ning Sun; Jun Yang; Ling Tan; Maoyu Zhao; Yuyao Fu; Gonghong Liu; Zhifu Song; Wenyou Wu

title: Mathematical analysis of electromagnetically driven squeezing flow in confined microchannels
abstract: Abstract Nanofluids flowing through confined channels are widely used in micro-cooling systems, miniature pumps, and other microfluidic technologies, where the combined effects of electromagnetic forces and variable fluid properties play an important role in transport phenomena. This study explores the squeezing flow of a nanofluid between two parallel plates, specifically focusing on a stretching, porous lower plate. We examine how external electric and magnetic fields influence flow transport. Temperature-dependent viscosity and thermal conductivity are included in the model to obtain a realistic thermophysical behaviour of the nanofluid flow. The novelty of the study lies in simultaneously considering electro-magnetohydrodynamic effects together with variable fluid properties within the Buongiorno nanofluid model. The governing equations are transformed using similarity transformations and solved by the Optimal Homotopy Analysis Method (OHAM). The results reveal that squeezing, electroosmotic, and electric field parameters enhance the forward flow, whereas suction and magnetic field intensity oppose the fluid motion. Brownian motion and thermophoresis increase the fluid temperature, while increasing the thermophoresis and Lewis number leads to a reduction in the nanoparticle concentration. The combined influence of electromagnetic effects and variable fluid properties demonstrates their importance in controlling flow and heat transfer in confined microfluidic systems.
authors: Mahantesh Chandaragi; Tripathi Dharmendra; Shruthi Karanth; Rajashekhar Choudhari; Hanumesh Vaidya; K. V. Prasad

title: Matrix-Based Specific T-Cell Activation Reporter for Nearly-Digital Mapping of Antigen-Specific T Cells via Heterotypic Cell Micro-Communities and Digital Microfluidics.
abstract: Antigen-specific T cells constitute a low percentage of peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) and require antigen presentation by autologous antigen-presenting cells for activation and cytokine secretion. Conventional interferon-γ release assay (IGRA) averages rare activation events beyond cellular resolution, while single-cell compartmentalization disrupts the intracellular synapses for T cell immunity. Here, we developed mSTAR (matrix-based Specific T-cell Activation Reporter), an active-matrix digital microfluidic platform that partitions microliters of PBMCs into a nanoliter-scale matrix of 16 cell microcommunities (CMCs), each retaining tens to hundreds of PBMCs in their native heterotypic composition to preserve the natural physiological immune response. In a proof of concept, mSTAR executes parallel IGRA for a tuberculosis disease model, including CMC stimulation and magnetic-bead-based immunofluorescence assay. The IGRA of the mSTAR system achieves a limit of detection of 3.70 pg/mL, yielding 16 interferon-γ quantification readouts and ratios between CMCs incubated with different stimulants (negative, positive, or specific antigen). This enables the mapping and reporting of activated antigen-specific T cells in the matrix, thereby achieving functional phenotyping of each CMC. Poisson-based modeling of the droplet matrix converts rare T-cell activation events into a nearly digital estimation, and the positive CMCs encapsulating target cells can be retrieved for further characterization without loss. By bridging functional phenotyping and molecular features without prior cell sorting or engineering, mSTAR provides a programmable immunoanalytical infrastructure for broad downstream applications such as antigen-specific immunotherapy development or T-cell receptor discovery.
authors: Hangjia Tu; Mengxing Mou; Chenxuan Hu; Jinxin Fu; Xiaotian Tan; Yuzhong Xu; Ji Huang; Wenxin Yan; Wenjuan Wu; Peijin Wang; Tianyuan Zhao; Jianheng Huang; Binmao Zhang; Chengbin Yang; Hanbin Ma; Siyi Hu; Yujuan Chai

title: Membrane-Integrated Organ-on-a-Chip Systems
abstract: Membranes play a key role in many organ-on-a-chip (OOC) platforms due to nutrient and mass transport, barrier formation, and mechanical signaling. However, despite their key role in OOC devices, the relationship between membrane design parameters and device performance is limited in the literature. Here, this review gives a critical overview of not only the types of membranes for OOC devices (natural, synthetic, hybrid, and emerging functional membranes) but also defines the key engineering design requirements for the selection and integration of membranes with microfluidic OOC platforms. Additionally, it presents types of organ-specific OOC devices (lung, kidney, liver, blood-brain barrier, and intestine models), highlighting existing challenges and limitations in the fabrication of such platforms. The paper also presents future directions toward smart, multifunctional membranes.
authors: Moldir Kali; Almas Rakhymzhanov; Gulsim Kulsharova

title: Mesenchymal stem cells and their exosomes modulate sebocyte fate and lipid-associated proteomic-lipidomic remodeling.
abstract: Sebocytes regulate skin lipid production and inflammatory homeostasis, yet how mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) and MSCs-derived exosomes reshape sebocyte function remains unclear. This study compared the effects of indirect MSCs co-culture and MSCs-derived exosome treatment on MTS-associated metabolic activity, intracellular lipid droplet accumulation, proteomic remodeling, and lipidomic profiles in sebocytes. Human sebocytes were indirectly co-cultured with bone marrow-derived MSCs using transwell inserts or treated with MSCs-derived exosomes under proliferative or low-serum, lipid accumulation-promoting conditions. MTS-associated metabolic activity was assessed using the MTS assay, intracellular lipid droplet accumulation using Nile Red staining, proteomic remodeling using label-free LC-MS/MS, and lipidomic changes using untargeted LC-MS lipidomics. Indirect MSCs co-culture reduced MTS-associated metabolic activity, particularly under low-serum conditions, while markedly increasing intracellular lipid droplet accumulation. Proteomic analysis indicated that MSCs co-culture promoted cytoskeletal, adhesion-related, and lipid-handling remodeling. Lipidomics further revealed broad lipid-class reprogramming, characterized by increased phospholipid-associated features and reduced lysophospholipid-associated features. In contrast, MSCs-derived exosomes increased MTS-associated metabolic activity under low-serum conditions, while intracellular lipid droplet accumulation remained largely comparable to control levels. Exosome treatment induced more selective proteomic changes related to proteostasis, mitochondrial adaptation, and vesicular trafficking/signaling, with limited lipidomic alterations that did not remain significant after FDR correction. MSCs co-culture and MSCs-derived exosomes exert biologically distinct effects on sebocytes. Whole MSCs co-culture drives extensive lipid-associated remodeling, whereas isolated exosomes mainly increase MTS-associated metabolic activity and induce adaptive proteomic responses, suggesting that exosomes transmit only part of the broader MSCs paracrine influence on sebocyte biology.
authors: Maryam Adelipour; Mohamed A Gab-Allah; Mingyu Kim; Sangsoo Lee; Kee K Kim; Ga Seul Lee; Jeong Hee Moon; David M Lubman; Jeongkwon Kim

title: Micro/Nanostructured Materials and Microfluidic Diagnostic Platforms Enable Multimodal Detection of Circulating Tumor Cells
abstract: Circulating tumor cells (CTCs), as pivotal targets in liquid biopsy, offer dynamic, multidimensional insights into tumor heterogeneity and metastatic progression. However, their extreme rarity, pronounced heterogeneity, and the complexity of the blood microenvironment severely constrain detection accuracy. Advances in micro/nanomaterials and functional device engineering have enabled substantial improvements in CTC enrichment efficiency by refining the topographical and chemical properties of capture interfaces. These innovations also provide a compatible foundation for multimodal molecular profiling. This review systematically outlines the structure-function relationships of functionalized nanomaterials, microfiltration substrates, and biomimetic microfluidic devices, highlighting how material parameters-such as nanoscale architectures and membrane pore sizes-govern CTC capture performance. We further explore the integration of micro/nanomaterials with functional platforms for multidimensional molecular analyses across DNA, RNA, and protein levels. Coupled with emerging digital PCR technologies, these systems show promise in overcoming the sensitivity barriers associated with rare mutation detection and protein quantification, enabling multi-omics data fusion. We also discuss how artificial intelligence (AI)-driven feature selection, clustering, and prediction integrate multidimensional data to decode tumor heterogeneity and guide disease monitoring. Despite rapid progress, key challenges remain-including the lack of standardization, limited integration of multi-omic datasets, and the need for robust clinical validation. Future directions may lie in the convergence of microfluidic-integrated materials, single-cell multi-omics, and AI-driven analytics to establish dynamic, high-resolution monitoring platforms that bridge the gap between fundamental research and clinical precision oncology.
authors: Hao Li; Jiaojiao Sun; Kunguo Liu; Shijie Wang; Bowen Fu; Hong Zhu; Peng Cao; Xin Han

title: Microcapillary-assisted acoustoelectric platform for selective single-cell isolation and in situ transfection
abstract: Single-cell transfection technologies hold tremendous promise for precision cell and immunotherapies. However, monolithic integration of cell isolation with targeted intracellular delivery remains technically challenging, especially within complex biological matrices. Herein, we present a microcapillary-assisted acoustoelectric single-cell selective isolation and sonoporative transfection platform (μC-ASSIST), which seamlessly sequences microcapillary-assisted dielectrophoresis (μC-DEP) for deterministic single-cell trapping with high-frequency surface acoustic waves (SAWs) for transient membrane poration within a unified workflow. We demonstrate the label-free, high-efficiency extraction of human non-small cell lung cancer (A549) cells from a complex white blood cell (WBC) background with a capture efficiency of 95%. Furthermore, we validate the highly efficient, contact-free intracellular delivery of diverse cargoes ranging from small dyes (PI) to functional small interfering RNA (siRNA) and large plasmid DNA (mRFP-C3), maintaining a high cell viability of 83.7% alongside a 78.1% transfection efficiency. Crucially, the targeted delivery of siBcl-xL significantly suppressed target mRNA expression and profoundly inhibited tumor cell motility. By circumventing off-target effects and cumbersome manual handling, the μC-ASSIST platform establishes a highly versatile, streamlined paradigm for precision single-cell engineering, holding immense potential for advancing functional genomics and next-generation gene therapies.
authors: Xuefeng Xu; Ziqiao Zhou; Guangyang Li; Jie Liang; Jianhui Wu; Jiaqi Lu; Fang Shen; Shengjun Wu; Zhi Ruan; Shurong Dong; Jikui Luo; Zhen Cao

title: Microchemical Strategies and AI-Enabled Biosensing for Non-Invasive Liquid Biopsy in Precision Oncology
abstract: Traditional blood-based liquid biopsy platforms have established crucial paradigms in precision oncology by enabling the longitudinal tracking of circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs). However, blood sampling remains minimally invasive, requires dedicated clinical infrastructure, and is restricted by physiological boundaries such as the blood-brain barrier (BBB). Non-Invasive Liquid Biopsy (NILB) addresses these limitations by utilizing painlessly collected alternative biological matrices, including saliva, urine, breath, stool, sweat, sputum, tears, and cervical secretions. From a microchemical and analytical perspective, these biofluids present extreme analytical challenges: target biomarkers exist at attomolar-to-picomolar concentrations within dense, highly variable chemical matrices containing high background noise and interference. This review outlines the microchemical, physical, and bio-sensing strategies developed to overcome these pre-analytical and analytical barriers. We evaluate advanced microfluidic architectures, nanoscale deterministic lateral displacement, functionalized surface chemistry, isothermal signal amplification, and label-free optical spectroscopy. Furthermore, we evaluate how Artificial Intelligence (AI) and chemometric algorithms—such as Support Vector Machines (SVM), Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), and multivariate spectral extraction—decode low-abundance, fragmented multi-omic signatures from complex noise. Finally, we propose a standardized analytical framework to bridge point-of-care microchemical devices with routine clinical diagnostic pipelines.
authors: Samuel Long; Abigail Long

title: Microfluidic Fabrication of Functional Micro-/Nanoparticles: From Structural Regulation to Scalable Integration
abstract: Ran Tian,1,* Jiani Liu,2,* Tao Liu,3 Hanyu Du,1 Geng Dou,2 Juan Tong,4 Xinyu Qiu,4 Linqian Hou,2 Xiaoju Lu,1 Yuting Su51School of Advanced Materials and Green Chemical Engineering, Hubei Polytechnic University, Huangshi, People’s Republic of China; 2State Key Laboratory of Oral & Maxillofacial Reconstruction and Regeneration, National Clinical Research Center for Oral Diseases, School of Stomatology, The Fourth Military Medical University, Xi’an, People’s Republic of China; 3Center of Biodiagnosis and Biotherapy, Precision Medical Institute, The Second Affiliated Hospital of Xi’an Jiaotong University, Xi’an, Shaanxi, People’s Republic of China; 4Department of Preventive Dentistry, State Key Laboratory of Oral & Maxillofacial Reconstruction and Regeneration, National Clinical Research Center for Oral Diseases, Shaanxi Clinical Research Center for Oral Disease, School of Stomatology, The Fourth Military Medical University, Xi’an, People’s Republic of China; 5Center of Clinical Aerospace Medicine, School of Aerospace Medicine, Air Force Medical University, Xi’an, People’s Republic of China*These authors contributed equally to this workCorrespondence: Yuting Su, Center of Clinical Aerospace Medicine, School of Aerospace Medicine, Air Force Medical University, Xi’an, People’s Republic of China, Email sssusyt@163.com Xiaoju Lu, School of Advanced Materials and Green Chemical Engineering, Hubei Polytechnic University, Huangshi, China, Email luxiaoju@hbpu.edu.cnAbstract: Functional particles play critical roles in biomedicine, sensing, catalysis, energy storage and conversion, and environmental remediation. Conventional bulk synthesis can provide limited control over local reaction environments when narrow size distributions, complex morphologies, or hierarchical architectures are required. Microfluidic synthesis addresses these limitations by confining reactions within microscale channels, droplets, or flow segments, thereby enabling controlled multiphase flow, rapid heat and mass transfer, and precise regulation of local reaction conditions. This review is organized around a particle formation/process control/particle properties/scale-up framework, linking microfluidic design and operating parameters to nucleation, growth, phase separation, interfacial assembly, and solidification, and subsequently to particle size, morphology, dispersity, and hierarchical structure. Representative strategies, including droplet microfluidics, hydrodynamic focusing, co-flow systems, structured microchannels, and integrated microreactors, are critically compared in terms of particle-quality control and manufacturing feasibility. Particular attention is given to scalability, productivity, process robustness, clogging, downstream processing, and internal and external integration. Although microfluidic processing can improve control and reproducibility, many reported systems remain at the proof-of-concept or laboratory scale. Future development therefore requires quantitative process-structured relationships, robust device engineering, in-line monitoring, feedback control, and validated scale-up strategies.Keywords: functional particles, microfluidic synthesis, micro-/nanoparticles, particle regulation, chip integration

title: Microfluidic Technologies for Seminal Fluid Analysis: from Sperm Selection to Liquid Biopsy in Prostate Cancer
abstract: Microfluidic technologies, which enable precise manipulation of cells and biological fluids at the microscale, represent a promising platform for reproductive medicine and urologic oncology. This review examines the operating principles, engineering features, and clinical potential of microfluidic systems for seminal fluid analysis, sperm selection, and liquid biopsy in prostate cancer. The reviewed domestic and international literature addresses microfluidic sperm selection, sperm DNA fragmentation, rheotaxis, inertial microfluidics, circulating tumor cells, and molecular biomarkers in seminal fluid. Microfluidic devices can facilitate gentle processing of spermatozoa, enrichment of samples with progressively motile cells, and isolation of tumor cells, extracellular vesicles, and cell-free DNA. Particular attention is paid to the potential for standardized processing of viscous and heterogeneous samples prior to molecular analysis and cytological evaluation in specialized laboratories. A particularly promising area is the development of integrated platforms suitable for clinical validation and subsequent incorporation into diagnostic pathways for patients with prostate diseases.
authors: S. P. Sametov; R. F. Gizatullin; R. I. Tukhvatullin

title: Microfluidic technology: from historical development to modern applications
abstract: Microfluidics is a rapidly evolving interdisciplinary field focused on the precise manipulation and control of fluids at the micrometre scale. The kingdom of microfluidics is ruled by tiny fluid volumes through the development of novel applications that benefit from the use of these small samples. Typical manipulations involve small volumes of fluid (microliters or sub-microliters) leading to improved capability to manipulate fluids, increased accuracy over traditional methodologies, and many successful implementations in diverse domains including health care, environmental capabilities, and chemical processing. Examples of microfluidic implementation that have significantly improved testing efficiency, effectiveness, and portability include lab on chip & point of care testing appliances. The primary advantages of microfluidics include lower sample use, faster analysis times, improved sensitivity, and the ability to combine with other systems for automated operation and control. This review highlights the historical development and fundamental principles of microfluidics along with its growing importance in modern science and engineering. Various applications of microfluidic systems in healthcare diagnostics, environmental monitoring, chemical synthesis, and biological analysis are comprehensively discussed. In addition, the review outlines the current limitations and challenges associated with microfluidic technologies, including fabrication complexity and scalability issues. Overall, this review offers a comprehensive understanding of both possible opportunities and existing limitations of microfluidics. Therefore, it is concluded that further development and improvement of this area are of significant importance, as it may become the basis for future scientific and engineering breakthroughs. Finally, future perspectives and trends in microfluidics are discussed, highlighting its potential to enable revolutionary approaches in subsequent analytical and biomedical technologies.
authors: Sourav Ghosh; Jit Chakraborty; Avishek Saha; Arijit Das; Kalachand Mahali; Sanjay Roy

title: Microfluidic-Based Molecular Diagnostics for Pathogen Detection in Urine Samples for Resource-Limited Settings: A Review
abstract: Urine is a convenient, noninvasive specimen for molecular diagnostics, offering advantages in scalability, patient compliance, and suitability for decentralized testing. However, its clinical adoption for molecular pathogen detection remains limited by intrinsic physicochemical variability, low target abundance, and the presence of inhibitors of enzymatic nucleic acid amplification that may seriously compromise assay sensitivity and reproducibility. In this review, we introduce a urine-first design paradigm in which device architecture and assay chemistry are codesigned around the unique biochemical constraints of urine rather than adapted from conventional blood-based workflows. This paradigm is built on three interdependent principles: matrix-aware sample processing with efficient inhibitor removal and multifraction nucleic acid capture; amplification chemistry with built-in tolerance to pH fluctuations, ionic variability, and residual urinary inhibitors; and closed, integrated microfluidic architectures that minimize contamination risk. We compare on-chip amplification strategies, including PCR, isothermal amplification methods such as LAMP and RPA, digital PCR, and CRISPR-assisted detection, and evaluate trade-offs in sensitivity, inhibitor tolerance, and deployability. Detection modalities, including fluorescence, colorimetric, electrochemical, and lateral-flow readouts, are assessed for analytical performance and compatibility with resource-limited settings. By integrating biological insight with engineering design, this review provides a practical roadmap for developing accessible, field-ready urine-based diagnostic platforms.
authors: E. Alperay Tarim; Natish Kumar; Michael Mauk; Mohamed El‐Tholoth

title: Microfluidics to assess the impact of transfused blood components
abstract: Assessing the function of transfused blood components within the dynamic environment of the vascular system remains challenging, as conventional assays are largely static and poorly represent the dynamic mechanical and biochemical interactions between blood cells and the vessel wall. Microfluidic approaches, which study blood flow within small-scale channels, provide an opportunity to bridge this gap by introducing physiologically relevant flow and shear rates into experimental models. This review synthesises the current literature describing the application of microfluidic technologies to the assessment of transfused blood components, with particular emphasis on platelet concentrates, red cell concentrates and plasma-derived products. Across existing studies, microfluidic models have demonstrated differences in component function related to storage conditions, manufacturing methods and emerging transfusion products that are not always detected using conventional bulk assays. These approaches have provided new insights into platelet haemostasis at defined shear rates, red cell deformability and gas exchange, and plasma-mediated coagulation in trauma and critical illness. However, substantial diversity in device design, experimental conditions and analytical endpoints limits direct comparison between studies and constrains translation into routine practice. The development of more standardised platforms, alongside integration with endothelialised and organ-on-a-chip models, may help to overcome these challenges. Overall, microfluidics represents a promising tool for improving functional assessment of blood components and supporting future advances in transfusion medicine research and personalised transfusion strategies.
authors: Edward John Sayers; Jamie Nash; E. M. Davies; Christine V. Saunders; Chloë E. George

title: Miniaturized Multifunctional Valves for Intelligent Pneumatic Systems in Soft Robotics
abstract: Soft robotics stands to benefit significantly from advances in pneumatic circuit‐based actuation, sensing, and on‐board logic. Soft pneumatic valves serve as vital components; however, existing implementations remain limited by insufficient function versatility, constraining their use in intelligent pneumatic architectures. Here, we present a unified framework for miniaturized functional pneumatic valves that provides both normally open (NO) and normally closed (NC) configurations. These valves can execute logic operations (AND, OR, NAND, and NOR) and can be rapidly reconfigured and programmed without physical replumbing or hardware modification. Fast dynamic response is achieved, with time constants as low as 5.2 and 6.1 ms for NO and NC valves, respectively. These valves enable embodied intelligence, as demonstrated in two representative robotic systems. First, we realize a reflexive response with an electronics‐free autonomous soft gripper capable of regulating grasping force. Second, we demonstrate a robotic gripper that integrates valve‐based tactile sensing to classify objects and support higher‐level intelligent control. Together, these results establish multifunctional pneumatic valves as foundational building blocks for intelligent pneumatic systems, enabling decentralized sensing, decision‐making, and adaptive control through physical embodiment. This approach advances soft robotics toward autonomy by embedding intelligence directly into the material and fluidic architecture of the system.
authors: Jing Xu; Xuezhi Niu; J. Andersson; D./G. Broo; Klas Hjort

title: Miniaturized biosensor platforms for early detection of neurodegenerative diseases and their potential for clinical translation
abstract: Neurodegenerative disorders (NDs), such as Alzheimer’s disease (AD), Parkinson’s disease (PD), and prion diseases, are defined by the gradual deterioration of neurons that frequently occurs prior to the onset of clinically observable symptoms. The early diagnosis of these conditions relies on analytical systems that are capable in detecting disease-related biomarkers at low concentrations within complex biological fluids. This analysis extensively evaluates miniaturized biosensor systems aimed at disease-specific biomarkers, such as amyloid-β and tau for Alzheimer’s disease, α-synuclein (α-syn) and DJ-1 for Parkinson’s disease, and prion protein isoforms for prion disorders. Electrochemical, optical, surface plasmon resonance, field-effect transistor, surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy, microfluidic lab-on-a-chip, portable, and wearable systems are assessed concerning their biorecognition methodologies, signal-transduction processes, linear ranges, detection thresholds, selectivity, sample matrices, and suitability for point-of-care applications. Recent research indicates that nanostructured sensing interfaces and microfluidic integration can improve analytical sensitivity, minimize sample needs, and facilitate biomarker identification in blood, plasma, cerebrospinal fluid, saliva, and other therapeutically pertinent matrices. However, remarkably low detection thresholds alone do not establish clinical significance. Biofouling, matrix influences, intricate production, prolonged stability, insufficient clinical validation, and the absence of standardized multicenter research persist in limiting clinical application. This review evaluates the development of biosensors for the diagnosis of neurodegenerative diseases towards miniaturized and portable systems based on current studies. It also comprehensively addresses the key limitations in the clinical validation, standardization, scalable production, and commercialization processes. Graphical abstract
authors: İnci Uludağ Anıl; Buse Sancakli; Nicole J. Jaffrezic-Renault; Hamdi Ben Halima; Mustafa Kemal Sezgintürk

title: Minimally Invasive In Vivo Fabrication of Multiscale Biohybrid Systems
abstract: Multiscale biohybrid systems integrating living materials with minimally invasive in vivo fabrication offer new opportunities for precise diagnosis, physiological monitoring, and tissue regeneration. This review provides a unified perspective on their design and therapeutic integration, organizing recent advances across multiscale material design, minimally invasive fabrication, spatiotemporal co-engineering, and functional applications. Three emerging principles are identified: multiscale coupling bridges material architectures with cellular and tissue responses; spatiotemporal coordination integrates precise in vivo construction with dynamic material and biological evolution; and sensing-regeneration feedback extends biohybrid systems from passive repair toward responsive therapeutic regulation. Building on these principles, we highlight machine learning-assisted material discovery, multi-site fabrication, and intelligent feedback control as key directions for developing adaptive, closed-loop therapeutic systems. Together, these insights provide design guidance for translating minimally invasive multiscale biohybrid systems toward next-generation patient-centered healthcare.
authors: Zhixing Ge; Yuji Gao; Elgene Chng Junyuan; Truong‐Son Dinh Le; Liang Lanfeng; Yu Zhang; Chwee Teck Lim

title: Modular Bio‐Integrated Materials and Devices for Advanced Theranostic Healthcare
abstract: Bio-integrated theranostic systems that combine sensing, analysis, interaction, and therapy are emerging as powerful platforms for personalized healthcare. Unlike conventional diagnostic or therapeutic devices, modular bio-integrated systems integrate body-conformal or implantable interfaces with analytical units, user-interaction platforms, and therapeutic modules to enable continuous monitoring, feedback-guided decision-making, and on-demand intervention. In this review, we summarize progress in modular bio-integrated theranostic systems (MBTS) from four functional perspectives. First, we discuss biophysical, biochemical, and multimodal sensing modules that provide physiological and molecular inputs across skin-interfaced, wound-integrated, ocular, oral, and implantable formats. We review analysis modules that convert sensor-derived signals into health-state assessments, risk estimates, and intervention guidance. Interactive interfaces and feedback modules are discussed, focusing on visual and graphical interfaces for data presentation and interactive feedback for user engagement and therapeutic response. Finally, programmable therapeutic modules for controlled drug delivery and nonpharmacological intervention are summarized, followed by biomedical implementations in drug delivery, neuromodulation, diabetes management, wound care, blood pressure regulation, and other healthcare scenarios. We further discuss engineering challenges related to module integration, bio-interface stability, power supply, data security, and cost-effective manufacturing. This review provides a modular framework for designing next-generation bio-integrated theranostic systems that connect sensing, analysis, interaction, and therapy within healthcare platforms.
authors: Zhenyou Ge; X Q Li; Bingbing Gao; Chwee Teck Lim; Yukun Ren

title: Modular construction of osteochondral organoids: Recapitulating gradients and microenvironment
abstract: In recent years, bone and cartilage organoid technology has attracted increasing attention and undergone rapid development, offering emerging approaches and broad prospects for osteoarthritis (OA) treatment, tissue engineering, regenerative medicine, and related fields. Despite the documented progress of bone and cartilage organoid models in structural biomimetic design, their limitation in the holistic reproduction of osteochondral unit, including interface gradient and physiological functions, remains a challenge for clinical application. Based on cutting-edge research, this review summarizes modular construction strategies of bone and cartilage organoids, targeting three types of signals in the osteochondral unit microenvironment: mechanical, metabolic, and immune. First, this review analyzes the microenvironment characteristics of the osteochondral unit, including the interface gradient and major signal pathways, then discusses the essential requirements for construction of osteochondral organoid. Then, based on different emphases, various osteochondral or cartilage organoid examples are classified and reviewed. Furthermore, this paper analyzes their advantages, bottlenecks, and feasibility, thereby outlining a design framework for modular organoids. Next, the technical pathways for functional coupling between modules are discussed, mainly including 3D bioprinting, organoid assembly, and microfluidic chips, in an attempt to provide solutions to the integrated challenge of osteochondral organoids. Then, the monitoring of multidimensional signals in organoids culture system is discussed. Finally, feasibility of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning in this field is discussed, with the aim to establish a closed-loop system for intelligent organoid culture.
authors: Zihan Xu; Yixing Ren; Xiaoming Li

title: Molecular point-of-care: technological evolution, clinical applications, and future perspectives
abstract: The landscape of clinical diagnostics is undergoing a fundamental shift from centralized laboratories toward decentralized point-of-care testing (POCT) models. Conventional molecular diagnostics often suffer from prolonged turnaround times, high operational costs, and a strict reliance on sophisticated infrastructure. To overcome these limitations, modern POCT platforms have deeply integrated advanced molecular techniques. These include diverse isothermal nucleic acid amplification methods (such as LAMP, RPA, and RCA) and highly specific CRISPR/Cas recognition systems. Furthermore, coupling these biochemical reactions with microfluidic chips and smartphone-based digital platforms has enabled fully automated, "sample-in, answer-out" diagnostic capabilities. This review systematically summarizes the technological evolution of these molecular POCT platforms. It highlights their transformative clinical applications across diverse fields, including infectious disease containment, early oncology screening, cardiovascular emergency triage, and metabolic disease management. Despite remarkable progress, several critical bottlenecks still prevent the widespread clinical translation of molecular POCT. These challenges include cross-interference in multiplexed detection, enzyme stability outside strict cold chains, high costs of core components, and the lack of tailored regulatory frameworks. Addressing these barriers via synthetic biology, robust system integration, and artificial intelligence is critical to advancing the core vision of delivering rapid, accessible, and precise healthcare solutions in resource-limited settings.
authors: Danfeng Zhang; Xin Cui; Ruijie Zhang; Wenlong Cai; Wang Li; Jichun Yang

title: Multi-Agent Scheduling of Instrument-Time for High-Throughput Palladium-Catalysed Cross-Coupling
abstract: NMR time and a shared liquid-handling robot are scarce, noisy and only partially observable, so the practical question is which experiment to run next on which instrument. Existing reaction-optimisation benchmarks measure budgets in experiments rather than instrumenthours, and they learn chemical feasibility only by paying for infeasible runs. We present CHASE, a centralised-training decentralised-execution scheduler with three coupled modules: a belief encoder (PEB) infers per-instrument throughput and channel health from local event histories and exchanges only low-bandwidth summaries; a chemistry feasibility gate (CFG) masks chemically impossible actions with a four-layer compatibility graph; and a counterfactual attribution module (CFA) converts delayed campaign reward into per-step credit through leave-one-experiment-out surrogate scoring. On the Buchwald–Hartwig (3,955 reactions) and Suzuki–Miyaura (5,760 nanomole-scale conditions) HTE datasets, the ten Olympus benchmarks and a plant-wide Tennessee Eastman process, CHASE reaches 94.1% best-found yield under a shared 60 instrument-hour budget, +3.3 points over the strongest same-setting baseline, attains 90% of the attainable optimum with 25.6% fewer experiments, and cuts infeasible actions to 0.7–1.6% across plate, flow and fault-injection settings.
authors: Yuhang Shao; Siqi Meng; Yutian Luo; Jiawei Tan; Chengyu He

title: Multi-mode droplet splitting on active-matrix digital microfluidics: quantitative boundaries and optimal sequential generation
abstract: Precise generation of microdroplets at picoliters to microliters scale is critical for advancing microfluidics technologies and precision life sciences research. Digital microfluidics enables programable individual droplet, however, there still lacks comprehensive characterization and analysis on optimal splitting modes, hindering its further application requiring extreme volume accuracy and splitting. Here, we report a systematic quantitative investigation of four droplet splitting strategies: symmetric splitting, asymmetric splitting, deformative splitting, squeezing, leveraging the high programmability advantage of large-scale active-matrix digital microfluidics. Droplet splitting is experimentally tested across varying droplet sizes, shapes, ratios and sub-droplet motion modes. Based on extensive experimental results, quantitative analysis is conducted to comprehensively characterize the splitting accuracy and effective ratio ranges. From these statistical results and optimal splitting modes, we establish an optimal sequential splitting decision framework. Aiming at precise generation for ultra-low-ratio sub-droplet through sequential splitting, the proposed framework can efficiently screen reasonable splitting paths from the combinatorial solution space. Ultra-low-ratio droplet generation at 0.78125% is realized, which is unattainable by any single-step method, with a cumulative accuracy of 1.05868 upon a target droplet of 12 nL. This work clarifies the quantitative performance boundaries of multi-mode droplet splitting strategies and demonstrates the capability of standardized optimal splitting sequence generation. These findings provide a theoretical and technical basis for customized multi-step droplet preparation and high-stability microfluidic manipulation.
authors: Chenxuan Hu; Hanbin Ma

title: Multimodal LLM-Assisted Diagnosis of Cryptic Failure Modes in High-Throughput Experimentation: A Case Study in Gold Nanorod Synthesis
abstract: Self-driving labs typically optimize experiments within a predefined design space. Yet high-throughput campaigns can fail for reasons outside this design space, in-cluding reagent state, stock solution quality, and handling history. Here, we present a case study of a five-plate high-throughput gold nanorod synthesis campaign in which a multimodal large language model (LLM) helped diagnose such cryptic failure modes. We used low-cost camera images for rapid assessment of seed and synthesis state, with UV–vis spectroscopy when the images were insufficient for failure diagnosis. The campaign included an abnormal seed batch, a visually plausible synthesis with hidden spectroscopic defects, and a plate-wide failed synthesis in which most wells showed weak spectra with a strong rise toward the near-infrared. In response, the LLM intervened by questioning the seed preparation step and reagent handling instead of optimizing the screened concentrations of silver nitrate and ascorbic acid. To quantify recovery, we defined a UV–vis spectral roughness metric based on local spectral interpolation across the synthesis grid. The final synthesis had the lowest roughness, Rspec = 0.636 compared with ∼ 0.772 for earlier successful runs, and the highest median longitudinal-window absorbance. Our results show the potential of multimodal LLMs upstream of autonomous optimization in self-driving labs to identify when an experiment has failed for reasons outside the nominal design space and when additional characterization is needed before optimization should continue.
authors: Riya Patel; Gabriela Briceno; Amirali Aghazadeh; Vida Jamali

title: Multimodal wearable biosensors in sports: integrating physical and chemical sensing for performance and health
abstract: Wearable technologies have emerged as essential tools for monitoring athletes’ performance and physiological states in real time. This review systematically examines advances in biosensing and wearable systems for sports applications, highlighting their design, sensing modalities, and integration strategies. Athlete tracking and data acquisition form the foundation for personalized training, injury prevention, and performance optimization. Biopotential sensors, including electrocardiography (ECG), electromyography (EMG), electroencephalography (EEG)/electroneurogram Electroneurography, and biopotential electrodes, provide insights into cardiac, muscular, and neural activity. Physical sensors, such as temperature, piezoresistive, piezoelectric, balance and acceleration, pressure, optical, and galvanic skin response (GSR) sensors, enable real-time assessment of movement, mechanical load, body posture, stress, and environmental interactions. Chemical sensors, including sweat and glucose sensors, facilitate non-invasive metabolic monitoring, supporting hydration and energy management. Integrated and hybrid biosensor systems combine multiple sensing modalities, offering comprehensive real-time feedback and personalized analytics for athletes. Despite these advances, challenges remain in sensor miniaturization, power efficiency, data accuracy, wireless communication, and user comfort. Future directions focus on artificial intelligence-driven data analysis, flexible and durable materials, multi-modal integration, and fully personalized wearable platforms. Collectively, wearable biosensing technologies present a transformative approach to sports monitoring, enabling enhanced performance evaluation, injury prevention, and long-term health management.
authors: Burhan Adıgüzel; Mansour Ghorbanpour; Begüm Sarac; Seydanur Yücer; Fatih Çiftçi

title: Multiscale mechanobiology of circulating tumor cells: microfluidics and atomic force microscopy
abstract: Cancer progression is shaped by coupled molecular, biochemical, and mechanical changes across multiple scales, from altered signaling and cytoskeletal organization to cellular deformation, adhesion, and metastatic dissemination. Circulating tumor cells (CTCs) are rare and heterogeneous in blood, occurring as single cells and multicellular clusters that provide access to evolving tumor phenotypes through liquid biopsy. Their apparent elasticity, deformability, adhesion, and viscoelastic behavior may reflect invasive potential, treatment response, and phenotypic state, while cytoskeletal proteins, membrane lipids, cell surface glycans, and receptors provide molecular context for these mechanical signatures. This review examines the complementary roles of microfluidics and atomic force microscopy (AFM) in multiscale CTC mechanobiology. Microfluidic platforms support label-free and affinity-based enrichment, capture, positioning, and recovery of viable cells. AFM provides localized measurements of apparent elasticity, deformation, adhesion, viscoelastic response, and nanoscale surface architecture in liquid, while functionalized probes enable molecular recognition and molecule-specific force measurements. We evaluate physical, affinity-based, cluster-preserving, open-space, and artificial intelligence-assisted microfluidic strategies together with reversible device assembly, automated AFM targeting, fluidic probes, advanced mapping modes, and treatment-response applications. Existing studies establish feasibility, including direct AFM measurements of individual patient-derived CTCs and automated analysis following microfluidic enrichment in model rare-cell mixtures. Clinical evidence remains limited, many integrated workflows rely on cultured cells or spiked samples, and within the literature identified in this review, direct AFM characterization of intact patient-derived CTC clusters was not found. Clinical translation will require confirmation of tumor identity, standardized acquisition, analysis, and reporting, increased throughput, statistical analysis that preserves the hierarchy of patients, cells, and force curves, and validation in independent patient cohorts. Integrated AFM-microfluidic platforms could extend CTC liquid biopsy beyond enumeration toward functional mechanobiological analysis relevant to metastasis, therapeutic response, and biomarker development.
authors: Ayoub Glia; Muhammedin Deliorman; Mohammad Ameen Qasaimeh
venue: Frontiers in Lab on a Chip Technologies

title: Multiscale wavelet Hurst analysis of pressure fluctuations in a jet impact negative pressure reactor
abstract: Abstract This work investigated the multiscale fractal dynamics of a jet impact‐negative pressure reactor (JI‐NPR) using an integrated wavelet‐Hurst methodology tailored to the JI‐NPR geometry. The analysis of pressure signals revealed a significant spatial diversity in the Hausdorff dimension (Dh). The negative pressure zone exhibited distinct spatial distribution characteristics of Dh compared to the slow flow zone, indicating that the turbulent sub‐atmospheric interaction resulted in characteristic flow complexity within the negative pressure zone. Two distinct Hurst exponent ( H ) regimes were identified: a persistent mode reflecting self‐similar flow patterns, and an anti‐persistent mode which at small scales reflects high‐frequency fluctuations yet re‐emerges at the largest scale (d8) in the negative‐pressure zone as low‐frequency vortex‐shedding structures. Furthermore, the evolution of the persistent H accurately captured hydrodynamic stability transitions. Dimensional convergence at the d4 scale served as a quantitative indicator of this transition. Through the parameter analysis, the targeted combination of wavelet and fractal analysis reveals flow dynamics specific to the coupled jet‐impingement and negative‐pressure environment. In a post‐hoc comparison, the regimes characterized by a persistent Hurst mode with H > 0.9 were found to coincide with the optimal operating conditions reported in our prior independently conducted trials. On this basis, the persistent Hurst exponent threshold is proposed as a candidate diagnostic indicator of favourable operating states, rather than as a validated efficiency criterion. The plausible rationale‐that persistent, self‐similar flow structures may reduce unnecessary turbulent dissipation relative to highly disordered states‐requires confirmation through future simultaneous measurement of pressure signals and process performance metrics.
authors: Fei Long; Yingying Dong; Zhongjun Li; Lingxing Hu; Facheng Qiu
venue: The Canadian Journal of Chemical Engineering

title: Nanofluid transport in Taylor bubble flows
abstract: Taylor bubble flows with nanoparticle suspensions are regularly encountered in non-isothermal chemical synthesis and microfluidics. Despite this, a complete mechanistic insight into the coupled thermal and hydrodynamic interactions remains unresolved. Here, a Eulerian-Lagrangian framework has been developed to address this, capturing two-way momentum, energy exchange, and nanoparticle interactions under non-isothermal conditions. We find that Brownian motion acts in two opposing ways, enhancing local particle-fluid energy exchange yet driving a thermophoretic drift away from the heated wall that strengthens as particle diameter is reduced below 100 nm. At particle volume fractions of $ϕ\sim 10^{-2}$, Taylor flow departs from the Nusselt scaling with dimensionless slug length, $\tilde{L}_s$, observed for particle-free flows. This coincides with alterations to bubble topology that co-benefit nanoparticle momentum and energy exchange with the carrier fluid. Examining both Poiseuille and Taylor flow problems, we observe contrasting, often opposing dimensionless heat transport behaviours, questioning the suitability of traditionally accepted mixture approaches. This work reveals that, in the visco-inertial regime ($Re > 500$), it is the interplay of hydrodynamic, Brownian, and interfacial forces, combined with the Taylor bubble and slug flow topology, which determine positive or negative $Nu$ outcomes. Interestingly, short-range particle forces at the liquid-gas interface work synergistically with the convective motion in the slug to alter local particle concentration and energy exchanges within downstream thin film and near-wall regions. The intensity of this convective flow was found to impact both slug and film transport phenomena, improving the redistribution of nanoparticles when $\tilde{L}_s \leq 1.6$ and with increasing $Re$.
authors: Fahad Al-Gburi; Faysal Khaleel; Yulong Ding; Jason Stafford

title: Nanomaterials in Solid-State Physics and Engineering: Synthesis Strategies, Structure-Property Relationships, and Emerging Applications
abstract: Nanomaterials often deliver impressive laboratory metrics, yet translation is weakened when the path from synthesis to operating-state behavior is poorly documented. This review asked whether performance claims could be traced consistently from controllable processing to verified structure, mechanism, function, and a stated translation boundary. Peer-reviewed literature published mainly from 2021 to 31 March 2026 was examined through a narrative review. During major revision, a structured OpenAlex and Crossref audit was added for operando and active-state characterization. The literature showed that size alone rarely determined performance. Surface chemistry, defects, interfaces, and process history often changed the outcome, and in many systems the functional state differed from the pristine or post-mortem structure. Translation problems were most visible when these changes were not connected to realistic measures of loading, yield, stability, or manufacturing compatibility. Stronger studies combined controlled processing with complementary characterization and measurements made under relevant operating conditions. They also made clear where the evidence stopped. Comparison across application areas showed markedly different levels of readiness, from manufacturing-scale evidence in a few device platforms to predominantly laboratory demonstrations in others. On this basis, the review treats the evidence chain as a practical traceability tool rather than a new materials theory and translates it into a domain-adaptable minimum evidence package for engineering claims.
authors: Thanh Van Nguyen
venue: Indonesian Journal of Modern Science and Technology

title: Nanoparticle-Based Drug Delivery Systems for Anticancer Therapy: Microenvironment-Driven Strategies, Advances, and Challenges
abstract: Cancer remains a major global health challenge, and nanoparticle-based drug delivery systems have emerged as a promising strategy for targeted cancer therapy. However, clinical translation is still limited by an incomplete understanding of how nanoparticles navigate the tumor microenvironment (TME) throughout the delivery process. This review presents an integrated, stage-by-stage framework for nanoparticle design that addresses the TME barriers encountered during systemic circulation, tumor-targeted enrichment, and drug release. During systemic circulation, PEGylation, hydrophilic polymer modification, cell membrane- or exosome-based biomimetic technologies, and biomolecular corona formation are employed to prolong circulation half-life. In the tumor-targeting stage, charge-reversal surfaces, ligand conjugation, ligand shielding, and tuning of physical properties enhance tumor accumulation and cellular internalization. For drug release, molecular and structural design enables intracellular responsive release, stepwise extracellular-to-intracellular release, and sequential release to distinct target cells. Beyond summarizing these strategies, we highlight the newly proposed active transport and retention (ATR) principle as a unifying mechanistic framework that explains how nanoparticles achieve tumor accumulation through active endothelial transport and retention via tumor component interactions. We further discuss translational barriers including complex fabrication, scalability hurdles, and biocompatibility constraints, and outline emerging solutions such as novel nanoparticle fabrication methods (microfluidics, turbulent jet, and microfluidic mixing), engineered biomimetic exosomes, organ-on-a-chip evaluation platforms, and AI-driven design screening. By connecting stage-specific design strategies to the ATR framework, this review offers a mechanistic foundation for the rational design of next-generation nanomedicines.
authors: Mengxin Ban; Sifang Zhao; Ziyu Liu; Lingling Zhao

title: New Era of Biosensors - Integration of Artificial Intelligence and Technology in Healthcare
abstract: The connection between biological systems and electronic devices has developed beyond simple glucose tests or pregnancy checks. It is now a transformative area in modern science. This chapter looks at the “New Era of Biosensors,” where molecular biology, materials science, and information technology come together to provide a clear view of our integration of Artificial intelligence in biosensors. We follow the transition from large, lab-based equipment to decentralized, patient-focused diagnostics. By moving the process from hospital beds to homes, these technologies change healthcare from a reactive approach to a proactive approach. Three advances enable this shift. Microfluidics and nanotechnology bring lab-grade sensitivity to chip-scale devices. Epidermal electronics maintain signal quality on flexible, skin-conformable substrates. Artificial intelligence removes noise from real-world recordings, identifies patterns that precede clinical symptoms, and tunes predictions to individual baselines. Translation from prototype to clinical deployment remains difficult. This chapter examines the technical, regulatory, and ethical barriers to implementation, including data privacy under Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) and General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), algorithmic bias arising from non-representative training data, and power constraints in implantable and energy-harvesting devices. Drawing on clinical applications such as smart bandages and remote cardiac monitoring, the chapter outlines how continuous, AI-supported sensing can shift healthcare from episodic consultation toward sustained physiological monitoring and earlier intervention.
authors: Sagar Pralhad Kanekar; Sahil Vaghole; Aarya Kamat; Anirjit Kartha

title: Next-Generation Liposomes for Drug Delivery: Engineering Strategies and Therapeutic Applications
abstract: Liposomes are versatile nanocarrier systems widely investigated for pharmaceutical drug delivery because of their biocompatibility, biodegradability, and ability to encapsulate both hydrophilic and lipophilic drugs. Since their discovery in the 1960s, liposomes have evolved into advanced nanomedicine platforms with applications in cancer therapy, antimicrobial treatment, gene delivery, vaccines, and personalised medicine. Advances in lipid chemistry, nanotechnology, and pharmaceutical engineering have enabled the development of long-circulating, targeted, stimuli-responsive, and multifunctional liposomal formulations. Several liposome-based products have received regulatory approval, demonstrating their clinical and translational potential. However, challenges related to formulation stability, encapsulation efficiency, large-scale manufacturing, storage, and regulatory requirements remain. Emerging approaches, including microfluidics, artificial intelligence-assisted formulation development, precision nanomedicine, and personalised drug delivery, are expected to address these limitations. This review discusses the historical development, structural characteristics, classification, preparation methods, therapeutic applications, clinical status, and future perspectives of liposomal drug delivery systems, with particular emphasis on recent innovations driving the development of next-generation liposomal therapeutics. Keywords: Liposome, Nanomedicine,Drug Delivery System, Phospholipid Vesicles, Targeted Drug Delivery, Nanotechnology, Lipid Nanocarriers, Controlled Drug Release.
authors: Shubham Sachdeva; Vikramjit Singh; Kaur Harwinder; Fairy Fairy; Jitender Singh
venue: Journal of Drug Delivery and Therapeutics

title: Noise-Aware Bayesian Optimization for Precision Improvement of Micro-Volume Liquid Handling in In Vitro Diagnostics
abstract: Micro-volume dispensing precision is critical for in vitro diagnostic (IVD) analyzers. We present a noise-aware Bayesian optimization framework that minimizes the within-run coefficient of variation (CV) of a 50 μL dispensing process by optimizing five pump-control variables. Each setting was tested in five independent batches; the group mean CV was used as the response, and the squared group standard error was supplied to an automatic relevance determination Gaussian process as observation-noise variance. From 33 tested combinations, the lowest measured mean CV was 0.266% (SD, 0.044%). An engineering-rounded setting then achieved 0.270% (SD, 0.050%), an 81.8% relative reduction versus engineer-selected settings (1.480%, SD, 0.083%). In a retrospective surrogate-based replay, the noise-aware strategy reached CV < 1.5% in 2.8 ± 1.2 iterations, compared with 4.1 ± 2.0, 6.5 ± 3.4, and 11.3 ± 5.1 for homoscedastic GP, standard GP, and random search. Deionized water, diluted human serum, and 5% bovine serum albumin all yielded mean CVs below 0.45%. The method thus identified a repeatable low-CV operating region with a limited physical-experiment budget; prospective algorithmic comparisons and multi-instrument validation remain necessary.
authors: Lihao Bai

title: On-board International Space Station Verification of Autonomous Emulsification Lab-on-Chip Payload: TIGERS-X Project
abstract: Abstract Sustained deep-space exploration under space programs places critical constraints on pharmaceutical and nutritional resupply, motivating fluid-processing systems, including emulsification, that can operate reliably in microgravity. Conventional terrestrial emulsification relies on high-shear, buoyancy-assisted processes unavailable in free fall, while passive, capillary-driven static mixers offer a compact, low-power alternative better suited to spaceflight constraints. This paper reports the design, ground verification, and on-orbit validation of TIGERS-X, a low-cost, teleoperated lab-on-chip experiment cube for the International Space Station (ISS). Ground testing, including chemical safety, electromagnetic compatibility, and structural verification, confirmed compliance with ISS pressurized-payload requirements. TIGERS-X uses multi-channel Tesla-valve microfluidic devices and optical diagnostics to observe oil-water mixing and emulsification behavior, operating under ground control via YAMCS-based command and telemetry with no astronaut interaction required beyond installation and removal. Across a 10-day flight campaign, TIGERS-X returned near-real-time video of fluid behavior under sustained microgravity, resolving a duration and environment inaccessible to prior parabolic-flight studies. Quantitative colorimetric analysis revealed substantial, geometry-dependent oil-water phase redistribution within short microfluidic channel lengths, extending prior ground- and parabolic-flight-based findings to realistic orbital conditions. These results establish TIGERS-X as a validated, accessible platform for microgravity fluid science, with potential extension to more complex biological applications such as cell culture systems in future missions.
authors: Saran Seehanam; Thakdanai Sirisombat; Rattanawalee Tobsri; Warisara Boonrueng; Potiwat Ngamkajornwiwat; Witsaroot Sripumkhai; Pattaraluck Pattamang; Wares Chancharoen

title: Ontology-enabled neuro-symbolic closed-loop control of laser powder bed fusion
abstract: A geometry-conditioned, neuro-symbolic closed-loop architecture is proposed for laser powder bed fusion, in which an ontology aligned with established standards and domain vocabularies operates inside the control loop and couples symbolic reasoning with statistical learning to set the targets of a constraint-aware predictive controller. The ontology links the process objectives and constraints to the signals a controller can observe. A description-logic reasoner selects the active constraints, which are converted into references and bounds enforced on each scan. The demonstrated case is overhang dross: a quality limit on the melt pool depth, which governs quality but is not measured in the present formulation, is mapped through a geometry- and power-dependent depth-to-width ratio onto a bound on the observable width. The ratio and its empirical uncertainty are estimated by a neural ensemble. The reasoner classifies each upcoming feature and selects the active constraints, adding a lack-of-fusion floor at overhangs and an extrapolation guard when the overhang angle falls below the calibrated range or uncertainty is high. It runs only when the symbolic context changes, and the inferred classification remains cached between changes. In an Eagar–Tsai surrogate calibrated to the NIST AM-Bench benchmark for IN625, the architecture reduced the mean total defect count at 45° from 6.0 to 6.2 tracks for the geometry-conditioned baselines to 3.2 per build and avoided their shift from dross to lack of fusion. Ablation attributed the ontology contribution to explicit representation of constraint applicability, inference, and consistency checking rather than separate numerical gains. The results establish architectural feasibility. Machine-specific calibration of the depth-to-width relation and physical validation are the principal next steps.
authors: Gisuk Hong; Jaebong Cho; Hyunbo Cho

title: Open-well compartmentalized microfluidic devices for reconstituting brain region connectivity
abstract: Microfluidics-based in vitro models provide powerful platforms for investigating disease mechanisms and screening therapeutic compounds. However, fabrication protocols for microfluidic devices that enable precise control over the directional connectivity between three-dimensional tissue models remain limited, restricting their applications in studying inter-regional interactions. In this study, we present an open-well polydimethylsiloxane microfluidic device that enables unidirectional axon connectivity between region-specific spheroids. We show that the combination of axon-diode microchannels and time-delayed spheroid plating effectively suppresses reverse projections and biases activity propagation. Using human midbrain and striatal spheroids, we further demonstrate that the platform reconstitutes 6-OHDA-induced dopaminergic axonal degeneration in vitro.
authors: Mamoru Sakaibara; Hideaki Yamamoto; Sota Endo; Kotaro Murata; Shigeo Sato; Yoshito Masamizu; Kaneyasu Nishimura; Ayumi Hirano-Iwata

title: Opportunities and Challenges of Generative AI for Cybersecurity in Sub-Saharan African Organizations: A Systematic Literature Review
abstract: Generative AI (GAI) is increasingly used and studied across various fields in different countries; however, its implications for cybersecurity in Africa remain underexplored. This study investigates the opportunities and challenges of GAI on cybersecurity within the Sub-Saharan African organizations through a systematic literature review. Peer-reviewed journal articles and conference proceedings papers were retrieved from five databases, yielding 51 relevant publications, which were synthesized. The literature review was guided by the PRISMA flow diagram to ensure a structured review. Thematic analysis informed a taxonomy of GAI-related challenges and opportunities, aligned with the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0. Key challenges include the absence of context-specific governance frameworks, technical and model-related limitations, data quality issues and people-related challenges. It was found that the reliance of GAI models on a few dominant languages limits their effectiveness in cybersecurity tasks such as threat detection within Sub-Saharan Africa’s multilingual context. Conversely, GAI presents opportunities to mitigate the region’s cybersecurity skills shortage by automating functions such as cybersecurity awareness and training, log analysis and continuous auditing. The findings provide valuable insights for policymakers, practitioners, and governments seeking to harness GAI for cybersecurity in Sub-Saharan Africa, while also highlighting avenues for future research.
authors: Thembekile O. Mayayise

title: Optimal strategies for the growth of dual-seeded lattice structures
