title: Role of Agentic Artificial Intelligence in Anatomical and Clinical Laboratory
abstract: Background: Laboratory medicine is transitioning from passive machine learning models and static decision-support algorithms toward agentic artificial intelligence (AI)—systems capable of goal-directed autonomy, environmental perception, multi-step reasoning, dynamic tool utilization, and iterative self-correction. This review synthesizes the operational frameworks and clinical implications of agentic AI across anatomical pathology and clinical laboratories (Biochemistry, hematology, microbiology, and molecular diagnostics). In anatomical pathology, multi-agent frameworks optimize whole-slide imaging workflows through adaptive region-of-interest navigation, autonomous pre-screening, automated biomarker quantification, and integrated multi-modal report generation. In clinical laboratories, agentic architectures streamline pre-analytic specimen quality verification, orchestrate real-time delta-check evaluations, resolve atypical hematologic cell flagging, guide microbiology culture plate selection, and automate complex next-generation sequencing variant curation. By interconnecting Laboratory Information Systems, digital instrumentation, and electronic health records, multi-agent networks bridge data silos to enable cross-disciplinary diagnostic synthesis. Despite substantial gains in diagnostic throughput, turnaround times, and quality assurance, clinical implementation is constrained by computational overhead, potential error propagation in reasoning chains, data privacy, and the risk of automated "hallucinations". Addressing these challenges necessitates robust human-in-the-loop oversight, standardized audit trails for decision chains, and evolving regulatory compliance frameworks (FDA, CE-IVDR). Agentic AI represents a paradigm shift from narrow analytical tools to collaborative diagnostic teammates, positioned to elevate precision medicine and operational efficiency while redefining the roles of pathologists and laboratory scientists.
authors: Vibhav Nigam; Atulya; Nidhi Mathur; Dilutpal Sharma

title: Scalable Arrayed T‐cell CRISPR Screening in Autologous Tumor Co‐cultures to Prioritize Combination Partners for T‐cell Engagers
abstract: T-cell-engaging therapies (TCE) have shown clinical promise in hematologic malignancies, but the T-cell-intrinsic determinants of TCE-mediated cytotoxicity remain incompletely defined. This is in part because functional studies in patient-derived primary samples have been technically challenging. Here, we describe a flow cytometry-based arrayed CRISPR knockout screening platform to prioritize regulators of TCE-mediated cytotoxicity in suspension tumor cells using patient-derived, autologous chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) samples. The principal advantage of this system is the use of matched T cells and tumor cells from the same patient, retaining patient-matched effector-target pairings that are not captured in donor-mismatched or cell line-based assays. In this workflow, CD3+ T cells isolated from viably frozen CLL peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC) are expanded and edited for 2 days using arrayed Cas9 ribonucleoprotein nucleofection. TCE-mediated cytotoxicity was assessed in a 72-hr, feeder-supported co-culture assay using patient-matched CLL tumor cells in the presence of CD20×CD3 TCE. In the current implementation, the workflow is organized into modules that accommodate up to 96 arrayed perturbations, with technical replicates evaluated under TCE and control conditions. Because perturbations remain physically indexed in an arrayed format, the workflow is amenable to parallelization and laboratory automation, providing a path toward substantially larger targeted screens. This platform therefore provides a scalable framework for mechanistic studies and combination-target discovery for TCE therapies. © 2026 The Author(s). title: Scalable Fabrication of Chemically Stabilized Gelatin Hydrogel Fibers by Thermal Drawing
abstract: ABSTRACT Gelatin represents a promising hydrogel fiber matrix for drug delivery, tissue engineering, and neural interfaces due to its inherent biocompatibility, biodegradability, and mechanical adaptability. Yet, existing soft‐material fabrication methods typically constrain fiber length, aspect ratio, throughput, and structural complexity, thereby restricting the capabilities of these fibers. Here, we introduce a multimaterial thermal drawing platform capable of continuously producing gelatin hydrogel fibers with lengths reaching tens of meters. Instead of relying on conventional synthetic crosslinkers, we leverage the Maillard reaction—adapted from food engineering—to induce in situ crosslinking under the heat generated during drawing. Guided by comprehensive rheological analyses, a moderate incubation step ensures a stable viscous flow regime essential for uninterrupted fiber production. This approach enables control over swelling and mechanical properties of hydrogel formulations, which exhibit elastic moduli in the tens to hundreds of kilopascals range and ultimate strains exceeding 100%. The hydrogel fibers can incorporate and gradually release therapeutic agents and generate low‐molecular‐weight species following collagenase exposure in vitro. By relying exclusively on naturally derived or naturally occurring constituents, the method circumvents the biocompatibility concerns associated with synthetic crosslinkers. The scalability and versatility of this fabrication platform open new design opportunities for hydrogel fibers tailored to diverse biomedical applications.
authors: Chaoqun Dong; Bastien Schyrr; Stella Laperrousaz; Hritwick Banerjee; Andreas Leber; Fabien Sorin

title: Scale‐Down Platforms for Process‐Oriented Enzyme Screening Using Microfluidics
abstract: Enzyme screening platforms are typically evaluated based on their throughput and analytical performance rather than their ability to mimic the conditions encountered at large scale. In bioreactors, enzymes experience gradients in substrate concentration, oxygen availability, pH, temperature, and interfacial exposure, caused by imperfect mixing and multiphase operation. These gradients affect both enzyme activity and stability, yet they are rarely incorporated into the assays used to select biocatalysts. Traditionally, a variant is chosen based on its performance under static, well-mixed laboratory conditions, yet those conditions do not necessarily represent the process conditions it must eventually perform under. Microfluidic devices can in principle recreate process-relevant conditions at a small scale since these devices offer precise control over the flow, residence time, and multiphase contact. Yet most current platforms are not built to mimic the scale-down process-derived conditions. Here, we assess current microfluidic tools against this process-relevant conditions and outline how modular designs can be combined into sequential screening platforms that generate the conditions in a bioreactor, for early-stage biocatalyst selection.

title: Scientific and methodological foundations for teaching physicochemical analysis methods in continuous chemical education: a scoping review
abstract: Background Rapid technological advancement, digitalization of analytical instrumentation, and the growing demand for interdisciplinary competence have significantly transformed the role of analytical chemistry in science and industry. These changes necessitate a systematic reconsideration of how physicochemical analysis methods are taught within continuous chemical education. Objective This scoping review aimed to map and systematize the structural components of modern analytical chemistry education, identify dominant pedagogical approaches, and conceptualize their functional interrelationships within an integrated educational framework. Design/methods The study was conducted as a scoping review in accordance with PRISMA-ScR guidelines. A comprehensive search was performed in Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, ACS Publications, SpringerLink, and RSCI (eLIBRARY.ru), covering publications from 1975 (the earliest eligible record retrieved) to 2024. Eligible studies addressed pedagogical, curricular, or methodological aspects of teaching analytical chemistry or physicochemical analysis methods. Extracted data were analyzed using qualitative thematic synthesis and conceptual mapping to identify recurring educational components and trends. Results The analysis revealed a consistent shift from method-centered instruction toward competence-oriented and system-based educational models. The most frequently reported components included integration of theoretical principles with laboratory practice, problem-based and research-oriented learning, incorporation of digital tools and chemometrics, emphasis on metrology and data interpretation, and increasing attention to sustainability and green analytical chemistry. The evidence indicates a transition from isolated presentation of analytical techniques to structured training focused on analytical thinking, decision-making, and interpretation of complex data. Conclusions Modern analytical chemistry education is evolving toward an integrated, interdisciplinary, and competence-driven model that prioritizes conceptual understanding, information processing, and real-world problem solving. The structural framework identified in this review may support curriculum development, modernization of laboratory courses, and alignment of educational programs with contemporary scientific and industrial demands.

title: Self-aggregated photo-heterostructures enhancing fluorescence for cancer diagnosis and treatment monitoring
abstract: Semiconductor zinc oxide (ZnO) nanostructures as classic photonic materials have sparked the development of low-cost, high-performance fluorescence sensors; however, their scalable clinical applications remain hampered by inadequate sensitivity. Here, we engineer a high-curvature photo-heterostructure aggregate-enhanced fluorescence (PAEF) sensor based on bubble-scaffolded ZnO nanorods. Leveraging synergistic evanescent field coupling and self-aggregation of photo-heterostructures, PAEF sensor streamlines efficient isolation (~90%) and ultrasensitive profiling of tumor extracellular vesicles (EVs) in a single assay, achieving sensitivity <10 EVs/μL (104-fold better than ELISA) without additional amplification, outperforming most state-of-the-art EV fluorescence assays. This self-sufficient sensor enables accurate monitoring of targeted therapeutic efficacy in mouse xenograft models via simultaneous dual-marker readout. We further show its clinical utility in hepatocellular carcinoma diagnosis with ≥96% accuracy (≥98% specificity) in two cohorts (n = 146), improving dynamic monitoring of surgical treatment responses, particularly in alpha-fetoprotein-negative patients. This work provides a cost-effective ultrasensitive liquid biopsy tool advancing non-invasive cancer diagnosis. Fluorescent detection approaches often require specialist equipment or have limited sensitivity. Here, the authors develop a bubble-scaffolded zinc oxide nanorod photo heterostructure aggregate for fluoresce enhancement demonstrating application for detection of circulating extracellular vesicles.

title: Self-buoyant cell-spheroid culture programming multi-spheroid assembly
abstract: Tempo-spatially controlled culture and assembly of cellular spheroids are fundamental in engineering tissue-like assembloids for scalable application, yet remain a technical challenge. Here, we show self-buoyant culture of cell spheroids and programmable assembly of multi-spheroid by microbubbles in a high-throughput, external field-free and miniaturized format. This approach allows one-step engineering of biocompatible cell-adhesive buoyancy interface that lifts the self-adaptive levitation growth of reliable one-drop-one-spheroid in an array without requiring any external fields. Using this self-floating spheroidal microarray, we find that a facile droplet 'kiss' facilitates the buoyancy-driven ultrafast transfer (∼1 s) of spheroids between top-down adjacent droplets, thus achieving rapid spheroid relocation, media exchange, and drug administration in parallel. Such a self-buoyant approach allows programmable horizontal/vertical bioassembly and enhanced fusion of homo/heterogeneous multi-spheroids into different "buoyantoid" patterns via sequential flash transfer along droplet array. This self-powered design provides a promising tool to enable mass production and smart manipulation of encoded assembloids for precision medicine, tissue engineering and high-throughput drug screening.
authors: Yuanhang Xiang; Binqi Wei; Yueyang Sun; Weifeng Liu; Hui Zhao; Xiaojie Qin; Changfeng Zhu; Xinchun Li; Fan Yang

title: Semantic Representation for Agentic Self-Play in Automated Laboratories
abstract: Navigating complex, high-dimensional biological search spaces necessitates scalable physical and computational intelligence to explore beyond local optima through iterative self-play across ideation, experimentation, and automation. Translating experimental designs into reliable physical execution remains bottlenecked by static laboratory automation and unmodeled physical variability. To address this, we introduce VERified Infrastructure for Discovery Laboratories, or VERID, a foundational infrastructure designed to bridge the gap between the high-level reasoning of artificial intelligence (AI) agents and complex, error-prone physical realities of wet labs. VERID is a persistent, high-fidelity semantic digital twin of the laboratory workcell that provides four core services: queryable introspection for agentic reasoning, time-compressed simulation for protocol validation, comprehensive trace persistence for a complete scientific record, and a framework for safe execution. We present three case studies using aqueous dye and deionized water mixtures to validate the optical and fluidic foundations of VERID. These studies demonstrate how VERID enables pre-emptive detection of critical errors in experimental protocols, stateful mid-run error recovery and post-hoc identification of subtle physical failures. The simulation functions as a discrete accounting engine, allowing agents to safely and inexpensively explore experimental designs in silico and refine experimental strategies through iterative self-play. VERID also captures structured multimodal experimental data for downstream analysis, knowledge mining and agent training. We argue that this semantic layer is an essential prerequisite for deploying autonomous agents in the biochemical and biomedical sciences, ensuring data integrity, operational safety, and paving the way for tackling previously intractable grand challenges in biology.

title: Silicon Photonics and Optically Controlled Microrobotics at the Limit English Introduction and Research Abstract This monograph asks whether silicon-photonic chips can create, observe, communicate, and close control around microscale agents with lower total burden than magnetic, wired, mechanical, microfluidic, or external-optical alternatives. It replaces impressive motion with a complete evidence chain from the commanded chip field to terminal task quality, thermal and photochemical exposure, recovery, and independent replay. Optical control is valuable only when usable control bandwidth and tracking success remain meaningful after coupling loss, absorbed heat, alignment, compute, calibration, packaging, missed agents, and failed recovery are counted. Unsafe exposure, runaway motion, lost identity, irreversible material change, corrupted command ancestry, or missing evidence are hard vetoes. Research architecture The PDF contains thirty gold derivations, eighty-two chapters with five single-page sections each, and two hundred detailed one-page Research Gates. Every derivation links to chapter, experiment, and Gate corridors. Every chapter opens with its governing formula. Fixed quotas for Easter-Egg Equations and Phoenix Answer Embryos are not used. Closed-loop multi-agent qualification: Join estimation latency constrained control identity occlusion collision recovery and independent task readout. The experiment compares integrated optical, external optical, magnetic, and wired control on identical path following, sensing, transport, and safe-stop tasks. title: Silk Fibroin-Based Flexible Electronics: A Mesoscopic Pathway Toward Human–Machine Interconnection
abstract: Silk fibroin, a natural textile material spun by silkworms over millennia, is emerging as a transformative platform for integrating human intelligence with artificial intelligence. Its core innovation lies in the meso-functionalization strategy, which precisely programs protein refolding and hierarchical assembly. This strategy groundbreakingly resolves the long-standing performance paradox among biocompatibility, mechanical compliance, and high-fidelity signal acquisition in bioelectronic interfaces, thereby providing a solution that is difficult to achieve with other material systems. This transformation elevates the traditional fiber into a programmable electronic material, capable not only of conformal and seamless skin contact but also of constructing dynamic conductive networks, and even pioneering the fabrication of neuromorphic memristors that emulate synaptic plasticity. Furthermore, silk fibroin systems, reshaped through meso-engineering, are poised to catalyze a novel paradigm for deep integration between biological systems and artificial intelligence. When coupled with AI-driven intelligent analytics and closed-loop feedback control, the system can decode human physiological states in real time into machine-interpretable command signals, while simultaneously delivering adaptive regulatory responses back to the body. This bidirectional interface breaks through the conventional boundaries of human–machine interaction, with application prospects spanning frontier domains such as wearable health monitoring, invasive brain–computer interfaces, and cognitive augmentation technologies. Ultimately, while honoring its heritage as a natural textile, silk fibroin opens a pathway toward deep biointegration that is both sustainable and exceptionally biocompatible. Along this pathway, ancient material wisdom collides with future artificial intelligence to spark synergistic innovation, ultimately empowering human intelligence to reach new heights through human–machine co-evolution.

title: Sliding rail-enabled capillary flow control on μPADs for programmable fluid delivery.
abstract: Precise control of fluid transport is critical for paper-based microfluidic analytical devices (μPADs), especially in point-of-care testing (POCT) applications involving multistep reactions and timed reagent delivery. Here, we propose a simple yet versatile strategy to regulate capillary flow on μPADs by overlaying a film above a paper strip as a sliding rail for liquid samples. By systematically investigating the surface wettability of the sliding rail and its distance (0.1-2.4 mm) from the NC paper strip, we demonstrate that flow velocity on μPADs can be efficiently modulated through geometric control and surface modification. The influence of the width of sliding rails is also investigated. For hydrophilic sliding rails, increasing the width of film will accelerate flow velocity, whereas for hydrophobic sliding rails, narrower film widths yield higher flow velocity. Furthermore, we use a three-branch μPAD to show that both sequential and synchronized fluid arrival can be achieved by fine-tuning gap distance and paper strip width. In addition, a proof-of-concept delay valve implemented by introducing a continuous hydrophilic sliding rail above the segmented NC paper strips is successfully validated. A 1 mm interval located at various positions of μPADs will lead to different time delays. Beyond flow control, the sliding rail also enables localized droplet delivery and transport using a Janus hydrophobic-hydrophilic film with defined apertures. This platform supports sequential and parallel reagent delivery, allowing chemical reactions on-chip. The feasibility of this approach is validated through precipitation reactions, colorimetric reactions, and an enzymatic colorimetric glucose assay, which exhibits a strong correlation (R2 = 0.9980) between gray intensity and glucose concentration under controlled laboratory conditions, suggesting its potential for quantitative applications in high-concentration samples. Overall, this work introduces a highly adaptable and fabrication-friendly μPAD platform with rapid flow tuning and multifunctional reaction capability. The mechanical support and alignment structure (3D-printed frame and spacers) are reusable across experiments, while the paper strips and surface-modified films are single-use consumables to ensure reproducible flow performance. This offers a powerful solution for efficient POCT applications and paper-based microfluidic systems.
authors: Shi Y, Zhong J, Li H, Chen H, Zhang H, Chu LT, Lin M, Guo W.

title: Smart materials for wound care: from passive dressings to autonomous bioelectronic systems
abstract: Background Chronic and infected wounds remain a major clinical challenge because of persistent inflammation, hypoxia, microbial biofilms, and dysregulated wound microenvironments. Conventional dressings provide passive protection but cannot monitor pathological changes or deliver targeted therapy. Smart wound dressings (SWDs), including stimuli-responsive hydrogels, bioelectronic interfaces, wearable sensors, and closed-loop systems, have emerged as multifunctional platforms capable of real-time monitoring and therapeutic intervention. Although preclinical studies consistently demonstrate antimicrobial efficacy, microenvironment regulation, and accelerated healing, particularly in diabetic and infected wounds, clinical translation remains limited. Objective To determine whether SWDs integrating sensing, biosignal interpretation, or responsive therapeutic functions improve wound healing, infection control, microenvironment regulation, or diagnostic accuracy compared with conventional passive dressings in preclinical and clinical wound models. Methods A structured literature search of PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus identified studies published between January 2018 and June 2026 following PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Eligible studies evaluated integrated sensing, wound microenvironment monitoring, stimuli-responsive therapy, bioelectronic actuation, or closed-loop control. Data on sensing modalities, biomarkers, therapeutic mechanisms, healing outcomes, antimicrobial performance, and engineering characteristics were extracted. Owing to substantial heterogeneity in materials, sensing technologies, biomarkers, and outcome measures, findings were synthesized narratively. Study quality was assessed qualitatively, and certainty of evidence was evaluated using a GRADE-informed approach. Results Of 2143 records screened, 312 studies met the inclusion criteria (298 preclinical and 14 clinical). Because many eligible studies reported overlapping technologies and outcomes, only 128 representative studies were cited to provide a concise synthesis of the evidence. Preclinical studies consistently demonstrated enhanced antimicrobial activity, regulation of pH, reactive oxygen species, oxygenation, and moisture, and accelerated healing in diabetic and infected wound models. Stimuli-responsive hydrogels enabled controlled therapeutic release, while nanozyme-enhanced systems improved oxygenation and reduced inflammation. Wearable, microfluidic, and bioelectronic platforms enabled continuous biomarker monitoring, electrical stimulation, and closed-loop therapeutic intervention, with machine learning improving wound classification and prediction of complications. Across representative studies, SWDs improved wound closure by 20–65%, reduced bacterial burden by 1–4 log units, and outperformed conventional dressings in regulating the wound microenvironment. However, clinical evidence is limited to small feasibility studies, and no controlled trials have demonstrated that continuous monitoring or closed-loop therapy independently improves healing outcomes. Limitations Evidence is dominated by heterogeneous preclinical studies, limiting quantitative meta-analysis. Sensor stability, calibration, biofouling, mechanical durability, and regulatory approval remain major barriers to clinical translation. In addition, standardized biomarker thresholds, clinical workflow integration, and long-term usability have not been established. The review was not prospectively registered, non-English studies were excluded, and publication bias may have influenced the findings.
authors: John H. T. Luong; Aharon Gedanken

title: Smartphone-based flow-controlled μPAD for automated nitrite determination.
abstract: We report a smartphone-based microfluidic platform for automated nitrite determination using a paper colourimetric assay. The system combines a V-shaped microfluidic paper-based analytical device (μPAD), a wireless electronic module for capacitive flow monitoring and thermal actuation, and a custom Android application that coordinates the measurement sequence and processes the captured image. Fluid arrival at the sensing zone is identified from changes in capacitance, which trigger the heating step required to collapse a NIPAM-based hydrogel reservoir and release sulfanilic acid from the hydrogel reservoir. Images are acquired under ambient lighting conditions and analysed by an image-processing algorithm that includes circle detection, saturation-value (SV)-based pixel selection, and colour correction using in-frame black and white references. Calibration with standard nitrite solutions showed that the platform achieved a limit of detection (LOD) of 7.63 × 10<sup>-6</sup> M (0.35 mg L<sup>-1</sup> as NO<sub>2</sub><sup>-</sup>) after colour correction, improving by about 17% with respect to the uncorrected response. The platform also showed good repeatability (CV < 6% at 10<sup>-4</sup> M) and consistent behaviour when tested with two different smartphones and several lighting conditions. Analysis of tap water and marine samples gave results in agreement with the reference method at the 95% confidence level. The platform combines automated fluid handling, thermally triggered reagent release, and adaptive image-based quantification in a portable format for nitrite analysis outside the laboratory.

title: Soft bioelectronics for wireless drug delivery: programmable, minimally invasive and closed-loop therapeutics
abstract: Soft bioelectronics is reshaping drug delivery from passive dosing to programmable, tissue-interfaced therapeutics. This Review examines the co-design of soft materials, wireless power, drug reservoirs, release mechanisms and feedback control for wearable and minimally invasive implantable therapeutic systems. We organize the field around key constraints including controllability, reversibility, payload capacity, dosing precision, drug stability and feedback latency, guiding the development of adaptive closed-loop drug delivery platforms for clinical translation.
authors: Feng Zhang; 孙富昌; Zheng Yan

title: Soil-on-chip for bioremediation studies in PAH-polluted soils: new insights into fungi-bacteria interactions and pollutant dynamics
abstract: Bioremediation of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) by fungi and bacteria is a sustainable and cost-effective approach for the depollution of soils. However, considering the complexity of soil matrix involving a wide range of parameters, the mechanisms by which microorganisms take up contaminants may vary depending on its composition and endogenous microbial communities. We used a compartmentalized microfluidic device in a soil-on-chip approach to study the bioremediation mechanisms of benzo[a]pyrene (B[a]P) adsorbed on soil-mimicking matrices and real soil particles. These microsystems were observed using confocal microscopy to investigate, at a cellular level, the desorption of B[a]P from soil and its internalization by fungi, either alone or in co-culture with bacteria. Rapidly after the fungal hyphae came in contact with the polluted particles, cellular labelling corresponding to B[a]P was observed, implying that the contaminant was taken up by the fungus. Cellular labelling enabled the localization of pollutant storage sites within model bacteria. Observations about mycelium influence on B[a]P transport and bacterial mobility at microscale were considered alongside macroscopic experiments. Results of this study demonstrate the ability of microorganisms to desorb hydrophobic organic pollutants adsorbed onto soil particles and highlight the potential of microfluidic devices to investigate PAH biodegradation in soils.
authors: Salomé Bertone; Léna Rasse; Fabrice Alliot; Sylvie Collin; Anne Le Goff; Antoine Fayeulle

title: Stability and lipolysis of W/O HIPEs under gastrointestinal conditions: Effects of fluid dynamics in static and microfluidic models
abstract: Water-in-oil high internal phase emulsions (W/O HIPEs) have potential applications in functional foods and nutraceuticals as replacements for conventional fats. Although structural characteristics influence lipid digestion, the impact of structural organization in W/O HIPEs, particularly those structured with vegetable waxes, remains poorly understood. This study evaluated the digestion of W/O HIPEs stabilized with polyglycerol polyricinoleate (PGPR), sunflower wax (SW), and hydrolyzed sunflower wax (HSW) under static and semi-dynamic (microchip) in vitro intestinal digestion conditions. Fresh PGPR- HIPEs exhibited a bimodal droplet size distribution, whereas SW-HIPEs showed smaller droplets, indicating greater structural stability. In contrast, HSW-HIPEs displayed larger and more heterogeneous droplets, suggesting a weaker structure. During digestion, all HIPEs coalesced in the gastric phase, followed by progressive structural reorganization toward an oil-in-water-like dispersion during intestinal digestion. At the end of digestion, SW-HIPE (2.0% w/w) retained smaller, more uniform droplets, whereas HSW-HIPE formed larger aggregates. Under static conditions, HSW-HIPE (0.5% w/w) showed the highest lipolysis (33.5%), while SW-HIPE (2.0% w/w) and PGPR-HIPE reached 17.8% and 12.6%, respectively, demonstrating an inverse relationship between structural stability and lipid hydrolysis. Hydrodynamic characterization showed physiologically relevant laminar flow in the microchip (Re ~0.4), compared with highly turbulent conditions in the static model (Re ≈ 13,000). Despite these differences, both systems showed comparable hydrolysis trends, although hydrolysis was lower in the microfluidic system. Overall, wax type and concentration, as well as digestion conditions, strongly influenced W/O HIPE stability and digestibility.
authors: Larissa Ribas Fonseca; Ana Elisa Ramos Magalhães; Fernando Divino Oliveira Júnior; Tatiana Porto Santos; Rosiane Lopes Cunha

title: State-of-the-art microfluidics technology for CO₂-foam flooding and geological CO₂ storage: A review
abstract: Microfluidic technology has been a powerful tool for exploring CO₂-foam flooding and CO₂ sequestration at the microscale. Traditional methods, e.g., core flooding experiments, are prone to facing challenges in simulating fluid dynamics in porous media accurately; however, microfluidic platforms allow for direct observation and real-time evaluation of multiphase flow dynamics. This review evaluates cutting-edge microfluidic techniques, such as rock-on-a-chip and high-temperature high-pressure (HTHP) chips, with enhanced functionalities in simulating reservoir conditions. Additionally, advances in image processing and machine learning greatly promoted data analysis in microfluidics-driven experiments. The integration of microfluidics with digital rock physics and reservoir simulations offers a platform for the translation of laboratory findings into field-applicable operations. Besides advances in technology, this review considers the economic feasibility and environmental benefits of microfluidic operations in enhanced oil recovery (EOR) and carbon capture and storage (CCS). The results show that microfluidics can play a key role in optimizing CO₂ injection strategies, enhancing oil recovery, and ensuring the security of long-term CO₂ storage, and thus promoting energy efficiency as well as climate change mitigation.
authors: Muhammad Raees Khan

title: Statistic Reability Test of Nozzle Geometry for Oil Well Hole Cleaning from Produced Sand
abstract: Sand production is a major operational challenge in the upstream oil and gas industry, leading to perforation blockage, equipment erosion, and increased non-productive time (NPT). This study investigates the optimization of upward-facing nozzle jetting technology to improve sand cleanout efficiency in oil wells. The research experimental model was designed using the Buckingham Pi Theorem and Reynolds number similarity by scaling field conditions into a laboratory prototype. The study concludes that upward-facing nozzle engineering significantly enhances sand lifting efficiency and accelerates wellbore cleanout operations.Furthermore, numerical simulations and statistical analyses—including ANOVA, Shapiro-Wilk normality tests, and coefficient of determination (R2) evaluations—are systematically applied to validate the performance of the re-engineered jetting tool under varied operational parameters such as injection pressure, fluid flow rate, and sand mesh size. The results demonstrate that the proposed sequential dual-function protocol—comprising initial downward disaggregation followed by upward-facing nozzle activation—significantly enhances upward transport velocity and sand-lifting efficiency. Ultimately, this study concludes that upward-facing nozzle engineering significantly enhances sand lifting efficiency, reduces casing erosion risks, and accelerates wellbore cleanout operations, offering an effective alternative for sand management in mature oil fields.
authors: Abdullah Rizky Agusman; Eko Prastio; Citra Wahyuningrum

title: Stimuli-responsive bioinks for bioprinted cancer models: Toward personalized drug screening and resistance modeling
abstract: Drug resistance remains the leading cause of treatment failure in solid tumors. Conventional two-dimensional (2D) cultures and animal models cannot reproduce the dynamic tumor microenvironment (TME) cues driving resistance evolution—matrix stiffening, acidification, hypoxia, and enzymatic remodeling. Most 3D-bioprinted constructs remain static matrices and share this limitation. This review proposes the spatiotemporal dynamics of the TME as a design criterion for stimuli-responsive ("smart") bioinks, whose stiffness, degradability, drug-release kinetics, and geometry change in response to endogenous TME cues or external triggers. This review distills the TME into a quantitative design blueprint; examines the printability, cytocompatibility, and responsiveness requirements of smart inks, together with the dynamic chemistries enabling them; and summarizes strategies for reconstructing an evolving TME, using pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma and glioblastoma as anchor case studies. The scope is restricted to cancer modeling and drug screening, excluding drug delivery and tissue regeneration. Current evidence remains proof-of-concept: printed models recapitulate resistance-associated phenotypes such as stiffness-mediated chemoresistance, cancer stem cell enrichment, dormancy, and phenotypic plasticity, whereas prospective validation of resistance models in patients has not been achieved. This review outlines the path from phenotype recapitulation to clinical prediction and analyzes prerequisites including vascularization, standardization, regulatory translation, and artificial intelligence (AI)-guided ink design.
authors: Jing Zeng; Wei-Jian Ni

title: Strategies for Enhancing the Performance of 3D ‐Printed Flexible Sensors and Their Applications
abstract: ABSTRACT In recent years, 3D printing technology has emerged as a promising approach for the fabrication of flexible sensors, owing to its advantages of low cost, high design flexibility, and simplified construction processes. The rapid progress of flexible electronics, smart wearable technologies, and soft robotics has driven the demand for flexible sensors with enhanced sensitivity, improved stability, and higher levels of system integration. However, existing 3D‐printed flexible sensors still face certain challenges in terms of sensing performance, long‐term reliability, and versatility. Consequently, developing effective performance improvement strategies has become a key area of research in this field. This paper provides a review of recent research progress in 3D‐printed flexible sensors. The discussion focuses on performance enhancement strategies, including microstructure design, embedded integration, and emerging auxiliary enhancement strategies. In addition, this article provides a systematic summary of the specific applications of these sensors, including soft robotics, human health monitoring, and human motion detection. It also analyzes the challenges and trends facing current technology, providing valuable guidance for bridging the gap between research and practical application and helping to accelerate the design and manufacturing of high‐performance, intelligent flexible sensors.
authors: Junru Wu; Xiaotong Zhang; Bin Wang; Yuping Bu; Weixin Dai; Minghao Zhu; Tianyi Gao; Linjun Huang; Jianguo Tang

title: Surface‐Enhanced Raman Spectroscopy Aptasensors for Nucleic‐Acid Detection: Advances, Challenges, and Future Perspectives
abstract: Nucleic-acid biomarkers play pivotal roles in disease diagnosis, therapeutic monitoring, and precision medicine, creating an urgent demand for analytical platforms combining high sensitivity, molecular specificity, and rapid detection. Surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS) integrated with aptamers, short single-stranded DNA or RNA oligonucleotides, has attracted considerable attention by coupling programmable molecular recognition with ultrasensitive plasmon-enhanced Raman detection. This review evaluates recent advances in aptamer-based SERS biosensors for nucleic-acid analysis, systematically examining sensing mechanisms, plasmonic substrate engineering, aptamer immobilization, signal-transduction pathways, and amplification approaches, including catalytic hairpin assembly, hybridization chain reaction, rolling circle amplification, and CRISPR-assisted systems. Recent developments in microfluidics, artificial intelligence-assisted spectral analysis, portable Raman instrumentation, and point-of-care platforms are assessed while distinguishing true aptamer-mediated sensing from conventional hybridization-based DNA detection. Rational hotspot engineering, deterministic nanogap architectures, and advanced amplification strategies have enabled detection from femtomolar to attomolar levels with improved selectivity, multiplexing, and reproducibility. Challenges including substrate variability, quantitative standardization, aptamer stability, biosafety, and clinical translation are discussed. Future directions toward standardized, intelligent, clinically deployable SERS platforms for next-generation molecular diagnostics and precision healthcare are proposed.
authors: MK Alam; Kazi Mohammed Mehedi Hassan; Monika Tarafdar; Mohammad Imran Hossain; Mohammad Anwar Parvez; Mostafizur Rahaman; Mohammad A. Hasnat

title: Synergistic engineering of organoids and organ-on-a-chip systems through microengineering and sensor integration for advanced biomedical research
abstract: Microphysiological systems, including organoids, organ-on-a-chip (OoC) platforms, and their integrated forms, are increasingly used to model human physiology in vitro. Organoids contribute self-organized cellular diversity and tissue architecture, whereas OoC platforms provide controlled geometry, perfusion, mechanical cues, and access to real-time measurements. Their integration into organoid-on-a-chip and multi-tissue systems can improve physiological relevance for efficacy evaluation, quality control, mechanistic studies, and personalized medicine. This review examines organoid generation, organ-specific OoC models, hybrid systems, 3D bioprinting, acoustic bioassembly, and sensor integration. It also discusses the principal barriers to translation, including scalability, reproducibility, standardization, and the responsible use of artificial intelligence and multi-omics data. Together, these advances position synergistically engineered microphysiological systems as promising translational tools, provided that performance is validated against standardized, reproducible, and clinically relevant benchmarks.
authors: Diantong Xie; Yixu Zhao; 冷予冰; Xiaorui Li; Hongxin Li; Hui Liu; Xudong Wang; Jingkai Liu; Yulong Liao; Tianyu Yang; Jie Liu; Yinuo Zhang; Fengde Peng; Ji Song; Zizheng Deng; Shiyao Chen; Kairui Sun; Yingran Liu; Keyi Chen; Jiashu Li; Yu Wang; Zhongze Gu; Fuyin Zheng

title: Synthesis-aware generative design in trillion-scale chemical spaces for automated drug discovery
abstract: Abstract Autonomous drug discovery via generative molecular design is critically bottlenecked by the production of chemically intractable structures. Multi-trillion-scale make-on-demand libraries guarantee synthetic feasibility, but conventional virtual screening cannot efficiently navigate these vast spaces or address multi-parameter optimization. We introduce Hyper Screening X, a generative AI framework integrating structure-based design with automated synthesis hardware. By encoding deterministic reaction logic in a generative flow network, the framework evaluates only 10 million candidates to navigate an 11-trillion-compound space, jointly optimizing physicochemical properties while ensuring compatibility with automated synthesis. Prospective validation against an SLC1A5 variant with a cryptic interface yielded a 96% synthesis success rate and a 50% functional hit rate, identifying two first-in-class lead compounds. This synthesis-aware strategy advances autonomous, closed-loop drug discovery.
authors: Seonghwan Seo; Yulseung Sung; Sang-Yeon Hwang; Mincheol Kang; JoonSeong Lee; Samuele Bordi; Luka Raguž; Jihye Choi; Daniil Melnichenko; Wan Namkung; Sehan Lee; Jaechang Lim; Benedikt M. Wanner; Jung Min Han; Woo Youn Kim

title: THE INTEGRATION OF TECHNOLOGIES OF NUCLEAR INDUSTRY INTO HEALTH CARE: THE ORGANIZATIONAL ECONOMICAL MECHANISM
abstract: The purpose of the study is to analyze organizational economical mechanism of integration of technologies of nuclear industry into health care. The methodology is based on systemic, institutional and intersectoral approaches using statistical and structural functional analysis. It is established that in Russia, in 2015-2025 volume of radionuclide therapy procedures increased more than twofold times (from 4-5 thousand to 13-15 thousand procedures annually). The number of centers of nuclear medicine reached 18-22. The percentage of state financing made up to 60%-70%, whereas deficiency of human resources reached 20%-30%. It is established that key limitations of integration are institutional barriers, high capital intensity of projects, regional differentiation of infrastructure. The scientific novelty is in development of organizational economic mechanism of integration of technologies of nuclear industry into health care as interdisciplinary system of interaction between industrial, scientific and medical sectors. The practical significance study results is associated with possibility to apply results under improvement of mechanisms of management of high-tech medical care.
authors: T. Yu. Dzholdosheva; A. B. Mottaeva; O. V. Suzeva; V. D. Petelina

title: Talking to instruments: device-integration standards for self-driving laboratories
abstract: Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) are rapidly outgrowing the single-instrument prototype, scaling into multi-instrument and multi-site platforms that run autonomous discovery across chemistry, materials science, biotechnology, pharmaceutical re-search and adjacent domains. What now decides whether an SDL can scale, share its integrations and federate experiments is no longer the algorithms or the robots, but the software layer that orchestrates heterogeneous devices. Today that layer is the bottleneck: a fast-growing ecosystem of open-source orchestrators in which most have built device integration on their own bespoke conventions instead of adopting a formally governed standard. The result is predictable and costly. Integrations do not transfer between laboratories, orchestrators cannot interoperate and many new SDLs rebuild their device-control layer from scratch. Crucially, this is an engineering coordination problem, not a fundamental scientific one and therefore among the most tractable bottlenecks in autonomous science. We map the device-integration standards landscape onto the open-source orchestrator ecosystem, compare the leading options and give scenario-driven guidance on when to use each. We then translate the requirements of autonomous operation into a concrete deliverable: a set of testable engineering criteria and a weighted procurement scorecard that defines an autonomous-ready control interface and gives institutional buyers the leverage to demand it; these requirements do not change as orchestration turns agentic: whether an instrument is driven by a program or by a language-model agent through a model-facing protocol, it is only as safe and reliable as the interface it exposes. Adopted at scale, these requirements turn device integration from a burden repaid lab by lab into shared infrastructure,

title: Temperature-Resolved Coding for Highly Multiplexed Digital PCR Using MeltArray.
abstract: Digital PCR enables sensitive absolute nucleic acid quantification, but its broader application remains constrained by limited multiplexing capacity. Here we report digital MeltArray (dMeltArray), a temperature-resolved endpoint decoding strategy that transfers MeltArray mediator-probe chemistry to a static droplet-imaging digital PCR system. In dMeltArray, target-specific mediator products generate fluorescent reporter duplexes with programmed melting temperatures. Post-amplification imaging at discrete temperatures progressively erases lower-T<sub>m</sub> signals while retaining higher-T<sub>m</sub> signals, allowing target-specific concentrations to be recovered from Poisson-corrected cumulative counts within each fluorescence channel. This strategy converts melting temperature into a programmable readout dimension requiring no real-time tracking or full-curve acquisition, addressing key trade-offs between multiplexing capacity, workflow simplicity, and cost. dMeltArray can be combined with 5'-hydrolysis probes, adding an orthogonal persistent-signal readout in the same optical framework. As proof-of-concept applications, we developed a 13-plex assay for post-transplantation viruses, an 11-plex assay for KRAS/BRAF hotspot mutations, and a 14-plex assay that integrates a 5'-hydrolysis probe into the 13-plex panel. These findings establish temperature-resolved endpoint decoding as a scalable route to multiplex digital PCR and support multidimensional target encoding by combining spectral, thermal and hydrolysis-probe readouts without requiring full melting-curve acquisition.

title: Temporary Uterine Artery Clamping During Laparoscopic Myomectomy and Perioperative Hemoglobin Decline: A Retrospective Single-Center Comparative Study
abstract: Background/Objectives: The aim of this study was to evaluate the adjusted association of temporary uterine artery clamping with the absolute and percentage decreases in hemoglobin during the perioperative period in women undergoing laparoscopic myomectomy, and to evaluate this association after multivariable adjustment for patient and leiomyoma characteristics. Methods: This single-center, retrospective, comparative observational study included 118 patients who underwent elective laparoscopic myomectomy for uterine leiomyomas between January 2021 and January 2026 (65 with temporary uterine artery clamping and 53 controls). The decision to perform clamping was based on the surgeon’s intraoperative assessment. The primary outcome measures were defined as absolute hemoglobin drop and percentage hemoglobin drop. The adjusted association of clamping with these measures was examined using multivariable linear regression models simultaneously adjusting for age, body mass index (BMI), and tumor burden (evaluated as dominant diameter in Model 1 and specimen weight in Model 2), with baseline hemoglobin additionally adjusted in absolute decline models. Results: No significant differences were found between the two groups in terms of baseline clinical and leiomyoma characteristics (age, BMI, number of pregnancies, preoperative hemoglobin level, leiomyoma size, and weight) (all p > 0.05). Although the difference in postoperative hemoglobin levels did not reach statistical significance (9.59 ± 1.70 vs. 10.01 ± 1.45 g/dL; p = 0.153), both the absolute hemoglobin decline (controls vs. clamping: 2.20 ± 0.90 vs. 1.83 ± 0.88 g/dL; p = 0.027) and the percentage hemoglobin decline (controls vs. clamping: 18.84 ± 7.77% vs. 15.24 ± 6.61%; p = 0.008) were significantly lower in the clamping group. Evaluated as a composite safety outcome across all 134 surgical patients (transfusion or conversion to laparotomy), procedural safety events occurred in 18.5% (12/65) of controls compared with 5.8% (4/69) of clamping cases, demonstrating a statistically significant reduction in composite major surgical morbidity in the clamping cohort (Fisher’s exact test p = 0.033; Relative Risk = 0.31, 95% CI: 0.11 to 0.92). In both the primary and sensitivity multivariable models, temporary uterine artery clamping demonstrated a significant adjusted association with lower values of approximately 0.38 g/dL in absolute hemoglobin decline (p = 0.015–0.016) and approximately 3.6 percentage points in percentage hemoglobin decline (p = 0.007–0.008). Furthermore, while the preoperative hemoglobin level was independently and positively associated with the absolute decrease in hemoglobin (p < 0.001 in both absolute decline models), age, BMI, leiomyoma size, and weight showed no independent association. Conclusions: Temporary uterine artery clamping demonstrated a significant multivariable adjusted association with a modestly attenuated perioperative hemoglobin decline during laparoscopic myomectomy. The finding that static postoperative hemoglobin levels alone did not differ significantly between groups underscores the importance of using dynamic hemoglobin parameters in the assessment of surgical blood loss. Although the retrospective design limits causal inferences, temporary uterine artery clamping appears to be a feasible surgical adjunct associated with reduced perioperative hemoglobin decline in experienced hands; however, prospective trials evaluating operative duration, clamping intervals, and long-term reproductive safety are warranted before broader clinical safety can be definitively established. Temporary uterine artery clamping demonstrated a significant multivariable adjusted association with a modest attenuation in perioperative hemoglobin decline (approximately 0.38 g/dL) during laparoscopic myomectomy, whereas static postoperative hemoglobin levels alone did not differ significantly between groups. Given the modest clinical magnitude of this difference, the lack of a significant difference in standalone transfusion rates, and the potential for residual confounding by indication in this retrospective cohort, temporary clamping should be considered a feasible adjunctive measure in experienced hands rather than a definitive routine intervention, and prospective randomized trials are warranted.
