title: The Cyber-Physical Attack Surface of Legacy Scada Networks: A Systematic Review of Vulnerabilities, Threats, and Detection Gaps in Critical Infrastructure
abstract: Legacy Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) networks remain the operational backbone of the electric power, water treatment, and oil-and-gas sectors, yet they were engineered in an era that prioritized deterministic availability and physical safety over information security. The progressive convergence of information technology (IT) and operational technology (OT) has dissolved the air gaps that once isolated these systems, exposing an attack surface for which their aging protocol stacks were never designed. Field-level communication standards such as Modbus and DNP3 typically transmit control directives without encryption, authentication, or message integrity, allowing an adversary who reaches the network to forge, replay, or manipulate commands at will. The defining hazard of this domain is the cyber-physical attack, in which a purely digital intrusion is translated into tangible physical damage, service disruption, or threats to human life. Against this class of threat, conventional signature- and rule-based intrusion detection is structurally inadequate, missing novel and stealthy manipulations while generating unsustainable false-alarm volumes. This review systematically synthesizes the vulnerability landscape, a taxonomy of cyber-physical threats, landmark incidents including Stuxnet, the 2015 Ukrainian grid attack, TRITON, and Maroochy, the protocol-level weaknesses of legacy assets, and the resulting detection gap. Drawing together the industrial-control and applied cybersecurity literature, it argues that intelligent behavioural anomaly detection offers the most credible path toward resilient protection of critical infrastructure
authors: Chukwunenye Amadi
venue: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF COMPUTER SCIENCE AND MATHEMATICAL THEORY E-ISSN

title: The Verification Wall in Microbial Metabolomics
abstract: Computational methods now propose structures for gut microbial metabolites faster than any laboratory can confirm them. We argue that verification, not generation, is the binding constraint, and that better models will not relieve it. Confirming a structure to the field's own standard means having the molecule in hand. Automation can lower what that costs per compound, but the cost stays proportional to the number of structures and never amortizes across them. Two substitutes are on offer and neither removes that requirement. In-silico spectral prediction ranks candidates instead of confirming one, and the strongest current model puts the right structure first 33.5% of the time on a scaffold-split benchmark. Any assignment resting on spectral similarity is, by the field's own definition, made without a reference standard. Microcrystal diffraction does return a structure, but it needs the compound to crystallize out of a trace mixture, which is a different problem rather than an easier one. We sorted 10,645 computationally inferred metabolite structures by what verifying each would take. Between 5% and 37% have no verification route identified under our analysis. That spread reflects where the thresholds are set rather than a measured count of unverifiable compounds, and the inaccessible ones cluster among the most speculative entries. Those figures understate the problem, because the gut makes far more compounds than any database records. HMDB holds only what someone has already thought worth cataloguing, and structure generators are bounded by nothing at all. The claim is easy to disprove. Show a route that confirms structures as fast as they are proposed. Until someone does, two problems stay unsolved. Nobody knows how to spend a verification budget that will always be too small, or what a biologist may conclude from a structure that was never confirmed.
authors: Takahiko Koyama

title: The ablation margin as a regenerative and immunosuppressive niche in hepatocellular carcinoma: multicellular remodeling and organoid-on-a-chip modeling.
abstract: Thermal ablation is an important local treatment for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), yet post-ablation local tumor progression remains a major obstacle to durable disease control. Traditionally, recurrence has been attributed mainly to incomplete thermal coverage, inadequate ablative margins, or heat-sink effects. However, increasing evidence suggests that the sublethal thermal injury (STI) zone at the ablation margin is not merely a passive physical boundary, but a biologically active injury-repair microenvironment. Within this region, gradients of thermal dose, hypoxia, damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs), extracellular matrix mechanics, and immune infiltration may interact to shape residual tumor cell behavior. Post-ablation remodeling is likely driven by coordinated crosstalk among myeloid cells, hepatic stellate cells/cancer-associated fibroblast-like stromal cells (HSCs/CAFs), endothelial cells, neutrophils, adaptive immune cells, and residual tumor cells. These interactions may promote epithelial-mesenchymal transition, stem-like plasticity, immune evasion, angiogenic repair, and local tumor progression. Current two-dimensional (2D) cultures lack three-dimensional architecture and multicellular spatial interactions, whereas animal models are limited by variable thermal dose control, restricted real-time imaging, and interspecies differences. Emerging HCC organoid-on-a-chip platforms may help address these gaps by integrating patient-derived organoids (PDOs), tunable extracellular matrix hydrogels, microfluidic thermal and hypoxic gradients, and defined multicellular co-culture modules. Importantly, immune checkpoint testing requires immune-competent extensions incorporating autologous T cells, and antigen-presentation studies require dendritic cells. This review discusses the ablation margin as a multicellular recurrence niche and evaluates organoid-on-a-chip systems as hypothesis-generating tools for mechanism-guided and safety-conscious adjuvant strategy development.
authors: Tingyue Qiao; Yang Zha; Honghua Dai; Yue Chai; Li Weng

title: The intelligence loop and value creation in the age of AI agents
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Artificial intelligence (AI) is moving from generating outputs to executing work. An agent that executes work autonomously produces something generative AI does not: operational experience that can raise its future intelligence. Prior research on AI emphasizes value creation through demand‐side feedback, notably data network effects, in which user data improve prediction and reinforce adoption. We develop the supply‐side counterpart, the intelligence loop: delegated usage generates operational experience, agentic capability converts it into future intelligence, and the resulting value maintains or expands usage. The loop cannot operate until autonomous execution is viable, a threshold we call minimum viable intelligence (MVI). Crossing MVI does not guarantee rising intelligence. Comparable deployments of AI agents can diverge as their loops decay, sustain, or accelerate. Three implications follow. Competitive advantage may depend more on the loop than on installed base. An above‐MVI agent supplies scarce expert skill as a non‐rival, replicable resource, so productive capacity can grow faster than expert headcount, with the one‐person company as a limiting case. And a venture with adequate demand, capital, and a capable team can still fail because its loop never functions or later deteriorates. Managerial Summary Artificial intelligence (AI) agents can execute work, and the experience generated through execution can raise their future intelligence, a feedback process we call the intelligence loop. An agent crosses a workflow's minimum viable intelligence (MVI) when it executes reliably without step‐by‐step direction, autonomous execution creates at least as much net value as the best alternative after oversight and correction costs, and governance arrangements keep residual risk acceptable and accountability clear. Investment belongs where one of these conditions keeps a valuable workflow below MVI. Deployment can begin with narrow, feedback‐rich workflows near MVI that ideally lead to harder workflows, since base model upgrades can match gains on simple work. Even above MVI, the loop is not automatic: it stalls when feedback is not timely and diagnostic, experience yields little intelligence gain, gains add little user value, or value does not maintain or expand usage. Human involvement shifts from executing work to specifying goals, evaluating outputs, governing execution, and supplying tacit knowledge. When the loop sustains or accelerates, productive capacity can grow faster than expert headcount. With capable base models widely available, advantage depends less on access to AI than on building and governing the loop, controlling proprietary operational experience, and converting it into intelligence more effectively than rivals. A venture with adequate demand, capital, and a capable team can fail because its loop never functions or later deteriorates. Cutting evaluation or oversight to scale faster may increase output in the short run but weaken the loop even while revenue remains healthy.
authors: Yong Li; Ming Zeng; Alexis Li

title: The microglial lineage: from molecular states to context-dependent functions
abstract: Microglial states are now being cataloged far faster than their associated cellular functions can be tested, widening the gap between molecular description and causal understanding of tissue impact. The gap becomes especially apparent as microglial biology moves beyond the rodent central nervous system (CNS). Peripheral nervous system (PNS) microglia, identified in human and other large-vertebrate ganglia, share major molecular features with CNS microglia and contribute to neuronal growth, yet their adult maintenance and responses to injury and disease remain unresolved. TREM2 exposes a second limit of state-based interpretation. The receptor supports recurring cellular processes, including myeloid fitness, lesion-associated accumulation and cargo handling, but their tissue consequences vary with the substrate, model and disease stage. This review separates population identity, molecular state, cellular function and tissue outcome, and outlines an experimental path that combines state-informed genetic screens, direct functional assays, multicellular human models and temporally controlled in vivo validation to connect molecular discovery with context-dependent function.
authors: Cuihua Li; Zhisheng Wu; Xianyuan Xiang; Hanjie Li

title: Theranostic Imaging Agents: Integrating Molecular Diagnostics, Precision Therapeutics, and Artificial Intelligence
abstract: Theranostic imaging agents combine molecular diagnosis, targeted therapy and monitoring of treatment response into a single paradigm of precision medicine. This review summarizes the current development and translational landscape of theranostic imaging agents, covering molecular targets, imaging platforms, principles of agent design, nanotheranostics, radiotheranostics, and disease-specific applications. Particular emphasis is given to clinically validated and emerging targeting strategies using prostate-specific membrane antigen, somatostatin receptors, fibroblast activation protein, C-X-C Chemokine Receptor 4 (CXCR4), Human Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor 2 (HER2) and other disease-associated biomarkers. Moreover, the review addresses Positron Emission Tomography (PET), Single-Photon Emission Computed Tomography (SPECT), Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI), optical, photoacoustic, Raman and multimodal imaging approaches, therapeutic payloads, stimulus-responsive systems, and pharmacokinetic optimization. Moreover, emerging applications of artificial intelligence, radiomics, radiogenomics, spatial and single-cell multiomics, liquid biopsy, digital pathology, personalized dosimetry, and digital twins are evaluated for their potential to improve patient stratification, treatment selection, response assessment and adaptive therapy. Despite tremendous progress, clinical translation is hampered by target heterogeneity, off-target accumulation, radionuclide availability, manufacturing complexity, dosimetric uncertainty, regulatory requirements, limited clinical validation, data interoperability, cost and unequal access. This review, overall, emphasizes the convergence of molecular imaging, targeted therapeutics, nanotechnology, and artificial intelligence in the development of next-generation theranostic platforms, and outlines critical priorities for their clinical translation.
authors: Shrestha Sharma; Syed Arman Rabbani; Mohamed El-Tanani; Mohamed Anas Patni; Rakesh Kumar; Manita Saini

title: Thermomechanical Noise Dilution by Low‐Q Cavity for Nanoparticles Detection
abstract: ABSTRACT Phonon laser sensors offer powerful label‐free detection, yet their sensitivity remains bounded by noise for which robust suppression strategies are still lacking. Here we introduce a technique for diluting thermomechanical noise that counter‐intuitively selects lower‐Q optical modes to suppress thermal fluctuations of phonon‐laser frequency, followed by active feedback locking for frequency stabilization. The combined approach enables real‐time detection of single 10 nm‐radius polystyrene particles based on a microbubble cavity with a 38 MHz phonon mode, estimating a mass limit of . We further apply the platform to study iron–oxide uptake and reaction dynamics in cells.
authors: Gui‐Wen Zheng; Rui Niu; Yi‐Wen Huang; Tian Tian; Yu‐Xuan Chen; Yu Wang; Hao Tian; Fang‐Wen Sun; Xi‐Feng Ren; Guo G; Zhen Shen; Chun‐Hua Dong

title: Toward autonomous chemical discovery: agentic AI in organic synthesis and nanochemistry
abstract: Conventional approaches to chemical discovery rely heavily on human expertise and experimental trial and error. This makes the process slow and resource-intensive when exploring large chemical spaces and designing novel compounds. Artificial intelligence (AI) has transformed this field by enabling predictive, generative, and increasingly autonomous approaches. In particular, machine learning, deep learning, generative AI, and autonomous laboratories allow systems to predict chemical outcomes, design molecules and synthetic routes, and perform experiments in closed loops. Agentic AI extends these capabilities by allowing AI systems to plan multistep tasks, use external tools, interpret experimental results, and adapt subsequent actions to pursue scientific objectives. These capabilities are being integrated into autonomous AI systems across multiple fields, including organic synthesis, nanochemistry, computational chemistry, robotics, and autonomous experimentation. Together, these developments support a comprehensive review of agentic AI and its potential to enable autonomous chemical discovery. However, existing reviews have primarily examined organic synthesis and nanochemistry separately, without a unified framework for how agentic AI can integrate these domains toward autonomous discovery. In this review, we integrate advances in predictive and generative AI, agentic systems, autonomous laboratories, and related computational and robotic technologies, while distinguishing capabilities demonstrated experimentally from those proposed for future applications. We also examine the major challenges that must be addressed to achieve reliable autonomous discovery, including model interpretability, data quality, reproducibility, experimental validation, scalability, safety, and governance.
authors: Boppudi Hari Babu; Pullaiah Chowdary Vutla; Jagadeesh Mahimaluru; Bryce Ke Jun Chong; Srinivasulu Kambam

title: Toward precision hernia surgery: integrating biomarkers, genomics, quantitative imaging, and artificial intelligence in abdominal wall repair
abstract: PURPOSE: Despite technical advances, the expansion of minimally invasive approaches and the development of novel biomaterials, recurrence and complications following abdominal wall hernia (AWH) repair remain frequent. This variability likely reflects anatomical and technical factors and host biological heterogeneity. Precision herniology is emerging as a translational paradigm integrating biomarkers, genetics, quantitative imaging, and artificial intelligence to refine risk stratification and therapeutic planning. METHODS: We conducted a critical narrative review with translational scope. PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and Embase were searched from January 2015 to June 2026. We prioritized adult studies across four axes: (i) biomarkers of collagen, extracellular matrix, and cellular mechanisms; (ii) genetics and susceptibility to AWH; (iii) immunonutritional markers; (iv) artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) for predicting complexity and complications. RESULTS: The literature reveals convergent, albeit heterogeneous, signals indicating that host biology may contribute to variability in hernia phenotype and surgical outcomes. Alterations in collagen turnover and in the MMP-TIMP axis, fibroblast heterogeneity, inflammatory signaling, polygenic architecture related to connective tissue integrity, immunonutritional markers associated with perioperative vulnerability, and quantitative imaging metrics analyzed by AI/ML models represent biologically plausible, clinically relevant domains. CONCLUSION: Available data support the plausibility that host biological heterogeneity contributes to the formation, healing, prosthetic integration, and recurrence of AWH, thereby broadening the traditional paradigm centered predominantly on defect anatomy. The main value of this work is the critical integration of molecular and cellular biomarkers, genetics, quantitative imaging, and AI/ML into a unified conceptual framework for future precision herniology research.
authors: Bruno Amantini Messias; Guilherme Costa e Silva; Pedro Henrique de Freitas Amaral; Diogo Parente Falcão; Sérgio Roll; Jaques Waisberg

title: Towards Intelligent Membrane Systems: A Critical Analysis of Digital Twin–ML Integration for Real–Time Process Optimization, Fouling Management, and Autonomous Design
abstract: Membrane separation is central to potable water production, wastewater reclamation, desalination, gas separation, and decarbonization, yet its economics remain constrained by fouling and by a gap between process data and timely operating decisions. Digital twins (DTs) offer live, bidirectionally coupled virtual representations of physical assets, while machine learning (ML) extracts predictive and prescriptive insights from operational data. Together, they are promising computational approaches for membrane systems. However, their applications have largely evolved independently across fouling prediction, DT development, and ML-based materials discovery. This review argues that these are converging strands of a single trajectory toward self-sensing, self-predicting, and eventually self-designing membrane systems, and that treating them separately obscures key interdependencies. The contributions are threefold. First, applying the digital model/digital shadow/digital twin taxonomy, it shows that most published membrane DTs are digital shadows (DSs). Second, it proposes a five-level autonomy framework, inspired by vehicle automation taxonomies, providing a unified scale for comparing applications ranging from LSTM-based fouling forecasting and reinforcement learning dosing control to autonomous materials laboratories. Third, it integrates autonomous materials design, including self-driving laboratories, inverse design, generative models, and Bayesian search, into the upper levels of this ladder. Evidence is synthesized across reverse osmosis, nanofiltration, ultrafiltration, microfiltration, membrane bioreactors, membrane distillation, and gas separation membranes, with emphasis on critically assessing model performance and generalizability. The study concludes with a roadmap for overcoming data limitations, poor interpretability, interoperability gaps, cybersecurity risks, techno-economic barriers, and regulatory trust deficits that block autonomous membrane systems.
authors: Olawumi O. Sadare; Samuel P. Alonge; A. O. Akinyemi; Abass A. Adesina; Shukrah Adesola-Olabiyi; Lanrewaju Ibrahim Fajimi

title: Transforming Brain Organoids Into Functional Platforms: Convergence of Engineering, Imaging, AI, and Ethics
abstract: Brain organoids are self-organizing 3D aggregates derived from pluripotent stem cells and thus mirror many aspects of human brain development, including gene expression programs, spatial organization, and neuron subtype specification. As a result, these organoids have been used to emulate neurodevelopmental, neuropsychiatric, and neurodegenerative diseases. Yet, their maturation remains fundamentally constrained by diffusion-limited necrosis, incomplete vascularization, limited visualization, and the absence of large-scale circuit integration, which collectively prevent progression beyond the fetal stage. These intrinsic limitations have catalyzed a convergence across microfluidics, biofabrication, imaging, and ethical frameworks, giving rise to a multidisciplinary movement aimed at enhancing organoid viability, reproducibility, and physiological relevance. This perspective examines how these technologies are transforming brain organoids from developmental models into experimentally robust, functional platforms.
authors: Aishwarya Pantula; Kaustubh G. Joshi; Swarangi Samant; Greta Babakhanova; Annie Kathuria

title: Translational Barriers and AI‐Driven Challenges of Microfluidics‐Enabled Wearables and Implantable Systems in Personalized Medicine
abstract: Wearable and implantable microfluidic systems have progressed from laboratory prototypes toward translational clinical deployment, enabling continuous, minimally invasive sampling of dynamic biomarkers across sweat, saliva, tears, and interstitial fluid. However, existing reviews often address materials chemistry or device fabrication in isolation, obscuring the systemic path to clinical translation. This review establishes a cohesive, translation-focused linear trajectory starting from foundational functional biomaterials and advanced fabrication techniques, transitioning into a performance benchmarking of diagnostics-oriented systems and closed-loop theranostic platforms. Through these vectors, we systematically evaluate how microfluidic transport, multiplexed molecular analytics, and autonomous therapeutic integration collectively drive the shift from passive tracking to adaptive intervention. Beyond physical hardware, we decode the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) across three precise pathways: sensor self-calibration, multiplexed molecular decoding, and on-device autonomous decision-making. Finally, we critically examine the socio-technical barriers to clinical translation, with a focus on how biofluid data heterogeneity and population baseline disparities propagate algorithmic bias. We propose that robust hardware interfaces, standardized validation benchmarks, and alignment with emerging regulatory frameworks are prerequisites for achieving equitable, responsible digital health protection.
authors: Ke Huang; Ching Yin Fong; Xin Huang; Bee Luan Khoo

title: Understanding and Mitigating Charge‐Trapping Induced Transfer Curve Drift in Electrolyte‐Gated Graphene Field‐Effect Transistors
abstract: Electrolyte-gated graphene field-effect transistors (EG-gFETs) have great potential for chemical and biosensing applications and are increasingly attractive platforms for synaptic or memristive elements in neuromorphic computing. However, EG-gFETs exhibit drift in their electrical response, a phenomenon that remains poorly understood. An in-depth understanding of EG-gFETs' responses is essential for fully exploiting their behavior in applications and to open a much-needed discussion and standardization of practices within the community. In this work, we show that drift is ubiquitous across all tested devices and experimental conditions, and present evidence indicating that it is driven by progressive charge trapping in the insulating layer beneath the graphene channel. We then discuss potential strategies to mitigate drift, including alternative interrogation schemes and fabrication processes. Additionally, we propose approaches to enhance signal readability and facilitate discrimination of the signal from noise and false-positive responses in biosensing applications.
authors: João Mouro; Tiago Pereira; Tiago Dias; Mohammadmahdi Faraji; Rui Campos; Jérôme Borme; Pedro Alpuim

title: VISION-BASED DRY-MATERIAL INVENTORY ESTIMATION IN AUTONOMOUS LABORATORIES: RGB SEGMENTATION VERSUS RGB-D SURFACE RECONSTRUCTION
abstract: Reliable dry-material inventory monitoring is needed for autonomous laboratory operation, but the suitability of a non-contact method depends on material behaviour, optical access, calibration requirements and the quantity to be estimated. We compared two vision-based approaches—material-specific RGB/YOLO level estimation and visible-surface reconstruction from an Intel RealSense D405—across three materials (black polypropylene pellets, wood powder, and microcrystalline cellulose fine powder) in small transparent laboratory tubes representative of common dosing instruments, with the aim of informing a practical, evidence-based framework for choosing between such methods in laboratory automation and similar industrial contexts. Software-coordinated records linked the two camera channels to a nominal mass-fraction inventory reference and a manual-height baseline. Across six runs and 133 paired, reference-eligible material states, D405 achieved lower error than YOLO in every run (mean absolute error of 3.26 vs. 7.14 percentage points), though YOLO offered higher valid-result coverage (97.2% vs. 95.1%). Both methods showed increased error under repeated surface disturbance, with YOLO degrading more sharply than D405. An exploratory correction fitted using the first observation at each mass level substantially improved YOLO but did not surpass D405’s uncorrected accuracy, while a single global correction worsened both methods—indicating that simple corrections do not transfer robustly across conditions. The results support a method-selection framework based on error, availability, viewing geometry, calibration-state representativeness and total resource requirements. Conclusions are limited to the tested materials and setups, and the mass-fraction reference is an operational inventory proxy rather than a direct measurement of true occupied volume.
authors: Mostafa Abd Al Kader; Miguel Hernández‐del‐Valle; Maciej Harańczyk

title: Vat photopolymerization additive manufacturing: A critical review of materials, processes, applications, and sustainability
abstract: Vat photopolymerization (VPP) has advanced from a laser-scanned prototyping into a multi-material additive manufacturing platform whose chemistry, process variants, application reach warrant critical appraisal. This review synthesizes 355 peer-reviewed articles indexed in Scopus between 2018 and 2026, retrieved through a structured query within article title, abstract, and keyword fields and filtered for English-language journal articles. A reproducible search strategy, a validated thematic classification protocol (inter-rater Cohen’s κ = 0.87 on a 20% double-coded subsample), and uncertainty intervals for every reported corpus share accompany the synthesis. The corpus is dissected across five analytical layers: photopolymer chemistry (initiators, monomers, oligomers, bio-derived feedstocks, fillers, and high-solid slurries); process variants spanning stereolithography, digital light processing, masked liquid-crystal-display printing, continuous liquid interface production, two-photon polymerization, and emerging volumetric and tomographic routes; ceramic VPP from slurry rheology through debinding and sintering of alumina, zirconia, bioactive ceramics, and polymer-derived SiC/SiOC; biomedical translation across bone, dental, drug delivery, hydrogel, and device subdomains; and the functional, smart, and sustainable frontiers. Two domains receive dedicated depth: biocompatibility-driven formulation design, covering cytocompatible photoinitiators, monomers and additives for biomedical VPP, and light-based 3D bioprinting of cell-laden hydrogels, analysed as a distinct biomedical frontier. Each process variant is discussed through governing parameters rather than publication chronology, and each application section closes with quantitative critical comparison. Quantitative trends show biomedical use, ceramic structural parts, and functional composites collectively account for more than half of recent output, whereas life-cycle assessment, fracture mechanics, and closed-loop recycling remain conspicuously underdeveloped. Twelve research gaps and ten actionable future directions are articulated, prioritized by technological maturity, evidence base, industrial relevance and feasibility, each paired with measurable targets, supported by fifteen schematic figures and comparative tables. The review positions VPP as a chemistry-led, process-flexible technology whose next decade will be defined by sustainability accounting, multi-material control, and clinically qualified translation.

title: Vision-Guided Closed-Loop Autonomous Navigation of Light-Driven Janus Microbots
abstract: Artificial microbots capable of precise and autonomous navigation could provide versatile platforms for microscale transport, manipulation, and task execution in complex environments. However, reliable navigation becomes increasingly challenging at the micrometre scale, particularly when the surrounding environment changes dynamically. Here, we develop a vision-guided closed-loop navigation framework for light-driven cube-shaped hematite/TiO2 Janus microbots with a characteristic size of approximately 3 μm. Real-time visual localization using a custom-trained YOLOv11 object-detection model is integrated with discretized waypoint-based magnetic steering to enable precise navigation along complex prescribed trajectories, with more than 90% of the measured trajectory deviations remaining below 6 μm across the tested path geometries. The framework further enables arbitrary user-defined free-hand trajectories and autonomous navigation through a physically confined maze. In dynamically changing environments, A* path planning enables real-time path replanning while avoiding multiple independently swimming 5 μm spherical Janus micromotors. Finally, the microbot selectively captures multiple cargo particles and autonomously transports and delivers them to a predefined location while simultaneously avoiding dynamic obstacles. These results establish an integrated platform combining programmable trajectory control, autonomous path planning, real-time environmental adaptation, and task execution within a single light-driven Janus microbot system.

title: When Can a Learned Design Surrogate Be Trusted in a Self-Driving Microfluidics Laboratory? An Offline Closed-Loop Framework Built and Tested on Six Public Tables
abstract: Self-driving laboratories couple a learned design surrogate to an instrument, and on every new target domain it must answer four questions: when it can be trusted, how many target measurements it needs, which to make first, and when to stop adapting, switch models or escalate. We state a framework making each measurable (a competence ratio, a budget $k^*(\varepsilon)$, a time-to-target and a priced decision) and instantiate it without wet experiments on six public droplet-microfluidic and liposome tables as offline laboratories: 107 leave-one-group tiers whose rows are hidden labels. A sealed, pre-registered programme (two sealed negative validations and a pre-registered test on three more tables) and seven frozen closed-loop protocols, each run twice, yield 23 findings. Shift cost is stratified by shift type; no label-free statistic certifies individual candidates; random-split model-family rankings predicted neither the sealed nor the loop rankings. Warm-start residual boosting returns a surrogate to $1.25\times$ its development reference within 20 target rows in 94% of chemistry tiers (27% under a strict noise-floor reading), 90% of laboratory and 40% of device tiers, and a budget planned from the shift type on other tables is not measurably worse on a new one. In the loop, one gain survives drift and shuffled-label controls on all tiers, carried by the sparsely sampled ones: proposing at once and warm-starting on every measurement reaches a 10% target in 2.80 measurements against 3.31 for the reference, and in 5.72 against 11.35 for random proposals on 301 hard units at a 3% tolerance. No label-free acquisition rule survives the shuffled-label control, no interval-aware proposal or other model family does better, and no threshold rule on the tested diagnostics beats always continuing once escalation is priced. No wet-lab validation is claimed.
authors: Zhiyuan Zhang

title: Whispering Gallery and Fabry‐Pérot Resonators for Photonics and Halide Perovskite Optoelectronics
abstract: ABSTRACT Halide perovskites, with their high refractive indices, strong excitonic interactions, and low optical losses, provide a unique platform for dielectric optical resonators. Among these, Whispering Gallery Mode (WGM) and Fabry–Pérot (FP) resonators enable light confinement through distinct yet complementary mechanisms based on total internal reflection and longitudinal interference. While both architectures have been widely explored in halide perovskite microlasers, optical sensors, and solar cells, their roles have largely been discussed in isolation. Here, we present a unified perspective on dielectric resonators in halide perovskite optoelectronics, identifying them as coherent, mode‐based light‐trapping systems. In contrast to conventional non‐resonant nanophotonic strategies that rely on scattering and geometric light management, WGM and FP resonators enhance optical path length, field localization, and photon lifetime through well‐defined cavity modes. This distinction underpins their performance in perovskite‐based low‐threshold lasing, high‐sensitivity sensing, and enhanced absorption in thin‐film photovoltaics, particularly near the band edge where photon recycling becomes critical. By systematically analyzing resonator implementations across these applications, we outline key design principles, performance trade‐offs, and integration challenges specific to halide perovskite platforms. Finally, we highlight the remaining challenges and emerging opportunities, including hybrid WGM–FP systems and resonator‐driven photon recycling for high‐efficiency perovskite devices.
authors: Ayusmin Panda; C. Sudakar; B. R. K. Nanda

title: YouRA: A Persistent-State Architecture for Evidence-Traceable Autonomous Research Agents
abstract: End-to-end research agents can now produce complete scientific papers, yet manuscript claims often diverge from executed experiments. This gap is structural: research state, failure histories, and claim-evidence alignment are not maintained as persistent, verifiable state across long-horizon pipelines. We present YouRA (Your Research Agent), an architecture for stateful, evidence-traceable autonomous research. YouRA preserves research state, execution evidence, and failure history across the research trajectory by integrating three components: a Verification State Architecture (VSA) that tracks hypotheses, gates, and evidence pointers; an Independent Controller that turns state and reflection records into lifecycle, recovery, and debate/review control while separating control from execution; and Stateful Reflection that logs failures as structured lessons and routes recovery through bounded repair, redesign, or reset. On MLR-Bench's predefined ten-task end-to-end subset, YouRA improves over both MLR-Agent and AI Scientist V2 on scalar Overall across all three matched backbones. An automated diagnostic using MLR-Bench's hallucination taxonomy reports intersection/union counts for four fact-based failure types, and data-provenance diagnostic shows more real-data-based outputs. Ablating each of the four components (the VSA, the Independent Controller, MCP tool access, and reflection-guided recovery) supports their separable contributions. Removing either core-state component drops YouRA below the full system. Code: https://github.com/PrayPrey/Your-Research-Agent.
authors: Yoonkyu Woo; Woojin Lee; Jin-Xia Huang

title: [Research progress of microfluidic technology in competitive sports].
abstract: Aiming at the practical requirements of point-of-care testing, dynamic functional monitoring of athletes, precise diagnosis and treatment of sports injuries, and rapid anti-doping screening for competitive sports, microfluidic technology, with the prominent advantages of miniaturization, high throughput, low sample consumption and fast response, has become a critical interdisciplinary technical tool for advancing the scientization of competitive sports. This review systematically summarizes recent research progress and typical applications of microfluidic technology in key fields of competitive sports, including anti-doping detection, monitoring of athletes' physiological and psychological status, management of sports injuries, development of intelligent sports equipment, and bionic research of exercise physiology. The technical characteristics and scenario adaptability of diverse microfluidic systems are further compared and analyzed. The development paths and application prospects of the integration between microfluidic technology and competitive sports are discussed. This review intends to provide theoretical basis and technical references for the scientific development of competitive sports in China.
authors: Chun Hu; Chao Zhang; Zhenmin Fan; Xiaoyan Deng; Ming Liu

title: A Computational Framework for Modelling Subject Specific Changes in Knee Ligaments and Tibiofemoral Contact Associated With Varus Deformity
abstract: Varus deformity is a pathological knee condition described by outward bowing of the joint and increased medial compartment loading, both of which contribute to the development and progression of knee osteoarthritis. This study presents a subject-specific musculoskeletal modelling framework to investigate ligamentous characteristics and tibiofemoral contact mechanics for subjects having a varus deformity. A cohort of osteoarthritic subjects with varus deformity and undergoing total knee replacement surgery was analyzed in a standing posture. For each subject, musculoskeletal models with subject-specific knee joint anatomy were developed. A Taguchi-based experimental design was implemented to quantify the influence of individual ligament group slack lengths on the varus alignment. Subsequently, subject-specific ligament slack lengths combinations were predicted using a search-based optimisation that minimises the muscle-volume-weighted sum of squared muscle activations. The MCL-G and LCL-G groups were identified as the dominant influencers of varus angles. Optimisation revealed that specific varus alignments were associated with distinct laxity of medial and lateral soft tissue. These ligamentous adjustments corresponded to a significant medial shift in the tibiofemoral contact centre relative to a neutral alignment. Furthermore, higher degrees of varus malalignment correlated with a substantial increase in the mean total knee joint reaction force and a concurrent increase in the knee adduction moment. The proposed framework provides a subject-specific in silico approach for quantifying ligament adaptations and contact forces associated with varus deformity.

title: A FOCUS-PDCA quality improvement model involving unlicensed assistive personnel for improving clinical effectiveness and efficiency in inpatient physical examination: a quasi-experimental, historical-control study
abstract: The accuracy and efficiency of inpatient examinations depend on a well-collaborated working team that involves doctors, nurses, and unlicensed assistive personnel (UAP). This study aimed to evaluate the clinical effectiveness and efficiency of a FOCUS-PDCA quality improvement model involving UAP in improving inpatient physical examinations. A quasi-experimental, historical-control before-and-after study was conducted among 372 patients who received the FOCUS-PDCA quality improvement examination management (the observation group) and another 385 patients under normal management (the control group). Clinical effectiveness and efficiency were compared between the two groups. Compared to the control group, the FOCUS-PDCA group had significantly lower rates of defect examinations (19.6% vs. 44.7%, p < 0.01), nursing interruption events (14.5% vs. 26.4%, p < 0.01), and nurse referral events (6.1% vs. 24.7%, p < 0.01). Furthermore, the FOCUS-PDCA group had higher patient satisfaction (9.04 ± 0.82 vs. 8.45 ± 0.96, p <0.01) lower hospital cost [Median: 29,434.70 RMB (IQR: 9,705.00–52,451.40) vs. 34,537.60 RMB (IQR: 14,689.98–64,222.12), p < 0.001], and shorter length of hospital stay [Median: 4.00 days (IQR: 3.00, 5.00) vs. 5.00 days (IQR: 4.00, 6.00), p < 0.001]. The FOCUS-PDCA model involving UAP was associated with improved clinical effectiveness and efficiency of inpatient physical examination, which may be applied in hospital management to enhance the quality of care and patient outcomes. Further validation in other clinical settings is needed to test its broader application.

title: A New Current Fingerprinting Sensing Method for Adaptive Protection of PV-Integrated Distribution Networks
abstract: Grid-following photovoltaic (PV) inverters inject fault currents whose magnitude and phase are set by the control mode active during the disturbance, so directional overcurrent relay (DOCR) settings coordinated for one inverter response can miscoordinate after a mode change. This paper proposes a communication-free adaptive protection scheme built on local sensing. A voltage-adaptive current fingerprinting classifier uses local positive sequence measurements to detect current-limiting (CL), active current priority (ACP) and reactive current priority (RCP) operation, as well as momentary cessation (MC) and asymmetrical faults. The classifier activates the relay setting group prepared offline for the detected mode. With pickup currents fixed, the coordination sub-problem is shown to be a linear program (LP), so every setting group is computed at its exact global optimum. Where the grid code droop law makes ACP and RCP indistinguishable by angle, the classifier declares the ambiguity and activates a group that is feasible for both. Under a class-0.5 instrument transformer noise model, the group placed in service is coordination-valid in 99.8% of cases and the expected residual miscoordination is 3.0×10-5 s, 0.01% of the 0.30 s margin. On the CIGRE medium-voltage benchmark, the scheme satisfies the margin in all operating modes for three-phase, line-to-line (LL) and single-line-to-ground (SLG) faults. The same fault types are then verified at three fault locations on a practical Egyptian 11 kV feeder model, where the sensing layer is confirmed on an electromagnetic transient (EMT) model and the scheme removes the violations of single-setting coordination using an estimated 4 kB of relay memory.
authors: Ahmed A. Salem; Emad Eldeen Omran; Azza Ahmed Eldesouky; Hany S. E. Mansour; Mohamed A. A. Mohamed; Eyad S. Oda

title: A Qualitative Case Study on the Implementation of an AI-Powered Gait Rehabilitation Robot Program for Students with Severe and Multiple Disabilities
abstract: This qualitative case study explored how an AI-powered gait rehabilitation robot program was implemented over one semester in a special school and how its participants experienced and made sense of it. The bounded case was the program itself; its participants comprised three students with severe and multiple disabilities, the teacher-researcher (a special education teacher), a collaborating physical therapist, and three guardians. Data were collected from multiple sources, including health-management records and assessment sheets, class documents and Individualized Education Program (IEP) team minutes, robot-recorded gait data, semi-structured surveys and interviews, participant-observation logs, and the researcher’s reflexive journal. The data were analyzed through iterative coding, pattern identification, and cross-source comparison, with attention to discrepant data, and trustworthiness was strengthened through triangulation, member checking, and peer debriefing. Three themes were identified. First, the program was implemented within a co-teaching model that connected the special education teacher and the physical therapist across the boundary of education and therapy, and it was organized as a related service through IEP team consultation under the 2022 revised special education curriculum. Second, the participants moved from initial expectation and concern toward a more nuanced appreciation of the program, while also raising practical concerns about safety, sensor limitations, and the burden of responsibility. Third, the students showed uneven but meaningful changes. Although gains on the ordinal functional indicators (MMT, BBS, FAC) were partial or limited to maintenance, clearer changes appeared in confidence, self-efficacy, and social participation. Rather than verifying effectiveness, this case illustrates the possibilities and conditions of school-based AI gait-robot education and points to the need for a sustainable policy and institutional support framework, including the placement of rehabilitation professionals within schools.

title: A Qualitative Examination of Perceptions Surrounding Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation Preferences in Head, Neck, and Lung Cancer Survivors
abstract: Abstract Purpose Head and neck cancer (HNC) and lung cancer (LC) survivors smoke at elevated rates at the time of diagnosis compared to other cancer survivors, and standard cessation interventions show suboptimal efficacy in this population. Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) is FDA-cleared for smoking cessation, and it may also address co-occurring depressive symptoms undermining cessation in cancer survivors. No studies have examined TMS acceptability for smoking cessation in cancer populations. Objective To examine HNC/LC survivors’ perceptions of TMS for smoking cessation as part of the assessment phase of the ADAPT-ITT framework. Methods HNC/LC survivors diagnosed within six months who currently smoked were recruited, and semi-structured interviews (45–60 minutes) were conducted via videoconference. Participants viewed a two-minute TMS educational video midway through the interview. Interview transcripts were analyzed using content and thematic analysis. Results Nine participants (7 head and neck cancer, 2 lung cancer survivors) provided data for this qualitative study. Smoking history ranged from 16 to 87.6 pack-years. Cancer diagnosis increased quit motivation, yet cessation was elusive. Despite no prior TMS knowledge, all nine participants expressed willingness to try TMS after the educational video, citing its non-invasive nature and independence from medications. The primary barrier was the six-week time commitment, with participants open to flexible, shorter treatment protocols. Facilitators included intrinsic motivation, family support, and structured accountability of clinic-based treatment. Participants recommended co-locating TMS with cancer care and providing educational materials through oncology providers. Conclusions HNC/LC survivors were receptive to TMS for smoking cessation after brief education. Findings support proceeding to subsequent ADAPT-ITT phases.

title: A Retensionable Inlay/Onlay Hybrid Double-Bundle Medial Collateral Ligament Reconstruction Produces Superior Restoration of the Uninjured State When Compared to a Single-Bundle Inlay Reconstruction
abstract: Background: Traditional superficial medial collateral ligament (sMCL) reconstruction techniques have not consistently restored native laxity. Purpose/Hypothesis: The purpose of this study was to develop a retensionable inlay/onlay hybrid medial collateral ligament (MCL) reconstruction through comparison to a biomechanically and clinically validated reconstruction. It was hypothesized that increasing the distal footprint on the tibia through a double-bundle construct and a retensionable construct would better restore native laxity. Study Design: Controlled laboratory study. Methods: A total of 27 cadaveric knees were tested on a 6 degrees of freedom robot system. Knees were tested with valgus and external rotation (ER). Each knee was tested in a native state and an injured state after sectioning of the sMCL. One of 3 reconstructions using an anterior tibialis allograft was then performed: (1) single-bundle inlay reconstruction, (2) double-bundle inlay/onlay hybrid reconstruction with tibial fixation at both the proximal and distal (PD) tibial insertions of the sMCL footprint, or (3) double-bundle inlay/onlay hybrid reconstruction with tibial fixation at the anterior and posterior (AP) aspects of the distal sMCL tibial insertion. The constructs used retensionable variable-loop devices, allowing for retensioning after knee cycling. The constructs were tested after cycling and retensioning. Results: Sectioning of the sMCL resulted in significantly increased laxity compared to the native state for both valgus and ER laxity testing ( P < .001). After flexion cycling and subsequent retensioning, both AP and PD double-bundle reconstructions demonstrated significantly higher restoration of stability compared to cycled single-bundle reconstructions ( P < .001). Both double-bundle reconstructions were significantly closer to the native state than the single-bundle reconstruction for valgus rotation ( P < .001) and ER ( P < .05). For valgus testing, there was no difference between retensioned double-bundle constructs and the native state, with a pooled valgus difference of 0.56° (95% CI, 0.05°-1.06°; P = .032). For ER testing, no differences were found between the retensioned AP double-bundle and the native state ( P = .836), suggesting more complete restoration was achieved by AP double-bundle restoration. Conclusion: A retensionable inlay/onlay hybrid double-bundle MCL reconstruction with a larger femoral footprint and 2 distal anterior-posterior tibial footprints produced superior restoration of the uninjured state when compared to a traditional single-bundle inlay reconstruction. For double-bundle reconstructions, an anterior-posterior tibial fixation achieved mean values closer to the native state than proximal-distal fixation. Clinical Relevance: A double-bundle retensionable inlay/onlay hybrid reconstruction is an effective alternative to a single-bundle inlay reconstruction technique. The double-bundle reconstruction may better withstand early unrestricted range of motion during postoperative phases.
authors: Adam William Anz; Garrett Waller; Jeremy D. Carroll; Gabe Colbrunn; Aiden Cole Magoolaghan; Jessi Truett; Achraf Cohen; Mangesh M. Kulkarni; Mark C. Callanan

title: A Review of Robotic Surgery: Engineering Considerations and Future Directions From Surgeons' Perspectives
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Since its initial inception, robotic-assisted minimally invasive surgery (RAMIS) is continually being applied to a wider array of procedures. However, there are significant limitations in current surgical subsystems, including a large learning curve, lack of effective haptic feedback, decreased surgical intuition, and decreased dexterity. METHODS: A narrative review of the literature was conducted to provide an overview of key developments in the field. Relevant articles were identified through searches of PubMed, IEEE, Google Scholar, and EMBASE, along with manual screening of references. RESULTS: A selection of representative articles covering topics including teleoperation, kinematics, dynamics, and haptic feedback is discussed to highlight major themes and recent advances. CONCLUSIONS: Despite recent advances, limitations to operator experience remain. Numerous strategies and approaches are currently being proposed and explored to further advance surgical subsystems, improving dexterity, haptic feedback, movement time delay, and learning curve.

title: A Review of Strip Shape Prediction Methods Transitioning From Mechanistic Models to Interpretable Deep Learning
abstract: Strip shape prediction is a core task in rolling process control, and its accuracy directly impacts product quality and production efficiency. However, complex multivariable nonlinear couplings, dynamic operating conditions, and strong environmental disturbances severely challenge the accuracy and adaptability of traditional mechanistic models. In recent years, machine learning (ML) has provided new pathways to overcome these limitations. Although research achievements are increasingly abundant, the field still lacks a systematic review that integrates technological evolution with industrial application experience. This paper systematically reviews the research progress of ML in strip shape prediction, tracing the evolution from mechanistic modeling to data‐driven approaches. By detailing the core modeling stages and using strip crown, flatness, and key influencing factors as specific contexts, we systematically categorize the functional positioning and applicable scenarios of various ML algorithms. Crucially, we outline their structural limitations in practical deployment, such as “black‐box” unreliability and a lack of physical consistency. Based on this synthesis, the paper explores current industrial bottlenecks and future development directions, specifically highlighting interpretable deep learning, mechanism‐data fusion, and causal inference. Ultimately, this review aims to provide valuable references and insights for academia and industry professionals striving to advance intelligent steel production and enhance process efficiency.

title: A Translational Approach for Treatment of Posterior Cruciate Ligament Injuries: From Foundational Anatomic and Biomechanical Studies to Validated Surgical Outcomes.
abstract: Posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) injuries were historically managed nonsurgically or with primary repairs, owing to limited anatomic knowledge, subjective diagnostic techniques, and nonvalidated reconstructions that frequently failed. We describe a two-decade, bench-to-bedside PCL research pyramid that progressively addressed these deficiencies. Foundational cadaveric work characterized the quantitative anatomy of the PCL, including the anterolateral and posteromedial bundles, yielding reproducible femoral and tibial osseous landmarks for tunnel placement. Robotic biomechanical testing established the codominant contribution of both bundles, optimal graft fixation angles, and the destabilizing influence of posterolateral corner injuries and flat tibial slope. Objective diagnostic methods, such as kneeling PCL stress radiography and posterior tibial translation on MRI, were validated to quantify laxity and detect chronic tears. These insights informed an anatomically grounded double-bundle reconstruction, complemented by multiligament tunnel convergence-avoidance strategies, evidence-based tensioning sequences, and a refined rehabilitation and bracing treatment protocol. Prospective outcome studies confirmed restoration of stability comparable to anterior cruciate ligament reconstructions, demonstrating how integrated translational research transformed treatment of this challenging injury.

title: A first realization of reinforcement learning-based closed-loop EEG-TMS.
abstract: Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) is a powerful tool to investigate neurophysiology of the human brain and treat brain disorders. Traditionally, therapeutic TMS has been applied in a one-size-fits-all approach, disregarding inter- and intraindividual differences. Brain state-dependent EEG-TMS, such as coupling TMS with a pre-specified phase of the sensorimotor μ-rhythm, enables the induction of differential neuroplastic effects depending on the targeted phase. But this approach is still user-dependent as it requires defining an a-priori target phase. Here, we present a first realization of a machine-learning-based, closed-loop real-time EEG-TMS setup to identify user-independently the individual μ-rhythm phase associated with high- vs. low-corticospinal excitability states. We applied EEG-TMS to 25 participants targeting the supplementary motor area- primary motor cortex network and used a reinforcement learning algorithm to identify the μ- rhythm phase associated with high- vs. low corticospinal excitability. We employed linear mixed effects models and Bayesian analysis to assess effects of reinforced learning on corticospinal excitability indexed by motor evoked potential amplitude, and functional connectivity indexed by the imaginary part of resting-state EEG coherence. Our results show that reinforcement learning identified the μ-rhythm phase associated with high- vs. low-excitability states, and their repetitive stimulation resulted in long-term increases vs. decreases in functional connectivity in the stimulated sensorimotor network. Our work demonstrated the feasibility of a reinforcement learning-based adaptive closed-loop EEG-TMS approach in a full experimental cohort, enabling user-independent identification of μ-rhythm phases associated with corticospinal excitability states.
authors: Dania Humaidan; Jiahua Xu; Jing Chen; Christoph Zrenner; David Emanuel Vetter; Laura Marzetti; Paolo Belardinelli; Timo Roine; Risto J Ilmoniemi; Gian Luca Romani; Ulf Ziemann

title: A new semi-automated, motility-based screening assay for discovery of compounds with activity against the juvenile stage of Fasciola hepatica
abstract: Abstract Fasciola hepatica is a trematode parasite responsible for fasciolosis, a liver disease that affects humans and livestock worldwide. Together with other food-borne trematode infections, fasciolosis is considered a neglected tropical disease. Further, it imposes substantial agricultural losses due to infections in ruminants. No vaccine is currently available, and control heavily relies on drug treatment, especially with triclabendazole (TCBZ). However, the intensive use of TCBZ over the past four decades has led to increasing rates of treatment failures and the emergence of drug-resistant parasites. Therefore, the identification of new treatment options is an urgent priority. The currently available toolset for drug screening, however, is limited. To address this need, we established a novel, semi-automated, standardized, and objective screening assay based on motility monitoring of newly excysted juveniles using microscopic live imaging. The assay was validated by testing a panel of ten compounds with known anthelmintic properties, amongst them TCBZ (IC 50 : 1.5 µM) and the new activator of the F. hepatica transient receptor potential melastatin (TRPM) ion channel, benzamidoquinazolinone (IC 50 : 1.05 µM). In addition to these two compounds with known activity against F. hepatica , three compounds were identified as particularly promising with a fast onset of action and IC 50 values in the nanomolar range: the salicylanilides MMV665807 (IC 50 : 44 nM), niclosamide (IC 50 : 32 nM), and its ethanolamine salt, niclosamide ethanolamine (IC 50 : 9 nM). Complementary live/dead staining revealed that only TCBZ displayed parasiticidal activity, while the other compounds, although leading to parasite paralysis, did not lead to parasite death within 72 hours. Scanning electron microscopy of drug treated parasites did not reveal any significant damage at concentrations corresponding to the IC 50 s, but strong phenotypes were visible at 20 µM. The presented motility assay provides a robust method for the discovery of novel anthelmintic compounds and facilitates the ongoing effort to combat fasciolosis. Author Summary Fasciola hepatica , the common liver fluke, is a parasitic platyhelminth that infects the liver and biliary ducts of humans and livestock, causing fasciolosis, a Neglected Tropical Disease as defined by the World Health Organization. Triclabendazole is the drug of choice to treat humans and animals. However, its intensive use has led to the emergence of drug resistance resulting in treatment failures worldwide. The identification of novel drugs is therefore urgent. Here, we present a semi-automated and objective method to assess the activity of compounds on one of the key life stages of the parasite: the newly excysted juveniles (NEJ). This stage is highly motile and motility assessment can be exploited to screen for bioactive compounds. Using time-lapse imaging, we quantified NEJ movement after drug exposure. From a panel of ten tested reference anthelmintics, two known fasciolicides (triclabendazole and benzamidoquinazolinone) and three additional compounds (MMV665807, niclosamide, and niclosamide ethanolamine) displayed particularly strong activity and were selected for further investigation. This method represents a robust tool for drug screening and facilitates the discovery of new compounds against F. hepatica .

title: A normative torque-profile approach for quantifying elbow and wrist flexor hyper-resistance after stroke: a proof-of-principle study
abstract: Abstract Background Post-stroke spasticity is commonly assessed using the Modified Ashworth Scale (MAS), despite its limited objectivity and variable reliability. This study introduces Score E , a novel isokinetic dynamometry-derived metric designed to quantify elbow and wrist flexor hyper-resistance by comparing patients’ torque-angle profiles with a healthy reference corridor. Methods Thirty-five post-stroke patients and twenty-one healthy controls were included. Elbow and wrist hyper-resistance was assessed using the MAS and an isokinetic dynamometer in two testing conditions: seated on the dynamometer chair (ergo chair) and seated in the patient’s wheelchair. Two dynamometer-derived metrics were analyzed: Score E and peak torque (Peakτ). Feasibility, inter-rater and test-retest reliability, and associations with MAS grades were assessed. Exploratory PRE-POST changes following a 10-min local vibration session were also described. Results Score E showed good to excellent inter-rater and test-retest reliability across joints and testing conditions. Inter-rater ICCs ranged from 0.81 to 0.89, and test-retest ICCs from 0.76 to 0.93. Peakτ showed moderate to good reliability. In contrast, MAS agreement was lower and more variable. Score E showed moderate associations with MAS grades, particularly at the elbow, with weaker and less consistent associations at the wrist. MAS assessment was faster, but all assessments were well tolerated, with median pain ratings of 0/10 in all testing conditions. PRE-POST vibration changes were small and heterogeneous, preventing formal assessment of responsiveness. Conclusion Score E provides a reliable, objective, and visually interpretable quantification of post-stroke elbow and wrist flexor hyper-resistance. By comparing the full torque-angle profile with normative data, this approach preserves information on both the magnitude and angular span of abnormal resistance, supporting its potential for targeted longitudinal monitoring.
authors: Sophie Julliand; Davy Laroche; D. Besson; Isabelle Fournel; Louis Riglet; Charalambos Papaxanthis; Jérémie Gaveau

title: A portable biomedical device for post-stroke spasticity assessment: preliminary validation study
abstract: Abstract Purpose This preliminary validation study investigated the feasibility of a portable biomedical device equipped with force and motion sensors for objectively quantifying resistance to passive movement in individuals with chronic post-stroke hemiparesis. The study examined associations between device-derived measurements and clinical spasticity scores obtained using the Modified Ashworth Scale (MAS). Methods Twenty-one individuals with chronic post-stroke hemiparesis were evaluated. MAS grading and device-based measurements were performed simultaneously during the same passive stretch to ensure comparable biomechanical conditions. Synchronized resistance-force and angular-displacement data were recorded during assessments of the shoulder adductors, elbow flexors, and wrist flexors. Associations between device measurements and MAS scores were analyzed using Spearman's rank correlation. Results Strong positive correlations were observed between device-derived resistance measurements and MAS scores for the shoulder adductors (ρ = 0.79, p < 0.001) and elbow flexors (ρ = 0.80, p < 0.001). A moderate correlation was found for the wrist flexors (ρ = 0.47, p = 0.003). Conclusion The findings provide preliminary evidence of concurrent associations between quantitative resistance measurements and MAS scores, supporting the device's feasibility as an adjunct tool for objective biomechanical assessment of post-stroke spasticity. However, larger studies incorporating independent blinded examiners, repeated measurements, and formal reliability analyses are necessary to establish its measurement properties and clinical applicability.

title: A reproducible safety assessment model for concurrent transcranial magnetic stimulation with implanted intracranial electroencephalography electrodes
abstract: BACKGROUND: Concurrent transcranial magnetic stimulation and intracranial EEG (TMS-sEEG) offers a powerful approach for interrogating human brain circuits with high spatiotemporal resolution. However, standardized safety testing procedures for TMS in the presence of implanted electrodes are lacking. OBJECTIVE: To establish and validate a reproducible methodological framework for assessing TMS safety with sEEG hardware, addressing potential risks of electrode displacement, heating, and secondary current induction. METHODS: A conductive agarose phantom implanted with clinical-grade platinum sEEG electrodes was exposed to single-pulse TMS (0.4 Hz), repetitive TMS (1-50 Hz), and intermittent theta burst stimulation. Electrode displacement was quantified via high-speed video and motion tracking. Temperature changes were measured with fiber-optic thermal probes positioned at stimulated electrode contacts. Induced voltages were recorded using an oscilloscope and intracranial EEG hardware, and secondary current and charge density were calculated from oscilloscope outputs and impedance measurements. RESULTS: sEEG lead displacement remained micrometer-scale across stimulation conditions, with a maximum transient displacement of 10.99 μm and a maximum 1-s mean displacement from the pre-TMS position of 16.27 μm. Temperature changes remained well within the 2°C safety threshold across all tested conditions; in the primary temperature series, the maximum observed increase was 0.073°C. Induced voltages and charge densities remained below established safety limits, exhibiting consistent exponential decay with increasing distance from the coil. All stimulation conditions, including those exceeding typical clinical ranges, remained well within safety margins. CONCLUSIONS: Under the tested conditions in a controlled phantom environment, TMS exposure produced micrometer-scale transient and longer-timescale displacement, temperature changes within established safety thresholds, and charge densities within established safety thresholds. This validated methodological pipeline provides a standardized framework for future safety experiments involving TMS and implanted devices and supports continued development of TMS-sEEG as a tool for studying human brain circuitry and neuromodulation.

title: A scenario-adaptive AHP-FCE framework for lithium-ion battery thermal management: Optimal strategy selection in energy storage, supercars, and marine propulsion
abstract: The suitability of lithium-ion battery thermal management strategies (TMSs) varies substantially across operating conditions and engineering constraints, limiting the effectiveness of single-metric or fixed-weight evaluation methods. This study develops a scenario-adaptive framework integrating the Analytic Hierarchy Process and Fuzzy Comprehensive Evaluation (AHP-FCE). The framework comprises four primary criteria (technical performance, economic viability, environmental safety, and sustainability) and 15 secondary indicators, with scenario-specific weights and evaluation boundaries established for energy storage systems (ESS), electric supercars (ESC), and electric propulsion ships (EPS). Among the evaluated candidates, single-phase immersion cooling, two-phase immersion cooling, and single-phase cold-plate cooling rank first for ESS, ESC, and EPS, with adaptability scores of 0.894, 0.930, and 0.885, respectively, highlighting the scenario dependence of TMS selection. Robustness analyses confirm the overall stability of these recommendations, although the ESC ranking is more sensitive to the weighting method. An external techno-economic benchmark further supports the engineering plausibility of the ESS recommendation. The proposed framework provides a transparent and interpretable quantitative basis for preliminary TMS screening and scenario-specific engineering decision-making.
authors: Xiaoyu Wang; Yanshun Yu; Zhihang Wang; Tengfang Chen

title: A story for Pepper and Nao: applying the learning by teaching paradigm in children with patterns of neuromotor impairment
abstract: Background Social robots are increasingly used in educational and clinical contexts to enhance engagement and learning, particularly in children with neurological and neurodevelopmental disorders. The Learning by Teaching paradigm, in which children actively teach social robots, promotes cognitive and metacognitive processes such as planning, self-efficacy, and executive functioning; however, controlled and systematic evidence supporting its effectiveness remains limited. Children with neuromotor disorders frequently present with closely intertwined motor and cognitive planning difficulties, which significantly impact learning and everyday functioning. In this context, social robot–mediated interventions based on the Learning by Teaching paradigm may represent a promising approach. The current multicenter randomized controlled trial (RCT) explores the feasibility and effectiveness of this approach to enhance cognitive and motor planning in children with neuromotor impairments, and to examine potential generalization effects on other cognitive domains and engagement. Methods The main aim of this RCT study is to evaluate the feasibility and effectiveness of a social robot-mediated Learning by Teaching intervention in children aged 7–16 years with neuromotor impairments. Eighty participants will be randomly assigned to an Experimental Group (EG) receiving social robot training or to a Control Group (CG) continuing standard care. The intervention consists of 20–25 sessions in which children teach a humanoid social robot (Pepper or NAO) to order picture-based stories of increasing complexity. Assessments will be performed at baseline (T0), post-intervention or control period (T1), and follow-up/post-treatment (T2). Primary outcomes include planning abilities assessed through picture arrangement and an ad hoc motor planning task. Secondary outcomes encompass executive functions, visuo-spatial memory, attention, inhibition, narrative production, visual-perceptual skills, and reading comprehension. Engagement will be measured using a multimodal approach integrating behavioral, cognitive, emotional, and physiological indicators derived from video, audio, and wearable sensors. Results The study will examine improvements in planning and motor programming abilities and potential generalization effects on executive functions and reading comprehension. Additionally, the predictive and mediating role of engagement in intervention effectiveness will be reported. Conclusions This research protocol proposes an innovative, engagement-focused rehabilitation approach integrating cognitive, motor, and narrative processes through social robotics. Findings are expected to inform the development of evidence-based, personalized interventions for children with neuromotor disorders and to advance methodological approaches for assessing engagement in human–robot interaction. Clinical Trial Registration ClinicalTrials.gov , identifier NCT06797050.

title: A study on Critical Factors for Blockchain Adoption in India: Analytic Hierarchy Process
abstract: Blockchain technology (BCT) has attracted a lot of attention because of its technological characteristics that improve the security, transparency, and operational efficiency of organizations. However, several considerations should be taken into account while evaluating its adoption. The aim of this study is to define and prioritize the factors influencing the adoption of BCT by organizations in India using Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) methodology. Five dimensions and nineteen sub-factors were evaluated using a literature review and interviews with experts. The results indicate that technology factors have the greatest impact on the adoption of blockchain, followed by organizational factors and regulatory factors. The most significant sub-factors were: security and privacy, relative advantage, and top management support. The study provides valuable implications for organizations and policymakers to address the challenges of successful implementation of blockchain and digital transformation initiatives.
