title: ADAPTIVE RISK MANAGEMENT IN INTERNATIONAL TRANSPORTATION AS A FACTOR IN ENHANCING ENTERPRISE COMPETITIVENESS
abstract: The article examines the specifics of risk management in international road transport within the context of a highly uncertain and dynamic transport environment. It substantiates the need to shift from reactive and proactive risk management to an adaptive approach, which entails continuous monitoring of changes, forecasting, the prompt adjustment of management decisions, and the use of digital technologies. The aim of the article is to substantiate an adaptive approach to risk management in international road transport and to develop a conceptual model for its implementation, focused on creating competitive advantages for road transport enterprises. The study systematizes the differences between reactive, proactive, and adaptive approaches to risk management based on objectives, the nature of managerial decision-making, tools, the level of digital technology adoption, flexibility, and the capacity to respond to new risks. It establishes that adaptive management combines the advantages of reactive and proactive approaches, entailing continuous monitoring of changes, real-time information updates, forecasting, dynamic adjustment of management decisions, and the use of digital technologies. External, internal, and integrated risks associated with international road transport are systematized, and corresponding adaptive response strategies are identified. It is proposed that risks be viewed not merely as sources of potential loss but as objects of management; an effective response to them can transform risk management outcomes into competitive advantages for the enterprise. A conceptual model of adaptive risk management has been developed, based on the cyclical interaction of monitoring, analysis, forecasting, decision-making, and feedback. A distinctive feature of the model is the integration of information regarding risk events, development scenarios, and the outcomes of implemented management measures, thereby creating the conditions for the continuous enhancement of the management system's adaptability. It has been demonstrated that adaptive risk management contributes to ensuring the continuity of the transport process, enhancing delivery reliability and quality, optimizing resource utilization, strengthening client and partner trust, and building long-term competitive advantages.
authors: Олена Михайлівна Ложачевська; Yulia Malakhova

title: ARAM: a threshold model for understanding occupant acceptance of architectural robot adaptations
abstract: Physical interior elements are increasingly becoming roboticised to support occupant needs. Partitions, ceilings, and furniture can now physically and autonomously change shape or move to architecturally “adapt” indoor spaces, with the aim of improving occupant comfort, satisfaction, and wellbeing. However, occupants sometimes reject these adaptations when they are perceived as disruptive, unpredictable, or difficult to control. Motivated by the goal of making architectural robots more acceptable, we involved an interdisciplinary team of experts in human-building interaction, human-robot interaction, psychology, anthropology, and human comfort to qualitatively re-analyze how occupants accepted adaptations across three previous studies on robotic partitions. We found that an occupant tended to accept an adaptation when they recognized a personal need that the architectural robot was capable of addressing in a socially justifiable way. Accordingly, we developed the Architectural Robot Acceptance Model (ARAM), in which three qualitative thresholds along a continuum of perceived stress severity define four distinct acceptance responses to a specific adaptation. As the positions of these thresholds may vary across occupants and situations, ARAM supports testable estimates of how an occupant may respond to different appraisal states of personal need, adaptation capability, and social justification. Because architectural robot adaptations may simultaneously be experienced as robotic behaviors, building automation, and socially situated environmental adjustments, ARAM is particularly relevant to individual adaptations that enter occupants' spatial experience and may affect co-located others. We then discuss how the model can inform situated estimates of occupant acceptance of architectural robot adaptations, and outline how its broader relevance to other robotic, automated, intelligent, and smart technologies embedded in the built environment may be evaluated in future work.
authors: Alex Binh Vinh Duc Nguyen; Rania Christoforou; Ilaria Pigliautile; Verônica Martins Gnecco; Anja Pogladič; Sara Arko; Anna Laura Pisello; Davide Schaumann; Marcel Schweiker; Andrew Vande Moere

title: AS-ULDAR: a ROS 2-based collaborative robotic platform for upper-limb rehabilitation — systems integration and pilot usability evaluation in a clinical environment
abstract: Robotic rehabilitation can increase the intensity and personalization of upper-limb therapy, but its clinical translation is hindered by the difficulty of integrating individually validated technical components into a single clinician-ready platform. This paper presents a platform which is intended to be an Auto-calibrating System for Upper Limb Disability Assessment and Rehabilitation (AS-ULDAR), a ROS 2-based platform built around a Franka Emika Panda robot that unifies motor/cognitive assessment, sensorless force estimation, and Cartesian and Human Joint-based Trajectory Tracking within a clinician-oriented GUI. While these functionalities were individually validated in prior work, the present contribution lies in their systems-level integration and in identifying the operational barriers that emerge when deploying such a platform in a real clinical workflow, targeting adult patients with chronic neurological conditions (stroke, Parkinson’s, ALS, MCI) and mild-to-moderate upper-limb impairment. The platform was evaluated through a formative usability study: the standalone GUI by five naïve users, and the complete system by seven physiotherapists performing the full clinical workflow (no patients were involved; clinical efficacy is outside this scope). The system was technically stable throughout. Usability (SUS) was high for the GUI (87.5 ± 1.8) but markedly lower and more heterogeneous for the complete platform (54 ± 16), with feedback pointing to robot setup and workflow operation—not interface design—as the main friction points for clinical staff. These results show that integrating multiple rehabilitation functionalities is technically feasible, but that usability must be treated as a system-level property, and they provide concrete operational lessons for the clinical translation of cobot-based rehabilitation platforms.

title: Academic Stress and Self-Regulation Skills among High School Mathematics Learners
abstract: Academic stress is one of the serious issues in mathematics education that is likely to undermine student performance and motivation. This study examines the relationship between academic stress and self-regulation skills among high school mathematics learners, focusing on how self-regulation can prevent the adverse effects of stress and enhance academic performance. With a descriptive-correlational research design, the research sampled 300 high school students from private schools in Davao City for the academic year 2024–2025. Data were collected using validated Likert-scale questionnaires to measure academic stress (e.g., teaching methods, parental expectations, and exam results) and self-regulation skills (planning, self-checking, effort, and self-efficacy). Statistical analysis indicated a significant negative correlation between academic stress and self-regulation skills. Among the stress indicators, only class tests and content difficulty stress showed a considerable relationship with self-regulation. These findings support the necessity to address these particular sources of stress in building resilience and improving performance in mathematics. Therefore, the study recommends that educational institutions emphasize developing interventions for reducing academic stress and enhancing student self-regulation through structured learning strategies, well-rounded support systems, and alternative assessment methods. Moreover, involving parents in nurturing supportive learning environments is essential. Future research should investigate the relative effect of digital tools and institutional policies for maintaining lower stress levels and improving academic self-regulation across diverse educational contexts. Addressing academic stress is crucial for fostering a positive learning environment and improving student achievements in mathematics education.

title: Accelerated TMS is associated with changes of subgenual cingulate–default mode network coupling in depression: an observational 7 Tesla fMRI study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Accelerated transcranial magnetic stimulation (aTMS) is an effective treatment for depression, but its neurobiological mechanisms of action remain to be elucidated. This study used high-resolution 7-Tesla MRI to investigate changes in resting-state functional connectivity (rs-FC) of the subgenual anterior cingulate cortex (sgACC) following a treatment series of aTMS. We hypothesized a decrease in sgACC rs-FC with key cortical regions of the default mode network (DMN), reflecting a downregulation of a network that is overactive in depression. METHODS: Twenty-two patients with current depression underwent 7-Tesla MRI scans before and after a two-week aTMS treatment series (24,000 pulses) targeting the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. Fourteen healthy participants were also scanned twice as a control group. Longitudinal changes in sgACC seed-based rs-FC were compared between groups. Furthermore, group differences were assessed at baseline and at follow-up. Exploratory correlations between longitudinal changes in sgACC rs-FC, depression severity, mindfulness, and affect were also evaluated. RESULTS: There was a reduction in rs-FC between the sgACC and bilateral precunei, and between sgACC and left frontal pole in patients receiving aTMS. At baseline, patients had increased rs‑FC between the sgACC and a cluster including the left precuneus and a cluster in the right superior frontal gyrus. Exploratory correlations suggest an association between sgACC-precunei rs-FC changes and mindfulness (p = 0.008, uncorrected for multiple comparisons), while no associations were found with depression severity or affect. CONCLUSIONS: Treatment with aTMS is associated with a reduction in rs‑FC between the sgACC and the DMN. Exploratory correlations with mindfulness warrant replication in larger, independent samples.
authors: Tobias Bracht; Pascal Borel; Stefan Dendorfer; Leila Maria Soravia; Kristina Adorjan; Sebastian Walther; Andrea Federspiel; Roland Wiest; Gianluca Andri Florineth; Niklaus Denier

title: Active Function Improvement with Repeated Injections of Botulinum Toxin A in Upper Limb Spasticity: A Longitudinal Analysis from the ULIS-III Study
abstract: Improvement in active function (making it easier to use the limb) is a common goal following treatment of upper limb spasticity with botulinum toxin (BoNT-A). ULIS-III was a large international, observational, longitudinal study (N = 953) conducted in the context of usual clinical practice over two years. In this secondary post hoc analysis, we examine whether goals for improvement in active function were met over repeated injection cycles. Patients were selected if improved active function (AF) was a primary/secondary goal for at least one cycle of treatment (n = 286/953). They were assessed at the start and end of each cycle using the Goal Attainment T-score alongside the Arm Activity measure (ArmA). Serial changes and predictors of improvement were explored. Across eight cycles, there were 1167 injections for active function, 875/1998 (44%) AF goals were set and 493 (57%) of those goals were achieved. Patients continued to show significant improvement in AF (p < 0.001) for each injection at least up to three cycles, which is likely to be clinically significant, especially in patients with milder spasticity who were naïve to BoNT-A. No statistically significant predictors were confirmed on mixed effects modeling. Conclusions: Repeated BoNT-A continued to produce significant improvement in active function for at least three cycles, regardless of patient- or treatment-related factors in this cohort, but type II errors due to small numbers cannot be excluded.
authors: Stephen A. Ashford; Mark Weatherall; Klemens Fheodoroff; Jorge Jacinto; Richard John Siegert; Christian Hannes; Lynne F. Turner‐Stokes

title: Advances in integrated surgical and rehabilitation treatment for cerebral palsy
abstract: Cerebral palsy (CP) is a group of motor disorders caused by non-progressive brain injury during development, often accompanied by sensory, cognitive, and behavioral impairments. It remains one of the most common causes of childhood disability. In recent years, the coordinated integration of surgical intervention and rehabilitation has transitioned from a conceptual framework to clinical practice, becoming a core strategy for improving patient function. However, integrated treatment still faces major bottlenecks: insufficient bridging between treatment phases, lack of individualized protocols, and inconsistent outcome measures. This review examines recent advances in integrated surgical and rehabilitative care for CP, covering four core domains: spasticity management (selective dorsal rhizotomy, botulinum toxin injection) with sequential rehabilitation; deformity correction (tendon lengthening, osteotomy) with biomechanically guided individualized rehabilitation; neuromodulation (deep brain stimulation, transcranial magnetic stimulation) with neuroplasticity-targeted training; and emerging technologies including robotic-assisted therapy, artificial intelligence, and digital therapeutics. Surgery creates the anatomical foundation for function; rehabilitation determines the ultimate functional value of surgery. The temporal coordination and strategic synergy between the two are critical for maximizing functional improvement. Future efforts should focus on establishing unified outcome measures for integrated treatment, promoting early intervention combined with regenerative medicine, and leveraging AI to shift from experience-driven to data-driven precision therapy.
authors: Zherui Zhang; Lou Li; Kezhi Li; Chuanxin Yu; Qinchuan Du; Zhiyan Hu; Xiaochao Yu; Jin Zhang; Jun Hu; Yucheng Zhou

title: Agreement and Systematic Differences Between Intraoperative ROSA Hip-Knee-Ankle Measurements and Standing Radiographic Alignment After Robotic-Assisted Total Knee Arthroplasty: A Retrospective Agreement Study
abstract: Background/Objectives: Intraoperative robotic hip-knee-ankle angle (HKA) measurements are obtained with the patient supine under operative conditions and may not directly represent postoperative standing weight-bearing alignment. This study quantified the correspondence and systematic differences between intraoperative ROSA HKA and standing radiographic HKA after robotic-assisted total knee arthroplasty. Methods: This retrospective single-center study included 208 knees from 178 consecutive patients, including 30 bilateral patients. The primary comparison was post-trial-component intraoperative ROSA HKA versus postoperative standing radiographic HKA; the secondary comparison was pre-cut intraoperative ROSA HKA versus preoperative standing radiographic HKA. Patient-cluster bootstrap confidence intervals used 10,000 resamples. Agreement was evaluated using Bland–Altman analysis, absolute-agreement ICC(A,1), and weighted kappa; Spearman ρ described association. Results: For the primary comparison, mean bias (ROSA minus radiographic HKA) was −1.75° (95% CI −2.08 to −1.43°), conventional limits of agreement were −6.36° to 2.85°, and ICC(A,1) was 0.472 (95% CI 0.379 to 0.557). Differences were within 3° in 70.2% of knees and exceeded 3° in 29.8%; proportional bias was present (slope −0.569, p < 0.001). The secondary comparison showed bias 0.97° and ICC(A,1) 0.956. Exact femoral and tibial size agreement was 42.3% and 80.8%, respectively. The standardized surgeon-entered 10 mm starting value was retained in 57.7% of knees. These systematic and angle-dependent differences may partly reflect the differing loading, positioning, and measurement conditions between the intraoperative trial construct and postoperative standing radiography. Conclusions: Post-trial-component ROSA HKA showed systematic and angle-dependent differences from postoperative standing HKA and should not be considered interchangeable with, or a fixed patient-level predictor of, postoperative standing alignment.
authors: Wei-Cheng Tseng; Ching‐Heng Lin; Yu-Tsung Lin; Cheng‐Chi Wang; Kao‐Chang Tu; Kun-Hui Chen; Cheng-Hung Lee; Cheng-Jung Ho; Chung‐Yuh Tzeng

title: An EEG-informed fNIRS framework uncovers stage-associated cortical dynamics during unassisted upper-limb movement after stroke
abstract: Abstract Background Upper-limb impairment after stroke is primarily characterized by the emergence and resolution of spastic synergies. Brunnstrom staging captures these recovery phases and provides a clinically grounded framework for studying cortical reorganization. Applying functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) during ecological gross-motor tasks introduces task-related systemic hemodynamic artifacts that obscure focal cortical signals. This study aims to determine whether an EEG-informed multimodal framework can effectively mitigate these artifacts and extract stage-sensitive patterns of cortical reorganization. Methods After multimodal quality control, 32 participants with stroke (Brunnstrom stages III–VI) and 15 healthy controls were enrolled. EEG and fNIRS were recorded simultaneously during an auditory-cued unilateral arm-raising task with concomitant fist clenching, comprising movement initiation, sustained elevation, and rest. Our framework combined Filter Bank Common Spatial Pattern (FBCSP) with an EEG-informed General Linear Model (GLM). FBCSP extracted focal sensorimotor features, while EEG-derived motor-intention regressors improved GLM modeling of task-related hemodynamic responses. Model performance was evaluated using R ² and ΔAIC, and feature discriminability using AUC from a linear discriminant analysis (LDA) classifier. Results The proposed FBCSP-GLM framework demonstrated improved model fit and spatial discriminability compared with conventional analytical approaches. Participant-level FBCSP estimates revealed a distinct non-linear, stage-associated trajectory of cortical reorganization. Specifically, the FBCSP-derived EW-LI significantly decreased from 0.46 at Stage III to − 0.55 at Stage IV, and rebounded to 0.13 at Stage V. The target-M1 response t -score similarly dropped from − 0.06 to − 1.05 before increasing to 0.85 at Stage V (all FDR-corrected q < 0.01). The standard GLM did not capture these stage-associated patterns, as its corresponding comparisons did not survive FDR correction. Conclusions By improving hemodynamic model fit during ecological gross-motor execution, the EEG-informed multimodal framework reveals cortical reorganization patterns associated with post-stroke synergistic recovery stages. Its artifact-resilient EW-LI and target-M1 response t -score provide a robust computational assessment of neural state transitions.
authors: 王鸣阳; Xiaojuan Chen; Zhenlan Li; Yulin Gong

title: Anatomic Anterolateral Ligament Reconstruction Using the Iliotibial Band Results in Less Internal Rotation Constraint and Lateral Compartment Joint Loading As Compared With the Modified Lemaire Procedure: A Robotic Biomechanical Study
abstract: Background: While current anterolateral complex knee procedures have been demonstrated to reduce anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) graft failures, concerns about potential lateral compartment overload are present. Purpose: To compare lateral compartment pressures and knee laxity between an anterolateral ligament reconstruction (ALLR) using the iliotibial band and the modified Lemaire lateral extra-articular tenodesis (LET) procedure by biomechanically testing for anterior tibial translation, a simulated pivot shift, and internal rotation (IR). Study Design: Controlled laboratory study. Methods: Seven paired cadaveric knees were utilized for this study. A 6 degrees of freedom robotic system was used to measure anterior tibial translation with an 88-N anterior drawer load, IR with a 5-N·m torque, and a simulated pivot-shift test using 5-N·m IR and 10-N·m valgus torques. Force sensors inserted under the lateral meniscus measured lateral compartment pressure during the simulated pivot shift. All specimens were tested in 3 states: intact, anterior cruciate ligament cut, and ACLR. The specimen pairs were then randomized to either an anatomic ALLR technique or a modified Lemaire LET. Results: When compared with the ALLR cohort, the modified Lemaire LET cohort had significantly increased lateral compartment peak pressure at 30° ( P = .047) and significantly decreased IR at all flexion angles (all P < .05). For the modified Lemaire cohort, lateral compartment peak contact pressures were significantly increased versus the intact and ACLR states at 30° of flexion, and IR was significantly decreased as compared with the intact state at 30°, 45°, and 90° during IR testing (all P < .05). For the ALLR cohort specifically, lateral compartment peak contact pressures were not significantly different from intact and ACLR states, and IR was significantly increased relative to the intact state at 30°, 45°, and 60° during IR testing (all P < .05). Conclusions: Lateral compartment peak contact pressure was restored to near intact values with an ALLR using the posterior third of the iliotibial band, while the modified Lemaire LET led to significantly increased pressures. Additionally, the modified Lemaire LET led to decreased IR at all flexion angles, while the ALLR had significantly increased IR between 30° and 60° of flexion. Clinical Relevance: Reconstruction of the anterolateral ligament using the posterior third of the iliotibial band is an option for knees requiring an anterolateral complex procedure. Modified Lemaire LET leads to increased lateral compartment pressures and decreased IR; however, no negative long-term outcomes of overconstraint have been agreed on in the literature.

title: Anatomical correlates of delivered TIS fields across deep and cortical targets
abstract: OBJECTIVE: The objective of this study was to quantify inter-individual variability in target-region TIS envelope amplitude and to examine its associations with anatomical features across deep and cortical targets. APPROACH: We built individualized finite element head models for 502 healthy HCP participants aged 22-35 years and evaluated five target ROI-montage pairs: hippocampus (two montages), left and right thalamus, and motor cortex. For each target ROI-montage pair, we quantified mean TIS envelope amplitude within target region (EA mean , V/m) and the target-to-brain envelope-amplitude ratio (TBR) as measures of target-field magnitude and spatial selectivity, respectively. Two prespecified global volume ratios were assessed with Pearson correlations, and 20 anatomical features were evaluated using two-stage LASSO-OLS models with an 80:20 internal hold-out split. Bootstrap selection frequencies were calculated for the EA mean models. MAIN RESULTS: EA mean showed substantial inter-individual variability (CV = 28.1-40.0%). Brain-TIV ratio and GM-head ratio were positively correlated with EA mean across all five target ROI-montage pairs (r = 0.281-0.420; all p < 0.001), with directions compatible with CSF-related current shunting. Pairwise EA mean correlations across the five target ROI-montage pairs were high (r = 0.749-0.957). Five two-stage LASSO-OLS models yielded in-sample R 2 values of 0.185-0.282. For TBR, MC1 showed the strongest model fit (R 2 = 0.311; hold-out R 2 = 0.267), while no predictor reached p < 0.05 in either thalamic model. Global predictors appeared repeatedly in the deep-target models. In MC1, the significant set also included skull-head ratio and W-scalp thickness (MC1), neither of which was significant in the deep-target models. The two hippocampal montages (H1 and H2) differed by 31% in EA mean , and their predictor sets reaching OLS p < 0.05 showed modest overlap (Jaccard = 0.33). SIGNIFICANCE: This population-scale computational dosimetry analysis quantifies how fixed TIS currents and montages translate into target-field magnitudes across individual head models. The results distinguish the anatomical correlates of delivered amplitude from those of spatial selectivity and provide quantitative information for anatomy-informed TIS planning.
authors: Tianxiang Guo; SuiPing Zhou

title: Aperiodic neural activity predicts cortical excitability in TMS-EEG
abstract:
Background

Fluctuating cortical excitability states are inherent to and critical for brain function. They can be probed non-invasively using transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) combined with electroencephalography (EEG) by measuring early local TMS-evoked potentials (EL-TEPs). Pre-stimulus periodic neural activity can predict fluctuating excitability states. To what extent aperiodic neural activity represents a marker of cortical excitability has not been explored.

Objectives

We investigated the relationship between pre-stimulus aperiodic and periodic neural activity and EL-TEP amplitude in both the primary motor cortex (M1) and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC).

Methods

Single-pulse TMS was delivered to the left M1 or left DLPFC in 29 and 11 healthy adults, respectively, while EEG was recorded simultaneously. Pre-stimulus EEG was parameterized into aperiodic and periodic components to extract the aperiodic exponent (slope of 1/f-like activity), alpha power (8–13 Hz), and beta power (13–30 Hz). EL-TEP peak-to-peak amplitudes were extracted from approximately 20-65 ms after the TMS pulse.

Results

Aperiodic exponent showed a strong negative relationship with EL-TEP amplitude in both M1 and DLPFC, with steeper 1/f-like slopes associated with smaller EL-TEP amplitudes. Inconsistent relationships were found between alpha and beta power with EL-TEP amplitude across the two regions.

Conclusions

These findings indicate that pre-stimulus aperiodic neural activity influences cortical excitability in both motor and prefrontal areas. Notably, the aperiodic exponent exhibited stronger associations with cortical excitability compared to periodic alpha or beta power. Brain-state-dependent protocols may benefit from real-time extraction of aperiodic exponent as a target feature to improve the precision and efficacy of TMS.

Highlights

Pre-stimulus aperiodic exponent predicts EL-TEP amplitude in M1 and DLPFC. Larger aperiodic exponent is associated with smaller EL-TEP amplitudes. Periodic alpha and beta power do not consistently influence EL-TEP amplitude. Aperiodic exponent may inform brain-state-dependent and closed-loop TMS.
authors: van Hattem T, Hougland JR, Gogulski J, Gordon PC, Belardinelli P, Ziemann U.

title: Applications of non-invasive brain stimulation in the treatment of children with cerebral palsy: a narrative review
abstract: Noninvasive brain stimulation has emerged as a promising adjunctive strategy for pediatric neurorehabilitation, particularly for children with cerebral palsy. This narrative review, informed by a structured literature search, summarizes current evidence on transcranial direct current stimulation and repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation in children with cerebral palsy, with emphasis on neurophysiological mechanisms, brain network targets, clinical outcomes, safety, and future translational directions. Cerebral palsy is a heterogeneous neurodevelopmental condition characterized by persistent motor impairment and frequent sensory, cognitive, communicative, behavioral, and musculoskeletal comorbidities. Although multidisciplinary rehabilitation remains the foundation of clinical management, improvements in higher level motor control, cognition, communication, and real world participation are often constrained by training intensity, adherence, developmental heterogeneity, and resource availability. Neuroimaging and electrophysiological studies indicate that children with cerebral palsy may present with corticospinal tract impairment, altered cerebellar thalamic cortical circuitry, interhemispheric inhibitory imbalance, and atypical development of frontoparietal executive control and language related networks. These findings provide a rationale for targeting the primary motor cortex, dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, and selected language related cortices with neuromodulatory interventions. At the mechanistic level, transcranial direct current stimulation and repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation may influence cortical excitability, NMDA receptor mediated long term potentiation and long term depression like plasticity, interhemispheric inhibition, and functional connectivity within distributed neural networks. Current evidence from small to moderate sized randomized trials and recent systematic reviews suggests that these techniques, when combined with task specific rehabilitation, may provide additional benefits for gross motor function, gait, balance, upper limb dexterity, spasticity, and selected cognitive, dual task, and communication outcomes. Available data also suggest acceptable short term safety and tolerability when appropriate pediatric screening and recommended stimulation parameters are applied. This review summarizes the current research progress on noninvasive brain stimulation in children with cerebral palsy and highlights its potential value for optimizing individualized neurorehabilitation strategies and improving motor, cognitive, and communication related outcomes.
authors: Ce Wang; Yuqiu Jia; Xiaoyan Ding; Dandan Wang; Qing Shi; 詹莎莎; Zhicheng Bao; Lei Huang

title: AquaMend: Minimal Re-probing and Conditional Rollback for Latent-Belief Failures in Embodied Agents
abstract: Physical changes or sensing errors can invalidate embodied agents' task-relevant beliefs. AquaMend compares re-probing, rollback, and supported continuation on a probe-belief-action graph under an expected-loss objective covering sensing, physical recovery, and uncorrected failures. A joint posterior guides a one-step policy with conditional detection-power screening. The per-belief three-way optimum requires independence, separability, and fully resolving probes; the general policy has no global optimality guarantee. Across 32 paired scenarios in a self-constructed simulation benchmark, AquaMend recovers in 28/32 cases and reduces mean complete loss by 21.6% versus restart. Its paired loss difference from decision-theoretic troubleshooting (DTT) is not statistically significant after Holm correction. Against the all-candidate ablation, online decision time decreases by 12.3% overall but increases by 3.4% in the uncovered late stage.
authors: Yufan Liu; Shang Luo; Yang Liu; Haoxuan Jia; Feiyu Han; Qian Li; Chen Li; Yingguang Yang; Chongyang Zhang; Hao Zheng; Kefu Xu; Bin Chong

title: Are We All Seeing the Same Gaps while performing robotic TKA? An Inter-operator Variability Study
abstract: Objectives: To evaluate the inter-operator variability in manual ligament laxity assessment, specifically varus/valgus stress angles and medial/lateral gap measurements, during robotic-assisted total knee arthroplasty (rTKA) using the ROSA® Knee system, and to determine its impact on femoral component sizing agreement. Methods: In a comparative cross-sectional study, 21 patients underwent rTKA with the ROSA® Knee system. Two surgeons (lead surgeon and first assistant) independently performed anatomical landmark registration and gap assessments in extension (0°) and flexion (90°) under varus and valgus stress before ligament release. Absolute differences between measurements were calculated, and paired t-tests assessed statistical significance. Pearson correlation coefficients (R) evaluated agreement for stress angles and gap measurements. Cohen’s kappa determined inter-observer agreement for Artificial Intelligence ROSA® Knee system suggested femoral component size. Results: Strong correlations were found between operators for varus/valgus stress angles in extension (R=0.91 and 0.77, p<0.01) and flexion (R=0.46 and 0.53, p<0.05), and for medial/lateral extension gaps (R=0.59 and 0.52, p<0.01). However, no significant correlation was observed for medial/lateral flexion gaps (R=0.23 and 0.10, p>0.05). Mean discrepancies in stress angles ranged from 1.7° to 3.5°. Femoral component sizing showed substantial agreement (κ=0.70, 95% CI: 0.41–0.92). Conclusion: Inter-operator variability in manual gap assessment during rTKA is low in extension but significantly higher in flexion, likely due to inconsistent force application and the absence of a reproducible stop. Despite this variability, femoral component sizing agreement remains substantial. Standardized force application protocols and enhanced robotic feedback in flexion are recommended to improve reproducibility and surgical outcomes.
authors: P. Meneguetti Filho; W.G. Lemos; T.V.D.O. Campos; M.L. Leite; R.S. Lazzarini; G.C. Rodrigues

title: Artificial Intelligence in European Healthcare
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted tools and systems are increasingly being applied and offer substantial potential for innovation across many scientific and societal fields.At the same time, appropriate policy guidance and regulation are crucial to ensure that the benefits of innovation are realised while effectively addressing the risks associated with implementing AI applications.Given this overall challenge of leveraging AI innovations for the benefit of society while simultaneously managing potential risks, AI developments in healthcare and public health bring specific opportunities, questions, and requirements.Therefore, with this report, the European Academies Science Advisory Council (EASAC) and the Federation of European Academies of Medicine (FEAM) aim to present a high-level, accessible overview of the opportunities and risks of AI systems in healthcare and focused recommendations.The intention is to assist European policy-makers -and other policy stakeholders -in promoting responsible innovation by formulating and implementing evidence-based policies, while ensuring appropriate methodological, ethical, security, and regulatory safeguards.The report therefore frames AI in healthcare as both an opportunity and a governance challenge.Its focus is on professional health and public-health uses of AI in Europe, including clinical care, population health, health-system management, and selected policy-relevant parts of medicines development, rather than on every possible consumer or wellness application of AI. Understanding AI systemsFor the purposes of this report, and given that the intended audience includes European Union (EU) policy-makers, we use the definition of an 'AI system' set out in the EU AI Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Article 3(1): 'A machine-based system designed to operate with varying levels of autonomy and that may exhibit adaptiveness after deployment, and that, for explicit or implicit objectives, infers, from the input it receives, how to generate outputs such as predictions, content, recommendations, or decisions that can influence physical or virtual environments.'This definition is part of the AI Act, which entered into force on 1 August 2024, with its provisions applying in phases from 2025.It is intended to help determine whether a software system falls under the scope of the AI Act or not.The European Commission (EC) gives non-binding guidelines clarifying how the definition should be applied in practice.The guidelines intend to support developers, providers, and users, including healthcare workers, in understanding whether their systems qualify, and are subject to its rules, as AI systems under the EU AI Act.This definition applies to healthcare; however, there are different regulatory implications from it.Certain healthcare AI systems, including regulated medical-device systems subject to third-party conformity assessment, are classified as highrisk under the AI Act and are consequently subject to stringent safety, accuracy, governance, and oversight requirements (EC 2025).We view this risk-driven definition as essential for balancing regulation (risk mitigation) and innovation (benefit), ensuring that the regulatory approach fosters innovation.For healthcare, the AI Act should be read together with the wider EU legal and regulatory ecosystem, including the Medical Device Regulation, the In Vitro Diagnostic Medical Device Regulation, the General Data Protection Regulation, and the European Health Data Space.The applicable obligations depend on intended use, clinical risk, data use, and whether the system functions as, or forms part of, a regulated medical device. Drivers of change in AI system useAI in healthcare is predicted to increase in application owing to converging drivers such as rising healthcare demand, workforce shortages, digitalisation of health records, and advances in computational power and data analytics.These pressures are prompting a shift towards more data-driven, personalised, and efficient healthcare models.At the same time, policy initiatives across the EU, alongside increased public and private investment, are accelerating AI integration.Together, these trends are reshaping expectations around healthcare delivery, prompting urgent attention to readiness, governance, and equity in implementation.A patient-centred approach should be operational rather than rhetorical.Patient organisations and patient representatives can contribute to priority setting, co-design, validation endpoints, procurement criteria, governance boards, communication materials, and post-deployment feedback.Evaluation should include patient-reported outcomes, patient experience, quality of life, accessibility, and the distribution of benefits and harms across patient groups. Regional/sub-sectoral differences in the use of AI systemsThe use of AI systems varies across Europe and healthcare sectors, reflecting disparities in digital infrastructure, investment capacity, regulatory readiness, and workforce expertise.While some regions and institutions lead in AI adoption, particularly in radiology, pathology, and administrative support, others lag relative to this because of resource constraints or limited technical capabilities.These differences risk deepening existing inequalities in healthcare access and quality.EU-level coordination and targeted support are needed to ensure balanced development and equitable AI integration across all Member States and health system segments.EU-level action should therefore support structured mutual learning across Member States, including identification, comparison, and dissemination of best practices for responsible AI implementation.This is especially important where differences in infrastructure, workforce capacity, data readiness, and procurement expertise risk widening inequalities in access to beneficial AI-enabled care. Current EU policies for AI systemsCurrent EU policies prioritise ethical, trustworthy, and human-centric AI systems, as reflected in initiatives such as the EU AI Act, the European Health Data Space, and Horizon Europe research funding.These frameworks aim to ensure safety, transparency, and equity while promoting innovation.However, gaps remain in harmonising implementation across Member States, aligning health-specific regulations, and addressing sector-specific challenges.Continued policy refinement and cross-sector collaboration are essential to translate these principles into effective, context-sensitive actions within healthcare systems. Policy shifts and integrated frameworks for AI systemsA proactive approach focusing on data protection and privacy, and energy and carbon footprint, is increasingly shaping AI-related policy developments (OECD 2025).To support sustainable and trustworthy AI in healthcare, integrated frameworks are needed that align digital health, environmental, ethical, and industrial strategies.Such coherence will help balance innovation with societal safeguards, ensuring that AI deployment contributes to broader EU goals, including climate neutrality, resilience, and social equity.Harmonised, forward-looking policies are key to managing complexity and fostering responsible AI adoption.Interoperability and sustainability should be treated as implementation conditions, not technical afterthoughts.Procurement, funding, and evaluation frameworks should encourage use of recognised standards such as HL7 (Health Level Seven), FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources), and DICOM (Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine) where relevant, assess cost-effectiveness and opportunity costs, and consider the energy and carbon footprint of compute-intensive AI systems. Urgent key messagesThis report aims to provide recommendations for embedding responsible AI practices into European healthcare, ensuring that AI deployment is managed proactively as part of a sustainable, anticipatory healthcare strategy, rather than merely responding to external factors such as emergencies or market inevitabilities.In the box below, we give the three urgent key messages of this report.1. Responsible AI integration must be proactive, not reactive.AI systems in healthcare should be guided by forward-looking policies that anticipate long-term impacts rather than reacting to crises or market pressures.Embedding responsibility requires early governance, inclusive design, and strategic investment to ensure AI strengthens -not destabilises -health systems.2. Equity and trust are essential for sustainable AI adoption.Without targeted action, AI systems risk widening health disparities and undermining public trust.EU policies must prioritise equitable access, transparency, and community engagement to ensure AI systems support universal healthcare goals and democratic values.3. Coordinated EU action is crucial for safe, scalable innovation.Fragmented approaches to AI-systems governance hinder safe implementation and slow progress.The EU must promote harmonised standards, interoperable cross-border data sharing, and collaborative oversight to enable robust, ethical, and scalable AI applications across Member States.report advocates for fit-for-purpose regulation such as regulatory sandboxes (controlled, time-limited environments in which innovators can test new tools under regulatory supervision, with safeguards for users and patients, while regulators learn how existing rules EU policy recommendationsThis report provides policy options that are a mix of regulatory, institutional, financial, and capacity-building measures to help embed responsibility, trust, and sustainability into healthcare AI across the EU.The FEAM is affiliated to the

title: Artificial Intelligence in Peroral Endoscopic Myotomy: Current Evidence, Limitations, and Future Directions
abstract: Peroral endoscopic myotomy (POEM) is an established treatment for achalasia and selected spastic esophageal motility disorders, but several aspects of care remain highly operator-dependent.These include early diagnosis, patient selection, procedural planning, myotomy length, intra-procedural safety, training assessment, and prediction of post-procedure reflux.Artificial intelligence (AI) may help address these limitations by integrating endoscopic video, high-resolution manometry, timed barium esophagram, EndoFLIP, clinical variables, procedural data, and follow-up outcomes into more personalized decision-support tools.This narrative review critically examines the evidence for AI across the POEM pathway and distinguishes direct achalasia or POEM evidence from adjacent and conceptual applications.Early AI applications are most likely to emerge in achalasia detection during diagnostic endoscopy, automated motility interpretation, video-based procedural assessment, and prediction of clinical response or post-POEM reflux.More ambitious applications, such as real-time tunnel orientation, vessel recognition, mucosal injury alerts, and personalized myotomy planning, remain largely investigational.Most AI-specific POEM applications remain at an early or conceptual stage and require multicenter validation, standardized outcomes, and careful clinical governance.AI should support, rather than replace, expert judgment, and an AI-derived reflux estimate cannot replace standard follow-up or objective reflux assessment.ÖZ Peroral endoskopik miyotomi (POEM), akalazya ve seçilmiş spastik özofagus motilite bozukluklarının tedavisinde yerleşik bir yöntem olmakla birlikte, tedavi sürecinin çeşitli aşamaları halen büyük ölçüde uygulayıcı deneyimine bağlıdır.Bu aşamalar; title: Artificial Intelligence in the Assessment and Management of Spasticity: A Scoping Review
abstract: Spasticity is a prevalent and disabling consequence of upper motor neuron disorders, yet its assessment and management remains clinically challenging. Artificial intelligence (AI) may offer opportunities to enhance the objective assessment, prediction, and management of spasticity; however, the current evidence base has not been comprehensively characterised. This review systematically mapped evidence on the application of AI across the continuum of spasticity care and identified key evidence gaps to inform future research. PubMed, Embase, CINAHL, and Web of Science were searched for peer-reviewed English-language studies evaluating AI in adult spasticity. Two reviewers independently screened studies, extracted data, and assessed methodological quality using NHLBI tools and PROBAST + AI. This scoping review was prospectively registered with the Open Science Framework Registries. The search yielded 1832 records, of which 21 studies were included after screening. One additional study was identified through citation searching, bringing the total to 22 studies involving 1114 participants. Applications spanned four clinical domains: discrimination between spastic and healthy individuals (n = 2), severity assessment (n = 18), risk prediction (n = 1), and treatment response prediction (n = 1). Most studies focused on post-stroke upper limb spasticity. Surface electromyography was the most frequently used input modality, often integrated with kinematic or kinetic sensors. Conventional machine learning predominated, with reported accuracies of 74–96% and the Modified Ashworth Scale as the most common reference standard. All 22 studies were at high overall risk of bias on PROBAST + AI, and none performed external validation, highlighting substantial methodological limitations that constrain clinical translation.
authors: Ruoxi Cao; Ruojin Li; Joon Sin Ser; Yeow Leng Tan; Jing Chen

title: Artificial Intelligence-Driven Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation(TMS) for Autism Spectrum Disorder
abstract: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a complex neurodevelopmental condition characterized by impairments in social communication, repetitive behaviors, sensory processing abnormalities, and variable cognitive deficits. Despite significant advances in behavioral therapies and pharmacological interventions, effective treatments capable of directly modulating dysfunctional neural networks remain limited. Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS) has emerged as a promising non-invasive neuromodulation technique that can alter cortical excitability, enhance neuroplasticity, and potentially improve cognitive and behavioral outcomes. Simultaneously, recent developments in Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML), Deep Learning (DL), Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI), Reinforcement Learning (RL), and Digital Twin technologies have created new opportunities to personalize TMS protocols using multimodal patient data, including structural and functional neuroimaging, electroencephalography (EEG), behavioral assessments, genetic information, and longitudinal clinical outcomes.
authors: Bahman Zohuri; Sana Fadavi
venue: Japan Journal of Clinical & Medical Research

title: Atomic cluster expansion potentials for screw dislocations in BCC refractory metals
abstract: Accurate atomistic modeling of screw dislocations in body-centered cubic (BCC) metals remains challenging because their plasticity is governed by complex dislocation glide behavior due to their compact threefold symmetric core structure and a strongly temperature-dependent flow stress induced by the large Peierls barrier. In the context of group 5 (V, Nb, and Ta) and group 6 (Mo and W) refractory metals (RMs), both classical interatomic potentials and some machine-learning potentials consistently fail to reproduce density functional theory (DFT) Peierls barriers and the glide plane. Here, we developed an array of atomic cluster expansion (ACE) potentials for these RMs by extending an existing DFT database. The developed ACE potentials significantly improve the description of screw dislocation properties, showing good agreement with the DFT references for Mo and W and substantial improvement for V, Nb, and Ta. The results show that transferability to screw dislocation behavior depends sensitively on both database composition and element-specific energetics and that achieving a single-humped Peierls barrier alone is not a sufficient validation metric for accurate prediction of dislocation glide. For Nb, Mo, and W, the developed ACE models also enable reliable calculation of kink-pair activation enthalpies, which are well described by both Kocks' law and a line-tension model.
authors: Lei Zhang; Francesco Maresca

title: Attention-Based Surface Representation Learning for Robot State Prediction and Open-Ended Surface Classification
abstract: For ground robots operating in outdoor environments, understanding the properties of the underlying terrain is essential for ensuring reliable operation. In most perception-based studies, this problem is formulated as categorical classification with a fixed number of classes defined during training. We propose an approach that enables new surface classes to be added as trainable vectors, which can subsequently be used to address higher-level tasks. By employing a learning paradigm based on predicting the robot's next state in time and using attention blocks, we improved classification accuracy to 98.56% on the Belyaev-Kushnarev dataset and 94.8% on BorealTC.
authors: Oleg Kushnarev; Alexander Belyaev

title: Automated and noninvasive in vivo mapping of brain functions in the human cortex
abstract: Mapping forms the basis for understanding the functional organization of the brain and for developing targeted interventions in neurological and psychiatric disorders. Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) is a non-invasive tool that allows causal mapping of cortical functions involved in motor control, speech, and connectivity. Since manual mapping procedures limit standardization, we present an automated cortical mapping method that integrates electronically controlled multi-locus TMS with a Bayesian optimization algorithm for identifying stimulation targets efficiently and objectively through a closed-loop framework. We localized individual motor representation area peaks with high accuracy (average 2.4 mm and 5° deviation from the optimum) in only approximately 4 minutes. This represents a substantial advancement over current mapping approaches, providing the means to greatly accelerate and standardize both research and clinical protocols while maintaining high reliability. We anticipate that our approach can further extend to map other cortical functions that cannot be easily analyzed online by a human operator.
