title: Ağız yoluyla endoskopik miyotomide yapay zekâ: Kişiselleştirilmiş miyotomiye, daha güvenli eğitime ve reflü tahminine doğru: AI in POEM
abstract: Peroral endoscopic myotomy (POEM) is an established treatment for achalasia and selected spastic esophageal motility disorders, but several aspects of care remain highly operator-dependent. These include early diagnosis, patient selection, procedural planning, myotomy length, intra-procedural safety, training assessment, and prediction of post-procedure reflux. Artificial intelligence (AI) may help address these limitations by integrating endoscopic video, high-resolution manometry, timed barium esophagram, EndoFLIP, clinical variables, procedural data, and follow-up outcomes into more personalized decision-support tools. This narrative review critically examines the evidence for AI across the POEM pathway and distinguishes direct achalasia or POEM evidence from adjacent and conceptual applications. Early AI applications are most likely to emerge in achalasia detection during diagnostic endoscopy, automated motility interpretation, video-based procedural assessment, and prediction of clinical response or post-POEM reflux. More ambitious applications, such as real-time tunnel orientation, vessel recognition, mucosal injury alerts, and personalized myotomy planning, remain largely investigational. Most AI-specific POEM applications remain at an early or conceptual stage and require multicenter validation, standardized outcomes, and careful clinical governance. AI should support, rather than replace, expert judgment, and an AI-derived reflux estimate cannot replace standard follow-up or objective reflux assessment.
authors: MD Ahmed Abdallah Salman; Ahmed Abdallah

title: BanglaBBQ: A Bias Benchmark for Question Answering in the Bangladeshi Context
abstract: This paper presents BanglaBBQ, a question-answering bias benchmark designed to capture stereotypes grounded in the Bangladeshi context, in both Bangla and English. Following KoBBQ and PakBBQ, BanglaBBQ adapts the original Bias Benchmark for Question Answering (BBQ) by classifying its templates into three groups: directly translated (DT), modified to align target groups or contexts with Bangladesh (TM), and removed when deemed unsuitable for the Bangladeshi context (SR). This process retains 140 templates across six categories, comprising 76 DT and 64 TM templates. Five newly authored (NA) categories, based on stereotypes common in Bangladeshi society, are then added: marital status, age and political perception, regional origin, educational background, and mental-health status. Native Bangladeshi annotators judged all 466 newly authored templates, and 372 were retained because a strict majority of English annotators identified the intended target and rated the attitude as common enough. Each newly authored template is linked to a documented source and a verbatim quote from it. Each evaluated template also has a counter-stereotypical version of its disambiguated context. The dataset was evaluated using two open-weight models (Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B) and two closed models (GPT-4.1-mini and Gemini 2.5 Flash). All four lean towards the stereotyped person when the context is ambiguous, in both languages, and the effect of language differs by model, so English results do not predict behaviour in Bangla. On the adapted BBQ templates, both Qwen3 models are also less accurate when the context contradicts a stereotype than when it confirms it. On the newly authored templates, the closed models follow counter-stereotypical evidence almost perfectly, and all four models are more biased on the templates that annotators validated than on those they rejected.
authors: Sumit Anthony Gomes; Yasin Rahman; Taeeba Tasnia; Faiza Nooren Suhita

title: Bayesian adaptive design for neural recruitment curves
abstract: Nonlinear response models remain ubiquitous across disciplines with recruitment curves describing muscle response to neural stimulation. Conventional acquisition methods typically rely on static uniform sampling, requiring many stimuli, while adaptive threshold-hunting designs such as ML-PEST forfeit accurate characterization of the overall curve. We present a Bayesian adaptive design that uses posterior uncertainty over curve parameters to propose stimuli that maximize information gain across the full recruitment curve. We additionally implement a focused acquisition method that can target arbitrary subset of curve parameters, which we use to evaluate and interpret our design. In simulations, our design outperforms uniform sampling in recovering threshold while matching ML-PEST, and outperforms ML-PEST in predictive curve accuracy while matching uniform. It likewise matches our threshold-focused acquisition, suggesting our design doesn't trade off threshold estimation for recovering the curve. We further show data collected using our design yields greater power when detecting a change in threshold in intervention studies. Our design proposes the next stimulus within 5 seconds, making it feasible for transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) experiments. Finally, we validate our design in TMS experiments and provide a library for Python, called onMEP, for online acquisition of neural recruitment curves.
authors: Vishweshwar Tyagi; Saihari S. Dukkipati; Daniel Twili; Jonas M. Mikhaeil; Andrew Gelman; Jason B. Carmel; James R. McIntosh

title: Behavioral Apathy and its Relationship with Physical Activity, Affective Attitudes, and Motor Cortex Excitability
abstract: Apathy is a multidimensional syndrome characterized by diminished motivation and reduced goal-directed behavior. Although apathy is commonly studied in neurological and psychiatric populations, it is also observed in otherwise healthy adults and may represent an important barrier to engagement in physical activity. Because physical activity requires effort, action initiation, and persistence, individuals with higher levels of behavioral apathy may be less likely to initiate and maintain active behavior. Despite growing interest in the relationship between apathy and physical activity, the behavioral and neurophysiological mechanisms underlying this association remain poorly understood. This thesis examined the relationship between behavioral apathy, physical activity, affective attitudes toward physical activity, and motor cortex neurophysiology. Across four complementary studies, behavioral and neurophysiological pathways that may contribute to reduced physical activity in individuals with higher apathy were investigated. Study 1 is a systematic review and meta-analysis examining the association between apathy and physical activity across clinical and non-clinical populations. Study 2 examined whether intentions, explicit affective attitudes, and approach-avoidance tendencies toward physical activity mediated the relationship between behavioral apathy and physical activity in healthy adults. Study 3 is a systematic review and meta-analysis investigating the association between habitual physical activity and measures of motor cortex neurophysiology, including corticospinal excitability, intracortical inhibition, and intracortical facilitation. Study 4 used transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) to examine whether behavioral apathy was associated with these neurophysiological measures in healthy adults. Across the four studies, results demonstrated that apathy is associated with physical activity, but that this association is more strongly explained by motivational and affective processes than by resting-state motor cortex neurophysiology. The systematic review and meta-analysis showed a significant negative association between apathy and physical activity, with stronger associations in older adults and individuals with Parkinson’s disease. Behavioral analyses further demonstrated that higher behavioral apathy was associated with lower physical activity, partly through weaker intentions to be physically active and less positive affective attitudes toward physical activity. Individuals with lower apathy also showed stronger tendencies to approach physical activity stimuli and avoid sedentary stimuli, although these tendencies did not mediate physical activity behavior. In contrast, the neurophysiological studies showed no reliable associations between habitual physical activity and measures of corticospinal excitability, intracortical inhibition, or facilitation. Similarly, behavioral apathy showed negligible associations with these measures, with equivalence testing indicating that any potential effects were too small to be practically meaningful. These results suggest that the relationship between apathy and physical activity is primarily linked to motivational and affective mechanisms rather than stable differences in primary motor cortex neurophysiology. Specifically, higher behavioral apathy was associated with weaker intentions to be physically active and less positive affective attitudes toward physical activity, whereas neither habitual physical activity nor behavioral apathy showed meaningful associations with resting TMS-derived measures of corticospinal excitability or intracortical circuitry. Overall, this thesis refines the understanding of how apathy contributes to physical inactivity and highlights the importance of targeting motivational processes when designing interventions aimed at increasing physical activity engagement.
authors: Ataallah Farajzadeh

title: Beyond Accurate Estimates: Planning Poker as Expertise Coordination in Agile Software Development
abstract: Planning Poker is one of the most widely adopted estimation techniques in agile software development, yet evidence on its forecasting accuracy remains mixed while the practice persists. We treat this paradox as a problematization opportunity and ask how Planning Poker can be understood through the lens of expertise coordination. Drawing on 14 practitioner interviews, we develop three propositions. First, Planning Poker sessions produce coordination value, including shared task understanding, transactive memory maintenance, and the surfacing of tacit knowledge, that is analytically distinct from the estimation value. Second, the coordination value of an estimation episode depends on the fit between its configuration, work granularity, and team scale and synchrony. Third, external forecasting and control pressure degrades the coordination function while its form persists, manifesting in four anti-patterns. We contribute a coordination-theoretic analysis of agile estimation and outline implications for research and practice.
authors: Nikolaus Obwegeser; Anna Wiedemann
venue: Journal of the Association for Information Systems

title: Beyond Cobots: Designing Collaborative Applications through Human-Centred Design
abstract: Early-stage specification of industrial human–robot collaboration often leaves operator roles, human-factor concerns, and performance objectives implicit or dispersed across documents. ISO 10218-2:2025 locates collaboration at the level of individual tasks and requires human-factor considerations to be addressed in design, but prescribes no representation for them. This paper introduces the Human-Robot Collaboration (HRC) Blueprint, a human-centred artefact that records roles, tasks, requirements, potential errors, physical and perceived safety risks, performance indicators, and criticality against a shared task-step and agent reference, together with a workshop-based protocol for multidisciplinary specification. Following a design science approach, the artefact was demonstrated in two industrial applications: crane-assisted assembly, and electric-vehicle battery assembly, inspection, and disassembly. A workshop with 24 participants in eight groups produced specifications examined alongside existing use-case narratives through descriptive document analysis. The Blueprint elaborated application-level descriptions into task-level specifications, made coordination transitions explicit through the role layer, incorporated human-factor concerns as specification content, and supported examination of tensions between operator authority and performance criteria. . These features bring early specification into closer correspondence with ISO 10218-2:2025 without constituting evidence of conformity. Post-workshop selections emphasised workload in both applications (seven and six of eight groups) and reliability in battery work (six). The findings characterise expert-generated specifications rather than comparative effectiveness or realised operational improvements. Within these boundaries, the HRC Blueprint offers a reusable means of integrating human-centred concerns into industrial collaboration before implementation.
authors: Nagore Osa; Ganix Lasa; Maitane Mazmela; Ainhoa Apraiz; Oscar Escallada

title: Beyond Completion Time: A Multimodal Approach to Characterizing Eye-Hand Coordination During the Nine-Hole Peg Test in Multiple Sclerosis
abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) can impair upper-extremity function through motor, sensory, cognitive, and visual deficits. Although the Nine-Hole Peg Test (9-HPT) is widely used to assess dexterity, completion time alone provides limited insight into the eye-hand coordination underlying performance. We characterized 9-HPT performance in nine people with MS (PwMS) and nine healthy controls using simultaneous eye tracking, markerless hand tracking, and object detection. Each peg cycle was divided into transport, manipulation and insertion, and return-to-bin phases. PwMS had longer overall completion times. Transport was prolonged with the non-dominant hand, manipulation was prolonged with the dominant hand, and return-to-bin duration was longer with both hands, representing the largest phase difference. PwMS also made approximately one additional fixation per peg and showed greater variability in gaze landing position during dominant-hand performance. Saccadic amplitude and mean placement error did not differ significantly between groups, and gaze generally preceded hand movement in both groups. These exploratory findings suggest that MS-related slowing is concentrated in phases requiring precise manipulation and transition to the next peg. Multimodal assessment of the 9-HPT can reveal coordination deficits not captured by completion time alone.
authors: Mahya Beheshti; Rajvardhan Gadde; Diana Maloku; Danae S Manta; Bethany Lum; Silvana Lopes Costa; Todd E. Hudson; John‐Ross Rizzo

title: Beyond technological readiness: How financial benefit and top management support drive public electric vehicle charging station investment in Indonesia
abstract: This study investigates what drives potential business partners in Indonesia to invest in public electric vehicle charging stations (PEVCS). Using the TOE framework and TPB, this study examines key determinants of investment decisions in a B2B context. Survey data from 242 organizational respondents were analyzed using PLS-SEM. Results indicate that Perceived Financial Benefit (PFB) is the strongest driver of investment intention, consistent with the economic logic that business decision-makers prioritize profitability and anticipated returns over other considerations. Top Management Support (TMS) also emerges as influential, directly affecting investment intention and reinforcing financial confidence among organizational stakeholders. A notable characteristic of the sample dominated by national private firms with highly centralized structures appears to meaningfully shape how decisions are made within organizations. One of the more striking outcomes of this study is that Government Support (GSP) showed no direct bearing on investment intention. Government incentives only drive investment when perceived as tangible financial gains via cost reduction or revenue growth confirming that policy instruments must translate into firm-level economic value to influence decisions. Perceived complexity, meanwhile, did not register as a meaningful obstacle within this sample, suggesting that surveyed organizations possess formalized capabilities to manage technical and integration challenges. On the other hand, perceived compatibility proved consistently relevant, particularly when the technology slots naturally into pre-existing systems such as parking facilities or customer loyalty programs, thereby amplifying perceived financial returns. From a practical standpoint, these findings carry important implications for policymakers, specifically the need to sharpen messaging on return on investment when engaging top management and to design incentive structures that speak directly to financial attractiveness. While contributing to the sustainable energy infrastructure literature, the cross-sectional design limits causal inference; future studies should examine how ownership type and competitive dynamics moderate investment decisions.
authors: sudianto d; Heronimus Yudhanto; Achmad Meidiansyah; Evi Rinawati Simanjuntak

title: Beyond the Paralyzed Arm: Quantifying Intentional Motor Control Capacity in People with Severe Arm Impairment Post-Stroke with High-Density Surface EMG
abstract: Abstract Background Standard clinical scales of motor impairment and activity limitation cannot detect whether a person with severe upper-limb impairment after stroke retains voluntary motor control. Consequently, the patient group that is most in need of active rehabilitation cannot be triaged for training using a/an biofeedback/intention-based interface. To address this gap, we tested whether people with stroke (PwS) with severe impairment (Action Research Arm Test [ARAT] ≤ 10) retain graded intentional motor control capacity (IMCC) that can be read from the myoelectric activity in the paretic arm. Methods Twelve severely impaired PwS (ARAT ≤ 10) and twelve healthy controls performed a movement-free myoelectric task in which high-density surface EMG (HD-sEMG) from two muscles belonging to distinct pathological synergies drove a cursor. Task success required genuine voluntary drive rather than spastic or synergetic co-activation. Principal-component analysis combined three performance measures (path length, radial target error, and Euclidean target error) into a composite IMCC score. We compared IMCC scores with those of healthy controls. Results PwS differed from controls in path length (p = 0.005) and radial target error (p = 0.033), yet the groups overlapped markedly: half of the PwS (6 of 12) produced IMCC scores inside the 85% confidence region of the healthy controls (the healthy reference range). This overlap was not predicted by ARAT or Modified Ashworth Scale scores. Conclusions Half of clinically non-functional arms retain IMCC within the healthy range. HD-sEMG allows measuring hidden intentional control capacity, providing a graded marker to identify which severely impaired PwS can be trained through an intention-based interface and possibly improving recovery prediction.
authors: Keren Pollack; Noy Goldhamer; Adi Lorber Haddad; Gil Meir; Hadar Idan; Tamar Mizrahi; Lior Shmuelof

title: Bio-inspired open ligamentous knee joint with extended pitch and yaw range of motion
abstract: This study presents a bio-inspired open knee joint for biofidelic robots with an anatomically correct range of motion. Bio-inspired joints contribute to robot performance and understanding living organisms by providing dynamic motion data as the real-world physical twin. The proposed joint structure features the integration of the open joint and ligamentous constraint. In particular, the spherical envelope of the condyles contributes to the rotation other than pitch rotation. By applying a bio-inspired ligament arrangement, the developed knee joint performed pitch and yaw motion. The relationship between the ligament length and joint orientation was derived by forward kinematics and the ligament wrapping. The arrangement of the bio-inspired collateral ligaments was determined with the iterative calculation method considering the object wrapping, which predicted the yaw range of motion. Verification of the proposed approach includes the evaluation of the range of motion on the robotic knee joint equipped with the motor-driven tendons. The robot validation tests include the rotational motions around the pitch and yaw axes. The tests showed that the proposed joint structure can be a relevant approach for replicating the range of motion of a human knee joint. Future work includes the motion control of the joint system and integration into a real robot.
authors: Shinsuke Nakashima; Yilun Sun; Julius Ambros; Robin Schregle; Christoph Rehekampff; Qi An; Atsushi Yamashita; Tim Christian Lueth

title: Biomechanical Effect of Medial Collateral Ligament Repair With and Without Suture Augmentation on Knee Laxity and Anterior Cruciate Ligament Force.
abstract: The medial collateral ligament (MCL) is the most frequently injured knee ligament. MCL repair is a surgical technique intended to acutely reduce medial side laxity that can be performed in isolation or combined with suture augmentation (SA). To assess the effect of MCL repair with and without SA on (1) valgus laxity and anteromedial rotational laxity and (2) force carried by the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) and (3) to quantify load-sharing between the MCL repair and SA components. Controlled laboratory study. Seven cadaveric knees were tested using a 6 degrees of freedom robotic manipulator in 4 states: (1) intact, (2) MCL cut, (3) isolated MCL repair, and (4) MCL repair combined with SA. Valgus laxity and anteromedial rotational laxity were measured at 0°, 15°, 30°, and 90° of flexion. In situ ACL force and forces carried by the MCL repair components were assessed at peak valgus moment using principle of superposition. Valgus laxity after isolated MCL repair was greater than the intact state at all flexion angles >0° (P≤ .01). The addition of SA to MCL repair significantly reduced valgus laxity at 15° and 30° of flexion only (P≤ .02). Anteromedial rotational laxity after both MCL repairs was greater than the intact state at 90° of flexion (P < .01), whereas no differences were detected at 0° and 30°. For both MCL repairs, ACL force was less than in the MCL cut state and did not differ from the intact state. In situ forces carried by the repair and SA components did not differ for the MCL repair combined with SA. Both MCL repair with and without SA reduced ACL force relative to the MCL cut state. Addition of SA to MCL repair resulted in less residual valgus laxity but not less anteromedial rotational laxity. These findings suggest that MCL repair may reduce medial side laxity and partially offload the ACL relative to the MCL cut state. This is particularly important for treatment of combined ACL and MCL injuries, where the protection of the ACL graft or repair is most important immediately after surgery.
authors: Fidelius von Rehlingen-Prinz; David Z Shamritsky; Sebastian Rilk; Kyle N Kunze; Maximilian M Mueller; Bryce Demopoulos; Carl W Imhauser; Gregory S DiFelice
venue: The American journal of sports medicine

title: Block-Based Programming for Educational Robotics in Lower Secondary Education: An Exploratory Challenge-Based Learning Study
abstract: Time-limited robotics assessments can misrepresent classroom performance when unfinished attempts are discarded or recorded as exact completion times. This exploratory study addresses a practical reporting need: describing immediate execution and post-task perceptions while retaining non-completion, rather than ranking educational technologies. Thirty-five novice lower-secondary students participated in an approximately 80 min challenge-based implementation in three intact cohorts (n=16, 11, and 8). A structured observation record and stopwatch captured completion of a movement-and-sensor task within 10 min; a six-item questionnaire captured task-specific perceptions. Completion proportions were 16/16, 11/11, and 5/8. Kaplan–Meier estimates and restricted mean time through 10 min yielded 3.05, 4.37, and 7.85 min, respectively. In the cohort with three unfinished attempts, the completer-only mean was 6.56 min, whereas the whole-cohort restricted mean was 7.85 min; these summaries address different questions. A compact exploratory analysis of all six survey items found no Holm-adjusted p<0.05. The main finding is that short challenge-based robotics activities are feasible and engaging, but performance differences cannot be attributed to the programming platform alone.
authors: José Varela Aldás; Gissela Gamboa; Carolina Del-Valle-Soto

title: Botulinum toxin type a within function-oriented management of post-stroke spasticity: a narrative review
abstract: Post-stroke spasticity (PSS) is a heterogeneous complication of stroke that affects motor recovery, care needs, pain, positioning, and participation in daily life. Current management frameworks commonly stratify patients by time since stroke, but disease duration alone does not capture differences in neural mechanisms, residual voluntary control, functional priorities, or response to intervention. This narrative review searched PubMed, the Cochrane Library, and Wanfang databases from inception to May 2026, prioritizing randomized controlled trials, prospective cohort studies, systematic reviews, real-world studies, Goal Attainment Scaling research, the Upper Limb International Spasticity cohort series, best-practice guidance, and clinical trials including BEST and InTENSE. We synthesize evidence that PSS heterogeneity can be understood across central and peripheral mechanisms, temporal trajectories, and active versus passive functional consequences. Available studies suggest that active and passive functional goals differ in baseline functional profiles, outcome assessment, treatment response, and intervention requirements. However, patients sharing a functional goal type may still differ in residual voluntary control, neural and non-neural contributors to movement restriction, pain, mobility, and care dependency. Botulinum toxin type A is well aligned with focal tone reduction and passive goals, including pain relief, hygiene, and limb positioning. It may also support contracture-prevention strategies when modifiable neural muscle overactivity remains, whereas active functional gains usually require preserved motor potential and integration with task-oriented training, rehabilitation, and adjunctive modalities. We propose that functional goal type should complement time-based staging as a decision dimension rather than serve as a complete clinical phenotype. This combined framework may better align patient selection, intervention matching, outcome assessment, and longitudinal treatment planning. Prospective goal-stratified studies and standardized assessment tools are needed to test its clinical utility.
authors: Baoling Su; Yating Huang; Xiaotong Li; Kun Wang; Bing Bao

title: Brief Trains of Closed-loop TMS Induce Controllable Power in FM-theta Oscillations
abstract:
Objective

Frontal-midline theta (FM-theta; 4–8 Hz) oscillations are thought to support cognition. Brief trains of transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) can probe these oscillations with high temporal precision but have rarely changed theta power. One possible reason is that prior studies ignored the instantaneous phase of the oscillation, which strongly shapes the cortical response to TMS. We tested whether brief TMS trains triggered at specific FM-theta phases in real time directionally modulate post-train FM-theta power.

Approach

Six healthy adults received TMS over dorsomedial prefrontal cortex (Fz) with concurrent electroencephalography during a whole-report working memory task. A beamformer and real-time phase-estimation pipeline triggered four-pulse 6 Hz trains (110% of resting motor threshold) at FM-theta peaks (0°) or troughs (180°), randomized trial by trial. Post-train spectral power was decomposed into total, induced (non-phase-locked) and evoked (phase-locked) components.

Main results

Trough-triggered trains transiently increased post-train FM-theta power relative to peak-triggered trains; task performance did not differ. Cluster-based permutation tests showed trough−peak differences in total (4.6–7.1 Hz) and induced (5.0–7.8 Hz) power ∼50–440 ms after the train, suggesting amplification of the oscillation . No evoked effect was detected. The total-power effect was robust at the subject level (Cohen’s dz = 1.32, p = 0.023). Within-train theta power did not differ between conditions, suggesting a cortical origin.

Significance

To our knowledge, this is the first study to lock brief rhythmic TMS trains to the real-time phase of an ongoing oscillation, and to show phase-dependent modulation of FM-theta power after individual trains on timescales relevant to behavior. Open-loop brief-train protocols may have missed such effects by mixing facilitatory and suppressive phases. Phase-locked brief trains offer a precise tool for testing the causal role of oscillations in cognition.

title: Causal evidence for the role of dorsolateral prefrontal cortex in the implementation of cognitive control adjustments
abstract: Abstract Cognitive control processes enable us to use recent contextual information to flexibly adapt to current task demands. This ability to adapt control processes is exhibited in response conflict tasks. In these tasks, participants must respond to a relevant piece of information while overcoming the tendency to respond to task-irrelevant information that cues an automatic or habitual response. Control demands can be updated in these tasks via two separate routes. Both errors and conflict between task-irrelevant and task-relevant information affect performance on subsequent trials. A body of work has implicated dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) in implementing these control adjustments. However, this work has primarily relied on correlational techniques or focused on a single index of control adaptation. Here, we combine inhibitory transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) over DLPFC with computational modeling of behavior to test the causal role of DLPFC in control adaptation. We show that inhibitory TMS to DLPFC reduces the effect of previous trial conflict, and committing an error on the previous trial further reduces adaptive effects. This result provides causal evidence for DLPFC playing a general role in implementing trial-to-trial control adjustments.
authors: Jacob Sellers; Han Zhang; John J. Jonides; Taraz G. Lee

title: Challenges of implementing Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) systems in Bangladesh
abstract: Goal: This study examines why Bangladeshi companies struggle to adopt ERP systems, looking at organizational, technical, and human hurdles. By combining the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and Critical Success Factors (CSF) frameworks, it shows how user acceptance and organizational readiness directly drive ERP success. Methodology: A sequential exploratory mixed-method design was used. First, a PRISMA-guided literature review mapped out key ERP challenges to shape the survey. Questionnaires were then gathered from 30 professionals across multiple Bangladeshi sectors with hands-on ERP experience. Finally, the data was analyzed using descriptive statistics, Cronbach’s alpha, one-sample t-tests, and Cohen’s d to evaluate reliability, significance, and practical effect size. Results: Cronbach’s alpha was 0.560, indicating moderate internal consistency. All seven ERP challenges were statistical significant. Budget limitations, lack of training and support, shortage of skilled personnel and maintenance costs demonstrated strong practical effects, whereas data migration, employee resistance and weak top management support also emerged as significant barriers. Limitations: The study is exploratory, cross-sectional, and based on a small sample. Practical implications: Organizations should focus on training, budgeting, skilled teams, leadership support, change management, and data governance. Originality/Value: The study adds Bangladesh-based ERP evidence using an integrated TAM-CSF perspective.

title: Cholinergic inputs to motoneurons in the spinal cord augment focal muscle spasticity in rodents
abstract: Background and Purpose Cholinergic premotor inputs to motoneurons support high levels of motor output when required. However, the possible role of these inputs in pathologically elevated muscle tone has not been characterised. To address this, we examined the modulatory effect of spinal acetylcholine (ACh) on experimental spastic paralysis. Experimental Approach Rats were injected with tetanus neurotoxin (TeNT, 33–100 pg, im) into gastrocnemius to induce sustained rigid hind‐paw extension and resistance to passive ankle flexion. The effects of spinal ACh on experimental hypertonia were probed by lumbar intrathecal application of the AChE inhibitor neostigmine (NEO) or a muscarinic M 2 receptor antagonist (AQ‐RA 741). Effects of NEO on extracellular ACh were measured in the facial nucleus after TeNT (33 pg) or botulinum toxin A (BoNT/A, 2 U) injection into the rat whisker pad. The intensity of TeNT‐evoked hindlimb hypertonia (10 pg, im) was assessed in mice with genetic ablation of cholinergic C bouton source interneurons (V0 C interneurons). Key Results NEO augmented the severity of TeNT‐evoked hypertonia, whereas AQ‐RA 741 attenuated it. Local perfusion of NEO caused a BoNT/A‐sensitive increase in extracellular ACh concentration. The involvement of cholinergic C boutons was corroborated by reduced hypertonia following TeNT challenge (10 pg, im) in V0 C ‐ablated mice. Conclusions and Implications Our results suggest that spinal cholinergic transmission, associated with vesicular ACh release and M 2 signalling at C boutons, exacerbates experimental spastic paralysis. We reveal a new role for endogenous spinal ACh, with implications for developing new therapeutic approaches to treat spasticity and hyperkinetic movement disorders.
authors: Patrik Meglić; Petra Šoštarić; Eirini Tsape; Melpomeni Galani; Ana Knezović; Laura Restani; Marco Pirazzini; Ornella Rossetto; Gareth Brian Miles; Laskaro Zagoraiou; Ivica Matak

title: Cognitive state dependent enhancement of cognitive control with transcranial magnetic stimulation
abstract: Abstract Background Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) is an effective treatment for major depressive disorder (MDD), yet variability of therapeutic responses remains high. A key contributor to this variability may be state-dependent effects of brain stimulation, where activity in underlying circuits can shape the propagation of TMS-evoked activity. Thus, constraining the target circuits’ state by engaging cognition may make TMS’ effects more consistent. Objective We tested whether TMS’ effects on cognitive control, a transdiagnostic construct implicated across psychiatric disorders and a putative mediator of TMS efficacy, are state-dependent. Methods Participants (N = 25) completed a context-dependent behavioural assay of cognitive control before and after we delivered rTMS to the prefrontal cortex (PFC). During rTMS, participants performed either the cognitive control task (active-state TMS), or performed a context-independent perceptual task (control-state TMS). We assessed changes in downstream behavioural metrics of circuit function, as well as neural indices of cognitive control measured from electroencephalography (EEG). Results rTMS enhanced downstream readouts of cognitive control only when stimulation was delivered concurrent with the cognitive control task. Similarly, only active-state TMS modulated theta band oscillatory activity, which is thought to be a marker of cognitive control engagement Conclusion These findings demonstrate that TMS’ effects on cognitive control are state-dependent, in which endogenous engagement of PFC-anchored networks can shape the magnitude and functional relevance of TMS-induced plasticity. Considering cognitive states during TMS may therefore offer a framework to enhance and/or accelerate TMS’ therapeutic effects.
authors: Aaron N. McInnes; Victoria L Pipia; Kiyana L Maynard; Güldamla Kalender; Alik S. Widge

title: Comparative pain relief and functional outcomes following robotic-assisted versus conventional total knee arthroplasty: a GRADE-assessed meta-analysis with meta-regression of randomized controlled trials
abstract: Although robotic-assisted total knee arthroplasty (RA-TKA) is increasingly adopted for its potential to improve surgical precision, its impact on functional outcomes compared with conventional TKA (C-TKA) remains unclear. Existing syntheses are limited by pooling observational and randomized data, focusing on absolute postoperative scores without evaluating recovery trajectories, and lacking rigorous exploration of heterogeneity. To overcome these limitations, we conducted a methodologically rigorous meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) only, incorporating comprehensive meta-regression, platform-specific subgroup analyses, and assessment of evidence certainty using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) framework. PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, the Cochrane Library, and Google Scholar (pages 1-50) were comprehensively searched from their inception up to December 27, 2025. Data were pooled using random-effects meta-analysis and Hartung-Knapp adjustments. Meta-regression of different moderators and subgroup analyses by robotic platforms were performed, when feasible, to identify sources of heterogeneity. A total of 24 RCTs encompassing 3,425 patients were included. The pooled analyses demonstrated no significant differences between RA-TKA and C-TKA for change in Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC) function score (MD 0.14; 95% CI - 5.88 to 6.16; p = 0.96), change in functional Knee Society Score (KSS) (MD 0.51; 95% CI - 3.43 to 4.44; p = 0.78), or change in Oxford Knee Score (OKS) (MD 2.07; 95% CI - 6.82 to 10.96; p = 0.51). Although a subgroup analysis revealed a significant improvement in OKS at 6 months only (MD 2.25; p = 0.01), this effect did not reach the minimal clinically important difference (MCID) and was not sustained at other time points. No significant differences were observed for range of motion, change in VAS pain score, KSS satisfaction, or length of hospital stay. Operative time was significantly longer for RA-TKA (MD 22.34 min; 95% CI 13.66 to 31.02; p < 0.01), though this estimate should be interpreted with caution given the very high heterogeneity (I² = 98.53%) and the likelihood that it includes cases performed during the early learning curve of robotic adoption. Trial Sequential Analysis suggested that this finding is unlikely to be attributable to random error, though the required information size was not reached. RA-TKA and C-TKA provide comparable functional improvement, pain relief, and most perioperative outcomes. The most consistent signal is a prolonged operative time with RA-TKA favoring conventional surgery, though the precise magnitude remains uncertain and may be influenced by the learning curve. The certainty of evidence is low to very low across all assessed outcomes, highlighting the need for cautious interpretation. Current evidence does not support the routine adoption of RA-TKA over C-TKA for TKA. Future adequately powered, multicenter RCTs with long-term follow-up and consistent reporting of surgeon experience are required to definitively clarify the role of RA-TKA in contemporary practice.
authors: Omar Abdelaziz; Ziad G. Zayed; Ahmed Mohamed Altukhy; Salem Waleed; Mohamed A. Hanafy; Rofida Hamdy; Haytham Abdelrahman; Abdalla Mohamed Hadhoud

title: Competency Development Strategies for Functional Entrepreneurship Development Officers in Indonesia's Ministry of MSMEs
abstract: Background: Functional Entrepreneurship Development Officers (JFPKWU) play an important role in MSME coaching; however, competency development within the newly established Ministry of MSMEs remains uneven, reactive, and lacks a position-specific competency-needs plan. This gap highlights the need to analyze competency development mechanisms and strengthening strategies. Objective: This study aims to analyze competency development strategies for JFPKWU within the Ministry of MSMEs to improve organizational performance and MSME coaching effectiveness. Methods: A qualitative case study approach was employed through in-depth interviews with nine key informants, participatory observation, and document analysis. Data were analyzed using SWOT and TOWS matrices to integrate internal conditions and external factors into strategic recommendations. Results: The findings indicate that JFPKWU competency development is influenced by three dominant factors: top management support, commitment of specialist and generalist officials, and training and development processes, supported by learning styles, organizational complexity, technology utilization, and human resource management functions. Key challenges include inconsistent leadership support, reactive training approaches, limited training participation, and the absence of position-specific competency planning. The study proposes a seven-strategy framework integrating governance strengthening, adaptive digital and hybrid learning, continuous position-based learning, practice-based collaboration, training transformation, HR optimization, and sustainable competency development. Conclusion: Effective JFPKWU competency development requires integrated strategies that align governance, learning systems, human resource management, digital transformation, and collaborative practices to strengthen organizational capacity and improve MSME coaching performance.
authors: Dendy Koswara; Firman Hadi Rivai

title: Coral Grow-out Robotic Assessment System (CGRAS): Scaling Coral Recruit Monitoring Through Robotics and Computer Vision
abstract: Climate change is the largest threat to coral reefs, with increasing global impacts accelerating the need for scalable reef restoration technologies. Large-scale reef restoration depends on the mass production of corals, such as through coral aquaculture. Coral seeding with recruits grown in aquaculture facilities is a feasible restoration approach, but effective production requires consistent, high-frequency monitoring of tens of thousands of macroscopic (0.5-2mm diameter) recruits, making conventional manual assessment prohibitively labor-intensive. To address this monitoring bottleneck, we introduce the Coral Grow-out Robotic Assessment System (CGRAS) which combines robotic imaging and computer vision to automate data acquisition, perform multi-species detection and counting of corals, and evaluate coral health. CGRAS automatically extracts coral growth, survival and spatial distribution metrics, with the aim of providing timely feedback to operators for optimizing production, grow-out and deployment workflow processes. We demonstrate CGRAS in a large aquaculture facility on standardized coral settlement tiles, reducing the time and labor costs by a factor of 9.6 as compared to manual monitoring, whilst achieving 96.4% agreement for Acropora kenti corals relative to expert counts.
authors: Dorian Tsai; Scarlett Raine; Emilio Olivastri; Riki Lamont; Andrew Lui; Timothy Morris; Joshua Esplin; Christopher A. Brunner; F. Mikaela Nordborg; Reginald Wardleworth; Garima Samvedi; Karen Jäckel; Matthew D. Dunbabin; Tobias Fischer; Andrea Severati

title: Corticospinal Excitability Depends on Hemodynamic Brain State: A Study using Optical Neuroimaging-Triggered, Brain-State-Dependent Stimulation
abstract: Background This study aimed to investigate whether a neural interface, which utilizes functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) to trigger transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) based on real-time hemodynamic signals, can modulate corticospinal excitability more effectively than brain-state-independent stimulation. Methods We developed an fNIRS-TMS interface that acquired oxyhemoglobin concentrations from the supplementary motor area (SMA) during kinesthetic motor imagery (KMI). In the brain-state-independent condition, participants performed continuous KMI while TMS pulses were delivered irrespective of their brain state. In the fNIRS-guided state-dependent condition, TMS was triggered to elicit motor evoked potentials (MEPs) only when real-time fNIRS signals from the SMA exceeded a predetermined activation threshold. MEP amplitudes were compared between conditions in both healthy and post-stroke participants. Results In 20 healthy participants, a generalized estimating equation adjusted for VAS revealed that SMA-fNIRS-guided TMS produced significantly larger MEP amplitude compared to the brain-state-independent TMS ( p = 0.010). Parameter estimates indicated that MEP amplitude was lower in the brain-state-independent condition compared to that collected during the brain-state-dependent condition ( B = −0.109, SE = 0.042, 95% CI: [−0.192, −0.026]). However, no significant difference between the two conditions was observed in the included eight patients with subcortical ischemic stroke. Above the individual activation threshold, higher hemodynamic signal levels were associated with lower MEP amplitude ( r = −0.15, p = 0.027). Conclusion The fNIRS-TMS interface shows preliminary technical feasibility for developing brain-state-dependent stimulation to probe and modulate brain function. Whether the absence of brain-state-dependent facilitation of SMA in post-stroke participants reflects impaired SMA-to-M1 facilitatory connectivity, and whether restoring such facilitation is clinically beneficial, warrant further investigation. Clinical trial registration NCT07088107.

title: Critical Success Factors for AI Training Robot Adoption in Accounting SMEs: An Integrated Delphi–DEMATEL–ANP Approach
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Robotic Process Automation (RPA) are transforming accounting services toward intelligent, data-driven professional services. However, small and medium-sized accounting firms (SMEs) face barriers to AI adoption, including limited resources, technological capabilities, employee skills, and regulatory uncertainty. This study identifies and prioritizes the critical success factors (CSFs) influencing AI training robot adoption in Taiwanese accounting SMEs. The framework integrates the Technology–Organization–Environment (TOE) framework, Task–Technology Fit (TTF), Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), Human–Computer Trust (HCT), and Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI). We used a two-round Delphi process with 15 experts to refine the CSFs, followed by DEMATEL to identify causal relationships and ANP to assess their relative priorities. The DEMATEL results indicate that the Technological dimension is the strongest causal driver (D−R = 1.355), followed by the Organizational dimension (D−R = 0.435), whereas Decision Making is the principal effect dimension (D−R = −1.781). The findings further emphasize task–technology alignment, AI maturity, regulatory conditions, top management support, employee AI competence, and human–computer trust. Overall, AI adoption represents an integrated organizational transformation rather than merely a technological investment. The proposed Delphi–DEMATEL–ANP framework provides systematic decision support for resource prioritization, organizational readiness, capability development, and sustainable AI-enabled digital transformation in accounting SMEs. JEL classification numbers: M15, M41, O33, C44. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, AI Training Robots, Accounting SMEs, Task-Technology Fit, DEMATEL, Analytic Network Process, Digital Transformation.

title: Decision-making styles, organizational ıinnovativeness, and change fatigue in healthcare
abstract: Introduction and Objective: Decision-making styles, organizational innovativeness, and change fatigue are three interrelated variables in healthcare management. This study aimed to explore health managers' experiences and perceptions of these variables and identify the individual, organizational, and contextual factors shaping their dynamics. Materials and Methods: Semi-structured in-depth interviews were conducted with 15 health managers from private healthcare institutions in Istanbul, Turkey, representing lower, middle, and upper management equally. Data were collected between April–October 2025 and analyzed through thematic analysis. Findings and Conclusions: Three main themes emerged: (1) Reasons for resistance to change and innovation (13 sub-themes including habitual resistance, staff turnover, and change fatigue from unplanned changes); (2) Facilitators of change and innovation (13 sub-themes including top management support, digitalization, and ownership capacity); (3) The influence of decision-making styles (7 sub-themes including inclusive decision-making, evidence-based rationality, and crisis-induced necessity). Inclusive and evidence-based styles were positively associated with innovativeness; change fatigue adversely affected both innovativeness and decision-making.Participatory and evidence-based decision-making styles are positively associated with organizational innovativeness and may mitigate change fatigue. These findings carry actionable implications for health managers and policymakers.
authors: Funda Topak; Ramazan Özgür ÇATAR

title: Deep Lunar Rock Assessment with Vision and Vibration
abstract: Autonomous lunar site preparation requires assessing individual rocks before excavation or relocation. Strong illumination contrast, occlusion, and burial make this difficult: observations from different viewpoints must be assigned to the same rock before its geometry can be estimated, while surface observations alone provide limited information about embedment. This dissertation develops visual methods for recovering rock identity and geometry, complemented by a separately evaluated vibration-based method for estimating burial depth. First, an RGB-plus-inverted-depth segmentation model identifies individual rocks, and calibrated projection converts their masks into metric three-dimensional surface observations. Second, ShadowCorr determines which observations belong to the same rock by projecting volumetric shadows behind visible surfaces and learning their shared spatial support. This approach does not require appearance similarity or direct surface overlap. Separate synthetic evaluations achieved average correspondence purity of 99.1% with complete masks and 98.9% with controlled mask erosion. Third, the associated observations support geometric completion using a covariance-ellipsoid prior, followed by mesh construction and volume and centroid estimation. In the four-view synthetic evaluation, matched, valid reconstructions achieved a median volume error of 16.5% and a median centroid error equal to 4.0% of the true longest rock dimension. Compared with visible-point convex-hull and alpha-shape closures, completion improved centroid accuracy while producing higher volume error. Fourth, impulse excitation and scanning laser Doppler vibrometry measure the response of partially buried specimens. A neural-network model uses vibration features and exposed geometry to estimate burial depth without measured rock mass or soil parameters as inputs. Separate laboratory experiments with 18 concrete specimens in sand achieved a root mean squared depth error of 0.94 cm under nested leave-one-rock-out evaluation, with each specimen excluded from model development when tested. Together, these studies establish methods for recovering individual-rock geometry from incomplete visual observations and obtaining complementary burial-depth information from vibration. The results support future robotic assessment before rock removal; validation with natural rocks and lunar conditions, automated measurement, and integration of the sensing methods remain future work.
authors: Yiyan Ruan

title: Deep TMS modulates neurovascular responses and enhances dual-task computation in healthy adults
abstract: Dual-task performance requires coordination between cognitive control and motor systems. This study examined how deep transcranial magnetic stimulation (DTMS) influences cortical responses and computational performance during dual-task processing. In a randomized crossover study, 19 healthy adults underwent DTMS targeting the bilateral prefrontal cortex and anterior cingulate cortex and sham stimulation in separate sessions, with functional near-infrared spectroscopy and dual-task assessments performed before and after each intervention. Compared with sham stimulation, DTMS increased task-related cortical activation in regions involved in cognitive-motor processing and improved computation number without affecting accuracy. Activation changes involving the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, secondary motor cortex, and language-related regions were associated with dual-task performance. These findings suggest that DTMS may modulate distributed cortical dynamics supporting cognitive-motor coordination and inform its potential application in populations with cognitive-motor impairments.
authors: Baoyao Zeng; Weining Wang; Zhengran Ding; Chen Wang; Ce Li; Runzhe Yuan; Bao Zhou; Yulian Zhu

title: Determinants influencing digital twin adoption decision in food supply chains
abstract: Digital Twins (DTs) are increasingly recognised as a promising solution for food supply chains (FSCs). However, existing DT research has focused mainly on conceptual development, technical applications, and pilot implementations, providing limited empirical evidence on the determinants influencing firms' adoption decisions. Thus, this study examines the determinants of DT adoption decisions in FSCs. Drawing on Diffusion of Innovation theory and the technology-organisation-environment (TOE) framework, the study develops a research model explaining how TOE factors shape firms' adoption decisions. Survey data from 260 respondents in food and technology-related firms across Western economies are analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling. Results show that compatibility, technology readiness, top management support, competitive pressure, and market uncertainty significantly influence the DT adoption decision, while complexity negatively affects adoption. Findings indicate that the DT adoption decision in FSCs is shaped not only by perceived technological characteristics but also by organisational support and external environmental pressures.
authors: Ying Huang; Abhijeet Ghadge; Nicky Yates

title: Digital multimodal vocabulary projects in Indonesian EFL higher education: Design, assessment, and students’ perceptions
abstract: Vocabulary assessment in Indonesian EFL higher education remains predominantly focused on discrete-item tests, prioritizing individual receptive knowledge. To address limitations of such tests, this study examined collaborative, digital, multimodal vocabulary projects in a pre-service teacher class in Indonesia and explored students’ perceptions. This study is an exploratory, single-case qualitative study conducted with a class of 30 third-semester EFL teacher-education students. They collaboratively created two digitally mediated multimodal projects: a Quizizz-based vocabulary quiz set and an idiom-based conversation video. The project artefacts, rubric notes, the lecturer’s reflection notes, and semi-structured interview scripts were analyzed thematically. The study revealed that students experienced gains in creativity, critical thinking, collaboration, digital skills, and enjoyment throughout the process. However, they reported time constraints, communication challenges, and performance anxiety. Group-based digital projects were evident to make vocabulary use in context observable, and multimodal assessment was found to support vocabulary learning and learning-oriented assessment. The research contributes empirical evidence on multimodal assessment for vocabulary learning in Indonesian EFL higher education, a context that remains underrepresented in the literature. It is recommended that collaborative, multimodal task design be integrated into pre-service teacher education to scaffold digital literacy, collaboration, culturally relevant development, and contextually grounded vocabulary assessment practices.
authors: Nurmala Hendrawaty; Zulfa Sakhiyya; Sri Wahyuni; Yuliati Yuliati

title: Disparity in Coronal Deformity Measurements: Standing Radiographs Versus Navigation in Varus Total Knee Arthroplasty.
abstract: This study aimed to ascertain whether a discrepancy exists between coronal deformity measurements obtained from radiographs and those from computer navigation, and to explore potential reasons for such discrepancy. This study assessed 621 primary navigated TKAs performed on varus arthritic knees. Preoperative and postoperative hip-knee-ankle angle (HKA), mechanical lateral distal femoral angle (LDFA), medial proximal tibial angle (MPTA), and joint congruence angle (JCA) were measured using scanograms. Initial coronal deformity after arthrotomy and prior to performing releases or bone cuts was recorded during navigation using a proven dynamic method. The difference between radiographic and navigation measurements of initial deformity was calculated. The mean preoperative HKA was 12.6º (SD ± 6.11, range 0.8º to 40.9º), while the mean initial alignment on navigation was 14° (SD ± 5.96, range 2º to 42º). The mean difference between these values of-1.42º was highly significant (SD ± 3.04, range -17º to 10.5º, P < 0.001 on t test,), with a correlation of r = 0.873 (P < 0.001). This difference exceeded ± 2º in over half of the knees (n = 314, 50.6%). There was a progressively increasing difference between the two measurements with an increase in mean initial HKA, LDFA, and JCA, and a decrease in mean MPTA (ANOVA, P < 0.001). Surgeons performing TKA surgery using navigation or robots should be aware of the potential discrepancies between coronal deformity measurements. Factors such as increased coronal deformity, medial bone deficiency, and lateral laxity may contribute to this discrepancy.
authors: Anand Kumar Gupta; Arun Mullaji

title: Disrupted bilateral co‐ordination of soleus motor units during early subacute stroke rehabilitation
abstract: Stroke can affect sensorimotor control, impairing balance and locomotion. These impairments increase fall risk, limit patient independence and reduce quality of life. Here, we investigated how stroke affects bilateral co-ordination of soleus motor units during standing in individuals undergoing subacute rehabilitation. Fourteen individuals were recruited after admission for inpatient rehabilitation with sixteen age- and sex-matched controls. Both groups attended two sessions separated by 1 week, during which high-density electromyography (EMG) signals were recorded from soleus muscles when standing on force plates. Patients also performed the Berg Balance Scale (BBS). EMG signals were decomposed into motor unit spike trains, from which peristimulus time histograms and EMG waveform averages were computed in relation to peaks in centre of pressure (COP). The amplitude of motor unit and EMG activity around COP peaks, directional tuning and bilateral synchronization were estimated. Individuals post-stroke improved their BBS score between visits, but COP displacement and speed were still greater than controls. Soleus activity was tuned anteriorly in both control and non-paretic limbs, whereas it was tuned laterally in paretic limbs. Synchronization of soleus activity was also reduced in the paretic limb compared to controls. Furthermore, cross-correlation lag between limbs was greater in individuals post-stroke than in controls at visit 1, whereas it decreased to control levels at visit 2 (P = 0.008). The decrease in lags was strongly correlated with improvement in BBS score (R = -0.94, P < 0.001). These results highlight the importance of bilateral motor unit co-ordination in balance, which is disrupted in both spatial and temporal domains following stroke. KEY POINTS: We examined bilateral motor unit co-ordination during quiet standing in individuals in the early subacute phase following unilateral stroke, whereas previous works have focused on the chronic phase post-stroke. Although the non-paretic limb of patients exhibited a spatial tuning of its activity oriented in the same direction as those of neurologically intact controls, the spatial tuning of the activity of the paretic limb was altered. Bilateral synchronization between soleus motor units was reduced in individuals post-stroke in comparison with neurologically intact controls. The level of bilateral synchronization between soleus motor units was associated with balance function and improved after one week of inpatient rehabilitation.
authors: Jackson T. Levine; Xin S. Yu; Alyssa Jones; Rebecca Munoz; Martin Zaback; Christopher K. Thompson; Dario Farina; Simon Avrillon; Jose L. Pons

title: Disrupting the Right Inferior Frontal Gyrus Increases ‘Social Brain’ Activity During Emotion Recognition
abstract: Abstract Neuroimaging studies have identified a specialised social brain network that supports emotion recognition and social cognition. This network performs a range of functions that include facial expression recognition and inferring the mental states of others. Studies of neuropsychological patients report that damage to the right inferior frontal gyrus (IFG), the top-down control area in this network, impairs facial expression recognition. To investigate how transient disruption of the right IFG affects the wider social brain we combined transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) with functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI). Participants ( n =20) were scanned across two sessions while performing a delayed match-to-sample emotion recognition task in which happy or fearful expressions were preceded by a congruent or incongruent word cue. Prior to each scan, thetaburst TMS was delivered over the right IFG or over the vertex control site (session order was balanced across participants). A group whole-brain analysis revealed that TMS to the IFG increased neural activity in multiple regions of the social brain network. These included the bilateral temporal pole, precuneus and medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC). This pattern of results shows that the disruption of top-down control mechanisms localised in the IFG alters the neural processing in remote nodes of the social brain network. Our findings are discussed within the wider context of how we recognise and understand the emotions of other people.
authors: Emel Küçük; Hannah Gofton; Cameron Smith; DANIEL H. KAISER; David Pitcher

title: Do Not Chase Symmetric Gaps: Native Asymmetry Linked to Better Recovery in Fixed-Deformity Total Knee Arthroplasty.
abstract:
Background

Non-correctable (fixed) knee deformities in total knee arthroplasty (TKA) are technically demanding, and the intraoperative factors driving recovery in this subgroup remain unclear. We hypothesized that, in non-correctable knees, a strategy that minimizes bone resection and preserves the patient's native medio-lateral laxity asymmetry, rather than chasing symmetric gaps through additional bone removal, would be associated with superior patient-reported functional outcomes at one year, whereas no such association would be observed in correctable knees.

Methods

We reviewed 861 consecutive primary robotic-arm-assisted TKAs (634 correctable, 227 non-correctable) at a single academic institution. Correctability was assessed intraoperatively by varus-valgus stress in extension: correctable if alignment came within 3° of neutral, non-correctable if it remained greater than 3° from neutral1-3. The robotic system quantified native and reconstructed compartment laxity in near extension (5 to 20°) and flexion (90 ± 10°) and recorded planned resection depths. Postoperative medial-lateral (M-L) laxity differential (reconstructed medial - lateral) was categorized as symmetric (less than 0.5 mm), partially corrected (0.5 to two mm), or preserved native asymmetry (two to five mm). The Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score for Joint Replacement (KOOS JR) and PROMIS (Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System) Physical Function were collected preoperatively and at six weeks, three months, and one year, stratified by correctability.

Results

The non-correctable knees showed greater PROMIS Physical Function improvement at three months (P = 0.003) and one year (7.0 ± 7.8 versus 4.9 ± 6.8; P = 0.036) despite similar preoperative scores. Among non-correctable knees, lower total bone resection volume was associated with greater KOOS JR improvement at one year (P = 0.016), strongest in the lateral flexion compartment (P = 0.039), indicating over-resection beyond implant thickness to achieve symmetric gaps is linked to poorer recovery. Greater postoperative flexion M-L laxity differential was also associated with greater KOOS JR (P = 0.009) and PROMIS (P = 0.044) improvement.

Conclusions

In non-correctable knees undergoing robotic-assisted TKA, preservation of native M-L laxity asymmetry is associated with superior patient-reported functional recovery. These findings challenge the universal goal of symmetric gaps and support an adaptive strategy that prioritizes bone preservation in fixed deformities.
authors: Suhardi VJ, Gwam C, DiGangi C, Hepinstall M, Rozell J, Meftah M.

title: Drivers and Barriers to Artificial Intelligence Adoption in the Banking Sector: Evidence from Cambodia
abstract: Driven by the Fourth and Fifth Industrial Revolutions, global financial institutions are aggressively deploying artificial intelligence (AI) technologies to optimize operations, risk management, and customer engagement. However, empirical investigation into AI adoption dynamics within emerging economies remains critically sparse, as established technology acceptance frameworks predominantly reflect advanced or industrialized environments. This study investigates the primary determinants—encompassing both technological, organizational, and environmental drivers and barriers—influencing AI adoption across the banking sector in Cambodia, evaluating 25 hypotheses to establish an integrated conceptual model tailored to emerging financial settings. A mixed-methods design with concurrent triangulation was executed. Quantitative data were gathered via a survey of 83 banking institutions and analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). Qualitative insights were extracted via content analysis on 17 semi-structured interviews. As a result, PLS-SEM path modeling confirmed 17 of 25 hypotheses as statistically significant drivers. Primary drivers include top management’s innovativeness, business scope, top management’s support, familiarity with innovation, and relative advantage. Surprisingly, traditional economic and structural inhibitors—technical complexity, cost, centralization, formalization, organization size, slack, government policies, and geographical settings—were statistically unsupported as firm-level barriers in the quantitative model. Nonetheless, qualitative content analysis supported 24 of 25 factors, exposing a profound perception-reality gap where operational friction is overridden by top-down executive mandates and competitive survival pressures. AI adoption in emerging banking markets operates under a Strategic Survival Mandate, wherein banking institutions bypass cost and complexity constraints to maintain market relevance. Policy interventions are critical to promoting sound adoption.
authors: Soklay Ky
venue: International Journal of Management and Economics Invention

title: EM-SNN: Efficiently Modulated Spiking Neural Network for Remote Sensing Image Dehazing
abstract: Although spiking neural networks (SNNs) provide an energy-efficient alternative to artificial neural networks (ANNs), their application to remote sensing image dehazing remains limited. A key challenge arises from the coupling between haze-induced high-frequency attenuation and discrete spike thresholding. This interaction suppresses weak responses and fundamentally limits the recovery of edges, textures, and fine details in spiking dehazing models. To address this challenge, we propose the Efficiently Modulated Spiking Neural Network (EM-SNN), a dedicated spiking framework tailored to remote sensing image dehazing. EM-SNN integrates a statistics-driven Threshold-Modulated Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (TM-LIF) neuron to adaptively compensate for haze-induced contrast compression, together with a Spike Sobel Modulation (SSM) module that enhances structural cues and reduces depth-wise attenuation during spiking feature propagation. By jointly modulating activation scales and structural representations, EM-SNN improves dehazing performance while preserving the inherent event-driven sparsity of SNNs. Experiments on HRSD, RICE, RRSHID, and SateHaze1K demonstrate that EM-SNN achieves competitive dehazing performance while consuming only one quarter of the energy of the strong ANN baseline SFRDP-Net.
authors: Jie Shao; Jiaqi Ma; Wenwen Min; Beihang Song; Ning Chen; Youfa Liu; Jun Wan

title: EVALUATING THE IMPACT OF SUPPLY CHAIN QUALITY ON SUPPLIER PERFORMANCE: A FIELD STUDY AT THE GENERAL COMPANY FOR ELECTRICAL INDUSTRIES, BAGHDAD
abstract: This study examined the impact of supply chain quality on supplier performance at the General Company for Electrical and Electronic Industries in Baghdad. Supply chain quality was measured through five dimensions: top management support, supplier relationships, total quality management, information integration, and continuous improvement. Supplier performance was assessed through quality, delivery, flexibility, and cost. The study adopted a descriptive-analytical approach. The population comprised 245 employees from relevant departments, from which a purposive sample of 150 employees was selected. A total of 127 valid questionnaires were collected and analyzed. Data were collected using a questionnaire whose validity and reliability were established. The overall Cronbach’s alpha coefficient was 0.947. Data analysis was conducted using SPSS version 26.The findings indicated moderate levels of both supply chain quality and supplier performance, with mean scores of 3.60 and 3.51, respectively. Total quality management recorded the highest mean among supply chain quality dimensions, while cost was the highest supplier performance dimension. The results also revealed a statistically significant positive relationship between supply chain quality and supplier performance. The combined dimensions of supply chain quality significantly explained 65.9% of the variance in supplier performance. Supplier relationships emerged as the most influential dimension.The study recommends strengthening long-term strategic supplier relationships, investing in digital infrastructure and information-sharing systems, establishing a specialized supplier development unit, adopting continuous improvement practices, and implementing supplier performance evaluation systems based on measurable indicators.
authors: Nawfal Kadhim Abd Oun

title: EXPRESS: BOLD Contrast in Cerebral Diffuse Glioma Imaging: Biological Foundations and Clinical Applications – A Review of the Literature
abstract: Diffuse cerebral gliomas are the most common malignant brain tumors in adults. In the present work we conducted a narrative review on the role of blood oxygen level-dependent (BOLD)-MRI in diffuse glioma imaging, from historical and clinical applications to recent translational studies including approaches to detect vascular and metabolic alterations as well as its expanding potential to enhance tumor infiltration assessment and treatment surveillance. Task-based and resting-state BOLD-MRI enable localization of eloquent cortical areas and assessment of functional reorganization, though their accuracy is challenged by neurovascular uncoupling and patient-related variability. Combination with vasoactive stimuli allows cerebrovascular reactivity mapping to uncover vascular dysfunction propagating beyond visible tumor margins, correlating with tumor grade and hemodynamic impairment. Quantitative and calibrated BOLD approaches as well as oxygen modulation during BOLD sequence acquisition provide noninvasive biomarkers of tissue hypoxia, oxygen metabolism, and tumor aggressiveness. Despite extensive research, BOLD contrast holds unexploited potential for enhancing glioma diagnosis and management by capturing critical vascular and metabolic alterations. Although challenges remain pertaining to accuracy and standardization, emerging techniques offer substantial potential for the assessment of tumor infiltration extent and therapy surveillance. Advancing clinical integration will require robust standardization, large-scale validation, and correlation with clinical, molecular, and histopathological data.

title: Editorial: Non-invasive brain stimulation: from basic science to clinical application
abstract: Non-invasive brain stimulation (NIBS) techniques are used both as causal probes of brain function and as clinically established or investigational interventions for neurological and psychiatric disorders. Transcranial electrical stimulation (tES), transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), and transcranial ultrasound stimulation (TUS) differ in their physical principles, spatial resolution, and biological effects, yet share a central translational challenge: stimulation must engage the right neural system, in the right patient, at an appropriate dose, and ultimately produce clinically meaningful benefit.
