title: Real-time noise cancellation for EEG monitoring and brain–computer interfaces
abstract: A bstract Raw electroencephalography (EEG) data suffer from a low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). Effective real-time cleaning of EEG would improve the robustness of EEG monitoring, brain–computer interfaces, and brain-state-dependent stimulation applications in both laboratory and real-life environments. Here, we present a real-time source-estimate-utilizing noise-discarding algorithm (rtSOUND) for EEG noise suppression. We adapted the established offline SOUND algorithm for real-time use and implemented it into an open-source EEG-processing software. Instead of using conventional temporal filtering, SOUND operates the data with a spatial filter. This makes it particularly suitable for real-time applications, since each streamed data sample can be cleaned separately in near real-time. Unlike temporal filtering methods, SOUND does not make assumptions about the frequency content of noise and brain signals but assumes that the noise topographies differ from those generated by brain activity. With an EEG forward model, rtSOUND cross-validates the EEG time series and estimates the spatial distribution of noise, resulting in a data-cleaning linear spatial filter. Each streamed EEG sample is processed synchronously, and the filter is periodically updated in an asynchronous parallel process. The algorithm rapidly updates the spatial filter in response to changes in the data, ensuring that noise reduction is both immediate and accurately adapted to the current EEG state. rtSOUND was validated with transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS)–EEG and resting-state EEG datasets measured from 25 healthy subjects. SNR of both TMS-evoked potentials and resting-state data consistently improved across various metrics. rtSOUND particularly benefitted channels with poor SNR, while retaining the waveforms in high-quality channels. The algorithm was fast enough to process data streamed at 5 kHz. rtSOUND improves the SNR of EEG in real time, providing a robust method to improve signal quality for brain-state-monitoring applications.
authors: Matilda Makkonen; Olli‐Pekka Kahilakoski; Johanna Metsomaa; Pantelis Lioumis; Risto Juhani Ilmoniemi; Tuomas P. Mutanen

title: Real-time posterior probabilistic TMS motor mapping with robust individualized stopping criteria
abstract: Abstract Background Electric-field-informed regression provides high-resolution transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) motor maps, but conventional nonlinear fitting is too slow to update the map during acquisition, so sessions rely on predefined stimulation budgets, despite sub-stantial inter-individual variability in the data required for stable localization. Objective To develop a real-time analysis updating a posterior probability map between pulses and compare its hotspots with finger-tapping functional MRI (fMRI). Methods We analyzed two independent cohorts (12 and 13 participants, one newly collected), analyzing each hand muscle independently. We replaced the conventional per-element sigmoid fit with Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient and transformed the resulting score map into a posterior probability map using marginal-likelihood evidence. Acquisition stopped once posterior mass within 5 mm of the hotspot passed a preset confidence level. Results The Spearman and linear scores updated the region of interest within milliseconds, versus tens of seconds for sigmoid fitting. Spearman more closely matched the full-data sigmoid hotspot in recorded sessions and converged faster and more precisely to the true source in virtual subjects. Across both fast scores, at a confidence level of 0.85 the stopping criterion was met after a median of 74-159 pulses, with 26-454 across individual problems. FDI hotspots lay 8.3 ± 4.3 mm from the fMRI center of gravity, in the precentral hand region. Conclusions Rank correlation reduces computation time without loss of accuracy relative to sigmoid fitting. The resulting posterior probability map provides a session-specific stopping criterion in place of a fixed pulse budget.
authors: Renxiang Qiu; Zi‐Jian Feng; Ole Numssen; Yu‐Feng Zang; Florian Wilhelmy; Erdem Güresir; Thomas R. Knösche; Konstantin Weise

title: Reinforcement learning guided robotic platform that investigates and discovers asymmetric reactions
abstract: Abstract Autonomous robotic platforms accelerate chemical discovery by coupling automated experimentation with algorithmic decision-making, but most lack integrated support for chirality and the sequential decision-making required to explore asymmetric reaction spaces with unknown reactivity and stereochemical outcomes. Here, we report a bespoke robotic platform guided by deep reinforcement learning that autonomously navigates a defined asymmetric reaction space by scouting reaction conditions, discovering chiral products, screening catalysts and mapping substrate scope. The structure-agnostic workflow is enabled by a digital twin of asymmetric catalysis, in which control policies are trained before transfer to the laboratory. We validate the approach in chiral phosphoric acid catalysis: over 30 days, the system made more than 3,000 decisions and uncovered four highly enantioselective transformations, including an axially chiral molecule and three allene syntheses, one involving the enantioselective functionalization of a pyrrolopyrrole moiety. These results highlight deep reinforcement learning-guided autonomy as a strategy for discovery in complex catalytic systems.
authors: Patryk Klochowicz; Ahmad F. Kassir; Chandrakanta Parida; Jarosław M. Granda

title: Reorienting TMS treatments for fear memories and posttraumatic stress disorder. The emerging potential of the anterior prefrontal cortex.
abstract: Posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is characterized by re-experiencing trauma through vivid and involuntary intrusions, avoidance of cues that could trigger traumatic memories, and alterations in mood and cognition. Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) offers a promising approach to modulating activity and functional coupling within neural circuits underlying these processes. To date, TMS studies in fear-conditioning research and PTSD have mainly focused on dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) and ventromedial (vmPFC)-connected or broader medial-prefrontal (mPFC) targets, yielding encouraging but heterogeneous effects on posttraumatic symptoms. In parallel, emerging evidence has implicated the anterior prefrontal cortex (aPFC; Brodmann area 10) in threat- and trauma-related processes, including memory retrieval, higher-order control of defensive responding, adaptive strategy selection, and resilience. Whereas the dlPFC and vmPFC have been incorporated into mechanistic models of fear regulation, the aPFC has received limited attention in theoretical frameworks of fear and PTSD. Here, we review TMS studies organized around dlPFC, vmPFC-connected or mPFC, and aPFC neuroanatomical targets, integrating evidence from experimental and clinical research. Based on the hierarchical model of prefrontal organization, we argue that these regions represent potential TMS targets or circuit nodes, but likely act on partially distinct mechanisms. The vmPFC appears primarily involved in early automatic downregulation of defensive responses; the dlPFC may support cognitive control strategies such as reappraisal; and the aPFC may enable a supraordinate influence over higher-order representations and avoidance-related circuitry, as well as flexible selection of emotion-regulation strategies. We conclude that integrating the aPFC into this framework may guide next-generation, mechanistically-informed TMS treatments for PTSD.
authors: Alba Chiara La Pastina; Eugenio Manassero; Benedetto Sacchetti

title: Repeated Head Impacts May Compromise White Matter Integrity and Bimanual Coordination in American Football Players
abstract: Abstract Objectives To determine whether repetitive subconcussive impacts in collegiate football are associated with altered white matter microstructure, motor control deficits, and changes in concussion symptoms across a single season. Design Cohort study with non-contact controls and stratification of contact athletes by head-impact exposure. Method Twenty-two male varsity football players and 27 non-contact controls underwent pre-season diffusion tensor imaging. Tract-specific fractional anisotropy (FA) and mean diffusivity (MD) were derived from commissural and association tracts using probabilistic tractography. Helmet-mounted accelerometers quantified head-impact frequency and gForce over the season, classifying athletes into high (HE) and low-exposure (LE) groups. Football players completed the Kinarm Ball-on-Bar bimanual coordination task and SCAT3 symptom checklist pre- and post-season. Results At pre-season, contact athletes showed altered white matter microstructure versus controls, with higher FA and predominantly lower MD across most tracts. Over the season, HE athletes sustained more total impacts and gForce than LE athletes and showed declining bimanual coordination on the Ball-on-Bar motor task. SCAT3 symptom and severity scores were low and showed no differences in change. Conclusions Repetitive subconcussive exposure in collegiate football is associated with persisting white matter differences and subtle bimanual motor coordination deficits that are not detected by routine symptom-based tools, supporting the use of advanced neuroimaging and robotic motor assessment to monitor athlete brain health.
authors: Sebastian D’Amario; Blaire T. Magee; Allen A. Champagne; Madison E. Wilson; Gabriel Ramirez‐Garcia; Nicole S. Coverdale; Douglas J. Cook

title: Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation paired with a 3D-printed ankle-foot orthosis for ankle-foot dysfunction among older adults following subacute stroke: clinical findings and exploratory neurophysiological analyses
abstract: Objective This work evaluated clinical effects of repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) plus custom-made 3D-printed ankle-foot orthosis (AFO) for older adults living with post-stroke ankle-foot impairment. Neurophysiological assessments were also carried out for exploratory purposes, drawing exclusively on indirect physiological readouts. Materials and methods Sixty older participants with ankle-foot dysfunction after subacute stroke were randomized into three parallel groups: conventional-only rehabilitation, 3D-printed AFO therapy, and combined rTMS-AFO intervention ( n = 20 per group). Evaluations including ankle active range-of-motion (AROM), resting motor threshold (RMT), integrated surface electromyography (iEMG), Clinical Spasticity Index (CSI), Fugl-Meyer Assessment of the Lower Extremity (FMA-LE), Berg Balance Scale (BBS), and 10-Metre Walking Test (10MWT) were performed at baseline and four-week post-intervention time-point. Results Noticeable within-group functional improvements emerged in all three study arms upon completion of treatment ( p < 0.001). Participants assigned to combined therapy achieved greater functional improvements compared with those receiving standalone 3D-printed-AFO or conventional rehabilitation ( p < 0.05). The conventional rehabilitation group produced the weakest magnitude of functional recovery across measured endpoints. Conclusion Compared with single-modality rehabilitation approaches, adding rTMS to 3D-printed AFO therapy brought measurable improvements in ankle mobility, muscle recruitment, balance and walking performance. These clinical benefits occurred alongside elevated excitability within the ipsilesional corticospinal tract. Explanations regarding sensorimotor integration and afferent-efferent circuit regulation should be regarded as exploratory hypotheses because direct neural measurements were not obtained in this investigation. Further independent research is needed to test these mechanistic assumptions.
authors: Yuting Zhang; Hehe Chen; Rui Xu; Lingyu Zhu; Siyuan Song; Weixin Zhu

title: Replication of the Robotic Evaluation of Articular Laxity (REAL) classification using intraoperative gap data in robot-assisted total knee arthroplasty.
abstract: Robot-assisted total knee arthroplasty (TKA) enables objective assessment of mediolateral (ML) balance; however, comparisons across cohorts remain difficult because "imbalance" has been poorly defined. The Robotic Evaluation of Articular Laxity (REAL) classification was proposed to standardize ML imbalance using a 3 × 3 framework, but independent replication of this novel classification has not been performed. We retrospectively reviewed 386 robot-assisted TKAs for osteoarthritis. Medial and lateral extension and flexion gaps were recorded before bone resection and at procedure end. ML imbalance was calculated as signed and absolute values. Primary outcomes were the distribution and normality of signed ML imbalance and the goodness-of-fit of varus REAL category frequencies versus the original REAL report using thresholds of 2.5 and 5.0 mm. Exploratory analyses evaluated patient-reported outcomes across initial REAL categories. In the full cohort, initial signed ML imbalance deviated from normality, whereas varus initial extension imbalance was nearly normal (1.08 ± 2.79 mm). Final absolute ML imbalance was about 1 mm in extension and 1.0-1.3 mm in flexion, with significant paired reductions in both (both p < 0.001). Varus REAL category frequencies differed from the original report, but deviations were modest and concentrated in a subset of cells. Patient-reported outcomes did not differ across initial REAL categories. In this independent robot-assisted TKA cohort, key features of the REAL framework were replicated in varus knees. Intraoperative balancing substantially improved ML balance, supporting the descriptive utility of REAL for organizing intraoperative balance phenotypes across cohorts.
authors: Yugo Morita; Nikolaos Mylonakis; Jonggu Shin; Mohammed El-Hassan; Ittai Shichman; Eustathios Kenanidis; Eleftherios Tsiridis; Peter K Sculco

title: Reticulospinal hyperexcitability after stroke: Associations with impairment severity and no evidence of functional advantage in severe cases
abstract: OBJECTIVE: Reticulospinal tract (RST) excitability increases after stroke. Although animal studies suggest that this hyperexcitability may compensate for corticospinal tract damage, its role in motor function in persons with stroke (PwS) remains debated. This study aimed to replicate RST hyperexcitability in PwS using the StartReact paradigm, examine associations with motor impairment, and explore whether heightened responses were associated with functional benefit in a subgroup with severe upper-limb impairment. METHODS: In this cross-sectional study, 46 PwS and 37 healthy controls completed a StartReact paradigm. Upper-limb impairment was assessed using the Upper Extremity Fugl-Meyer, Action Research Arm Test (ARAT), grip strength, and Modified Ashworth Scale. PwS were classified as having high or typical StartReact effects based on the control 90th percentile. Severe impairment was defined as ARAT ≤10. RESULTS: PwS showed greater StartReact effects than controls (median: 15.00 vs. 5.21 ms; U = 667.5, p = 0.047, rank-biserial correlation = 0.22). StartReact effects were negatively correlated with ARAT (r = -0.44, p < 0.01), Fugl-Meyer (r = -0.51, p < 0.01), and grip strength (r = -0.36, p = 0.01). The high StartReact subgroup showed poorer upper-limb function, weaker grip strength, and greater biceps spasticity (U = 266, p = 0.02). Within the severe impairment subgroup, high StartReact effects were not associated with greater grip strength. CONCLUSIONS: StartReact-derived RST hyperexcitability was associated with greater post-stroke upper-limb motor impairment. In the severe subgroup, heightened responses were not associated with greater grip strength. These findings cannot establish that RST hyperexcitability supports functional recovery.
authors: Adi Lorber-Haddad; Noy Goldhamer; Tamar Mizrahi; Shirley Handelzalts; Lior Shmuelof

title: Reusing Statistical Guarantees Under Change: Selection Costs and Event Ownership
abstract: An adaptive system can retain an earlier estimate while changing what that estimate is used to guarantee. The guarantee depends on the experiment that produced the evidence, including how its target was selected and which assumptions connect it to the current claim. We show that past-measurable selection preserves future martingale dynamics without preserving a unit expected starting value. An exact finite counterexample, using a strictly positive family, refutes a published changing-prior extension as stated with probability one and rules out unrestricted bounds based only on switch count and the error level. We give a paid-start multi-switch correction and establish $m$ as the sharp worst-case expected starting-moment cost for an unstructured family of $m$ hypotheses. We then develop Adaptive Assurance, a framework in which statistical events retain their experiment, funding and outcome bindings while claims and premise dependencies change. Compatible-outcome projection supports reuse, selective invalidation, fresh acquisition and auditable decisions. Two histories can have identical current regions yet require different responses to a later edit, making evidence origin part of the assurance state. Studies in six public-recorded domains exercise heterogeneous outcomes and access contracts. Component interventions expose erroneous inheritance and unnecessary resets. The framework separates conditional guarantee recovery from competence adaptation, with explicit costs for evidence, computation and verification.
authors: Ao Li; Weitong Chen

title: Robotic Assessment of Thumb Proprioception after Stroke: Reliability, Validity, and Sensitivity.
abstract:
Objective

Despite the thumb's critical role in dexterity and its dense sensory innervation, thumb proprioceptive deficits after stroke remain limited due to the limited nature of clinical assessments. This study evaluated the reliability, validity, and sensitivity of a novel robotic assessment of thumb proprioception, SomatoCircleJump (SCJ), in individuals with chronic stroke.

Design

Cross-sectional psychometric study evaluating the reliability, validity and sensitivity of SCJ using baseline data from a clinical trial, with assessments conducted twice 5-10 days apart. In SCJ, a robot moved the visually occluded thumb, and participants indicated when the thumb passed a visual target.

Setting

University-based rehabilitation research laboratory.

Participants

Thirty-five stroke survivors with residual unilateral hand weakness and 24 healthy age-matched controls.

Interventions

Not applicable.

Main outcome measures

SCJ proprioceptive error, defined as the angular difference between actual thumb position and the visually presented target. Test-retest reliability was assessed with Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC). Validity and sensitivity were evaluated by comparing SCJ with the Fugl-Meyer Assessment Sensory Scale for the upper extremity (FMA-S) thumb position item, and two robotic proprioception tests, one for the thumb (ThumbSense) and one for the fingers (Crisscross).

Results

SCJ demonstrated good test-retest reliability (ICC = 0.82, 95% CI [0.72-0.87]). SCJ error correlated significantly with FMA-S (ρ = -0.56, p < 0.001), ThumbSense accuracy (ρ = -0.62, p < 0.001), and Crisscross error (ρ = 0.61, p < 0.001). Using a 2SD criterion relative to controls, SCJ identified thumb proprioceptive impairment in 61% of stroke participants, compared with 23% identified by FMA-S.

Conclusions

SCJ is a reliable, valid, and sensitive assessment of dynamic thumb proprioception after stroke. It revealed that thumb proprioceptive deficits are common and related to finger proprioception deficits, supporting its use in future studies of sensory impairment and rehabilitation outcomes.
authors: Garcia-Fernandez L, Farrens AJ, Chan V, Rojas RD, Wolbrecht ET, Perry JC, Do AH, Cramer SC, Reinkensmeyer DJ.

title: Robotic Visually Guided Reaching Assessments of Upper-Limb Sensorimotor Function in Subacute Stroke Patients and Healthy Controls (KINARM Exoskeleton Lab)
abstract: This dataset contains KINARM Exoskeleton Lab visually guided reaching assessments. It includes raw exam archives (KINARM .zip files containing C3D trial files) for each stroke and healthy control participant, and two processed MATLAB files. The main processed file holds demographic, clinical (Chedoke-McMaster, Purdue Pegboard, grip and pinch, thumb localization, Behavioural Inattention Test, Folstein MMSE, Functional Independence Measure) and twelve robotic reaching features for 52 stroke participants and 91 healthy controls. We split by dominant hand or affected arm. The second file holds inter-rater reliability data for 8 stroke participants and 6 controls. We also include a data dictionary and the KINARM Standard Tests summary.
authors: Angela M. Coderre; Amr Abou Zeid; Sean Peter Dukelow; Melanie Joy Demmer; Kimberly D. Moore; Mary Jo Demers; Helen Bretzke; Troy M. Herter; Janice Glasgow; Kathleen E. Norman; Stephen D. Bagg; Stephen Harold Scott

title: Robotic assessment of spasticity in neurological conditions: measurement properties and clinical applications. A scoping review protocol
abstract: This scoping review maps robotic and motorized systems used to assess spasticity and passive hyper-resistance in neurological clinical populations. It examines populations, devices, perturbation protocols, measured constructs, measurement properties and clinical interpretation. The review follows JBI scoping review methodology, with PRISMA-ScR and PRISMA-S reporting. This registration documents an ongoing review after search activity, evidence charting and manuscript development have begun.
authors: Salvatore Facciorusso; Stefania Spina

title: Robotic exoskeleton Remotion in outpatient gait rehabilitation for young adult patients with cerebral palsy
abstract: Background. Although a significant number of studies have focused on the rehabilitation of children patients with cerebral palsy (CP), the use of restorative treatment in the adult population with this pathology remains understudied. High-technology robot-assisted rehabilitation using exoskeleton systems for gait restoration has proven effective in various neurological disorders, including the rehabilitation of children with CP. However, questions concerning the application of these methods in adult patients require further clarification. Aim. To investigate the effect of robot-assisted gait training in an exoskeleton in an outpatient setting on mobility, gait speed, and gait biomechanics in adult patients with CP (students of an inclusive university), and to determine the feasibility and effectiveness (i.e., the appropriateness) of outpatient motor rehabilitation using such training for this patient population. Materials and methods. The study included 11 patients with spastic CP (spastic diplegia), classified as Gross Motor Function Classification System levels II–III. All patients underwent 10 training sessions on the Remotion robotic exoskeleton system (JSC "Volzhsky Electromechanical Plant", Russian Federation) once a day, 5 days a week. Clinical assessment included the timed up and go test and the 10-meter walk test. To objectify the clinical assessment data, biomechanical analysis of cyclic walking was performed using the Biomekhanika Nevrokor system (LLC Nevrokor, Russian Federation). Results. The study demonstrated a clinically significant improvement in mobility as assessed by the timed up and go test (p 0.05) and in fast walking speed measured by the 10-meter walk test (p 0.05). Based on the gait biomechanics analysis, the patients were divided into two groups: a symmetric gait group (n = 5) and an asymmetric gait group (n = 5). In the asymmetric gait group, a statistically significant improvement in step phase symmetry was observed after the rehabilitation course using the Remotion exoskeleton system. These changes occurred due to a reduction in compensatory movements at the hip joint and normalization of the phase characteristics of the flexion/extension angles of the lower limb joints. Conclusion. The present study confirmed that outpatient motor rehabilitation using robot-assisted therapy with an exoskeleton system is feasible, appropriate, and effective in adult patients with a previously established diagnosis of CP who are continuing their higher education.
authors: Anastasia E. Khizhnikova; A. S. Glukhov; А. Н. Островский; K. A. Sargsyan; L.A. Savin; Иконникова Екатерина Сергеевна; Олена Анатоліївна Кириченко; Sergey Nikolaevich Illarioshkin; I. V. Mikhalyov; Natalia A. Suponeva

title: Robotic-assisted knee arthroplasty methods provide insight into Homo neanderthalensis gait and the evolutionary origins of modern human knee variation
abstract: Abstract Lower-limb alignment is central to human bipedal locomotion and a key determinant of joint kinematics and osteoarthritis risk in modern clinical practice. However, its significance in hominins, and therefore its evolutionary implications, remain poorly understood. Advances in robotic-assisted total knee arthroplasty (TKA) provide highly precise measurements of lower-limb alignment, joint morphology and soft-tissue balance that can elucidate these understudied aspects of hominin functional morphology. Here, we perform a proof-of-concept robotic-assisted TKA on an anatomically accurate model of the Spy II Neandertal. Using a robotic-assistance system, we registered bony morphology and replicated soft-tissue laxity extrapolated from a modern patient with a comparable alignment phenotype. We confirmed a pronounced constitutional varus alignment, classifying Spy II as a CPAK type I knee. This phenotype resembles that of modern athletes engaged in significant weight-bearing sports or intense physical activity during growth. The demonstration of constitutional varus in a hominin fossil thus suggests a deep evolutionary origin for this alignment pattern in modern humans, contextualizing normal knee variation and supporting an individualized alignment approach to modern TKA.
authors: Hendrik Pott; Peter Savov; Ricarda D. Stauss; Lara Watson; Ottmar Kullmer; Max Ettinger; Nicole M. Webb; Tara Chapman

title: SAFER: a simulation-based assessment tool for emergency robotic undocking with multisource validity evidence
abstract: BACKGROUND: Emergency undocking is a high-acuity, low-occurrence event in robotic surgery. Existing robotic curricula do not address this skill, and no validated instrument has been developed to assess performance. We developed the Structured Approach for Fast Emergency Robotic-Undocking (SAFER), a simulation-based assessment tool, and hypothesized it would be reliable, responsive to educational intervention, and able to distinguish between trainee experience levels. We present multisource validity evidence. METHODS: Using a quasi-experimental design, 58 general surgery residents at a single academic institution completed two simulation assessment scenarios-hemorrhage and hemodynamic instability-at two timepoints 6 months apart. Each scenario was evaluated using a 9-item checklist and a global rating scale (maximum score 20 points), scored independently by two trained faculty raters. Between timepoints, participants received a structured teaching session and self-directed learning materials. Validity evidence was gathered across five domains: content, response process, internal structure, relationships to other variables, and consequences of testing. Psychometric analyses included intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC), Cronbach's α, standard error of measurement (SEM), and minimal detectable change at the 95% confidence level (MDC95). RESULTS: Interrater reliability was excellent overall (ICC = 0.95, 95% CI 0.94-0.96) and across both scenarios and timepoints. Internal consistency was acceptable to good (Cronbach's α = 0.72-0.83). The MDC95 was 2.5 points, with 72% of paired learners exceeding this threshold at the second assessment. Mean total score improved by 5.73 points (Cohen's d = 1.38), with largest gains among junior residents. Baseline scores increased significantly with postgraduate year (PGY) level [F(4,102) = 3.99, p = 0.005], supporting known-groups validity. CONCLUSIONS: SAFER, a novel assessment tool for robotic emergency undocking, demonstrated strong reliability, acceptable internal consistency, large responsiveness to training, and expected performance patterns across trainee levels. Further multicenter validation and transfer studies are needed before use in higher-stakes assessments, such as credentialing or advancement decisions.
authors: Blake T Beneville; Abigail J Hatcher; Michael M. Awad

title: Scientific Curiosity Building through Guided Inquiry in Secondary Science
abstract: This study examined how guided inquiry contributed to the development of scientific curiosity among Grade 9 learners in San Pablo, Isabela. Using a cross-sectional predictive survey design with a quantile-regression framework, the research involved 190 learners selected through proportionate stratified random sampling. Data were gathered using validated measures of guided inquiry experiences and scientific curiosity. Median, interquartile range, and median absolute deviation were used to describe the distributions of the variables, while quantile regression with 5,000 bootstrap resamples determined whether the predictive contribution of guided inquiry varied across levels of scientific curiosity. Results showed that learners experienced guided inquiry at a moderate level, while overall scientific curiosity was also moderate. Among the dimensions of curiosity, stretching and engagement in science practices were relatively stronger, whereas embracing uncertainty emerged as the weakest area. Guided inquiry significantly predicted scientific curiosity at the 25th, 50th, and 75th percentiles, with the strongest coefficient observed among learners in the lower curiosity group. The findings indicate that guided inquiry may be particularly beneficial for learners who demonstrate limited inclination to question, investigate, or persist in uncertain scientific situations. Strengthening guided questioning, evidence-based investigation, experimentation, and reflective explanation is therefore recommended, with differentiated teacher scaffolding based on learners’ levels of scientific curiosity.
authors: Amilyn P. Maramag; Alma P. Gonzales
venue: International Journal of Education, Research, and Innovation Perspectives

title: Screening novel cathode materials from the Energy-GNoME database using foundation machine learning force fields and DFT
abstract: Abstract The development of new cathodes is essential for enabling next generation energy storage technologies. Here, we introduce a multi-fidelity workflow that bridges AI-based candidate identification and density functional theory refinement for accelerated discovery of cathode materials. Starting from the Energy-graph networks for materials exploration (GNoME) database, we use foundation machine-learning force fields (MLFFs) as an intermediate-fidelity layer to screen Li-, Na-, K-, Mg-, and Ca-ion intercalation cathodes. We assess dynamical stability and simulate intercalation voltage profiles to determine the average operating voltage and specific energy. The surviving candidates are further prioritized using experimentally motivated filters based on space-group prevalence, elemental availability, and cost, followed by DFT+U refinement of the most promising structures. Finally, combined MLFF and DFT nudged elastic band calculations are used to assess ion-migration kinetics and identify candidates with the potential for good rate capability. The workflow reduces 615 high-confidence Energy-GNoME cathodes to 10 prioritized candidates with favorable electrochemical properties and manageable volume changes. In addition to delivering a shortlist of promising candidates, this work benchmarks the consistency of Energy-GNoME, ML interatomic potential, and DFT predictions and demonstrates how MLFFs can transform AI-prioritized materials databases into physics-grounded discovery pipelines.
authors: Nada M. Alghamdi; Paolo De Angelis; Pietro Asinari; Eliodoro Chiavazzo

title: Shared Leadership and Team Performance: A Systematic Literature Review of Mechanisms and Contextual Conditions
abstract: The increasing complexity, digitalization, and uncertainty of contemporary organizations have heightened the need for leadership approaches that facilitate the integration of distributed knowledge and expertise. Shared leadership has therefore gained increasing scholarly attention as an alternative to traditional vertical leadership. However, existing research remains fragmented in explaining how and under what conditions shared leadership contributes to team performance. This study conducts a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines to examine the evolution of shared leadership research, the theoretical mechanisms underlying its relationship with team performance, and the contextual conditions shaping its effectiveness. The findings reveal three major shifts in the literature: from direct relationships to underlying mechanisms, from variable-based approaches to relational and network-oriented perspectives, and from viewing context as a research characteristic to recognizing contextual configurations as determinants of effectiveness. Four complementary mechanisms are identified: relational capability, collective cognition, collective coordination and knowledge integration, and adaptive capability. These mechanisms are explained through complementary theoretical perspectives, including Social Exchange Theory, Social Identity Theory, the Input–Mediator–Output–Input framework, Transactive Memory System, and Complexity Leadership Theory. The findings further indicate that effectiveness depends on organizational, team, task, and environmental configurations, particularly collaborative culture, task interdependence, competency diversity, task complexity, digitalization, virtuality, and environmental uncertainty. Based on these findings, an Integrative Framework is proposed that repositions shared leadership as an organizational capability enabler that transforms distributed knowledge into collective capability and coordinated action, thereby enhancing team performance.
authors: Muhammad Fajrul Islam F; Muh Alim Fasieh; Gd Pandya Wicaksana Gara; Jemmy Regri Ferdianto; Ni Wayan Mega Sari Apri Yani; Theresia Dirda Rosari Widyadara

title: Showering Barriers and Interaction Preferences of Older Adults with Mobility Disabilities for a Robotic Showerhead
abstract: Bathing and showering are among the most challenging daily activities for individuals with long-term mobility impairments, requiring substantial physical effort, coordination, and environmental support. Background/Objectives: This study aimed to understand showering challenges faced by older adults with long-term mobility disabilities who used wheeled mobility devices. We evaluated user and caregiver perspectives on three Soft Robotic Showerhead (SoRoSh) concepts: Elongation, Swing, and Two Showerhead designs. We explored preferred interaction modes (user-guided, voice-controlled, gesture-controlled), desired features, and perceptions of how such technologies could improve independence, safety, and usability. Methods: We conducted semi-structured interviews with 12 participants: 6 older adults aged 63–77 (M = 72.83; SD = 5.03) with at least 10 years of lower-body mobility disabilities, and 6 subject matter experts aged 30–78 (M = 60.83; SD = 16.82), including professional caregivers and family care partners. Participants discussed current routines, unmet needs, and provided feedback on the concepts and interaction modes. Data were thematically analyzed. Results: Participants reported challenges such as difficulty lifting arms, reaching body areas, handling showerheads, maintaining balance, and using unstable shower chairs. Voice control was strongly preferred due to low physical effort, whereas gesture control was viewed as impractical. Manual control was valued for familiarity, with many favoring hybrid approaches. Desired features included integrated controls, joystick input, adjustable spray modes, wake-word activation, and streamlined design. Participants believed these technologies could enhance independence, safety, and emotional well-being. Conclusions: Adaptive showering technologies should prioritize accessibility, intuitive multimodal control, customization, safety, and privacy to support independence and quality of life.
authors: Pallabi Bhowmick; Kainat Shahid; Zhiyu Ren; Girish Krishnan; Wendy A. Rogers; Ian M. Rice

title: Simulation-based optimization of look up tables for TMS ASM operation at the Large Binocular Telescope
abstract: Gravity and temperature induced deformations in extremely large telescopes are commonly compensated using look up tables (LUTs). At the Large Binocular Telescope (LBT), the existing LUTs were derived from focal plane aberration minimization and do not explicitly enforce geometric constraints required for metrology operation. They also do not account for rapid environmental variations or long-term structural evolution. We present a simulation-based framework that integrates the Telescope Metrology System into the control strategy to redesign the LUTs. A sequential optical model of the LBT was used to reproduce the active optics loop and to evaluate the sensitivity of wavefront error and pointing to Adaptive Secondary Mirror rigid body motions. The optimized LUTs will be validated through dedicated on sky tests to assess their suitability for routine operation.
authors: Byeongjoon Jeong; Luca Rosignoli; Heejoo Choi; John M. Hill; Brandon Mechtley; Olga Kühn; Gabriele Rodeghiero; C. Veillet; J. Chu

title: Single‐strand superficial medial collateral ligament reconstruction with a peroneus longus split graft provides reliable control of anteromedial rotatory instability combined with anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction: A 2‐year clinical cohort study
abstract: Abstract Purpose To evaluate 2‐year clinical, radiological, and patient‐reported outcomes after combined anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction and single‐strand superficial medial collateral ligament (sMCL) reconstruction using a peroneus longus split graft (PLSG) in patients with anteromedial rotatory instability (AMRI). Methods Patients with ACL insufficiency and clinically and intraoperatively confirmed AMRI who underwent combined ACL and sMCL reconstruction using a PLSG were retrospectively identified and prospectively followed. AMRI was diagnosed in this study based on a combination of ACL insufficiency, increased anteromedial drawer in external tibial rotation, medial laxity on valgus stress testing at 20° of knee flexion, pivot‐shift grading as an indicator of overall rotatory instability of the knee, and supportive arthroscopic findings such as the medial meniscus squeeze sign. At a minimum follow‐up of 2 years, 59 of 63 patients (mean age 30 years, 48% female) were available for evaluation. Postoperative stability was assessed using KT‐1000 instrumented side‐to‐side measurements for the Lachman test and anterior drawer test at 90° flexion with neutral and 15° external tibial rotation (AMRI‐related). Pivot‐shift grading and valgus stress radiographs obtained at 20° of knee flexion were additionally performed. Patient‐reported outcome measures (PROMs) included International Knee Documentation Committee (IKDC) Subjective, Lysholm, Tegner activity scale, and return‐to‐any‐sport rate. A non‐inferiority margin of 3 mm for side‐to‐side differences was predefined. Results The mean side‐to‐side difference for the AMRI‐related anterior drawer was 0.0 ± 1.3 mm (95% CI: −0.4 to 0.3 mm), meeting the predefined non‐inferiority criterion (upper one‐sided 95% confidence limit 0.3 mm; p < 0.001). The mean Lachman side‐to‐side difference was 1.8 mm ± 1.3 mm and remained within clinically acceptable limits. A negative pivot‐shift was observed in 93% of patients. IKDC (59 ± 20 to 85 ± 12; p < 0.001) and Lysholm (61 ± 25 to 89 ± 11; p < 0.001) scores improved significantly, whereas the Tegner Activity Scale (5.8 ± 1.7 to 5.2 ± 1.6; p = 0.007) showed a small but significant decrease. The mean side‐to‐side difference in medial joint opening on valgus stress radiographs was 0.6 mm ± 1.0 mm, remaining below the predefined clinical reference threshold. At 2 years, 66% of patients had returned to any sports. Conclusion Combined ACL and single‐strand sMCL reconstruction using a PLSG was associated with low postoperative side‐to‐side differences, satisfactory postoperative stability, favourable postoperative PROMs and low ankle donor‐site morbidity at 2‐year follow‐up. This tunnel‐sparing technique may be considered a reasonable surgical option for patients with ACL insufficiency and clinically relevant concomitant AMRI. Level of Evidence Level IV.
authors: Philipp Weber; Simone Maxand; Michael Wagner

title: Smartphone-Based 3D Ocular Reconstruction for Automated Quantitative Blepharoptosis Evaluation
abstract: Importance: External ocular examination is central to ptosis evaluation, yet it often relies on manual, experience-dependent measurements with variable accuracy and reproducibility. Objective: To develop and prospectively evaluate the Digital Rulers of Ptosis (DRP), a smartphone-based 3-dimensional (3D) reconstruction system for automated quantitative external ocular assessment in blepharoptosis, including marginal reflex distance 1 (MRD1) and levator muscle function (LF), and clinical classification. Design, Setting, and Participants: This diagnostic/prognostic study was conducted prospectively across 5 hospitals in 2025. Participants 3 years and older underwent smartphone video capture and same-day oculoplastic specialist assessment as the reference standard. Participants undergoing surgery received repeat specialist measurements of MRD1 and LF at 3 months postoperatively to assess recurrence. Exposure: DRP uses a 10-second smartphone video for 3D reconstruction with metric unit conversion and real-time quality control. Main Outcomes and Measures: Agreement between DRP and specialist measurements was assessed by mean absolute error (MAE) and intraclass correlation coefficient. Diagnostic performance was assessed by area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, negative predictive value. For patients who underwent surgery, 3-month postoperative recurrence was assessed. Results: Among 952 participants (1904 eyes), the mean age was 27.9 years (range, 3-86 years); 493 participants were female (51.8%) and 459 were male (48.2%). A total of 1862 eyes were included in MRD1 analysis and 1830 eyes in LF analysis after quality control. DRP demonstrated high agreement with specialist measurements for MRD1 (MAE, 0.52 mm; 95% CI, 0.50-0.54 mm) and LF (MAE, 0.95 mm; 95% CI, 0.91-0.98 mm). For diagnosing ptosis, DRP achieved an AUC of 0.97 (95% CI, 0.96-0.97). For identifying surgical approach, DRP achieved an AUC of 0.98 (95% CI, 0.97-0.98). Performance remained consistent across sex, age, and geographic region. Among 206 surgical participants (248 eyes), the 3-month postoperative recurrence rate was 7.3% (95% CI, 4.4%-11.2%; 18/248 eyes), within the lower range of previously reported rates. Conclusions and Relevance: This study found that accurate, standardized quantitative blepharoptosis assessment might be supported by commercially available smartphones, demonstrating the potential of smartphone-based 3D reconstruction for external ocular assessment and clinical decision-making. Further studies are needed to evaluate its clinical impact.

title: Spasticity in Multiple Sclerosis: 2026 Expert Consensus
abstract: Background: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic neuroinflammatory disease that significantly impairs quality of life. Spasticity is one of the most frequent and highly disabling features of MS, often accompanied by cramps, pain, bladder dysfunction, sleep disturbances, fatigue, and tremor. Recently, the concept of ‘spasticity-plus syndrome’ (SPS) has emerged to reflect the interplay among these symptoms. This work aims to update the Spanish clinical guideline for managing MS-related spasticity (MSS) by adopting this evolving concept. Methods: A panel of 14 Spanish neurologists assessed the available evidence using a two-level literature review strategy, combining a systematic review focused on SPS with a rapid review of MSS management. Building on the previous guideline, the panel formulated updated recommendations with the scientific endorsement of the Spanish Society of Neurology (SEN). To support a structured and transparent development process, an adapted GRADE-informed framework was used to guide the appraisal of the evidence and formulation of recommendations. Results: A total of nine publications addressing the SPS concept were identified. Based on the evidence and expert consensus, the panel developed 13 recommendations covering triggering and aggravating factors, the diagnosis and evaluation of spasticity, and therapeutic strategies for patient management. In addition, a comprehensive treatment algorithm was proposed to guide therapeutic decision-making according to patients’ clinical profiles. Conclusions: This work provides updated recommendations for the management of patients with MSS, integrating the SPS concept into clinical practice. The panel highlights the importance of a symptom-oriented approach that considers the full spectrum of clinical manifestations to individualize treatment, simplify the therapeutic approach, and minimize the risk of polypharmacy.

title: Splenectomy, indications and outcomes: a 12-year experience in a community hospital
abstract: Background: Splenectomy volume has declined as improved imaging, nonoperative management of blunt trauma, and novel medical therapies such as rituximab and thrombopoietin receptor agonists have narrowed its indications, making elective splenectomy uncommon and raising concern about maintaining operative proficiency. Methods: We conducted a single-center retrospective chart review at Flushing Hospital Medical Center in Queens, NY of patients who underwent splenectomy between October 2012 and March 2025. Eligible patients were identified by institutional record review using diagnostic codes and confirmed by chart review. Inclusion criteria were patients 18 years and older who underwent splenectomy for any indication. Patients under the age of 18 or who required transfer to another institution were excluded. Data collection included patient demographics, medications, splenectomy indication, emergent versus elective, surgical approach (laparoscopic, robotic, or open), length of stay (LOS), morbidity, and in-hospital mortality. Descriptive statistics were calculated; chi-square tests with Bonferroni correction and Fisher's exact test assessed categorical relationships, and Pearson's correlations assessed continuous variables. IRB approval was obtained. Results: Twenty-two patients were included (mean age 59.2±18.7 years; 54.5% male; 63.6% Hispanic), with hypertension (45.5%) and diabetes (22.7%) the most prevalent comorbidities; 50% were on steroids and approximately one-third on immunosuppressive therapy or chemotherapy. Most cases were elective (90.9%) and open (68.2%), with robotic (18.2%) and laparoscopic (9.1%) approaches less common. Immune thrombocytopenic purpura and neoplasm were the leading indications (40.9% each), while 9.1% (n=2) were urgent or emergent for massive splenomegaly. Postoperative bleeding occurred in 22.7% (n=5/22), mean LOS was 8.4±7.3 days, readmission rate was 27.3%, and there was no mortality. Surgical indication was significantly associated with complication type (p<0.03), and average volume was 2 cases per year. Conclusions: Splenectomy has become a rare elective operation but remains highly effective and often life-saving; community and teaching surgical services should deliberately maintain minimally invasive splenectomy skills, recognizing that outcomes vary by indication.
authors: Jordan Stone; Candance Wong; Nana Yaa A. Marfo; Mrinalini Alla; Catherine J. Kilada; Camille Mai-Phuong Tran Quang; Christina Montesano; David Egbo; Tereque Raeburn; Matthew Roland; Martine A. Louis; Nageswara Rao Mandava

title: Standardized Localization of Intraoperative Direct Electrical Stimulation Sites in Awake Brain Surgery Using MRI-Based 3D Cortical Mapping
abstract: OBJECTIVE: Intraoperative direct electrical stimulation (DES) remains the gold standard for mapping motor and cognitive cortical functions during awake brain surgery. However, a reproducible method to relocate these stimulation sites on the common brain template is still lacking, hindering reproducibility and data integration. Here, we propose our tested corticotopography method, as a reliable technique for mapping cortical DES sites onto brain atlases. METHODS: Corticotopography was applied by matching the intraoperative image of the exposed cortex with the preoperative 3D MRI-based brain reconstruction using anatomical landmarks (i.e., sulci, gyri, and cortical vessels). Coordinates of the stimulation sites were then extracted using FSLeyes and mapped to MNI152 space. The method's reliability was then evaluated through an inter-rater comparison. Lesion volume, tumor relapse status, and extent of craniotomy were tested for their potential bias on localization reliability. RESULTS: Ninety eloquent cortical sites were identified in 19 patients undergoing awake surgery for glioma resection. Inter-rater analysis showed high concordance with 87% of stimulated sites presenting a spatial discrepancy below 2.5 mm. No significant differences in localization agreement were observed between newly diagnosed or relapsing tumors or as a function of lesion volume or craniotomy size. CONCLUSIONS: We introduce a standardized and reproducible corticotopography technique to localize intraoperative cortical stimulation sites on preoperative anatomical MRI. By formalizing the procedure used to map cortical functions, this method reduces inter-study variability, enabling DES to serve as a cumulative and interoperable resource for functional brain mapping. This allows cortical DES-derived information to be integrated with other neuroimaging modalities and leveraged across neuroscientific domains, including large-scale brain mapping and connectomics.
authors: Eleonora Grande; Andrea Bartolo; Chiara Rita Masotti; Alice Esposito; Vincenzo Esposito; Marco Ciavarro

title: State-Dependent Modulation of Corticospinal and Cortical Responses by Closed-Loop Paired-pulse TMS.
abstract: Brain oscillations shape cortical excitability in a phase-dependent manner. Cortical excitability reflects the net output of intracortical circuits, including inhibitory and facilitatory pathways. However, whether the phase of ongoing brain rhythms differentially modulates inhibitory and facilitatory responses remains unknown. Paired-pulse transcranial magnetic stimulation (ppTMS) can selectively engage these circuits, providing a unique tool to dissociate their contributions. We combined real-time EEG-guided closed-loop TMS with single- and paired-pulse TMS in 24 healthy adults (13 female) to probe how sensorimotor mu (8-13 Hz) and beta (14-30 Hz) oscillatory phase shapes responses associated with intracortical inhibitory and facilitatory processes. Single-pulse TMS (spTMS), short-interval intracortical inhibition (SICI), and intracortical facilitation (ICF) were delivered at four phases (peak, falling, trough, rising). Motor evoked potentials (MEPs) and TMS-evoked potentials (TEPs) were recorded to assess corticospinal and cortical responses, respectively. We found that MEP amplitude was phase-dependent across all three stimulation types, with spTMS-evoked and ICF-conditioned MEPs showing the largest amplitudes at the rising phase, whereas SICI-conditioned MEPs were largest at the peak phase of the mu oscillation. TEP P60-N100 amplitude was modulated by oscillatory phase across all stimulation types, with maximal responses at the trough phase. SICI showed opposing phase patterns between the two measures, revealing a dissociation between cortical and corticospinal responses. MEP and TEP preferred phases were correlated across participants only in the ICF condition. These findings extend phase-dependent spTMS effects to paired-pulse stimulation and show that ongoing mu phase differentially shapes responses to SICI and ICF across cortical and corticospinal levels.Significance Statement Ongoing brain oscillations are known to shape cortical excitability across their phase cycle. However, whether this effect differentially influences inhibitory and facilitatory responses has remained unresolved. Here, using closed-loop EEG-guided transcranial magnetic stimulation in healthy adults, we probed how SICI- and ICF-conditioned responses vary across different phases of the sensorimotor mu and beta rhythms. We show that corticospinal and cortical responses to inhibitory and facilitatory paired-pulse protocols exhibit distinct phase-dependent patterns in the sensorimotor mu rhythm. These findings extend phase-dependent stimulation effects beyond single-pulse TMS and reveal that the relationship between cortical state and stimulation response differs across paired-pulse protocols.
authors: Choi DS, Güth MR, Ma M, Harmon M, Wischnewski M, Park J, Blenker A, Lee S, Opitz A.

title: Stimulation parameters of epidural spinal cord stimulation for functional recovery after spinal cord injury: a narrative review
abstract: Spinal cord injury (SCI) causes persistent motor, sensory, and autonomic deficits that conventional rehabilitation only partly mitigates. Epidural spinal cord stimulation (EES) can re-enable standing, walking, upper-limb control, and autonomic regulation, yet clinical translation is constrained by pronounced heterogeneity in stimulation parameters and by a weakly controlled evidence base. This narrative review maps stimulation parameters—electrode placement, frequency, intensity, pulse width, waveform, and stimulation mode—onto functional targets after SCI, critically appraises the supporting evidence, and maps scenario-specific parameter considerations onto a descriptive evidence hierarchy. Evidence was identified through targeted, non-systematic searches of PubMed/MEDLINE and citation tracking of key primary studies and reviews through 30 June 2026; human epidural-stimulation studies in SCI reporting parameters or functional outcomes were prioritized, with preclinical studies retained for mechanistic synthesis, transcutaneous trials used only as contextual evidence, and preprints labeled as such. Because no systematic search was performed, the review is presented as a narrative review: evidence is appraised using a design-based hierarchy, human, animal, and preprint findings are explicitly distinguished, and all parameter-level considerations are offered as preliminary observations rather than graded recommendations. Two reproducible motor parameter philosophies emerge—tonic, individually titrated lumbosacral stimulation embedded in intensive activity-based training, and programmed biomimetic (spatiotemporal, dual-mode, closed-loop) approaches—whereas hemodynamic management now has the most standardized parameter set. Evidence for upper-limb, bladder, spasticity, and pain indications remains case-level, and for neuropathic pain no SCI-specific parameter evidence exists. Mechanistic evidence derives predominantly from animal models, and clinical reports are dominated by small uncontrolled series in which stimulation is delivered as one component of a combined stimulation-plus-training intervention. Parameter-level conclusions are therefore preliminary and hypothesis-generating rather than practice-defining; standardized parameter reporting, physiology-based stratification, and adequately powered controlled trials are the priorities for converting EES from individualized experimentation into evidence-based neurorehabilitation.
authors: Jingkai Wang; Yermike Bieshanbieke; He Wang; JiChao Yang; Shanfeng Ji; Yulong Li; HaoYuan Gu; Yongli Lou

title: Stimulus predictability rather than inter-trial interval itself affects motor evoked potential amplitudes
abstract: Abstract The inter-trial interval (ITI) of transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) can modulate motor-evoked potential (MEP) amplitude and may thus confound assessments of corticospinal excitability. We tested whether this effect depends on the ITI duration per se or the associated temporal predictability and whether intracortical inhibitory processes mediate these effects on. In 26 healthy participants, we recorded single-pulse MEPs and paired-pulse measures of short-interval intracortical inhibition (SICI; 2-ms interstimulus interval) and long-interval intracortical inhibition (LICI; 100-ms interstimulus interval) at ITIs of 2, 5, and 10 s. ITIs were presented in different Patterns, i.e., separate fixed blocks (FXD), randomly intermingled within blocks (RND), or randomly intermingled but auditorily cued at 950 ms pre-TMS (RNDC). MEPs showed significant effects of ITI, Pattern, and their interaction, being smaller at 2 s than at longer ITIs in FXD but not in RND and RNDC. However, RNDC produced marked MEP suppression across all ITI. SICI showed a Pattern × ITI interaction but no main effect of Pattern or between-pattern differences per ITI, whereas LICI showed complex Pattern × ITI interaction and both main effects. Notably, ITI affected SICI and LICI oppositely. While GABA-A-receptor mediated inhibition (SICI) showed an ITI dependency compatible with the ITI effects on single-pulse MEPs, it was unlikely mediating the predictability effects but may rather relate to an independent ITI driven suppression. In contrast, GABA-B-receptor mediated inhibition (LICI), was clearly modulated by predictability, but incompatible with the observed ITI effects on MEP amplitude. In summary, the effect of ITI duration on MEP amplitude seems to be largely explained by anticipatory suppression of corticospinal excitability based on the predictability of TMS pulses as derived from their temporal context, being easier for shorter and more regular ITIs and maximal for explicit cues immediately preceding the TMS pulse. SICI and LICI are modulated by ITI as well, with the latter affected by predictability, but neither can explain the observed predictability effects on single-pulse MEP amplitudes.
authors: Saman Seifpour; Nele Haferkorn; S. Vijayakumar; Til Ole Bergmann

title: Stochastic Adaptive Fourier Decomposition for Operator Learning
abstract: Fourier Neural Operators (FNOs) offer an efficient paradigm for solving partial differential equations (PDEs). However, FNOs rely on a fixed Fourier basis and hard frequency truncation, which inherently limit their ability to model non-periodic, localized, and fine-scale solution structures. We propose the Stochastic Adaptive Fourier Decomposition Neural Operator (SAFDNO), a spectral neural operator that replaces predefined Fourier modes with an adaptive Takenaka-Malmquist (TM) orthonormal system derived from the theory of Stochastic Adaptive Fourier Decomposition (SAFD). Instead of performing an expensive greedy pole search in classical SAFD, SAFDNO amortizes stochastic pole selection through a neural pole predictor and constructs the adaptive TM system directly from latent features. The resulting operator performs learned filtering on coefficients of analytic branches in the Hardy space with respect to the input-adaptive TM system, preserving the global receptive field of spectral operators while providing a more flexible representation than using fixed spectral bases. Across nine PDE benchmark problems, SAFDNO achieves the best performance on all six regular-grid problems among strong neural operator baselines, with especially notable gains on Darcy, Burgers, and Navier-Stokes, where fixed Fourier modes are often less effective at modeling localized oscillations, sharp transitions, and multiscale structures. SAFDNO also exhibits stronger zero-shot super-resolution performance and shows less performance degradation when deployed on finer discretizations. These results suggest that the input-adaptive TM system provides a promising alternative to fixed spectral representations for neural operator learning.
authors: Pengqing Shi; Liming Zhang; Tao Qian; Stephen Tierney; Jie Yin; Junbin Gao

title: Strategic Orientation, Dynamic Capabilities, and Business Model Innovation: The Emergent Role of Top Management Support
abstract: Background: As connectivity becomes commoditized amid over-the-top (OTT) competition and stagnant average revenue per user (ARPU), business model innovation, rather than network expansion, has become a primary determinant of incumbent telecommunications operators’ continued relevance. Objective: This study examines how strategic orientation translates into business model innovation (BMI) through dynamic capabilities (DC) and under what conditions top management support (TMS) influences this relationship among incumbent telecommunications firms in Indonesia. Methods: This study tests direct and DC-mediated effects of SO on BMI, with TMS as a potential boundary condition moderating the DC–BMI relationship. Analysis uses two-stage partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) applied to survey data from 130 executive respondents. Results: SO positively influences DC (β = 0.610, p < .001) and exerts both a significant direct effect on BMI (β = 0.377, p < .001) and a significant indirect effect through DC (β = 0.125, p = .025), indicating partial rather than full mediation. TMS does not significantly moderate the DC–BMI relationship (p = .313) but emerges as a significant direct predictor of BMI (β = 0.324, p = .001), with an effect larger than that of DC itself. Eliminating the reconfiguring dimension of DC on discriminant validity grounds left sensing and seizing as the final indicators of DC. Conclusion: Findings suggest a shift in the interpretation of TMS’s role, from a boundary condition consistent with upper echelons theory toward a direct antecedent consistent with dynamic managerial capabilities theory.
authors: Topaz Malik Aziz; Luqman Satria Manggala; Ervina Priyanti; Mira Maulida

title: Subject-Independent EOG-Based Classification of Horizontal Eye Movements for Real-Time Robot Control
abstract: Background/Aim: Neurodegenerative diseases and severe neurological trauma can substantially impair conventional communication and control channels, while ocular motor functions may remain preserved until advanced stages. This study proposes a subject-independent electrooculography (EOG)-based framework for classifying horizontal gaze directions and controlling an omnidirectional mobile robot without user-specific calibration.Methods: EOG signals acquired from 12 healthy participants were filtered using a fourth-order Butterworth band-pass filter between 0.1 and 15 Hz and segmented into non-overlapping 5-second windows. Twelve time- and frequency-domain features were extracted from each window. Five classifiers—k-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), Random Forest (RF), Support Vector Machine (SVM), Decision Tree (DT), and a multilayer perceptron-based artificial neural network (ANN)—were evaluated using Leave-One-Subject-Out cross-validation.Results: SVM achieved the highest participant-wise mean accuracy of 79.61%, followed by KNN (74.47%), RF (72.19%), DT (68.69%), and ANN (66.11%). Pooled out-of-fold analysis further showed that SVM obtained a macro specificity of 0.911 and a macro one-vs-rest ROC-AUC of 0.907. The classified gaze commands were transmitted wirelessly to the mobile robot for real-time motion control.Conclusion: The results demonstrate that the proposed framework provides a practical and computationally efficient solution for subject-independent assistive robotic control.
authors: Emre DEMİRÖZ; Ayşe Nur Ay

title: Surgical Skill Transference: Independent Development of Complex Technical Skills Across Open, Laparoscopic, and Robotic Platforms in Residency Training
abstract: OBJECTIVE: To evaluate whether technical performance in open, laparoscopic, and robotic gastrojejunostomy simulation transfers across operative platforms among general surgery residents completing structured curricula. It was hypothesized that residents would improve within each curriculum, but that final technical performance in one modality would not reliably predict performance in the others. DESIGN: Retrospective single-institution cohort study using a prospectively maintained simulation performance database. Final technical performance within each modality was used as the primary outcome. Residents were stratified within each modality as low-, middle-, or high-performing based on final assessment score, and cross-platform performance tier concordance was assessed. SETTING: Grainger Center for Simulation and Innovation at Endeavor Health Evanston Hospital, Evanston, Illinois. PARTICIPANTS: Thirty-two University of Chicago general surgery residents who completed open, laparoscopic, and robotic side-to-side gastrojejunostomy simulation curricula between 2019 and 2025. RESULTS: Only 7 residents (21.9%) remained in the same performance tier across all 3 modalities, including 2 residents (6.3%) who were high performers across open, laparoscopic, and robotic simulation. Pairwise categorical tier concordance was not significant between open and laparoscopic performance (p = 0.1980), open and robotic performance (p = 0.3366), or laparoscopic and robotic performance (p = 0.5084). Score-based analyses similarly showed no consistent pattern of cross-platform performance transference. Despite this, residents improved significantly from initial to final assessment in open (19.9 ± 4.9-31.6 ± 1.9), laparoscopic (16.4 ± 3.8-22.6 ± 1.6), and robotic simulation (19.3 ± 2.1-25.8 ± 2.2; all p < 0.0001). Prior operative experience, self-reported skill, comfort, and robotic workload measures were not consistently associated with final performance. CONCLUSIONS: Structured simulation improved technical performance within each modality, but final performance did not reliably transfer across open, laparoscopic, and robotic platforms. These findings suggest that complex technical skill development remains platform specific and support early, dedicated, and longitudinal simulation-based training across all 3 domains during residency.
authors: Colin M. Johnson; Laura A. Eldridge; Sangrag Ganguli; Aram Eduardo Rojas; Syed A. Mehdi; Alessia Vallorani; Silvia Zenuni; Arjun Thapa Chhetri; Miral Sadaria Grandhi; Melissa Ellen Hogg; Stephen P. Haggerty

title: Surgical approach and insert constraint are associated with small differences in patellar tilt after robotic‐assisted total knee arthroplasty: A retrospective comparative radiographic study
abstract: Abstract Purpose Patellofemoral alignment remains important after total knee arthroplasty (TKA). Robotic‐assisted functional positioning may reduce the impact of approach‐ and implant‐related factors on the patellofemoral joint. This study evaluated the association between surgical approach and insert constraint with postoperative static patellar alignment following robotic‐assisted TKA. Methods This retrospective comparative radiographic study included 320 primary nonresurfaced robotic‐assisted TKA performed with the MAKO system between March 2021 and December 2024. Patients were divided into four groups: mini‐subvastus condylar‐stabilised (MSV‐CS, n = 134), mini‐subvastus posterior‐stabilised (MSV‐PS, n = 63), medial parapatellar condylar‐stabilised (MPP‐CS, n = 75) and medial parapatellar posterior‐stabilised (MPP‐PS, n = 48). Standardised Merchant axial radiographs at 30° and lateral radiographs were obtained at 2 months and 1 year. Patellar tilt was the primary outcome. Secondary outcomes were qualitative patellar centreing, patellar thickness and the modified Blackburne–Peel index. Two‐way factorial analysis assessed surgical approach, insert constraint and their interaction. Results Baseline characteristics and final intraoperative robotic alignment parameters were comparable across groups. MSV and CS implants were associated with statistically greater patellar tilt than MPP and PS implants, respectively, but the absolute differences were small, approximately 1°. No significant interaction was observed between surgical approach and insert constraint. Patellar height did not differ between groups. Conclusion Robotic‐assisted functional positioning provided consistent static patellofemoral alignment regardless of surgical approach or insert constraint. Although statistically significant differences in patellar tilt were detected, their approximately 1° magnitude suggests a negligible radiographic effect. Their clinical significance remains unknown because clinical outcomes and dynamic patellar tracking were not assessed. Level of Evidence Level IV.
authors: Clément Favroul; Mehdi Drissi Kaitouni; Elvire Servıen; Cécile Batailler; Sébastien Lustıg

title: Systematic Literatur Review: Implementation of Risk-Based Internal Audit (RBIA) in Hospitals
abstract: Risk-Based Internal Audit (RBIA) is an internal audit approach that focuses audit activities on areas with the highest level of risk to provide strategic added value to the organization. In the hospital context, RBIA plays a crucial role due to the high complexity of clinical, operational, financial, legal, and reputational risks, which directly impact patient safety and organizational sustainability. This paper aims to develop a systematic review of RBIA implementation in hospitals. The method used is a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) with the PRISMA approach to data collection. A literature search was conducted through the Scopus database between 2010 and 2025, with 12 selected articles that met the criteria. The synthesis results reveal that RBIA implementation is significantly influenced by top management support, the role of the board of directors and audit committee, the competence of internal auditors, and the level of risk management maturity. Risk maturity is proven to play a role as a structural foundation and a mediator, determining the effectiveness of RBIA in improving internal audit effectiveness, hospital governance, and patient safety.
authors: Tita Ratya Utari; Arlina Dewi
