title: Mosaicism for Cohen–Gibson Syndrome in a Female Individual With Overgrowth and Neurodevelopmental Delay
abstract: BACKGROUND: The Embryonic Ectoderm Development (EED) gene encodes a core component of the Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2), which regulates chromatin structure and plays a key role in embryonic development and cell differentiation. Pathogenic variants in EED are associated with overgrowth-intellectual disability syndrome (Cohen-Gibson syndrome, OMIM #617561), though reported cases are rare and typically involve heterozygous germline variants. This study presents an individual with confirmed postzygotic mosaicism in EED, contributing to diagnostic complexity. METHODS: A 12-year-old girl with tall stature, dysmorphic features, developmental delay, and congenital anomalies underwent clinical and genetic evaluation. Exome sequencing and targeted deep sequencing were used to identify and validate the genetic variant across multiple tissues. RESULTS: A likely pathogenic mosaic EED variant c.1091G > T; p.(Trp364Leu) was identified in the patient with a 31% variant allele fraction in peripheral blood. Deep sequencing confirmed the variant and its de novo origin in the parents' samples. Mosaicism was also detected in two independently collected buccal mucosa samples (dry swab and buccal swab collection kit; 11% and 17%) and in saliva (30%), indicating somatic mosaicism in multiple tissues. DNA methylation profiling revealed a high-confidence epigenetic signature consistent with a PRC2 complex-associated disorder, further supporting the likely pathogenic classification of the identified variant. CONCLUSION: This case broadens the molecular understanding of EED-related disorders and highlights the clinical significance of mosaicism. Deep sequencing and multi-tissue analysis are crucial for accurate diagnosis, management, and genetic counseling in overgrowth syndromes.
authors: Fei Song; Manuel Michels; Beate Betz; Walburga Vorhoff; Teresa Neuhann; Lisa Senninger; Dagmar Wieczorek

title: Multicenter evaluation of Coyote FlashDetect LyocartE multiplex assays for six respiratory pathogens: a comparative analysis with Sansure and Cepheid assays.
abstract: Respiratory diseases caused by common respiratory pathogens, such as influenza A/B (Flu A/B), severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus-2 (SARS-CoV-2), respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), adenovirus (ADV), and Mycoplasma pneumoniae (MP), share many of the same symptoms and may progress to severe complications in some cases. Multiplex molecular point-of-care testing (mPOCT) enables automated and rapid differential diagnosis for timely intervention. This study independently evaluated the clinical performance of Coyote FlashDetect LyocartE SARS-CoV-2/FluA/FluB and FlashDetect LyocartE RSV/MP/ADV multiplex mPOCT assays using the Sansure as the primary comparator, followed by a subset-based, target-specific paired comparison with Cepheid mPOCT assay for selected respiratory pathogens (FluA, FluB, and RSV). Specifically, 642 and 427 throat swab specimens were used to evaluate the Coyote SARS-CoV-2/FluA/FluB and Coyote RSV/MP/ADV multiplex mPOCT assays against Sansure assays, respectively. Coyote assays demonstrated high concordance with Sansure assays, with overall percent agreement (OPA) values ranging from 93.8% to 100.0% for six pathogens covered by two Coyote assays. Most discrepancies with Sansure assays occurred in samples with cycle threshold (Ct) values ≥35, especially among FluA samples. Moreover, 414, 414, and 215 specimens were allocated for FluA, FluB, and RSV, respectively, to conduct target-specific paired comparison between Coyote and Cepheid. Each Coyote assay also demonstrated high concordance with the Cepheid assays, with PPA values of 96.0%, 100.0%, and 98.3% for FluA, FluB, and RSV, respectively. These results support the use of Coyote mPOCT assays in specific settings. Coyote assays demonstrated a high degree of concordance for shared targets with comparator methods, supporting their use as a rapid and user-friendly diagnostic approach for multiplex respiratory pathogen detection.IMPORTANCEThis study highlights the value of multiplex molecular point-of-care tests. The POCT assays demonstrate high concordance with the laboratory-based lab tests in this retrospective specimen cohort, offering a viable, rapid, and user-friendly alternative for multiplex respiratory pathogen detection and hold the promise to be used in primary healthcare settings and public health surveillance.
authors: Cong Liu; Lei Feng; Gaowei Fan; Huiying Lai; Linlin Xiao; Yanxi Han; Duo Wang; Wangyu Feng; Yingshuo Ma; Ziqiang Li; Qiang Zhang; Jinming Li; Rui Zhang

title: Multicentre Evaluation of Loop-Mediated Isothermal Amplification (LAMP) for Environmental Monitoring of Nosocomial Pathogens in Italian Hospitals.
abstract:
Background

Environmental contamination of hospital surfaces, especially in high-risk clinical areas, partly sustains healthcare-associated infections. The detection of microbiological contamination in hospital settings using culture-based methods remains fundamental, even though these methods are not rapid, show moderate sensitivity in areas with low microbial loads, and are unsuitable for some microbial species. This multicentre study evaluated the performance of loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) for the rapid detection of major nosocomial pathogens on hospital surfaces.

Methods

A multicentre observational method-comparison study was conducted in three Italian hospital centres. Overall, 298 environmental surface samples were collected from clinical areas included in local infection-prevention monitoring plans. For each sampling point, LAMP swab sampling was paired with an adjacent contact plate culture. LAMP assays targeted Staphylococcus aureus, Acinetobacter baumannii, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Manual and automated nucleic acid extraction workflows were analysed separately. Diagnostic performance, agreement metrics, and discordant paired results were assessed using a contact plate culture as the microbiological comparator.

Results

No LAMP-negative/RODAC-positive pairs were observed. Positive percent agreement (PPA) relative to contact plate culture was therefore 100% in the subgroups evaluated. Relative specificity ranged from 90.9% to 98.6%, while overall accuracy ranged from 93.8% to 98.6%. Discordant results were exclusively LAMP-positive/contact plate-negative and were more frequent for S. aureus and P. aeruginosa. Selective culture verification supported several LAMP-positive findings not recovered by routine contact plates.

Conclusions

LAMP showed high negative agreement, high specificity, and rapid target-specific detection of selected nosocomial pathogens on hospital surfaces. It may complement conventional cultures in environmental surveillance, particularly when timely feedback is needed to guide infection-prevention and sanitation-monitoring strategies.

title: Nanoplatform-Enhanced Therapies for Adenoid Cystic Carcinoma: Integrating Pathobiology, Microenvironment Modulation, and Synergistic Treatment Strategies
abstract: Abstract: Adenoid cystic carcinoma (ACC) is an indolent yet aggressive malignancy characterized by perineural invasion, local recurrence, and distant metastasis. Current clinical management, primarily surgical resection and postoperative radiotherapy, offers limited efficacy, and systemic therapies have yielded unsatisfactory outcomes for recurrent and metastatic ACC, largely due to its unique molecular drivers and a structurally and immunologically complex tumor microenvironment (TME). Nanoplatforms, with their tunable physicochemical properties, surface functionalization, and designable stimuli-responsive release capabilities, offer a promising strategy for overcoming the barriers that hinder the efficacy of conventional therapies, which is crucial for improving treatment outcomes. In this review, we first summarize the key pathogenic features of ACC and the critical TME components, including immunosuppressive landscape, aberrant vasculature, stroma, and neural niches. We then outline rational design of nanoparticle system suited for ACC, highlighting active targeting and responsive strategies. Finally, we highlight recent advances in nanoplatform-based ACC therapies, from enhanced chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and ablation, to emerging therapeutic mechanisms, such as ferroptosis, cuproptosis, and TME reprogramming via cGAS-STING activation. By bridging ACC pathobiology with nanomedicine engineering, this review aims to provide insights that may accelerate the development of comprehensive and personalized therapeutic approaches for this challenging disease. Keywords: adenoid cystic carcinoma, nanoparticles, molecular drivers, tumor microenvironment, personalized therapy
authors: Yana Ma; Weijia Zhu; Hang Yuan; Ruican Nie; Wen Luo; Hong-Tao Hu

title: Nanopore metagenomic sequencing links clinically relevant resistance determinants to pathogens
abstract: Abstract Culture-independent metagenomics enables the detection of plasmid-encoded antimicrobial resistance (AMR) genes directly from clinical samples; however, the clinical significance of these genes depends on their bacterial host and genomic context, which metagenomics cannot fully infer. Nanopore sequencing technology intrinsically encodes epigenetic modifications such as methylation, which can be leveraged for plasmid-host associations from metagenomic data. Existing methods rely on the recovery of metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs), which can introduce bias toward abundant taxa and leave clinically relevant, low-abundance pathogens unassociated. To address this limitation, we extended methylation-based plasmid-host association from the MAG level to individual assembly contigs and sequencing reads. The CUPID pipeline implements the calculation of contig and read similarity scores, which compare weighted mean methylation rates across motifs genetically shared between any contig or read pair. We validated this approach on a mock metagenomic community composed of ten carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales isolates, where we achieved 93.8% accuracy at the contig level and 100% at the read level for carbapenemase plasmid-host associations. When applied to metagenomic and quasimetagenomic data of sixteen patient rectal swabs collected during routine hospital surveillance, our approach assigned every detected plasmid-encoded carbapenemase to its correct bacterial host at the contig level, using matched culture-based diagnostics and whole-genome sequencing as a ground truth. Read-level analysis identified additional associations that were missed at the contig level, including a multi-host plasmid confirmed by established diagnostics. These findings demonstrate a pathway from rapid AMR gene detection using metagenomics to actionable surveillance for infection prevention, transmission tracing, and outbreak investigation. Impact statement Culture-independent metagenomics can detect antimicrobial resistance genes, but their clinical significance depends on the bacterial host and genomic context. Here, we show that nanopore-derived bacterial DNA methylation patterns can link carbapenemase genes to pathogenic hosts and plasmid context directly from patient samples. This provides a route from rapid antimicrobial resistance gene detection to actionable public health surveillance. Data summary All sequencing data after human content filtering have been deposited at the European Nucleotide Archive (ENA, BioProject accession PRJEB108076, with all isolate sequencing data for mock community generation available under the sample accession numbers SAMEA121375149-58, all isolate sequencing data from the rectal swabs available at SAMEA121334008-24, all metagenomic data from the rectal swabs available at SAMEA121325220-27, and all quasimetagenomic data available at SAMEA122914816-23, SAMEA122920068-74). All code is available at GitHub: https://github.com/harikaurel/cupid . All other supporting data are provided in the article and supplementary tables.
authors: Harika Ürel; Ela Sauerborn; Michael Biggel; Friedemann E. Gebhardt; Ebenezer Foster-Nyarko; Silvio D. Brugger; Rhys T. White; Søren Heidelbach; Mads Albertsen; Francis Muchaamba; Tim Reska; Marc J. A. Stevens; Roger Stephan; Richard Fetherston; Lara Urban

title: Navigating the transition to digital transfusion safety in a resource-limited setting: a prospective implementation study and operational workflow analysis
abstract: Background Manual verification in transfusion medicine is prone to human error. We evaluated the impact of implementing electronic crossmatching (EXM) to replace manual serological crossmatching in a resource-limited setting.Methods We conducted a prospective implementation study over 25 months (May 2022 to May 2024) at a tertiary hospital in Thailand. The intervention involved implementing EXM for eligible patients. To ensure patient safety, a parallel validation protocol (shadow mode) was employed, where all eligible units underwent both digital and manual verification. A paired time-motion substudy (n=130) was conducted to compare processing time (efficiency) and interoperator variability (reliability) against the parallel manual immediate-spin crossmatch.Results Of 100 835 requests, 12 267 units (9871 patients) were processed using EXM. Across all digitally verified units, we observed 100% concordance with the manual reference method during shadow-mode validation, with no safety signal detected. Implementation reduced median processing time by 93.9% (246.0 vs 15.0 s; Wilcoxon signed-rank p<0.001), while interoperator variability was comparable between methods (coefficient of variation 17.2% vs 19.7%, p=0.13). No ABO (blood group system)-incompatible transfusions were detected. However, given the rarity of such events, these findings indicate no detected safety signal rather than proof of safety.Conclusions Implementing EXM in a safety-critical workflow dramatically improved efficiency and standardisation, with no safety signal detected, although the study was underpowered to confirm safety equivalence with manual crossmatching. This study demonstrates that transitioning from human-dependent checks to robust digital systems is feasible and effective even in resource-limited healthcare settings.

title: Navigation Bronchoscopy Specific Cone-Beam CT Software Enabling Pre- And Intraprocedural Guidance
abstract: BACKGROUND: Cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT)- guided bronchoscopy is an established technique for diagnosing peripheral pulmonary lesions, offering 3-dimensional imaging for both navigation and confirmation. However, its usability as a stand-alone modality is limited by a substantial learning curve and a lack of integrated planning tools. This study evaluates the feasibility and performance of navigation bronchoscopy-specific CBCT software that enables preprocedural CT-planning fusion with intraprocedural CBCT imaging and provides intraprocedural support algorithms. METHODS: This prospective, single-center clinical feasibility study exploratively assessed the usability of the AirWaze investigational software. Usability was measured using a standardized system usability score, with scores of 70 or higher considered indicative of good usability (range, 0-100). The performance of the individual software components ('planning,' 'image fusion,' and 'guidance') was evaluated. An ultralow-dose CBCT protocol was compared with conventional CBCT scans for accuracy and radiation exposure. RESULTS: The study enrolled 34 patients with 37 lesions. The investigational software achieved a system usability score of 45. The planning component was available in all cases and was unanimously rated by the endoscopists as accurate and intuitive. In contrast, the image fusion and guidance components were rated as insufficient. The ultralow-dose CBCT protocol provided clinically accurate imaging in 84% of cases and reduced the radiation dose by 94%. CONCLUSION: Integrating planning and procedural guidance within stand-alone CBCT-guided navigation bronchoscopy procedures has great potential. Although several components of the investigational software were considered valuable, further development is required to ensure comprehensive procedural guidance.

title: Olfactory Swab-Derived Human Neuroepithelium Cell Culture as a Novel Model to Study Neurodegeneration-Related Proteins
abstract: The olfactory neuroepithelium (ON) collected with nasal swabs (NS) is a valuable source for studying brain processes in physiological and pathological conditions, due to its anatomical proximity to the brain and heterogeneous neural cell population. In this proof-of-concept study, we developed a protocol for co-culturing distinct cellular populations from ON, establishing a human olfactory neuroepithelium cell culture (hON) model from healthy individuals (HIs) without differentiation factors. We characterized the cellular composition of ON samples at harvesting, identifying sustentacular cells (Pan-CK+), neuronal cells (PGP9.5+), and ciliated respiratory cells (βIV-tubulin+) by immunofluorescence and flow cytometry. We assessed the expression and distribution of TDP-43, Tau, and α-synuclein, together with their phosphorylated isoforms, to establish a physiological reference profile. Furthermore, Seeding Amplification Assay (SAA) analysis, including disease-positive and healthy control cohorts, confirmed the absence of aggregated protein species in HIs. While p-Tau and p-α-syn localization was preserved between collection and culture, p-TDP-43 displayed neuron-specific nuclear redistribution upon culture, suggesting distinct regulatory dynamics. Longitudinal monitoring revealed that hON cultures maintain a stable neuronal population for up to 21 days, after which cells transition toward a fibroblast-like phenotype. This study establishes NS-derived hON as a feasible model for investigating neurodegenerative mechanisms, providing a baseline for disease comparisons.

title: On-Device Multimodal Small Language Models for Privacy- Preserving Edge Intelligence Through Quantization Pruning Distillation and Energy-Efficient Inference
abstract: On-device multimodal small language models are emerging as a practical foundation for privacypreserving edge intelligence, enabling devices to interpret and generate language while processing images, audio, video, sensor streams, and contextual signals without continuous cloud dependence. Their deployment can reduce data exposure, network latency, connectivity costs, and centralized infrastructure demand; however, limited memory, compute capability, battery capacity, thermal headroom, and accelerator support constrain model design and inference. This review examines architectures, compression techniques, privacy mechanisms, and energy-efficient inference strategies for multimodal small language models operating on smartphones, wearables, vehicles, robots, cameras, and embedded Internet of Things platforms. It develops a deploymentcentric taxonomy covering weight, activation, cache, and modality-encoder quantization; structured, unstructured, token, channel, and modality-aware pruning; response, representation, cross-modal, and task-specific knowledge distillation; and hybrid compression pipelines. The review analyzes how these methods affect language quality, visual and acoustic understanding, cross-modal alignment, robustness, fairness, privacy leakage, memory consumption, latency, throughput, energy per inference, and thermal stability. Particular attention is given to local retrieval, adaptive modality selection, speculative decoding, cache management, early exiting, hardware-aware scheduling, and heterogeneous CPU, GPU, neural, and digital-signal processing. The paper also evaluates secure personalization, federated updates, trusted execution, encrypted storage, sensor permission controls, and data-minimizing telemetry. Comparative evidence is organized by device class, workload, compression target, and evaluation objective. The gap analysis identifies limited reproducibility, inconsistent energy measurement, weak lowresource language coverage, underdeveloped multimodal privacy benchmarks, and insufficient study of sustained inference under thermal throttling. It distinguishes theoretical compression savings from measurable device-level efficiency improvements. The review concludes with standardized reporting recommendations and research priorities for compact, private, reliable, and energy-efficient multimodal intelligence at the edge.

title: PHI for adverse pathology and PHI density for upgrading: two complementary predictors in localized prostate cancer
abstract: BACKGROUND: The Prostate Health Index (PHI) has emerged as a promising biomarker for improving prostate cancer (PCa) detection. However, its role in predicting pathological aggressiveness at radical prostatectomy (RP) requires further elucidation. We aimed to assess the ability of PHI and PHI density (PHId) to predict adverse pathological features and ISUP upgrading in men undergoing robot-assisted RP. METHODS: We conducted a prospective, single-center observational study including 130 patients who underwent RP. Total PSA, free PSA, and p2PSA were measured using the Access 2 platform, and PHI and PHId were calculated accordingly. Multivariable logistic regression models evaluated the association of PSA, PSA density, PHI, and PHId with two predefined endpoints: (i) adverse pathological features (pT ≥3 and/or pN1), and (ii) upgrading from biopsy to RP. Models were adjusted for DRE status, PI-RADS score, and biopsy ISUP grade. Discrimination was assessed using AUC and the DeLong test. RESULTS: Median PSA, PHI, PSA density, and PHId were 6.21 ng/mL, 58, 0.15 ng/mL/cc, and 1.40, respectively. Adverse pathological features were identified in 39% of cases, and upgrading occurred in 59% (after exclusion of biopsy ISUP 5 cases). PHI emerged as the strongest independent predictor of adverse pathology (OR 1.04; 95% CI 1.02-1.07), yielding the highest model accuracy (AUC 0.86) and showing a sharp risk increase above PHI > 40. PHId was the only marker independently associated with upgrading (OR 1.54; 95% CI 1.10-2.29), achieving the best discrimination (AUC 0.83), with risk escalation particularly evident in patients with PI-RADS 4-5 lesions. CONCLUSIONS: PHI and PHId provide complementary information in localized PCa. PHI accurately identifies patients at risk of adverse pathological extension, whereas PHId effectively captures the probability of grade reclassification at RP. Integrating these biomarkers into patient assessment may support precision-based decision-making and helping to minimize undertreatment.

title: Patient Experience with Phlebotomy and Laboratory Testing at a University Hospital: A Mixed-Methods Exploratory Study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Patient satisfaction with the phlebotomy center or the laboratory in general is often only infrequently measured in single touchpoint surveys. In addition, patient complaints are scarce and patients rarely proactively provide feedback by themselves. The aim of this single-center study was to explore patient satisfaction and perceived improvement opportunities regarding phlebotomy and laboratory testing at a university hospital phlebotomy center. METHODS: We conducted a mixed-methods study combining survey data (including Net Promoter Score [NPS] and Customer Effort Score [CES], n = 109) and semi-structured interviews with 8 patients frequently visiting the phlebotomy center. RESULTS: In the survey, 34.9% of the respondents were promoters, 53.2% were passives, and 7.3% were detractors, resulting in an NPS of 27.6%. The median CES was 1 (interquartile range 1-2), indicating low perceived effort. Interview findings suggested that while the service was considered well-organized, "waiting"-rather than the phlebotomy procedure itself-emerged as the most important theme. Key recommendations included reducing waiting times, improving the waiting area, providing more instructions on the phlebotomy process, offering reliable online information on laboratory tests and results, and facilitating phlebotomy close to home. While most recommendations addressed functional needs, some also targeted emotional needs (e.g., free coffee, private seating). CONCLUSIONS: This mixed method study illustrates how involving patients in examining the laboratory-related patient journey can yield concrete, patient-reported insights and suggestions for improvement. Implementing recommendations derived by open-ended survey responses and interviews is likely to improve the patient journey, on both functional and emotional levels.

title: Perilesional Biopsy in—Systematic Out? Comparative Analysis of Targeted, Perilesional, and Systematic Core Yield by Needle Tracking With Robotic-Assisted Transperineal Magnetic Resonance Imaging/Ultrasound Fusion Prostate Biopsy
abstract: OBJECTIVE: To characterize prostate cancer (Pca) detection rates by Gleason Grade Group (GG) in targeted, perilesional, and systematic cores sampling the remaining prostate using robotic-assisted transperineal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) /ultrasound fusion biopsy (RA-TP-FBx), enabling precise spatial documentation of every core relative to MRI-lesions and the prostate. METHODS: We analyzed prospectively collected RA-TP-FBx cases between 2020 and 2024. Biopsies were performed with the iSR'obot Mona Lisa (Biobot). Sampling included a traditional targeted + systematic strategy and a Trizonal approach: targeted + perilesional + systematic. Perilesional cores were defined at biopsy as samples within 10 mm of the MRI-lesion margin and systematic cores as samples outside the targeted-perilesional areas. Individualized 3D prostate maps were correlated with per-core histopathology. Clinically significant PCa (csPCa) was defined as GG ≥ 2. RESULTS: The full cohort included 566 RA-TP-FBx cases. Diagnosis of csPCa (n=131 in the Trizonal cohort) was exclusively due to perilesional sampling in 6.1% (8/131). Systematic biopsy detected csPCa not captured by targeted or perilesional cores in 3.8% (5/131), but only 1.5% (2/131) originated from MRI-negative lobes. Overdetection of GG 1 (n = 58 in the Trizonal cohort) would be reduced by 24.1% (14/58) by omitting systematic cores when targeted and perilesional cores were negative. CONCLUSION: Robotic-assisted mapping demonstrated that perilesional sampling effectively complemented targeted biopsy, while systematic cores yielded minimal additional csPCa detection but increased GG 1 overdetection. These data support adopting targeted + perilesional sampling and omitting or deintensifying the routine addition of systematic cores in the remaining prostate.

title: Perioperative Blood Management in General Surgery: Recent Advances, Current Limitations, and the Emerging Role of Artificial Intelligence—A Narrative Review
abstract: Patient blood management (PBM) is a patient-centered approach to blood use that aligns with modern medical practice. It is based on multidisciplinary collaboration and evidence-based medicine. Its aim is to improve clinical outcomes by correcting preoperative anemia, reducing perioperative blood loss, standardizing transfusion practices, and optimizing the management of coagulation function. Patients undergoing general surgery, particularly complex liver surgery or gastrointestinal cancer surgery, often face preoperative anemia, intraoperative bleeding, increased transfusion requirements, and postoperative coagulation abnormalities. These factors make perioperative blood management more complex. This narrative review searched PubMed, Web of Science, Google Scholar, and the China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI) for relevant studies published over the past 10 years. It summarizes recent advances, current limitations, and challenges in the clinical translation of perioperative blood management in general surgery. This review focuses on the assessment and management of preoperative anemia, bleeding control and hemostatic strategies, transfusion management, coagulation monitoring, and thrombotic risk management. It also discusses recent advances and current limitations in the use of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) for risk prediction, clinical decision support, and individualized management. Current evidence suggests that PBM may help optimize perioperative care in general surgery. AI/ML may also support clinical decision-making by predicting bleeding risk, estimating transfusion requirements, and stratifying thrombotic risk. However, studies specifically focusing on general surgery patients remain limited. Most available evidence comes from cardiac surgery, orthopedics, or other surgical populations. In addition, current prediction models still have several limitations, including insufficient external validation, a lack of prospective evaluation, and limited interpretability. Therefore, these models should currently be used only as tools to support clinical judgment. Therefore, future studies should include more multicenter prospective research in general surgery populations. AI/ML-assisted decision support should also be further explored within standardized PBM pathways to improve the precision and standardization of perioperative blood management in general surgery.
authors: Long Zhang; Guoxin Liu; Shuyuan Guo; Yan Wu; Jing Yu; Xin Song; Hao Jiang

title: Persistent gut microbiota alterations after ischemic stroke are modifiable by probiotic intervention
abstract: SUMMARY The gut-brain axis has emerged as a critical modulator in neurological diseases, including stroke. While acute post-stroke dysbiosis is well established, it remains unclear whether these alterations persist long-term and can be therapeutically modulated. This study addresses this gap through integrated metagenomic and metabolomic profiling in two independent clinical stroke cohorts, complemented by experimental models. Experimental stroke induced persistent changes in gut microbiota composition and altered short-chain fatty acid profiles. In patients, microbiota composition remained distinct from controls up to three months after ischemic stroke or transient ischemic attack (TIA), accompanied by persistent reductions in propionic and valeric acid and reduced abundance of Prevotella -associated microbial signatures. We performed a randomized, double-blind interventional trial (PRISE) testing a multispecies probiotic versus placebo, using household members as additional controls. Probiotic intervention led to microbiome compositional changes with increased abundance of beneficial taxa and significantly improved functional recovery. The tested probiotic strains showed anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects in vitro. These findings suggest that targeted modulation of the microbiome represents a promising therapeutic avenue to improve chronic stroke recovery, warranting validation in larger Phase III clinical trials.
authors: Philip William Melton; Adam Sorbie; Velma Tea Essi Aho; Christina Haslinger; Maili Zimmermann; Wiola Marut; Christian Jaeger; Paul Wilmes; Corinne Benakis; Arthur Liesz

title: Phenotypic and Molecular Characterization of Heme Release in Selected Clinical Isolates of Staphylococcus aureus: Expression Analysis of PSMA and HLD Genes by RT-PCR and Quantification by HPLC.
abstract: This study evaluated whether the expression of psmα and hld is associated with HPLC-detected heme release from human erythrocytes after exposure to clinical S. aureus isolates. A total of 90 human clinical samples were examined, including wound swabs, pus aspirates, blood-culture isolates and catheter-tip isolates. S. aureus was identified using culture, Gram staining, catalase, coagulase, mannitol fermentation and automated biochemical confirmation. Thirty confirmed S. aureus isolates were selected for the erythrocyte-exposure experiment. Bacterial isolates were incubated with washed human erythrocytes for 2 h at 37°C. Total RNA was extracted from bacterial pellets, converted into cDNA and analyzed by RT-qPCR for psmα and hld, using gyrB as the housekeeping gene. Free heme released into the supernatant was quantified by reverse-phase HPLC using a hemin chloride calibration curve. S. aureus was recovered from 42/90 samples, giving an isolation rate of 46.7%. Among the 30 selected isolates, 15 were classified as high heme-release isolates and 15 as low heme-release isolates. High heme-release isolates showed significantly higher psmα expression than low heme-release isolates, with mean fold expression of 3.41±1.02 versus 1.48±0.51, respectively. The hld gene was also significantly upregulated in high heme-release isolates, with mean fold expression of 2.87±0.94 versus 1.26±0.42. HPLC analysis showed significantly higher free heme concentration in the high heme-release group than in the low heme-release group, 38.6±9.4 µM versus 12.4±5.1 µM. psmα expression correlated positively with HPLC-detected heme concentration, while hld expression also showed a significant positive correlation. Clinical S. aureus isolates with increased psmα and hld expression showed greater HPLC-detected erythrocyte heme release.
authors: Shahad Mudheher Ismael; Hiba Ali Hilal; Ruaa Hussein NADA

title: Pilot Evaluation of Saliva Samples as An Alternative to Blood for Large-scale Whole-genome Sequencing Studies
abstract: Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) studies have traditionally relied on blood as the primary DNA source and manual workflows. As population-based genomics studies expand, minimally invasive and easily deployable biospecimen collection methods compatible with high-throughput automation are increasingly needed. In this pilot study, we established a real-world, end-to-end automated WGS workflow, encompassing robotic DNA extraction, library preparation, sequencing and quality control. We compared saliva- and blood-derived WGS across key analytical parameters, including performance at each step of the workflow, overall cost, and feasibility for future large-scale implementation. First, germline variant calls from saliva and blood samples showed high concordance, reaching 97% genome-wide and over 99% in high-confidence genomic regions. Second, key workflow metrics, including DNA quality and sequencing quality, were comparable between saliva and blood samples, while saliva samples had a lower per-sample cost. We compared three commercially available saliva collection kits and found that all achieved at least 95% genome-wide concordance with matched blood samples, with differences primarily driven by cost. Finally, automated saliva processing produced sequencing and short variant calling metrics broadly comparable to manual processing in a small paired comparison. Collectively, these results provide a practical and scalable solution for incorporating saliva into future large cohort sequencing studies. Larger and more diverse studies are needed to further validate the robustness and generalizability of this pilot study.
authors: Susu Qu; Ruijun Meng; Ran Wu; Yi Shao; Xinshuang Zhang; Yi Wei; Jingxuan Zhang; Lu Yang; Min Li; Li Zhang

title: Platelet-Based Blood Products in Bovine and Equine Medicine: A Systematic Scoping Review of Blood Collection, Preparation Methods, and Reporting Completeness
abstract: Platelet-based blood products, including platelet-rich plasma, platelet concentrate, and platelet lysate, are increasingly investigated in veterinary medicine as biological preparations with proposed regenerative, anti-inflammatory, and immunomodulatory properties. In bovine and equine medicine, their use has expanded across several clinical fields, but blood collection and product preparation methods have not been systematically synthesized. This systematic scoping review aimed to describe the literature on platelet-based blood products in bovine and equine medicine, summarize methodological characteristics of blood collection and preparation methods, and analyze studies addressing bovine mammary disorders. Searches were performed in Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, CAB Abstracts, and PubMed on 25 August 2026, with no publication-year or start-date restriction. Eligible studies were original peer-reviewed articles in English; fibrin- or gel-based preparations were excluded when the corresponding liquid platelet-based product could not be separately characterized or evaluated, as were scaffold or combined constructs when the platelet-based component could not be evaluated separately. No formal review protocol was registered or published. Studies providing eligible bovine and/or equine data and reporting at least one methodological aspect related to collection, preparation, activation or lysis, storage, characterization, or administration were eligible. A total of 191 studies were included. Studies contributing equine data only among the target species predominated (161/191; 84.3%), whereas 29 studies (15.2%) contributed bovine data only and one study (0.5%) included both bovine and equine data. The PRP family, including PRP and related PRP-type preparations, was the most frequently investigated product group (134/191; 70.2%), followed by platelet lysate (46/191; 24.1%) and platelet concentrate (19/191; 9.9%); categories were not mutually exclusive. Methods varied in donor source, collection site, blood volume, anticoagulant, collection system, centrifugation workflow, activation or lysis, storage, and characterization. The main blood collection and preparation workflow was reconstructable in 111 studies (58.1%) and partially reconstructable in 80 studies (41.9%). Methodological reporting was frequently incomplete, particularly for leukocyte concentration, activation or lysis procedures, storage conditions, and product-level sterility or microbiological quality control. Product-level sterility or microbiological quality control was explicitly reported in 7 studies (3.7%) and partially reported in one study (0.5%). Only five studies addressed bovine mammary disorders and investigated methodologically distinct products. More complete and consistent methodological reporting is needed to improve reproducibility and comparability across studies.
authors: Filippo Rigo; Caterina Marcon; Margherita Soncin; Flaviana Gottardo

title: Prediction of Elastic Properties for Thermoplastic Composites In Situ Manufactured Using Laser‐Assisted Automated Fiber Placement
abstract: ABSTRACT The mesoscale finite element simulation method based on the Representative Volume Element (RVE) can predict the elastic properties of composites according to the dimension and distribution characteristics of fibers and voids. Nevertheless, affected by the non‐uniform distribution of fibers and voids as well as crystallization behavior in thermoplastic composite specimens in situ manufactured via laser‐assisted automated fiber placement, the RVE generated by conventional fiber generation algorithms fails to accurately forecast the elastic properties of in situ manufactured specimens. In this paper, on the basis of experimentally observed microstructures of in situ manufactured specimens, a subregional random fiber generation algorithm and a gradient random void generation algorithm were proposed. A mesoscale finite element model was established to predict the elastic properties of in situ manufactured thermoplastic composites. The results of the nearest neighbor distribution function, pair distribution function, and Ripley's K function verify that the fiber distribution of the generated RVE was in good agreement with the microstructure of the in situ manufactured specimens. Compared with autoclave‐consolidated specimens, the transverse elastic modulus and out‐of‐plane shear modulus of in situ manufactured specimens decrease by 13.38% and 18.54%, respectively. The proposed method provides a foundation for predicting the properties of thermoplastic composite structures manufactured by laser‐assisted automated fiber placement and shows potential applicability to thin‐shell composite structures.
authors: Yonglong Ma; Teng Yue; Zheng Zhang; Baisong Pan; Xiangdong Yuan

title: Protocol for the Assessment of Endogenous Platelet-Associated Tissue Factor-Dependent Thrombin Generation in Human Platelets Using the Calibrated Automated Thrombogram.
abstract: Platelet-associated Tissue Factor (TF) is increasingly recognized as a functionally active determinant of platelet procoagulant activity, enabling platelets to initiate and sustain thrombin generation beyond their established role as a phospholipid surface for coagulation factor assembly. However, its specific functional assessment remains challenging, as conventional Calibrated Automated Thrombogram (CAT) assays rely on exogenous TF to trigger thrombin generation, thereby masking the endogenous contribution of platelet-associated TF. Here, we describe a Calibrated Automated Thrombogram (CAT)-based workflow that enables the selective assessment of TF-dependent thrombin generation in isolated intact human platelets under conditions that preserve the contribution of endogenous platelet-associated TF. The protocol integrates key methodological steps, including inhibition of contact pathway activation through the use of microvesicle-free plasma pool containing a contact pathway inhibitor, normalization of the procoagulant membrane surface by exogenous phospholipids, and functional validation through neutralizing antibodies against TF and Tissue Factor Pathway Inhibitor (TFPI). The workflow also addresses key pre-analytical variables related to blood collection and platelet-rich plasma (PRP) preparation. Under these controlled conditions, thrombin generation kinetics -particularly LagTime- reflect the functional activity of platelet-associated TF, as demonstrated by their modulation upon TF and TFPI inhibition and their association with TF<sup>pos</sup>-platelets levels measured by flow cytometry. By avoiding the addition of exogenous TF, this approach overcomes key methodological limitations that have contributed to the ongoing controversy surrounding platelet-associated TF, providing a functional readout that complements antigen-based measurements. This protocol therefore represents a robust and reproducible framework for investigating platelet-associated TF in both mechanistic and clinical studies.
authors: Camera M, Becchetti A, Brambilla M, Valle PD, Giesen PLA, Tremoli E.

title: Pulmonary Sarcoidosis Mimicking Multifocal Adenocarcinoma: An Atypical Radiologic and Diagnostic Dilemma
abstract: Known as "the great mimic," sarcoidosis often poses a diagnostic challenge.Although common radiological manifestations include hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy and micronodules, atypical patterns can also be encountered, requiring awareness of the disease's potential radiological manifestations to allow for prompt diagnosis and management.We report a case of sarcoidosis presenting with predominant groundglass opacities (GGOs) on high-resolution CT (HRCT) of the chest, mimicking adenocarcinoma in situ.The diagnosis was established by histopathology after other causes of pulmonary GGOs had been excluded.This report highlights the importance of maintaining a high degree of clinical suspicion and pursuing a comprehensive workup, including tissue diagnosis, even in minimally symptomatic patients.
authors: Aya Gohar; Alaa Hmeedan; Ashraf Saeed; JEHAD J AZAR; Muhammad Naeem

title: Quality control of blood components: A Six-Year Multicentre Retrospective Study in Tertiary Care Hospitals in Bangladesh
abstract: Background Before prescribing blood components physicians must know the quality of blood that actually fulfil the requirements of patients. In the field of transfusion medicine, blood components therapy is also a standard care therapy globally. In this study we evaluated three hospital data related to quality control of blood components that we prepare and issue. Objectives To evaluate compliance of blood components with AABB quality standards. Materials and Methods A multicentre retrospective study with 95% confidence interval, the study were done in three tertiary care hospitals in Dhaka, Bangladesh. In which total number of Whole Blood (WB) were 55650, RCC were 45420, SDP were 20124, RDP were 25264 and FFP were 48530. Sampling method was simple random sampling technique. Four of each blood components were analyzed every monthly throughout the study period. All blood units (RBCs, RCCs, RDPs, SDPs and FFP) from donors in Ibn Sina Medical College, Delta hospital and Green Life Hospital blood bank were included in the study with the exclusion of blood units which were not processed in these hospital (Outside Blood), leucocyte depleted blood products and washed blood products. Automated cell counter Sysmex XN-1000, and XN -2000, Stago auto analyser were used to obtain desired parameters. Results In our study, 91% of WB, 91% of RCC, 92% of RDP, 95% of SDP and 80% of FFP met the quality compliance with international standard. Conclusion The quality control (QC) data generated in this study provides essential insights into the performance of modern blood collection and processing systems. More than 90% studied blood components like WB, RCC, RDP, SDP strictly complied with international standards. However, FFP analysis could not be done according to AABB and international guideline due to financial constrain rather it was surrogate study. Ultimately, establishing a comprehensive QC program, alongside strict adherence to departmental protocols and manufacturer instructions is vital for blood centers to ensure effective and reliable operational outcomes. authors: Rafiqul H; Habibur R; Tahmina S; Tasminah N L; Daanish A B

title: Repurposing a commercial artificial intelligence vision platform for automated surgical instrument identification: a proof-of-concept study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Retained surgical items are classified as never events but continue to occur, and the count meant to prevent them is often recorded as correct even when an item is retained. Computer vision could provide an independent check on what is on the instrument table, but purpose-built surgical systems are scarce. Industrial vision platforms offer a faster route, although their surgical performance is unknown. METHODS: In a prospective experimental study, a commercial artificial intelligence vision platform developed for industrial inspection was applied to 19 surgical instruments and 3 suture items, each presented once in 100 runs (2,200 experiments). No software redesign was required, but the classifier had been trained on this item set, making this a supervised rather than a zero-shot setting. Two outcomes were recorded: whether the platform assigned the exact item identity, and whether it registered an item as present at the packing step irrespective of type, termed count-presence detection. Because experiments are clustered within items and runs, the primary estimate is the mean per-item accuracy with cluster-adjusted intervals. RESULTS: The correct instruments were identified in 2,036 of 2,200 experiments (92.5%). The mean per-item accuracy was 92.5% (95% confidence interval 88.4 to 96.7; cluster-adjusted 87.7 to 95.6). Count-presence detection was 99.1% (98.7 to 99.4). Performance was reproducible across runs (intraclass correlation 0.02), whereas variance clustered by item (0.12). Accuracy ranged from 64% (suture needle 6-0) to 100% (six items). Errors were directional and almost always within visually near-identical sub-types. CONCLUSIONS: An industrial vision platform detected item presence with high reliability and identified item type with high accuracy, however, with a residual error rate of 7.5%. The errors were predictable and confined to visually similar classes, pointing to correctable mitigations rather than a fundamental limit. These figures represent an upper bound under highly controlled conditions rather than expected intraoperative performance. Such a system is intended to support rather than replace the perioperative team. This study establishes feasibility rather than clinical benefit; a prospective intraoperative study is the necessary next step.
authors: Simon Stoerzer; Klinto Xhemo; Felix Gronau; Linda Feldbruegge; Philipp Felgendreff; Maximilian Kaltenecker; Jacques Hahn; Gerrit Grannas; Moritz Schmelzle

title: Risk Stratification of Incidental Pulmonary Nodules: A Fully Automated Approach to CT Imaging Analysis.
abstract: Incidental detection is the most common pathway through which pulmonary nodules are identified. With the advancement of navigational and robotic-assisted bronchoscopy, existing risk stratification models often lack sufficient discrimination power, particularly for intermediate-risk nodules. Bronchosolve is a fully automated, imaging-only risk stratification tool that was previously validated in lung cancer screening cohorts. We applied Bronchosolve to a cohort of adults with incidentally detected pulmonary nodules identified from registries at 2 large health care systems between 2006 and 2019. Nodules were classified as malignant or benign based on biopsy or extended clinical follow-up. Discrimination was assessed and compared with the VA Model. Sensitivity and specificity were reported at the Youden and high-sensitivity operating points. Additional analysis was performed in cases with nodule diameter 8 to 15 mm. Among 187 patients, malignancy prevalence was 70%. Bronchosolve achieved an AUC of 0.895 versus 0.870 for the VA model. Among nodules 8 to 15 mm, discrimination differences were larger (AUC 0.808 vs. 0.701). In nodules of 8 to 15 mm in diameter with an intermediate risk for malignancy by the VA model, Bronchosolve reclassified 51 patients to high risk and 23 to low risk; 33/37 (89%) malignancies were up-classified and 19/37 (51%) benign nodules were down-classified. In a nonscreening setting, Bronchosolve demonstrated robust discrimination for lung nodule malignancy risk using imaging alone compared with a widely used clinical risk model, with more pronounced separation in intermediate-sized nodules. In this subgroup, Bronchosolve also yielded clinically meaningful risk reclassification, with potential implications for downstream management.
authors: Hongli Liu; Himmat Grewal; Joshua Reicher; Michael Muelly; Angad Kalra; Don Bigler; Omid T Omran; Hitesh Batra

title: Robotic Beyond Total Mesorectal Excision With Synchronous Perineal Flap Reconstruction: Feasibility and Early Outcomes
abstract: BACKGROUND: Advanced rectal and anal malignancies often require dissections beyond total mesorectal planes for improved oncological outcomes. While minimally invasive techniques facilitate this approach, they result in larger perineal defects, creating reconstructive challenges. Robotic-assisted surgery enhances precision, visualisation, and ergonomics, potentially optimising outcomes. However, data on robotics beyond total mesorectal excision (bTME) remain limited. This study evaluated robotic bTME and synchronous gracilis or PAP (profunda artery perforator) flap reconstruction. METHODS: This retrospective case series reviewed 10 patients with locally advanced or recurrent anorectal cancer who underwent elective robotic bTME with synchronous perineal gracilis or PAP flap reconstruction. RESULTS: Median operative time was 465 minutes. Gracilis flap harvest was concurrent. No major flap-related complications or reoperations. R0 resection was achieved in 80%. At 1-year, local recurrence was 0%, distant metastases 30%, and disease-free survival 70%. CONCLUSION: Robotics bTME with synchronous gracilis or PAP flap reconstruction is feasible, efficient, and oncologically safe.
authors: Ahlam Alharbi; Muhammad Rafaih Iqbal; Dolly M. Dowsett; Eleanor J. M. Rudge; Hassan I. Shah; Sandeep Kapur; Richard Matthew Haywood; Anais Rosich‐Medina; Irshad Shaikh
venue: International Journal of Medical Robotics and Computer Assisted Surgery

title: Robotic bronchoscopy in early lung cancer: a biomarker-driven platform for genomic profiling and immunotherapy-oriented decision-making
abstract: Robotic bronchoscopy is increasingly used to sample peripheral pulmonary lesions as lung cancer screening detects more small, distal, subsolid and ground-glass nodules. Most evidence has assessed the technology by diagnostic yield and safety, but these endpoints only partly capture clinical value. In early lung cancer care, the relevant question is whether bronchoscopy provides information that is sufficient for diagnosis, staging, molecular profiling and treatment-ready decision-making. This state-of-the-art review examines robotic bronchoscopy as a potential diagnosis-to-treatment platform rather than an isolated navigation device. We summarise evidence on distal airway access, procedural stability, CT-to-body divergence, tool-in-lesion confirmation, cone-beam CT, mobile cone-beam CT and radial endobronchial ultrasound. We also discuss tissue stewardship, rapid on-site evaluation, cell block preparation, next-generation sequencing, PD-L1 testing and same-session endobronchial ultrasound-guided transbronchial needle aspiration (EBUS-TBNA) and, when appropriate, endoscopic ultrasound with bronchoscope-guided fine-needle aspiration (EUS-B-FNA) as determinants of molecular adequacy and clinical actionability. We propose clinically actionable yield as a pragmatic, complementary, and currently unvalidated reporting construct linking lesion access, confirmed targeting, pathological diagnosis, molecular adequacy, staging completeness, and management decisions. For prospective evaluation, Level 5 (treatment decision informed or changed) should be assessed within 30 days after the index bronchoscopic procedure or before definitive therapy, whichever occurs first. Bronchoscopic ablation is considered as a future therapeutic extension, but current evidence remains early and does not establish equivalence with surgery, stereotactic body radiotherapy or percutaneous ablation. Future studies should evaluate decision-centred and patient-centred endpoints, including molecular-testing success, repeat biopsy avoidance, time to treatment, local control, pulmonary function, quality of life and cost-effectiveness.
authors: Dengxia Zhang; Yahui Han; Haonan Zhang; Chaoyang Yu; 张师前; Teng Li

title: Robotic systems in cranial surgery: a systematic review of accuracy, clinical outcomes, and adverse events
abstract: Robotic-assisted surgery is becoming more prevalent in neurosurgery. Many studies have classified the advantages and disadvantages, particularly in spinal robotic surgeries. However, the use of robotics in cranial procedures has been limited to individual studies without large-scale review of the different modalities. This study is a comprehensive systematic review of the major robotics utilized in cranial neurosurgical procedures and their respective outcomes. Following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines, a systematic review was conducted over PubMed, Cochrane, and Embase for articles published between January 2000 to February 2025. EndNote and Rayyan were utilized to organize the 1,409 identified studies and conduct a blinded multiphase process for including and excluding studies. Originally, studies were intended to be run as a meta-analysis to compare robotic modalities, but the existing data was too heterogeneous to statistically contrast outcomes. Overall, 51 studies were included, with six robots being discussed in more than one study. The use of robotics in cranial neurosurgery stretches mostly across functional neurosurgery, with different applications in brain tumor biopsies and resection, hemorrhage drainage, and endoscopic surgeries. Cranial neurosurgical procedures primarily apply robotics in the world of functional neurosurgery. Outside of this subspecialty, robotic-assisted cranial surgery remains sparse in the literature. As technology evolves, more use cases may be realized.
authors: Alison E. Burgess; Bailey D. Lupo; Luke P. Landry; Ben V. Peco; Nadia V Haik; Zack Karzoun; Norris C Talbot; James R. Bridges; Michael S. Folse; Ryan Diaz; Jamie Toms

title: Robotic-Assisted Bronchoscopy for Peripheral Pulmonary Lesions: Current Evidence, Clinical Applications, and Future Directions
abstract: The evaluation of peripheral pulmonary lesions (PPLs) represents a persistent clinical challenge, particularly in the context of rapidly expanding lung cancer screening programs generating unprecedented volumes of screen-detected nodules requiring tissue evaluation. Conventional bronchoscopic techniques and earlier navigation platforms, including electromagnetic navigation bronchoscopy (ENB), improved access to peripheral airways but demonstrated variable and generally suboptimal diagnostic performance—historically plateauing at 60–70%—attributable principally to CT-to-body divergence and the diagnostic drop-off phenomenon. Robotic-assisted bronchoscopy (RAB) has emerged as a significant advancement integrating robotic catheter control, shape-sensing or electromagnetic navigation, and adjunctive intraprocedural imaging—principally cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT)—to improve lesion localization and procedural stability. Available evidence suggests that RAB achieves improved diagnostic yields compared with conventional bronchoscopic techniques, particularly when combined with real-time CBCT-guided tool-in-lesion confirmation and multimodal biopsy strategies including transbronchial cryobiopsy. Reported diagnostic yields generally range from 70% to 87% across pooled meta-analytic datasets, with higher yields described in centers employing CBCT and cryobiopsy. A favorable safety profile—with pooled pneumothorax rates of approximately 2%, substantially below the 20–25% associated with CT-guided transthoracic needle biopsy—represents a clinically important differentiator, particularly in patients with emphysema, coagulopathy, or contralateral lung compromise [1,3]. RAB additionally enables procedural capabilities beyond peripheral lesion biopsy, including simultaneous mediastinal lymph node staging, bilateral same-session lesion sampling, fiducial marker placement for stereotactic body radiotherapy, and investigational therapeutic applications. However, current evidence is largely derived from observational studies and single-arm prospective cohorts, with limited randomized data directly comparing RAB with transthoracic biopsy approaches. Outcomes are meaningfully influenced by lesion characteristics, operator experience, institutional volume, and availability of advanced imaging infrastructure. This review summarizes current evidence on RAB platforms, procedural optimization, diagnostic performance, safety, molecular tissue adequacy, and emerging applications, while explicitly addressing limitations, controversies, and areas requiring further investigation. This review was conducted and reported in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines adapted for narrative reviews (SANRA framework).
authors: Venkatkiran Kanchustambham

title: Robotic-assisted bronchoscopic biopsy and EBUS-TBNA in lung cancer: An outcome comparison between clinical and pathological staging.
abstract: Accurate mediastinal staging of suspected lung cancer is critical for guiding treatment and determining prognosis. While computed tomography (CT) and positron emission tomography (PET) are integral to initial staging, both modalities have limitations for detecting nodal metastases. Endobronchial ultrasound-guided transbronchial needle aspiration (EBUS-TBNA) provides a minimally invasive option for obtaining tissue confirmation. This study evaluates the impact of adding EBUS-TBNA at the time of lung tumor biopsy on mediastinal staging accuracy. We conducted a retrospective study of patients who underwent shape-sensing robotic-assisted bronchoscopy (ssRAB) with concurrent EBUS-TBNA between June 2020 and December 2025. Preprocedural CT and PET findings were compared with EBUS-TBNA cytopathology to assess their diagnostic performance and to evaluate stage migration in patients with primary pulmonary malignancies. A total of 1,234 patients underwent ssRAB with EBUS-TBNA, of whom 123 (10.0 %) had malignant lymph nodes on cytopathology. Among these, 23 patients (18.7 %) had no suspicious lymphadenopathy on preprocedural CT and/or PET imaging. The sensitivity of CT and PET for detecting malignancy at specific lymph node stations was 44.5 % and 68.5 %, respectively. In the clinical-to-EBUS staging analysis, 66 (74.2 %) demonstrated no major stage change, while 23 (25.9 %) experienced stage migration. Concurrent EBUS-TBNA identified occult nodal involvement and resulted in stage migration. These findings underscore the critical role of EBUS-TBNA in identifying clinically occult nodal disease and optimizing lung cancer treatment.
authors: Sebastian Fernandez-Bussy; Regina M Murillo-Torres; Tatiana A Rojas-Zapata; Alejandra Yu Lee-Mateus; Paola Gutierrez-Gallegos; David Abia-Trujillo; Linh H Vu; Ryan M Chadha; Kelly S Robertson; Bryan C Husta

title: Robotics in neurosurgery: past, present, and future
abstract: Background Robotics has progressed from stereotactic positioning and instrument guidance toward integrated platforms combining navigation, intraoperative imaging, immersive visualization, and computer-assisted control. However, technical accuracy and clinical benefit are not interchangeable, and the maturity of evidence differs markedly across neurosurgical indications. Objective To critically synthesize the historical development, contemporary applications, supporting evidence, implementation constraints, and research priorities of robotic and complementary augmented-reality (AR)/virtual-reality (VR) technologies in neurosurgery. Methods This is a critical narrative review and technology-focused synthesis, informed by the literature and reference set of the original manuscript (which described searching PubMed, Google Scholar, and ScienceDirect through January 2021), supplemented by selected contemporary publications and the two VOSTARS studies suggested during peer review. No new reproducible systematic search, dual-reviewer screening, formal risk-of-bias assessment, or quantitative synthesis was performed; therefore, PRISMA study counts are not reported. Synthesis Cranial robotic systems facilitate trajectory planning and reproducible positioning for stereotactic biopsy, stereoelectroencephalography, deep brain stimulation, and related interventions. Spine robotics can support pedicle screw placement, although comparative estimates depend on platform, comparator, experience, and outcome definition. Endovascular and microsurgical robotics remain heterogeneous, with many applications at feasibility or early clinical stages. Wearable AR systems such as VOSTARS illustrate the convergence of visualization and navigation but require validation under real operative conditions. Acquisition and maintenance costs, registration error, line-of-sight constraints, human factors, training, and cybersecurity are distinct adoption barriers. Conclusions The most defensible current contribution of robotics is task-specific assistance within surgeon-led workflows, not universal superiority or autonomy. Future studies should prioritize patient-important outcomes, transparent technical reporting, prospective comparisons, and context-sensitive economic evaluation.
authors: Hosam Maher Al-Jehani; Ahmed Hafez Mousa

title: STEAM and educational robotics in the development of statistical literacy
abstract: In primary school, the teaching of mathematics and natural sciences should promote meaningful, context-based learning that enables students to apply knowledge in real-life situations. Interdisciplinary approaches such as STEAM foster 21st century competences through active and collaborative methodologies, while educational robotics (ER) supports the development of computational thinking and social skills. This study analyses the influence of a STEAM practice, incorporating ER on the development of statistical literacy and learning about ocean plastic pollution among 4th grade students. The research adopted a mixed-methods, interpretative action research design. Data were collected by the trainee teacher as participant researcher through performance tasks, field notes, photographs and audio recordings, later used to construct multimodal narratives. Findings reveal statistically significant improvements in global level of knowledge and global performance. The study concludes that steam practices incorporating ER and grounded in real-world problem-solving constitute an effective strategy for fostering statistical literacy.
authors: Vanda Santos; Ana Silva; Filipa Pinto; Marisa Alexandra Maia Machado; Fernando Martíns
venue: Eurasia Journal of Mathematics Science and Technology Education

title: Safety and Efficacy of Endobronchial Ultrasound
abstract: Abstract Purpose of review The use of bronchoscopy with endobronchial ultrasound (EBUS) to aid in lymph node and lung biopsy is relatively new. This review will summarize the literature surrounding the efficacy of bronchoscopy with EBUS. Safety of bronchoscopy with EBUS is not markedly different that procedure with EBUS and is impacted by patient features including co-morbidities as well as different sedation modalities. This paper reviews the impact on both safety and diagnostic yield. Recent Findings The yield from using EBUS guided biopsy varies with the diagnosis but is high with linear EBUS. Recent data incorporating other technologies (electromagnetic navigation, robotic assistance) with bronchoscopy has potential to increase diagnostic yields, appears to be equivalent to transthoracic needle biopsies performed by radiology. Different sedation modalities are utilized, including the use of dedicated anesthesia providers, for bronchoscopy with EBUS but do not appear to significantly affect the diagnostic yield. Summary Bronchoscopy with EBUS (both linear and radial) is a safe procedure with acceptable yields. The type of sedation does not appear to affect the diagnostic yield or the safety of the procedure. Further research into incorporation of other technologies may provide for higher diagnostic yields.
authors: Travis Yamanaka; Kevin P. Haas

title: Safety and diagnostic performance of robotic-assisted bronchoscopy in higher-risk and complex patients
