title: Artificial intelligence-assisted art therapy in digital psychiatry: Clinical applications, mechanisms, and ethics
abstract: Artificial intelligence-assisted art therapy should be understood as a therapistmediated extension of creative practice rather than an autonomous treatment.This structured narrative review synthesizes eleven directly relevant publications, including preliminary patient studies and adjacent creative-activity research, alongside transferable evidence from art therapy, conversational artificial intelligence, digital psychiatry, immersive technologies, affective computing, social robotics, and health-care artificial intelligence ethics.Direct patient-level evidence remains limited and heterogeneous, with mixed, domain-specific findings that do not establish general efficacy, comparative effectiveness, or safety; clinicianperspective evidence is limited, and most proposed applications and mechanisms derive from conceptual or transferable evidence.We therefore distinguish artificial intelligence used in visual creation, therapeutic dialogue or documentation, behavioral or emotional inference, and immersive or embodied interaction, and separate professional art therapy from broader digital creative activity.Supervised image-making, reflective preparation, patient-selected monitoring, and recoveryoriented follow-up are candidate uses for prospective research.The proposed taxonomy, pathway, risk framework, mechanisms, and safeguards are conceptual, research-oriented, provisional, and non-validated; they are not clinical guidance or a validated practice standard.Key risks include privacy loss, culturally stereotyped imagery, hallucinated feedback, misinterpretation, uncertain authorship, dependency, and image-specific provenance and secondary-use concerns.Future research should test clearly defined therapist-mediated protocols using explicit risk stratification, adverse-event monitoring, and transparent data governance.
authors: Ke Meng; Mingzhi Hou; Heeju Chae

title: Audit-first rollback semantics for safety–critical deployment pipelines
abstract: Deployment runtimes for safety–critical embodied agents keep two records: the live state components execute and the audit chain operators and regulators read. When an upgrade crashes mid-flight, a runtime that fails open keeps the partial deployment running, so the audit chain misstates what runs. We propose audit-first rollback semantics: the revert is attempted before any terminal record is written, and the record states what it did. Provisional state machines with a rollback closure and a bounded soak budget realize the rule; a protocol design extends it to coordinated bridges. We implemented it in a robot-manipulator deployment runtime and compared it with fail-open at 23 enumerated fault sites plus a control and over 10 runs of a 12-point crash grid. The sweep exposed two writes the first implementation left outside its guard and a fallback that lost the divergence flag. With the guard widened, every audit-first trial ended in the specified state; under our stricter coherence check fail-open did so at 5 sites, the ones needing no revert. Over the guarded trials that ended ROLLED_BACK, a terminal record followed within 35.7 ms at the 99th percentile. A terminal record then states what is running or flags that it must be reconciled.
authors: Xue Qin; Simin Luan; Cong Yang; Zhijun Li

title: Automated 3D morphological analysis of calcaneal fractures on CT-scans using deep learning-based segmentation and rule-based geometric measurements
abstract: Background The calcaneus is a complex anatomical structure essential for upright posture and movement. Calcaneal fractures can result in substantial disability. Treatment varies from non-operative to surgical fixation, depending on fracture morphology. Current assessment relies on subjective interpretation of 2D and 3D imaging, limiting reproducibility and standardization. Quantitative and automated tools may improve fracture characterization, although clinical application requires further validation. Purpose To develop and evaluate an automated method for 3D morphological analysis of the calcaneus and its joint surfaces. Methods nnU-Net models were trained to segment the calcaneus, talus, cuboid, and calcaneocuboid joint on CT images using a development dataset (n=35 non-fractured, n=38 fractured) and were evaluated on an external test dataset (n=46 non-fractured, n=38 fractured). Segmentation performance was evaluated using the Dice Similarity Coefficient, mean surface distance, and 95 th percentile Hausdorff distance, with manual segmentations serving as the reference standard. Morphological measurements were then computed using surface-based geometry. Agreement between measurements derived from manual and automated segmentations was assessed. In addition, exploratory between-cohort comparisons were performed to evaluate whether the measurements showed differences between non-fractured and fractured calcanei. Results Automated segmentation achieved high performance for the calcaneus, talus, and cuboid, with Dice similarity coefficients of at least 0.98. For the calcaneocuboid joint, Dice similarity coefficients ranged from 0.79 to 0.89. Most morphological measurements showed agreement between manual- and automated-segmentation-derived models. Significant between-cohort differences were observed for several measurements, including posterior talocalcaneal joint incongruence, Böhler’s angle, varus/valgus angulation, and calcaneal/talocalcaneal height, whereas the calcaneocuboid joint distance measurements and Critical angle of Gissane showed less consistent differences. Conclusion The method provides a reproducible and quantitative CT-based workflow for automated 3D analysis of calcaneal fracture morphology using deep learning-based segmentation and rule-based geometric measurements. The between-cohort comparisons are exploratory, and within-subject and clinical validation are required before use in clinical decision-making.
authors: Alexander M. Wakker; Jacob J. Visser; Esther M.M. Van Lieshout; Cornelis H. van der Vlies; M.H.J. Verhofstad; Theo van Walsum; Mark G. van Vledder

title: Awareness perception and attitude towards neglected tropical diseases among health professionals in South-West Nigeria
abstract: Abstract Background Health professionals play an important role in the management and control of neglected tropical diseases (NTDs). However, variations in awareness, knowledge, and attitudes among healthcare workers in South-West Nigeria may limit the effectiveness of NTD control programmes. This study assessed the awareness, perception, and attitude of health professionals towards NTDs and related control activities in South-West Nigeria. Methods A cross-sectional descriptive study was conducted between 18th October 2021 and 31st March 2022 using structured close-ended questionnaires administered to health professionals across South-West Nigeria. Data were analysed by descriptive statistics and “ Chi -Square” test at 95% level of significance with SPSS software (version 20.0). A 67% response rate was achieved. Results Out of 1556 respondents surveyed, 765 (49.2%) were females. Significant associations were observed between respondents’ location, gender, age group and occupation (p < 0.05 for all). Accurate recognition of NTDs among participants was 86.4% for correct definition, 85% for identification of one or more NTDs, 68.5% for involvement in NTDs programmes, and 46.4% for academic sources of information. Readiness for future engagement in NTDs was high, with 90.7% indicating support for required intervention, and 83.7% expressing willingness to participate in NTDs-related activities. Knowledge based on definition of NTDs showed no statistical difference across the South-West zone (P-value > 0.05). Conclusion Health professionals in South-West Nigeria demonstrated generally high awareness and positive attitudes toward NTDs. These findings provide an important framework for targeted capacity building, training and policy interventions to strengthen NTD management and control.

title: Backdoors in Learning-Based Industrial Robotic Arm Manipulation: An Empirical Security Study
abstract: Learning-based models (e.g., visuomotor and Vision-Language-Action (VLA)) are increasingly explored for industrial robotic manipulation, where model predictions are directly translated into physical actions. This tight coupling between model behavior and physical execution makes hidden security vulnerabilities particularly consequential. While backdoor attacks have been widely studied in conventional AI models, their effects on deployed learning-based robotic arm manipulation systems remain less understood: a backdoored robot can behave normally during benign operation while inducing attacker-specified behaviors only when specific triggers are present, posing potentially serious risks in physical environments. In this work, we present a preliminary empirical security study of backdoor attacks and defenses in learning-based robotic manipulation on two real commercial industrial robotic arms (FANUC and xArm). We investigate whether a backdoor can reliably induce semantically incorrect manipulation behaviors while remaining stealthy under nominal task execution. We then develop an online defense pipeline that detects and neutralizes triggers at runtime, and compare its effectiveness against an offline fine-tuning defense. Beyond defense effectiveness, we further evaluate the computational latency and execution overhead introduced by the defense pipeline to assess its suitability for high-throughput industrial operation.
authors: Zijian Zhang; Zhen Zeng; Zhongshu Gu; Sandeep Pisharody

title: Between Knowledge and Care: A Mixed-Methods Evaluation of Generative AI for T2DM Self-Management from Patient and Physician Perspectives
abstract: Generative AI is increasingly used for everyday health guidance, yet its clinical appropriateness in chronic disease contexts remains poorly understood. This paper presents a two-part mixed-methods study on Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM), examining how patients and physicians assess AI-generated health information. Study 1 analyzes 784 participant reported patient queries to characterize seven informational need categories and develops a structured five dimensional physician rating rubric informed by patient query categories and clinician priorities (Accuracy, Safety, Clarity, Integrity, Action Orientation). Study 2 engages seven physicians scoring responses from four AI models and discussing evaluative reasoning through in-depth interviews. Models perform well on factual explanation and lifestyle guidance but consistently underperform on medication reasoning and emotional support. Two analytic concepts emerge from the data. The pre-visit primer frames AI as preparation for clinical encounters rather than as a replacement for physicians. The fluency illusion describes how polished language may convey epistemic authority that the clinical content does not support. Patients and physicians converged on three shared limitations (role boundaries, emotional inadequacy, personalization gaps) while diverging in evaluative emphasis, which informed four design directions, task-aware orchestration, risk-aware fallback, dynamic personalization, and emotionally attuned interaction.
authors: Ruiqi Chen; Yibo Meng; Huidi Lu; Xiaolan Ding

title: Beyond Tasks: A Vision for Reproducing an Animal-like Behavioral Substrate Using Modern Robot Learning Techniques
abstract: Recent advances in robot learning have produced increasingly capable embodied agents. Yet comparatively less attention has been given to a more basic form of competence that animals exhibit continuously: the ability to remain situated, responsive, and behaviorally coherent as physical, environmental, and social demands change over time. We propose the ethological behavioral substrate as a conceptual lens for studying this form of competence in artificial agents. Rather than treating these behaviors that animals exhibit as a set of isolated skills, we argue that their continual coordination under competing demands constitutes an important and underexplored target for modern robot learning. We further propose robotic animal companions as a useful research setting for studying sustained interaction and adaptation in human-centered environments. Such systems provide an opportunity to investigate how social behavior, memory, and continual learning develop over long periods of interaction. This perspective motivates further investigation of how such persistent behavioral competence may complement higher-level capabilities in embodied agents.
authors: Samiyuru Menik; Hemadri Jayalath

title: Bioassays in Allergy: Technical Characteristics, Limitations, and Pathways to Clinical Implementation—An EAACI Position Paper
abstract: Bioassays offer functional readouts of immune responses through specific biomarkers, providing mechanistic insight beyond conventional serology. By capturing cellular activation, tissue-level changes, and molecular signaling, they hold promise for refining allergy diagnosis, risk stratification, and treatment monitoring, contributing to precision medicine. This review summarizes the current landscape of three allergy-relevant bioassays: basophil activation test, histology, and molecular biology-based assays. We discuss their underlying principles, clinical utilities as well as methodological and translational challenges and translational barriers. Attention is given to unmet needs such as assay standardization, reproducibility, and integration into clinical workflows. Finally, we outline future directions for research and clinical implementation, emphasizing the potential of bioassays to refine personalized management of allergic disorders. This position paper clearly distinguishes between descriptive summaries of the available evidence and the potential applicability recommendations of the EAACI Task Force, thereby enhancing clarity and interpretability for clinicians and researchers.

title: Blood‐ and Liver Stiffness‐Based Non‐Invasive Tests for Clinically Significant Portal Hypertension in Patients With cACLD and HCC
abstract: BACKGROUND AND AIMS: The applicability of non-invasive tests (NITs) for clinically significant portal hypertension (CSPH) in patients with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is controversial. We performed a head-to-head comparison of various NITs for CSPH and evaluated rule-in/-out criteria. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective study including 283 patients with HCC undergoing hepatic venous pressure gradient (HVPG) measurement at the Vienna Hepatic Haemodynamic Lab with available, same-day data on NITs (i.e., liver stiffness measurement [LSM], platelet count [PLT], von Willebrand factor antigen [VWF:Ag], and the ratio of VWF:Ag and PLT [VITRO]). For the subsequent analysis, we focused on patients with compensated advanced chronic liver disease (cACLD). RESULTS: Among 164 patients with cACLD, most were BCLC 0/A (50.6%) and CSPH prevalence was 46.3%, the median LSM was 20.0 kPa (IQR: 13.3-37.9), and mean VWF:Ag/VITRO was 266 ± 119%/2.30 ± 1.81. The VITRO score yielded the highest discriminative ability to detect CSPH (AUROC: 0.834), followed by ANTICIPATE ± NASH (AUROC: 0.822), PLT (AUROC: 0.803), LSM (AUROC: 0.779), and VWF:Ag (AUROC: 0.707). The application of the Baveno VII criterium (LSM ≤ 15 kPa & PLT ≥ 150G/L) and the VITRO score (≤ 1.0) individually showed an excellent performance for ruling-out CSPH (sensitivities: ≥ 95%, NPV: 100%/87.9%). For ruling-in CSPH by individual criteria, the VITRO score provided the highest PPV (≥ 2.5, specificity/PPV: 89.8%/83.0%), followed by the Baveno VII criteria (specificity/PPV: 81.8%/74.6%). When sequentially applying Baveno VII criteria and VITRO, the grey zone could be significantly reduced to 16% (sensitivity/NPV: 94.7%/92.2%; specificity/PPV: 73.9%/84.4%). CONCLUSION: The discriminative ability in patients with cACLD and HCC was comparable to patients without HCC. However, PPVs of established criteria were < 90%, which may be explained by the comparatively low prevalence of CSPH in this context.

title: Brain-Inspired Hierarchical Modularity for General Continual Learning
abstract: Continual learning, the ability to learn from sequential experience while retaining and adapting prior knowledge, is central to intelligent systems operating in changing environments. However, conventional continual learning is typically studied with offline task-wise training and clear task boundaries, leaving a substantial gap from general continual learning under online, uncertain, and evolving data streams. In this regime, intelligent systems must separate conflicting experience to reduce interference while integrating compatible experience to promote generalization. Inspired by the organization of the Drosophila learning and memory system, we identify a hierarchical modular principle that coordinates both functions through expert specialization and ensemble integration. We instantiate this principle as lightweight modular adaptation of pretrained foundation models, combining brain-inspired random expansion for expert routing and diversified modular integration across spatial and temporal scales. Across visual recognition, vision-language understanding, ego-exo video understanding, and embodied vision-language-action learning, our method consistently improves learning under online and uncertain data streams, with gains exceeding 50 percentage points over replay-free alternatives in embodied manipulation. These findings support hierarchical modularity as a biologically grounded path for learning from dynamic experience.

title: Caring for a Life: Medical Treatment and Biographical Futurity
abstract: Abstract Medical care is commonly understood through the aims of cure, restoration, functional recovery, symptom relief, and survival. Yet medical treatment may extend biological futurity while contracting biographical futurity: it may give a person more time while leaving fewer meaningful and practically realisable possibilities within that time. This article develops the concept of biographical futurity to describe the field of possibilities within which a person can still project, choose, revise, and make a life. Building on literature on biographical disruption, phenomenology of illness, treatment burden, embodied autonomy, and transformative experience, the paper argues that existing approaches often presuppose goals and projects that radical illness may itself render unavailable. Drawing principally on José Ortega y Gasset’s conception of life as quehacer , with Benedetto Croce’s account of concrete volition providing a further conceptual distinction, biographical futurity is presented as a way of conceptualising care beyond restoration. The argument distinguishes goal preservation from goal formability, examines treatment’s role in the reconstitution of circumstance, and proposes future re-choosing as an important temporal dimension of autonomy. Good care, on this account, does not guarantee a future but helps preserve the conditions under which a future can still become the patient’s to make.
authors: Massimo Vittorio

title: Cell‐Based Micro/Nanorobots: From Living Carriers to Living Therapeutic Specialists
abstract: ABSTRACT Cell‐based micro/nanorobots (CMNRs) integrate intrinsic biological functions with engineered capabilities, constituting an emerging class of biohybrid robotic platforms. Unlike fully synthetic micro/nanorobots, whose functions depend entirely on artificial materials, CMNRs are constructed from living cells or cell‐derived components and can exploit unique biological capabilities. Over the past decade, CMNR research has progressed from the development of simple delivery carriers toward therapeutic specialists capable of performing diagnostic and therapeutic tasks within distinct organs. Although the complex and highly heterogeneous physiological environments of different organs impose formidable barriers, CMNRs possess intrinsic organ‐specific compatibility shaped by evolution, offering a promising strategy for improving their performance in specialized medical tasks. Here, we propose a novel framework for constructing organ‐specific therapeutic platforms. Guided by this framework, we systematically review and critically assess the biological properties, robotic functions, and recent in vivo applications of CMNRs. Despite substantial progress, a considerable gap remains between laboratory prototypes and clinical translation. This Review identifies key translational barriers that must be addressed to ensure the safety, controllability, and functional reliability of CMNRs in clinical use. Overall, a future trajectory toward organ‐specific theranostic systems is outlined to provide a conceptual basis for the clinical development of next‐generation CMNRs.

title: Changes in Body Weight and Radiographic Cardiac Indices Following Furosemide Treatment in Maltese Dogs with Cardiogenic Pulmonary Edema
abstract: Background: Cardiogenic pulmonary edema (CPE) is a life-threatening condition in dogs with myxomatous mitral valve disease (MMVD). Diagnosis and monitoring of CPE typically rely on repeated radiographic examinations, including vertebral heart size (VHS) and vertebral left atrial size (VLAS), which may be challenging in critically ill patients. Although diuretic therapy is routinely used for treatment, the relationship between body weight loss during treatment and changes in cardiac size has not been fully investigated. This study aimed to evaluate the association between body weight reduction and radiographic cardiac size changes following furosemide treatment in Maltese dogs with CPE. Because no previous studies have evaluated whether body weight reduction reflects complete radiographic resolution of pulmonary edema during treatment of cardiogenic pulmonary edema, we investigated whether body weight loss could serve as a practical adjunctive monitoring parameter. Methods: Medical records of 48 Maltese dogs diagnosed with cardiogenic pulmonary edema (CPE) and treated with continuous rate infusion (CRI) of furosemide between June 2020 and June 2022 were retrospectively reviewed. Dogs were divided into two groups according to prior administration of heart medications (pimobendan and enalapril). Body weight, vertebral heart size (VHS) and vertebral left atrial size (VLAS) were measured at presentation (D0) and after complete radiographic resolution of pulmonary edema (D1). Changes and change rates were calculated and correlations among body weight reduction, VHS and VLAS were analyzed. Group comparisons were performed using the Mann-Whitney test and pre- and post-treatment changes were analyzed using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Result: A total of 48 Maltese dogs met the inclusion criteria. Mean body weight decreased from 3.56±1.30 kg at D0 to 3.31±1.19 kg at D1, corresponding to a mean reduction rate of 6.89%. Mean VHS decreased from 11.76±0.93 to 11.03±0.96 and mean VLAS decreased from 3.04±0.33 to 2.86±0.32 after treatment. No significant differences in body weight loss rate, VHS change rate, or VLAS change rate were observed between dogs receiving heart medications and those not receiving such medications. Correlation analysis showed positive correlations between pre- and post-treatment body weight and between pre- and post-treatment VHS and VLAS values. However, body weight loss was not significantly associated with changes in radiographic cardiac indices.
authors: Youngsin Seung; Jihyun Kim; Yunji Lim; Jimin Yoo; Young-Min Yun

title: ChunkVLA-AM: Parallel Action Chunking for Vision-Language-Action Robot Control in Additive Manufacturing
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models unify visual perception, language understanding, and action generation, offering new opportunities for automation in additive manufacturing (AM). However, deployment in AM remains challenging because adapting these models to unseen robot embodiments is costly, and performance can degrade under environment changes. In this work, we present a framework for deploying OpenVLA-OFT on a FAIRINO FR3 robot in a fixed AM workcell. A data pipeline converts monocular real-world demonstrations into OpenVLA-compatible TFDS/RLDS datasets to support adaptation to the FR3 embodiment. At runtime, each inference request predicts an eight-step chunk of 7-D actions. The FR3 executes each chunk open loop before capturing a new observation, providing closed-loop feedback between chunks. The system uses a cloud-edge architecture in which the FR3 client streams observations to a remote inference server through a FastAPI interface. In 42 physical A-to-B object-transfer trials, evenly split between red and blue targets, the system succeeded in 39 (92.9%). All three failures occurred during final placement, when insufficient release-height control caused the object to topple. An illumination sweep identified a low-error luminance range of 85-125 on a 0-255 scale, with the lowest mean spatial error at 95.

title: Clinical-scale manufacturing of CD137+ enriched tumor-reactive T cells for glioblastoma in the CliniMACS Prodigy
abstract: Background: Most tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte (TIL) studies and therapies have focused on tumors with high T-cell infiltration and mutational burden. Glioblastoma (GBM) represents a challenging indication for TIL therapy because of its limited T-cell infiltration and low mutational burden. We investigated whether targeted enrichment of tumor-reactive T cells using CD137-based selection could enable robust, clinical-scale production of TIL products from GBM. Methods: Ultrasonic aspirates (UAs), routinely collected during GBM resections, were evaluated as a source of TILs for clinical manufacturing. TILs were generated from GBM UAs under GMP-like conditions at clinical scale using the closed, automated TRT Process on the CliniMACS Prodigy. Matched TRT products that were enriched for CD137+ cells, depleted of CD137+ cells, or left unselected were generated in parallel at full manufacturing scale. Products were characterized by cellular and transcriptomic analyses and evaluated in functional assays for cytotoxicity against autologous and non-autologous patient-derived GBM cell lines. Results: Cellular and transcriptomic analyses revealed that UA-derived CD137+ (4-1BB/TNFRSF9) T cells were clonally expanded, exhibited activated and memory phenotypes, and displayed transcriptional profiles associated with tumor reactivity. The closed manufacturing process preserved phenotypic features previously associated with clinical benefit in other TIL indications. Functional assays demonstrated potent, tumor-reactive cytotoxicity of CD137-enriched TRT products against autologous GBM cell lines compared with TILs generated in parallel without selection. Discussion/Conclusions: These findings establish the feasibility of a clinical-scale TIL manufacturing approach using the CliniMACS Prodigy that enables production of clinically relevant quantities of TILs from GBM while enriching for cells with tumor-reactive characteristics. This approach may broaden the application of TIL therapy to immunologically cold tumors with limited T-cell infiltration or low mutational burden that have historically been challenging to manufacture using conventional TIL production methods.

title: Comparing large language models and prompting techniques to control an embodied persuasive coach
abstract: Embodied agents play a crucial role in applications designed to influence user behaviour. Traditionally, crafting these agents requires considerable human effort. Large Language Models (LLMs) might open the possibility of creating agents capable of autonomous, open-ended interactions without labour-intensive development processes. We explore creating an embodied agent to coach users in real-time through slow and deep breathing exercises using an LLM. The LLM exploits a text-based context to generate a composition of predefined behaviours for interacting with the user through both verbal and nonverbal communication. This context includes essential details like the user’s respiratory rate to monitor the exercise. First, we assess the feasibility of this approach, showing that the LLM-based coach generates believable contingent behaviour compositions. Then, we conduct a 4 × 2 × 2 study evaluating how four different LLMs and two prompting techniques (reasoning- and learning-oriented) affect latency, appropriateness, and reliability of the behaviour compositions. Our findings show that more recent LLM models, combined with appropriate prompting techniques, improve appropriateness and reliability over previous models. However, our two studies also identify challenges, including latency, inappropriate feedback, and hallucinations. We discuss the limitations of using only LLMs to create persuasive agents capable of real-time user interactions, suggesting a need for hybrid approaches.
authors: Christian Corrò; Luca Chittaro

title: Content analysis of the range of anthelmintic drugs on the pharmaceutical market of the Republic of Uzbekistan, 2016–2025
abstract: Background. Helminthiases remain a significant medical and social concern, necessitating rational pharmaceutical supply and regular analysis of the available range of anthelmintic drugs. Objective: To perform a content analysis of the range of anthelmintic drugs registered on the pharmaceutical market of the Republic of Uzbekistan and assess its structure, changes over time, and key trends from2016 to 2025. Material and methods . The study was based on data from the State Register of Medicines and Medical Devices of the Republic of Uzbekistan for 2016–2025, officially finalized as of 2025. Content, structural, comparative, and trend analyses, as well as descriptive statistics, were used. The medicines were analyzed by international nonproprietary name (INN), dosage form, country of origin, and manufacturer. Results. During the study period, the range of anthelmintic drugs underwent substantial structural changes and showed a trend toward ationalization. The total number of registered medicines decreased from 72 INNs in 2016 to 35 INNs in 2025. The range consisted mainly of drugs from domestic and foreign manufacturers, with drugs from CIS countries accounting for only a small proportion. Approximately 50% of anthelmintic drugs contained albendazole. Oral dosage forms were the most common, particularly tablets and suspensions. Conclusion. The findings indicate a shift toward a more rational structure of the anthelmintic drugs range on the pharmaceutical market of the Republic of Uzbekistan. The identified trends inform the planning of drug supply and subsequent pharmacoeconomic studies.

title: Deep Reinforcement Learning and Explainable Artificial Intelligence for Autonomous Systems
abstract: Autonomous systems are quickly journeying from research laboratories into everyday existence. Autonomous vehicles drive on the roads in cities, unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) monitor structure health, mobile robots and humanoid robots and intelligent controllers collaborate with a human. The common thing with these machines is that they are required to sense, reason and act independently of human intervention. One of the most powerful methods to provide them with that capability is deep reinforcement learning (DRL), where agents learn human-level, sequential decision-making policies directly from their experiences. But the powerful neural networks that power these policies are very opaque, which makes trust, certification and accountability challenging. This book, Deep Reinforcement Learning and Explainable Artificial Intelligence for Autonomous Systems, aims to unite these two areas to fill this gap. Chapters 1 is laying the foundation. It explains the Markov decision process (MDP) and the partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) and overviews the key families of algorithms: value-based methods like deep Q-network (DQN), policy gradient methods, actor-critic methods like proximal policy optimization (PPO) and soft actor-critic (SAC), model-based reinforcement learning and offline reinforcement learning. Also covered are sim-to-real transfer, digital twins, reward design, sample efficiency, and generalization. Chapter 2 focuses on explainable reinforcement learning (XRL). It presents a taxonomy of explainable AI (XAI) approaches from post hoc feature attribution, to interpretable policies, causal, counterfactual, and language-based explanations, along with discussing human-centered evaluation of explanation quality. Causal and counterfactual explanations are explored in greater detail in Chapter 3, with a focus on counterfactuals generated using world models and diffusion models, causal reinforcement learning, reward decomposition and structural causal models, and the ladder of causation. Co-operative autonomy is discussed in Chapter 4 using Multi Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL). It includes chapters on Markov games, decentralized POMDPs, centralized training with decentralized execution, value decomposition, and credit assignment, as well as how Shapley value attribution, attention analysis, and policy distillation can be used to render multi-agent systems transparent. Chapter 5 discusses foundation models, multimodal AI, and vision-language-action (VLA) models, and how reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) and fine-tuning modules can modify such generalist robot policies for embodied AI, end-to-end autonomous driving, and robotic manipulation respectively. Chapter 6 deals with the topic of generative AI and agentic AI, in which LLMs serve as a planner, diffusion policies determine actions, and multi-agent systems collaborate with each other according to shared protocols, and all of this under the umbrella of AI safety, alignment, and governance. Chapter 7 ties up these concepts for autonomous vehicles and robotics, comparing with different ways and outlining some open problem areas. A common thread that weaves through the text is the concept of safe reinforcement learning, as well as topics such as robustness, human-in-the-loop oversight and trustworthy AI. We are saying that we need to perform in a high way but it's not enough. An autonomous agent also has to be able to describe their behaviour in ways that will be understood and verified by engineers, regulators and end-users. Explainability is thus not considered an add-on feature but is instead viewed as a design constraint that helps facilitate safety assurance, debugging, and responsible deployment of machine learning. It is especially written for graduate students, researchers and practitioners of artificial intelligence, robotics, control engineering and intelligent transportation systems. Every chapter is a mix of the foundations of the enthusiasm, the latest advances, comparison tables, and software applications case studies, allowing the readers to ramp up from theory to practice. We hope that this volume is a reference and that it is a "springboard" for developing autonomous capable, safe and interpretable systems.

title: Deployment of a Multilingual, Embodied, Holographic Artificial Intelligence Concierge in Ambulatory Care: Early Implementation Lessons From the Artificial Intelligence Responsive Interactive Agent
abstract: Healthcare environments can be difficult to navigate, particularly for individuals with limited language proficiency, hearing impairment, low digital literacy, or unfamiliarity with the facility. Conversational artificial intelligence (AI) systems may support accessibility and navigation, although descriptions of real-world implementation in healthcare settings remain limited. As a descriptive, single-site quality-improvement pilot, this report characterizes the experience of implementing a conversational AI agent in the lobby of a large, outpatient, academic practice. The Artificial Intelligence Responsive Interactive Agent (ARIA) is a multilingual, three-dimensional, holographic conversational AI concierge developed to provide real-time assistance with navigation, digital onboarding, and information regarding amenities and services. ARIA leverages natural language processing and large language model technology to provide voice-enabled interactions in English, Spanish, Mandarin, and Arabic, with real-time closed captioning. The system can also generate quick response (QR) codes that push information directly to users' mobile devices. Piloted in a large ambulatory lobby from October 21, 2025, to February 2, 2026, ARIA recorded 1,429 device-activation sessions. Of these, 689 sessions (48%) contained analyzable user interaction data. Wayfinding and general information requests were the most common use cases. Deployment surfaced operational challenges, including audio capture, network reliability, interaction timing, workflow integration, QR transfer, and content governance. As the use of AI in clinical settings expands, there may be a role for an embodied agent serving as a digital concierge if these barriers can be addressed. Future evaluations should prospectively define implementation outcomes, use systematic utilization denominators, and assess user experience and operational impact with validated measures.

title: Diagnostic Accuracy of a Novel Chemiluminescent Immunoassay for Strongyloides stercoralis in a Non-Endemic Clinical Setting
abstract: Background/Objectives: Strongyloides stercoralis is a soil-transmitted helminth that can cause severe disease in immunocompromised individuals. In non-endemic clinical settings, recommended diagnostic strategies rely on serology alone or in combination with a sensitive fecal test, maximizing sensitivity to avoid missed infections. The S. stercoralis VirClia® IgG monotest (Vircell, Spain) is a novel automated chemiluminescent immunoassay (CLIA) that detects IgG antibodies against the recombinant NIE and SsIR antigens. This study evaluated its diagnostic accuracy (sensitivity and specificity) in a non-endemic clinical setting. Methods: In this monocentric retrospective study, 245 serum samples from the Tropica Biobank of a referral centre for parasitic diseases in Italy were analyzed. Samples originated from individuals from Africa (n = 85), America (n = 31), Asia (n = 53), and Europe (n = 76). Diagnostic accuracy was estimated using Bayesian latent class analysis based on a model including five routinely used diagnostic tests. Results: The S. stercoralis VirClia® IgG monotest showed a sensitivity of 95.0% (95% credible interval [CrI]: 90.1–98.2%) and a specificity of 90.8% (95% CrI: 85.1–96.0%) for the tested population. Conclusions: In immunocompetent individuals with a risk of previous exposure to S. stercoralis, the S. stercoralis VirClia® IgG monotest showed high diagnostic accuracy. Its high sensitivity supports current recommendations favouring highly sensitive serological assays for screening and diagnosis in non-endemic clinical settings.

title: Diagnostic Utility of Pentraxin-3 Compared With N-terminal-prohormone of B-Type Natriuretic Peptide (Nt-probnp) and Tumour Necrosis Factor-α (Tnf-α) in Dogs With Degenerative Mitral Valve Disease
abstract: Abstract Pentraxin-3 (PTX3) is a novel biomarker of interest in cardiovascular disease and injury. Despite this, there is limited literature on PTX3 as a veterinary biomarker. Another ubiquitous inflammatory marker, tumour necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), has been studied extensively in dogs with DMVD, with mixed findings. The N-terminal-prohormone of B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) is a routinely used biomarker of canine cardiac dysfunction. This study compared the diagnostic utility of PTX3 with TNF-α and NT-proBNP in dogs with DMVD. Serum NT-proBNP, PTX3, and TNF-α were measured in 50 client-owned dogs diagnosed and staged according to the ACVIM stages A-D. Echocardiographic variables, radiographic vertebral heart score (VHS) and vertebral left atrial size (VLAS), systolic blood pressure (SBP), and quality of life (QoL) scores were assessed. The Kruskal-Wallis test was used to compare PTX3, TNF-α, and NT-proBNP levels between different stages of DMVD, and the Jonckheere-Terpstra test assessed whether serum biomarker concentrations showed a significant ordered trend across progressively worsening DMVD across stages. Spearman’s correlation was used to assess the associations between biomarker levels, disease stage, QoL scores, SBP, radiographic, and echocardiographic parameters. Concentration of PTX3 and TNF-α did not differ significantly across DMVD stages, while only NT-proBNP showed significant variation between stages (p = 0.02). Jonckheere-Terpstra trend test revealed a significant ordered trend in serum NT-proBNP (p < 0.01), but not PTX3 and TNF-α across DMVD stages. NT-proBNP correlated significantly with DMVD stage, QoL score, VHS, VLAS, and echocardiographic variables including LVIDdn, LA:Ao (p < 0.01), and EF%, FS% (p = 0.02). NT-proBNP remains a reliable biomarker for diagnosis, disease monitoring, and prognosis assessment in canine DMVD. Future studies employing larger longitudinal cohorts will be essential to better elucidate the role of inflammatory markers in canine heart disease.
authors: Umaya Gunaratne; Kuan Hua Khor; Farina Mustaffa-Kamal; Mun Keong Kok; Norhidayah Noordin; Eddie Yian Ming Tan

title: Distribution and Seasonal Variation of Snail Vector of Medical and Veterinary Importance in Communities Around Challawa Dam, Karaye Local Government Area, Kano State
abstract: Snail are generally aquatic upon found in almost all fresh water bodies ranging from rivers, lakes, streams, irrigation channels, lakes, streams, Ponds and marshes attached to the water plants. The epidemiology of schistosomiasis involves a mollucs (snail) as an intermediate host, various species of fresh water snails are known to act as intermediate host of schistosomiasis. This study aims to determine the distribution and seasonal variation of snail vector species of medical and veterinary importance in communities around Challawa Dam, Karaye Local Government Area, Kano State. Three communities, Challawa, Kauyan Mata and Magasawa were selected based on their proximity to Dam and the Challawa River. Snails are collected on monthly basis for twelve consecutive months, using forceps technique. A total of six hundred and seventy-four (674) freshwater snails were collected from the three selected sampling sites, based on morphological appearance of the snail shells, three species were identified in all the sampling sites namely; Bulinus globosus 433 (64.24%), Bulinus forskalii 41 (6.08%) and Biomphalaria spp 200 (29.67%). All snail species were identify in all sampling site with Bulinus globosus the most abundant. Snails were more abundant during rainy season (Wet, n = 603. 89.47%, Dry, n = 71. 10.53%). In conclusion, Challawa Dam is a dwelling site for freshwater snails. Therefore, there is a great need for regular vector control such as use of molluscicides.
authors: Abdullahi Umar Bature; Abdulrahman Umar; Saminu Atiku Lawan; Kilawa Aishatu Sale

title: ExplaiNavility: Interpretable Vision-and-Language Navigation with Reasoning Supervision
abstract: Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) requires embodied agents to follow natural language instructions while grounding their decisions in complex visual environments. Despite recent progress, most VLN agents remain difficult to interpret, providing limited insight into why a navigation action is selected. In this work, we introduce ExplaiNavility, an interpretable VLN framework that augments navigation with explicit reasoning supervision. Our model combines a visual scene encoder with a multimodal LLM, using structured prompts to jointly condition on the instruction, the navigation history, and the candidate viewpoints available at each step. Beyond predicting the next navigable location, the model is trained to produce human-readable explanations of its decisions and descriptive low-level action labels, such as turning left, turning right, moving forward, or stopping. To supervise these outputs, we augment R2R trajectories with speaker-style action explanations generated from consecutive observations, together with action labels obtained from the simulator. By fine-tuning the embodied multimodal agent with these auxiliary reasoning objectives, ExplaiNavility encourages more transparent decision-making while preserving strong navigation ability. Experiments on the R2R benchmark show that our approach improves over prior explainable VLN methods on unseen environments, while producing interpretable rationales that make the agent's behavior easier to inspect. These results suggest that explicit reasoning supervision can benefit both navigation performance and interpretability in embodied instruction-following agents.
authors: William Raccagni; Niyati Rawal; Marcella Cornia; Lorenzo Baraldi; Rita Cucchiara

title: Federated privacy-preserving facial paralysis severity classification using hybrid deep learning and pufferfish optimization
abstract: Abstract Facial paralysis (FP) severity assessment requires accurate identification of subtle facial asymmetry while maintaining the confidentiality of sensitive patient information. Conventional centralized deep learning approaches require patient images to be transferred to a central repository, which can increase privacy risks and limit collaborative learning across healthcare institutions. To address these challenges, this study proposes a Federated Learning-based Secure and Privacy-Preserving Hybrid Deep Learning with Pufferfish Optimization (FLSDPP-HDLPO) framework for automated FP severity classification. The proposed framework first performs image preprocessing and augmentation to improve facial-image quality and class representation. A hybrid feature extraction strategy integrating Capsule Network (CapsNet), ResNet50, and LeViT is then employed to learn complementary spatial, hierarchical, and attention-based facial representations. The extracted features are classified using a CNN-BiGRU architecture, while the Pufferfish Optimization Algorithm (POA) is employed to optimize the relevant model parameters. To preserve data confidentiality during distributed learning, homomorphic encryption is incorporated into the federated learning process so that sensitive model information can be securely exchanged without exposing the original patient data. The framework is evaluated using combined MEEI and YFP facial paralysis datasets containing six severity classes. Experimental evaluation under different training and testing configurations demonstrates that the proposed FLSDPP-HDLPO framework achieves a maximum classification accuracy of 97.56%, with precision, sensitivity, specificity, and F1-score of 92.48%, 92.53%, 98.54%, and 92.50%, respectively. Repeated experiments further produced an accuracy of 97.56% ± 0.42%, demonstrating consistent performance. The proposed framework therefore provides an accurate and privacy-preserving approach for distributed FP severity assessment. Future work will focus on larger multi-center datasets, stronger robustness evaluation, computational optimization, and real-world clinical validation.
authors: S. Kiruthiga; C. Anbuananth; V. Dhilipkumar

title: From Biological Precursors to Artificial Cognition: Consciousness, Embodiment, and the MEM Architecture
abstract: This article asks under what conditions artificial intelligence could warrant a rational attribution of consciousness. Linguistic ability, multimodality, memory, planning, action control, and humanoid embodiment are not sufficient evidence of phenomenal experience. Biological precursors such as excitability, homeostasis, neural networks, and hierarchical representation instead identify functions whose counterparts may be engineered. The paper compares conventional LLMs, hybrid h-LLMs, vision-language-action systems, and embodied agents with the Motivated Emotional Mind (MEM) architecture. MEM adds receptor-grounded representations, regulatory self-monitoring and interoception, affect, semblion-based associative memory, and re-entry into lower sensory and interoceptive maps. A related formulation defines a phenomenal state as a dynamic, integrated state of the whole embodied system in which sensor-grounded modal content is recurrently stabilized and coupled to a suprathreshold interoceptive representation of the system's regulatory state. The mathematical model of MEM published on arXiv specifies implementable relations among these components and makes the proposal more precise and testable. Comparative and causal tests in humans, invertebrates, and artificial systems could strengthen or weaken the MEM capabilities. MEM is therefore presented as a falsifiable research program requiring empirical validation and ethical caution.
authors: Janusz A. Starzyk; Wiesław L. Galus

title: Frozen Models, Evolving Expertise: Model-Agnostic Learning from Deployment Experience for Multimodal Medical AI
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) are usually frozen after deployment, so they do not learn from the cases they solve. This is especially concerning in medicine, where new clinical evidence, updated guidelines, and new therapies can change established practice. Fine-tuning can update the model, but it requires access to model weights and additional training. Parameter-free methods avoid training, but they may overfit a fixed validation set, lack reliable domain knowledge, or lose visual details by saving experience only as text. To address these limitations, we present a model-agnostic framework that allows frozen LLMs and VLMs to learn from deployment experience through three forms of external expertise: a Skill that guides reasoning and tool use, a Knowledge Memory that stores reliable facts supported by earlier cases or trusted external evidence, and a Multimodal Knowledge Base that keeps visual examples and guides the model to relate each retrieved case to the current image. Instead of relying on a fixed validation set, a validation strategy keeps an update only if it helps on new cases without degrading performance on earlier ones. Across six benchmarks covering clinical diagnosis, clinical workflows, medical reasoning, and medical and non-medical visual reasoning, and with four open-weight and closed-source base models, our framework improves performance during online deployment by up to 34.2% over the base model on medical tasks, generalizes to unseen cases, transfers to other models without further optimization, and works in non-medical domains.
authors: Yexiao He; Yucheng Tang; Pengfei Guo; Yufan He; Andriy Myronenko; Can Zhao; Ang Li; Daguang Xu; Dong Yang

title: Generative AI as a process of socio-technical co-evolution: a structured review of the transition from content generation to operational intelligence
abstract: In the era of the digital economy, generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has become a transformative force, and its impact extends far beyond the scope of content creation. GenAI has rapidly evolved from generating text, images, and code to assuming operational roles across industries, science, healthcare, and governance. Tracing this evolution requires more than a catalog of technical milestones. A dedicated analytical framework is therefore needed. This study constructs a comprehensive analytical framework organized around three intertwined axes: technology generation, operational intelligence, and socio-technical co-evolution. The framework is applied comparatively across five domains: industry, healthcare, education, finance, and public governance. Three cross-cutting principles emerge from this cross-domain analysis. These are situation-sensitive anchoring, dynamic trust calibration, and responsibility-aware delegation. Risk tolerance, cultural background, and the depth of domain-specific knowledge are identified as key moderators that shape the transition from generative tools to operational intelligence. By synthesizing evidence across these dimensions, this review identifies future directions for research, design, and governance of GenAI systems.
authors: Haowei Zhang; Ruobing Wu; Wenjie Hou; Ping Lan; Senchang Hu

title: Geometric morphometric analysis of cardiac shape changes associated with myxomatous mitral valve disease in Cavalier King Charles Spaniels
authors: Caner Bakıcı; Murat Vurucu; İhsan Berat Kılıçlı; Ezgi Deniz Mavili; Barış Batur

title: Gym-Anything for Robotics: Scaling physical simulations with digital agents
abstract: Realistic, fast robotics simulations could enable large-scale training of embodied AI models that transfer to the real world. However, despite decades of progress, available simulations cover only a narrow range of real-world tasks and physical phenomena. The core bottleneck is that creating better simulations requires significant expert effort and therefore does not scale. To address this, we introduce Gym-Anything for Robotics, a framework in which coding agents create realistic robotics simulations. Our core insight is that simulation creation is a coding agent task, so improvements in coding agents translate directly into richer and more faithful simulations. We select simulations based on U.S. GDP data to cover economically valuable physical work, define what makes a good simulation and a good task, and develop an adversarial creation-audit loop that checks each simulation and task against these definitions. Using this pipeline, we build RoboWorld, a set of 25 simulations with 25 test and 175 training RL environments of varying difficulty. Even the best frontier models fail on every RoboWorld test task, achieving an average reward of only 0.06. Building on RoboWorld, we introduce several new ways for frontier models to improve, including in-context learning across repeated attempts, a privileged teacher that reads the simulator state and teaches a student in context, self-assisted learning from the model's own privileged experience, and code policies that generate demonstrations across varied scenes to train vision-language-action models (VLAs) such as $π_{0.5}$. Each of these substantially improves performance. We release our pipeline, RL environments, and benchmark to facilitate future research. Code and data are available at https://gym-anything.github.io/robotics
authors: Pranjal Aggarwal; Sean Welleck

title: HEIR: Learning Human-Entity Interactions with Functional Roles
abstract: Understanding human-entity interactions requires recovering each person-action event's participants, roles, and shared identities. This structure can support embodied agents by clarifying who acts on which entities and how, informing anticipation and coordination in shared environments. Standard HOI metrics score individual links, leaving complete event composition undermeasured. We introduce HEIR (Human-Entity Interactions with Functional Roles), an image benchmark for complete grounded participant-role sets across object, interpersonal, and self-directed interactions. It contains 18,730 images, six roles, 105 actions, and 437 nouns, with shared entities, role changes, and repeated fillers; 51.6% of images contain multiple actors and 62.1% contain multiple actions. HEIR pairs relation AP with complete-set AP and structural evaluation. We also introduce CoRISP (Compositional Role-aware Interaction Set Prediction), which uses shared entity identities to combine role-conditioned evidence and predict normalized participant-role sets. Cardinality and role-multiplicity potentials couple assignments through event size and role composition, with exact per-event normalization. Across 16 baselines, relation and complete-event rankings diverge even after aligning action weights. CoRISP leads the evaluated systems on repeated-role events and shared-participant images in HEIR by 2.87 and 3.82 Set mAP points, respectively. On V-COCO, CoRISP achieves 73.72/76.23 role AP and 61.06/68.59 complete-set AP on two-slot actions under Scenarios 1/2. These results show the value of learning and evaluating event composition alongside individual relations. The code and dataset are publicly available at https://github.com/Kratos-Wen/HEIR.
authors: Di Wen; Wenhao Guo; Yuedong Tan; Yun Huang; Minheng Wu; Zhihang Chen; Haiwen Sun; Fei Teng; Zhiyuan Gao; Yufeng Zhang; Yuanhao Luo; Jingqi Zhang; Yufan Chen; Junwei Zheng; Ruiping Liu; Jiale Wei; Kailun Yang; Kunyu Peng

title: Hospital Bed Utilization Patterns across Healthcare Sectors in Türkiye: A Sector-Level Analysis for 2020–2024
abstract: This study analyzes how hospital bed occupancy and related operational indicators changed across three healthcare sectors in Türkiye (public, university, and private hospitals) over the 2020–2024 period. The analysis is based on 15 aggregated sector-year observations, comprising three hospital sectors across five years. Average length of stay (ALOS), bed turnover rate (BTR), and bed turnover interval (BTI) were derived from raw sectoral data, with total hospital beds used as the consistent denominator for BTR and BTI. The data were examined using descriptive statistics, a descriptive sector-year trend analysis, and Pabon Lasso mapping of all 15 observations. In public hospitals, BOR and BTR increased over the period, while ALOS and BTI decreased. University hospitals showed the highest mean BOR and the longest mean ALOS, and their corrected BTI values were positive across all years. Private hospitals had the highest mean BTR and the lowest mean ALOS, although their BOR declined after 2022. The Pabon Lasso results describe the relative operational profiles of sector-year observations rather than the efficiency of individual hospitals. The study documents sector-specific bed utilization patterns relevant to sector-sensitive capacity planning.
authors: Öner Gümüş; Dilek Gümüş; Onur Celebi

title: How To Train Your World Model: Fine-tuning vs RAG for LM-based World Modeling
abstract: World models (WMs) simulate the transition dynamics of environments, enabling agents to plan over the consequences of their actions. In text-based environments, fine-tuning a Language Model (LM) to serve as a WM has emerged as a dominant paradigm. However, despite the widespread success of non-parametric approaches such as Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG), retrieval for LM-based world modelling remains underexplored. We conduct a systematic evaluation across five diverse environments spanning embodied, web navigation and social settings, comparing fine-tuning and RAG-based approaches for LM-based world modelling. Our study reveals that fine-tuning often outperforms RAG, with fine-tuned WMs enabling agents to obtain higher rewards on 15/20 settings. While both construction paradigms benefit from additional and more diverse exploration, RAG-based approaches prove more data-efficient, and fine-tuning approaches disproportionately benefit from scaling the amount of experience collected. With a focus on RAG-based WMs, we devise a procedure that uses counterfactual intervention to estimate the error rate of the retrieval stage, and show that retrievers consistently surface suboptimal transitions from the experience buffer. Hoping to address this failing, we study a variety of query reformulation strategies, demonstrating that a hierarchical approach outperforms the traditional retrieval pipeline. Finally, we compose our findings into a hybrid world modelling system that parametrically captures core environment dynamics, while learning to rely on retrieval from an actively maintained memory store. Our hybrid system consistently outperforms other methods across multiple environments and models, showcasing the robustness of the approach and the applicability of our findings.
authors: Dhananjay Ashok; Shantanu Agarwal; Vivek Datla; Jonathan May; Alfy Samuel

title: Identifying adverse event clusters and treatment effects in randomised trials using latent class analysis: an application in the COV-BOOST trial
abstract: Abstract Background Randomised Controlled Trials (RCTs) are essential for evaluating treatment efficacy and safety, particularly in vaccine trials, where adverse events are systematically collected and assessed. The high volume of reported adverse events often presents challenges in discerning meaningful associations between treatments and adverse events. Traditional analytical approaches rely on multiple pairwise treatment comparisons of individual adverse events, which can be difficult to interpret. This study explores the use of Latent Class Analysis (LCA) to identify adverse event profiles and estimates the Average Treatment Effects (ATE) for these in an RCT setting. Methods Data from the COV-BOOST trial (ISRCTN registration 73765130), which assessed the safety and efficacy of seven COVID-19 booster vaccines was used. This trial monitored a predefined set of 17 adverse events, graded by severity, over a seven-day period following immunisation. LCA was applied to classify participants into adverse event subgroups based on shared event profiles. After identifying these classes, the ATE was estimated for each identified adverse event profile to quantify the causal impact of different vaccine boosters. This was achieved by regressing treatment on the latent adverse event class membership outcome. Results Fatigue, pain, and headache were commonly reported adverse events across all vaccine arms. LCA identified three distinct adverse event profiles among participants: (class 1) Minimal AEs, (class 2) Mild AEs, and (class 3) Severe AEs reports. Four vaccines, ChAd after BNT/BNT primer, Ad26, CVn, and MOD after both primer vaccines, were associated with higher reactogenicity, with most recipients falling into classes 2 or 3. Conclusion This study demonstrates the utility of LCA in identifying adverse event profiles within an RCT and uniquely integrates the latent adverse event class membership of participants as an outcome for ATE estimation. By examining the varying effects of booster vaccines in the COV-BOOST trial, this method advances the understanding of these vaccines’ safety. The successful application of this innovative approach in this study could pave the way for its adoption by researchers in future clinical trials across various medical domains. More broadly, integrating LCA with ATE estimation provides a novel framework for enhancing vaccine pharmacovigilance and improving safety assessments for medical interventions.
authors: Lea Maria Khoueiry; Eleanor Van Vogt; Leila Janani; Victoria R.
