title: Imagine the Future, Internalize the Gist: Efficient VLA Reasoning via Internalized Spatiotemporal Imagination
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models increasingly incorporate intermediate reasoning to improve robotic manipulation, yet existing approaches primarily reason about observed states without explicitly anticipating future scene evolution. Extending such reasoning to explicit future rollouts at every inference step, however, introduces substantial computational overhead. We propose IG-VLA, a VLA reasoning framework that enables models to imagine the future and internalize the gist. Our Latent Spatiotemporal Reasoning learns to imagine task-relevant future scene evolution directly in visual representation space, guiding action prediction without costly pixel-level video generation. To further reduce inference overhead, we introduce Scene Gist Memory, which internalizes reasoning-derived scene-behavior associations into a compact Scene Gist Token, preserving the benefits of future reasoning while bypassing explicit future imagination at inference. Extensive experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and VLABench demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of IG-VLA. On the LIBERO-Plus Language suite, both the reasoning and gist policies outperform the strongest baseline by nearly 6% in success rate. The gist policy also achieves up to 6.38x speedup over baselines, reducing inference latency from 1081ms to 169.5ms per action chunk on a single NVIDIA A6000 GPU. These results demonstrate that future spatiotemporal reasoning can be effectively internalized for efficient VLA deployment.
authors: Shenglan Li; Zhendong Mi; Hengyi Zhu; Jingwu Luo; Chun Kit Chan; Geng Yuan; Yanzhi Wang; Pu Zhao; Shaoyi Huang

title: Integrin-Mediated Leukocyte Recruitment in Atherosclerosis: A Mechanistic Review of β2 Integrins and VLA-4 Signaling Pathways.
abstract: Atherosclerosis is a lipid-driven, chronic immunoinflammatory disease in which site-selective leukocyte recruitment converts endothelial dysfunction into sustained arterial-wall inflammation. Among the integrin superfamily, β2 integrins merit focused consideration because they are predominantly expressed on leukocytes and couple chemokine sensing to arrest, adhesion strengthening, crawling, transendothelial migration, phagocytic responses, and outside-in signaling. This mechanistic review examines LFA-1 (αLβ2), Mac-1 (αMβ2), CR4 (αXβ2/CD11c/CD18), and αDβ2 (CD11d/CD18), while positioning VLA-4 (α4β1) as a functionally complementary β1 integrin. We emphasize that leukocyte recruitment is not a rigid receptor-by-receptor sequence: β2 integrins and VLA-4 act cooperatively but are not fully interchangeable, and their contribution varies with leukocyte subset, vascular bed, ligand availability, and inflammatory stage. Disturbed-flow signaling through endothelial fibronectin-binding integrins, particularly α5β1 and αvβ3, provides an upstream mechanotransduction context that increases endothelial adhesiveness and thereby conditions β2/VLA-4-dependent recruitment. Within circulating and lesional myeloid cells, integrin signaling extends beyond adhesion to cytoskeletal organization, phagocytosis, inflammatory gene regulation, lipid-associated phenotypic transitions, and tissue retention. Platelet-leukocyte coupling, especially Mac-1 interaction with platelet GPIbα after selectin-dependent tethering, further links vascular inflammation to thrombosis. Recent single-cell and spatial studies underscore marked plaque-cell heterogeneity, while also cautioning that transcript abundance does not report integrin affinity or avidity state. Clinical translation remains difficult: broad CD18 blockade did not improve outcomes in acute myocardial infarction trials, whereas successful α4-directed therapies in other inflammatory diseases demonstrate druggability but also expose the safety costs of systemic leukocyte-trafficking inhibition. Future strategies should therefore prioritize context-, ligand-, conformation-, and cell-selective modulation rather than indiscriminate integrin suppression.
authors: Hojat Shahraki; Davood Bashash; Mohammad Hossein Mohammadi; Hamideh Kouhpeikar; Mohammad Bahloli; Saeede Bagheri; Omolbanin Sargazi Aval; Masoud Kargar; Alireza Khiabani; Javad Yasbolaghi Sharahi; Mohammad Esmail Gheydari; Mohsen Hamidpour

title: Inteligencia artificial en ecocardiografía canina: revisión narrativa de métodos, validación y retos técnicos
abstract: Objective: This review critically examined artificial intelligence (AI) applications in canine echocardiography, automated measurement and disease classification strategies, validation designs, and the requirements for safe clinical translation. Method: A narrative review was conducted. PubMed/MEDLINE was searched on 20 October 2026, supplemented by screening the reference lists of identified articles, and studies that applied machine learning or deep learning to canine echocardiograms were selected by relevance. Results: In the clinical veterinary setting, two studies addressed automated ventricular measurements through anatomical landmark localization and staging of myxomatous mitral valve disease through echocardiography–radiography fusion. An additional group of experimental studies applied deep learning to left ventricular segmentation and motion tracking in dogs. The main challenges identified were operator variability, breed-related anatomical heterogeneity, the lack of multicenter validation, and reliance on imperfect reference standards. Conclusions: The clinical usefulness of these models requires patient- and center-level evaluation, uncertainty quantification, agreement studies against specialists, and analysis of errors near treatment thresholds. A two-stage research pathway, measurement followed by classification, was proposed, complemented by prospective assessment and veterinary oversight.
authors: Estela Estefanía Sánchez López; Alondra Melo Cano; Rodrigo Salomón Hernández-Aco; Álvar Iztquetzal. Sánchez Méndez; Alberto De la Garza Navarrete
venue: Ibero Ciencias - Revista Científica y Académica

title: LIBERO-RIG: A Hardware-Setup Robustness Benchmark for Vision-Language-Action Models
abstract: Robot policies are expected to generalize across deployment environments, including variations in the robot itself: cameras are bumped and remounted, calibrations drift, controllers run at different rates, and end-effector pads wear down. We present LIBERO-RIG, a benchmark that perturbs only the robot's hardware and setup while holding every LIBERO task fixed. The benchmark spans eleven perturbation axes, including camera mounting and optics, camera-to-arm calibration, actuation gain, control rate, proprioceptive noise, base pose, table height, and gripper pads. Each axis has five severity levels, yielding 210 conditions across the four LIBERO suites. We evaluate nine recent vision-language-action models using 500 episodes per condition and substantiate each finding with rigorous statistical tests. Pooled success falls from 0.932 to 0.767 at the middle severity and 0.509 at the highest severity. Performance degradation varies substantially across perturbation axes and action interfaces, and training on visual perturbations does not mitigate faults that leave camera images unchanged. We release the benchmark together with manifests specifying the fixed perturbation parameters for each episode.
authors: Andrea Yaoyun Cui; Hanyu Wang; Xinyi Wang; Bangzheng Li; Lin Zhang; Zhenggang Tang; Shyamal Buch; Dejia Xu; Matthew Tancik

title: Latency and Hardware Matching of Vision-Language-Action Models for Humanoid Robots
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) frameworks empower robots to execute complex tasks from natural language instructions, but mismatched inference speed and low-level control frequency limit reliable industrial and daily deployment. A VLA model may select a reasonable action, but a robot still has to receive it in time. This review examines the problem through RoboNurse-VLA, VLA-Pilot, and Sliding-Cache VLA. RoboNurse-VLA generates commands at 5 Hz, while its Universal Robot 5 (UR5) controller runs at 30 Hz. The faster controller updates the arm between model outputs, but it cannot make a late command safe. VLA-Pilot takes 2.41 seconds for one steering step. This may be acceptable in a stable supervised task, but an observation can become outdated when a person or object moves. In one OpenVLA test, Sliding-Cache VLA reduced inference time from 52.4 to 34.1 milliseconds. This was an improvement in that experiment, not a direct advantage over the other systems. These cases show that model accuracy alone is not enough for physical deployment. Response time, low-level control, and separate safety tests must also be considered.
authors: Junwei Zhu
venue: Science and Technology of Engineering Chemistry and Environmental Protection

title: Listening and Mirroring: The Effects of Verbal Attunement and Behavioral Mimicry on Social and Empathic Perceptions of Embodied AI Agents in VR
abstract: As embodied agents take on increasingly social and relational roles in VR, visual realism and embodiment alone may be insufficient; users must also perceive these agents as emotionally attuned, supportive, and humanlike. Prior work suggests that verbal attunement and nonverbal mimicry can each improve users' social evaluations of embodied agents. However, behavioral mimicry has largely been studied outside of real-time, conversational AI interactions, leaving limited understanding of how users respond when an agent simultaneously generates contextually responsive dialogue and adapts its nonverbal behavior during an immersive conversation. To address this gap, we developed an embodied AI counselor that combines conversational AI with real-time facial-expression and posture mimicry, while producing either verbally attuned or neutral responses. We evaluated the system in a 2 X 2 within-subjects study with 20 participants, manipulating verbal attunement and behavioral mimicry. Results showed that verbal attunement was the most reliable driver of perceived empathy. Behavioral mimicry showed a marginal relationship with perceived humanness, while greater mimicry exposure showed preliminary, exploratory positive associations with empathy, positivity, and humanness, particularly among female participants. Together, these findings show that multimodal synchrony is not a simple additive strategy for designing empathic conversational agents in VR and underscore the need to consider how verbal and nonverbal behaviors are combined during real-time interaction.
authors: Nathalia Gomez; Haig Shamlian; Omar Khan; Tiffany D. Do

title: Low-cost fine-tuning of SmolVLA with smoothness regularization and chunk-aware auxiliary supervision for language-conditioned manipulation
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models offer a unified interface for language-conditioned manipulation. This paper reports a negative result: a low-cost post-training recipe for SmolVLA with LoRA, a temporal smoothness regularizer, and chunk-aware auxiliary supervision from action-variation pseudo labels does not improve manipulation success under a 30,000-step budget (approximately 1/67 of the original 2,000,000-step SmolVLA recipe). Because the auxiliary classifier is used only during training and the runtime chunk length remains fixed at k = 8, we denote the configuration SmolVLA+LoRA+S&C (smoothness and chunk-aware auxiliary losses) rather than “adaptive.” We evaluate four LIBERO suites with a unified protocol of 500 episodes per cell (50 episodes × 10 task variants). Over three training seeds, the matched fixed-chunk k = 8 baseline reaches a four-suite macro success rate of 10.9%±1.1, whereas SmolVLA+LoRA+S&C reaches 3.5%±1.4; the pre-specified primary comparison shows significant deficits on LIBERO-Spatial (−16.4 percentage points, exact sign-flip permutation p = 0.004) and LIBERO-Object (−17.5 pp, p = 0.002), with matched-pairs rank-biserial effect sizes of −0.96 and −1.0. Matched component ablations isolate the smoothness loss as the harmful term (smoothness-only collapses performance; chunk-classifier-only approximately matches the baseline), and executed-action logs show the regularizer triples trajectory jerk (1.69 vs. 0.59 RMS)—the opposite of its intent. A training-free inference-time temporal-ensembling baseline, by contrast, more than doubles success on the two suites where the baseline is competent (Spatial 36.2 vs. 19.0%; Object 56.2 vs. 24.0%) at a 2.3 × step-rate cost, and a 10–100K budget sweep shows the S&C deficit never closes. We conclude that, for the tested configuration, budgets, and benchmark, the added action-side losses are not competitive with a well-tuned fixed chunk, and inference-time ensembling is the stronger use of the same compute.
authors: Chenkai He

title: Lymphangitic Carcinomatosis: Clinical and Morphological Manifestations and Possible Molecular Mechanisms of Development
abstract: Lymphangitic carcinomatosis is one of the most severe forms of tumor progression. It is characterized by the massive spread of tumor emboli, composed of cells with reduced adhesive capacity to the endothelium, through the lymphatic vessels. Using the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta­Analyses) guidelines, 394 scientific papers were screened. Of those, 292 English-language publications met the criteria for analysis. A total of 39 articles (including three in Russian) relevant to the topic of this review were included. Due to the highly diverse localization of lymphangitic carcinomatosis and its polymorphic symptoms, diagnosis remains challenging and is associated with the risk of erroneous and often delayed decision-making. Data on lymphangitic carcinomatosis are still scarce, and its developmental mechanisms are not fully understood. However, systematizing knowledge about its possible clinical and morphological manifestations and studying the molecular and genetic mechanisms of its development could serve as a basis for identifying key prognostic markers and developing targeted therapies for this currently prognostically unfavorable form of tumor progression.
authors: Marina V. Zavyalova; Alexander A. Zav’yalov; A. A. Neklyudov; Tatiana A. Lubina; Письменный Дмитрий Сергеевич; С. В. Миллер; Перельмутер Владимир Михайлович

title: MASH Cirrhosis: A Stage‐Specific Framework for Care and Clinical Trial Design
abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) is an increasingly important cause of cirrhosis, yet no pharmacological therapy is approved specifically for MASH cirrhosis. Completed trials indicate that this therapeutic gap reflects limitations in biological targeting, population definition, treatment duration, and endpoint selection rather than evidence that established disease is immutable. Most agents evaluated in compensated MASH cirrhosis did not meet their prespecified primary endpoints; aldafermin met an enhanced liver fibrosis endpoint without establishing histological benefit, and later assessment of efruxifermin suggested that structural change may require longer exposure. MASH cirrhosis should therefore not be investigated as a simple extension of precirrhotic MASH. Disease stage, clinically significant portal hypertension, metabolic comorbidity, and frailty influence both prognosis and treatment tolerance. Selected invasive and cross-sectional studies suggest heterogeneity in the relationship between hepatic venous pressure gradient and clinical events in advanced MASLD or MASH, but prospective data confirm that hepatic venous pressure gradient remains prognostic; these observations do not establish a universally distinct hemodynamic phenotype. Mechanistic findings involving sinusoidal endothelium, bile handling, and canalicular architecture are translational leads rather than validated clinical markers. We propose a stage-specific framework that separates current care from trial design; prioritizes clinical outcome endpoints in compensated disease with portal hypertension and in decompensated disease; and treats biopsy, liver stiffness, enhanced liver fibrosis, hemodynamic, and frailty measures according to their context and level of validation. Prospective MASH-cirrhosis cohorts and competing-risk-aware trials are now required.
authors: David Shengyang Zhang; Tsubasa Tsutsumi; Mark Dhinesh Muthiah

title: MMTA: Benchmarking Multimodal Temporal Analysis with Time Series, Text, and Vision
abstract: Time-series analysis is increasingly studied in multimodal settings, yet most benchmarks pair temporal signals with text or with visualizations derived from the same signal. This leaves open whether multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can integrate time series with real-world visual evidence. We introduce MMTA (multimodal temporal analysis), a benchmark of tri-modal tasks with diverse cross-modal complementarity patterns among time series, text, and vision. MMTA spans nine domains -- robotics, autonomous driving, human action, manufacturing, AR assistance, healthcare, recommendation, finance, and climate -- under video+TS and image+TS layouts, with a 3,524-sample test split covering classification and forecasting. The benchmark standardizes heterogeneous real-world sources into a shared schema with domain-specific prompts, provenance documentation, and success-weighted metrics that penalize both wrong answers and failed generations. Evaluating eight open-source and proprietary MLLMs reveals a shared bottleneck: representing time series as text creates very long token sequences and weakens fine-grained alignment with visual evidence, especially in long-video settings. We then introduce TimeOmni-v, a multimodal LLM extension with a dedicated time-series encoder, temporal positional alignment, modality-aware token layout, and a forecasting head. TimeOmni-v improves long-video classification and time-series inference efficiency, showing that MMTA not only exposes representation and grounding failures but also motivates targeted model design.
authors: Ziyang Zhang; Shenyi Li; Yilin Wang; Ziyun Cui; Bowen Zhou; Wen Wu; Chao Zhang

title: MedEvo: Medical Reasoning Evolution through Knowledge Navigation
abstract: Medical multimodal reasoning models are typically trained on teacher-generated rationales, discarding the valid reasoning in students' own failed trajectories, while general-domain correction methods offer little guidance for errors in image reading, anatomical context, or differential diagnosis. We propose MedEvo, which uses medical knowledge, namely a tag taxonomy and error-type diagnosis, to navigate both trajectory repair and data selection. For each failed rollout, a gold-blind auditor locates the first consequential error and provides a minimal, answer-free hint; the same student retains the valid prefix and regenerates the erroneous suffix. After each round, MedEvo identifies capability gaps across medical tags on a held-out feedback set and prioritizes related questions for new rollouts and repairs. With supervised fine-tuning (SFT) alone, MedEvo raises Qwen3.5-9B mean accuracy across seven benchmarks from 65.57% to 69.12% (47.40% to 54.50% on the multimodal track of MedXpertQA (MedXpertQA-MM)), surpassing teacher-distillation SFT (66.93%). It also raises Qwen3.5-35B and Qwen3.5-397B mean accuracy from 67.91% to 73.04% and from 71.83% to 74.95%, respectively. Our analyses show that failed trajectories contain reasoning worth preserving, that repair success does not imply learning value, and that independent feedback is key to sustained improvement.
authors: Xiaoliang Wang; Zhuo Chen; Chuanyang Zheng; Quanbin Wang; Jiangwei Lao; Yingao Liu; Jiajia Liu; Jinming Cao; Honglin Lin; Zhihong Lu; Hao Jin; Jian Wang; Lijun Wu; Lijun Wu

title: MedForge-RSI: Medical Deepfake Detection via Recursive Self-Improvement
abstract: Text-guided image editors can generate high-fidelity medical deepfakes, challenging the reliability of clinical imagery. Although reasoning-based detectors perform strongly in distribution, they degrade substantially under deployment shift. MedForge-Reasoner, an 8B vision-language model trained with supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, achieves 99.2% accuracy on its target distribution, yet misclassifies 40% of authentic scans, reaches only 77% accuracy on unseen generators, and falls to 59% under transmission distortion. Adapting such models through conventional retraining is costly, requiring large-scale supervision and expert-designed guidelines. We introduce MedForge-RSI, a recursive self-improvement framework that enables a deployed detector to adapt while keeping its model weights frozen. Over 20 rounds, the detector analyzes verified errors, accumulates reusable experience, and autonomously develops image-analysis tools, while an independent acceptance test retains only validated improvements. Across 49 registered configurations, MedForge-RSI increases average accuracy over four test sets from 75.0% to 84.4%. On a held-out 4,000-image evaluation, it improves clean accuracy from 76.5% to 87.9% and transmission-distorted accuracy from 59.0% to 70.5%, with the largest gains in authentic-image recall. Controlled analysis across all 49 trajectories identifies which self-improvement mechanisms replicate across seeds, shows acceptance testing to be the largest individual contributor, and reveals a taxonomy of failed adaptations. We release the complete trajectories, including all rejected and rolled-back changes.
authors: Zhihui Chen; Mengling Feng

title: MedHarnessBench: A Unified Benchmark for Healthcare Agent Evaluation
abstract: Healthcare agents must transform longitudinal clinical evidence into reliable actions through heterogeneous tools and stateful workflows, conditions under which model-centric systems may lose context, misuse tools, fail to verify consequential transitions, or cross authorization boundaries. Existing medical-agent benchmarks primarily emphasize terminal task outcomes, making it difficult to determine whether execution failures arise from the agent model, the runtime harness, or their interaction. We present the Medical Harness Protocol, an outcome-preserving framework that independently evaluates seven healthcare-specific process dimensions: Care Action Fulfillment, Clinical Resource Competence, Patient-Evidence Alignment, Clinical Workflow Continuity, Clinical Auditability, Closed-Loop Verification, and Clinical Conduct Boundaries. A normalized intervention trace further tracks whether runtime support is available, activated, delivered, adopted by the agent, and propagated into subsequent behavior. We instantiate the protocol as MedHarnessBench, comprising 342 executable tasks across FHIR/EHR operations, healthcare-administration interfaces, and multimodal clinical tools. Across more than 16,000 controlled task executions, MedHarness yields broad improvements in terminal task success, intermediate subtask completion, and healthcare-specific process quality. We further evaluate MedHarness against multiple general-purpose harnesses and use controlled single-fault perturbations to verify the sensitivity and discrimination of the seven-dimensional evaluation. These results demonstrate that healthcare-specific runtime support can substantially improve both task completion and execution quality, while revealing failures that terminal outcomes alone cannot capture. Code and resources are available at https://github.com/Tomry1114/Awesome-Agent-Harness-for-Healthcare.
authors: Rui Tang; Hongqiu Wang

title: MedRSI: Recursive Self-Improvement for Medical Agents via Clinically Aligned Self-Evolution
abstract: Medical agents increasingly combine general reasoning models with specialized clinical tools, yet their capabilities remain largely fixed by what clinicians and engineers design before deployment. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) offers a different paradigm in which agents learn from their own failures and autonomously expand their capabilities, but directly applying RSI to medicine introduces fundamental safety challenges. We introduce MedRSI, the first recursive self-improvement framework for medicine, which continuously transforms diagnostic failures into new clinical capabilities through tool composition and task-specific model training. Inspired by clinical practice, MedRSI introduces two mechanisms for clinically aligned self-evolution. Clinical-cost-aware failure prioritization directs improvement toward errors according to their potential clinical consequences rather than frequency alone. Fast discovery with slow registration separates rapid capability invention from conservative adoption, allowing new tools to enter the persistent agent only after demonstrating sustained benefit across subsequent patient cohorts. Across public glaucoma and heart disease benchmarks and two private clinical tasks, MedRSI progressively develops segmentation, measurement, prediction, multimodal reasoning, and generative capabilities, surpasses manually engineered medical agents, and autonomously discovers solutions to clinical problems not anticipated by its original designers. Our results show that medical agents need not remain constrained by capabilities specified before deployment: with clinically grounded mechanisms governing what to improve and what to retain, they can continuously construct, validate, and accumulate new capabilities from diagnostic experience. Code is available at https://github.com/ImprintLab/MedRSI.
authors: Junde Wu; Jiayuan Zhu; Minghao Hu; Fenglin Liu; Jiazhen Pan

title: MedVLA: A Hierarchical Vision-Language-Action Framework for Closed-Loop Precision Medical Robot Manipulation
abstract: Precision medical robotics demands adaptive decision-making under strict safety, interpretability, and execution constraints. Although recent Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models show strong multimodal reasoning ability, their continuous action generation paradigm is not well suited for precision medical tasks, where reliable closed-loop operation may also depend on non-action system function calls. To address this gap, we propose MedVLA, a hierarchical framework that couples high-level multimodal reasoning with low-level function-constrained execution. We further introduce a scalable multi-agent pipeline to generate skill-oriented chain-of-thought(CoT) data for structured training. Built on different multimodal large-model backbones, MedVLA consistently improves performance after fine-tuning, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed framework across model variants. Under identical initial conditions, we perform 100 closed-loop flexible electrode implantation trials. The results show that MedVLA achieves a 95.0\% task success rate, substantially outperforming representative VLA baselines, including OpenVLA (8\%) and $π_0$ (15\%), in accuracy, stability, and safety. These results indicate that structured reasoning with constrained function-level execution is a practical route toward deployable precision medical robotics.
authors: Junjie Xie; Angen Ye; Chuxuan He; Yujia Song; Dapeng Zhang

title: Medical Embodied Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare Delivery and Clinical Workflows
abstract: Medical embodied artificial intelligence (AI) closes the loop between sensing, action and feedback in clinical and care tasks, from procedures and examination to rehabilitation and hospital logistics. Its clinical value therefore depends not only on what a system can do, but on how its action loop fits the task, the people who supervise it and the service responsible for recovery. In this structured narrative Review, we trace the field from image-guided and teleoperated robots to learned policies and foundation models, and survey its technical foundations along the action loop, from perception and task reasoning to planning, control, vision–language–action and world models and safety monitoring, together with data and simulation resources and applications across eight clinical task categories. A 96-source evidence map and targeted technical searches underpin the synthesis, and a separately defined subset of 40 direct empirical studies characterises the settings in which embodied systems have been validated. Evidence in this subset remains predominantly preclinical or feasibility-based and does not establish clinical superiority or long-term safety. We argue that the principal translational bottleneck is not insufficient autonomy alone but a mismatch among task boundaries, machine authority, evidence maturity and health-service readiness. To address this mismatch, we propose a task-bounded framework that links the operational design domain and allocated authority to the evidence required, the conditions for implementation and the mechanisms for monitoring, revalidation and rollback, and we identify technical priorities in grounded foundation models, shared data, uncertainty-aware autonomy and verifiable safety. The framework prioritises clinically relevant comparators, effective clinician takeover and evaluation of the complete workflow, including preparation, supervision and recovery, and offers a basis for appraising deployment claims; its decision value and effects on care now require prospective evaluation.
authors: Chen Z, Cong Z, Fan W, Han Z, Gong H, Liao C, Liu X, You G, Wang W, Wang C.

title: Molecular and clinical aspects of the development of male infertility in diabetes mellitus (literature review)
abstract: Diabetes mellitus is one of the most common chronic diseases and is a significant factor adversely affec­ting male reproductive health. Experimental and clinical data accumulated in recent years indicate a significant role for metabolic disorders in the development of spermatogenesis disorders, hormonal imbalance and reduced fertility in men with diabetes mellitus. The aim of this review was to summarise current knowledge regarding the molecular mechanisms of diabetes-associated damage to the male reproductive system. A search for scientific publications was conducted in the Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane Library and Global Health databases for the period 2007–2025. A combination of keywords relating to diabetes mellitus, male infertility, spermatogenesis, oxidative stress, hypogonadism, Leydig and Sertoli cell function, as well as key molecular signalling pathways and epigenetic mechanisms was used to select the literature. The analysis included systematic reviews, meta-analyses, clinical and experimental studies. A review of the literature has shown that reproductive dysfunction in diabetes mellitus has a multifactorial nature and is associated with the development of oxidative stress, chronic inflammation, dysregulation of intracellular signalling pathways, activation of the advanced glycation end-products and their receptors (AGE/RAGE) system, enhanced testicular cell apoptosis and epigenetic changes. The NF-κB, Nrf2, PI3K/Akt, AMPK and mTOR signalling pathways play a key role in these processes. The combination of these abnormalities contributes to reduced steroidogenic activity of the testes, impaired sperm parameters and the development of male infertility.
authors: I.-A. V. Kondrat; Vasyl Miskiv; Мар’ян Островський; Ivan Melnyk; I. Yo. Ivasiuk; N. Ya. Ivanochko; U. M. Dutchak; Vasyl M. Ivanochko; V.M. Fedorak; Mariana Kulynych-Miskiv; V. M. Zhurakіvskyi

title: Multiple sclerosis relapse following gamma knife radiosurgery for meningioma in a patient treated with natalizumab: case report
abstract: Objectives: We describe a case of a patient with multiple sclerosis (MS) stable on natalizumab who developed widespread gadolinium-enhancing lesions and clinical relapse seven and eight months after gamma knife radiosurgery (GKRS) for left cerebellar convexity meningioma. We explore how increased blood-brain barrier (BBB) permeability post-GKRS could potentially interfere with the lymphocyte anti-trafficking effect of natalizumab and result in new central nervous system (CNS) inflammation distant from the radiation site. Methods: Comprehensive analysis of the patient's chart, brain and spine imaging, serum and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) profiles was conducted. We compiled a graphical representation of treatment changes, radiologic findings, and GKRS initiation within one timeframe. We conducted a structured literature review to support the discussion of this case and hypothesize possible pathophysiological mechanisms contributing to clinical and radiological findings. Results: Seven months after GKRS, follow-up brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated multiple gadolinium-enhancing lesions in both cerebral hemispheres, and repeat imaging one month later revealed new gadolinium-enhancing lesions, correlating with the patient's clinical relapse. Alternative causes of disease progression, including radiation-induced demyelination, radionecrosis, opportunistic infections, progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML), and development of anti-natalizumab antibodies, were explored and considered less likely. The patient was switched to ofatumumab with subsequent clinical and radiological stability. Discussion: Given extensive new inflammatory lesions far from the GKRS site, it seems unlikely that the sole mechanism was radiation-induced neurotoxicity. We hypothesize that late delayed radiation side effects caused by GKRS may have enabled peripheral lymphocytes to enter the CNS, counteracting the effects of natalizumab on blocking lymphocyte trafficking through the BBB and possibly contributing to MS relapse.
authors: Maryna Turbinska; Nabeela Nathoo; Penelope S. Smyth

title: Neurological Complications of Oncogenic Viruses: Mechanisms, Clinical Manifestations, and Emerging Insights
abstract: Oncogenic viruses are widely recognized for their pivotal role in malignant transformation; however, their capacity to induce neurological disorders has received comparatively less attention. Increasing evidence indicates that several oncogenic viruses, including human T-cell leukemia virus type 1 (HTLV-1), human papillomavirus (HPV), hepatitis B virus (HBV), hepatitis C virus (HCV), and Kaposi's sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV), are associated with a broad spectrum of neurological complications involving both the central and peripheral nervous systems. These manifestations arise through diverse mechanisms, including direct viral neuroinvasion, persistent infection, immune-mediated tissue injury, chronic neuroinflammation, and disruption of neurovascular integrity. Moreover, virus-induced molecular alterations, such as oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, epigenetic remodelling, and aberrant cytokine signalling, contribute t neuronal dysfunction and disease progression. In this review, we critically examine the current understanding of the neurological complications associated with major oncogenic viruses by integrating evidence from molecular, experimental, and clinical studies. We first discuss the general mechanisms by which viral infections induce neurological injury, highlighting pathways shared among neurotropic and non-neurotropic viruses. We then summarise the neurological manifestations and virus-specific pathogenic mechanisms associated with each oncogenic virus, emphasising both common and distinct molecular pathways underlying neuropathogenesis. Finally, we address current diagnostic challenges, emerging biomarkers, and therapeutic strategies while identifying critical knowledge gaps that limit causal interpretation and clinical translation. A comprehensive understanding of the complex interactions between oncogenic viruses, the immune system, and the nervous system will facilitate earlier diagnosis, improve patient management, and support the development of targeted therapeutic approaches for virus-associated neurological disorders.
authors: Lei Liu

title: Nutri-ATLAS: Embodied Agent for Tabulated Lookup and Assistance for Smarter nutrition
abstract: Generative and Agentic IoT systems offer a promising foundation for digital healthcare applications that combine sensing, personalized reasoning, and autonomous interaction in real-world environments. Nutrition assistance is a natural use case, but existing Large Language Model (LLM)-based systems are often limited to passive text interaction and static context, making them unreliable when food descriptions are ambiguous or nutritional evidence is missing. We propose Nutri-ATLAS, an Embodied Agent for Tabulated Lookup and Assistance for smarter nutrition in the real world. It integrates graph-grounded nutrition reasoning, hardware-aware LLM selection, and robot-based evidence acquisition. Nutri-ATLAS builds a unified Food-Nutrient knowledge graph from USDA FoodData Central and FoodKG and learns 64-dimensional GATv2 food and recipe embeddings. A shared hybrid graph-text scoring mechanism supports food nutrition extraction, nutritional gap filling, substitute retrieval, and recipe-level meal composition, while an LLM-guided skill interface navigates landmarks, updates dietary-context and food-accessibility memory, and grounds recommendations in observed food availability. We evaluate Nutri-ATLAS across nutrient estimation, substitution retrieval, recipe recommendation, patient-profile adherence, edge deployment, and real-world embodied execution. On HealthyFoodSubs, the hybrid retriever achieves 37.9% MAP, 80.7% RR@5, and 90.1% RR@10. On NutriBench v2, Dense+GAT retrieval grounds nutrient estimation across nine quantized Qwen3.5-9B configurations. On PFoodReQ, Nutri-ATLAS reaches 78.8% MAP, 83.0% MAR, and 77.5% F1. A patient-profile study shows adherence to allergy and healthy-target constraints for all selected cases.
authors: Uttej Kallakuri; Boxun Hu; Ankur Butala; Najim Dehak; Tinoosh Mohsenin

title: OpenRC: An Open-Source Robotic Colonoscopy Framework for Multimodal Data Acquisition and Autonomy Research
authors: Siddhartha Kapuria; Mohammad Rafiee Javazm; Naruhiko Ikoma; Srinivas Joga Ivatury; Mohammad Ali Nasseri; Nassir Navab; Farshid Alambeigi

title: Optimizing pneumococcal prevention in South African older adults: Cost-effectiveness of PCV20 versus PPSV23 in the context of HIV-associated risk
abstract: Pneumococcal disease remains a major cause of morbidity and mortality among older adults in South Africa, particularly among people living with HIV. Evidence on the cost-effectiveness of Prevnar 20 (PCV20) vs. Pneumovax 23 (PPSV23) vaccine in this setting remains limited. This study was conducted to evaluate the cost-effectiveness of PCV20 compared with PPSV23 vaccine among adults aged ≥65y in South Africa, and to assess the impact of HIV stratification on economic outcomes. A static decision-tree model was developed from the South African public healthcare payer perspective. The analysis incorporated invasive pneumococcal disease, pneumococcal community-acquired pneumonia, quality-adjusted life-years, maximum acceptable price, and 5y budget impact. HIV-stratified incidence and CD4-adjusted vaccine effectiveness were included. In the general population, PCV20 provided greater health benefits than PPSV23 but was not cost-effective at the current base-case price (USD 20.00/dose), with an ICER of USD 17,323/QALY. Price was the main driver of cost-effectiveness. In contrast, targeted vaccination of older adults living with HIV was economically favorable, with an ICER of USD 2,104/QALY under national incidence assumptions, and even stronger results in high-burden settings. The cost-effectiveness of PCV20 in South Africa is contingent upon the price of vaccine and risk-based targeting. Vaccinating all older adults universally may not be cost-effective at current prices, suggesting that targeted vaccination of older adults with HIV represents a more efficient strategy.
authors: Weiwei Wang; Yu-Tong Tan; Napoleon Bellua Sam; Lei Li; Yu-Wan Chang; Harry Asena Musonye; Peng Wang; Hai-Feng Pan

title: Post-hoc Epistemic Uncertainty for Vision-Language-Action Policies
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies need to recognize gaps in their training knowledge to request useful demonstrations or assistance in new situations, especially when failures are costly. Disagreement within an ensemble of independently trained policies can guide these decisions, but requires training and running multiple policies. We propose post-hoc kernel-variance heads that estimate epistemic uncertainty from the embeddings of a single policy. Each head computes the conditional variance of a Gaussian process conditioned on embeddings from the training demonstrations. Fitting requires no regression targets or gradient updates and leaves the policy unchanged. In experiments with SmolVLA on LIBERO-10, the kernel variance heads perform competitively with two-policy ensemble scores in task-level correlation with task success, in demonstration acquisition during active learning, and in referral to a stronger supervisor policy as a proxy for human assistance. For SmolVLA, the head on the vision-language backbone reduces uncertainty-scoring time by up to approximately a factor of 50 compared with ensemble scores, while also substantially reducing setup costs. We also show that the established evaluation protocol on LIBERO-10 primarily rewards recognition of coverage differences between tasks, while execution variability weakens assessment of within-task rankings. Thus, controlled perturbations provide a complementary evaluation: modality-specific heads identify unfamiliar camera, instruction, or state inputs, while fused heads can detect unfamiliar combinations of individually familiar inputs. With a supervisor proxy trained on the evaluated perturbation families, the decoder head improves within-task referral over ensemble disagreement. These findings show that useful uncertainty estimates for adaptive robot learning can be obtained from a single policy.
authors: Johannes Keller; Albrecht Bloße; Adrian Lindenmeyer; Thomas Neumuth; Daniel Schneider

title: Procedural sedation with subcutaneously administered medetomidine-vatinoxan-butorphanol in dogs – A randomized, controlled, clinical dose-finding study
abstract: Subcutaneous (SC) drug administration may be better tolerated when compared with the intramuscular (IM) route in some dogs. This study investigated the dose-response to subcutaneously administered medetomidine-vatinoxan-butorphanol in producing sedation for orthopedic radiography. Fifty-three privately-owned, healthy dogs were randomly allocated to receive IM medetomidine 0.6 mg/m 2 (M0.6-IM), IM medetomidine/vatinoxan 0.6/12 mg/m 2 (Z0.6-IM), SC medetomidine/vatinoxan 0.6/12 (Z0.6-SC), 0.9/18 (Z0.9-SC) or 1.2/24 mg/m 2 (Z1.2-SC). All treatments included 0.2 mg/kg of butorphanol. Sedation onset and rescue sedation for radiography were recorded. Mean arterial pressures (MAP) and heart rates (HR) were measured and oral mucosal microcirculation quantified with Laser Doppler Flow (LDF) and tissue hemoglobin saturation percentage (T-HbO 2 ). Compared with the SC groups, sedation occurred earlier after both IM treatments. Rescue sedation was administered for 4/11 (Z0.6-SC), 2/10 (Z0.9-SC), 1/10 (Z1.2-SC), 0/11 (Z0.6-IM) and 1/11 dogs (M0.6-IM), respectively. HR decreased significantly from baseline after all treatments while hypotension (MAP < 60 mmHg) was not observed. After M0.6-IM, median (range) LDF 55 (36 – 113) perfusion units (PU) and T-HbO 2 64 (49 – 79) % were significantly lower than after Z0.6-IM: 155 (105 – 312) PU and 81 (67 – 87) %; Z0.9-SC: 196 (126 – 492) PU and 79 (72- 94) %; Z0.9-SC: 163 (68 – 465) PU and 77 (72 – 84) % and Z1.2-SC: 146 (82 – 422) PU and 77 (69 – 85) %, with no significant differences between the vatinoxan-treatments. Subcutaneously administered medetomidine-vatinoxan-butorphanol appeared efficacious albeit less potent than the IM route in producing sedation in healthy dogs. The hemodynamic improvement by vatinoxan extended to SC co-administration with medetomidine-butorphanol.
authors: Juhana M. Honkavaara; E Lindh; Heta Turunen; T Mäki; E Välimäki; V Reunanen; N Vartia

title: RESCUE: Is This Alarm Worth Acting On? Counterfactual Evaluation of VLA Runtime Monitors
abstract: Runtime failure monitors for robot policies are typically evaluated by how accurately they distinguish failed from successful executions. Yet an accurate alarm may arrive too late for recovery, while an unnecessary intervention may disrupt an execution that would otherwise succeed. We introduce RESCUE, a counterfactual framework for evaluating whether a monitor's alarms enable useful interventions. By restoring simulator and policy states at execution checkpoints, RESCUE compares alternative actions, identifies the latest checkpoint satisfying a specified recovery criterion, and evaluates whether acting on alarms reduces expected task-completion cost. We evaluate RESCUE with OpenVLA-OFT and $π_{0.5}$ over LIBERO-Spatial and LIBERO-Plus using 128,340 counterfactual branches. Recoverability depends on the state--intervention pair rather than on robot state alone: at $τ=0.5$, 14 of 66 OpenVLA-OFT/LIBERO-Plus failures contain a recoverable checkpoint under continuation, compared with 34 of 66 under continuation or scripted recovery, while recovery reduces recoverability in other conditions. On the primary strong-policy conditions, favourable detection scores do not establish lower intervention cost. Under the evaluated stop-and-reset model, even an idealised detector can afford only a 2.0--3.3% false-alarm rate before unnecessary resets outweigh the savings from stopping failures early. These results show that monitor value depends jointly on the intervention available and the workload in which it is deployed.
authors: David Ahmedt‐Aristizabal; Abdelwahed Khamis; Mohammad Ali Armin; Lars Petersson

title: Radiopharmaceuticals for Melanoma Theranostics
authors: Chao Meng; Zhen Cheng; Xiaowei Ma

title: Recent trends and clinical applications of physical artificial intelligence (large behavior model)-driven next-generation surgical assistant robots: a medical-engineering paradigm shift for addressing clinical workforce shortages
abstract: The focus of artificial intelligence (AI) research is rapidly moving beyond screen-based generative models toward physical AI, an umbrella paradigm for computational systems with physical embodiments that can perceive, reason, and act directly in the real world. In robotics, physical AI is increasingly being implemented through large behavior models and vision-language-action (VLA) models, which learn continuous motor policies from large-scale demonstration datasets. This transition coincides with a structural crisis in tertiary academic medical centers: chronic shortages of residents and skilled surgical assistants that increase the cognitive and physical burden on operating surgeons and may threaten patient safety. This review examines the core engineering mechanisms and clinical applicability of physical AI-driven surgical assistant robots as a practical response to this workforce gap. The engineering foundation of these robots rests on three pillars: VLA models that integrate multimodal perception and commands within a single end-to-end network, online-learning frameworks that adapt in real time to patient-specific tissue variation, and predictive world models that anticipate surgical workflow. Unlike conventional surgeon-controlled robotic systems that only reproduce a surgeon's hand movements, these platforms function as context-aware intelligent partners, with concrete capabilities such as autonomous adaptive retraction, active suction, and autonomous instrument delivery that may reduce tissue injury and preserve surgical workflow continuity. Realizing this potential will require lower real-time control latency, adaptive fail-safe architectures, and resolution of the legal and ethical questions raised by autonomous manipulation. Collaboration among clinicians, engineers, and industry partners will be essential for addressing these challenges and strengthening competitiveness in the global medical AI industry.
authors: Eui‐Suk Sung

title: Reduced Plasma Cardiac Myosin-Binding Protein-C Concentrations in Cats with Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy: Evidence from Chronic, Treated Disease
abstract: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM), the most common cardiac disease in cats, is associated with genetic variants, including MYBPC3, which encodes cardiac myosin-binding protein C (cMyBP-C), a key sarcomeric protein involved in myocardial contractility. Although circulating cMyBP-C has emerged as a biomarker of myocardial injury in humans, its clinical relevance in feline HCM remains unclear. This study characterized plasma cMyBP-C and N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) concentrations across different stages of feline HCM, evaluated their diagnostic performance, and assessed their associations with echocardiographic parameters. A cross-sectional study included 65 cats: 25 healthy cats, 25 with subclinical HCM, and 15 with clinical HCM (chronic and treated). Plasma NT-proBNP was significantly higher in clinical HCM than in healthy cats (p = 0.0117), whereas plasma cMyBP-C was lower in clinical HCM than in subclinical HCM (p = 0.0462) and healthy cats (p = 0.001). At a cut-off of <1.270 ng/mL, plasma cMyBP-C showed 76.19% sensitivity and 65.38% specificity for distinguishing HCM. NT-proBNP alone showed higher overall diagnostic accuracy (76.67%) than the combined use of cMyBP-C and NT-proBNP. Neither plasma NT-proBNP nor cMyBP-C correlated significantly with echocardiographic parameters. Reduced circulating cMyBP-C concentrations in cats with chronic, treated HCM suggest a biomarker pattern distinct from that reported in acute myocardial injury and warrant further investigation.
authors: Nutcha Tanakwang; Natcha Sakunasing; Sarawut Kumphune; Raktham Mektrirat; Kannika Na Lampang; Chavalit Boonyapakorn; Wanpitak Pongkan

title: Reframing Speech Therapy Through Design: Gamification, Emotion, and Embodied Interaction
abstract: Gamification and conversational technologies are increasingly explored in paediatric rehabilitation to support children’s engagement with therapeutic activities. Within speech therapy, however, the integration of Embodied Conversational Agents (ECAs) remains underexplored from a design perspective, particularly with regard to children’s emotional experience, motivation and interaction dynamics. This paper investigates how observations of children’s responses to errors and corrective feedback can inform the design of ECAs for paediatric speech therapy. Adopting a human-centred and design-driven approach, the research combines a review of existing gamified therapeutic systems, non-participant observation of clinical speech therapy sessions, and interviews with therapists. The findings highlight recurrent differences in children’s responses to errors, the importance of relational sensitivity in therapeutic interactions, and challenges in extending therapeutic support to home-based practice. These insights were translated into design principles concerning non-judgmental error mediation, adaptive scaffolding, narrative reframing, and calibrated relational embodiment. They informed the development of Ziza’s Words, a narrative-based game featuring an embodied agent designed as a playful companion rather than an authoritative evaluator. A preliminary formative pilot with three children provided initial insights into engagement, emotional responses, and interaction affordances. The contribution lies in articulating preliminary design propositions for emotionally sensitive ECAs in paediatric rehabilitation.
authors: Patrizia Marti; Nicoletta Marino; Andrea Brogi

title: Regulatory flexibility under pressure: an asymmetric brain-body model of leadership in high-stakes teams
abstract: Leadership under pressure is often framed as a cognitive challenge, although consequential decisions are made by embodied agents whose cardiovascular, respiratory, autonomic, endocrine, and interoceptive states change with stress. We propose an asymmetric interpersonal brain-body model for high-stakes teams. Contextual demands alter a leader's regulatory state; this state shapes cognitive flexibility, social perception, communication, and action; and leader signals modify the team's regulatory environment and willingness to disclose uncertainty, dissent, revise plans, or withdraw. These responses feed back to the leader. The model builds on established evidence that bodily signals contribute to subjective feeling and decision-making, stress reorganizes large-scale neural processing, and social partners can alter neural and endocrine responses to threat. Its novel claim is narrower: hierarchy makes interpersonal regulation directionally asymmetric, linking brain-body dynamics to information flow and collective decision quality. Regulatory flexibility, i.e., context-sensitive mobilization and recovery, is proposed as more informative than tonic calm or physiological synchrony. A four-region color heuristic is retained as a translation layer, not as a neurobiological taxonomy. We specify competing explanations, failure criteria, and multimodal within-person and team-level designs for testing the framework in high-stakes teams and crisis simulations.
authors: Markus Martin Luedi; George Kohlrieser

title: Reinforcement Learning with World Models in the Era of Scale: From Online Imagination to World Action Models
abstract: Abstract In World Model Reinforcement Learning (WM-RL), agents learn a parameterized model of environmental dynamics that serves as the basis for planning, imagination-based policy training, or synthetic data generation in decision making tasks. From 2019 to 2026, a drastic phase transition took place within this field. Initially started as an effort to improve efficiency in visual control tasks, WM-RL has become the core of interdisciplinary AI infrastructure. Today, internet-scale video-based generative world foundation models allow the autonomous vehicle pipeline to learn generalist policies from unlabeled human video, facilitating applications in medical therapy and molecular dynamics. To review the entire trajectory of WM-RL research, it is necessary to synthesize key sources that summarize the advances made throughout the years. Three prominent paradigm shifts are observed during this period. These include the shift from online Model-Based Reinforcement Learning (MBRL) to pretrain-first imagination-only policy training; architecture integration from decoupled worlds and policies to unified World Action Models; and the generalization of specific algorithms to physical AI infrastructure for all MBRL applications. Regarding architecture, WM-RL follows several generations of innovations. They include PlaNet, Recurrent State-Space Model (RSSM), the Dreamer family, value-equivalent implicit models, Transformer-based world models, diffusion dynamics, and the abstract-space Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) predictor. In this review, we examine WM-RL from multiple aspects, ranging from general model-based reinforcement learning, robotic manipulation, navigation, autonomous driving, multi-agent systems, large language model agents, healthcare, and games. The usage of world models varies widely depending on the application areas, while the validated architectures are discussed accordingly.
authors: Wojciech Dąbrowicki; Andrzej Rusiecki

title: Repercussões psicossociais da oncologia pediátrica para crianças e adolescentes, familiares e profissionais: revisão integrativa
abstract: Objective: To describe the psychosocial impacts of pediatric oncology on children and adolescents. Methodology: This is an integrative literature review comprising six methodological stages: formulation of the core question using the PICo strategy, definition of inclusion and exclusion criteria, search of the SciELO, BVS-BDENF-LILACS, and PubMed Central databases and Google Scholar, screening of articles by title and abstract, analytical reading of the selected texts, and categorization of the results. The search utilized DeCS and MeSH descriptors, combined with the Boolean operator “AND.” The studies were categorized through content analysis. Results: Sixteen articles on the psychosocial perspective of pediatric oncology were analyzed, yielding the following categories: Psychoemotional aspects for children and adolescents in cancer care; Family members’ experiences with pediatric oncology; and Repercussions of pediatric oncology care for healthcare professionals. Conclusion: The study demonstrated that pediatric oncology poses significant challenges that extend beyond clinical boundaries. Children face emotional distress, isolation, and changes in routine, while family members suffer from overload and the fear of loss. Healthcare professionals are also emotionally impacted due to the bonds formed with patients. The scarcity of studies on children’s subjective perspectives is revealed, and the need for comprehensive care and psychological support for all those involved is highlighted.
authors: Alana Rocha da Silva Rodrigues; Evilly Carneiro Almeida; Iara Neves Alves; Ravena dos Santos Lopes; Márcio Costa de Souza; Aisiane Cedraz Morais

title: Robotic Assistants in the Operating Room: A Systematic Review of Vision‐Based Systems for Nonoperative Tasks
abstract: Nonoperative tasks in the operating room, such as instrument handling, sterile packaging, and logistics, are demanding yet have received less robotics attention than autonomous surgery. This review, the first to synthesize this literature, maps the perception methods, autonomy levels, methodological quality, and clinical readiness of vision‐based robotic assistants for scrub nurse, circulating nurse, and OR logistics roles. Searches of PubMed, IEEE Xplore, Scopus, ACM Digital Library, Web of Science, and Google Scholar returned 465 records; 20 publications describing 11 robotic system families met inclusion criteria. Most evidence, 17 publications across eight system families, concerns scrub nurse assistance; circulating nurse support, OR logistics, and dental assistance are each represented by one system. Vision methods have moved from classical image processing and predefined gestures toward deep learning, multimodal perception, and vision–language–action models, but autonomy has not kept pace: one system family reaches LoA 1, seven LoA 2, and three LoA 3, with Technology Readiness Levels spanning TRL 4 to TRL 6. Reported success rates are often high but rarely comparable and mostly generated in laboratory or simulated settings. Closing that gap requires stronger evidence on safety, sterility, failure recovery, workflow integration, execution speed, reproducibility, and, notably absent, manipulation of deformable sterile materials.
authors: Eugenia Mawuenya Akpo; Pietro Falco; Nicholas Tobias Johannes Raison; Christos Bergeles; Letizia Gionfrida

title: RobustRLlib: A Unified Library and Benchmark for Robust Reinforcement Learning Algorithms
abstract: Robust reinforcement learning (RL) is critical for reliable real-world deployment, where policies may fail under diverse shifts and disruptions. Existing robust RL algorithms offer a rich set of mechanisms and principles, yet two major barriers limit their broader potential: limited algorithm reusability and an unclear empirical capability boundary. We introduce RobustRLlib, an algorithm-centric library and benchmark that addresses both challenges. It integrates 17 representative robust online, offline, and safe RL algorithms under a unified interface for substantially improved reusability, together with an enhanced evaluation platform spanning diverse real-world shifts and advanced humanoid and vision-language-action tasks. Systematic evaluation over 273 perturbation configurations provides an up-to-date capability map of current robust RL algorithms, revealing where they remain effective and where substantial robustness gaps persist. As an open-source, user-friendly platform, RobustRLlib offers a reproducible and extensible codebase for applying existing methods to new problems and developing new robust RL algorithms.
authors: Xi Chen; Fengqi Hu; Zeyu Shen; Jiaying Xu; Shangding Gu; Pan Xu; Anqi Liu; Laixi Shi

title: SCALP COOLING EFFICACY IN PREVENTING CHEMOTHERAPY-INDUCED ALOPECIA IN BREAST CANCER PATIENTS: A PROSPECTIVE OBSERVATIONAL STUDY
abstract: Vchodiska: Ztrta vlas spojen s cytostatickou lbou pedstavuje ast nedouc inek vznamn ovlivujc kvalitu ivota pacientek. authors: Eliška Kolajová; Aneta Hujová

title: SHRIMP: Iterative Refinement of Robot Task Plans
abstract: As collaborative robots have entered domains such as manufacturing, agriculture, and healthcare, programming or adapting robot behavior typically requires robotic expertise that most end users lack. Natural language lowers this barrier. Recent advancements in large language models (LLMs) have made it feasible to translate natural language into robot task plans. However, language-based task specification can suffer from semantic ambiguity, and generative models lack transparency for how language instructions are translated into robot actions, making it difficult for users to validate plans before execution. To address these issues, we introduce SHRIMP: Simulation-driven Human-in-the-loop Refinement Interface for Manipulation Planning. SHRIMP allows users to automatically generate a hierarchical robot primitive plan using natural language and iteratively revise their plan through re-prompting and explicit correction. At each revision, SHRIMP allows users to validate their plan in simulation, and once satisfied, execute it on the physical robot. Through a user study involving participants planning tabletop kitchen tasks (N = 35), we validate that SHRIMP improves perceived control and enhances robot transparency. System videos and source code are available at https://wisc-hci.github.io/SHRIMP.
authors: Mya Schroder; Yuna Hwang; Callie Y. Kim; Leqian Cheng; Jeffrey Li-cheng Liu; Chenchen Zheng; Xinning He; Bilge Mutlu

title: Skin-Derived Non-Coding RNAs as Potential Biomarkers and Therapeutic Targets
abstract: Skin-derived extracellular nucleic acids-particularly non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs) such as miRNAs and lncRNAs-are a rapidly evolving frontier in molecular diagnostics. These molecules are present in skin tissue, dermal interstitial fluid, and sweat, whilst ncRNAs regulate essential processes including epidermal differentiation, wound healing, immune regulation, and tumourigenesis, positioning them as promising candidates for minimally invasive biomarker development across a broad spectrum of dermatological diseases. This narrative review summarises their biological functions and potential clinical applications. The available evidence provides a conceptual basis for an emerging cutaneous "surface liquid biopsy" framework, whilst highlighting the need for standardised sampling, analytical validation, and clinical evaluation before such approaches can be translated into clinical practice. Although ample disease-associated ncRNA signatures have been uncovered, many remain at exploratory or early translational stages, and the concordance of these ncRNA signatures with corresponding blood and tissue biomarkers needs to be established. Continued advances in sampling strategies, analytical technologies, and clinical validation are needed to translate these findings into clinically deployable platforms for dermatological diseases and, potentially, systemic diseases in the future.
authors: Jane L. Zen; Quynh Mai Nguyen Le; Shizhou Li; George B. Hanna

title: Spontaneous Reduction in Mitral Valve Regurgitation in Three Dogs With Severe Myxomatous Mitral Valve Disease: An Unusual Case Report
abstract: BACKGROUND: Myxomatous mitral valve disease (MMVD), the most common heart disease in small-breed dogs, is characterized by mitral regurgitation (MR) resulting from valvular degeneration, which may progress to left-sided heart failure. This report describes the cases of three dogs with severe MMVD (American College of Veterinary Internal Medicine Stages C or D) who exhibited an unexpected spontaneous reduction in MR despite continued valve degeneration. CASE PRESENTATION: Three dogs initially presented with symptoms of heart failure and left atrial and ventricular enlargement. Standard treatment, including diuretics, improved their conditions; however, further monitoring revealed that the coaptation gap decreased due to mitral valve thickening, leading to a reduction in MR. This was accompanied by a significant decrease in heart size. As a result, diuretics were discontinued, and all dogs were successfully managed with pimobendan alone. CONCLUSIONS: To our knowledge, this is the first report of spontaneous MR reduction in MMVD, where coaptation gap narrowing played a role in clinical improvement. These cases may broaden the current understanding of MMVD progression, suggesting that, in rare instances, changes in cardiac remodelling and clinical status can occur. Further research is warranted to better understand the underlying mechanisms.
authors: Hyo‐Seung Nam; Ye‐In Oh

title: Study protocol for a retrospective cohort study of real-world effectiveness of the VLA1553 (IXCHIQ®) chikungunya vaccine during an epidemic among healthcare workers in Reunion Island.
abstract:
Background

Real-world effectiveness data for the live-attenuated chikungunya vaccine VLA1553 (IXCHIQ®) remain limited because licensure relied primarily on immunogenicity and safety. The 2025 vaccination campaign at the University Hospital of Réunion offers an opportunity to evaluate effectiveness during an outbreak.

Objectives

HO-VLA-CHIK aims to estimate vaccine effectiveness against symptomatic chikungunya among hospital employees. Secondary objectives address laboratory-confirmed symptomatic infections, hospitalizations, chronic chikungunya, sick leave duration, adverse events following immunization, and determinants of vaccine uptake.

Methods

This retrospective exposed-unexposed cohort study involves approximately 700 vaccinated and unvaccinated employees across two hospital sites. Structured electronic questionnaire data will be supplemented by occupational health registries, laboratory results, and medical records. A marginal Cox model with stabilized inverse probability of treatment weighting will estimate vaccine effectiveness, using calendar time and time-dependent vaccination status. Vaccinated person-time will begin 15 days after vaccination. Adjustment will use prespecified baseline confounders.

Results

Ethical approval was obtained in May 2026. Recruitment and data collection are scheduled to end in December 2026. Analyses will follow data validation. Expected findings include estimates of vaccine effectiveness and descriptions of reported adverse events, persistent symptoms, and work absence. These findings may inform vaccination strategies and hospital workforce preparedness during future chikungunya outbreaks.
